new_text: A relevant contribution in the field of computer vision is the development of Slimmable Neural Networks <cit.>. These networks were introduced to train a single neural network capable of operating at varying widths, enabling real-time and adaptive trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency. This study adopts the training strategies from slimmable networks, specifically employing distinct normalization layers for each sub-network (task) as conditional parameters and utilizing the teacher network's predictions to guide the student network through in-place distillation. In contrast to traditional slimmable networks, where a larger model supervises a smaller one, our method distills knowledge from the full-context mode (teacher) to the streaming mode (student) dynamically within a unified Universal ASR model.

Self-attention (a.k.a. intra-attention) is an attention mechanism weighting different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the same sequence. It is heavily used in Conformer <cit.> ASR networks. The attention layer itself is parameter-free (projection layers before attention are fully shared), and is composed of matrix multiplication of the key and the query, followed by softmax over keys, before another matrix multiplication with the value. As shown in Figure <ref>, in dual-mode attention layer, the softmax is performed on the left context only in streaming mode (rectangle with solid line), compared with the full-context mode (rectangle with dash line). Self-attention (a.k.a. intra-attention) weights positions within a single sequence to compute its representation. It is widely used in Conformer<cit.> ASR networks. QA is an active research area, including machine reading comprehension (MRC) <cit.>, visual question answering (VQA) <cit.>, table-based QA <cit.>, and graph-based QA <cit.>.
EHR QA is a research area with great potential for real-world impact, as it provides an interface where both medical experts and ordinary users can easily query clinical facts and statistics via natural language.
Previously, <cit.> constructed `emrQA`, an MRC dataset based on clinical notes.
`emrQA`, however, focuses only on the free-text notes, thus not being able to be used to train machines to leverage the structural properties of EHR.
Recently, <cit.> used MIMIC-III <cit.>, a publicly available EHR dataset, to construct `MIMICSQL`, a table-based (i.e., text-to-SQL) QA dataset.
However, while constructing `MIMICSQL`, they preprocessed the tables of MIMIC-III such that the original schema was heavily modified.
Therefore the final dataset (questions and tables) does not reflect the complex, yet interesting structure of MIMIC-III, thus losing real-world applicability and the value as a tool for fostering machine intelligence.
new_text: QA is an active research area encompassing machine reading comprehension (MRC) <cit.>, visual question answering (VQA) <cit.>, table-based QA <cit.>, and graph-based QA <cit.>. EHR QA is a research area with significant potential for real-world impact, as it provides a platform enabling medical experts and lay users to query clinical facts and statistics through natural language. Previously, <cit.> developed `emrQA`, an MRC dataset based on clinical notes. However, `emrQA` focuses exclusively on free-text notes and is not suitable for training models to exploit the structural properties of EHR. Recently, <cit.> leveraged MIMIC-III <cit.>, a publicly available EHR dataset, to develop `MIMICSQL`, a table-based (i.e., text-to-SQL) QA dataset. During the construction of `MIMICSQL`, they substantially altered the schema of MIMIC-III by preprocessing its tables. Consequently, the final dataset (questions and tables) fails to reflect the complex yet clinically meaningful structure of MIMIC-III, thereby reducing its real-world applicability and utility for advancing machine learning systems.

We introduced a broader concept of approximate teaching that generalizes exact teaching. To the best of our knowledge, the exact teaching dimensions introduced here for linear and polynomial perceptron learners are novel, as is our establishment of an upper bound on the approximate teaching dimension for RBF perceptron models, along with the associated analytical methods. Several potential avenues for extending our current research exist. For instance, relaxing the assumptions on data distribution for polynomial and RBF perceptrons could be addressed by analyzing the linear perceptron and developing techniques to neutralize non-orthogonal subspaces. This approach may generalize the exact teaching results for polynomial perceptrons and yield tighter bounds on the approximate teaching dimension of RBF perceptrons.

old_text: The key idea of our multigrid architecture is to design a hierarchy of grids in the channel space (also referred to as “levels”), where the number of channels in the finest level corresponds to the original width of the network. The number of channels is halved between the levels until reaching the coarsest level, where the number of channels is smaller or equal to the parameter s_c. Our multigrid architecture is accompanied by a CNN block, like the ResNet block in Eq. (<ref>), which is applied on each level. On the finest and intermediate levels, we only connect disjoint groups of channels using grouped convolutions. These convolutions have 𝒪(c_ in) parameters, as we keep the group size fixed throughout the network, and as the network widens, the number of groups grows. We allow interactions between all the channels on the coarsest grid, where we use the original CNN-block without additional grouping. Since the coarsest grid contains only a few channels, this is not a costly operation.
new_text: The multigrid architecture organizes a hierarchy of grids in the channel space (levels), with the finest level matching the original network width. Channel counts are halved between successive levels until reaching the coarsest level, where they are ≤ s_c. A CNN block (e.g., ResNet in Eq. (<ref>)) is applied to each level. Finest and intermediate levels use grouped convolutions to connect disjoint channel groups, resulting in 𝒪(c_in) parameters due to a fixed group size; as the network widens, the number of groups increases. The coarsest level employs the original CNN-block without grouping, enabling full channel interactions. This remains computationally efficient due to its reduced channel count.

Residual Policy Learning. An alternative to typical transfer learning techniques is to directly improve the underlying policy itself. Instead of re-training an agent from scratch when policies perform sub-optimally, the sub-optimal policy can be used as prior knowledge in RL to speed up training. This is the main idea behind residual policy learning, in which a residual policy is used to augment an initial policy to correct for changes in the environment. <cit.> demonstrated that combining residual policy learning with conventional robotic control improves the robot's ability to adapt to variations in the environment for manipulation tasks. Our method builds on this line of research by augmenting the simulator using a neural network that learns the residual error between simulation and reality.
new_text: Residual Policy Learning. An alternative to conventional transfer learning techniques involves directly enhancing the underlying policy. Rather than retraining an agent from scratch when policies perform suboptimally, the sub-optimal policy itself can serve as prior knowledge to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL). This forms the core concept of residual policy learning, where a residual policy complements an initial policy to adapt to environmental changes. <cit.> demonstrated that integrating residual policy learning with traditional robotic control enhances a robot’s ability to adapt to environmental variations in manipulation tasks. Our approach extends this work by augmenting the simulator with a neural network that learns the residual error between simulated and real-world environments.

We opt for real2sim observation adaptation over sim2real as it decouples sensing mechanisms from acting components. new_text: A road network ℜ is represented as a graph ℜ = (G, E), where G denotes the collection of grid points and E consists of edges that capture immediate adjacency in a Cartesian coordinate system between these points. This adjacency implies that connected grid points are neighbors in either horizontal or vertical directions within a two-dimensional grid. Each grid point g ∈ G is associated with a set of properties 𝒫 = {p, d, `lo`}, which encode key spatial and navigational attributes. Specifically, **p** represents the Cartesian coordinate of the grid point, defined as a pair of integer values (p ∈ ℤ²); **d** is a binary flag indicating whether the grid point is drivable (d = 1) or impassable (d = 0); and **`lo`** specifies the set of legal orientations permitted at the point, consisting of cardinal directions (ϕ_l ∈ {`north`, `east`, `south`, `west`}). These properties collectively define how agents or vehicles can interact with the grid in terms of location, accessibility, and directional constraints.

new_text: Chinese is a hieroglyphic language that contains minimal morphological cues (e.g., capitalization) to indicate word usage. The absence of clear boundaries between words complicates the differentiation between monosyllabic words and monosyllabic morphemes. Nevertheless, Chinese exhibits two defining traits. First, Chinese characters are square-shaped [They are known as square-shaped characters.], with spatial symmetry in their composition. Second, since the meaning of a Chinese word is typically derived from its component characters, each character conveys meaningful information. Consequently, character-based representations effectively capture the syntactic and semantic properties of a sentence. The BR model performs robustly on Chinese corpora. To demonstrate its adaptability, the BR model is subsequently applied to an English corpus in the next experiment.

Following the footsteps of <cit.>, a promising approach based on approximate value iteration was proposed for MDPs with CVaR objectives in <cit.>. But, it is not clear how one can extend this method to other coherent risk measures. An infinite-dimensional linear program was derived analytically for MDPs with coherent risk objectives in <cit.> with implications for solving chance and stochastic-dominance constrained MDPs. Successive finite approximation of such infinite dimensional linear programs was suggested leading to sub-optimal solutions. Yet, the method cannot be extended to constrained MDPs with coherent risk objectives and constraints. A policy iteration algorithm for finding policies that minimize total coherent risk measures for MDPs was studied in <cit.> and a computational non-smooth Newton method was proposed in <cit.>. Our work, extends <cit.> to constrained problems and uses a DCCP computational method, which takes advantage of already available software (DCCP and CVXPY).
new_text: Building on prior work in <cit.>, a method for MDPs with CVaR objectives was introduced using approximate value iteration. However, this approach lacks clear generalization to other coherent risk measures, such as entropic or conditional value-at-risk, which differ in mathematical properties and optimization requirements. Subsequently, <cit.> analytically derived an infinite-dimensional linear program for MDPs with general coherent risk objectives, offering theoretical insights for addressing constrained problems like those with chance or stochastic-dominance constraints. While this formulation enabled successive finite approximations to be studied, these approximations yield suboptimal solutions and are not adaptable to constrained MDPs with coherent risk objectives and constraints, as demonstrated by the lack of feasible transformations in such settings. Later, <cit.> proposed a policy iteration algorithm specifically tailored to minimize total coherent risk measures in MDPs, while <cit.> introduced a computational non-smooth Newton method to address its optimization challenges. Our work bridges a critical gap by extending <cit.>’s framework to constrained problems and employing a difference-of-convex (DCCP) computational method, leveraging existing tools like DCCP and CVXPY to ensure practical implementation.

In this work, we aim to extend and explore the analysis of lottery tickets to fundamental visual recognition tasks of object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint detection. Popular methods for such recognition tasks use a two-stage detection pipeline, with a supervised pre-trained convolutional neural network (ConvNet) backbone, a region proposal network (RPN), and one or more region-wise task-specific neural network branches. Loosely speaking, a ConvNet backbone is the most computationally intensive part of the architecture, and pre-training is the most time-consuming part. Therefore, as part of this study, we explore the following questions: (a) Are there universal sub-networks within the ConvNet backbone that can be transferred to the downstream object recognition tasks? (b) Can we train sparser and more accurate sub-networks for each of the downstream tasks? And, (c) How does the behavior or properties of these sub-networks change with respect to the corresponding dense network? We investigate all of these questions under the dominant settings used in object recognition frameworks. Specifically, we use ImageNet <cit.> pre-trained ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 <cit.> backbones, Faster R-CNN <cit.> and Mask R-CNN <cit.> modules for object recognition on Pascal VOC <cit.> and COCO <cit.> datasets.

In this work, we seek to extend and investigate the analysis of lottery tickets to fundamental visual recognition tasks—object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint detection. Most popular approaches employ a two-stage detection pipeline comprising a supervised pre-trained convolutional neural network (ConvNet) backbone, a region proposal network (RPN), and one or more region-wise task-specific neural network branches. Loosely speaking, the ConvNet backbone constitutes the most computationally intensive component, with pre-training being the most time-consuming aspect. To address these challenges, we explore the following questions: (a) Do universal sub-networks exist within the ConvNet backbone that can generalize across downstream object recognition tasks? old_text: Recent literature in cognitive science <cit.> has examined the use of DNNs for model-agnostic fits to human behavior. <cit.> model a simple probability tracking task using LSTMs, instead of the classical reinforcement learning models popular in the literature. They show that LSTMs, being model agnostic, can capture arbitrary policies like deterministic switching irrespective of historical value, policies that are actually seen in behavior but not captureable by simple value-based models such as Q learning. In subsequent work <cit.>, they learned disentangled embeddings for each subject using behavioral data. We build substantially on these promising initial drections with the following additional contributions: (1) application to a multi-stage sequential decision-making task, and recovery of idiosyncratic biases (“suboptimalities”) from behavior, and critically, (2) demonstration that pooling together large numbers of subjects can enable learning individual behavior from very small sample sizes (5-10 trials per subject).

new_text: When a new user initiates a request, NGINX first redirects them to a noVNC front-end interface, which signals that the simulation is booting up. Simultaneously, NGINX forwards the request to a Flask webserver. The Flask webserver plays two key roles: it first sanitizes and filters request parameters to mitigate potential security vulnerabilities. After this validation step, the Flask webserver acts as a process manager, responsible for launching the core components required for the simulation session. These components include noVNC (for graphical display), Unity (for running the simulation environment), and ROS (for robotic system management). To ensure responsiveness, the execution of these components is handled asynchronously via a background queue. On average, the boot-up process takes 18.9 seconds. The queue follows a staged approach: it first initializes the noVNC service to establish an X Window session for rendering the simulation output. Next, it deploys a Docker container where ROS is started alongside a ROSbridge server, enabling communication with Unity. At this stage, any necessary ROS nodes—such as those controlling simulated robots or logging navigation data—are also deployed within the Docker container. Finally, Unity is launched under the noVNC display environment, executing the SEAN simulation with input parameters like the initial positions of the human avatar and robot. Once Unity is running, the noVNC interface connects to its display output, allowing the user to interact with the fully initialized simulation environment.

Data removal from machine learning models has been paid more attentions due to the demands of the “right to be forgotten” and countering data poisoning attacks.
In this paper, we frame the problem of federated unlearning, a post-process operation of the federated learning models to remove the influence of the specified training sample(s).
We present FedEraser, the first federated unlearning methodology that can eliminate the influences of a federated client's data on the global model while significantly reducing the time consumption used for constructing the unlearned model.
The core idea of FedEraser is to trade the central server's storage for unlearned model's construction time.
In particular, FedEraser reconstructs the unlearned model by leveraging the historical parameter updates of federated clients that have been retained at the central server during the training process of FL.
A novel calibration method is further developed to calibrate the retained client updates, which can provide a significant speed-up to the reconstruction of the unlearned model.
Experiments on four realistic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedEraser, with an expected speed-up of 4× compared with retraining from the scratch.
new_text: Data removal from machine learning models has received increasing attention due to the demands of privacy regulations such as the “right to be forgotten” and the need to counter data poisoning attacks. In this paper, we formalize the problem of federated unlearning, which refers to a post-processing operation in federated learning (FL) systems aimed at eliminating the influence of specific training samples from a global model. We introduce FedEraser, a novel federated unlearning framework that enables the removal of a federated client’s data influence from the global model while significantly reducing the computational cost associated with reconstructing an updated model. The underlying principle of FedEraser is to prioritize storage efficiency at the central server in exchange for faster unlearning performance. Specifically, the method leverages historical parameter updates retained by the central server throughout the FL training process to reconstruct the unlearned model. To enhance efficiency, we propose a novel calibration technique that adjusts the retained updates, accelerating the reconstruction process. Experimental evaluations on four real-world datasets validate the efficacy of FedEraser, achieving a 4× speedup compared to conventional retraining approaches. This approach addresses the computational limitations of existing unlearning methods in distributed learning environments.

This dataset contains longitudinal records of shopping activities spanning one year, documenting transactions from several thousand shoppers. A key limitation of the dataset is the absence of pre-assigned class labels, which necessitates the use of alternative methods for categorization. To address this, we follow prior approaches <cit.> by applying an unsupervised clustering algorithm to infer meaningful groupings within the data. Specifically, we partition the dataset’s 197,324 records into two distinct clusters, allowing us to identify and differentiate consumer segments based on their purchasing patterns. This approach aligns with established practices in unsupervised learning for customer segmentation and provides a foundation for tailoring promotional strategies to each group’s behavior.

RL is a semi-supervised machine learning field in which the agent learns what to do through interaction with the environment. The milestone in the RL field is the combination of DL with traditional RL methods, which is known as deep reinforcement learning (DRL). This made it possible to apply RL in problems with enormous state and action spaces, including self-driving cars <cit.>, robotics <cit.>, industry automation <cit.>, finance <cit.>, healthcare <cit.>, and RSs. From the architectural point of view, most of the existing RLRSs exploit available DRL architectures that were developed and successfully tested for other domains with different applications, like Atari games <cit.>. Equally important, previous RL methods are typically designed based on physics or Gaussian processes, not based on complex and dynamic nature of users. Although it makes sense to not reinvent the wheel, sometimes thinking out of the box could make a substantial improvement in the field. For example, instead of usual MDP-based RL algorithms, Ref. <cit.> uses evolution strategies <cit.> to optimize the recommendation policy. Also, as mentioned earlier, some RL algorithms (e.g., Q-learning) have been more popular among RLRSs compared to other RL methods. new_text: Most existing RLRSs leverage DRL architectures originally developed for domains like Atari games <cit.>, often relying on physics or Gaussian processes rather than capturing the complex, dynamic nature of user behavior. While avoiding redundant work is standard, unconventional approaches—such as replacing traditional MDP-based RL algorithms with evolution strategies <cit.>—can yield significant improvements. As surveyed <cit.>, numerous DL models exist for RSs, and strategically combining these with RL algorithms may surpass current DRL performance. Q-learning, for instance, has dominated RLRSs, but no rigorous rationale justifies algorithm choice in RS applications. old_text: In this paper, we investigate a new variant of neural architecture search (NAS) paradigm – searching with random labels (RLNAS). The task sounds counter-intuitive for most existing NAS algorithms since random label provides few information on the performance of each candidate architecture. Instead, we propose a novel NAS framework based on ease-of-convergence hypothesis, which requires only random labels during searching. The algorithm involves two steps: first, we train a SuperNet using random labels; second, from the SuperNet we extract the sub-network whose weights change most significantly during the training. Extensive experiments are evaluated on multiple datasets (e.g. NAS-Bench-201 and ImageNet) and multiple search spaces (e.g. DARTS-like and MobileNet-like). Very surprisingly, RLNAS achieves comparable or even better results compared with state-of-the-art NAS methods such as PC-DARTS, Single Path One-Shot, even though the counterparts utilize full ground truth labels for searching. We hope our finding could inspire new understandings on the essential of NAS.
new_text: In this paper, we propose a novel variant of the neural architecture search (NAS) paradigm—searching with random labels (RLNAS). This approach contradicts expectations for most existing NAS algorithms, as random labels provide little information about the performance of candidate architectures. Instead, we introduce a framework based on the ease-of-convergence hypothesis, which requires only random labels during the search process. The algorithm comprises two stages: first, a SuperNet is trained using random labels; second, a sub-network is extracted from the SuperNet based on the architectures whose weights undergo the most substantial changes during training. Extensive experiments are conducted on multiple datasets (e.g., NAS-Bench-201 and ImageNet) and search spaces (e.g., DARTS-like and MobileNet-like). Remarkably, RLNAS achieves comparable or superior results to state-of-the-art NAS methods such as PC-DARTS and Single Path One-Shot, despite these counterparts utilizing full ground-truth labels during search. Our findings aim to inspire new insights into the fundamental principles of NAS.

new_text: Stochastic ordering serves as a well-established method for comparing two random variables (RVs) in terms of their relative magnitudes. Specifically, it provides a rigorous framework to determine when one RV can be said to consistently exceed another in value—essentially quantifying the probabilistic notion of "bigness." This becomes particularly relevant when analyzing how the distribution of a random variable evolves as its defining parameters change. In such contexts, stochastic ordering allows researchers to systematically study how perturbations in parameters influence the variability and behavior of the resulting RVs. Building on this, the sub-section at hand extends the analytical approach used in prior work <cit.> to investigate how stochastic ordering can be applied to the k-th maximum RV. Our focus is on understanding how variations in specific parameters—denoted as a_M^(1), b_M^(1) and a_M^(2), b_M^(2)—affect the ordering of the k-th maximum RV. In this setting, the k-th maximum RV X, characterized by parameters a_M^(1) and b_M^(1), is considered stochastically smaller than another k-th maximum RV Y, with parameters a_M^(2) and b_M^(2), when certain conditions on these parameters are met.

new_text: The tool accepts as input an automaton representation of a regular Kripke structure ℳ and, for each specification φ, determines the set of states in ℳ where φ is satisfied. If the complement of this satisfaction set (i.e., the states where φ does not hold) is non-empty, the tool generates a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) that encodes the counterexamples to φ. To improve usability, the PPAL^* syntax incorporates additional syntactic constructs (syntactic sugars) and supports the inclusion of dummy formulae logically equivalent to the tautology ⊤. These dummy formulae, when evaluated, prompt the visualization of intermediate automata generated during the tool’s execution.

Joint detection and tracking. The recent success of multi-task learning in deep neural networks <cit.> has led to models that jointly learn detection and tracking tasks. Tracktor <cit.> adapts the Faster RCNN detector <cit.> to estimate the location of a bounding box in the new frame from the previous frame. Tracktor's drawback is that it works well only on high frame-rate videos where inter-frame motion is low. In <cit.>, authors extend R-FCN <cit.> detector to compute correlation maps between high level feature maps of consecutive frames to estimate inter-frame offsets between bounding boxes. Similarly, CenterTrack <cit.> extends the CenterNet detector <cit.> to estimate inter-frame offsets of bounding boxes. CenterTrack is a state-of-the-art method, but only associates objects in consecutive frames. Our method is more robust for longer occlusions and large inter-frame displacements, thus improving tracking under more challenging conditions, which we show in <ref>. Xu et al. <cit.> presents an end-to-end MOT training framework, using a differentiable approximation of MOT metrics in the loss functions. They show improvements for existing deep MOT methods when extended with their training framework. Chaabane et al. <cit.> propose an approach to jointly optimize detection and tracking, with a focus on static object tracking and geolocalization. Their model makes strong use of learned pose estimation features, and is less suitable as a general tracker for dynamic objects. JDE <cit.> extends YOLOv3 <cit.> with a reID branch to extract object embeddings for association. The feature extractor and detection branches share features and are jointly learned. Similarly, FairMOT <cit.> improves on JDE and makes use of the CenterNet detector to improve tracking accuracy.
new_text: Recent advances in multi-task learning within deep neural networks <cit.> have motivated the development of models that simultaneously perform detection and tracking. Tracktor <cit.> adapts Faster RCNN <cit.> to estimate bounding box locations in a new frame by leveraging information from the previous frame. However, Tracktor performs poorly in low-frame-rate videos with large inter-frame motions. In <cit.>, the authors extend the R-FCN <cit.> detector to compute correlation maps between high-level feature representations of consecutive frames for estimating inter-frame bounding box offsets. Similarly, CenterTrack <cit.> extends the CenterNet detector <cit.> to infer these offsets, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Despite this, CenterTrack only supports associations between consecutive frames, limiting its robustness to longer occlusions or larger displacements. Our method addresses these limitations, offering improved tracking under challenging conditions, as demonstrated in <ref>. Xu et al. <cit.> propose an end-to-end MOT training framework incorporating a differentiable approximation of MOT metrics into the loss function, demonstrating enhanced performance when integrated with existing deep MOT approaches. Chaabane et al. <cit.> present a joint detection and tracking model optimized for static object tracking and geolocalization, leveraging learned pose estimation features. This specialized approach, however, is less suited for dynamic object tracking. JDE <cit.> enhances YOLOv3 <cit.> by adding a reID branch for object embedding extraction during association, with shared features learned between the feature extractor and detection branches. FairMOT <cit.> further refines this approach by incorporating the CenterNet detector to achieve higher tracking accuracy.

This section proposes a general approach for the implementation of a system capable of predicting Road Traffic Incidents using methods of Machine Learning.
In this work we have chosen to follow the CRISP Data Mining framework <cit.> to build a system that can eventually be taken to production. The requirements for our system are to first receive a request sent by a specific vehicle which contains the current position of the vehicle.
The prediction system then retrieves the current external conditions of the vehicle at its given position and passes these along to its prediction model as input variables.
The model then produces a prediction of the likelihood of a traffic indent under the current circumstances of the vehicle.
Finally, the result is sent back to the vehicle as a response to its request.
new_text: This section presents a general approach for implementing a system designed to predict Road Traffic Incidents using Machine Learning methods. This approach follows the CRISP Data Mining framework <cit.> to develop a system suitable for eventual production deployment. The system operates by first receiving a request from a specific vehicle containing its current position. The prediction system then retrieves the environmental conditions surrounding the vehicle's location and transmits these variables to its prediction model. The model evaluates these inputs to estimate the probability of a traffic incident occurring under the current conditions. Finally, the prediction result is returned to the vehicle as a response to its initial request.

We provide some intuitions about why—in contrast to the gap_ε defined in Section <ref>—our sample complexity depends on this newly defined gap_ε here. Observe that, gap_ε measures the max gap between ψ_ε(a) - ψ_0(a), over all possible a's whose ψ_ε can compete with the best ψ_0. For any of these a's, statistically (if we only have O(AB/ε^2) samples), the best response set BR_ε(a) is indistinguishable from BR_0(a), and we may well pick these a's as the Stackelberg equilibrium. The DeepReDuce method enables users to create networks with trade-offs between ReLU count and accuracy by strategically removing ReLUs in ascending order of criticality. Evaluation on CIFAR-100 demonstrates a 3.5% accuracy improvement at iso-ReLU and a 3.5× reduction in ReLUs at iso-accuracy. We conduct experiments on TinyImageNet—a dataset rarely used in private inference research due to its computational demands—to further validate the approach. Although DeepReDuce advances the state-of-the-art, real-time private inference remains an unmet objective. We anticipate that DeepReDuce will stimulate future optimizations and novel perspectives on network design toward achieving this goal.

The recent rise of privacy concerns has led researchers to devise
methods for private neural inference—where
inferences are made directly on encrypted data, never seeing inputs.
The primary challenge facing private inference is that computing on encrypted data
levies an impractically-high latency penalty, stemming mostly from non-linear operators like ReLU.
Enabling practical and private inference requires new optimization methods that
minimize network ReLU counts while preserving accuracy.
This paper proposes DeepReDuce: a set of optimizations for
the judicious removal of ReLUs to reduce private inference latency.
The key insight is that not all ReLUs contribute equally to accuracy.
We leverage this insight to drop, or remove, ReLUs
from classic networks to significantly
reduce inference latency and maintain high accuracy.
Given a target network,
DeepReDuce outputs a Pareto frontier of networks
that tradeoff the number of ReLUs and accuracy.
Compared to the state-of-the-art for private inference
DeepReDuce improves accuracy and reduces ReLU count by up to
3.5% (iso-ReLU count) and 3.5× (iso-accuracy), respectively.
new_text: The recent increase in privacy concerns has led researchers to devise methods for private neural inference—where inferences are made directly on encrypted data, without ever decrypting the inputs. The primary challenge facing private inference is that computing on encrypted data imposes an impractically high latency penalty, stemming mainly from non-linear operations such as ReLU. Enabling practical and private inference requires new optimization methods that minimize the number of ReLUs in a network while preserving accuracy. This paper proposes DeepReDuce: a set of optimizations for the judicious removal of ReLUs to reduce private inference latency. The key insight is that not all ReLUs contribute equally to accuracy. We leverage this insight to remove ReLUs from classic networks to significantly reduce inference latency and maintain high accuracy. Given a target network, DeepReDuce outputs a Pareto frontier of networks that trade-offs the number of ReLUs and accuracy. Compared to the state-of-the-art for private inference, DeepReDuce improves accuracy and reduces ReLU count by up to 3.5% (iso-ReLU count) and 3.5× (iso-accuracy), respectively.

Compared with all-hex mesh generation, a hex-dominant mesh generation,
which combines advantages of both tetrahedral and hex elements, is
more automatic and robust for complex solid models. In the literature,
several strategies have been proposed to generate hex-dominant
meshes. An indirect method was suggested by <cit.>,
the domain is first meshed into tetrahedral elements and then merged
into a hex-dominant mesh with the packing technology. Several other
hex-dominant meshing techniques were also presented
in <cit.>. Such
indirect methods create hex-dominant meshes with too many
singularities, and the tetrahedral mesh directly influences the
quality of the hex-dominant mesh. Similar to unstructured all-hex mesh
generation, the direct method is also more preferable for hex-dominant
meshes <cit.>. The polycube-based
method <cit.> is an attractive direct approach
to obtain hex-dominant meshes by using degenerated cubes. The
polycube-based method was mainly used for all-hex meshing. A smooth
harmonic field <cit.> was used to generate polycubes for
arbitrary genus geometry. Boolean operations <cit.> were
introduced to deal with arbitrary genus geometry. In <cit.>, a
polycube structure was generated based on the skeletal branches of a
geometric model. Using these methods, the structure of the polycube
and the mapping distortion greatly influence the quality of the hex
mesh. The calculation of the polycube structure with a low mapping
distortion remains an open problem for complex geometry. It is important
to improve the quality of the mesh for analysis by using methods such
as pillowing, smoothing, and optimization <cit.>. Pillowing is an
insert-sheet technique that eliminates situations where two adjacent
hex elements share more than one face. Smoothing and optimizing are
used to further improve the quality of the mesh by moving the
vertices. In our software, we implement all of the above methods to
improve the quality of hex elements.
new_text: Hex-dominant mesh generation combines tetrahedral and hex element advantages, offering greater automation and robustness for complex solids compared to all-hex approaches. Literature strategies include indirect methods that first mesh domains into tetrahedra and merge them into hex-dominant structures via packing technology *<cit.>*, though these generate excessive singularities with tetrahedral quality directly affecting final output. Direct methods, preferred over indirect ones *<cit.>*, include the polycube-based approach *<cit.>*, originally applied for all-hex meshing. Polycube structures are derived using degenerated cubes, with harmonic fields *<cit.>*, Boolean operations *<cit.>*, and skeletal branching *<cit.>* enabling arbitrary genus geometry handling. However, polycube structure and mapping distortion significantly impact hex mesh quality, and calculating low-distortion configurations remains an open challenge for complex geometries. Mesh quality improvement for analysis can be achieved through pillowing (inserting sheets to avoid co-located hex faces), vertex smoothing, and optimization *<cit.>*. Our software integrates all these techniques to enhance hex element quality.

new_text: Each prism-shape degenerated cube within the polycube structure serves as a volumetric representation of a portion of the geometry. Importantly, each of these cubes is paired with a prism-shape degenerated unit cube that acts as its parametric domain. This relationship is illustrated in Fig. <ref>(b), where a specific example is shown: the degenerated cube is depicted alongside its corresponding volumetric region, highlighted by black boxes. Given this structure, the process for each degenerated cube involves identifying its boundary surface P̅_i and establishing a mapping between this surface and a parametric surface U̅_k within the associated unit cube. The mapping procedure begins by aligning the boundary edges of the segmented surface patch S̅_i with those of U̅_k. Once this edge correspondence is established, a parameterization of S̅_i is computed using the cotangent Laplace operator to solve for a harmonic function <cit>. This method ensures a smooth and distortion-minimized mapping. Compared to non-degenerated cubic regions, which rely on axis-aligned faces and require only two parametric variables, the degenerated case introduces an additional variable due to the non-orthogonality of one face. However, this extra complexity is not applied uniformly: for interior surfaces I̅_j within the polycube, the parametric mapping step is omitted entirely, as these surfaces do not contribute to the external geometry representation.

The basic HotStuff approach works sequentially to commit a single client request per four phases. This approach underutilizes the system. However, chained HotStuff approach improves the system throughput to commit one client request per phase and pipeline commit mechanism. Basically, each elected leader propose a new client request on every phase in new view for all replicas. Then, the leader at the same time piggybacks pre-commit, commit, and decide messages for previous client requests that passed to him from the previous leader through commit certificate. This lead to reduction in messages and increasing in throughput by four times. For example, the prepare phase for block k simultaneously serves as the pre-commit phase for block k -1. It also simultaneously serves as the commit phase for block k -2, and simultaneously serves as the decide phase for block k -3, these transactions are now final. This is possible because all the phases have identical structure.
new_text: The fundamental HotStuff protocol operates by processing a single client request through four sequential phases (prepare, pre-commit, commit, and decide), which limits system throughput due to the serialized nature of these steps. To address this inefficiency, the chained HotStuff approach optimizes throughput by allowing one client request to be committed per phase, leveraging a pipelining mechanism. In this method, each elected leader proposes a new client request during every phase while simultaneously handling messages related to previously processed requests. Specifically, the leader piggybacks pre-commit, commit, and decide messages for earlier requests—received from prior leaders via a commit certificate—onto the new proposal. This concurrent processing reduces the total number of required messages and increases throughput by approximately four times compared to the basic protocol. For instance, the prepare phase for block *k* concurrently functions as the pre-commit phase for block *k*−1, the commit phase for block *k*−2, and the decide phase for block *k*−3, effectively finalizing these earlier transactions. This overlap is feasible because all four phases in HotStuff share an identical message structure, enabling the same communication format to be reused across overlapping requests in the pipeline.

The PBFT uses partially synchronous model for guarantee its liveness and asynchronous model for guarantee its safety. PBFT has an optimal bound of N ≥ 3f+1 replicas and adversary can only control lower bound assumed f replicas. PBFT uses encrypted messages that used to prevent spoofing and replay attacks, as well as detecting corrupted messages. PBFT is leader-based paradigm similar to Paxos but differs in all-to-all communications and byzantine tolerance mechanism. In PBFT, leader ensures that all the non-faulty replicas execute each client request in the same order. The normal path consists of 𝒪(1) rounds of voting and when the normal path does not make progress, the protocol falls back to a view change protocol to elect a new leader. PBFT is responsive similar to HotStuff <cit.>. PBFT has implemented in Hyperledger Fabric platform v0.6 <cit.> and many other blockchain systems due to its robust security under attacks and well-tested.

Spoken language understanding (SLU) is a crucial component of task-oriented dialogue systems, that typically handles natural language understanding tasks including intent detection and slot filling. In particular, intent detection aims to identify speaker's intent from a given utterance, while slot filling is to extract from the utterance the correct argument value for the slots of the intent <cit.>. Despite being the 17th most spoken language in the world <cit.> (about 100M speakers), data resources for Vietnamese SLU are limited. There is only one Vietnamese dataset somewhat relevant to intent detection, that is a dialog act corpus containing ISO-24617-2 based annotations over communication acts <cit.>, however, this corpus is not publicly available for the research community.
To the best of our knowledge, there is no public Vietnamese dataset available specifically for either intent detection or slot filling.
new_text: Spoken language understanding (SLU) plays a central role in task-oriented dialogue systems, which rely on it to process and interpret user input for actionable responses. Specifically, SLU encompasses two key tasks: intent detection, which determines the user’s goal or purpose in an utterance, and slot filling, which identifies and extracts specific argument values (e.g., time, location, or object) required to fulfill that intent <cit.>. While these tasks are foundational for enabling effective dialogue systems, challenges arise when applied to less-resourced languages. Vietnamese, despite being the 17th most spoken language globally with approximately 100 million speakers <cit.>, lacks sufficient annotated data to support robust SLU models. To date, only one dataset exists that could marginally contribute to intent detection research in Vietnamese: a dialog act corpus annotated with ISO-24617-2 standards <cit.>. However, this resource focuses on categorizing communication acts rather than intents, and it is not publicly accessible, limiting its utility for model training or evaluation. Consequently, researchers currently face a significant gap, as no publicly available datasets exist specifically for Vietnamese intent detection or slot filling. This scarcity of resources hampers progress in developing effective dialogue systems for Vietnamese speakers and underscores the need for targeted data collection efforts.

new_text:
We also provide illustrative examples to compare the prediction outputs of JointIDSF and JointBERT+CRF, focusing on their ability to identify intent and extract slot information from Vietnamese utterances. Consider the validation utterance “chuyến bay nào rời sân_bay vân_đồn đến côn_đảo và hạ_cánh lúc 10 giờ tối” (What flights leave Van Don airport for Con Dao and arrive at 10 pm). Both models correctly identify the intent as “flight,” accurately recognizing the user’s query about flight details. However, their performance differs in slot tagging. Specifically, our JointIDSF successfully detects the compound term “sân_bay vân_đồn” (Van Don airport) as a departure airport, assigning it the slot type “fromloc.airport_name.” This reflects its capacity to disambiguate nested entities in low-resource languages like Vietnamese. In contrast, JointBERT+CRF misidentifies the entity by tagging only “sân_bay” (airport) as “fromloc.city_name,” incorrectly interpreting it as a city name rather than an airport, and completely omitting “vân_đồn” (Van Don) from the slot recognition process.  

A second example further highlights these distinctions: “cho tôi danh_sách các chuyến bay vào ngày 27 tháng 12 từ đài_bắc đến singapore và giá vé tương_ứng” (Give me a list of flights on December 27 from Taipei to Singapore and their corresponding airfare). Here, both models accurately extract slot information, correctly identifying dates, locations, and destinations. However, their intent predictions diverge. While JointIDSF assigns the combined intent label “airfare#flight,” appropriately reflecting the dual focus on flights and pricing, JointBERT+CRF simplistically labels the intent as “flight,” neglecting the additional airfare information specified in the query. This example underscores how intent modeling capabilities can vary, even when slot tagging is successful. These cases collectively demonstrate that accurate joint intent and slot recognition requires nuanced handling of both semantic compositionality and structural ambiguity in natural language queries.

The overview of our algorithm is shown in Fig. <ref>. The key algorithmic innovation of our approach is to create two distinct MCTS policies to bridge the gap between high-performance simulation and real-world robotic application: the “expert” tree search is centralized and has access to perfect information and large computational resources, whereas the “learner” tree search is decentralized and has access to partial information and limited computational resources. During the offline phase, the neural networks are trained in an imitation learning style using the self-play states of the learner and the high-quality demonstrations of the expert. The expert's high-quality demonstrations enable policy improvement through iterations and incrementally improve the policy and value networks. The learner samples states that should appear more frequently at runtime. For deployment, each robot uses the learner tree search to effectively plan online with partial information and limited computational budget.
Our contributions are extending Biased Neural Monte Carlo Tree Search to (i) decentralized evaluation with local information, (ii) continuous state-action domain, and (iii) limited computational resources.

new_text: While significant progress has been made in object detection over the past decade, the performance of the most advanced detectors remains far from reaching a plateau. As applications in object detection expand into critical real-world domains—such as autonomous vehicles, augmented reality, and surveillance—there is an escalating demand for models that balance high accuracy with computational efficiency. This growing demand is driven by the need to deploy these models on resource-constrained platforms like mobile devices and embedded systems, where real-time performance and minimal power consumption are essential. Although interest in developing lightweight detectors has surged, achieving this balance remains a significant and unresolved challenge. In this paper, we examine the evolution of detector architectures, particularly the advancements of two-stage and single-stage models over their predecessors. Traditionally, two-stage detectors have offered higher accuracy by first generating region proposals and then classifying them, but their computational complexity makes them unsuitable for real-time tasks such as self-driving cars or video surveillance. In contrast, single-stage detectors bypass the region proposal step, enabling faster inference at the cost of some accuracy. However, recent advancements in the past few years have narrowed this gap, with state-of-the-art single-stage detectors now achieving comparable accuracy while maintaining their speed advantage. As illustrated in Figure <ref>, the Swin Transformer represents a notable breakthrough, currently holding the highest accuracy among existing detectors. These developments, along with the ongoing trend of improving detector performance, suggest a promising trajectory toward systems that combine both high accuracy and real-time efficiency.

new_text: From a probabilistic standpoint, post-hoc interpretability methods predominantly center around the model’s predictive posterior probability P_ℳ, aiming to disentangle P_ℳ(Y=y^*|X) through diverse analytical approaches. For instance, LIME <cit.> constructs an interpretable surrogate model f̃(x) to approximate the model’s prediction f(x) = P_ℳ(Y | X=x) locally around an input x_0. In contrast, the WOE approach emphasizes the conditional likelihood P(X = x | Y), either directly (in the evidence-likelihood interpretation) or indirectly (in the hypothesis-odds interpretation). Specifically, a WOE explanation derives from the probability attributed by the model to an input x (or subsets of its features) under the condition Y=y^*, such as Y=y^*=-1.

The main idea of differentiable programming is to leverage gradient-based approaches to optimize the input parameters to obtain a specific target output, allowing for end-to-end trainable systems (particularly useful in deep neural networks). This approach has found use in a large variety of applications such as scientific computing <cit.>, image processing <cit.>, physics engines <cit.>, computational simulations <cit.>, and graphics <cit.>. For differentiable programming of NURBS, we need to compute gradients of the NURBS surface points with respect to the parameters of the NURBS representation. However, since the NURBS surface points are a function of knots, control points, and weights, the partial derivative with respect to each input parameter needs to be computed, which makes the backward evaluation challenging. Further, due to the use of basis functions (which are piecewise-continuous polynomials), the gradients might be discontinuous (or even zero) at certain locations. To alleviate this issue, we exploit the recent theoretical advances in the paradigm of differentiable programming. It has been theoretically proven that if a weak form of the Jacobian for the “forward” evaluation operator can be represented using a block-sparse matrix, then this approximate Jacobian can be used for performing the “backward” evaluation of that operation <cit.>. This approach has been used to define approximate derivatives for operations such as sorting <cit.>, loops and algorithmic conditions , and even derivatives for piecewise polynomial functions <cit.>. We use a similar approach by defining a block-sparse Jacobian for NURBS surface representation and evaluation.
new_text: Differentiable programming uses gradient-based methods to optimize input parameters for target outputs, enabling end-to-end trainable systems (notably in deep neural networks), with applications in scientific computing <cit.>, image processing <cit.>, physics engines <cit.>, simulations <cit.>, and graphics <cit.>. For NURBS, gradients of surface points with respect to knots, control points, and weights must be computed for backward evaluation, a task complicated by the need to calculate partial derivatives for each parameter. The piecewise-continuous nature of basis functions further complicates gradients, which may become discontinuous or zero at certain locations. We address this using recent advances in differentiable programming, where theoretical results show that a block-sparse matrix representing the weak form of the Jacobian for the forward evaluation operator enables approximate backward evaluation <cit.>. This has been applied to sorting <cit.>, loops, conditions, and piecewise polynomials <cit.>. We apply this by defining a block-sparse Jacobian for NURBS.

new_text: When an interface contains “dents”—regions where the structure is temporarily incomplete—these features can appear in any row or column before reaching the end of the plane. Specifically, if such dents occur along the path where interface information propagates (i.e., mid-plane), the system initially places tiles at those dented locations to facilitate the continuation of the propagation process. This temporary placement allows signals to traverse the gaps in the structure, ensuring continuity in the growth of the plane. However, over time, the same signals that initially enabled placement will trigger the deactivation of specific bonding mechanisms (glues) associated with the tiles. As a result, the tiles at dented locations will eventually dissociate and be removed. The design of tile types required for interfaces in these intermediate positions is detailed in Figure <ref>, which illustrates the template configurations necessary to enable this dynamic behavior. An example of how this mechanism unfolds over time—showing the initial deposition of tiles in dented regions followed by their gradual removal—is presented in Figure <ref>, which captures a segment of the growing plane and interface during this process.

Most of the work in the literature relies solely on pixel information inherent in digitized paintings and drawings that is suitable for being fed into Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models for solving classification and retrieval tasks, e.g. <cit.>. Some other works integrate this information with textual metadata or comments, so that computer vision systems are integrated with natural language processing techniques to address multi-modal learning problems, e.g. <cit.>. This means that the information exploited
is often just the visual features extracted from the digitized artworks. Alternatively, these features are used in conjunction with textual features to create a shared embedding where the two representations are projected and compared.
These approaches lead to ignoring a large amount of domain knowledge as well as already known relationships and connections that could increase the quality of existing solutions. Instead, having a knowledge base in which not only artworks but also a rich plethora of metadata, contextual information, textual descriptions, etc., are unified in a structured framework can provide a valuable resource for more powerful information retrieval and knowledge discovery tools in the artistic domain. Such a framework would be beneficial not only for enthusiastic users, who can take advantage of the encoded information to navigate the knowledge base, but also especially for art experts, interested in finding new relationships between artists and/or artworks for a better understanding of the past and modern art.
new_text: The majority of existing studies focus exclusively on the pixel-based data from digitized artworks, such as paintings and drawings, which are input into Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models to perform tasks like classification and retrieval <cit.>. Additional research combines these visual features with textual metadata or annotations, integrating computer vision with natural language processing to address multimodal learning challenges <cit.>. In these cases, the primary data utilized typically consists of visual features derived from digitized artworks, while alternative approaches merge these features with textual attributes to construct a shared embedding space where both representations are projected and compared. These methods often neglect substantial domain-specific knowledge and established relationships that could enhance solution accuracy. A structured knowledge base incorporating not only artworks but also extensive metadata, contextual details, and textual descriptions could serve as a robust foundation for improved information retrieval and knowledge discovery in art history. Such a framework would support both casual users, who benefit from accessible navigation tools, and art scholars, who seek deeper insights into historical and contemporary artistic connections through systematic exploration.

old_text: Deep Learning of neural networks has progressively become more prominent in healthcare with models reaching, or even surpassing, expert accuracy levels. However, these success stories are tainted by concerning reports on the lack of model transparency and bias against some medical conditions or patients' sub-groups. Explainable methods are considered the gateway to alleviate many of these concerns. In this study we demonstrate that the generated explanations are volatile to changes in model training that are perpendicular to the classification task and model structure. This raises further questions about trust in deep learning models for healthcare. Mainly, whether the models capture underlying causal links in the data or just rely on spurious correlations that are made visible via explanation methods. We demonstrate that the output of explainability methods on deep neural networks can vary significantly by changes of hyper-parameters, such as the random seed or how the training set is shuffled. We introduce a measure of explanation consistency which we use to highlight the identified problems on the MIMIC-CXR dataset. We find explanations of identical models but with different training setups have a low consistency: ≈ 33% on average. On the contrary, kernel methods are robust against any orthogonal changes, with explanation consistency at 94%. We conclude that current trends in model explanation are not sufficient to mitigate the risks of deploying models in real life healthcare applications.
new_text: Deep learning of neural networks has increasingly gained prominence in healthcare, with models achieving or surpassing expert-level accuracy. However, these success stories are marred by concerns raised by reports highlighting the lack of model transparency and potential bias toward certain medical conditions or patient sub-groups. Explainable methods are considered the gateway to alleviating these concerns. In this study, we demonstrate that the generated explanations are volatile to changes in model training that are perpendicular to the classification task and model structure. This raises further questions about trust in deep learning models for healthcare, particularly whether these models capture underlying causal links in the data or rely on spurious correlations that become apparent via explanation methods. We show that the output of explainability methods on deep neural networks can vary significantly due to hyper-parameter changes, such as the random seed or the shuffling of the training set. We introduce a measure of explanation consistency to highlight these issues on the MIMIC-CXR dataset. Explanations from identical models trained under different setups exhibit low consistency: approximately 33% on average. In contrast, kernel methods demonstrate robustness against orthogonal changes, achieving 94% explanation consistency. We conclude that current trends in model explanation are insufficient to mitigate the risks of deploying such models in real-life healthcare applications.

As can be seen in Table 1, DCCA and B-DCCA, lead to accurate alignments across the board.
In the case of aligning morphologically dissimilar signals, the two ECG-ECG alignments (EE1 and EE2), CC based alignment is sufficient and even slightly more accurate than DCCA.
However, as already observed on the synthetic datasets, when morphologically distinct signals come into play (as in PE, EVL and ACC), the nonlinear transformation functions used with DCCA seem to matter.
Please note that in the case of PE and ACC, a perfect alignment is not possible as we calculated the ground-truth based on the ECG signals. Due to this there is a variable time delay between the registration of the electrical ECG signal and the arrival time of the pulse wave that the optical/mechanical signals of the PPG and accelerometer represent. As such, alignments within a single heartbeat (approximately 1000ms) should be considered mostly accurate for the PPG and accelerometer.
Nonetheless, especially with the accelerometer to ECG alignment, all methods struggled, although to varying degrees (note that we had to use the median due to too many heavy outliers, where no alignment was found).
This intuitively makes sense, as it shows an extremely difficult alignment scenario because the signals are only very weakly correlated and the used accelerometers were not configured to measure cardiac activity at all - in that sense it was actually quite surprising to us that this alignment was even possible at all.
Again results between DCCA and B-DCCA are somewhat balanced, given the increased computational cost of training an additional f_2, one might consider it sufficient to train only one transformation function.
DTW performed relatively poorly overall.

new_text: Table 1 shows DCCA and B-DCCA produce accurate alignments universally. For morphologically dissimilar signals, such as EE1 and EE2, CC-based alignment suffices and slightly outperforms DCCA. When dealing with morphologically distinct signals (e.g., PE, EVL, and ACC), DCCA’s nonlinear transformation functions prove critical. Perfect alignment is unattainable since ground truth is derived from ECG signals, introducing variable time delays between ECG and pulse wave arrival (as represented by PPG/accelerometer signals). Alignments within a single heartbeat (~1000ms) are largely accurate for PPG and accelerometer signals. Accelerometer-to-ECG alignments performed poorly for all methods, with median used due to numerous heavy outliers (no alignment found). This reflects a challenging scenario: signals are weakly correlated, and accelerometers were not designed to measure cardiac activity. Surprisingly, alignment remained feasible under these constraints. DCCA and B-DCCA show balanced results, but the increased computational cost of an additional transformation function (f₂) may justify using only one transformation. DTW performed poorly overall; while more sophisticated variants could improve results, noise, signal drift, morphological dissimilarities, and collapsing links render it suboptimal in this constrained alignment task.

In the present paper, we propose a novel model called error loss network (ELN) to build an error loss function for supervised learning. The ELN is in structure similar to a radial basis function (RBF) neural network, but its input is an error sample and output is a loss corresponding to that error sample. That means the nonlinear input-output mapper of ELN creates an error loss function. The proposed ELN provides a unified model for a large class of error loss functions, including the previously mentioned ITL loss functions as special cases. The activation function, weight parameters and network size of the ELN can be predetermined or learned from the error samples. On this basis, we propose a new machine
learning paradigm where the learning process is divided into two
stages: first, learning a loss function using an ELN; second, using
the learned loss function to continue to perform the learning.
Moreover, we propose a probability density function (PDF) matching approach to train the ELN and a fixed-point iterative algorithm to train the learning machine with a linear-in-parameter (LIP) model.
new_text: We propose a novel model, the error loss network (ELN), to construct an error loss function for supervised learning. The ELN, structurally similar to an RBF neural network, uses error samples as inputs and generates corresponding loss outputs via its nonlinear input-output mapping. This approach unifies a broad class of error loss functions, including ITL loss functions as special cases. The activation functions, weights, and architecture of the ELN can be predetermined or learned from error samples. We introduce a two-stage learning paradigm: first, training the ELN to learn a loss function, followed by applying this loss function in subsequent learning. Additionally, we develop a PDF matching approach for ELN training and a fixed-point iterative algorithm for learning with linear-in-parameter (LIP) models.

* The ELN1 and ELN2 have the ability to obtain a comparative and even smaller RMSD than QMEE. A possible reason for this is that QMEE is built with a simple online-vector quantization (OVQ) technology <cit.>. Although this technology also chooses the centers of kernels from error samples, it however can not keep the distribution information of the original samples well <cit.>. Moreover, in the process of performing quantization operator, the contribution of a discarded error sample is directly measured by its closest center, which ignores the difference between two adjacent error samples. In contrast, the proposed ELN model is built based on the idea of RBF networks, whose centers do not depend on any specific manner. Once an approriate sampling technology, such as the random sampling technology adopted in ELN1 or the probability density rank-based quantization technology in ELN2, is adopted, it can capture more distribution information hidden in the original error samples. Meanwhile, the combination coefficient in the ELN model are determined by the idea of PDF matching, which can, to some extent, allocate the coefficients of different kernels in a more reasonable manner.
new_text: The ELN1 and ELN2 models demonstrate the potential to achieve a lower, or even lower, root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) compared to the QMEE method. This performance advantage can be attributed, in part, to the inherent limitations of QMEE’s underlying online-vector quantization (OVQ) technology <cit.>. While OVQ selects kernel centers from error samples, it fails to adequately preserve the statistical distribution characteristics of the original data <cit.>. Specifically, during quantization, OVQ assigns discarded error samples to a single nearest kernel center, treating all such samples as equivalent in their contribution. This approach overlooks subtle variations between adjacent error samples, leading to a loss of information about how errors are distributed. In contrast, the ELN model leverages principles from radial basis function (RBF) networks, which do not enforce rigid constraints on kernel center selection. By incorporating sampling strategies like random sampling (in ELN1) or probability density rank-based quantization (in ELN2), the ELN models can capture a richer representation of the original error distribution. Furthermore, the ELN model determines combination coefficients through probability density function (PDF) matching. This method enables a more systematic allocation of weights to different kernels, aligning them with the statistical properties of the errors. Together, these design choices enhance the model’s ability to approximate the target function with greater fidelity, reducing RMSD relative to QMEE.

Usually, neural networks are trained by minimizing the loss which is obtained at the final layer. We ask whether it is beneficial to let the network know the loss it is currently producing and adapting its output correspondingly. That is not possible with the traditional supervised losses since labels are not available at the inference time. Yet, such an approach is sound for an unsupervised loss and, indeed, provides an excellent basis for designing a neural SAT solver.
new_text: Traditional neural network training involves optimizing a loss function calculated at the final layer. This study explores the potential advantages of enabling the model to access its current loss value during execution, allowing dynamic adjustment of its outputs. While conventional supervised learning approaches cannot implement this strategy due to the absence of ground truth labels at inference time, such a mechanism is viable when using unsupervised loss functions. This insight forms a robust foundation for developing neural SAT solvers that leverage real-time loss feedback.

Upsampling Real-Scanned Data. Among the supervised methods, PU-GAN achieved the best performance in our quantitative study. Here, we further compare our model with PU-GAN on real-scanned point clouds using LiDAR from the KITTI dataset <cit.> that contains mixed shapes of car, bike, scrub and ground. Some exemplar results are shown in Fig <ref>. We carefully set up NoP in PU-GAN to ensure all points can be covered. Although PU-GAN is designed to fill the tiny gaps through the optimization of the uniformity metric, in practice it leads to the potential interference between different parts of an object (e.g, the interference between car wheels and car body as zoomed in orange frames or the back wheel of bike as zoomed in red frames in Fig <ref>fig3:v1, and scrub and ground as zoomed in purple frames or ground lines as zoomed in yellow frames in Fig <ref>fig3:v2). new_text: Upsampling Real-Scanned Data. Among supervised methods, PU-GAN demonstrated the best performance in our quantitative analysis. However, when applied to real-world data, we conducted a direct comparison between our model and PU-GAN using point clouds from the KITTI LiDAR dataset, which includes diverse object categories such as cars, bicycles, scrub (e.g., bushes or low vegetation), and ground surfaces. To ensure a fair comparison, we meticulously configured the number of points (NoP) in PU-GAN’s framework to ensure complete coverage of the original input points. PU-GAN employs a uniformity metric to prioritize filling small gaps in the point cloud. While this approach theoretically reduces sparsity, it does not account for the spatial relationships between distinct parts of objects, leading to unintended consequences in practice. For instance, in the KITTI test cases, the uniformity-based upsampling created conflicts between adjacent or overlapping components of objects. In Fig. <ref>fig3:v1, orange frames highlight problematic regions where the car’s wheels and body are incorrectly merged during upsampling, while a red frame isolates a similar issue on the rear wheel of a bicycle. In Fig. <ref>fig3:v2, purple frames show misaligned representations of scrub and ground surfaces, and yellow frames reveal blurred boundaries between ground lines and surrounding geometry. These examples underscore a critical limitation of PU-GAN’s patch-based strategy: by focusing solely on global uniformity, it fails to preserve structural coherence in heterogeneous real-world scenes. In contrast, our holistic, zero-shot model inherently respects contextual relationships between objects and their components, making it more robust for real-world point cloud upsampling tasks.

new_text: Role of batch normalization. Consistent with observations in Lucas2020, our analysis reveals that incorporating batch normalization (BN) results in non-monotonic behavior when interpolating linearly between model checkpoints for ResNet and VGG architectures (see Appendix <ref>). These findings underscore the nuanced role of BN in shaping the geometry of interpolation paths across different network structures.

old_text: Model-based RL algorithms have been studied for a long history and generally obtain higher sample efficiency over model-free algorithms <cit.>. Dyna <cit.> generates virtual samples with a trained dynamics model to augment training data. Learned dynamics models can also be incorporated into model-free algorithms to accelerate learning <cit.>. Model-based value expansion (MVE) <cit.> improves model-free value estimation with predictive transitions. To tackle with the model bias in learned models, STEVE <cit.> uses an ensemble of models for a robust prediction. Model-Based Policy Optimization (MBPO) <cit.> proves a monotonic improvement with limited use of a predictive model. However, most of the model-based methods are designed for tasks with dense rewards. PlanGAN <cit.> is the first algorithm to use GANs and models for planning in sparse-reward multi-goal tasks. But PlanGAN is a planning method and requires a huge amount of computation to simulate trajectories for selecting a single action, and it may also suffer from the accumulated model-based errors in the long planning horizon. Different from these works, our work only utilizes the virtual achieved goals to avoid training with full virtual states and alleviate the impact of model bias.
new_text: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have a long-standing history and typically demonstrate superior sample efficiency compared to their model-free counterparts <cit.>. Dyna <cit.> employs a learned dynamics model to generate synthetic data, enhancing the training dataset. Integrating learned dynamics models into model-free methods can expedite the learning process <cit.>. Model-Based Value Expansion (MVE) <cit.> enhances the accuracy of model-free value estimation by leveraging predicted transitions. To address model bias inherent in learned dynamics, STEVE <cit.> utilizes an ensemble of models for more robust predictions. Model-Based Policy Optimization (MBPO) <cit.> achieves monotonic improvement through strategic, limited use of a predictive model. However, most model-based techniques are optimized for tasks with dense reward signals. PlanGAN <cit.> is the first method to combine generative adversarial networks (GANs) with model-based planning for sparse-reward, multi-goal environments. Despite this, PlanGAN relies on a planning-based strategy that demands significant computational resources to simulate extensive trajectories for action selection and is vulnerable to accumulated model errors over long planning horizons. In contrast, our approach replaces full virtual state sequences with virtual achieved goals, eliminating the need for training with generated states and reducing sensitivity to model inaccuracies.

Robust AC.
Algorithms learning from off-policy data are sample-efficient but are also at the risk of divergence.
To solve the divergence problem, an approach is to incorporate the importance sampling (IS) ratio <cit.>.
However, the resultant algorithms typically have large variance as the IS ratio is the product of many potentially unbounded terms.

Retrace (λ) has motivated recent successful AC methods <cit.> that exploit both on- and off-policy samples for better stability while retaining sample-efficiency.

To address this, importance sampling (IS) ratios <cit.> are often incorporated, though resulting algorithms suffer from high variance due to the IS ratio's multiplicative nature with potentially unbounded terms. We validate our approach on an extended graph model of a road network from North Bethesda, Montgomery County, Maryland. We slightly modified the geometry of this network with additional links to be able to test a bigger number of OD-pairs and routes. We were able to demonstrate up to 12% delay reduction on this extended network. Despite this improvement, we do not claim the proposed route removal strategy is optimal. new_text: Unlike other approaches to detecting and eliminating the Braess paradox, our model explicitly incorporates intersection structures and queue dynamics, which are often overlooked in traditional methods. This is achieved through a more precise graph representation, where link and queue delays are modeled using functions fitted to real-world data. By capturing these delays with empirical accuracy, the model bridges the gap between abstract theoretical frameworks and practical applications, enabling the deployment of analytical methods in complex, real-world transportation networks. To validate this approach, we applied it to an extended graph model of a road network in North Bethesda, Montgomery County, Maryland. This model was modified to include additional links, thereby expanding the network’s complexity and allowing us to test a broader range of origin-destination (OD) pairs and potential routes. Our experiments revealed a maximum 12% reduction in travel delay on this extended network, demonstrating the potential benefits of the proposed strategy. However, we emphasize that this route removal strategy does not guarantee optimality. In fact, as shown in <cit.>, identifying the optimal subnetwork for eliminating the Braess paradox is an NP-hard problem, rendering exact solutions computationally infeasible for large-scale systems. Consequently, our method prioritizes computational efficiency and practical usability in real-world scenarios by accepting a suboptimal yet tractable solution. This trade-off ensures that the approach remains viable for real networks, where scalability and real-time applicability are critical.
