In this paper, we bridge the gap between current multi-view 3D reconstruction and physically-based
differentiable rendering, and demonstrate high-quality reconstructions at competitive runtime performance.
We attack the challenging case of extracting explicit triangle meshes, PBR materials and environment
lighting from a set of multi-view images, in a format directly compatible with current DCC tools and game engines.
For improved visual fidelity, we compute direct illumination using Monte Carlo integration with ray tracing,
and add several techniques to combat the increased noise levels. By carefully trading variance for bias,
we enable efficient gradient-based optimization in a physically-based inverse rendering pipeline.
Compared to previous 3D reconstruction methods, our formulation primarily improves material and light separation.
new_text: This work establishes a connection between existing multi-view 3D reconstruction techniques and physically-based differentiable rendering, showcasing high-quality reconstructions with comparable runtime efficiency. We tackle the complex problem of generating explicit triangle meshes, physically-based rendering (PBR) materials, and environment lighting from multi-view image sets, ensuring compatibility with mainstream digital content creation (DCC) tools and game engines. To enhance visual accuracy, direct illumination is computed via Monte Carlo integration combined with ray tracing, alongside strategies to mitigate elevated noise levels. Through strategic variance-bias trade-offs, we facilitate efficient gradient-based optimization within a physically-based inverse rendering framework. Relative to prior 3D reconstruction approaches, our method markedly improves the separation of material properties and lighting conditions.

The ML research community have embraced DP as the gold standard for privacy protection. Yet, none of the related works in the literature employs the original formulation of DP, but relaxations of it, such as (ϵ,δ)-DP and others. On top of that, the privacy parameters used are quite far from what is considered theoretically “safe” (i.e., ϵ≤ 1 and negligible δ w.r.t. the population size). For such loose implementations, the
privacy guarantees of DP do not hold, and what is done can only be viewed as old plain noise addition, which at best provides ex post protection depending on the amount of noise added for a given ϵ, rather than on the ϵ value itself. This renders it rather pointless to claim use of the DP privacy model and comes close to the (often criticized) utility-first paradigm used in SDC for decades. Thus, the use of the “differential privacy” label by a lot of works whose implementations offer an actual privacy very far from truly sound DP can only be regarded as deceptive. To aggravate the matter, most of those works systematically omit empirical privacy analyses, because they consider any relaxation and parameterization of DP to be privacy-preserving enough.
new_text: The ML research community has adopted DP as the gold standard for privacy protection. However, no work in the literature uses the original DP formulation, instead relying on relaxations like (ε,δ)-DP and others. The privacy parameters employed are far from the theoretically “safe” thresholds (i.e., ε ≤ 1 and negligible δ w.r.t. population size), rendering DP guarantees invalid. Such implementations amount to traditional noise addition, offering at best ex post protection dependent on noise magnitude for a given ε, not ε itself. This undermines DP claims and aligns with the (often criticized) utility-first paradigm in SDC, as the actual privacy provided deviates significantly from rigorous DP. Further, most of these works systematically omit empirical privacy analyses, since they consider any relaxation of DP sufficient for privacy.

new_text: This study investigates the resilience of deep learning architectures against watermark shortcuts in chest X-ray (CXR) datasets. new_text: A fundamental principle underlying integrated gradients is “implementation invariance,” which requires that networks with equivalent functionality yield identical attribution results <cit.>. Scaling up language models has been shown to predictably improve performance and sample efficiency on a wide range of downstream tasks.
This paper instead discusses an unpredictable phenomenon that we refer to as emergent abilities of large language models.
We consider an ability to be emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models.
Thus, emergent abilities cannot be predicted simply by extrapolating the performance of smaller models.
The existence of such emergence implies that additional scaling could further expand the range of capabilities of language models.
new_text: Scaling up language models has been shown to consistently improve performance and sample efficiency on a broad array of downstream tasks. This paper introduces an unanticipated phenomenon we term emergent abilities in large language models. We define an emergent ability as one that is absent in smaller-scale models but present in larger-scale models. Thus, emergent abilities cannot be predicted by merely extrapolating the performance of smaller-scale models. The existence of these emergent abilities suggests that additional scaling could further broaden the range of language model capabilities.

old_text: The original CXRs were corrupted by synthetic shortcuts by adding label-associated watermarks. A unique symbol was assigned to each of the five labels, and at train time, each image was selected to be corrupted by shortcut features with a probability of 0.9. If selected to be corrupted, the image was given “correct" shortcuts with a probability of 0.9, meaning all positive label symbols were watermarked onto the image. Otherwise (with a probability of 0.1), the corrupted image was given “incorrect" shortcuts and all negative label symbols were watermarked onto the image.
new_text: To simulate the presence of synthetic shortcut features in the original chest X-ray (CXR) images, researchers introduced label-associated watermarks that acted as artificial cues. Each of the five possible labels in the dataset was assigned a unique symbolic identifier. During training, every image had a 90% probability of being corrupted with these synthetic shortcut features. When an image was selected for corruption, it could either receive "correct" or "incorrect" shortcuts. Specifically, if a corrupted image received a "correct" shortcut (which occurred in 90% of cases), its true label’s corresponding symbol was applied as a watermark, reinforcing an accurate association between the image and its label. Conversely, in the remaining 10% of corrupted images, the shortcuts were considered "incorrect," meaning that symbols linked to all other (negative) labels were watermarked instead, creating misleading associations. This process aimed to challenge models by introducing biases that could either align with or contradict the true labels.

It is also important to consider the evaluation metrics used to measure emergent abilities <cit.>.
For instance, using exact string match as the evaluation metric for long-sequence targets may disguise compounding incremental improvements as emergence.
Similar logic may apply for multi-step or arithmetic reasoning problems, where models are only scored on whether they get the final answer to a multi-step problem correct, without any credit given to partially correct solutions.
However, the jump in final answer accuracy does not explain why the quality of intermediate steps suddenly emerges to above random, and using evaluation metrics that do not give partial credit are at best an incomplete explanation, because emergent abilities are still observed on many classification tasks (e.g., the tasks in <ref>D–H).
new_text: The evaluation metrics used to assess emergent abilities <cit.> critically influence their perceived emergence. For example, relying on exact string matching for long-sequence targets risks obscuring gradual improvements as abrupt emergent behavior. A similar issue arises in multi-step or arithmetic reasoning tasks, where models receive credit solely for correct final answers, regardless of intermediate step accuracy. This creates a disconnect: while final answer accuracy improves sharply with scale, the sudden emergence of high-quality intermediate reasoning remains unexplained. Evaluation metrics that ignore partial correctness offer at best an incomplete account, since emergent abilities persist even in classification tasks (e.g., <ref>D–H), where such stepwise dependencies do not apply.

We analyzed the search behavior of ACG on a WideResNet-34-10 model trained by the method proposed in <cit.> using CIFAR-100, the only model in which the ASR of ACG was lower than that of APGD in the experiment using the CW loss (see <Ref>).
From <Ref>, it may be observed that the DI  of ACG of this model was lower than that of ACG on the other models.
This means that the search for ACG in this model tended to be more intensified than the attacks on the other two models <cit.>.
By contrast, the DI  of APGD on this model was higher than that of APGD in the other models, indicating that it tended to be more diversified.
These results suggest that the reason why APGD was superior to ACG for this model was because intensification was required to achieve a higher ASR.
However, the models requiring intensification for more effective attacks were rare because ACG exhibited a higher ASR than APGD for most of the models in <Ref>.
new_text: We analyzed the search behavior of ACG on a WideResNet-34-10 model trained using the method described in <cit.> on the CIFAR-100 dataset, the only model in which ACG’s ASR was lower than APGD’s ASR in the CW loss-based experiment (see <Ref>). Observations from <Ref> indicate that the Diversification Index (DI) of ACG for this model was lower compared to ACG’s DI on other models. This suggests that ACG’s search process for this specific model was more focused or "intensified"—prioritizing a narrower range of attack strategies—relative to its behavior on other models <cit.>. Conversely, APGD exhibited a higher DI on this model than on others, implying its attack strategies were more "diversified" here. These contrasting patterns point to a critical distinction: for this model, the lower ASR of ACG compared to APGD likely arose because the attack required a greater degree of intensification to overcome the model’s defenses. However, such a scenario was uncommon. In most models tested in <Ref>, ACG outperformed APGD in terms of ASR, suggesting these models did not demand the same level of intensification. In our study all models are pre-trained on ImageNet (upstream dataset) and then fine-tuned on downstream data. In this section, we explore if upstream robustness propagates downstream.

new_text:
Robustness to upstream dataset shifts  
In our study, all models are pre-trained on ImageNet (an upstream dataset) and then fine-tuned on downstream data. In this section, we explore whether upstream robustness transfers downstream. First, we observe in <ref> (left) that the original performance on ImageNet is linked to out-of-distribution (OOD) classification error in accordance with previous studies <cit.>. When adjusted for in-distribution (ID) classification error, clean ImageNet performance emerges as one of the strongest predictors of OOD classification error. Second, we find that robustness to ImageNet shifts provides little additional information about downstream robustness compared to clean performance. The performance on ImageNet shifts is nearly perfectly correlated with ID performance (in this setting, accuracy falls precisely on the line; c.f., <ref>), but this relationship does not generalize to our diverse set of downstream shifts.

The model is transferred using a set of (potentially few) examples from a new distribution. At test time, we assume that the classes remain the same (closed-world setting), but that the distribution may otherwise change. We specifically focus on the effect of distribution shifts after a model has been transferred to a new distribution (i.e., the downstream implications) and discuss the empirical differences and similarities compared to results concerning upstream OOD robustness that were discussed in previous studies <cit.>.
new_text: We follow the standard workflow for applying computer vision models to downstream tasks—particularly long-tail problems—by building on pre-trained backbones. Model transfer is performed using a limited set of examples from a new data distribution. At inference time, we assume class labels remain consistent with the training set (closed-world setting), while other distributional aspects may vary. Our analysis specifically targets distribution shifts that occur after model transfer (i.e., downstream implications) and systematically evaluates empirical patterns, contrasting these findings with upstream out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness results from prior studies <cit>.

Object detection, a dense prediction task characterized by complex network architectures comprising backbone, neck, and head components, forms the foundation of this study. We adopt Mask-RCNN <cit.> as the baseline model, replacing its backbone with ViT-B/L <cit.> pretrained using our proposed CSPT framework. The performance is evaluated on the publicly available remote sensing dataset DIOR <cit.>, which contains 23,463 images with 192,472 annotated instances across 20 object categories: airplane (AL), airport (AT), baseball field (BF), basketball court (BC), bridge (B), chimney (C), dam (D), expressway service area (ESA), expressway toll station (ETS), golf course (GC), ground track field (GTF), harbor (HB), overpass (O), ship (S), stadium (SD), storage tank (ST), tennis court (TC), train station (TS), vehicle (V), and windmill (W). Following DIOR’s data division protocol <cit.>, we benchmark our approach against state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods and advanced pretraining techniques. Classical detectors, including Faster-RCNN <cit.>, YOLOv5 <cit.>, Mask-RCNN <cit.>, PANet <cit.>, and CenterNet <cit.>, are selected for comparison, alongside RSD-specific SOTA models such as MSFC-Net <cit.>, CANet <cit.>, and FSoD <cit.>.  

As shown in the 9th and 14th rows of Table 6, our method outperforms the baseline Mask-RCNN <cit.> by 3% mAP using ViT-B <cit.> as the backbone, without requiring additional architectural modifications. Furthermore, with ViT-L <cit.> as the backbone—deployed in its standard configuration—we achieve 71.7% mAP, a result competitive with and in some cases superior to existing SOTA methods.  

Additionally, self-supervised pretraining approaches (e.g., MAE <cit.>, MoCo <cit.>, and SimMIM <cit.>) are compared in rows 9 to 12 of Table 6, each integrated as a backbone within Mask-RCNN <cit.>. These comparisons demonstrate that CSPT enables Mask-RCNN to achieve the highest performance among the tested pretraining strategies.

The IoU-based metric. The IoU-based trajectory metric is computed as follows: given two predicted trajectory sets (with and without perturabtion), we first upsample all predicted trajectories (6 of them in each set) to 100Hz, and then voxelize them into a 2D top down grid with resolution of 0.5 meters. We then count the number of voxels both sets occupy, divided by the total number of voxels either output set occupies. To simplify computation, we explicitly ignore the probabilities and speeds of trajectories. This measure quantifies "how geometrically different the trajectories look". An IoU of 1 means the trajectories did not meaningfully change, and an IoU of 0 means the trajectories do not overlap at all. While more complicated versions of this metric could be computed (e.g. earth movers distance), we found this metric intuitive and useful for finding interesting shifts due to perturbation.
new_text: The IoU-based trajectory metric is computed as follows: given two predicted trajectory sets (with and without perturbation), we first upsample all predicted trajectories (six in each set) to 100 Hz, then voxelize them into a 2D top-down grid at a resolution of 0.5 meters. We calculate the IoU by dividing the count of voxels shared by both sets by the total count of voxels occupied by either set. To simplify computation, we explicitly disregard trajectory probabilities and speeds. This measure quantifies how geometrically distinct the trajectories appear. An IoU of 1 indicates the trajectories underwent no meaningful changes, while an IoU of 0 indicates no overlap. While more complex variants of this metric could be computed (e.g., Earth Mover’s Distance), we found this version intuitive and effective for identifying significant shifts caused by perturbation.

In this paper, we propose Point-McBert, a Bert-style pre-training method for point cloud pre-training, which tackle the problem of improper tokenizer in previous work.
We release the previous strict single-choice constraint on patches and utilize the probability distribution vector of token ids as supervision signals to avoid semantically-similar patches corresponding to different token ids.
In addition, we use the high-level semantics generated by transformer to refine the probability distribution vector to further avoid semantically-dissimilar patches corresponding to the same token ids.
Extensive experiments on different datasets and downstream tasks are conducted to evaluate the performance of our Point-McBert.
The results show that our Point-McBert not only improves the performance of previous work on all downstream tasks with almost no extra computational overhead, but also achieve new state-of-the-art on point cloud classification and point cloud few-shot learning.
The experiments also reveal that our pre-training method successfully transfer knowledge learned from unlabeled data to downstream tasks, which has great potential in point cloud learning.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were recently proposed for the session-based recommendation task. The models showed promising improvements over traditional recommendation approaches.
In this work, we further study RNN-based models for session-based recommendations.
We propose the application of two techniques to improve model performance, namely, data augmentation, and a method to account for shifts in the input data distribution.
We also empirically study the use of generalised distillation, and a novel alternative model that directly predicts item embeddings.
Experiments on the RecSys Challenge 2015 dataset demonstrate relative improvements of 12.8% and 14.8% over previously reported results on the Recall@20 and Mean Reciprocal Rank@20 metrics respectively.
new_text: Recent studies have introduced RNNs for session-based recommendation tasks, with these models demonstrating significant performance enhancements compared to conventional recommendation systems. Building on these findings, this research extends the investigation of RNN-based models within session-based recommendation systems. Two strategies are introduced to enhance model effectiveness: data augmentation techniques and a method addressing changes in the input data distribution. Additionally, the study explores generalized distillation and a novel model variant that directly predicts item embeddings. Experimental results using the RecSys Challenge 2015 dataset show relative performance gains of 12.8% in Recall@20 and 14.8% in Mean Reciprocal Rank@20 compared to prior studies.

old_text: Users of e-commerce websites are often inundated by the huge number of items available for sale. Recommender systems can be used to enhance user experience by making personalized and useful recommendations for each user. For example, the system could automatically display items of interest, or suggest new discounts relevant to each user. In order to personalize recommendations, traditional recommender systems often need to build up a user profile. Collaborative filtering approaches <cit.> can define user-user similarity based on their history of purchases, or they could rely on matrix factorization to build latent factor vectors for each user. Crucially, these approaches require the user to be identified when making recommendations. This may not always be possible: new users to the site will not have any profile, or users may not be logged in, or they may have deleted their tracking information. This leads to the problem of cold-start for recommendation methods that require user history.
new_text: Users of e-commerce websites are often inundated by the vast selection of products available for purchase. To address this, recommender systems enhance user experience by offering personalized and useful recommendations. These systems might, for example, automatically highlight items of interest or promote new discounts tailored to individual preferences. Traditional recommendation approaches typically require constructing user profiles to enable personalization. Collaborative filtering methods can define user-user similarity based on purchase histories or employ matrix factorization to generate latent factor vectors for users. Crucially, these strategies necessitate identifying users at the time of recommendation. However, this requirement presents challenges: new users may lack profiles, users might not be logged in, or tracking data could have been deleted. These scenarios highlight the limitations of user-history-dependent methods, ultimately leading to the cold-start problem.

The reasons of the significant increase in the KV store sizes of HyperLevelDB
and PebblesDB are two-fold. First, both HyperLevelDB and PebblesDB compact
only selected ranges of keys to reduce write amplification. Specifically,
HyperLevelDB selects the largest range of keys in the upper level that covers
the smallest range of keys in the lower level to perform compaction, and
places a limit on the total volume of KV pairs in each compaction. This
reduces the amount of invalid KV pairs being reclaimed from the lower level
during compaction. PebblesDB divides keys in each level into disjoint ranges
and compacts each range only when its size reaches a predefined threshold. To
enable fast compaction, PebblesDB only partitions KV pairs in the selected
ranges and directly inserts them into the lower level, without removing
invalid KV pairs in the lower level. This also reduces the amount of invalid
KV pairs being reclaimed.
new_text: The significant increase in KV store sizes in HyperLevelDB and PebblesDB stems from their compaction strategies aimed at reducing write amplification. HyperLevelDB compacts only selected key ranges by choosing the largest overlapping range between upper and lower levels and limiting the total KV pairs per compaction. This minimizes invalid KV pairs reclaimed from lower levels. PebblesDB partitions each level into disjoint key ranges, compacting a range only when its size meets a threshold. To accelerate compaction, it inserts selected ranges directly into the lower level without removing invalid KVs, similarly reducing reclamation of invalid data. Both approaches curtail invalid KV pair retrieval during compaction.

new_text:
**Experiment 7 (Selective Key-Value (KV) Separation):**  
We assess the influence of selective KV separation on the update efficiency of `HashKV`. Three configurations of small-to-large KV ratios are tested: 1:2, 1:1, and 2:1. Small KV pairs are defined as 40 B, while large KV pairs are either 1 KiB or 4 KiB. With the selective KV separation threshold set to 192 B (<ref>), small KV pairs are stored in their entirety within the LSM-tree, whereas large KV pairs are managed through separation. Figure <ref> presents performance comparisons with and without selective KV separation. Enabling this technique boosts throughput by 23.2–118.0% for 1 KiB large KVs and 19.2–52.1% for 4 KiB large KVs. Higher gains are observed in workloads with a larger proportion of small KVs, owing to the elevated overhead of updating small KVs under separation. Additionally, selective KV separation reduces total write sizes by 14.1–39.6% for 1 KiB large KVs and 4.1–10.7% for 4 KiB large KVs.

We propose a novel sparse spectrum approximation of Gaussian process
(GP) tailored for Bayesian optimisation. Whilst the current sparse
spectrum methods provide good approximations for regression problems,
it is observed that this particular form of sparse approximations
generates an overconfident GP, i.e. it predicts less variance than
the original GP. Since the balance between predictive mean and the
predictive variance is a key determinant in the success of Bayesian
optimisation, the current sparse spectrum methods are less suitable.
We derive a regularised marginal likelihood for finding the optimal
frequencies in optimisation problems. The regulariser trades the accuracy
in the model fitting with targeted increase in the variance of the
resultant GP. We first consider the entropy of the distribution over
the maxima as the regulariser that needs to be maximised. Later we
show that the Expected Improvement acquisition function can also be
used as a proxy for that, thus making the optimisation less computationally
expensive. Experiments show an increase in the Bayesian optimisation
convergence rate over the vanilla sparse spectrum method.
new_text: We propose a novel sparse spectrum approximation method for Gaussian processes (GPs) specifically designed for Bayesian optimisation (BO). While existing sparse spectrum techniques effectively approximate GPs in regression tasks, they tend to produce an overconfident model that underestimates predictive variance compared to the original GP. This issue arises because the sparse approximations prioritize fitting the mean response while discarding certain spectral components, which inadvertently reduces the model’s uncertainty estimates. In BO, however, the interplay between predictive mean and variance is critical for effective decision-making. An overconfident GP biases acquisition functions, leading to suboptimal exploration-exploitation trade-offs, and ultimately degrading the performance of BO algorithms. To address this, we introduce a regularised marginal likelihood framework that optimizes the selection of spectral frequencies. The regulariser introduces a controlled trade-off between fitting the data and explicitly increasing the predictive variance of the resulting GP. Initially, we formalize the regulariser as the entropy of the distribution over potential maxima, ensuring that the model maintains a diverse set of plausible optimal regions. This entropy-based approach, however, can be computationally demanding. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition function—already central to BO—can serve as a computationally efficient proxy for this entropy maximisation. By leveraging EI during the regularisation process, we maintain the variance-increasing benefits of the entropy objective while reducing computational overhead. Empirical results confirm that this method accelerates the convergence of Bayesian optimisation compared to the standard sparse spectrum approach, without compromising model accuracy.

Actually, cut deletion or clean-up strategies are important when multiple cuts are added to the master problems at each iteration <cit.>. Most existing works use mathematical methods to develop cut clean-up strategies. A similar work that has leveraged ML techniques to develop cut clean-up strategies can be found in <cit.>, where the authors have accelerated Benders decomposition <cit.> especially for the two-stage stochastic programming problems. Specifically, the authors have used ML techniques to evaluate cuts and their proposed method is instance-specific, which means a specific model is needed for each instance and the training process is conducted online. new_text: Cut deletion or clean-up strategies become critical in optimization frameworks when multiple cuts are iteratively added to the master problem. This necessity arises because excessive or redundant cuts can hinder solver efficiency or slow convergence. While most prior research relies on mathematical criteria—such as angle-based or distance-based metrics—to design clean-up strategies, a recent study <cit.> has explored machine learning (ML) as an alternative for accelerating Benders decomposition in two-stage stochastic programming. The authors trained ML models to evaluate and select informative cuts, aiming to reduce computational overhead. However, their approach is instance-specific: a separate model must be trained for each problem instance, with the training conducted online (during the solving process). This contrasts with typical requirements in wireless network optimization, where pre-trained, generalizable models and offline training are preferred for scalability and deployment efficiency. Furthermore, two-stage stochastic programming problems differ fundamentally from mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problems commonly encountered in wireless resource allocation. Generalized Benders Decomposition (GBD) in MINLP generates cuts that are structurally more complex and harder to characterize than those in Benders decomposition, complicating direct adaptation of the ML strategy. Consequently, the methods in <cit.> cannot be straightforwardly applied to wireless scenarios without significant modifications to address these differences in problem structure and cut behavior.

To the best of our knowledge, it has not been proven that deciding the existence of a valid itinerary for the unlabeled version (assuming T is stationary, and allowing one move per disc) is NP-hard, but similar reconfiguration problems, such as those called OMC <cit.> and U-TRANS-RP <cit.>, have been shown to be NP-hard.
Both problems seek to find a valid itinerary of translations of discs from a start configuration to a target configuration.
Specifically, in OMC (one move per coin), each of the discs is given a subset of possible final targets, and can move (as in our model) exactly once.
In U-TRANS-RP, the goal is to decide whether a valid itinerary of at most k moves exists, for the unlabeled variant.
The NP-hardness of U-TRANS-RP is shown for the case where k is smaller than n (some discs are already at the target locations, and some may move more than once).

new_text: To the best of our knowledge, it has not been formally established whether determining the existence of a valid itinerary for the unlabeled version—where the translation model assumes a stationary target configuration *T* and permits exactly one move per disc—is NP-hard. However, related reconfiguration problems with analogous constraints have been proven to be NP-hard, providing a benchmark for reasoning about computational complexity in similar contexts. For example, the One Move per Coin (OMC) problem involves determining if a set of unlabeled discs can be moved in a single step from an initial configuration to a target configuration, where each disc has a predefined subset of possible final positions. This aligns with the model considered here, as each disc is allowed to move exactly once under the same translation rules. Similarly, the U-TRANS-RP problem focuses on deciding whether an unlabeled reconfiguration can be achieved using at most *k* moves. Crucially, this variant is proven NP-hard when *k* is less than the total number of discs *n*, which implies that some discs must already be at their target locations, while others may require multiple moves. These results suggest that reconfiguration problems with move constraints share intrinsic computational challenges, even when the specific details of the problem instances differ. While no formal reduction has yet been established from OMC or U-TRANS-RP to our unlabeled setting, the structural similarities between these problems lead us to conjecture that the unlabeled version of our model is also NP-hard. Consequently, optimizing for certain criteria—such as minimizing the total displacement in the SA-UST(*S*,*T*) framework—would likely inherit or even amplify the computational difficulty, making it likely NP-hard as well.

new_text: Spatial blockages are categorized as static (e.g., buildings and immobile fixtures), dynamic (e.g., humans and moving obstructions), and self-blockages (e.g., self-hand blocking). Static blockage impacts are traditionally modeled via shadowing <cit.>, while stochastic models characterize statistics of dynamic and self-blockages <cit.>. To address channel uncertainties from random blockages, robust beamforming strategies have been proposed <cit.>. Blockage probability learning through spatiotemporal image sensing side information <cit.> enabled worst-case robust beamforming in CoMP systems, considering all blockage pattern combinations <cit.>. However, the ergodic method’s high computational complexity prompted outage-minimum strategies using stochastic optimization for CoMP <cit.>. Deploying multiple BSs in CoMP leverages spatial diversity to compensate for blockage-induced performance loss but incurs high hardware and power costs. An alternative cost-efficient solution <cit.> involves reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs), creating alternative communication links via RIS-assisted mmWave systems.

If Δ t < 0, the new packets from ⟨ f,p' ⟩ arrive too early.

new_text: When the time difference Δ t between consecutive packet batches is positive (Δ t > 0), it introduces a measurable delay between the final packet of the sequence ⟨ f,p ⟩ and the initial packet of the subsequent sequence ⟨ f,p' ⟩. Conversely, if Δ t is negative (Δ t < 0), the packets from ⟨ f,p' ⟩ arrive at the network before the final packets of ⟨ f,p ⟩ have been fully transmitted, creating a temporal misalignment. This misalignment can result in packets from ⟨ f,p' ⟩ overtaking packets from ⟨ f,p ⟩ if the system allows end-to-end deadlines to exceed the defined cycle time (t_cycle). Such overtaking disrupts the expected transmission order, as packets are processed based on arrival time rather than sequence order. To quantify this effect, the number of packets that arrive out of their original order and lack a guaranteed inter-arrival time of t_cycle can be bounded. This upper bound is calculated as n_transition ≤ 2·⌈|Δ t|/t_cycle⌉, where the ceiling function accounts for discrete cycle time intervals and the factor of 2 accommodates both early and delayed packets in the worst-case scenario.

the VP's runtime environment. This means our device customization is invisible to VP's user-mode apps.
Although our user-level device virtualization allows the VP's process to share certain services in the host system,
with the `device` namespace isolation, a user-mode app running in the VP is still unaware of device-specific differences.
Second, our VP's customization does not interfere with normal operations on the host device.
System modifications without leveraging OS-level virtualization lack flexibility and compatibility.
Besides, they are very difficult to achieve the same transparent and stealthy capability as VPDroid,
as blindly changing return values of APIs/syscalls is likely to cause system crashes or exceptions (e.g., Bluetooth system services keep restarting).
Due to the multiplexing of hardware devices, VPDroid avoids incompatibility issues by
decoupling device-attribute editing operations from normal operations on the host device.

new_text: Lastly, we analyzed the performance of reduce tasks during indexing 1TB of data under the default configuration. The system was configured with 8 reduce tasks per node, resulting in a maximum of 848 reduce tasks across all nodes (calculated as 8 tasks × 106 total nodes). To establish a reference point, the reduce phase was assumed to begin at time 0s, while the overall indexing job had already started 716 seconds earlier (at -716s). Within the first 26 seconds of the reduce phase, all 848 reduce tasks were launched and running concurrently, indicating rapid task initiation. By 3926s—when the fastest reducer completed its task—the number of active reduce tasks began to decline, gradually reducing to just one active task by 4976s (when the final reducer completed). As illustrated in Figure <ref>, this decline in running tasks is evident from 3800s through 4976s, marking the end phase of the indexing job. During the critical time window of 3926–4976s, the system experienced resource underutilization: many nodes that had already completed their assigned reduce tasks remained idle. For instance, the final 50 reduce tasks—completing between 4809s and 4976s—were distributed across only 7 nodes, leaving the remaining 99 nodes (out of 106) with no active tasks, thereby underutilizing their computational capacity. This highlights inefficiencies in resource allocation toward the conclusion of the indexing job.

It is also known as strict or hard sparsity since it counts the cardinality of the support of a function, i.e., the number of non-zero elements in a vector. old_text: Since quantizes C best among all imaginary quadratic integers, at first glance, it appears that there is no need to pursue lattices over rings other than . However, this is not the case when we have feedback. This scenario was first studied by Niesen and Whiting in <cit.> where the global channel knowledge is perfectly fedback to the transmitters. Using the theory of Diophantine approximation, they show that the traditional lattice-based scheme in <cit.> is inefficient in the asymptotically high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime. They then propose a novel coding scheme which is a clever combination of compute-and-forward and real interference alignment. Their scheme achieves the full degrees of freedom (DoF); but in order to see a gain, it requires an enormously high SNR. Another approach proposed in <cit.> is to phase-precode the lattice-based scheme in <cit.>. In this approach, one rotates the transmitted signal space according to the channel realization in such a way that the received signal space is close to a linear integer combination of the codebook. Hence, instead of the global channel knowledge, the phase-precoding approach only requires limited feedback. i.e., transmitters only need to know the optimal (or reasonable) phases for precoding. In this paper, we propose a novel framework called adaptive compute-and-forward which makes use of the proposed lattices. The idea is to let the transmitters adaptively choose the best ring of imaginary quadratic integers to work with according to the channel coefficients. It is worth noting that this approach only requires the knowledge of which ring the transmitters should work with and hence limited feedback suffices. We show that the proposed adaptive compute-and-forward can achieve increased computation rates. Further, this can be used in conjunction with the phase precoding scheme in <cit.>.

Multi-atlas based methods (such as <cit.>) are widely used methods. For a new query image to segment, such methods usually consist of the following steps: first, the n most similar atlases to the query image are selected and registered to the query image; second, the same registration transformations are applied to the labels of the n atlases, and these labels are propagated to produce n segmentations of the query image; finally the segmentations are combined using a fusion strategy. These methods heavily rely on a registration step, in which the atlases are non-linearly registered to the query image. A global affine or rigid registration is usually first performed and then followed by a local non-rigid registration. This latter registration step relies on the critical assumption that brains are similar enough to be accurately mapped from one to another. However, this is unlikely to be the case if the query brain is too different from the atlases in a local area (e.g. if the subject has a neurodegenerative disorder that introduces drastic structural changes). Furthermore, regions whose boundaries are clearly identifiable by a contrast in intensity but arbitrarily defined by the segmentation protocol are likely to be less accurately registered. These errors will inevitably have an effect on the final segmentation. Registrations are also computationally intensive and are usually responsible for the slowness of atlas-based methods.
new_text: Multi-atlas based methods (such as <cit.>) are widely used for image segmentation. For a query image, these methods first select the *n* most similar atlases and register them to the query; second, apply the same registration transformations to atlas labels, generating *n* segmentations; third, combine these segmentations via fusion. They depend on non-linear registration of atlases to the query image, typically starting with global affine/rigid registration followed by local non-rigid registration. This relies on the assumption that brains are sufficiently similar to allow accurate inter-subject mapping. However, this assumption fails when the query brain differs significantly from the atlases locally (e.g., neurodegenerative disorders causing structural changes). Additionally, regions with intensity-defined boundaries not aligned with segmentation protocols may be poorly registered, leading to errors in the final segmentation. Registration is computationally intensive, contributing to the slow performance of atlas-based methods.

old_text: In this paper we take a machine learning approach whereby, given a training set consisting of several atlases, a model is trained to classify each voxel into its corresponding anatomical region. In particular, we investigate whether recent advances in representation learning (the field of machine learning that aims to automatically extract useful representations of the data) may prove beneficial for the segmentation problem. Deep learning is the sub-field of representation learning concerned with learning multi-level or hierarchical representations of the data, where each level is based on the previous one <cit.>. Lately there has been a burst of activity around deep neural networks, and in particular convolutional neural networks, for medical imaging segmentation problems. These include approaches for the segmentation of the lungs <cit.>, cells of C. elegans embryos <cit.>, biological neuron membrane <cit.>, tibial cartilage <cit.>, bone tissue <cit.> and cell mitosis <cit.>, amongst others. All these applications mostly use 2D convolutional networks which take intensity patches as inputs; occasionally spatial consistency is enforced at a second stage through post-processing computations such as probabilistic graphical models. Despite this increasing interest in medical imaging, deep neural networks have not yet been considered for the problem of the whole brain segmentation into anatomical regions. Initial work has been carried out for the segmentation of a single (central) 2D slice of the brain using local 2D patches as input <cit.>. By comparison, our approach tackles the segmentation of the whole 3D brain and introduces multi-scale input features to enforce the spatial consistency of the segmentation.
new_text: This paper presents a machine learning approach where a model trained on multiple atlases classifies each voxel into its anatomical region. We explore whether recent advances in representation learning—machine learning focused on hierarchical data representations—benefit segmentation <cit.>. Recent interest in deep neural networks, particularly convolutional variants, has driven progress in medical imaging segmentation, including lung <cit.>, C. elegans embryo cells <cit.>, neuron membranes <cit.>, tibial cartilage <cit.>, bone tissue <cit.>, and cell mitosis <cit.> applications. Most use 2D convolutional networks with intensity patches, sometimes enforcing spatial consistency via post-processing techniques like probabilistic graphical models. Despite this interest, whole-brain segmentation into anatomical regions has not been addressed with deep networks. Prior work segmented a single 2D brain slice using local 2D patches <cit.>. In contrast, our method segments the entire 3D brain using multi-scale input features to ensure spatial consistency.

We call this strategic exploration (SE). It should be noted that the value of each node is dynamically updated by SE across rounds so it effectively should result in maximizing the amount of exploration across the network.

In formal verification temporal logics are widely used for formulating behavioural specifications and regarding data the concept of storing values in registers for comparison at different points in time is very natural.
This paper is therefore concerned with the logic Freeze LTL <cit.> that extends classical Linear-time Temporal Logic (LTL) by registers and was extensively studied during the past decade.

new_text: In formal verification, temporal logics are widely used for formulating behavioral specifications. When it comes to data, the concept of storing values in registers for comparison at different points in time is very natural. This paper therefore addresses the logic Freeze LTL <cit.>, which extends classical Linear-time Temporal Logic (LTL) by incorporating registers and has been extensively studied over the past decade. Since the satisfiability problem for Freeze LTL is undecidable in general, we focus on the decidable fragment LTL^↓_1 <cit.>, which is restricted to a single register and future-time modalities. More precisely, we propose a generalization of this fragment and analyze its implications in terms of decidability and complexity.

The fundamental decision problem related to OBDA is the following:
is a Boolean
conjunctive query (CQ) entailed from a KB?
This problem has long been known to be undecidable for general existential rules
(this follows e.g., from <cit.>). Consequently,
a significant amount of research has been devoted to the issue of
finding decidable subclasses with a good expressivity / tractability
tradeoff.
It has been observed that most exhibited decidable classes fulfill one of the
three following properties <cit.>:
finiteness of a forward chaining mechanism known
as the chase, which allows inferences to be materialized
 in the data
(we call such rule sets finite expansion sets, fes);
finiteness of query rewriting into a union of CQs, which
allows to the rules to be compiled into the query (finite unification sets, fus);
tree-like shape of the possibly infinite chase,
 which allows one to finitely encode the result
(bounded-treewidth sets, bts). The class of guarded rules <cit.>
is a well-known class satisfying the latter property.
new_text: A core decision problem in ontology-based data access (OBDA) is determining whether a Boolean conjunctive query (CQ) is entailed by a knowledge base (KB). It is well-established that this problem is undecidable for general existential rules <cit.>, prompting extensive research into identifying decidable subclasses that balance expressiveness and computational efficiency. Research has shown that most decidable classes exhibit one of three characteristics <cit.>: the finiteness of a forward-chaining process called the chase, which enables materialization of inferences within the data (finite expansion sets, fes); the ability to rewrite queries into a union of CQs, allowing rules to be compiled into the query (finite unification sets, fus); and the potentially infinite chase having a tree-like structure, enabling finite encoding of results (bounded-treewidth sets, bts). The class of guarded rules <cit.> is a prominent example of a rule set fulfilling this last property.

The left options of a game form the left cut, the right options the right cut, and the game itself represents a number strictly between the two. new_text: Numeric games derive their name from the fact that their values behave analogously to real numbers; a key characteristic is their total order under ≤. These games are constructed using a method similar to the construction of real numbers from rationals through Dedekind cuts. In this analogy, the left options of a game constitute the left cut, while the right options form the right cut, with the game itself representing a number strictly lying between them. A notable distinction lies in the potential separation between the two cuts (one or both could be empty), and the left cut may contain a maximum element, unlike classical Dedekind cuts.

The learning-based approaches can be grouped into three categories according to the degree of supervised information of labeled data used: unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised methods.

In this paper, we present a detail achievable rate analysis of regular and LS-MIMO systems under transceiver hardware impairments and Rician fading conditions. New analytical achievable rate results are derived for finite and infinite number of transceiver antennas. We obtain asymptotic high-SNR achievable rate expression to reveal a finite ceiling in regular MIMO systems. Moreover, the impact of the Rician K-factor and hardware impairments on the achievable rate performance are investigated. Our findings reveal that the achievable rate ceiling vanishes by increasing both the number of transmit and receive antennas in LS-MIMO systems. Finally, we conclude that the achievable rate loss due to hardware impairments increases with the value of the Rician K-factor.
new_text: This paper provides a detailed achievable rate analysis of regular and LS-MIMO systems subjected to transceiver hardware impairments and Rician fading. We derive new analytical expressions for achievable rates under finite and infinite transceiver antenna configurations. An asymptotic high-SNR achievable rate expression is obtained to demonstrate a finite performance ceiling in conventional MIMO systems. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of the Rician K-factor and hardware impairments on achievable rate performance. Our results demonstrate that in LS-MIMO systems, the achievable rate ceiling disappears as both transmit and receive antenna numbers increase. Finally, our analysis confirms that hardware impairment-induced achievable rate losses grow proportionally with increasing Rician K-factor values.

new_text: A recurring assumption in these studies is the use of Rayleigh fading channel models, which simplify the theoretical analysis of multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems by neglecting the presence of a dominant line-of-sight (LoS) propagation path. While this approach significantly reduces analytical complexity, it fails to capture the statistical properties of real-world wireless environments where LoS components are frequently present, such as in urban or indoor scenarios. In such cases, the Rician fading model—a more generalized framework that accounts for both scattered and direct LoS signal paths—provides a more accurate representation of channel conditions. Despite the practical relevance of Rician fading, existing literature has not thoroughly addressed the performance of MIMO systems operating under this model, particularly when transceiver hardware impairments—such as phase noise, amplifier nonlinearities, or quantization errors—are considered. Although recent advances have derived the high-SNR capacity limit of conventional MIMO systems in Rician fading environments <cit.>, these results do not incorporate hardware imperfections, which are known to degrade system performance in practical deployments. The D-preserving scheme presented in <cit.> relies on an application of the probabilistic
method and can be rephrased as follows.
We fix one shortest path between every pair of nodes in the same connected component.
The goal is to find a set S of vertices intersecting with (covering) many such shortest paths
that are of length at least D.
We proceed in stages. At each stage of the algorithm, if there are x
still uncovered paths, by greedily picking a new vertex we can surely cover
Ω(x·D/n) new paths. Thus, since initially there are at most n^2 paths,
we obtain a set S of size 𝒪(n/Dlog D) covering all but n^2/D^2 paths.
Now let T be the set of vertices being the endpoints of at least n/D still uncovered
paths, and notice that |T|=𝒪(n/D). The label of every node consists of the distances
to all nodes from S and T. Additionally, every node v∈ V∖ T also stores the distances
to all nodes which are the other endpoints of the shortest paths starting at v; by the definition
of T there are 𝒪(n/D) such nodes. The total number of distances stored
at every node is thus n/Dlog D, and they can be stored with log D mutliplicative

new_text: The D-preserving approach outlined in <cit.> employs the probabilistic method and can be formalized as follows. For each pair of nodes within a connected component, we fix one shortest path. The objective is to identify a vertex set S that intersects (covers) as many of these shortest paths of length ≥ D as possible. The algorithm operates iteratively: in each iteration, given x uncovered paths, a greedy choice of a vertex guarantees coverage of Ω(x·D/n) new paths. Starting with at most n² paths, this yields a set S of size 𝒪(n/D log D) that covers all but n²/D² paths. Let T denote the set of vertices that are endpoints of ≥ n/D uncovered paths, with |T|=𝒪(n/D). Each node’s label includes distances to all nodes in S and T. Additionally, nodes not in T store distances to the other endpoints of their shortest paths (which, by the definition of T, are 𝒪(n/D) in number). Consequently, every node stores 𝒪(n/D log D) distances, encoded with log D multiplicative overhead (as per Lemma <ref>), resulting in label size n/D log² D.

From a more general perspective, Kanatani <cit.> reformulated motion segmentation as a subspace separation problem, and showed that under the
condition that the subspaces are linearly independent, the SIM is block-diagonal (up to a permutation of the data).
Later, Zelnik-Manor and Irani <cit.> considered the degenerate cases of the motion segmentation problem when the motions are not independent. They analyzed the causes of these degeneracies and proposed to overcome some of them by using the eigenvectors E=[ e_1^T⋯ e_N^T]^T of the row-normalized matrix X^T X and constructing a new shape interaction matrix as Q_ij = ∑_k=1^r exp(( e_i(k)- e_j(k))^2).

They analyzed degeneracy causes and proposed overcoming them by leveraging the eigenvectors E = [e₁ᵀ⋯eₙᵀ]ᵀ of the row-normalized matrix XᵀX, defining a new shape interaction matrix: Q_ij = ∑_{k=1}^r exp( (e_i(k) - e_j(k))² ).

If the claim fails, there exists a set U ⊆ V(G”) such that G”[U] induces a subgraph isomorphic to R. Since R ∖ V' is connected, we can partition U into subsets U' and U ∖ U' such that G”[U ∖ U'] is connected and G”[U'] induces H'. As G' − F' is H'-free, at least one vertex v ∈ U' must belong to a branch V_j. By construction, V_j induces a connected subgraph in both G and G”, and every vertex in V_j has degree r in G”. Invoking Observation <ref> (with G = G”, W = V_j, and W' = U), we conclude that every vertex in V_j is in U. Since |V'| = 3 by construction, the size of V_j is |U| − 3. Applying Observation <ref> (with V' = U ∖ V_j), we find that V_j is a dominating set in G”[U]. This decomposition implies U = V_j ∪ B_j, where B_j denotes the base vertices of V_j in G. A subsequent edge-counting argument reveals that E(G”[B_j]) must contain exactly |E(H')| edges. Since |B_j| = 3, Observation <ref> implies that B_j induces H' in G' − F', contradicting the assumption. Lemma <ref> proves the converse.

old_text: In an ideal scenario (i.e., without noise), after row normalization the inter-cluster affinities are all zero and the intra-cluster affinities all one. However, in noisy cases, the elements of the affinity matrix (i.e., the absolute value of the new SIM) lie in the interval [0,1], and the inter-cluster affinities are often nonzero, but have rather small values. Elementwise powering of the new SIM will thus virtually suppress these small values while keeping the large affinities mostly unaffected. This operation is quite intuitive and just aims to denoise the SIM (affinity matrix). It was first used in <cit.> to increase the gap between inter-cluster and intra-cluster affinities. The result of this step is illustrated in Fig. <ref>. Since, after row normalization, the data in V_r always has a similar magnitude, independently of the problem of interest, the same powering factor can always be employed, thus preventing the need to tune a parameter for the data at hand. In our experiments, we always used γ = 3.5, but observed that values in [3,4] generally yield good results.
new_text: In the absence of noise, row normalization yields inter-cluster affinities of zero and intra-cluster affinities of one. With noise, the affinity matrix (i.e., absolute values of the new SIM) contains entries in [0,1], where inter-cluster affinities are small but nonzero. Elementwise powering of the new SIM suppresses these small values while preserving large affinities, effectively denoising the matrix (as introduced in <cit.> to amplify the inter-intra cluster affinity gap; see Fig. <ref>). Row normalization ensures consistent magnitude in V_r across problems, enabling a universal powering factor to avoid parameter tuning. We used γ = 3.5, noting that γ ∈ [3,4] generally suffices.

The total estimated runtime is decomposed into execution time and data transfer
times. There are rules when contributions can overlap with each other. Times
are always in CPU core cycles. This is convenient as everything on a processor
happens in units of cycles and thus the model is independent of a specific
variant of the processor. Modern processors have multiple clock domains, cores,
caches and memory might have a different clock speed. For memory transfers the
time is converted to the standard bandwidth unit bytes/cycle. While different
clock domains make it more complicated to set up the model, the generic
formulation of the model supports it. The granularity of data transfers inside
the cache/memory hierarchy is that of cache lines (CL). As a consequence the
ECM model considers instructions equivalent to process one CL length. Note
that a kernel might involve multiple data streams and therefore also multiple
CLs.
new_text: The overall predicted runtime is split into execution and data transfer durations. Overlapping contributions are permitted under certain conditions. Time is universally expressed in CPU core cycles, aligning with the processor's operation and enabling model independence from specific processor variants. Contemporary processors feature diverse clock domains, cores, caches, and memory operating at distinct clock speeds. For memory transfers, duration is normalized to the standard bandwidth metric (bytes/cycle). Although clock domain variability complicates model configuration, the model's general formulation accommodates these complexities. Data transfer granularity within the cache/memory hierarchy corresponds to cache lines (CL), which defines the ECM model's assumption that the number of instructions required equates to those processing a single CL. It should be noted that kernels may involve multiple data streams, each associated with distinct CLs.

Figure <ref> illustrates the simplified core layout of the
Haswell microarchitecture. As all modern designs, this microarchitecture uses a
Harvard design for the innermost cache level, i.e. instructions and data are
stored in separate caches. Starting with the L2 cache it is based on a von
Neumann design with unified caches for instructions and data. The core fetches
instructions in chunks of 16 byte from the address provided by the
BPU—typically this address is just a 16 byte increment of the last
address from which data was fetched; in the case of branches it will be the
address of instructions that are the most likely to be executed. After
instructions have been fetched, a pre-decoder determines the bounds of the
various instructions that were included in a given 16 byte block. In the next
phase, decoding from CISC instructions to μops occurs. A simple
example would be a single arithmetic operation with memory address as operand
(e.g. `vaddpd ymm0, ymm0, [rax+r11*8]`) that is split into two μops:
one dedicated load operation and a dedicated arithmetic operation with
register-only operands. This decoding phase is superscalar, with one complex
and three simple complex decoders; also featured is a MSROM decoder which is
responsible for seldom used RISC instructions that decode to more that
4 μops. Decoded μops are stored in the μop cache, which can hold
up to 1536 micro-ops, and enables the reuse of previously decoded instructions,
e.g. in the event of loops. The motivation for this cache is energy saving:
whenever micro-ops from the cache are used, the legacy decode pipeline can be
powered down.
new_text: Figure <ref> illustrates the simplified core layout of the Haswell microarchitecture. Like all modern designs, this microarchitecture employs a Harvard design for the innermost cache level, that is, instructions and data are stored in separate caches. Starting with the L2 cache, the design follows a von Neumann architecture with unified caches for instructions and data. The core fetches instructions in 16-byte blocks from the address provided by the BPU—typically the next 16-byte increment from the last fetched address, or the address of instructions most likely to be executed in the case of branches. After fetching, a pre-decoder identifies the boundaries of individual instructions within each 16-byte block. In the subsequent phase, decoding occurs from CISC instructions to μops. A simple example is a single arithmetic operation with a memory address as an operand (e.g., `vaddpd ymm0, ymm0, [rax+r11*8]`), which splits into two μops: a dedicated load operation and a dedicated arithmetic operation with register-only operands. This decoding phase is superscalar, using one complex and three simple decoders; also present is a MSROM decoder for seldom-used RISC instructions that decode to more than 4 μops. Decoded μops are stored in the μop cache, which holds up to 1536 micro-ops and enables reuse of previously decoded instructions, such as during loop execution. The purpose of this cache is energy conservation: when micro-ops from the cache are used, the legacy decode pipeline can be powered down.

old_text: We prove the existence of an efficient algorithm to find perfect matchings in bipartite hypergraphs whenever a stronger version of Haxell's condition holds. Our algorithm can be seen as a generalization of the classical Hungarian algorithm for finding perfect matchings in bipartite graphs. The techniques we use to achieve this result could be of use more generally in other combinatorial problems on hypergraphs where disjointness structure is crucial, e.g. Set Packing.
new_text: We establish an efficient algorithm for identifying perfect matchings in bipartite hypergraphs provided a reinforced variant of Haxell’s condition is satisfied. This approach extends the classical Hungarian algorithm, which addresses perfect matchings in bipartite graphs, to the hypergraph setting. The methodologies employed here—focusing on maintaining disjointness constraints—have broader potential applications in hypergraph-related combinatorial problems where such independence is critical, including problems like Set Packing.

old_text: Recognizing 3D objects from 2D images is a central problem in computer vision. In recent years, there has been an emerging trend towards analyzing 3D geometry of objects including shapes and poses instead of merely providing bounding boxes <cit.>. The 3D geometric reasoning can not only provide richer information about the scene for subsequent high-level tasks such as scene understanding, augmented reality and human computer interaction, but also improve object detection <cit.>. 3D reconstruction has been a well studied problem and there have been many practically applicable techniques such as structure from motion, multi-view stereo and depth sensors, but these techniques are limited in some scenarios. For example, a large number of acquisitions from multiple views are often required in order to obtain a complete 3D model, which is not preferred in some real-time applications; the depth sensors in general cannot work outdoor and have a limited sensing range; and reconstructing a dynamic scene is still an open problem. In this paper, we aim to investigate the possibility of estimating the 3D shape of an object from a single 2D image, which may potentially address the aforementioned issues.
new_text: Recognizing 3D objects from 2D images is a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Traditionally, object detection systems have relied on 2D bounding boxes to localize objects within an image, but recent advancements have shifted focus toward capturing detailed 3D geometric information, such as object shapes and poses. This transition reflects a growing recognition that 3D data offers significant advantages over 2D representations. Specifically, understanding 3D geometry enables richer scene interpretation, which is critical for applications like augmented reality, human-computer interaction, and advanced scene understanding. Additionally, 3D reasoning can enhance the accuracy of object detection by providing contextual spatial relationships. However, existing 3D reconstruction methods, such as structure from motion, multi-view stereo, and depth sensors, face practical limitations in real-world scenarios. For instance, structure from motion and multi-view stereo typically require numerous images from multiple viewpoints to reconstruct a complete 3D model, making them unsuitable for real-time applications where speed is essential. Depth sensors, while useful in controlled environments, are constrained by short operational ranges, poor performance in outdoor settings, and an inability to capture dynamic scenes involving moving objects. These challenges highlight a gap in the field: the need for a method that can estimate accurate 3D object models using minimal input. This paper addresses this gap by investigating techniques to infer 3D geometry from a single 2D image, a strategy that could overcome the limitations of multi-view and sensor-based approaches by reducing data acquisition requirements and enabling analysis in unstructured or dynamic environments.

new_text: KineographKineo decouples graph updates from queries by executing queries on an outdated snapshot of the graph. It employs a timestamping mechanism similar to Weaver’s, but delays all writes for an epoch (10 seconds in the paper) and applies them as a batch. Kineograph processes queries on the most recent snapshot while buffering new updates until the end of the epoch. Transactions within an epoch are applied in a deterministic order, but the method by which Kineograph resolves conflicts across shards remains unclear. In contrast, refinable timestamps enable low-latency transaction processing and fine-grained resolution of conflicts among concurrent, overlapping transactions. This ensures Weaver’s node programs operate on the latest graph snapshot at execution initiation and supports historical queries for graph snapshots at specific timestamps.

new_text: Our new bilingual distributed representation learning model relies on the creation of pseudo-bilingual documents by combining the content of two documents from a paired source and target language. To construct these pseudo-bilingual documents, we propose and evaluate two strategies: first, the *merge and randomly shuffle* strategy, in which words from both languages are randomly interspersed within the document, breaking all original word order constraints; second, the *length-ratio shuffle* strategy, a deterministic approach that preserves the word order within each language while alternating words between the two languages in proportion to their relative lengths. These shuffling techniques are designed to generate documents where source and target language words co-occur in shared contexts, ensuring that each word—regardless of language—is repeatedly exposed to both linguistic environments. This contextual overlap is critical for building meaningful bilingual associations, as it allows the model to learn alignments between words based on how they appear together in the shuffled documents rather than relying on rigid structural cues. To train the model, we apply a monolingual method like the skip-gram with negative sampling (from the `word2vec` package <cit.>), adapted to process the pseudo-bilingual documents as inputs. By doing so, the model implicitly maps semantically related words across languages into similar regions of a shared embedding space, leveraging the artificially created bilingual contexts instead of monolingual co-occurrence patterns. Importantly, this approach simplifies document processing by treating all text as unordered bags-of-words, ignoring syntactic structure and sentence boundaries. This design emphasizes statistical co-occurrence over grammatical relationships, enabling efficient scaling while still capturing cross-lingual semantic alignment. SLS algorithms under focused random walk framework first choose an unsatisfied clause c, then choose a flip variable from c according to some rules (Algorithm 1).
These rules are usually based on variables' information like break and make.
The break value of v is the number of clauses which will become unsatisfied from satisfied after flipping v. While the make value is the number of clauses which will become satisfied from unsatisfied after flipping v.
A traditional SLS algorithm called WalkSAT/SKC uses a simple rule to pick variable: if there exists a variable with break=0, flip it, otherwise flip a random variable with probability p, or a variable with minimal break with probability 1-p.
Another SLS algorithm called probSAT also uses break value only, but in a completely probabilistic way.
Some recent SLS algorithms also utilize some other information of variables to obtain more complex rules <cit.>: the neighborhood of a variable v are all the variables that occur in at least one same clause with v. The score of a variable is defined as the sum
of weights of clauses (at least 1) which will become satisfied from unsatisfied after flipping that variable. If variable v's neighborhood has been flipped since v's last flip, v is called configuration changed variable, and configuration change decreasing(CCD) variables if score(v)>0 too.

old_text: There are a number of challenges in dealing with POMDPs, including the curse of dimensionality and curse of history. Curse of dimensionality refers to the high dimensions of the belief space. If the underlying robotic system evolves in a discrete grid world with n cells, the corresponding belief space is an n-dimensional continuous space. Moreover, if the underlying state space is continuous (which is the case for most real robotic applications), then the belief space is an infinite dimensional space. Methods such as <cit.> alleviate these issues and aim at taking POMDPs to more challenging and realistic problems. In this paper, we consider a class of POMDPs that commonly arise in modeling the SLAP problem. The settings are similar to the ones used in KF-based localization literature, such as (i) the system model is given as closed-form nonlinear equations, (ii) the state/action/observation spaces are continuous, and (iii) belief is unimodal, thus it is well-approximated by a Gaussian.

There are some centrality measures, that can be calculated using local information of the node like degree centrality <cit.> and semi-local centrality measure <cit.>. Others uses global information of the network like closeness centrality <cit.>, betweenness centrality <cit.>, eigenvector centrality <cit.>, katz centrality <cit.> and so on. These properties are used to show the importance of a node in the given network under different contexts. Calculation of different centrality measures based on global structure of the network is very costly. new_text: In addition to these properties, nodes possess distinct features known as centrality measures that highlight their individual importance within the network. Centrality metrics are categorized based on whether they rely on local node information or global network structure. Local measures include degree centrality <cit.> and semi-local centrality <cit.>, whereas global measures encompass closeness centrality <cit.>, betweenness centrality <cit.>, eigenvector centrality <cit.>, Katz centrality <cit.>, and others. The computational expense of deriving these global metrics has driven the development of approximation algorithms that leverage sampling techniques and localized node data. These algorithms prioritize efficiency by incorporating random walk-based or sampling-driven methods <cit.>, which require minimal data storage since only sampled subsets are retained.

old_text: Degree centrality ranking of a node can be calculated by collecting degree centrality value of all nodes and sort them. But for this we should have complete information of the network. Size of complex networks is increasing exponentially with time. It is a very tedious task to collect and store complete data on a single system, and process it. In the present work, we calculate ranking of a node based on degree centrality using BA model. In real world networks, degree centrality follows power law distribution. We use the evolving process of real world networks and power law distribution to calculate the ranking of a node. Error in the estimated ranking is calculated as the modular difference in actual and estimated ranking. Simulation results show that there is very less error in the estimated ranking. Probabilistic method to estimate the degree ranking is proposed by A Saxena et al. <cit.>. As per the best of our knowledge, this is the first work of its kind. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the properties of the BA model followed by the mathematical analysis of the degree centrality ranking. Section 3 shows experimental results and section 4 concludes the paper.
new_text: Degree centrality rankings of a node can be calculated by collecting the degree centrality values of all nodes and sorting them. However, this requires complete information about the network. The size of complex networks increases exponentially over time, and collecting, storing, and processing complete data on a single system becomes extremely tedious. In the present work, we calculate node rankings based on degree centrality using the BA model. In real-world networks, degree centrality follows a power law distribution. We use the evolutionary process of real-world networks and the power law distribution to estimate the rankings. The error in the estimated rankings is calculated as the modular difference between actual and estimated rankings. Simulation results show that the estimated rankings have very little error. A probabilistic method to estimate degree rankings was proposed by A. Saxena et al. <cit.>. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work of its kind. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the properties of the BA model and the mathematical analysis of the degree centrality ranking. Section 3 presents experimental results, and Section 4 concludes the paper.

Our work falls into the research area of Semantic Parsing, where the key problem is to parse Natural Language queries into logical forms executable on KBs. Classical approaches for Semantic Parsing can be broadly divided into two categories.
The first line of research resorts to the power of grammatical formalisms (e.g., Combinatory Categorial Grammar) to parse NL queries and generate corresponding logical forms, which requires curated/learned lexicons defining the correspondence between NL phrases and symbolic constituents <cit.>. The model is tuned with annotated logical forms, and is capable of recovering complex semantics from data, but often constrained on a specific domain due to scalability issues brought by the crisp grammars and the lack of annotated training data.
Another line of research takes a semi-supervised learning approach, and adopts the results of query execution (i.e., answers) as supervision signal <cit.>.
The parsers, designed towards this new learning paradigm, take different types of forms, ranging from generic chart parsers <cit.> to more specifically engineered, task-oriented ones <cit.>. Semantic parsers in this category often scale to open domain knowledge sources, but lack the ability of understanding compositional queries because of the intractable search space incurred by the flexibility of parsing algorithms. Our work follows this line of research in using query answers as indirect supervision to facilitate end-to-end training using QA tasks, but performs semantic parsing in distributional spaces, where logical forms are “neuralized” to an executable distributed representation.
new_text: Semantic parsing focuses on converting natural language (NL) queries into logical representations that can be executed on knowledge bases (KBs), and our work contributes to this field. Traditional methods in semantic parsing fall into two main categories. The first employs grammatical formalisms, such as Combinatory Categorial Grammar, to derive logical forms from NL inputs, relying on curated or learned lexicons that map linguistic elements to symbolic components <cit.>. These models are trained on annotated logical forms, enabling them to extract intricate semantic structures from data. However, they are often confined to narrow domains due to scalability limitations from rigid grammatical rules and the scarcity of annotated data. The second approach utilizes semi-supervised learning, leveraging query execution outcomes (i.e., answers) as indirect supervision <cit.>. Parsers in this paradigm vary from general-purpose chart parsers <cit.> to task-specific, engineered architectures <cit.>. While these systems excel at scaling to broad knowledge sources, they struggle with compositional queries caused by the exponentially growing search spaces inherent to flexible parsing algorithms. Our approach aligns with this semi-supervised framework, using query answers to enable end-to-end training via QA tasks, but introduces semantic parsing in distributional spaces. Here, logical forms are transformed into executable neural representations, allowing for scalable and domain-adaptive parsing without explicit symbolic intermediaries.
