old_text: Due to the extreme scarcity of urban airspace and safety critical nature of drone operations, we believe it is necessary to highly regulate its use through a model such as collision free network of airways and intersections as alluded to above. As such, notions like free flight as described in the context of NextGen are unlikely to be practical at least in the urban environment. At the same time we do not take the freedom away completely as free flight is possible inside the nodes by default with the extra flexibility for having collision free maps and other information if needed as the meta-data for the nodes. Nodes can have any geometries which means they have no restriction on the size. Once the drone enters a node, the ZSP no longer provides a specific trajectory as in the case of airways or intersections. ZSP will only provide the meta data about that particular node to the drone. Hence a farming drone is in the free flight mode inside a node representing a farm. If on the other hand, ZSP's help with navigation is needed for a node representing a large national park, the node must be divided into multiple nodes each connected through a network of airways and intersections, but again inside the newly formed nodes, free flight is the mode of operation.
new_text: Given the extreme scarcity of urban airspace and the safety-critical nature of drone operations, we argue that highly regulated use is necessary through a collision-free network of airways and intersections, as discussed previously. In this context, concepts such as free flight—prominent in NextGen frameworks—are unlikely to be practical in urban environments. However, this does not entirely restrict freedom: free flight remains possible within nodes, with optional enhancements through collision-free maps and other metadata available as node-specific information. Nodes are unconstrained in geometric configuration and size. Upon entering a node, the ZSP ceases to enforce specific trajectories, as it does in airways or intersections, instead supplying the drone with metadata corresponding to that node. For example, a farming drone operates in free flight mode within a node representing a farm. Conversely, if ZSP-assisted navigation is required for a node representing a large national park, the node must be subdivided into multiple connected nodes via airways and intersections. Yet, within each newly defined node, free flight remains the operational mode.

old_text: The congestion status must be known in IoD within each of ZSPs for two reasons. First, running a congested airspace translates into grounding or holding which are both expensive operations. Second, in the Internet, the ACKs happen on the orders of few hundreds of milliseconds. This fast feedback loop allows implicit congestion probing as a viable option. In IoD, probing directly with drones (i.e. by seeing if drones get stuck in the congestion or not) is orders of magnitude slower. Because of especially high cost of congestion for the IoD, we believe we have to require a feature in the IoD architecture for explicit congestion notifications to at least the neighbouring zones in the E2E level. This is not needed in the N2N level, as any ZSP has complete knowledge of the congestion on all the airways, intersections, and nodes due to the broadcasts from the drones. A major difference with ATC is that there is no central controller for the whole network (ATCSCC) that regulates the load on the whole network while each ARTCC only ensures separation, which would have a negative effect on scalability.
new_text: The congestion status must be known in the IoD for each Zone Service Provider (ZSP) for two key reasons. First, operating a congested airspace results in grounding or holding operations, which are costly. Second, in the Internet, ACK feedback occurs within hundreds of milliseconds, enabling implicit congestion probing as a viable option. In IoD, however, probing by observing if drones become stalled in congestion is significantly slower. Due to the exceptionally high cost of congestion in the IoD, we propose that the IoD architecture must include explicit congestion notifications for neighboring zones at the end-to-end (E2E) level. This is unnecessary at the node-to-node (N2N) level, as each ZSP has full visibility of congestion on all airways, intersections, and nodes via drone broadcasts. A major difference compared to ATC is the absence of a centralized controller (e.g., ATCSCC) regulating network-wide load. In ATC, each ARTCC only ensures separation, which impedes scalability.

old_text: Optimizing the joint mmWave radar and communication system is not a trivial problem. Each system has different objectives, e.g., radar requires high target detection accuracy and resolution even at low received signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR), while communication requires high data rate. The two goals may conflict with each other when optimizing the waveform. Full duplex, which is commonly assumed in radar but not in communications, is also a problem that should be resolved for the joint mmWave radar and communication system.
new_text: Designing an integrated millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar and communication system poses significant challenges due to conflicting performance requirements. Radar systems prioritize high target detection accuracy and resolution, particularly under low received signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, whereas communication systems emphasize maximizing data throughput. These mutually exclusive requirements create inherent trade-offs when optimizing the transmission waveform. Additionally, the implementation of full-duplex operations—commonly employed in radar to enable simultaneous transmission and reception but typically avoided in communication systems due to self-interference—introduces further complexity for coexistence in the shared mmWave band.

old_text: In the early stage of deploying mmWave V2X communication systems, the insufficient penetration rate of V2X capable vehicles would be an issue to exploit the full benefit of V2X (especially V2V) communications. High penetration rates may cause excessive interference in highly-loaded traffic conditions, which could be mitigated with narrow mmWave beams and advanced MAC protocols. Because automotive radars already exploit mmWave spectrum, it may be possible to implement joint mmWave radar and communication systems and increase the penetration rate of mmWave V2X capable vehicle in the early deployment stage. Joint systems will also save space in a vehicle and reduce cost and power consumption. A preliminary study on designing a joint mmWave radar and communication framework for vehicular environment based on the IEEE 802.11ad system (operating in the 60 GHz unlicensed spectrum) was conducted in <cit.>. It was shown in <cit.> that a range estimation accuracy within 0.1m and a velocity estimation accuracy within 0.1m/s could be achieved by using the IEEE 802.11ad preamble as a radar signal and standard WiFi receiver algorithms. It may also be possible to add communication functions on existing mmWave automotive radars operating in 76-81 GHz frequencies.
new_text: During the initial deployment of mmWave V2X communication systems, the limited adoption rate of V2X-enabled vehicles poses a challenge to fully realizing the potential of V2X (particularly V2V) communication. Conversely, excessively high penetration rates in dense traffic could lead to significant interference, potentially alleviated through the use of focused mmWave beamforming and advanced MAC protocols. Given that automotive radars already operate in the mmWave spectrum, integrating joint mmWave radar and communication systems could accelerate the deployment of V2X-capable vehicles by leveraging existing infrastructure. Such integrated designs offer advantages such as reduced hardware footprint, lower costs, and decreased power consumption. An initial investigation into developing a combined mmWave radar-communication framework for vehicular environments, based on the IEEE 802.11ad standard (operating at 60 GHz in the unlicensed band), was reported in <cit.>. This study demonstrated that range estimation with an accuracy of 0.1m and velocity estimation within 0.1m/s could be achieved by repurposing the IEEE 802.11ad preamble as a radar signal and utilizing conventional WiFi receiver algorithms <cit.>. Additionally, enabling communication capabilities in existing mmWave automotive radars operating in the 76–81 GHz range may also be feasible.

old_text: As driving becomes more automated, vehicles are being equipped with more sensors generating even higher data rates. Radars (RAdio Detection and Ranging) are used for object detection, visual cameras as virtual mirrors, and LIDARs (LIght Detection and Ranging) for generating high resolution depth associated range maps, all to enhance the safety and efficiency of driving. Connected vehicles can use wireless communication to exchange sensor data, allowing them to enlarge their sensing range and improve automated driving functions. Unfortunately, conventional technologies, such as dedicated short-range communication (DSRC) and 4G cellular communication, do not support the gigabit-per-second data rates that would be required for raw sensor data exchange between vehicles. This paper makes the case that millimeter wave (mmWave) communication is the only viable approach for high bandwidth connected vehicles. The motivations and challenges associated with using mmWave for vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure applications are highlighted. A solution to one key challenge — the overhead of mmWave beam training — is proposed. The critical feature of this solution is to leverage information derived from the sensors or DSRC as side information for the mmWave communication link configuration. Examples and simulation results show that the beam alignment overhead can be reduced by using position information obtained from DSRC.
new_text: With increased automation, vehicles now incorporate an expanding array of sensors that generate substantial data rates. These sensors include radar systems for object detection, visual cameras serving as digital mirrors, and LIDAR units for creating high-resolution depth-range maps, all aimed at improving driving safety and efficiency. Connectivity among vehicles, enabled by wireless communication, facilitates sensor data sharing, thereby expanding their perceptual range and enhancing autonomous driving capabilities. However, conventional communication standards such as dedicated short-range communication (DSRC) and 4G cellular networks cannot achieve the gigabit-per-second speeds necessary for exchanging raw sensor data between vehicles. This paper argues that millimeter wave (mmWave) communication is the sole feasible solution for high-bandwidth connected vehicles. The paper examines the rationale and challenges of implementing mmWave for vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure scenarios, proposing a method to address the challenge of mmWave beam training overhead. The core innovation of the proposed method involves utilizing side information derived from onboard sensors or DSRC to optimize mmWave link configuration. Simulation results indicate that leveraging position data from DSRC significantly reduces beam alignment overhead.

Functions in this class admit simple iterative methods (including the noisy gradient method, curvilinear search, and trust-region methods), which avoid being trapped near saddle points, and efficiently obtain a local minimizer. The goal of our evaluation was to answer the following questions: (1) does continuous servoing significantly improve grasping accuracy and success rate? (2) how well does our learning-based system perform when compared to alternative approaches? To answer question (1), we compared our approach to an open-loop method that observes the scene prior to the grasp, extracts image patches, chooses the patch with the highest probability of a successful grasp, and then uses a known camera calibration to move the gripper to that location. This method is analogous to the approach proposed by <cit.>, but uses the same network architecture as our method and the same training set. We refer to this approach as “open loop,” since it does not make use of continuous visual feedback. To answer question (2), we also compared our approach to a random baseline method, as well as a hand-engineered grasping system that uses depth images and heuristic positioning of the fingers. This hand-engineered system is described in Appendix <ref>. Note that our method requires fewer assumptions than either of the two alternative methods: unlike <cit.>, we do not require knowledge of the camera to hand calibration, and unlike the hand-engineered system, we do not require either the calibration or depth images.
new_text: Our evaluation aimed to address two key questions: (1) whether continuous servoing significantly enhances grasping accuracy and success rates, and (2) how our learning-based system compares to alternative methods. To investigate question (1), we evaluated our approach against an open-loop baseline that pre-grasp scene observations to extract image patches, selects the patch with the highest predicted grasp success probability, and computes gripper positions using a known camera-to-hand calibration. This method shares the same network architecture and training data as our system but lacks real-time visual feedback, aligning with the method described in <cit.>. For question (2), we also compared against a random baseline and a hand-engineered system utilizing depth images and rule-based fingertip positioning, detailed in Appendix <ref>. Our approach imposes fewer assumptions than both alternatives: unlike <cit.>, it does not require camera-to-hand calibration, and in contrast to the hand-engineered system, it operates without calibration or depth image inputs.

old_text: We describe a learning-based approach to hand-eye coordination for robotic grasping from monocular images. To learn hand-eye coordination for grasping, we trained a large convolutional neural network to predict the probability that task-space motion of the gripper will result in successful grasps, using only monocular camera images and independently of camera calibration or the current robot pose. This requires the network to observe the spatial relationship between the gripper and objects in the scene, thus learning hand-eye coordination. We then use this network to servo the gripper in real time to achieve successful grasps. To train our network, we collected over 800,000 grasp attempts over the course of two months, using between 6 and 14 robotic manipulators at any given time, with differences in camera placement and hardware. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that our method achieves effective real-time control, can successfully grasp novel objects, and corrects mistakes by continuous servoing.
new_text: We present a learning-based method for enabling robotic grasping through hand-eye coordination using monocular visual input. At its core, this approach employs a large convolutional neural network (CNN) trained to estimate the likelihood that a specific gripper movement in task space will lead to a successful grasp. The CNN operates on monocular images alone and does not rely on knowledge of the robot’s current pose or precise camera calibration. This design challenges the network to infer the spatial relationship between the gripper and objects within the scene purely from visual cues, effectively enabling it to learn hand-eye coordination implicitly through data-driven pattern recognition. Once trained, the model guides real-time control of the gripper by continuously predicting and adjusting motions to achieve successful grasps. To develop this system, we gathered an extensive dataset comprising over 800,000 grasp attempts across two months, using up to 14 robotic manipulators simultaneously. These robots operated with varying camera placements and hardware configurations, ensuring the model generalizes across diverse observational conditions. Our experiments confirm that the approach enables reliable real-time grasping, adapts to previously unseen objects, and recovers from initial errors through persistent, closed-loop servoing adjustments.

The assumption is that the actions induce a transitive relation between states: that is, that moving from p_1 to p_2 and then to p_3 is equivalent to moving from p_1 to p_3 directly. This assumption does not always hold in the case of grasping, since an intermediate motion might move objects in the scene, but it is a reasonable approximation that we found works quite well in practice. The major advantage of this approximation is that fitting the Q function reduces to a prediction problem, and avoids the usual instabilities associated with Q iteration, since the previous Q function does not appear in the regression. An interesting and promising direction for future work is to combine our approach with more standard reinforcement learning formulations that do consider the effects of intermediate actions. This could enable the robot, for example, to perform nonprehensile manipulations to intentionally reorient and reposition objects prior to grasping.

The latest study with the best-reported results in emotion classification from the speech <cit.> has used a basic Deep Neural Network, which has a limited capacity. In the proposed study a newer form of Deep Neural Network (DNN) will be utilised, which is known as Deep Belief Networks (DBN). A DBN is better than a conventional DNN because it offers the layer-wise training (known as “pretraining”) as opposed to the conventional “feed-forward” training. The layer-wise training is unsupervised and it does not require labeled data, therefore, a DBN can have a deeper architecture compared to a DNN. A deeper architecture offers a better representation of data compared to a shallow architecture.
new_text:
A deep network is selected for this study due to its established effectiveness in discriminative feature learning, which is critical for tasks like emotion classification where distinguishing subtle patterns is essential. The architecture of a deep network is fundamentally structured as a directed graph: each hidden unit in a layer is connected to multiple hidden units in the subsequent, deeper layer. This connectivity creates a cascade of interactions, where the outputs of units in earlier layers are combined and recombined through nonlinear activation functions (e.g., sigmoid or ReLU). As a result, each subsequent hidden layer generates a nonlinear transformation of the information from all preceding layers. When an optimization algorithm, such as gradient descent, is applied during training, the network iteratively adjusts the weights of these connections. This process ensures that each hidden layer becomes an optimally weighted, nonlinear combination of the layer below it, effectively extracting hierarchical representations of the input data. 

The latest benchmark study in emotion classification from speech <cit.> employed a standard deep neural network (DNN) with limited capacity, constrained by its reliance on fully supervised training, which requires extensive labeled data. In contrast, the proposed study utilizes a Deep Belief Network (DBN), a more advanced form of DNN. A DBN improves upon conventional DNNs by incorporating layer-wise training, also known as pretraining, which is unsupervised. This approach allows each layer to be trained independently using unlabeled data, capturing meaningful features without explicit supervision. Because pretraining does not depend on labeled examples, DBNs can achieve deeper architectures—comprising more hidden layers—than traditional DNNs, which rely on end-to-end supervised learning. A deeper architecture enables the network to model more abstract and hierarchical representations of the input data. This enhanced representational capacity is particularly valuable for emotion classification, where nuanced patterns in speech signals require multi-level feature abstraction for accurate discrimination.

old_text: Currently, we are evaluating various integration strategies of SRC and DBN and running simulation experiments to find a optimal feature set. As a next step we will impute synthetic noise available from publicly available datasets ([URL] fr/DEMAND/), which involves 18 types of noises including white noise and noises at the cafeteria, car, restaurant, train station, bus and park. We will then train the classification framework to handle noise. Signal-to-noise ratio will be varied by varying the noise intensity (from the noise dataset) in the speech signal and the optimal configuration for the DBN parameters (such as, number of layers, number of hidden units per layer etc.) and optimal construction of the training matrix for SRC will be learned through solving an optimisation problem. A general model will be developed that given the noisy intensity will be able to yield the optimal configuration of the DBN and SRC to maximise the accuracy.
new_text: We are currently assessing different integration strategies for the Sparse Representation Classification (SRC) and Deep Belief Network (DBN) models to identify an optimal feature set, using simulation experiments as a foundation for subsequent improvements. To enhance robustness in real-world conditions, the next phase involves incorporating synthetic noise samples from the publicly accessible DEMAND dataset ([URL] fr/DEMAND/). This dataset encompasses 18 distinct noise categories, such as white noise and environmental sounds recorded in settings like cafeterias, vehicles, restaurants, train stations, buses, and parks. The classification framework will be trained to effectively process these noisy inputs. To simulate varying real-world acoustic challenges, the signal-to-noise ratio will be systematically adjusted by modulating the intensity of the noise applied to speech signals. Simultaneously, we will optimize DBN architecture parameters—such as the number of layers and hidden units per layer—and refine the training matrix construction for SRC through an optimization problem. The goal is to develop a generalized model that, given a specific noise intensity level, automatically determines the most effective configuration of DBN and SRC components to maximize classification accuracy. This approach ensures the system adapts dynamically to environmental noise variability.

An optimal feature set will be determined from the pool of available features including pitch, energy and formant related features etc. For every instance of the dataset, features would be extracted using the DBN network and will be stored as a column of the “Training Matrix A”. When a test speech arrives, similarly the features are first extracted and solved with regards to the “Training Matrix A” to identify the test class. For the segment-level emotion recognition, the training target is the label of the utterance. The same labels are assigned to all the segments in one utterance. new_text: As a foundational step, speech signals are first segmented into smaller, manageable units. These segments serve as the basis for extracting relevant acoustic features, which are critical for training a Deep Belief Network (DBN). The selection of an optimal feature set involves evaluating various characteristics from the available pool, such as pitch (related to vocal tone), energy (amplitude strength), and formants (resonance frequencies). These features are chosen because they collectively capture phonetic and prosodic aspects that correlate with emotional expression. For each dataset instance, the DBN processes the extracted features and compiles them into a structured representation. Specifically, the features are organized as individual columns in a matrix termed “Training Matrix A.” This matrix becomes the core training data for the model. During testing, when a new speech input is received, the same feature extraction process is applied. The derived features are then compared against Training Matrix A to infer the emotional class of the test sample. For segment-level emotion recognition, the training labels correspond to the emotion class assigned to the entire utterance. These labels are uniformly applied to all segments within the utterance, assuming consistency in emotional expression across the speech segment. However, recognizing that emotional cues may not be uniformly distributed, the method prioritizes segments with the highest energy. This is based on the rationale that high-energy segments are more likely to contain prominent emotional cues, such as increased intensity or stress, which are characteristic of affective states. Consequently, these segments are selected as representative training samples to enhance the model’s focus on the most informative parts of the speech.

The skip connections from convolutional layers to their mirrored
  corresponding de-convolutional layers exhibit two main advantages.
  First, they allow the signal being back-propagated to
  bottom layers directly, and thus tackles the problem of gradient vanishing, making
  training deep networks easier and achieving denoising performance gains
  consequently. Second, these skip connections pass image details from
  convolutional layers to de-convolutional layers, which is beneficial in
  recovering the clean image. Experiments are carried out on benchmark

new_text: Skip connections between convolutional layers and their mirrored de-convolutional counterparts offer two key benefits that enhance the network’s functionality. First, these connections facilitate the direct transmission of gradients during backpropagation, bypassing intermediate layers. This mechanism addresses the gradient vanishing issue commonly encountered in deep networks, where gradients weaken as they propagate through many layers. By preserving gradient magnitude, the network trains more effectively, leading to improved denoising performance. Second, the skip connections transfer detailed structural information captured by the convolutional layers—such as edges, textures, and fine-grained patterns—directly to the de-convolutional layers. This ensures that the de-convolutional stages retain critical spatial details during image reconstruction, which is essential for synthesizing a clean, high-quality output. To validate these advantages, experiments were conducted on benchmark datasets. The results demonstrate that the network outperforms all previously reported state-of-the-art methods in denoising accuracy, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed architecture.

One application of geometric descriptors is the registration of two fragments from a 3D scan, a subcomponent of some 3D reconstruction approaches <cit.>. The goal of surface registration is to determine if two fragments (P_i,P_j) overlap, and if they do provide an estimate of their relative geometric transformation T_ij. To focus our evaluation on a registration method's ability to detect and align loop closures, we only consider pairs of fragments that are not time-based adjacent to each other.
We start by showing the results of registration over an existing synthetic dataset designed for indoor scene reconstruction, and then demonstrate the results on fragments scanned from real-world environments. We show that a standard RANSAC-based registration approach using 3DMatch significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art geometric registration methods for loop closure detection and fragment-to-fragment alignment.
new_text:
Geometric descriptors play a crucial role in various computer vision tasks. One such application is the registration of 3D scan fragments, which serves as a key component in broader 3D reconstruction pipelines. Surface registration involves determining whether two fragments (P_i and P_j) exhibit overlapping regions and, if they do, estimating their relative geometric transformation T_ij. This transformation aligns the coordinate systems of the fragments to reconstruct a coherent 3D model. To isolate the evaluation of a registration method's effectiveness in detecting and aligning loop closures—critical for creating globally consistent reconstructions—we focus on fragment pairs that are not sequentially adjacent in time. Time-based adjacency often simplifies alignment due to minimal motion between scans; excluding such pairs ensures that the assessment prioritizes the ability to resolve non-consecutive overlaps, a more challenging scenario. 

We first present our findings using an existing synthetic dataset designed for indoor scene reconstruction, providing a controlled baseline for comparison. Subsequently, we validate these results through experiments on real-world scanned fragments, where sensor noise and environmental variability further challenge registration accuracy. Our results demonstrate that a standard RANSAC-based registration approach, leveraging the 3DMatch descriptor, outperforms other leading geometric registration methods in both detecting loop closures and aligning fragments. This superior performance highlights the effectiveness of integrating 3DMatch with robust consensus estimation techniques for fragment-level alignment tasks.

old_text: Stereo vision is considered to be a more robust method for the purpose of obstacle avoidance. The main advantages are that objects can also be detected in the direction of motion and that it provides absolute distance estimates to these objects. These advantages were demonstrated on a relatively heavy platform equipped with optical flow and stereo vision systems <cit.>. Onboard stereo vision has also been demonstrated on a fixed-wing vehicle of over 500 g flying at 9 m/s <cit.>. In flight tests small obstacles right ahead of the vehicle are detected at a range of 5 m and at a frame rate of 120 Hz. This approach shows that stereo vision can be used to combine short-term path planning with reactive avoidance control.
new_text: Stereo vision is a robust method for obstacle avoidance, enabling detection of objects in the direction of motion and providing absolute distance estimates. These advantages were demonstrated on a heavy platform with optical flow and stereo vision <cit.>. Onboard stereo vision has been applied to a fixed-wing vehicle over 500 g flying at 9 m/s <cit.>. Flight tests detected small obstacles directly ahead at 5 m range with 120 Hz frame rate, demonstrating its capability to integrate short-term path planning with reactive avoidance control.

Based on the shape of this region, a threshold disparity value can be calculated for each camera pixel such that the Droplet shape is defined in a reference disparity map. Every time a sparse disparity map has been generated by the stereo vision algorithm, it is compared to this reference disparity map. The number of pixels with a disparity value higher than the reference provides information about obstacles. This number is compared to a threshold (τ_d>ref=7 px) to deal with outliers. new_text: The stereo vision system's primary function is to determine whether obstacles exist within the Droplet area. A threshold disparity value is computed for each pixel based on the Droplet's geometric configuration, establishing a reference disparity map that defines the static shape. After a sparse disparity map is produced through stereo matching algorithms, it is cross-referenced with the precomputed reference. The count of pixels in the resulting map exceeding the reference disparity indicates potential obstructions; however, to mitigate outlier effects, this count must surpass a threshold (τ_d>ref=7 px) to flag the area as occupied. As long as the threshold remains unexceeded, the Droplet region is deemed unobstructed. The static nature of the Droplet shape allows the reference disparity map to be precomputed, significantly reducing computational overhead during obstacle detection.

Both <cit.> and <cit.> use versions of Async-SGD where
the main potential problem is that each worker computes gradients
over a potentially old version of the model.
In order to remove this discrepancy, we propose here to reconsider
a synchronous version of distributed stochastic gradient descent (Sync-SGD),

new_text: Both <cit.> and <cit.> employ variants of Async-SGD, where the primary issue lies in workers computing gradients over potentially outdated model versions. To address this discrepancy, we propose adopting a synchronous formulation of distributed stochastic gradient descent (Sync-SGD). In this approach, parameter servers await receipt of gradients from all workers before aggregating them and distributing the updated parameters to all workers. This ensures the algorithm functions as a true mini-batch SGD, where the effective batch size equals the sum of the workers' individual mini-batch sizes.

old_text: We introduce the problem of counting everyday objects in everyday scenes. While previous works have studied specific counting problems such as pedestrian counting in surveillance videos, or biological cell counting, we are interested in counting common objects in natural scenes. We study this problem in a setup similar to traditional scene understanding problems. Given an image, we consider the task of predicting the counts (or the numerosity) of categories of interest. We study some simple approaches and applications for this counting problem. Our `detect` approach adapts an object detector to perform counting, while our `glance` approach regresses to ground truth counts. Our associative subitizing (`aso-sub`) approach divides an image into regions and regresses to fractional object counts in each region. We create an ensemble (`ens`) of these counting methods which improves performance. We demonstrate counting performance on the PASCAL and MS COCO datasets. We show proof-of-concept applications of our automatic counting methods to 1) improve object detection performance, and 2) visual question answering (on VQA and COCO-QA). Our code and datasets will be publicly available.
new_text: This study addresses the challenge of quantifying common objects in naturalistic environments. Unlike prior research focused on domain-specific tasks such as pedestrian detection in surveillance footage or cellular counting, our work investigates general-purpose object enumeration in everyday scenes. The problem is approached within a conventional scene analysis framework, where the objective is to estimate the numerical distribution of object categories within a given image. We evaluate three foundational techniques for this task: a detection-based method (`detect`) that leverages object detection models for counting, a direct regression approach (`glance`) that predicts ground-truth counts, and an associative subitizing method (`aso-sub`) that partitions images into regions and estimates fractional object counts per region. These approaches are combined into an ensemble (`ens`) to enhance accuracy. Evaluation is conducted on the PASCAL and MS COCO benchmarks, with experimental results demonstrating applications including 1) boosting object detection efficacy and 2) supporting visual question answering on VQA and COCO-QA datasets. Code and associated datasets will be shared publicly.

old_text: We also evaluate mRMSE values for ground truth instances with non-zero counts (mRMSE-nonzero). This metric reflects more clearly how accurate the counts produced by a method (beyond predicting absence) are.

* We formulate the problem of allocating such D2D links for cooperation within the utility maximization
framework (Section <ref>). We propose a scheduling policy for such D2D-enabled networks (Section <ref>). The policy consists of an extension of the single-user scheduling algorithm of <cit.> to the cooperative MU-MIMO scenario with incomplete network state knowledge, and a novel flow control component based on an explicit characterization of an inner bound on the stability region of the system. The proposed algorithm is shown to be optimal with respect to this inner bound on the stability region (Section <ref>). new_text: We also conducted experiments on large-scale character-based language models (LMs) trained using the One Billion Word Benchmark dataset (<cit.>), a widely adopted standard for assessing language model performance. These experiments aimed to evaluate the model's ability to predict the next character in a sequence given a sequence of prior words. To achieve computational efficiency, we leveraged a pre-trained model (<cit.>) designed to process characters as inputs and generate probabilistic predictions for subsequent words. However, since our objective was to predict characters rather than whole words, we modified the model by replacing its final layer with a smaller, custom LSTM architecture. This adjustment enabled the model to sequentially predict characters, one at a time, which is crucial for tasks requiring fine-grained, character-level generation. The revised architecture offers an important advantage: it inherently supports an unbounded vocabulary, meaning it can process and generate any input string without being constrained by a predefined set of word tokens—a limitation common in word-based models. Further technical details about the experimental setup are detailed in Section 5.5 of <cit.>. During training, we observed that deploying 32 synchronized workers resulted in a modest but measurable improvement in performance, achieving a per-word perplexity of below 49. In contrast, training with Async-SGD proved problematic, exhibiting significant instability characterized by occasional surges in training loss. This instability necessitated the use of a substantially reduced learning rate to avoid divergence. Synchronous SGD, on the other hand, demonstrated robustness under higher learning rates—up to 100 times greater than in the Async-SGD setup—without encountering similar issues, highlighting its greater stability for this task.

old_text: Inspired by the index of beauty coefficient <cit.>, we introduce a parameter-free framework to identify two sleeping beauties in each meme diffusion. We demonstrate that the phenomenon of two sleeping beautifies is pervasively existing in diffusion of different memes and time intervals between the two awakening stages follow an exponential distribution. Besides, the second awakening stage generally rises to peak at a higher velocity and thus brings a wider dissemination. Based on these findings, we model the two sleeping beauties through the classical Bass diffusion model and produce promising predictions for the meme diffusion. We disclose a common mechanism beyond meme diffusion in terms of two sleeping beauties and our results will shed lights on revealing the essential rule that drives the popularity dynamics of memes in different media.
new_text: Building upon the index of beauty coefficient <cit.>, we present a parameter-free framework to detect two distinct "sleeping beauty" phases within the diffusion of each meme. Our analysis reveals that this phenomenon is prevalent across the diffusion of various memes, with the temporal gaps between the two awakening stages adhering to an exponential distribution. Furthermore, the secondary awakening phase typically reaches its peak at a faster rate, resulting in broader dissemination compared to the initial phase. Leveraging these insights, we apply the classical Bass diffusion model to simulate the two sleeping beauty dynamics, yielding accurate forecasts of meme diffusion trajectories. By elucidating a shared mechanism underlying this two-stage diffusion pattern, our findings provide insights into uncovering the fundamental principles governing the popularity dynamics of memes across diverse media platforms.

old_text: Robust environment perception is essential for decision-making on robots operating in complex domains. Principled treatment of uncertainty sources in a robot's observation model is necessary for accurate mapping and object detection. This is important not only for low-level observations (e.g., accelerometer data), but for high-level observations such as semantic object labels as well. This paper presents an approach for filtering sequences of object classification probabilities using online modeling of the noise characteristics of the classifier outputs. A hierarchical Bayesian approach is used to model per-class noise distributions, while simultaneously allowing sharing of high-level noise characteristics between classes. The proposed filtering scheme, called Hierarchical Bayesian Noise Inference (HBNI), is shown to outperform classification accuracy of existing methods. The paper also presents real-time filtered classification hardware experiments running fully onboard a moving quadrotor, where the proposed approach is demonstrated to work in a challenging domain where noise-agnostic filtering fails.
new_text: Robust environment perception is critical for autonomous decision-making in robots navigating complex domains. Accurate mapping and object detection require a principled approach to addressing uncertainty sources in a robot’s observation model. Such considerations are vital across all levels of perception, ranging from low-level observations (e.g., accelerometer data) to high-level inferences, such as semantic object labels. This paper introduces a method for filtering sequences of object classification probabilities through online modeling of classifier output noise characteristics. By employing a hierarchical Bayesian framework, the approach models per-class noise distributions while enabling the sharing of high-level noise patterns across classes. The proposed filtering scheme, termed Hierarchical Bayesian Noise Inference (HBNI), demonstrates superior classification accuracy compared to existing methods. The paper further validates the method through real-time onboard experiments on a moving quadrotor, showcasing its effectiveness in challenging environments where noise-agnostic filtering fails.

new_text: Response mechanisms of adblockers against blocking attempts are increasingly sophisticated. Anecdotal evidence suggests the adblocking arms race has progressed to a new stage: certain adblockers now identify anti-adblocking measures and preemptively block them <cit.>. To evaluate this capability, we tested a representative website featuring each anti-adblocking script using AdBlock Plus, Ghostery, and Privacy Badger on the Chrome browser. The experiment was repeated thrice, with Chrome Developer Tools employed to trace all HTTP requests during website loading. A counter-blocking inference was made if requests to retrieve anti-adblocking scripts were entirely omitted. As detailed in Table <ref>, 6 out of 12 anti-adblocking vendors were blocked by at least one adblocker. Ghostery and Privacy Badger neutralized four anti-adblockers each, while AdBlock Plus countered only one. Anti-adblocking scripts from `Taboola` and `Outbrain` were blocked by both Ghostery and Privacy Badger; `PageFair` scripts were blocked by AdBlock Plus and Privacy Badger; and `Doublepimp`, `Ensighten`, and `Cloudflare` scripts were blocked by a single adblocker at most. Notably, undetected anti-adblocking vendors were linked to content delivery, Google advertising services, analytics, or overarching website scripts.

These codes have length N=q^n, where n is the number of steps in the polarization process. When one of these codes is transmitted over a q-ary erasure channel with erasure probability ϵ, its effective channels are q-ary erasure channels and their erasure rate satisfy a closed-form recursion. By analyzing this recursion, we show that , for any γ>0 and δ>0, there is a q_0 such that, for all q≥ q_0, the fraction of effective channels with erasure rate at most O(N^-γ) is at least 1-ϵ-O(N^-1/2+δ). Thus, the gap to capacity scales at a rate very close to the optimal rate of O(N^-1/2).

We believe that the risks of unmanaged sensors on mobile phones, specially through JavaScript code, are not known very well yet. More specifically, many OS/app level solutions such as asking for permissions at the installation time, or malware detection approaches would not work in the context of a web attack.
In our previous work <cit.>, we suggested to apply the same security policies as those for camera, microphone, and GPS for the motion and orientation sensors. Our suggestion was to set a multi-layer access control system on the OS and browser levels. However, the usability and effectiveness of this solution are arguable.
First, asking too many permissions from the user for different sensors might not be usable.
Furthermore, for some basic use cases such as gesture recognition to clear a web form, or adjusting the screen from portrait to landscape, it might not make sense to ask for user permission for every website.
Second, with the increase of the number of sensors accessible through mobile browsers, this approach might not be effective due to the classic problem of sidestepping the security procedure by users when it is too much of a burden <cit.>.
As stated by one of our participants: “I don't mind these sensors being risky anyway. I don't even review the permission list. I have no other choice to be able to use the app”.
Moreover, as we have shown in Section <ref>, users generally do not understand the implications of these sensors on discovering their PINs for example, even though they know how these sensors work. Hence, such an approach might not be effective in practice.

Our earlier work <cit.> proposed applying camera-, microphone-, and GPS-like security policies to motion and orientation sensors using a multi-layer OS/browser access control system. However, its usability and effectiveness are questionable. First, excessive permission requests for sensors hinder usability, especially for common tasks like gesture recognition or screen rotation, where frequent prompts are impractical. Second, as more sensors become browser-accessible, the system’s effectiveness may decline due to user fatigue and workarounds <cit.>. As one participant noted: “I don’t mind these sensors being risky. I ignore permission lists to use apps.” Moreover, as shown in Section <ref>, users often fail to grasp sensor risks (e.g., PIN inference), despite understanding sensor functionality. Thus, this approach may lack practical effectiveness.

In this paper, we presented a context-aware proactive caching algorithm based on contextual multi-armed bandits for cache content placement at a local caching entity in a wireless network.
To cope with unknown and fluctuating content popularity among the permanently changing local user population, the algorithm regularly observes context information of connected users,
updates the cache content and observes the demands for cached content.
Thereby, the algorithm learns context-specific content popularity online over time,
which allows for a proactive adaptation of cache content according to fluctuating local content popularity.
We derived a sub-linear regret bound, which characterizes how fast the algorithm converges to optimal cache content placement and proves that our proposed algorithm asymptotically maximizes the average number of cache hits.
Moreover, the algorithm supports customer prioritization.
Additionally, the algorithm can be combined with multicast transmissions and it can be extended to allow rating-based caching decisions.
Numerical studies showed that by exploiting contextual information, our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in a real world data set.
new_text: We propose a context-aware proactive caching algorithm based on contextual multi-armed bandits for optimizing cache content placement at local caching entities in wireless networks. To address unknown and fluctuating content popularity in dynamic local user populations, the algorithm periodically observes user context, updates cache content, and monitors demand for cached items. This enables online learning of context-specific content popularity, allowing proactive cache adaptation to evolving popularity patterns. The algorithm achieves a sub-linear regret bound, characterizing the rate of convergence to optimal content placement and proving asymptotic maximization of average cache hits. It supports customer prioritization, integrates with multicast transmissions, and extends to rating-based caching decisions. Numerical studies on real-world datasets demonstrate that exploiting contextual information outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms.

For r=1, the round of exchanging the input values, this completes the protocol. In all future rounds, there is an additional step (step 5) of waiting for all messages that are causally prior to the current message to be accepted (and processed), before the current message will be accepted. The content of the message, v, specifies explicitly the set of prior messages we need to wait for. If the sender is correct this will eventually happen at every processor.
If the sender is faulty and claimed to receive messages from a processor that never sent it a message, the waiting for prior messages might not end, and the state machine of that (faulty) sender will practically be blocked at every processor.
However, if any correct will agree to accept the message, eventually everyone will receive all the prior messages and will accept the message.
new_text: In the initial round (r=1), where input values are exchanged, the protocol concludes without requiring additional verification, as there are no prior messages to consider. However, in subsequent rounds, an additional step (step 5) is introduced: before a processor can accept a current message, it must first wait for all messages that are causally necessary for it to be processed (i.e., those that logically precede it in the protocol’s sequence) to be accepted and processed by other processors. The content of each message, denoted by *v*, explicitly lists the set of prior messages that must be confirmed before the current one can proceed. If the sender is correct, this causal dependency is valid, and all processors will eventually process the required prior messages, ensuring the current message is accepted in due course. Conversely, if the sender is faulty and incorrectly claims to have received messages from a processor that never sent them, this dependency check cannot complete, leading to indefinite waiting. As a result, the protocol’s state machine for that (faulty) sender will effectively stall at all processors, preventing progress. However, this situation is mitigated if at least one correct processor agrees to accept the message, as it will propagate and validate the required prior messages. Once those are confirmed, all processors will eventually receive them, allowing the current message to be accepted and maintaining the protocol’s consistency.

Furthermore, the performance gap between low-cost fast methods versus high-accuracy slow methods grows with increasing content length. In conclusion, our results suggest the optimal strategy for time-based data annotation is to minimize per-iteration cost by using multiple questions and running multiple annotation iterations.

We presented our findings
as the first quantification of Aristotle's famous adage: The whole is more than the sum of its parts. In contrast, Scholtes et al. referred to Maximilien Ringelmann, a French agricultural engineer (1861-1931) who discovered the tendency for individual members of a group to become increasingly less productive as the size of their group increases <cit.>. Since Ringelmann, the topic of collective intelligence has interested numbers of researchers in social sciences, as well as practitioners in management aiming at improving the performance of their team. And indeed, in most research and practice case studies, the Ringelmann effect has been found to hold. Our results challenge common wisdom, precisely because the Ringelmann effect has been replicated in countless experiments.
We are glad that the study by Scholtes et al. allows us to explain further our findings by highlighting the
methodological aspects that condition our diverging results. In particular, the definitions of group sizes and measurement
periods are essential to explain the different conclusions. This healthy debate enriches the understanding
on group productivity, in particular in the case of open source software production.
new_text: On December 19, 2015, Scholtes et al. published online in the Journal of Empirical Software Engineering <cit.> challenging our 2014 finding that open source software production exhibits superlinear productive bursts <cit.>. We framed our results as the first quantification of Aristotle’s adage: "The whole is more than the sum of its parts." Scholtes et al., however, cited Ringelmann’s effect—the observation that group productivity declines as group size increases <cit.>—a phenomenon documented since 1861 by French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann. While most empirical studies confirm Ringelmann’s effect, our findings contradict this consensus. The Scholtes et al. critique enables us to clarify methodological differences, particularly in defining group size and measurement periods, critical to divergent conclusions. This debate advances understanding of group productivity, particularly in open source software contexts.

We nevertheless recognize that productivity may be defined in a variety of ways, each with their advantages and shortcomings.
Scholtes et al. considered productivity as production per team (as an aggregate of working developers in large – 295 days – time windows), while we considered productivity as production per developer and per time unit (i.e., over a short time period of 5 days). For instance, Scholtes et al. operationalized productivity as total output per team, aggregating contributions across all working developers within extended periods (specifically, 295-day intervals). In contrast, our approach defines productivity at a more granular level: measuring output per individual developer and per time unit, using a shorter evaluation window of 5 days. While neither definition is without flaws, we argue that our method provides a more detailed perspective on individual performance dynamics. Specifically, this level of granularity enables us to track short-term variations in developer activity, such as the brief but intense productivity surges we observed in our dataset. These transient spikes in engagement are obscured when activity is averaged across teams or over long timeframes, as in Scholtes et al.’s approach. By focusing on individual contributions within compressed windows, our metric retains sensitivity to localized changes in workload or focus that aggregate measures inevitably smooth out.

In existing literature, the semantics of a Probabilistic Argumentation Graph (PrAG) is grounded in the concept of "possible world." A possible world, in this context, is a specific configuration or scenario derived from the PrAG by selecting subsets of its arguments and attacks. For example, consider a PrAG containing *n* arguments (nodes); each argument can either be included or excluded independently in a scenario. This binary choice for each argument leads to up to 2^n possible subgraphs, many of which may have nonzero probabilities depending on the graph’s probability distribution. A subgraph induced by a subset of arguments *A’* ⊆ *A* is formally defined as *G’* = (*A’*, *R’*), where *R’* represents the attacks in the original graph that involve only arguments in *A’*. To simplify notation, the same subgraph can be denoted as *G*↓*A’* or *G^i* (for *i* = 1, 2, 3, …), enabling concise references to specific subgraphs when necessary.  

When analyzing a PrAG under a semantics *σ* (e.g., admissible, conflict-free, preferred, grounded, or stable extensions), the classical argumentation semantics are applied to each subgraph. This involves computing the *σ*-extensions—sets of arguments that satisfy the criteria defined by the semantics—for every possible subgraph. The probability of a particular set of arguments *E* ⊆ *A* being a *σ*-extension, denoted *p(E^σ)*, is then determined by summing the probabilities of all subgraphs in which *E* qualifies as a *σ*-extension.  

This probabilistic aggregation relies on the assumption that the inclusion or exclusion of arguments in a subgraph is independent of one another. That is, the presence of one argument in a scenario does not influence the likelihood of another being included. This independence assumption simplifies the calculation of subgraph probabilities but may not always reflect real-world dependencies, a limitation further discussed in Section 7.1.

We start by a fundamental conceptual remark that illuminates one key difference between the approach of
Scholtes et al. <cit.> and our's <cit.>. Scholtes et al. consider production
in the mean, using as metric the “average output per team member" (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, line 3), and argue
that it increases when synergy effects are present and decreases due to
“communication and coordination overhead” (which surges with larger teams).
In contrast, we argued and demonstrated <cit.> that using an average output is
misleading if not plain wrong in the presence of a highly bursty dynamics characterised by power law tail distributions
with small tail exponents. Indeed, we reported that the distribution of contributions per developer
is heavy-tailed. This empirical fact is also cited by Scholtes et al. and
well-documented in the open source software production literature
and for other open collaboration projects, such as wiki's and Wikipedia <cit.>.
In open collaboration, a few contributors account for a majority of the performed work, whether it is counted in lines of code, commits, files modified, and so on. This is one of the features associated with the fact that the distribution of contributions,
counted in commits or in lines of codes, possesses a power law tail of the form P(X>x) ∼ 1/x^μ with μ < 1 <cit.>. Such distributions are wild <cit.> in the sense that
their two first statistical moments (mean and variance) are undefined and diverge as the sample grows.
For such heavy-tail distributions, reasoning in mean is fundamentally erroneous. For a finite number n
of developers in the project, it is easy to show that the average production scales as ∼ n^1/μ for μ < 1
and ∼ n for μ≥ 1.
Defining productivity as the ratio of the total production by the number n of team members,
this shows that productivity scales as ∼n^1/μ/n = n^1 μ - 1 for μ < 1
and is constant for μ≥ 1. This latter case is the null hypothesis of an approximate
constant output per team member. Superlinear production is quantified by μ < 1, leading to
a growing productivity per team member, the larger the team.
Searching for a superlinear productivity is different from seeking a superlinear production, the former
requiring 1 μ - 1 >1, i.e., μ < 1/2, while the later just needs μ < 1.
In our dataset of 168 projects, we found that only four projects are characterised by μ < 0.5 (while most
obey μ<1).
Scholtes et al. have used a dataset of 58 projects, which implies a ≈ 0.8% chance of finding one project where the average productivity scales superlinearly with the team size. But, as mentioned, the novel non-trivial
discovery that we previously reported <cit.> deals with the superlinear production,
and not superlinear productivity.
new_text: A key conceptual distinction between Scholtes et al. and our approach lies in the metrics used. Scholtes et al. define productivity as average output per team member (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, line 3), arguing it rises with synergy effects and declines due to communication/coordination overhead scaling with team size. Conversely, we demonstrated <cit.> that averages are misleading in systems with bursty dynamics and power-law tail distributions with exponents μ < 1. We showed that contributions per developer are heavy-tailed—confirmed by Scholtes et al. and open-source literature on Wikipedia and wikis <cit.>—with P(X>x) ∼ 1/x^μ (μ < 1) <cit.>. Such distributions lack defined mean and variance, rendering mean-based analysis invalid. For finite teams of size n, total production scales as ∼n^(1/μ) (μ < 1) and ∼n (μ ≥ 1). Productivity (total output/n) scales as ∼n^(1/μ-1) for μ < 1 and remains constant for μ ≥ 1. The latter corresponds to the null hypothesis of constant output per member. Superlinear production (μ < 1) indicates growing productivity per member with team size. Notably, superlinear productivity (1/μ - 1 >1, i.e., μ < 0.5) is rarer than superlinear production (μ <1). In our 168-project dataset, only four exhibited μ < 0.5 (most had μ <1), while Scholtes et al.’s 58-project dataset yielded ~0.8% chance of observing superlinear productivity. Our earlier finding <cit.> of superlinear production remains distinct from, and independent of, superlinear productivity debates.

The collision probability in (<ref>) is always positive due to the uncertainty of the future human position, and we compute a trajectory which is probabilistically guaranteed to be collision-free.
For a given confidence level δ_CL, we compute a trajectory that its probability of collision is upper-bounded by (1 - δ_CL).
If it is unable to find a collision-free trajectory, a new waypoint 𝐪_new is appended next to the last column of 𝐐 to make the robot waits at the last collision-free pose until it finds a collision-free trajectory.
This approach computes a guaranteed collision-free trajectory, but leads to delay, which is fed to the Q-learning algorithm for the MDP task planner.
The higher the delay that the collision-free trajectory of a task has, the less likely the task planner selects the task again.
new_text: The collision probability in (<ref>) remains strictly positive due to inherent uncertainty in predicting the future position of humans, which necessitates a probabilistic approach to safety. To address this, we compute a trajectory that is guaranteed, with a specified confidence level δ_CL, to be collision-free; specifically, the probability of collision along this trajectory is mathematically bounded above by (1 − δ_CL). This ensures robustness against uncertainty while maintaining operational safety. However, in cases where a valid collision-free trajectory cannot be computed within the allowed time, the algorithm appends a new waypoint, q_new, to the trajectory matrix Q. This waypoint instructs the robot to pause at the last verified collision-free pose, allowing additional time to resolve the uncertainty and identify a safe trajectory. While this strategy guarantees safety, it introduces a delay, which is quantified and used as a feedback signal in the Q-learning algorithm governing the MDP-based task planner. The Q-learning framework incorporates this delay as a cost metric, such that tasks associated with higher delays—which reflect greater collision risk or uncertainty—are penalized. Consequently, the task planner reduces the probability of reselecting such tasks, prioritizing alternatives with lower delay and, by extension, lower risk of collision.

We present an efficient method for detecting and localizing anomalies
in videos showing crowded scenes. Research on fully convolutional neural networks (FCNs) has shown the potentials of this technology
for object detection and localization, especially in images. We
investigate how to involve temporal data, and how to transform
a supervised FCN into an unsupervised one
such that the resulting FCN ensures anomaly detection. Altogether,
we propose an FCN-based architecture for anomaly detection
and localization in crowded scenes videos. For reducing computations
and, consequently, improving performance both with respect
to speed and accuracy, we investigate the use of cascaded
out-layer detection. Our architecture includes two main components,
one for feature representation, and one for cascaded out-layer detection.
Experimental results on Subway and UCSD benchmarks
confirm that the detection and
localization accuracy of our method is comparable
to state-of-the-art methods, but at a significantly increased speed of
370 fps.
new_text: We propose an efficient method for detecting and localizing anomalies in videos of crowded scenes. Fully convolutional neural networks (FCNs) have demonstrated their potential for object detection and localization in images. Here, we investigate strategies for incorporating temporal information and transforming a supervised FCN into an unsupervised one, enabling effective anomaly detection. Our approach proposes an FCN-based architecture for anomaly detection and localization in crowded scenes. To reduce computational load and thereby improve performance in both speed and accuracy, we explore cascaded out-layer detection. The architecture comprises two main components: one for feature representation and another for cascaded out-layer detection. Experimental results on the Subway and UCSD benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves detection and localization accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art approaches while attaining a significantly higher speed of 370 fps.

Highway Networks <cit.> were amongst the first architectures that provided a means to effectively train end-to-end networks with more than 100 layers. By introducing the bypassing layers along with gating units, <cit.> showed that Highway Networks with hundreds of layers can be optimized with SGD effectively. The bypassing paths are perhaps the key factor that eases the training of very deep networks. This point is further supported by ResNet <cit.>, in which pure identity mappings are used as bypassing layers. ResNets have achieved impressive (often record breaking) achievements on most challenging image recognition, localization and detection tasks, such as ImageNet and COCO object detection dataset <cit.>. Recently, <cit.> successfully trained a 1202-layer ResNet with stochastic depth <cit.>. Stochastic depth is a mechanism to improve the training of deep residual networks by dropping layers randomly. It also shows that not all layers may be needed and highlights that there is a great amount of redundancy in deep (residual) networks. This paper was in part inspired by this observation. <cit.> introduces ResNets with pre-activation, which similar to stochastic depth allow state-of-the-art performance with > 1000 layers.

In this section we analyze the quality of different layers of
 pre-trained CNN for generating regional feature vectors. As mentioned, adapt a classification CNN to a FCN by just using convolutional layers. Selecting the best layer for
representing the video is important with respect to two different aspects:
(1) Usually the deeper features are more discriminative, but deeper is also
more time-consuming. Also, as the CNN is trained for image classification,
going deeper may create over-fitted features for image classification.
(2) Going deeper leads to larger receptive fields on input data, consequently an increased likelihood of

new_text: This section analyzes the quality of different layers in pre-trained CNNs for generating regional feature vectors. Adapting a classification CNN to a FCN involves retaining only convolutional layers. Selecting the optimal layer for video representation depends on two considerations: (1) Deeper features are more discriminative but computationally expensive; since CNNs are trained for image classification, deeper layers may produce overfitted features for that task. (2) Deeper layers increase receptive field size, thereby raising the risk of inaccurate localization and reduced detection performance.

The adaptive gradient online learning method known as AdaGrad has seen widespread use in the machine learning community in stochastic and adversarial online learning problems and more recently in deep learning methods. The method's full-matrix incarnation offers much better theoretical guarantees and potentially better empirical performance than its diagonal version; however, this version is computationally prohibitive and so the simpler diagonal version often is used in practice. We introduce a new method, CompAdaGrad, that navigates the space between these two schemes and show that this method can yield results much better than diagonal AdaGrad while avoiding the (effectively intractable) O(n^3) computational complexity of full-matrix AdaGrad for dimension n. CompAdaGrad essentially performs full-matrix regularization in a low-dimensional subspace while performing diagonal regularization in the complementary subspace. We derive CompAdaGrad's updates for composite mirror descent in case of the squared ℓ_2 norm and the ℓ_1 norm, demonstrate that its complexity per iteration is linear in the dimension, and establish guarantees for the method independent of the choice of composite regularizer. Finally, we show preliminary results on several datasets.
new_text: AdaGrad, an adaptive gradient method, is widely used in stochastic and adversarial online learning, as well as deep learning. While the full-matrix variant provides stronger theoretical guarantees and potential performance gains, its O(n³) computational complexity makes it impractical, leading to reliance on the simpler diagonal version. We propose CompAdaGrad, an intermediate approach that combines full-matrix regularization in a low-dimensional subspace with diagonal regularization in the complementary subspace. This method achieves performance surpassing diagonal AdaGrad while avoiding the intractable cost of the full-matrix variant. We derive CompAdaGrad updates for composite mirror descent under the squared ℓ₂ norm and ℓ₁ norm, show linear per-iteration complexity in the dimension, and establish regularizer-independent guarantees. Preliminary results across multiple datasets demonstrate its effectiveness.

Recent approaches often prioritize low-level features such as histograms of gradients (HoG) or histograms of optic flow (HoF) to model spatio-temporal properties in video data. Trajectory-based methods struggle with occlusion scenarios and exhibit high computational complexity in crowded scenes. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), widely adopted in computer vision, have achieved state-of-the-art results in tasks including image classification <cit.>, object detection <cit.>, and activity recognition <cit.>. However, it is argued that handcrafted features are insufficient for efficiently representing normal video content <cit.>. Notably, CNNs are computationally expensive, particularly when applied block-wise <cit.>. Dividing video sequences into patches and processing them via CNNs necessitates further investigation into potential speed-up techniques. Key challenges in applying CNNs to anomaly detection include: (1) the computational burden of patch-based methods; (2) the reliance on fully supervised training, which is incompatible with real-world settings where anomaly classes are typically absent in training data; and (3) the time-intensive nature of training even small CNNs. To address these limitations, researchers have explored strategies from related domains. For instance, object detection frameworks like Faster-RCNN <cit.> employ convolutional layers to generate feature maps for all regions of input data. Similarly, semantic segmentation methods, such as <cit.>, utilize fully convolutional networks (FCNs) to transform traditional CNNs into regional feature extractors, thereby reducing computational costs. While traditional CNNs are not well-suited for direct use in anomaly detection, adapting them as FCNs offers a viable alternative. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel FCN architecture for extracting discriminative features from video regions. Our FCN integrates the initial convolutional layers of a pre-trained CNN with an additional convolutional layer. The pre-trained CNN, modeled after AlexNet <cit.> [A version of the AlexNet model is available on [URL]; similar to the network in <cit.>], was trained on ImageNet <cit.> and the MIT Places dataset <cit.> for image classification. We found the features extracted from its convolutional layers provide sufficient discriminative power for video anomaly detection. Unlike patch-based methods, which first decompose video frames into discrete patches and process them individually for feature extraction, our FCN-based approach enables more efficient regional analysis.

old_text: The proposed approach for transfer from simulated to real robot domains is based on a progressive network with some specific changes. First, the columns of a progressive net do not need to have identical capacity or structure, and this can be an advantage in sim-to-real situations. Thus, the simulation-trained column is designed to have sufficient capacity and depth to learn the task from scratch, but the robot-trained columns have minimal capacity, to encourage fast learning and limit total parameter growth. Secondly, the layer-wise adapters proposed for progressive nets are unnecessary for the output layers of complementary sequences of tasks, so they are not used. Third, the output layer of the robot-trained column is initialised from the simulation-trained column in order to improve exploration. These architectural features are shown in Fig. <ref>.
new_text: The proposed approach for transferring learning from simulated to real robot domains leverages a progressive network with three key modifications. First, columns within a progressive network do not require identical capacity or structure, offering advantages in sim-to-real settings. The simulation-trained column is designed with sufficient capacity and depth to learn the task de novo, while robot-trained columns employ minimal capacity to facilitate rapid learning and constrain overall parameter proliferation. Second, since layer-wise adapters—typically proposed for progressive networks—are unnecessary for the output layers of complementary task sequences, they are omitted. Third, to enhance exploration, the output layer of the robot-trained column is initialized using the simulation-trained column’s parameters. These architectural adaptations are illustrated in Fig. <ref>.

section: Game Models for Resource Allocation in Code-Domain NOMA
old_text: To alleviate network congestion, reduce collisions, and improve fairness, an efficient distributed medium access protocol is necessary to share the radio resources efficiently. To this end, game theory is a proper tool used to design the distributed protocols for CD-NOMA networks. The contention based MAC can be formulated by a random access game, in which the multiple mobile users want to maximize their utilities individually by sharing a common channel. A selfish user typically waits for a smaller backoff interval to increase its chance of accessing the medium, which hence may reduce the channel access chance of those well behaved users. The difference with traditional carrier sense multiple access protocols is to also consider the selection of the proper frequency segment and the spreading sequence for users to get access, which can improve the connectivity possibility. The resource allocation problems in this scheme involve contention window length adjustment, power control, and subcarrier allocation, etc.

To this end, game theory serves as an appropriate tool for designing distributed protocols in CD-NOMA networks. Contention-based MAC can be formulated as a random access game in which multiple mobile users seek to maximize their individual utilities by sharing a common channel. A selfish user typically waits for a shorter backoff interval to increase its chance of accessing the medium, which in turn may reduce the channel access opportunity for well-behaved users. The difference from traditional carrier sense multiple access protocols lies in also considering the selection of an appropriate frequency segment and spreading sequence for users to access the channel, which can improve connectivity probability. The resource allocation challenges in this scheme involve contention window length adjustment, power control, and subcarrier allocation, among others.

section: Game Models for Resource Allocation in Code-Domain NOMA
old_text: Consider a downlink single-cell CD-NOMA network as shown in Fig. <ref>, in which a set of mobile users, denoted by N = {1, ⋯ ,N}, communicate with a single BS. The BS divides the available bandwidth into a set of subcarriers, denoted by K_SC = {1, ⋯ ,K}. There are J codebooks assigned by the BS to the users, and each user is characterized by a codebook, which contains M sparse codewords of length K. At the transmitter, bit streams of each user with length of log_2M bits are directly mapped to different sparse codewords of the corresponding codebook, in which the codewords are generated through a multi-dimensional constellation. After the data stream of each user is mapped to a sparse codeword, different CD-NOMA codewords are multiplexed over K shared subcarriers. The objective of system design is to maximize the total sum-rate of the system through optimally allocating subcarrier to the users. This optimization problem can be formulated as a many-to-many two-sided matching problem, which can be solved by utilizing the matching theory <cit.>.

This paper is inspired in DPCNs but substitutes the top down inference step in DPCN by a recurrent
convolutional encoder-decoder that predicts the next frame of the video, can be trained with backpropagation,
and does simples recall in test phase. The paper consists of three main contributions.
First, we evolved the self-organizing object recognition in video work of
Chalasani and Principe <cit.><cit.> by developing a scalable

new_text: This paper draws inspiration from Deep Predictive Coding Networks (DPCNs) but introduces a key modification: it replaces the top-down inference mechanism in DPCNs with a recurrent convolutional encoder-decoder architecture. This encoder-decoder framework is designed to predict the next frame in a video sequence, is trained using backpropagation, and performs a simplified recall process during testing. The paper presents three main contributions. First, it advances the work on self-organizing object recognition in video by Chalasani and Principe <cit.><cit.>, proposing a scalable counterpart to the original DPCN architecture and its associated algorithms. This adaptation retains the core principles of DPCNs while enhancing scalability for practical applications. Second, the authors integrate recent advancements in two emerging areas: convolutional winner-take-all autoencoders <cit.> and convolutional-recurrent neural networks <cit.><cit.>. By adapting winner-take-all autoencoders to handle temporal data, the approach extends their utility beyond static image domains. The paper demonstrates improvements in tasks such as video prediction, object recognition, and action recognition. Third, the authors address the findings of Luong et al. <cit.>, who showed that recurrent neural networks benefit from unsupervised pre-training and multi-task learning. The proposed method demonstrates how the recurrent encoder-decoder can function as a pre-training strategy for initializing convolutional RNNs, potentially improving their performance on downstream tasks.
