With the rapid growth of the Internet-of-Things (IoT), concerns about the security of IoT devices have become prominent. Several vendors are producing IP-connected devices for home and small office networks that often suffer from flawed security designs and implementations. They also tend to lack mechanisms for firmware updates or patches that can help eliminate security vulnerabilities. Securing networks where the presence of such vulnerable devices is given, requires a brownfield approach: applying necessary protection measures within the network so that potentially vulnerable devices can coexist without endangering the security of other devices in the same network.
In this paper, we present IoT Sentinel, a system capable of automatically identifying the types of devices being connected to an IoT network and enabling enforcement of rules for constraining the communications of vulnerable devices so as to minimize damage resulting from their compromise. We show that IoT Sentinel is effective in identifying device types and has minimal performance overhead.
new_text: As the Internet of Things (IoT) continues to expand rapidly, security concerns have come to the forefront. Numerous manufacturers are developing IP-connected devices for residential and small business networks, which frequently exhibit inadequate security architectures and flawed implementations. These devices often lack built-in mechanisms for firmware updates or patches, preventing timely mitigation of vulnerabilities. Mitigation strategies in such environments require a brownfield approach: implementing security measures at the network level to enable potentially compromised devices to coexist without jeopardizing the rest of the network. This paper introduces IoT Sentinel, a system designed to automatically classify connected devices and enforce communication policies that restrict vulnerable devices, thereby reducing potential impact from compromises. Experimental results demonstrate its accuracy in device identification and its low computational overhead.

Gini coefficient of transition counts.
The previous analyses have suggested a discrepancy between the link network D_wikiand actually transitioned links in D_transand D_trans_w.
The Gini coefficient is a measure of statistical dispersion allowing us to quantify the inequality of link popularity within articles. We calculate the Gini coefficient for each article based on a vector containing the transition counts for all links (including zeros) in this article from D_trans_w. A Gini coefficient of 0 indicates complete equality, while a result of 1 would mean that only a single link gets the whole attention. We visualize the histogram of all coefficients for each article in Figure <ref>; results indicate that there is a clear inequality of link popularity within articles, i.e., attention focuses on just a few links.
new_text: The Gini coefficient of transition counts provides insight into the disparity between theoretical link structures and actual user navigation patterns. Prior analyses revealed inconsistencies between the static link network in D_wiki and the dynamic transition data in D_trans and D_trans_w, suggesting users do not uniformly follow available links. To quantify this disparity, we apply the Gini coefficient, a statistical measure of inequality. Originally developed to assess income distribution, the Gini coefficient here evaluates how evenly attention is distributed among hyperlinks within articles. Specifically, for each article, we compute the Gini coefficient by analyzing a vector of transition counts derived from D_trans_w, including all links—even those with zero transitions. A Gini coefficient of 0 would imply all links receive equal attention, whereas a coefficient of 1 indicates extreme concentration, with nearly all attention directed to a single link. By calculating this metric for every article, we observe a systematic skew: most articles exhibit high Gini coefficients, confirming that user attention is disproportionately focused on a small subset of links. The histogram in Figure <ref> visualizes this distribution, demonstrating that inequality in link popularity is not an isolated phenomenon but a widespread characteristic of the dataset. This result reinforces the importance of distinguishing between the structure of hyperlinks and the actual pathways users follow.

old_text: Recently, it has been shown that in a cache-enabled interference channel, the storage at the transmit and receive sides are of equal value in terms of Degrees of Freedom (DoF). This is derived by assuming full Channel State Information at the Transmitter (CSIT). In this paper, we consider a more practical scenario, where a training/feedback phase should exist for obtaining CSIT, during which instantaneous channel state is not known to the transmitters. This results in a combination of delayed and current CSIT availability, called mixed CSIT. In this setup, we derive DoF of a cache-enabled interference channel with mixed CSIT, which depends on the memory available at transmit and receive sides as well as the training/feedback phase duration. In contrast to the case of having full CSIT, we prove that, in our setup, the storage at the receive side is more valuable than the one at the transmit side. This is due to the fact that cooperation opportunities granted by transmitters' caches are strongly based on instantaneous CSIT availability. However, multi-casting opportunities provided by receivers' caches are robust to such imperfection.
new_text: It was recently shown that in a cache-enabled interference channel, transmit and receive storage are equally valuable in terms of Degrees of Freedom (DoF) under full Channel State Information at the Transmitter (CSIT). This work considers a more practical scenario requiring a training/feedback phase to obtain CSIT, where transmitters lack instantaneous channel knowledge, resulting in mixed CSIT (a combination of delayed and current). We derive the DoF of a cache-enabled interference channel under mixed CSIT, which depends on transmit/receive memory sizes and the training duration. In contrast to full CSIT scenarios, receive-side storage proves more valuable than transmit-side storage. This is because cooperative transmission via transmit-side caches requires instantaneous CSIT, whereas multicast opportunities via receive-side caches remain robust to CSIT imperfections.

Our aim here is to minimize the total insertion time in cuckoo hashing, thereby minimizing the total time required to construct the hash table. We propose a deterministic strategy of how to select a vertex for placing an item when all its choices are occupied.
We assign to each vertex v_i∈ V an integer label, L(v_i). Initially all vertices have 0 as their labels. Note that at this stage, for all j∈ [n], L(v_j) =d(v_j,F), i.e., the labels of all vertices represent their shortest distances from F. When an item x appears, it chooses the vertex with the least label from among its k choices. If the vertex is free, the item is placed on it. Otherwise, the previous item is kicked out. The label of the location is then updated and set to one more than the minimum label of the remaining k-1 choices of the item x. The kicked out item chooses the location with minimum label from its k choices and the above procedure is repeated till an empty location is found.
Note that to maintain the labels of the vertices as their shortest distances from F we would require to update labels of the neighbors of the affected vertex and the labels of their neighbors and so on. This corresponds to performing a breadth first search (bfs) starting from the affected vertex. We avoid the bfs and perform only local updations. Therefore, we also call our method as local search allocation.

Tree hash constructions appear to be a good way to utilize SIMD instructions.
However, the SipHash add-rotate-XOR construction is not ideally suited for
current instruction sets.
As previously mentioned, bit rotations must be implemented by ORing together
the result of left and right shifts. Although rotations of multiples of 8 bits
can be implemented with very fast byte permute instructions, this would weaken
SipHash to an unacceptable degree <cit.>.
The individual add and XOR instructions also only achieve a weak mixing effect.
By contrast, AVX2 includes 32 × 32 bit multiplication instructions that
mix their operands much more thoroughly. Although their latency is higher than
non-SIMD multiplies (5 vs 3 cycles <cit.>), we believe the increase in
mixing efficiency vs. add/XOR is still worthwhile. The 64-bit Intel
architecture also provides 16 SIMD registers, which is enough to perform two
multiplies in parallel and thus hide some of the latency. Given that
multiplications are efficient, we now propose a new permutation step for
strong hashing.
new_text: Tree hash constructions offer an effective approach for leveraging SIMD instructions. However, the SipHash add-rotate-XOR construction is not optimally suited for current instruction sets. Specifically, bit rotations require combining the results of left and right shifts via OR operations, which introduces inefficiencies. While byte permute instructions can accelerate rotations for multiples of 8 bits, doing so would compromise SipHash’s security to an unacceptable degree <cit.>. Furthermore, the individual add and XOR instructions achieve only limited mixing effectiveness. In contrast, AVX2 incorporates 32 × 32 bit multiplication operations that thoroughly mix their operands. While these multiplications have higher latency compared to non-SIMD counterparts (5 versus 3 cycles <cit.>), the improved mixing efficiency still justifies the tradeoff. The 64-bit Intel architecture provides 16 SIMD registers, sufficient to execute two multiplies in parallel, thereby mitigating some of the latency. Given these advantages, we propose a revised permutation step tailored for robust hashing via multiplication-based operations.

We presented an optimization formulation for device-to-device networks in terms of SIR and coverage probability. We showed that if we wish to maximize the device spatial throughput of such a network, then the optimal proportion of active devices is given by a simple formula, serving as a useful guide. These results suggest that the price for allowing device-to-device communication is potentially high in terms of device-to-base-station coverage, but further further investigation is needed. A key step in our results is introducing the interference of other Poisson networks easily into our SIR expressions, which gives another way to model heterogeneous networks with closed and open access.

new_text: This study introduces an optimization framework for device-to-device (D2D) networks based on signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) and coverage probability metrics. It demonstrates that maximizing spatial throughput in such networks requires an optimal active device ratio defined by a closed-form expression, offering practical design insights. The findings highlight a potential trade-off between D2D communication gains and degradation in device-to-base-station coverage, though further study is necessary. A core contribution lies in accounting for interference from other Poisson-distributed networks in SIR calculations, enabling a novel modeling approach for heterogeneous networks with mixed closed and open access policies. These outcomes reaffirm the analytical advantages of Poisson network models. Future work should validate these theoretical results through simulations and experiments, as well as explore protocols to mitigate coverage loss in hybrid D2D-cellular environments.

Maximizing performance on modern CPUs usually requires the use of
SIMD instructions. These apply the same operation (e.g. addition) to
multiple `lanes' (elements) of a vector. This works best for data-parallel
problems. However, the SipHash dependency chain offers limited parallelism and
cannot fully utilize the four AVX2 vector lanes.
Our SIMD implementation was actually slower than the scalar version,
presumably because of the lack of bit rotation instructions. We instead
compute four independent hash results by
logically partitioning input buffers into interleaved 64-bit pieces.
For example, consider a 64 byte input interpreted as eight 64-bit words:
A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3, B_0, B_1, B_2, B_3. These can be combined into four
hash results with two updates, one with A_i and the other with B_i.
We must then fold the four results into a single hash. XOR reduction is
unsuitable because it cannot distinguish between permutations of the
64-bit words. Instead, we can just hash the results. This is known as a
tree-hash construction and has been used to accelerate SHA-256 <cit.>.
new_text: Maximizing performance on modern CPUs typically requires leveraging SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions, which enable parallel execution of the same operation across multiple data elements, or "lanes," within a vector. This approach is particularly effective for data-parallel tasks, where operations on independent data elements can be executed simultaneously. However, the SipHash algorithm presents a challenge due to its inherently sequential dependency chain, where each computation step depends on the previous one, leaving little opportunity for parallel execution. As a result, even with AVX2's four vector lanes, the potential for parallelism is severely constrained. This limitation becomes critical in practice: our initial SIMD implementation for SipHash proved slower than the scalar version, likely because AVX2 lacks dedicated bit rotation instructions—a key operation in SipHash that serializes computations across lanes. To address this, we adopted an alternative strategy: partitioning input buffers into interleaved 64-bit segments and processing each partition independently. For instance, a 64-byte input (eight 64-bit words) could be divided into two groups—A_0 to A_3 and B_0 to B_3—and used to compute four separate hash results through two sequential updates (one per group). After obtaining these four outputs, we faced the problem of combining them into a single hash. A simple XOR reduction would fail to preserve input order, as it produces the same result regardless of the arrangement of 64-bit words. Instead, we opted to hash the four results hierarchically using a "tree-hash" method. This approach, inspired by techniques in SHA-256 acceleration <cit.>, ensures that the final hash reflects both the individual components and their order by recursively hashing sub-results until a single output remains.

Specifically, given N training 3D poses—each represented as a (3 × L) matrix P_i containing the 3D coordinates of L human joints—our goal is to estimate four key components simultaneously. First, we compute a global average 3D pose, denoted by μ, which serves as a central reference configuration. Second, we derive a set of J orthonormal basis matrices (e). These matrices, when converted into vectors, must be unit-norm and mutually orthogonal, forming a structured, low-dimensional representation of pose variations. Third, we estimate the noise variance σ, which quantifies the uncertainty in the data. Finally, we determine per-sample parameters: rotation matrices R_i to align each pose to the average, and basis coefficients a_i that describe how each individual pose deviates from the mean. Together, these variables are optimized to minimize a specific cost function, ensuring that the reconstructed poses align as closely as possible with the observed data while maintaining the desired mathematical constraints.

As discussed in <cit.>, the computing environments in virtualized data centers are heterogeneous and algorithms based on homogeneous assumptions can result in significant performance reduction. In this paper, we focus on general heterogeneous distributed computing clusters consisting of a variety of computing machines with different capabilities. Specifically, we propose a coding framework for speeding up distributed matrix multiplication in heterogeneous clusters with straggling servers, named Heterogeneous Coded Matrix Multiplication (HCMM). Matrix multiplication is a crucial computation in many engineering and scientific disciplines. In particular, it is a fundamental component of many popular machine learning algorithms such as logistic regression, reinforcement learning and gradient descent based algorithms. Implementations that speed up matrix multiplication would naturally speed up the execution of a wide variety of popular algorithms. Therefore, we envision HCMM to play a fundamental role in speeding up big data analytics in virtualized data centers by leveraging the wide range of computing capabilities provided by these heterogeneous environments.
new_text: Prior coded computing approaches target homogeneous clusters. As discussed in <cit.>, virtualized data centers feature inherently heterogeneous environments, and algorithms designed under homogeneous assumptions often incur substantial performance losses. This work addresses general-purpose heterogeneous distributed computing clusters composed of diverse computing resources with varying capabilities. Specifically, we introduce Heterogeneous Coded Matrix Multiplication (HCMM), a novel coding framework that accelerates distributed matrix multiplication in heterogeneous clusters with straggling servers. Matrix multiplication serves as a fundamental operation in numerous engineering and scientific domains, forming the core of widely used machine learning algorithms including logistic regression, reinforcement learning, and gradient descent-based methods. Accelerating matrix multiplication inherently accelerates the execution of these algorithms. Consequently, we position HCMM as a key enabler for optimizing big data analytics in virtualized data centers by effectively harnessing the diverse computing capabilities of heterogeneous environments.

In this paper, we study the CTVM problem, aiming to optimally solve the problem. We first highlight that using a traditional two stage stochastic programming to exactly solve CTVM is not possible because of scalability. We then propose an almost exact algorithm TipTop, which has an approximation ratio of (1 - ϵ). This result significantly improves the current best solutions to both IM and CTVM. At the heart of TipTop lies an innovative technique that reduces the number of samples as much as possible. This allows us to exactly solve CTVM on a much smaller space of generated samples using Integer Programming. While obtaining an almost exact solution, TipTop is very scalable, running on billion-scale networks such as Twitter under three hours. Furthermore, TipTop lends a tool for researchers to benchmark their solutions against the optimal one in large-scale networks, which is currently not available.
new_text: In this paper, we study the CTVM problem, aiming to find an optimal solution to it. We first note that solving CTVM exactly using a traditional two-stage stochastic programming approach is infeasible due to scalability limitations. We propose an algorithm called TipTop, which achieves an approximation ratio of (1 - ϵ). This result significantly improves upon the best existing solutions for IM and CTVM. At the heart of TipTop is an innovative technique that minimizes the number of required samples. This allows us to solve CTVM exactly in a much reduced sample space using integer programming. While producing an almost exact solution, TipTop is highly scalable, handling billion-scale networks such as Twitter within three hours. Furthermore, TipTop provides a tool for researchers to benchmark their solutions against the optimal one in large-scale networks, which are currently unavailable.

Unfortunately, obtaining exact solutions to CTVM (and thus to IM) is very challenging as the running time is no longer in polynomial time. Due to the nature of the problem, stochastic programming (SP) is a viable approach for optimization under uncertainty when the probability distribution governs the data is given <cit.>. However traditional SP-based solutions to various problems in NP-hard class are only for small networks with a few hundreds nodes <cit.>. Thus directly applying existing techniques to IM and CTVM is not suitable as OSNs consist of millions of users and billions of edges. Furthermore, the theory developed to assess the solution quality such as those in <cit.>, and the references therein, only provide approximate confidence interval. Therefore, sufficiently large samples are needed to justify the quality assessment. This requires us to develop novel stochastic programming techniques to exactly solve CTVM on large-scale networks.
new_text: Exact solutions to CTVM (and thus to IM) are intractable due to superpolynomial running time. Stochastic programming (SP) is a viable approach for optimization under uncertainty when the probability distribution is known <cit.>. However, traditional SP-based solutions for problems in the NP-hard class are limited to small networks with a few hundred nodes <cit.>. Applying these techniques to IM and CTVM is inapplicable, as online social networks (OSNs) contain millions of users and billions of edges. Existing theories for solution quality assessment, such as those in <cit.> and references therein, only provide approximate confidence intervals. Hence, sufficiently large samples are required to justify these assessments, necessitating novel SP techniques to exactly solve CTVM on large-scale networks.

We show that the task of question answering (QA) can significantly benefit from the transfer learning of models trained on a different large, fine-grained QA dataset.
  We achieve the state of the art in two well-studied QA datasets, WikiQA and SemEval-2016 (Task 3A), through a basic transfer learning technique from SQuAD.
  For WikiQA, our model outperforms the previous best model by more than 8%.
  We demonstrate that finer supervision provides better guidance for learning lexical and syntactic information than coarser supervision, through quantitative results and visual analysis.
  We also show that a similar transfer learning procedure achieves the state of the art on an entailment task.
new_text: We demonstrate the potential benefits of transfer learning using models trained on a distinct, large, fine-grained QA dataset. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on two widely studied QA datasets, WikiQA and SemEval-2016 (Task 3A), using a basic transfer learning approach from SQuAD. For WikiQA, our model outperforms the previous best model by more than 8%. Quantitative results and visual analysis demonstrate that finer-grained supervision provides more effective guidance in learning lexical and syntactic information than coarser supervision. Additionally, a similar transfer learning procedure achieves state-of-the-art performance on an entailment task.

old_text: A QCOMP emulator/simulator is basically an analogue machine: an engineered qubit-array where the interactions between qubits (memory cells) are implemented by substrate-defined or externally induced local and global couplings. The static or quasi-static (adiabatic) interactions can be tuned to implement specific Hamiltonians describing physical models or systems (or even something unphysical), and time-dependent driving will implement dynamic response. All the interactions provide together an effective time-dependent Hamiltonian and a corresponding time-evolution operator U = exp[-iH_eff(t) t ]. The induced time-evolution will be characteristic for the system and can be analysed (measured) to provide deterministic or statistical answers to various questions. Note that there is no fundamental difference between digital and analogue QCOMP: if we drive the qubits by, e.g., fast external microwave pulse trains, we can design the time-evolution operator U to generate the specific elementary universal 1q and 2q gates of the quantum circuit model.

Vector CiM operations. Many modern computing workloads exhibit significant data parallelism.
To further enhance the efficiency of STT-CiM for such applications, we introduce Vector Compute-in-Memory (VCiM) operations. The key idea behind VCiM operations is to exploit the internal memory bandwidth to perform CiM operations on the elements of a vector simultaneously. Figure <ref> shows how the internal memory bandwidth (32xN bits) can be significantly larger than the limited I/O bandwidth (32 bits) visible to the processor. We exploit this internal bandwidth to perform vector operations (N words wide) within STT-CiM. However, the computed vector cannot be directly transferred to processor in one access due to I/O limitations. To address this issue, we leverage the reduction computation patterns commonly observed in several applications and introduce a Reduce Unit (RU) shown in Figure <ref>. The RU takes an array of data elements as inputs and reduces it to a single data element. A reduce unit can support various reduction operations such as summation, zero-compare (shown in Table <ref>). The overheads of the RU depend on two factors: (i) the number of different reduction operations supported, and (ii) the maximum vector length allowed (can be between 2 to N words). In our evaluation, we have included the timing and area overheads associated with the proposed RU. To limit the area overheads, we support two reduction operations, i.e., summation and zero-compare, and evaluate our design for vector lengths of 4 and 8. Consider an example VCiM operation which computes ∑_i=1^N A[i] + B[i], where arrays A and B are stored in rows i and j respectively (shown in Figure <ref>). To compute the desired function using VCiM operation, we activate rows i and j simultaneously, and configure the sensing circuitry to perform an ADD operation and the RU to perform accumulation of the resulting output. Note that the summation would require 2N memory accesses in a conventional memory. With STT-CiM (but not the proposed vector operations) it requires N memory accesses. With the proposed VCiM operations, only a single memory access is required.
new_text: Vector Compute-in-Memory (VCiM) operations exploit internal memory bandwidth to perform simultaneous CiM operations on vector elements. Modern computing workloads exhibit significant data parallelism, motivating enhanced efficiency for STT-CiM in such applications. The internal bandwidth (32×N bits) is substantially larger than the visible I/O bandwidth (32 bits), enabling N-word-wide vector operations within STT-CiM (Figure <ref>). However, I/O limitations prevent direct single-access transfer of computed vectors to the processor. To overcome this, we introduce a Reduce Unit (RU) (Figure <ref>) that reduces arrays to single elements via operations like summation and zero-compare (Table <ref>). RU overheads depend on supported reduction types and maximum vector lengths (2–N). We evaluate timing and area overheads for RU designs supporting two operations (summation, zero-compare) and vector lengths of 4 and 8. For example, computing ∑<sub>i=1</sub><sup>N</sup> A[i] + B[i]—where A and B reside in rows i and j (Figure <ref>)—requires 2N accesses in conventional memory, N with STT-CiM, and a single access with VCiM. This is achieved by activating rows i and j while configuring sensing circuits for ADD and the RU for accumulation.

new_text: We categorize the 20 object classes into symmetry-available and symmetry-unavailable groups, as illustrated in Fig. <ref>. Of these, 31.3% contain multiple objects, and 45.6% exhibit partial invisibility of object parts, reflecting the complexity of real-world scenes.

For this reason, A/B tests are of widespread use, where the new policy to be evaluated is fielded to a subsample of the user population. Unfortunately, A/B tests come with two drawbacks. First, they can be detrimental to the user experience if the new policy to be evaluated performs poorly. Second, the number of new policies that can be evaluated in a given amount of time is limited, simply because each A/B test needs to be run on a certain fraction of the overall traffic and should ideally span any cycles (e.g. weekly patterns) in user behavior.

Communication complexity and query complexity are two concrete models of computation which are very well studied. In the communication model there are two parties Alice, with input x and Bob, with input y, and they wish to compute a joint function f(x,y) of their inputs. In the query model one party Alice tries to compute a function f(x) by querying bits of a database string x. There is a natural way in which a query protocol can be viewed as a communication protocol between Alice, with no input, and Bob, with input x, in which the only communication allowed is queries to the bits of x and answers to these queries. Given this, we can (informally) view the query model as a “simpler” sub-model of the communication model. Indeed several results in query complexity are easier to argue and obtain than the corresponding results in communication complexity. One interesting technique that is often employed with great success is to first show a result in the query model and then “lift” it to a result in the communication model via some “lifting theorem”.

To reduce data collection time for deep learning of robust robotic grasp plans, we explore training from a synthetic dataset of 6.7 million point clouds, grasps, and robust analytic grasp metrics generated from thousands of 3D models from Dex-Net 1.0 in randomized poses on a table.
We use the resulting dataset, Dex-Net 2.0, to train a Grasp Quality Convolutional Neural Network (GQ-CNN) model that rapidly classifies grasps as robust from depth images and the position, angle, and height of the gripper above a table.
Experiments with over 1,000 trials on an ABB YuMi comparing grasp planning methods on singulated objects suggest that a GQ-CNN trained with only synthetic data from Dex-Net 2.0 can be used to plan grasps in 0.8s with a success rate of 93% on eight known objects with adversarial geometry and is 3× faster than registering point clouds to a precomputed dataset of objects and indexing grasps.
The GQ-CNN is also the highest performing method on a dataset of ten novel household objects, with zero false positives out of 29 grasps classified as robust and a 1.5× higher success rate than a point cloud registration method.
new_text: To minimize the time required for data collection in deep learning-based robotic grasp planning, we developed a synthetic dataset comprising 6.7 million point clouds, grasps, and analytically computed robustness metrics derived from thousands of 3D models from Dex-Net 1.0, randomized in table-top configurations. This dataset, labeled Dex-Net 2.0, was used to train a Grasp Quality Convolutional Neural Network (GQ-CNN) capable of rapidly classifying grasps as robust using depth images and the gripper’s position, orientation, and height relative to a surface. Evaluations involving over 1,000 trials on an ABB YuMi robot demonstrated that a GQ-CNN trained solely on synthetic data from Dex-Net 2.0 achieves a 93% success rate for eight objects with adversarial geometries, planning grasps in 0.8s—3× faster than point cloud registration to precomputed object datasets followed by grasp indexing. Furthermore, the GQ-CNN outperformed alternative methods on ten previously unseen household objects, achieving zero false positives among 29 classified robust grasps and a 1.5× higher success rate than point cloud registration approaches.

If the mind is the result of the computation of the brain, there is nothing that prevents the creation of a mind, and thus everything that may derive from it, from general-purpose intelligence to consciousness itself. new_text: The nature of intelligence remains an open question. If the mind arises from the computational processes of the brain, then, in principle, there is no obstacle to creating a mind—and with it, phenomena ranging from general-purpose intelligence to consciousness itself. What is increasingly evident is that humans have partnered with computers to reprogram matter and life, and our ability to describe or explain ourselves is now inextricably linked to computational tools. Computers surpass human capabilities in executing calculations and performing tasks, achieving outcomes that far exceed what we can accomplish independently.

old_text: Multiple object detection in wide area aerial videos, has drawn the attention of the computer vision research community for a number of years. A novel framework is proposed in this paper using a fully convolutional deep neural network, which is able to detect all objects simultaneously for a given region of interest. The network is designed to accept multiple video frames at a time as the input and yields detection results for all objects in the temporally center frame. This multi-frame approach yield far better results than its single frame counterpart. Additionally, the proposed method can detect vehicles which are slowing, stopped, and/or partially or fully occluded during some frames, which cannot be handled by nearly all state-of-the-art methods. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of a multiple-frame, fully convolutional deep model for detecting multiple small objects and the only framework which can detect stopped and temporarily occluded vehicles, for aerial videos. The proposed network exceeds state-of-the-art results significantly on WPAFB 2009 dataset.
new_text: Multiple object detection in wide-area aerial video analysis has become a critical focus within computer vision research over the past decade. This paper introduces a novel framework based on a fully convolutional deep neural network, designed to simultaneously detect multiple objects within a defined region of interest. Unlike traditional methods that analyze individual video frames independently, the proposed architecture processes multiple sequential frames as input, enabling the network to leverage temporal context. This approach produces detection outputs specifically for the central frame within the input sequence, allowing the model to infer object positions and states by analyzing motion patterns across adjacent frames. The multi-frame processing strategy significantly outperforms single-frame detection techniques, as demonstrated through rigorous evaluation. Critically, the framework addresses limitations of existing methods by detecting vehicles that are stationary, moving slowly, or experiencing partial/full occlusion across certain frames—scenarios where most state-of-the-art systems fail due to their inability to maintain contextual information across time. By integrating temporal data with spatial feature extraction, the network achieves robust performance in challenging conditions. To date, no prior work has successfully combined a fully convolutional deep learning model with multi-frame analysis for aerial small-object detection, particularly for tracking stopped or temporarily occluded vehicles in wide-area surveillance. The proposed method achieves a substantial improvement in detection accuracy compared to existing solutions, as validated by experimental results on the WPAFB 2009 dataset.

new_text: In most publicly available aerial video datasets—such as the WPAFB 2009 dataset (see <cit.>)—object annotations typically consist of (x,y) coordinates paired with vehicle IDs and supplementary metadata. These coordinates represent the precise detected locations of objects in each video frame. However, a significant challenge arises when training deep learning models: a single point cannot effectively guide the model to learn object localization from noisy or spatially ambiguous input. To address this limitation, the raw (x,y) annotations are transformed into heat-map representations. This process involves placing a Gaussian filter at each coordinate, with the peak intensity at the original (x,y) point and decreasing intensity outward, controlled by a pre-defined variance parameter, σ. The resulting heat-map visually encodes the likelihood of an object being present at any spatial location, with brighter spots indicating higher probabilities. For each frame, the heat-map integrates all annotated objects by overlapping these Gaussian "spots," which may number in the hundreds or thousands depending on scene density (see Fig. <ref>). During training, the network’s predicted heat-map is compared to the ground-truth heat-map, and the loss is calculated as the Euclidean distance between the two, as formalized in Eq. <ref>. This approach ensures the model learns to approximate the spatial distribution of objects rather than relying on precise point-level accuracy.

This distinction matters because, in conjunction with (<ref>), an ASP solver may generate multiple constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) in a non-optimized manner—essentially testing each one independently through the constraint solver. This approach, while functional, lacks strategic coordination between the ASP and constraint solving components, leading to potentially redundant computations. However, by incorporating (<ref>), clingcon introduces a mechanism where the computational workflow can be initiated earlier during problem solving. This improvement arises from its algorithm’s design, which tightly integrates the ASP solver and the constraint solver. Specifically, clingcon interweaves the processing of the logical (qualitative) and numerical aspects of the problem, rather than separating them into sequential phases. This interleaving allows the constraint solver to begin refining solutions during the early stages of the ASP solving process, enabling faster identification of infeasible paths and thus enhancing overall performance.

old_text: Torsello et al. has shown that dominant sets, a well known clustering notion which generalizes the maximal clique problem to edge weighted graphs, can be bijectively related to Evolutionary Stable Strategies (ESS) <cit.>. Since the formalization of clustering problem as a game, replicator dynamics has been used to address different problems <cit.>. Players simultaneously select an object to cluster and receive a payoff proportional to the similarity of the selected objects. Since clusters are sets of objects that are highly similar, the competition induced by the game forces the players to coordinate by selecting objects from the same cluster. Indeed, by doing so, both players are able to maximize their expected payoff. The clustering game is a non-cooperative game between two-players, where the objects to cluster form the set of strategies, while the affinity matrix provides the players’ payoffs. The dynamics is also able to solve multiple affinities by extending the clustering game, which has a single payoff, to a multi-payoff game <cit.>. Since the introduction of the connection, replicator equation helps dominant set formulation be a robust clustering approach with many interesting and powerful properties such as: it makes no assumption on the underlying data representation, it makes no assumption on the structure of the affinity matrix, being it able to work with asymmetric and even negative similarity functions alike; it does not require a priori knowledge on the number of clusters; able to solve one-class clustering problems (figure ground separation); it allows extracting overlapping clusters <cit.>; it generalizes naturally to hypergraph clustering problems, in which the clustering game is played by more than two players <cit.>. The dominant sets formulation, using replicator equation, have proven to be an effective tool for graph-based clustering and have found applications in a variety of different domains, such as bioinformatics <cit.>, computer vision <cit.>, image processing <cit.>,<cit.>, group detection <cit.><cit.><cit.>, security and video surveillance <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.> etc.
new_text: Torsello et al. demonstrated that dominant sets, a clustering concept extending the maximal clique problem to edge-weighted graphs, can be bijectively linked to Evolutionary Stable Strategies (ESS) <cit.>. Since then, replicator dynamics has been employed to tackle clustering as a game-theoretic framework <cit.>. In this formulation, each player selects an object to cluster, with payoffs determined by the similarity between chosen items. The game's competitive structure incentivizes players to coordinate their selections on objects from a shared cluster, as this maximizes individual expected rewards. Clustering is modeled as a two-player non-cooperative game, where the set of objects serves as strategies and the affinity matrix defines payoffs. Extending this to handle multiple affinities involves generalizing the single-payoff game to a multi-payoff version <cit.>. This approach leverages replicator dynamics to produce a robust clustering method with several key properties: it requires no assumptions about data representation or affinity matrix structure (including compatibility with asymmetric and negative similarity functions); it determines cluster count automatically without prior knowledge; it enables one-class clustering (figure-ground separation); it supports overlapping clusters <cit.>; it naturally extends to hypergraph clustering via games involving more than two players <cit.>. The dominant sets method, grounded in replicator equations, has proven effective for graph-based clustering, with applications spanning bioinformatics <cit.>, computer vision <cit.>, image processing <cit.><cit.>, group detection <cit.><cit.><cit.>, and security/video surveillance <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>.

new_text: The agent's behaviour is defined by sampling actions from the current policy π_t and storing observed states, actions, rewards, and selected action probabilities (x_t, a_t, r_t, μ_t) into the replay memory. Retrace uses an off-policy correction that requires knowledge of the probability in which actions are generated (i.e., the trace cutting coefficient c_s in Equation <ref> depends on μ(a_s|x_s)). We can either use the stored behavioural probabilities μ(a_s|x_s) of the chosen actions or estimate μ̂ by training a model to predict previously taken actions P(a_s | x_s) using past samples. The replay memory contains a mixture of trajectories generated by the sequence of policies π_1, π_2, ..., π_t during the learning process. To see the difference between μ and μ̂, consider that from a state x, if actions 1 and 2 have been chosen deterministically in equal proportion, the replay memory contains an equal number of samples for both actions in that state. From an off-policy batched learning perspective, the empirical distribution of actions in that state resembles that of a stochastic policy with equal probabilities of 1/2 for both actions. Thus, the memorized probabilities μ(a_s|x) are either 1 or 0, whereas a learned μ̂(a_s|x) would predict 1/2. Using μ̂ can be beneficial since the trace cutting coefficients c_t would be higher, leading to reduced trace cutting and faster reward propagation through the Retrace algorithm. This might make the off-policy corrected returns less biased but at the cost of higher variance. On the other hand, if behavioural probability estimates are inaccurate, the Retrace algorithm may produce biased returns.

old_text: The replicator equation is a simple model of evolution that leads to stable form of Nash Equilibrium, Evolutionary Stable Strategy (ESS). No individuals get an incentive unilaterally deviating from the equilibrium. It has been studied in connection with Evolutionary Game Theory, a theory John Maynard Smith and George R. Price developed to predict biological reproductive success of populations. Replicator equation was originally developed for symmetric games, games whose payoff matrix is skew-symmetric and in general tells us, in a game, how individuals or populations change their strategy over time based on the payoff matrix of the game. Consider a large population of players where each player is assigned a strategy and players cannot choose their strategies which means rationality and consciousness don't enter the picture (players play based on a pre-assigned set of strategies). Evolutionary game theory assumes a scenario where a non-rational pairs of players, which play based on a pre-assigned set of strategies, repeatedly drawn from a large population plays a symmetric two-player game which drives the strategies with lower payoff to extinction . Since players interacts with another randomly chosen player in the population, a player’s expected payoff is determined by the payoff matrix and the proportion of each strategy in the population. The limiting behavior of the replicator dynamics (i.e., the evolutionary outcome) are the Evolutionary Stable Strategies, a NE with additional stability properties.

Endoscopic capsule robots are one of the most exiting novel technological
developments in the area of medical devices in the last decade. In that paper, we have presented to our knowledge for the ﬁrst time in literature a deep learning based 6 DoF localization approach for endoscopic capsule robots. The proposed architecture is unique in its kind by embedding RNN layers into the CNN architecture. The proposed system was able to stay close to the ground truth endoscopic capsule robot trajectory even for very challenge datasets confronted with sharp rotations and fast translations, heavy specular reﬂections and noise. Our system proved qualitatively and quantitatively its eﬀectiveness in occasionally looping capsule robot motions and comprehensive inner organ scanning tasks. In future, we aim to extend our work into the stereo capsule endoscopy applications to achieve even more accurate localization and mapping results.
new_text: Endoscopic capsule robots represent a groundbreaking technological advancement in medical devices over the last decade. This paper presents the first deep-learning-based 6 DoF localization approach for endoscopic capsule robots. The architecture uniquely integrates RNN layers into the CNN framework. The system maintains proximity to ground truth trajectories even in challenging datasets with sharp rotations, fast translations, heavy specular reflections, and noise. Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations validate its effectiveness for looping capsule motions and comprehensive organ scanning. Future work includes expanding the method to stereo capsule endoscopy to enhance localization and mapping accuracy.

new_text: In this paper, we reframe the spelling correction problem as a machine translation task within the encoder-decoder framework. This approach enables the use of a single model to address the problem and supports end-to-end training. We evaluate the effectiveness of this model using an internal dataset, with training data automatically extracted from user logs. Despite the model's simplicity, it competes favorably with state-of-the-art methods that require extensive feature engineering and human intervention.

old_text: The input/output vocabulary problem can be solved by using a character based encoding scheme. Although it seems appropriate for encoding the input, this scheme puts unnecessary burden on the decoder, since for a correction the decoder need to learn the correct spelling of the word, word boundaries, and etc. We choose the byte pair encoding (BPE) scheme <cit.> that strikes the balance between too large output vocabulary and too much learning burden for decoders. In this scheme, the vocabulary is built by recursively merging most frequent pairs of strings starting from character, and the vocabulary size is controlled by the number of merging iterations.
new_text: The input/output vocabulary problem can be addressed using a character-based encoding scheme. However, while this approach is suitable for encoding the input, it imposes an unnecessary burden on the decoder, which must learn not only the correct spelling of words but also word boundaries and other linguistic features. To resolve this, we adopt the byte pair encoding (BPE) scheme <cit.>, which effectively balances the trade-off between an excessively large output vocabulary and the excessive learning burden on decoders. In this approach, the vocabulary is constructed by recursively merging the most frequent pairs of strings, starting from individual characters, and the vocabulary size is regulated by adjusting the number of merging iterations.

During prediction, we face the problem of deciding on a concrete word ŵ^(t) given the predicted probabilities ŷ⃗^(t).
As mentioned before, we use beam search as a middle ground between greedily selecting the word with highest probability and performing an exhaustive search in the space of possible word sequences.
More concretely, we expand each of the candidate sequences by predicting W different probability vectors ŷ⃗_1^(t), …, ŷ⃗_K^(t) (beam search of width W) for each timestep.
Given a vocabulary of size V, this yields W · V new candidates, of which we only keep around the W most likely sequences under our model.
This process is then repeated iteratively until each candidate has been completed as indicated by the `EOS` token, resulting in W different descriptions.
new_text: During prediction, the challenge lies in selecting a concrete word ŵ^(t) based on the predicted probabilities ŷ⃗^(t). To address this, we employ beam search as a compromise between greedy selection (choosing the highest-probability word at each step) and exhaustive search over the space of possible word sequences. Specifically, at each timestep, we expand each candidate sequence by predicting W probability vectors ŷ⃗_1^(t), …, ŷ⃗_K^(t) (beam width W). With a vocabulary size V, this generates W · V new candidate sequences, from which we retain approximately the top W most probable ones according to the model's probability distribution. The process repeats until all candidates are completed, marked by the end-of-sequence (EOS) token, yielding W distinct descriptions.

We consider the synthesis of distributed implementations for specifications
in parameterized temporal logics such as PROMPT–LTL, which extends LTL by
temporal operators equipped with parameters that bound their scope. For
single process synthesis it is well-established that such parametric
extensions do not increase worst-case complexities. For synchronous
distributed systems we show that, despite being more powerful, the
realizability problem for PROMPT–LTL is not harder than its LTL
counterpart. For asynchronous systems we have to express scheduling
assumptions and therefore consider an assume-guarantee synthesis problem. As
asynchronous distributed synthesis is already undecidable for LTL, we give
a semi-decision procedure for the PROMPT–LTL assume-guarantee synthesis
problem based on bounded synthesis. Finally, we show that our results extend
to the stronger logics PLTL and PLDL.

Execution Stacks for a General Scheduler.
We observe that when using a general scheduler,
additional execution stacks may be needed.
For suppose that processor P is executing a task τ from which a deep steal of subtask
σ occurs.
Let P' be the processor executing σ.
Suppose that P is the first of P and P' to reach the join node at which the steal ends.
Then P will leave the continuation of the execution of τ to P'.
But P needs to continue the execution of the
parallel tasks still on its task queue,
performing them in dfs order (i.e. from the
rear of the queue).
However, P cannot use the execution stack for τ to store the variables
for these subtasks as (a) this would violate the standard practice in which the current variable
order on the execution stack corresponds to the current path of open procedure calls,
and (b) additional space on this stack may be needed for the execution by P' of the portion of
τ following the join node.
In these circumstances P will create a new execution stack for each such
pseudo-stolen task on its
task queue as and when it starts its execution.
This is exactly what would happen were the task to be stolen.
The difference is that this will not count as a steal.
In fact, whether P reaches the join node first or not, it will need to execute the
tasks remaining on its task queue, and it will use a new execution stack for each
such pseudo-stolen task.
P will continue to have a single task queue, however.

old_text: As an attempt to more quantitatively evaluate generative models, we introduced Flow-GAN. It is a generative adversarial network which allows for tractable likelihood evaluation, exactly like in a flow model. Since it can be trained both adversarially (like a GAN) and in terms of MLE (like a flow model), we can quantitatively evaluate the trade-offs involved. In particular, we also consider a hybrid objective function which involves both types of losses. On MNIST, our hybrid Flow-GAN objective outperforms both pure MLE and a pure adversarial training, both in terms of sample quality and log likelihood. On CIFAR-10, our Flow-GAN objective outperforms a pure MLE approach in terms of visual sample quality, and is only slightly worse in terms of log-likelihood. old_text: Orman2015 formalize the community characterization problem as a sequential pattern mining problem Mabroukeh2010. Each node is represented through a sequence of individual descriptor values, describing its evolution through time. A descriptor can directly correspond to a nodal attribute, but it can also be a topological measure: this allows to represent simultaneously attributes and various aspects of the network topology (degree, centrality, transitivity, etc.). A community is therefore described by the set of sequences representing its nodes. It is characterized by identifying the most relevant sequential patterns among these nodal sequences, which allows detecting common changes in topological features and attribute values over time periods. This relevance is enforced through various constraints. First, to get prevalent patterns, they focus on frequent ones (i.e. those supported by a at least a certain number of nodes). Second, to get informative patterns, they only detect closed ones, i.e. patterns not included in larger patterns possessing the same support. Third, to get distinctive patterns, they select those with the highest growth rates. The growth rate of a pattern is a measure showing how much representative a sequence is inside of a group, relatively to the whole studied population. In this case, a group corresponds to a community.
new_text: Orman2015 frame the community characterization problem as a sequential pattern mining task (Mabroukeh2010). Each node is encoded as a sequence of descriptor values capturing its temporal evolution. These descriptors may represent node attributes or network topology metrics (e.g., degree, centrality, transitivity), enabling simultaneous representation of both attribute dynamics and structural changes. A community is defined by the collective set of such nodal sequences. Its characterization relies on extracting the most significant sequential patterns across these sequences, revealing shared temporal variations in topological properties and attribute values. This significance is ensured via three constraints: (1) *frequency*—retaining only patterns supported by a minimum number of nodes in the community; (2) *closedness*—excluding patterns subsumed by larger patterns with identical support; and (3) *distinctiveness*—selecting patterns with maximal growth rates. The growth rate quantifies the relative representativeness of a pattern within a community compared to the entire network, with higher values indicating stronger differentiation of the community.

This dataset includes interactions from 810k users with 380k videos over the same 2-month period, totaling 33 million events and 8.5 million sessions [We retained the preprocessing steps applied to the original VIDEO dataset.]. We refer to this as the VIDEOXXL dataset. Given constrained computational resources, we restricted experiments to small network configurations (100 hidden units for RNNs and 100+100 HRNNs) on this large-scale data. All RNN and HRNN models were trained once using hyperparameters optimized on the smaller VIDEO dataset, acknowledging this suboptimal setup provides initial insights into scalability. Summary results in <ref> align with findings from the smaller dataset: RNN Concat consistently underperformed compared to session-based RNNs, and similarly, HRNN All showed poor performance. In contrast, HRNN Init significantly outperformed session-based RNNs, achieving improvements of up to ∼10% in Recall@5 and MRR@5. These outcomes reinforce HRNN Init’s effectiveness for personalized session-based recommendations.

This conforms with the intuition that past user activity can be effectively used to predict the first actions of the user in the forthcoming session with greater accuracy. After the first few events the gain in Recall of personalized over pure session-based models reduces, while the gain in MRR stays stable. In other words, after a few events, the session-level dynamics start to prevail over longer-term user interest dynamics, making personalization strategies less effective. However, personalization still provides superior ranking quality all over the session, as testified by the higher MRR of both HRNN Init and RNN Concat over RNN. HRNN Init demonstrates significant improvements over RNN and RNN Concat early in the session (up to 10% higher Recall and 20–25% higher MRR, respectively), aligning with the intuition that prior user activity effectively predicts initial actions in upcoming sessions. After the first few events, the improvement in Recall by personalized models over pure session-based models diminishes, while MRR gains remain stable. Session-level dynamics begin to outweigh long-term user interest patterns after a few interactions, reducing the effectiveness of personalization strategies. However, personalization consistently maintains superior ranking quality throughout the session, as evidenced by higher MRR scores for both HRNN Init and RNN Concat compared to RNN. Additionally, improved recommendation quality at the session's onset enhances user retention more effectively than later recommendations. Finally, HRNN All consistently represents the worst-performing method, further reinforcing the superiority of the HRNN Init variant.

In this paper we addressed the problem of personalizing session-based recommendation by proposing a model based Hierarchical RNN, that extends previous RNN-based session modeling with one additional GRU level that models the user activity across sessions and the evolution of her interests over time. HRNNs provide a seamless way of transferring the knowledge acquired on the long-term dynamics of the user interest to session-level, and hence to provide personalized session-based recommendations to returning users. The proposed HRNNs model significantly outperform both state-of-the-art session-based RNNs and the other basic personalization strategies for session-based recommendation on two real-world datasets having different nature. In particular, we noticed that the simpler approach that only initializes the session-level representation with the evolving representation of the user (HRNN Init) gives the best results.
We delved into the dynamics of session-based RNN models within and across-sessions, providing extensive evidences of the superiority of the proposed HRNN Init approach and setting new state-of-the-art performances for session-based recommendation.
new_text: In this paper, we address the problem of personalizing session-based recommendation by proposing a model based on a Hierarchical RNN, which extends previous RNN-based session modeling by introducing an additional GRU layer that captures both the user’s activity across sessions and the evolution of their interests over time. HRNNs enable the seamless transfer of knowledge regarding the long-term dynamics of user interests to the session level, thereby enabling personalized session-based recommendations for returning users. The proposed HRNN model significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art session-based RNNs and other baseline personalization strategies for session-based recommendation on two real-world datasets of different natures. In particular, we observe that the simpler approach, which initializes the session-level representation with the evolving user representation (HRNN Init), achieves the best performance. We analyze the dynamics of session-based RNN models within and across sessions, providing extensive evidence of the superiority of the proposed HRNN Init approach and establishing new state-of-the-art performance levels for session-based recommendation.

old_text: For the infinite battery scenario, we adopt a best-effort uniform status update policy and show that it minimizes the long-term average AoI. For the finite battery scenario, we adopt an energy-aware adaptive status update policy, and prove that it is asymptotically optimal when the battery size goes to infinity. For the last scenario where the battery size is one, we first show that within a broadly defined class of online policies, the optimal policy should have a renewal structure, i.e., the status update epochs form a renewal process, and the length of each renewal interval depends on the first energy arrival over that interval only. We then focus on a renewal interval, and prove that if the AoI in the system is below a threshold when the first energy arrives, the sensor should store the energy and hold status update until the AoI reaches the threshold; otherwise, it updates the status immediately. We analytically characterize the long-term average AoI under such a threshold-based policy, and explicitly identify the optimal threshold. Simulation results corroborate the theoretical bounds.
new_text: For the infinite battery scenario, we consider a best-effort uniform status update policy, in which the sensor transmits status updates at fixed intervals without regard to energy constraints. We demonstrate that this policy minimizes the long-term average age of information (AoI), as it ensures the most frequent and consistent updates possible. Turning to the finite battery scenario, we analyze an energy-aware adaptive status update policy, which accounts for the available battery level before scheduling updates. We prove that this policy achieves asymptotic optimality as the battery size grows arbitrarily large, meaning its performance converges to the theoretical minimum AoI achievable under ideal conditions. Finally, for the case where the battery capacity is limited to one unit, we first establish that any optimal policy within a broad class of online strategies must exhibit a renewal structure. Specifically, the sequence of status update events forms a renewal process, where each cycle begins after an update and is defined by the time until the next energy arrival. The length of each renewal interval depends solely on the timing of the first energy arrival during that interval, reflecting the system’s reliance on sporadic energy availability. Within this renewal interval, we then specify an optimal threshold-based decision rule: if the AoI at the moment of the first energy arrival is below a predefined threshold, the sensor should defer the update, storing the energy until the AoI reaches the threshold; if the AoI exceeds the threshold, the update should occur immediately. By analyzing this policy, we derive an explicit expression for the long-term average AoI and identify the optimal threshold that minimizes this metric. Simulations confirm the theoretical results, validating the efficiency of the proposed strategies.

Formally, a circuit layout consists of several sub-blocks (or cells) with input/output ports (or pins). Connections between pins use channels (or tracks) in several metal layers that run orthogonal to one another, separated by insulating layers with connecting vias. If we treat cells as edges, then a node in a circuit graph corresponds to a net in the layout, which connects the driver's output pin with the input pin(s) of the receiver(s). Traditionally, when the circuit sizes were tractable, routing was primarily a manual task. However, in the past couple decades with exploding circuit sizes and more than a few billion transistors to be routed, the use of auto-routers is indispensable. Shrinking technology nodes and more stringent design rules further impact routability. Commercial electronic design automation (EDA) tools try to tackle this non-linear optimization problem using various algorithmic approaches <cit.> such as (i) exponential algorithms to exhaust the search space for a solution, (ii) heuristic algorithms, (iii) optimal algorithms for special cases of the problem, or (iv) approximation techniques. These approaches are iterative in nature and rely on a continually evolving/changing set of design rules. The routed layouts may further require significant manual effort and fine tuning to improve the non-optimal routes.
new_text: A circuit layout comprises multiple sub-blocks (also known as cells) equipped with input/output ports (referred to as pins). Interconnecting these pins involves channels (or tracks) across multiple metal layers, which are oriented perpendicularly to each other and separated by insulating layers via vias. When modeling the layout as a graph, treating cells as edges allows a graph node to represent a net, linking the driver’s output pin to one or more receiver input pins. Historically, routing was conducted manually due to manageable circuit sizes, but over the past two decades, the exponential growth in circuit complexity—exceeding a few billion transistors—has rendered automated routers essential. Advancements in smaller technology nodes and stricter design requirements further complicate routability. Commercial electronic design automation (EDA) tools address this complex, non-linear optimization problem through diverse algorithmic strategies <cit.>, including (i) exhaustive search algorithms to explore the solution space, (ii) heuristic-based methods, (iii) optimal algorithms for specific subproblems, or (iv) approximation techniques. These methods are iterative and depend on dynamically changing design rules. Even after routing, layouts often necessitate substantial manual intervention to refine suboptimal routes.

These regional outputs are then integrated via a secondary classifier to infer overall driver behavior.

old_text: Although activation maps of the last convolutional layer carry most discriminative information, they are usually greatly down-sampled from the original image resolution due to pooling operations. We hereby introduce a multi-GAP CNN model that takes advantage of shallower layers with higher spatial resolution. Similar to the idea of the skip architecture proposed in fully-convolutional network (FCN) <cit.>, shallower layers can be directed to the final classification task skipping the following layers. We also add a Conv+GAP structure following the shallow layers. The concatenation of feature vectors generated by each GAP layer is fed into the final FC layer. The NAM generated from the multi-GAP CNN model (multi-GAP NAM) is a weighted activation map involving activations at multiple scales.
new_text: Activation maps from the last convolutional layer contain most discriminative information but are typically downsampled via pooling operations, reducing spatial resolution. To address this, we propose a multi-GAP CNN model leveraging shallower layers with higher spatial resolution. Inspired by FCN’s skip architecture <cit.>, these layers bypass subsequent stages and contribute directly to classification. A Conv+GAP structure follows each shallow layer, and the concatenated feature vectors from all GAP layers are input to the final FC layer. The resulting NAM, termed multi-GAP NAM, integrates activations across multiple scales to form a weighted activation map.

old_text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been widely used for supervised image classification and segmentation tasks. It was very recently discovered in a study <cit.> on natural images that CNNs trained on semantic labels for image classification task (“what”), have remarkable capability in identifying the discriminative regions (“where”) when combined with a global average pooling (GAP) operation. This method utilizes the up-sampled weighted activation maps from the last convolutional layer in a CNN. It demonstrated the localization capability of CNNs for detecting relatively large-sized targets within image, which is not the general scenario in medical imaging domain where pathological changes are more various in size and rather subtle to capture. However, this work sheds light on weakly-supervised disease detection.
new_text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely employed for supervised image classification and segmentation tasks. A recent study <cit.> has demonstrated that CNNs trained using semantic labels for image classification tasks (the “what”) have demonstrated remarkable capability in identifying the discriminative regions (the “where”) when combined with a global average pooling (GAP) operation. This approach leverages up-sampled weighted activation maps from the final convolutional layer of a CNN to highlight relevant features. The method revealed the localization capabilities of CNNs for detecting relatively large targets in images, a scenario that contrasts with the medical imaging domain, where pathological changes exhibit greater variability in size and are more subtle to detect. However, this study provides valuable insights for weakly-supervised disease detection.

The FCN comprises 15 convolutional stages (see Section <ref> for further explanation on the choice of network depth), as fully connected layers or excessively deep architectures were avoided. All convolutional stages, except the final one, are followed by batch normalization (BN) <cit.> and leaky rectified linear unit (leaky ReLU) <cit.>. The final convolution stage (L_15), which outputs class scores, omits BN and leaky ReLU since these operations would not influence the relative score comparisons. The FCN receives encoded inputs as tensors of shape N × 1 × H × W, where N denotes the mini-batch size and H = W = 32 represent the spatial dimensions. The first stage (L_1) utilizes 33 × 33 convolution with 16 filters, whereas stages L_2 through L_15 employ 3 × 3 convolution with 16 filters. We posit that the large receptive field at the head of the network enables rapid acquisition of overall pin locations and facilitates improved learning of spatial information, as detailed in Section <ref>. Convolutional strides and padding are configured to maintain the spatial dimensions of feature maps across stages. Consequently, activations after each stage adopt the shape N × 16 × 32 × 32, or more generally N × (α.β) × H × W, where α represents the number of layout layers to be learned and β corresponds to the number of segmentation classes (two in our case). Activations from the final FCN stage, which contain class scores, are processed through a score comparator to select the class with the higher score. This reduces the tensor shape from N × (α.β) × H × W to N × α × H × W, where each pixel is assigned a '1' (indicating presence) or '0' (indicating absence) of a given layer at its spatial location. In Figure <ref>, we notice that the most confusing posture is the “safe driving”.
This is due to the lack of temporal context in static images.
In a static image, a driver would appear in a “safe driving” posture.
However, contextually, he/she was distracted by doing some other activity.
“Text Left” is mostly confused for “Talk Left” and vice versa.
Same applies to “Text Right” and “Talk Right”.
“Adjust Radio” is mainly confused for a “safe driving” posture.
That is due to lack of the previously mentioned temporal context.
Apart from safe driving, “Hair & Makeup” is confused for talking to passenger.
That is because, in most cases, when drivers did their hair/makeup on the left side of their face, they needed to tilt their face slightly right (while looking at the frontal mirror).
Thus, the network thought the person was talking to passenger.
“Reach Behind” was confused for both talking to passenger and drinking.
That makes sense as people tend to naturally look towards the camera while reaching behind.
As for the drinking confusion, it is due to right-arm movement from the steering wheel to the back seat.
A still image in the middle of that move could be easily mistaken for a drinking posture.
“Drink” and “Talk to Passenger” postures were not easily confused with other postures as 98% and 97.67% of their images were correctly classified.
new_text: In Figure <ref>, the most confusing posture is identified as "safe driving." This misclassification is primarily attributed to the absence of temporal context inherent in static images. A driver's apparent "safe driving" posture in a static image may misrepresent the actual context, where the individual was distracted by other activities. "Text Left" is frequently misclassified as "Talk Left" and vice versa, with the same pattern observed for "Text Right" and "Talk Right." "Adjust Radio" is predominantly mistaken for the "safe driving" posture, again due to the absence of temporal context. Additionally, "Hair & Makeup" is frequently confused with "talking to passenger." This occurs because drivers adjusting their hair or makeup on the left side of their face often tilt rightward while viewing the frontal mirror, leading the network to misinterpret the action as conversing with a passenger. "Reach Behind" is frequently misclassified as either "talking to passenger" or "drinking." This is logical, as individuals tend to look toward the camera while reaching behind. The confusion with "drinking" arises from the right arm’s movement from the steering wheel to the back seat, where a still image captured mid-motion might resemble a drinking posture. Conversely, "Drink" and "Talk to Passenger" postures exhibited minimal confusion, with 98% and 97.67% of their images correctly classified, respectively.

old_text: Data used in this study contains 1,010 thoracic CT scans from the public LIDC-IDRI database. Details about this database, such as acquisition protocols and quality evaluations, can be found in <cit.>. Lungs were segmented and each axial slice was cropped to 384`x`384 pixels centering on the lung mask. Nodules were delineated by up to four experts. Voxel-level annotations are used to generate slice-level labels, and are used as ground truth for segmentation evaluation. Nodules with diameter <3mm are excluded <cit.>. Given the high false positive rate of nodule detection, we select slices with nodule if there were overlapped annotations by at least two experts, and select slices without nodule if no expert reported a nodule in the slice. Annotations from different experts were merged using the STAPLE algorithm <cit.>. A total of N_slice=8,345 slices with nodule are selected, and an equal number of slices without nodule are randomly extracted. The total number of voxels belonging to nodule is N_voxel=1,658,981. Segmentation evaluation is focused on slices with one nodule. Rare cases of slices with two nodules are discussed in the end of Section <ref>. Training, validation and test sets are generated by distributing the full set of subjects in a ratio of 4:1:1 through stratified sampling so that they have non-overlapping subjects and similar distribution of nodule occurrence.
new_text: The dataset used in this study consists of 1,010 thoracic CT scans sourced from the publicly available LIDC-IDRI database. Comprehensive details regarding the acquisition protocols, imaging parameters, and quality assessments for this database are provided in the cited reference <cit.>. To prepare the data for analysis, the lungs in each scan were segmented, and each axial slice was then cropped to a resolution of 384 × 384 pixels, with the cropping centered on the segmented lung region. Pulmonary nodules within these scans were annotated by up to four expert radiologists, ensuring a multi-expert consensus. For the segmentation task, voxel-level annotations—representing the precise three-dimensional locations of nodules—were aggregated to create slice-level binary labels. These labels serve as the ground truth for evaluating segmentation accuracy. To focus on clinically relevant structures, nodules smaller than 3mm in diameter were excluded from the dataset <cit.>. Given the inherent challenges of false positives in nodule detection, a two-tiered selection criterion was applied to axial slices: a slice was labeled as containing a nodule only if at least two of the four experts identified a nodule in that slice, and a slice was labeled as nodule-free if no expert reported a nodule in that slice. To reconcile discrepancies among the experts’ annotations, the STAPLE (Simultaneous Truth and Performance Level Estimation) algorithm <cit.> was employed, a consensus method that generates a fused, reliable annotation set. Using these criteria, a total of 8,345 axial slices with confirmed nodules were selected, paired with an equal number of nodule-free slices chosen randomly to maintain balanced class distribution. The dataset includes 1,658,981 voxels annotated as nodules. For segmentation evaluation, the analysis primarily focuses on slices containing a single nodule; however, cases with two nodules are acknowledged and addressed in Section <ref>. To ensure robust model evaluation and generalizability, the dataset was stratified into training, validation, and test sets in a 4:1:1 ratio. This stratified sampling approach ensures that each subset contains non-overlapping patient scans and maintains a similar distribution of nodule occurrence across all sets.

new_text: Community detection in networks, also known as network partitioning, is a critical area that has drawn significant research attention. Here, we highlight several major categories of methods used for network partitioning. The first major category leverages spectral properties of network matrices, such as the adjacency matrix and Laplacian (see e.g., the survey <cit.> and references therein). The second category, closely linked to the first, employs random walk techniques (see e.g., <cit.> for the most representative works in this research direction). A third approach draws from principles in statistical physics <cit.>. The fourth category, most pertinent to our approach, is centered on the concept of modularity and its various generalizations <cit.>. For an extensive overview of community detection methods, we recommend consulting the survey <cit.>.
