old_text: To address this significant gap in the literature, here we introduce the first (to our knowledge) systematic, real-world comparison of autonomous driving performance across multiple, contemporary deep neural networks in a setup that can be easily and inexpensively replicated. We use a simple platform assembled from commercially available components (all hardware and software specs are described below; software is publicly available as a Docker repository). The setup consists of an off-the-shelf, remotely operated vehicle (Brookstone Rover 2.0), a GPU equipped computer and an indoor foam-rubber racetrack. The vehicle communicates with the computer over wifi in order to send its camera images, which are then run through a trained neural network in real time in order to output an action decision that the computer sends back to the rover over the wifi network. This setup allows us to test computing intensive deep learning models without the need to “onboard” the GPU hardware. We used this platform to train 8 different contemporary deep neural networks, across three image input classes, on data from multiple humans driving around the track. We then compared autonomous performance on the track under identical experimental conditions for each of the 21 (7 × 3) conditions. We report performance along multiple metrics including the percentage of successful loops (i.e. without crashing) and the average time in seconds needed to complete a loop.
new_text: To address this critical research gap, we present the first (to our knowledge) empirical, real-world evaluation of autonomous driving systems across multiple modern deep neural networks, using a framework designed for straightforward, low-cost replication. Our implementation employs a modular system built from commercially available components (detailed hardware and software configurations are provided below; software is accessible via a public Docker repository). The core architecture integrates an off-the-shelf remotely controlled vehicle (Brookstone Rover 2.0), a GPU-powered computer, and an indoor foam-rubber racing circuit. The rover transmits live camera footage to the computer via Wi-Fi, where a pre-trained neural network processes the inputs in real time to generate action commands relayed back to the vehicle through the same wireless network. This design enables high-computation deep learning experiments without embedding the GPU directly into the vehicle. We trained eight contemporary deep neural networks across three distinct image input modalities using datasets collected from multiple human drivers navigating the track. Autonomous performance was benchmarked across 21 (7 × 3) configurations under standardized experimental conditions. Evaluation metrics included the proportion of completed laps without collisions and mean lap duration in seconds.

old_text: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have seen great success in a range of computer vision tasks, including image classification <cit.>, semantic segmentation <cit.>, depth estimation <cit.>, and style transfer <cit.>. However, these networks are typically designed to achieve only one particular task. For more complete vision systems in real-world applications, a network which can perform multiple tasks simultaneously is far more desirable than building a set of independent networks, one for each task. This is more efficient not only in terms of memory and inference speed, but also in terms of data, since related tasks may share informative visual features. For example, the task of depth estimation with supervised learning may help with a semantic segmentation task, by learning features which are responsive to depth discontinuities, and hence which may provide cues for segmentation.
new_text: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated significant effectiveness across diverse computer vision tasks, including image categorization <cit.>, semantic segmentation <cit.>, depth estimation <cit.>, and artistic style transfer <cit.>. Nevertheless, most CNNs are conventionally engineered to execute a single, discrete task. In practical real-world vision systems, however, deploying a single model capable of handling multiple tasks concurrently is often more advantageous than constructing separate, independent networks for each function. This approach offers efficiency gains in terms of computational memory, inference latency, and data utilization, as correlated tasks frequently rely on overlapping discriminative visual patterns. For instance, supervised depth estimation can enhance semantic segmentation by learning features sensitive to depth boundaries, thereby generating contextual cues that improve the accuracy of object boundary detection in the segmentation process.

In order to satisfy the input requirement of the classification networks, most two-stage object detection algorithms, e.g., SPP <cit.>, Fast RCNN <cit.> and Faster RCNN <cit.>, represent each proposal as a fixed-size feature vector by RoI pooling <cit.>.
As shown in Fig. <ref> (c), the RoI pooling divides every proposal into H× W sub-windows and uses the max pooling to extract one value for each sub-window so that the output can have a fixed-size of H× W.
If a proposal is smaller than H× W, it is enlarged to H× W by simply replicating some parts of the proposal to fill the extra space.
Unfortunately, such a scheme is not appropriate as it may destroy the original structures of the small objects (see Fig. <ref> (c)).
During the network training process, filling with replicated values not only leads to inaccurate representations in the forward propagation, but also accumulates errors in the backward propagation. The inaccurate representations and accumulated errors mislead the training and prevent the network from correctly detecting small scale vehicles.
In our experiments, we find that this problem is critical for the low detection accuracy of small vehicles.
new_text: Two-stage object detection algorithms (e.g., SPP, Fast R-CNN, and Faster R-CNN) represent each proposal as a fixed-size feature vector using RoI pooling (Fig. <ref> (c)). RoI pooling partitions each proposal into H×W sub-windows, applies max-pooling to extract one value per sub-window, producing a fixed-size H×W output. When a proposal is smaller than H×W, it is upscaled to H×W by replicating parts of the proposal to fill the extra space. This approach is problematic because it can distort the original structures of small objects. During training, replicated values cause inaccurate forward representations and error accumulation during backpropagation. These issues mislead the training, hindering small-scale vehicle detection. Our experiments reveal this issue is a major cause of low detection accuracy for small vehicles.

new_text:
Training Strategies  
We employ stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to optimize our SINet. To stabilize the training process, we begin by using a small learning rate to pre-train the RPN, then transition to a larger learning rate for end-to-end network training. Initially, we set the learning rate to 0.0001 for 10,000 iterations with a weight decay of 0.0005 to train the RPN. For full-network training, the learning rate is set to 0.0005, reduced by a factor of 0.1 at 40,000 and 70,000 iterations, and training ceases after 75,000 iterations. When using VGG, the initial learning rate is adjusted to 0.00005 and 0.0001 for the first and second stages, respectively. To accelerate training and mitigate overfitting, we initialize the RPN’s convolutional layers using weights pretrained on ImageNet or Pascal VOC. The fully connected layers of the newly added multi-branch decision network are initialized with weights from the corresponding layers of VGG or PVA, while other layers use random noise. Each training batch contains four images. Additionally, data augmentation methods and hard example mining strategies are adopted as in MS-CNN.

old_text: This paper presents a measurement-based evaluation of channel hardening in a practical scenario. The measurements were taken in an indoor auditorium with a cylindrical array, implying that some antennas are in LOS and some NLOS. The amount of channel hardening that can be expected when increasing the number of base station antennas is in this scenario highly dependent on the order in which the antennas are chosen. Depending on whether the antennas in the chosen subset are in LOS or in NLOS, both the starting point for a single antenna as well as the slope of the standard deviation curve are affected due to the large variations of channel gain over the cylindrical base station array. Also, even if the number of antenna elements at the base station side is 128, the number of actually effective channels is less than that. Another important point in this analysis is that here, the standard deviation measured is still a result of both small-scale and large-scale fading due to interaction with the users and antenna alignments. This affects both the starting point and the slope of the standard deviation curve. Overall, based on the analysis and the specific scenario in this paper, the channel hardening, in terms of decrease of the standard deviation of the experienced channel gain, varies between 3.2–4.6 dB, depending on the user's position and the order in which the antenna elements are chosen. This can be compared to the Gaussian case, where a channel hardening of 10.5 dB is expected. Future work will include extending this analysis, to further narrow down the parameters which creates channel hardening in a practical scenario.
new_text: This study provides a measurement-driven assessment of channel hardening in a realistic setting. Data was collected in an indoor auditorium using a cylindrical array, resulting in a mix of line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) antennas. The degree of channel hardening observed with an increasing number of base station antennas is critically influenced by the selection order of antennas. The starting point for a single antenna and the slope of the standard deviation curve are altered depending on whether the selected subset includes LOS or NLOS antennas, owing to the pronounced variations in channel gain across the cylindrical array. Furthermore, even though the base station is equipped with 128 antenna elements, the actual number of effective channels is lower due to combined small-scale and large-scale fading effects caused by interactions between users and antenna orientations. These effects modify both the initial magnitude and the rate of decline in the standard deviation curve. In this context, the channel hardening, defined as the reduction in the standard deviation of the channel gain, ranges between 3.2–4.6 dB, contingent on user position and antenna selection sequence. This contrasts sharply with the Gaussian channel scenario, where a 10.5 dB reduction is anticipated. Future research aims to expand this analysis to identify the specific parameters driving channel hardening in real-world conditions.

Starting from the same motivation, the order embeddings method <cit.> explicitly models the partial order induced by entailment relations between embedded objects. Formally, a vector x∈ℝ^n represents a more general concept than any other embedding from the Euclidean entailment region 𝒪_x:={ y|∀ i∈[n], y_i≥ x_i}. A first concern is that the capacity of order embeddings grows only linearly with the embedding space dimension. This also implies that Euclidean distances would no longer be capable of reflecting the original tree metric.

new_text: The analysis of shoe tread impressions is particularly challenging due to the diverse nature of crime scene evidence. This is complicated by the wide range of environmental conditions in which such evidence may be found, including trace dust or oil on hard surfaces, as well as impressions embedded in soil or other soft materials. Additionally, the scarcity of comprehensive reference datasets for shoe outsole tread patterns (see Fig. <ref>) further limits the development of robust analytical methods. To address these issues, it is necessary to design models capable of cross-domain matching, where tread features extracted from controlled, clean test impressions—such as those from laboratory settings or direct outsole images—can be reliably compared to real-world crime scene data. This requires accounting for the stark differences in imaging conditions between these domains. Another layer of complexity arises when attempting to match features derived from crime scene impressions to a large, open-ended database of reference tread patterns. In such scenarios, the system must efficiently search an extensive and potentially unbounded collection of exemplars, demanding both computational efficiency and high discriminative accuracy in feature representation.

We propose a framework for extreme learned image compression based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), obtaining visually pleasing images at significantly lower bitrates than previous methods.
This is made possible through our GAN formulation of learned compression combined with a generator/decoder which operates on the full-resolution image and is trained in combination with a multi-scale discriminator.
Additionally, our method can fully synthesize unimportant regions in the decoded image such as streets and trees from a semantic label map extracted from the original image, therefore only requiring the storage of the preserved region and the semantic label map.
A user study confirms that for low bitrates, our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, saving up to 67% compared to the next-best method BPG.
new_text: We propose a framework for extreme learned image compression based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which achieves visually pleasing images at significantly lower bitrates than previous methods. This is made possible through our GAN formulation of learned compression combined with a generator/decoder that operates on the full-resolution image and is trained alongside a multi-scale discriminator. Additionally, our method can fully synthesize unimportant regions in the decoded image, such as streets and trees, from a semantic label map extracted from the original image, thus requiring only the storage of the preserved regions and the semantic label map. A user study confirms that at low bitrates, our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, saving up to 67% relative to the next-best method, BPG.

Arguably the most closely related work to ours is <cit.>, which uses an adversarial loss term to train a deep compression system. However, this loss term is applied to small image patches and its purpose is to suppress artifacts rather than to generate image content.
Furthermore, it uses a non-standard GAN formulation that does not (to the best of our knowledge) have an interpretation in terms of divergences between probability distributions, as in <cit.>.
<cit.> uses a GAN framework to learn a generative model over thumbnail images, which is then used as a decoder for thumbnail image compression. Other works use adversarial training for compression artifact removal (for engineered codecs) <cit.> and single image super-resolution <cit.>.
Finally, related to our SC mode, spatially allocating bitrate based on saliency of image content has a long history in the context of engineered compression algorithms, see e.g. <cit.>.
new_text: Arguably the most closely related to our approach is the work in <cit.>, which employs an adversarial loss term to train a deep image compression system. However, in this method, the adversarial component is specifically applied to small, localized image patches, and its primary objective is to reduce compression artifacts rather than to generate or enhance perceptual quality in global image content. Additionally, the formulation of the GAN in this approach deviates from standard frameworks, lacking a clear interpretation in terms of statistical divergences between probability distributions—a characteristic central to many conventional GANs, such as those described in <cit.>. In contrast, <cit.> employs a GAN-based framework to learn a generative model for thumbnail images, which is then adapted as a decoder for thumbnail compression tasks. Adversarial training has also been explored in related contexts, including artifact suppression in engineered codecs <cit.> and enhancing resolution in single-image super-resolution scenarios <cit.>. Notably, our SC mode, which dynamically allocates bitrate based on the saliency of visual content, draws on techniques with a long-standing history in traditional, manually designed compression algorithms. For example, saliency-driven bitrate allocation strategies have been widely studied in the context of handcrafted codecs, as demonstrated in <cit.>. These prior approaches highlight the broader relevance of perceptual modeling and efficient resource distribution in achieving high-quality compression.

The success of approximate DP in addressing challenging large-scale applications owes much to an enormously beneficial cross-fertilization of ideas from decision and control, and from artificial intelligence. The boundaries between these fields are now diminished thanks to a deeper understanding of the foundational issues, and the associated methods and core applications. Unfortunately, however, there have been substantial discrepancies of notation and terminology between the artificial intelligence and the optimization/decision/control fields, including the typical use of maximization/value function/reward in the former field and the use of minimization/cost function/cost per stage in the latter field. The notation and terminology used in this paper is standard in DP and optimal control, and in an effort to forestall confusion of readers that are accustomed to either the reinforcement learning or the optimal control terminology, we provide a list of selected terms commonly used in reinforcement learning (for example in the popular book by Sutton and Barto [SuB98], and its 2018 on-line 2nd edition), and their optimal control counterparts.

old_text: Finally, let us mention a potential weakness of using the features obtained at the output of the last nonlinear layer of the neural network in the context of aggregation: the sheer number of these features may be so large that the resulting number of aggregate states may become excessive. To address this situation one may consider pruning some of the features, or reducing their number using some form of regression, at the potential loss of some approximation accuracy. In this connection let us also emphasize a point made earlier in connection with an advantage of deep (rather than shallow) neural networks: because with each additional layer, the generated features tend to be more complex, their number at the output of the final nonlinear layer of the network can be made smaller as the number of layers increases. An extreme case is to use the cost function approximation obtained at the output of the neural network as a single feature/scoring function, in the spirit of Section 4.2.
new_text:
One potential limitation in using features extracted from the output of a neural network’s final nonlinear layer arises in aggregation tasks: the high dimensionality of these features can result in an excessive number of aggregate states. This scalability challenge occurs because the raw feature set may contain redundancies or unnecessary complexity for the specific aggregation purpose. To mitigate this, two approaches are commonly considered: first, feature pruning—selectively removing less informative features—and second, dimensionality reduction techniques such as regression, which compress the feature space while preserving meaningful structure. However, these methods may come at a cost, as they could degrade the model’s ability to approximate the underlying function accurately.  

Crucially, this trade-off between feature richness and computational tractability connects to a key benefit of deep neural networks over their shallow counterparts. In deep architectures, each additional layer refines and abstracts the learned representations, progressively generating more complex features. As a result, deeper networks can achieve equivalent or superior performance with fewer output features compared to shallow models, where feature count must grow rapidly to capture equivalent complexity. For instance, a deep network with many layers might produce a compact set of highly descriptive features at its final layer, whereas a shallow network would require a much larger feature set to encode similar information. Extending this logic to its logical extreme, one might even reduce the aggregated feature set to a single function—the network’s final output—mirroring the approach outlined in Section 4.2, where the cost function itself serves as the sole representation for aggregation. This highlights the interplay between network depth, feature efficiency, and the design of aggregation strategies.

To overcome the limitations of Dedicated Short Range Communications (DSRC) with short range, non-supportability of high density networks, unreliable broadcast services, signal congestion and connectivity disruptions, Vehicle-to-anything (V2X) communication networks, standardized in 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 14,
		have been recently introduced to cover broader vehicular communication scenarios including vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), vehicle-to-pedestrian (V2P) and vehicle-to-infrastructure/network (V2I/N). Motivated by the stringent connection reliability and coverage requirements in V2X ,
		this paper presents the first comprehensive and tractable analytical framework for the uplink performance of cellular V2X networks, where the vehicles can deliver its information via vehicle-to-base station (V2B) communication or directly between vehicles in the sidelink, based on their distances and the bias factor. By practically modeling the vehicles on the roads using the doubly stochastic Cox process and the BSs, we derive new association probability of the V2B communication, new success probabilities of the V2B and V2V communications, and overall success probability of the V2X communication, which are validated by the simulations results. Our results reveal the benefits of V2X communication compared to V2V communication in terms of success probability.
new_text: To overcome the limitations of Dedicated Short Range Communications (DSRC), such as short range, lack of supportability for high-density networks, unreliable broadcast services, signal congestion, and connectivity disruptions, Vehicle-to-anything (V2X) communication networks—standardized in 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 14—have recently been introduced to address broader vehicular communication scenarios, including vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), vehicle-to-pedestrian (V2P), and vehicle-to-infrastructure/network (V2I/N). Motivated by the stringent requirements for connection reliability and coverage in V2X, this paper presents the first comprehensive and tractable analytical framework for the uplink performance of cellular V2X networks, where vehicles can transmit their information via vehicle-to-base station (V2B) communication or directly using the sidelink between vehicles, depending on their distances and a bias factor. By practically modeling vehicles on the roads using the doubly stochastic Cox process and base stations (BSs), we derive the new association probability for V2B communication, new success probabilities for V2B and V2V communications, and the overall success probability for V2X communication, validated by simulation results. Our results reveal the benefits of V2X communication compared to V2V communication in terms of success probability.

In <cit.>, an exact closed-form expression for the SCF of FD-MIMO channels constituted by antenna ports arranged as shown in Fig. <ref> was developed using ITU's antenna port radiation pattern expression. The proposed SCF is general in the sense that it can be used for any arbitrary choice of antenna pattern and distribution of azimuth and elevation angles and can be computed using knowledge of the Fourier Series (FS) coefficients of the Power Azimuth Spectrum (PAS) and the Power Elevation Spectrum (PES) of the propagation scenario under study. new_text: Several recent studies have addressed the issue of spatial correlation in Full-Dimension (FD) MIMO antenna systems <cit.>. In <cit.>, researchers derived an exact closed-form expression for the Spatial Correlation Function (SCF) of FD-MIMO channels, where the antenna ports are arranged as depicted in Fig. <ref>. This was achieved by leveraging the International Telecommunication Union's (ITU) standardized antenna port radiation pattern model. The resulting SCF offers a high degree of flexibility, as it can be applied to any arbitrary antenna pattern configuration and any distribution of azimuth and elevation angles. Furthermore, its computation only requires knowledge of the Fourier Series (FS) coefficients of the Power Azimuth Spectrum (PAS) and the Power Elevation Spectrum (PES) of the specific propagation environment being analyzed. A similar analytical approach was subsequently applied in <cit.> to study a Uniform Circular Array (UCA) of antenna ports, again utilizing the ITU-based channel representation framework.

Both copying and anonymization alleviate the data sparsity problem by handling the open-class tokens.
However, the copy mechanism has the following advantages over anonymization:
(1) anonymization requires significant manual work to define the placeholders and heuristic rules both from subgraphs to placeholders and from placeholders to the surface tokens,
(2) the copy mechanism automatically learns what to copy, while anonymization relies on hard rules to cover all types of the open-class tokens,
and (3) the copy mechanism is easier to adapt to new domains and languages than anonymization.
new_text: Copying and anonymization both address the data sparsity issue by managing open-class tokens. Nonetheless, the copy mechanism offers three key advantages over anonymization: first, anonymization demands extensive manual effort to establish placeholder definitions and heuristic rules for mapping subgraphs to placeholders and placeholders to surface tokens; second, copying mechanisms automate the decision-making process, whereas anonymization depends on predefined, rigid rules to handle all open-class token types; and third, copy mechanisms are more easily transferable to new domains and languages compared to anonymization approaches.

The face anti-spoofing is considered as the two-class classification problem in this paper. The two classes are real face class and spoofed face class. Fig. <ref> shows the training and testing framework for real and spoofed face classification using CNN model such as Inception-v3, ResNet50 and ResNet152. During training phase, the CNN model predicts the class score for training images, computes the categorical cross-entropy loss, and finally update the weights of network using gradient descent method by back-propagating the gradient w.r.t. loss function. During training, the CNN predicts class scores for training images, calculates categorical cross-entropy loss, and updates network weights via gradient descent using backpropagation of gradients relative to the loss function. Each epoch employs the learned weights from training images to compute class scores and classification accuracy on validation images. After training completes, the model parameters achieving the highest validation accuracy are selected for testing. In testing, the trained CNN computes class scores for input face images and assigns the class label with the highest score as the prediction.

Measuring utility loss
A user's (noisy) public data are often leveraged by a service provider to provide services. For instance,
in a recommender system (e.g., Amazon, Google Play, Netflix), a user's public data are rating scores or likes/dislikes to items, which are used to recommend items to users that match their personalized preferences. Therefore, utility loss of the public data can essentially be measured by the service quality loss.
Specifically,
 in a recommender system, the decreased accuracy of the recommendations introduced by the added noise can be used as utility loss. However, using such service-dependent utility loss makes the formulated optimization problem computationally intractable.
new_text:
Measuring utility loss  
A user's (noisy) public data are leveraged by service providers to deliver services, such as in recommender systems (e.g., Amazon, Google Play, Netflix), where data like ratings or likes/dislikes are used to recommend items aligned with user preferences. Utility loss can be measured by service quality loss. In recommender systems, reduced recommendation accuracy due to added noise constitutes utility loss. However, service-dependent utility loss renders the optimization problem computationally intractable.

Unless a multitude of users are in the network, the cooperative feedback strategy might not be an effective solution because the multiuser diversity gain is limited in a small-users regime. new_text: Adaptive cooperative feedback algorithm: The number of users in the cooperative feedback strategy is halved by combining two users into a single cooperative unit (CU) to achieve a more accurate channel state information (CSI) selection. However, if the network contains a limited number of users, the cooperative feedback strategy may be ineffective due to the constrained multiuser diversity gain in a small-user regime. Consequently, efficient allocation of limited multiuser resources is essential to acquire accurate CSI while leveraging the benefits of multiuser diversity gain. In this paper, we analyze the sum-rate throughput of the multiuser MIMO system using the proposed algorithm. Based on the analytical studies, we develop a cooperation mode switching criterion to activate the cooperation mode depending on channel environments and network conditions.

old_text: In Phase I, for each possible attribute value, the defender finds a minimum noise such that if we add the noise to the user's public data, then the attacker's classifier predicts the attribute value for the user. From the perspective of adversarial machine learning <cit.>, finding such minimum noise is known as evasion attacks to classifiers. Specifically, in our problem, the defender adds minimum noise to evade the attacker's classifier. However, Phase I faces two challenges. The first challenge is that existing evasion attack methods <cit.> did not consider the unique characteristics of privacy protection, as they were not designed for such purpose. In particular, in defending against attribute inference attacks, different users may have different preferences on what types of noise can be added to their public data. For instance, in recommender systems, a user may prefer modifying its existing rating scores, or adding new rating scores to items the user did not rate before, or combination of them. Existing evasion attack methods did not consider such constraints. To address the challenge, we optimize an existing evasion attack, which was developed by Papernot et al. <cit.>, to incorporate such constraints.

section: Embedding into Extreme points of a Convex Set (EmECS)
old_text:
Let us now compare EmECS and TC-NN.
They both map the original inputs to the extreme points of a convex set—in the case of tile coding, the convex set is a hypercube and the extreme points are its vertices, and they both use the topological structure of the original space to do so. A difference between them is that for EmECS the input transformation is an embedding, whereas for tile coding it is not. As a consequence, in TC-NN, an activation region of a neural node, viewed in the original input space, can (and usually do, as observed in our experiments) contain multiple disconnected components. This suggests that one may be able to further improve the performance of TC-NN by initializing the neural net in a certain way or by monitoring and “pruning” the activation regions of its nodes during training.
Another difference between the two methods is in computational complexity. For TC-NN, suppose each dimension of the inputs can be tile-coded separately; then the dimensionality of the transformed inputs will still depend on the size of the original input space along each dimension. In contrast, EmECS only increases the dimensionality of the inputs by the number of component spaces that are embedded separately (cf. Example <ref>). So, given the same number of hidden-layer nodes, the neural net with EmECS has much fewer parameters than the TC-NN network.
new_text: Both EmECS and TC-NN map inputs to the extreme points of a convex set: tile coding uses a hypercube with vertices as extreme points, while EmECS leverages the original space's topology. A key distinction is that EmECS employs an embedding for input transformation, whereas TC-NN does not. Consequently, in TC-NN, neural nodes' activation regions in the original input space often contain multiple disconnected components (observed experimentally). This suggests potential TC-NN improvements via strategic initialization or activation-region pruning during training. Another difference lies in computational complexity. If each input dimension is tile-coded separately, TC-NN's transformed dimensionality depends on the original space's size per dimension. By contrast, EmECS increases dimensionality only by the number of embedded component spaces (cf. Example <ref>). Thus, for equal hidden-layer node counts, EmECS-based networks have significantly fewer parameters than TC-NN networks.

section: Relating the Metric to Model Development
old_text:
For any practical ML applications, humans usually do the clever part of the programming by defining a template, such as determining the candidature variables for a decision tree, the order of nodes in a neural network, or the possible connectivity of a Bayesian network.
The ML tool then does the tedious and repetitive part of the programming for fine-tuning the template using training data to make a function.
It is known that most commonly used ML platforms, such as forward neural networks, decision trees, random forests, and static Bayesian networks are not Turing complete.
Some others are Turing complete (e.g., recurrent neural networks and dynamic Bayesian networks), but their demand for training data is usually exorbitant.
For any ML model, once a template is determined by the humans, the parameter space that the ML tool can explore is certainly not Turing complete.
This implies that the “intelligence” or “creativity” of the ML tool is restricted to the tedious and repetitive part of the programming for fine-tuning the template.
new_text: In practical ML applications, humans define templates (e.g., selecting variables for decision trees, node order in neural networks, or connectivity in Bayesian networks), while the ML tool handles repetitive fine-tuning with training data. Common ML platforms like forward neural networks, decision trees, random forests, and static Bayesian networks lack Turing completeness, whereas recurrent neural networks and dynamic Bayesian networks are Turing complete but require excessive training data. Once human-defined templates are fixed, the ML tool’s parameter space is non-Turing complete, restricting its “intelligence” to repetitive programming tasks for template optimization.

section: Relating the Metric to Model Development
old_text:
“Model” is an overloaded term. Here we use this term strictly for referring to an executable function in the form of F: ℤ_in→ℤ_out.
Hence, a software program is a model, a machine-learned algorithm (e.g., a decision tree and a neural network) is a model, a human's heuristic function is a model, and so on.
When a data intelligence workflow in Figure <ref> is used to obtain a model, the final alphabet ℤ_n+1 consists of all possible models that meet a set of conditions in a specific application context.
Although the number of letters in a typical model alphabet seems to be extraordinarily large, many letters do not meet the predefined conditions in the specific application context.
Hence, the actual entropy of ℤ_n+1 would be much lower than the maximal amount of entropy derived by enumerating all combinations of the model components.
For example, the number of all possible programs with n or fewer lines of code, the number of all possible neural networks with m or fewer neurons, or the number of all possible Bayesian networks with l or fewer nodes and probability values rounded off to k decimal digits would be intractable, but there will only be proportionally a much smaller subset of programs, neural networks, or Bayesian networks that meet the predefined requirements for such a model in a specific application context.
However, the main challenge in model development is that the strategy for finding an acceptable model while filtering out the extraordinarily large number of unacceptable models is often not well-defined or ineffective.
For example, one often refer to programming as “art” and parameter tuning as “black art”, metaphorically reflecting the lack of well-defined or effective strategy in dealing with the NP search space.
new_text: The term "model" is ambiguously used across disciplines, and here it is defined strictly as an executable function represented by F: ℤ_in→ℤ_out. Under this definition, diverse constructs—such as software programs, machine learning algorithms (e.g., decision trees and neural networks), human-derived heuristic functions, and others—qualify as models. When a data intelligence workflow, as depicted in Figure <ref>, is employed to generate a model, the resulting alphabet ℤ_n+1 encompasses all possible models satisfying a predefined set of application-specific conditions. While the total number of potential elements in such a model alphabet (e.g., all programs with ≤n lines, all neural networks with ≤m neurons, or all Bayesian networks with ≤l nodes and probabilities rounded to k decimal digits) is computationally intractable, the vast majority fail to meet the specified criteria, drastically reducing the actual entropy of ℤ_n+1 compared to the theoretical maximum entropy derived from exhaustive enumeration. The core challenge in model development lies in the absence of a precise or efficient strategy to identify acceptable models while discarding the overwhelming number of invalid ones. This is often reflected metaphorically in descriptions of programming as an "art" and hyperparameter tuning as a "black art," highlighting the intractability of NP search spaces and the lack of systematic solutions for this combinatorial problem.

We analyze the methods using two sets of metrics. First in ResultsBaselines(a) we show metrics from existing work: syntactic validity, novelty (i.e. fraction of sampled molecules not appearing in the training data) and uniqueness (i.e. ratio of sample set size before and after deduplication of identical molecules). Second, in ResultsBaselines(b) we introduce new metrics to measure how well each model captures the distribution of molecules in the training set. new_text: We evaluate the methods using two distinct metric sets. It first encodes the source sentence into a continuous space and then performs decoding based on this space, employing attention to indicate the relevance of each source word to the current translation. new_text: Attention-based neural machine translation (NMT) models utilize an encoder-decoder structure augmented by an attention mechanism. These models operate under the premise that the source sentence and its corresponding target translation exist within a shared continuous space. The process involves encoding the source sentence into this continuous space, followed by decoding that leverages attention weights to determine the relevance of each source word to the target translation. Figure <ref> illustrates the architecture of the attention-based NMT <cit.>, consisting of three main components: the encoder, the attention module, and the decoder.

As RNNs are not good at remembering the old history and cannot consider word relationship either, sometimes conventional NMT cannot get enough source information and hence emphasizes too much on the fluency of the target. As a result, it suffers from meaning-drift and generates “inaccurate” translation. Even so, NMT can still benefit from the recurrence of RNNs. In this paper, we propose to incorporate RNLs into the attentional NMT. The RNs employs CNNs to collect information around one word and explicitly connect each word with all the other words. In this way, it provides the opportunities for NMT to capture relationship between source words and hence leads to a better source representation.
Our method can get better translation on NIST Chinese-English data set and WMT English-German data set and can even outperform the system with supervised syntactic knowledge.
new_text: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), due to their inability to effectively retain long-term memory and model word relationships, often limit conventional neural machine translation (NMT) systems in capturing sufficient source-side context. This limitation causes such systems to prioritize fluency in the target language over accuracy, leading to semantic distortion and mistranslations. However, the sequential processing capabilities of RNNs still offer potential benefits for NMT. To address these challenges, this work introduces a framework integrating recursive neural layers (RNLs) into attention-based NMT architectures. The proposed approach leverages convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract local contextual features for each word while establishing explicit connections between all word pairs, enabling the model to better encode inter-word relationships in the source sentence. This enhancement results in improved source representations, achieving superior translation quality on the NIST Chinese-English and WMT English-German benchmarks, even surpassing systems enhanced with explicit supervised syntactic features.

In contrast, the proposed Rnmt-CNN model, as demonstrated by the boldfaced sections in its outputs, successfully retains and translates a greater proportion of source-side information, including the adversative relations. old_text: Interpreting Equations (<ref>) - (<ref>), we can regard D2L as a simulated annealing algorithm that attempts to find an optimal trade-off between subspace dimensionality and prediction performance. The role of α is an exponential decay factor that allows for interpolation between raw and predicted label assignments according to the degree of dimensional expansion observed over the learning history. Here, dimensional expansion is assessed in terms of the ratio of two average LID scores: the score observed at the current epoch, and the lowest score encountered at earlier epochs. As the learning enters the dimensional expansion stage, this ratio exceeds 1, and the exponential decay factor begins to favor the current predicted label. The complete D2L learning strategy is shown in Algorithm <ref>.
new_text: By analyzing Equations (<ref>) - (<ref>), we can understand the Distilled Dimensional Learning (D2L) algorithm as a variant of simulated annealing, which seeks to balance two competing objectives: reducing the subspace dimensionality of learned representations while maintaining or improving prediction accuracy. Central to this strategy is the parameter α, which functions as an exponential decay factor. Over the course of training, α dynamically adjusts how heavily the model relies on either the original ("raw") label assignments or the model’s own predicted labels. This interpolation is driven by the observed degree of dimensional expansion, which is quantified by comparing two averaged Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) scores. Specifically, the current epoch’s LID score is divided by the minimum LID score recorded during earlier epochs; this ratio serves as a metric for detecting meaningful increases in the complexity of the learned subspace. When dimensional expansion occurs—marked by this ratio rising above 1—the exponential decay factor α shifts the model’s behavior, giving greater weight to the predicted labels as the learning process progresses. This mechanism ensures that the model adapts to increasing representational complexity while mitigating overfitting. A detailed outline of the D2L training procedure is provided in Algorithm <ref>.

In their work, they analyzed the problem of model degradation, which present as saturation and then degradation of accuracy as the network depth increasing. They argued that the degradation problem is an optimization problem, and as the depth of the network increase, the network gets harder to train. It was assumed that the desired mapping of a convnet is comprised of an identity mapping and a residual mapping. Therefore, a deep residual learning framework is proposed. Instead of letting a convnet learn the desired mapping, it fits the residual mapping and uses shortcut connection to merge it with the identity input. With this configuration, the residual network become easy to optimize and can enjoy accuracy gains from greatly increased depth. Veit et al. <cit.> presented a complementary explanation of the increased performance of residual networks, i.e., the residual networks avoid the vanishing gradient problem by introducing the short paths between input and output. Later, He et al. <cit.> analyzed the propagation formulations behind the connection mechanisms of residual networks and proposed a new structure of residual unit. In their work, they extended the depth of a deep residual networks to 1001 layers. Zagoruyko et al. <cit.> investigated the memory consumption of residual networks and propose a novel residual unit that aims to decrease depth and increase width of a deep residual network.
new_text: Residual networks (ResNets) were first introduced by He et al. <cit.> to address a critical challenge in deep learning: the degradation problem. Their analysis revealed that as neural networks grow deeper, training accuracy initially improves but eventually plateaus and then declines—a phenomenon they termed "saturation followed by degradation." He et al. argued that this issue stems from optimization difficulties rather than overfitting, as deeper networks become increasingly challenging to train due to complex error surfaces. To resolve this, they proposed decomposing the desired mapping into two components: an identity mapping (where the output equals the input) and a residual mapping (the difference between the input and output). By reformulating the learning objective to focus on the residual function instead of the full mapping, they developed a framework where shortcut connections bypass non-linear transformations. These skip connections concatenate the input of a layer to its output, enabling gradients to flow unimpeded through the network. This architectural innovation simplified optimization, allowing models to benefit from extreme depth without suffering from degradation. Subsequently, Veit et al. <cit.> offered a complementary perspective, highlighting that residual networks mitigate the vanishing gradient problem by creating direct pathways between input and output layers. Further advances were made by He et al. <cit.>, who mathematically analyzed gradient propagation in ResNets and introduced an improved residual unit design. Their work demonstrated the scalability of the framework by training a residual network with 1,001 layers. Meanwhile, Zagoruyko et al. <cit.> focused on computational efficiency, proposing a modified residual unit that reduces depth while increasing width—thereby lowering memory usage without sacrificing performance. Together, these contributions underscore the versatility of residual learning in addressing both theoretical and practical challenges in deep neural network design.

old_text: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have demonstrated excellent performance in solving many complex problems, and have been widely employed for tasks such as speech recognition <cit.>, computer vision <cit.> and gaming agents <cit.>. DNNs are capable of learning very complex functions, and can generalize well even for a huge number of parameters <cit.>. However, recent studies have shown that DNNs may generalize poorly for datasets which contain a high proportion noisy (incorrect) class labels <cit.>. It is important to gain a fuller understanding of this phenomenon, with a view to development of new training methods that can achieve good generalization performance in the presence of variable amounts of label noise.
new_text: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have shown remarkable capabilities in addressing intricate challenges and are extensively used in applications like speech recognition <cit.>, computer vision <cit.>, and gaming agent development <cit.>. These networks excel at approximating highly complex functions and maintain strong generalization abilities even when utilizing an extensive number of parameters <cit.>. However, recent research indicates that DNNs often exhibit suboptimal generalization when trained on datasets containing a substantial proportion of noisy or incorrect class labels <cit.>. A deeper comprehension of this issue is critical for the creation of novel training methodologies capable of maintaining effective generalization despite varying degrees of label noise.

section: Principles for EA benchmarks on constrained optimization tasks
old_text:
Taking into account that current algorithms have to deal with continuously increasing problem complexity, the constrained functions are ideally designed in a scalable fashion <cit.>. Scalability with respect to the search space dimension, and also the number of constraint functions, permits an understanding of the inherent problem complexity. It further allows assessing these factors of influence on the algorithm performance.
    In this regard, the creation of artificial test problems represents a much easier way to generate constrained test functions.
    On the downside, such test problems are usually easier to solve than real-world problems.
    However, real-world problems are hardly scalable as they often state a purpose-built mathematical representation of a certain application. Modifications in terms of dimension or constraint numbers may result in a change of the problem structure.
    Further, the design of constrained test functions should incorporate characteristics that are commonly observed in real-world situations. This way, algorithmic ideas that proved themselves successful on the benchmark suite can be transferred to corresponding real-world applications with partly similar characteristics.
new_text: Given the increasing complexity of problems, current algorithms require constrained functions to be scalable <cit>. Scalability in search space dimension and constraint count enables understanding of inherent problem complexity and assessment of algorithm performance. Artificial test problems are easier to generate, though they often remain simpler to solve than real-world problems. Real-world problems are purpose-built and rarely scalable; modifying their dimension or constraint count can alter the problem structure. Constrained test functions should incorporate common real-world characteristics to enable transferability of algorithmic ideas between benchmarks and applications with similar features.

old_text: Estimating lighting from images enables a wide range of possible applications, ranging from the realistic insertion of virtual content in augmented reality <cit.>, shadow or highlight removal <cit.>, image matching <cit.>, appearance transfer <cit.> or reflectance and/or geometry estimation <cit.> to name just a few. However, estimating light from an image is a challenging problem. Indeed, light is just one of the many components in the image formation process, which also involves camera parameters, scene material reflectance, the geometry of objects and other post-processing operations. Disentangling one of these components from the others is an ill-posed inverse problem, since infinitely many of their combinations can create the same image.
new_text: Estimating lighting from images enables numerous applications, including the realistic integration of virtual content in augmented reality <cit.>, the removal of unwanted shadows or highlights <cit.>, improved image matching across different conditions <cit.>, and techniques for transferring material appearances between objects <cit.>. Additionally, accurate lighting estimation supports the recovery of surface reflectance properties and three-dimensional scene geometry <cit.>. Despite these potential benefits, solving this problem remains highly challenging. To understand why, consider that an image is not solely shaped by lighting; it also depends on camera-specific parameters (e.g., exposure, sensor characteristics), the reflective properties of materials in the scene, the spatial arrangement of objects, and post-capture image processing. These interdependent factors collectively determine the final image, and isolating one component—such as lighting—requires disentangling them, a task complicated by the lack of unique solutions. Specifically, an infinite number of combinations of lighting, camera settings, and material properties could produce the same visual outcome, rendering the inverse problem inherently ill-posed. This ambiguity limits the reliability of lighting estimation without additional constraints or contextual information.

Modeling and prediction of spatiotemporal behavior of complex physical systems is an important problem in science and engineering. The physical systems are mostly defined by coupled partial differential equations (PDEs). Traditionally, computationally expensive numerical methods running on high-performance computing systems have been used to study these systems. The success of deep learning has motivated recent developments in machine learning algorithms for analysis and forecasting of physical systems, for example, motion tracking <cit.>, video prediction <cit.>, weather forecasting <cit.>, to name a few. In this section, motivated by the discussion in the previous section, we propose a new transceiver architecture for K-user Gaussian MISO BCs in order to enhance the diversity order of the resulting individual user channel under Rayleigh fading as compared to linear ZF downlink beamforming. The proposed architecture is based on adaptive user grouping, which enforces the "angle" between the subspace of each group and the orthogonal complement of the union of all other groups' subspaces to be less than a certain threshold by grouping closely-aligned channel users as one group so that inter-group ZF beamforming does not harm the overall diversity order. On the other hand, to deal with users with closely-aligned channel vectors in each group, we apply superposition coding and SIC to the users in each group, since ZF beamforming cannot handle closely-aligned channel users without degrading the diversity order.
new_text: Motivated by the preceding discussion, we introduce a novel transceiver design for K-user Gaussian multiple-input single-output (MISO) broadcast channels (BCs) to improve the diversity order of individual user channels under Rayleigh fading conditions relative to conventional linear zero-forcing (ZF) downlink beamforming. The core idea relies on adaptive user grouping, where users with highly aligned channel vectors are clustered into groups. This ensures the angular separation between a group’s subspace and the orthogonal complement of the combined subspaces of all other groups remains below a specified threshold, thereby enabling inter-group ZF beamforming without undermining the system's diversity gains. For intra-group users with closely aligned channel vectors, however, ZF beamforming is insufficient to maintain diversity order, so we implement superposition coding and successive interference cancellation (SIC) within each group to resolve interference effectively without sacrificing diversity performance.

We study the verification of safety properties over data-aware processes,
establishing for the first time a correspondence with model checking based on
Satisfiability-Modulo-Theories (SMT). Specifically, we consider a very general
model for artifact-centric systems, following the well-accepted setting
consisting of a read-only relational database, an updatable artifact database,
and rich actions to evolve it. For this model, we study (parameterized) safety
problems where safety is assessed irrespectively of the instance of the
read-only database. We encode such artifact systems into array-based systems,
by representing database relations with sorted unary function symbols. The
encoding pursues the twofold purpose of strengthening relevant decidability
results from the literature, and of exploiting the SMT technology in
implementations. In particular, we show how safety can be checked by adapting
standard backward reachability. The main difficulty towards this goal is that
quantifier elimination techniques for array-based systems cannot be readily
applied in our richer framework. To recover quantifier elimination, we make use
of the model-theoretic machinery of model completions, which represents the
main original contribution of this paper. Using them, we prove that the runs of
artifact systems can be faithfully lifted to richer structures admitting
quantifier elimination. We then give strong evidence that model completeness
turns out to be quite effective to attack the verification of dynamic systems
operating over relational databases. From the foundational point of view, we
isolate three notable classes of artifact-centric systems where backward
reachability guaranteed to terminate. Two of them reconstruct and generalize
the essence of some of the most important decidability results obtained in the
literature, while the third is genuinely novel. As for practical development,
we build on the well-known MCMT model checker for array-based systems, and
extend it make all foundational results presented in the paper fully
operational.
new_text: We study the verification of safety properties over data-aware processes, establishing for the first time a correspondence with model checking based on Satisfiability-Modulo-Theories (SMT). Specifically, we consider a very general model for artifact-centric systems, following the well-established setting comprising a read-only relational database, an updatable artifact database, and rich actions to evolve the latter. For this model, we study (parameterized) safety problems where safety is assessed regardless of the instance of the read-only database. We encode such artifact systems into array-based systems, representing database relations with sorted unary function symbols. The encoding serves the dual purpose of strengthening relevant decidability results from the literature and of exploiting SMT technology in implementations. In particular, we show how safety can be checked by adapting standard backward reachability. The main difficulty toward this goal is that quantifier elimination techniques for array-based systems cannot be readily applied in our richer framework. To recover quantifier elimination, we employ the model-theoretic machinery of model completions, which is the main original contribution of this paper. Using them, we prove that the runs of artifact systems can be faithfully lifted to richer structures admitting quantifier elimination. We then give strong evidence that model completeness turns out to be quite effective in attacking the verification of dynamic systems operating over relational databases. From a foundational perspective, we isolate three notable classes of artifact-centric systems where backward reachability is guaranteed to terminate. Two of them reconstruct and generalize the essence of some of the most important decidability results obtained in the literature, while the third is genuinely novel. As for practical development, we build on the well-known MCMT model checker for array-based systems and extend it to make all foundational results presented in the paper fully operational.

The general idea is to take advantage of the quantum interference terms produced in the quantum-like Bayesian Network to influence the probabilities used to compute the expected utility of some action. This way, we are not proposing a new type of expected utility hypothesis. On the contrary, we are keeping it under its classical definition. new_text: This work aims to expand and investigate the quantum-like Bayesian networks <cit.> framework to address decision-making contexts by integrating the concept of maximum expected utility within influence diagrams. The core approach involves utilizing quantum interference terms generated by the quantum-like Bayesian network to modify the probability distributions used in calculating the expected utility of actions. Importantly, this does not introduce a novel expected utility theory but retains its classical formulation. Instead, it embeds this classical utility framework as an extension within a compact probabilistic graphical model—the influence diagram—where the utility function is determined by the probabilistic interactions inherent in the quantum-like Bayesian network.

old_text: Analyzing job hopping behavior is important for the understanding of job preference and career progression of working individuals. When analyzed at the workforce population level, job hop analysis helps to gain insights of talent flow among different jobs and organizations. Traditionally, surveys are conducted on job seekers and employers to study job hop behavior. Beyond surveys, job hop behavior can also be studied in a highly scalable and timely manner using a data driven approach in response to fast-changing job landscape. Fortunately, the advent of online professional networks (OPNs) has made it possible to perform a large-scale analysis of talent flow. In this paper, we present a new data analytics framework to analyze the talent flow patterns of close to 1 million working professionals from three different countries/regions using their publicly-accessible profiles in an established OPN. As OPN data are originally generated for professional networking applications, our proposed framework re-purposes the same data for a different analytics task. Prior to performing job hop analysis, we devise a job title normalization procedure to mitigate the amount of noise in the OPN data. We then devise several metrics to measure the amount of work experience required to take up a job, to determine that existence duration of the job (also known as the job age), and the correlation between the above metric and propensity of hopping. We also study how job hop behavior is related to job promotion/demotion. Lastly, we perform connectivity analysis at job and organization levels to derive insights on talent flow as well as job and organizational competitiveness.
new_text: Analyzing job-hopping behavior is important for understanding job preferences and career progression of working professionals. When analyzed at the workforce level, job-hopping analysis provides insights into talent flow across various jobs and organizations. Traditionally, surveys are administered to job seekers and employers to analyze job-hopping behavior. Beyond surveys, job-hopping behavior can also be studied in a scalable and timely manner using a data-driven approach in response to the rapidly evolving job market. Fortunately, the advent of online professional networks (OPNs) has enabled large-scale analyses of talent flow. In this paper, we present a new data analytics framework to analyze talent flow patterns of nearly 1 million working professionals from three different countries/regions using their publicly accessible profiles in an established OPN. As OPN data are originally generated for professional networking applications, our proposed framework repurposes the same data for a different analytics task. Prior to performing job-hopping analysis, we devise a job title normalization procedure to reduce noise in the OPN data. We then devise several metrics to measure the work experience required to assume a job, to determine the duration of the job’s existence (also known as the job age), and to assess the correlation between these metrics and the propensity to hop. We also study how job-hopping behavior correlates with job promotion or demotion. Lastly, we perform connectivity analysis at both job and organizational levels to gain insights into talent flow as well as job and organizational competitiveness.

new_text: Each corner corresponds to a single ground-truth positive location, with all remaining locations classified as negative. During training, we modify the penalty for negative samples by applying a reduced loss weight to those within a defined radius around the positive location. This adjustment is motivated by the observation that false corner predictions in proximity to their true counterparts may still produce bounding boxes with sufficient overlap to the ground-truth annotation (Fig. <ref>). The radius is calculated based on object size, ensuring that any two points within this radius generate a bounding box with at least t intersection-over-union (IoU) relative to the ground-truth, where t is fixed at 0.7 across experiments. The penalty reduction is implemented through an unnormalized 2D Gaussian function, e^{-x² + y²/2σ²}, centered at the positive location with σ defined as one-third the radius.

new_text: Figure <ref> illustrates the error-correction performance of TSCF decoding relative to SC, SC-Flip, SC-Flip-EIS <cit.>, and SC-List (L=4) decoding for the PC(1024,512) code. For consistency, a CRC remainder length of C=32 is applied to all decoders except SC, while SC-Flip-based variants use a maximum of T_max=10 iterations. This comparison complements Figure <ref>, which focuses on low-rate codes. In the present case, the performance gap between SC-Flip and the SCO-1 FER curve is narrower. This observation aligns with prior findings that higher code rates reduce the occurrence of E₁ errors, as visually demonstrated in Figure <ref>. The reduced E₁ error count directly limits the effectiveness of flip-based strategies, narrowing discrepancies between decoding methods. Notably, TSCF outperforms SC-Flip and SC-Flip-EIS, with its performance curve closely matching the optimal SCO-1 benchmark. Furthermore, the error-correction capability of SC-List (L=4) is indistinguishable from TSCF, suggesting both approaches achieve comparable trade-offs between complexity and accuracy. Conversely, SC-Flip-EIS exhibits inferior performance compared to SC-Flip. This degradation, as described in <cit.>, arises from the diminishing utility of its search criteria as code rate increases. Higher rates expand the critical set of potential error patterns, and SC-Flip-EIS lacks additional constraints to limit the search space for the optimal flip index, exacerbating its performance shortfall.

It is one of the important puzzles in robotics that has to be solved for creating the next generation of consumer robotics systems. Equipping the robots with observation learning methods will make them capable of learning new skills by only visually observing a demonstrator. Even though researchers have been trying to address this problem for the past several years and are able to come up with several ways of tackling it, the field is still in its infancy and has a lot of room for development, especially in the implicit observation learning branch of observation learning problem. More advanced algorithms and methods have to be developed for giving robotic systems human like learning capability to learn new skills/tasks.

By equipping robots with observation learning methods, they can acquire new skills through visual demonstrations alone. Despite ongoing research over the past decade and diverse approaches developed, the field remains immature, particularly in implicit observation learning. Advanced algorithms must be developed to enable robotic systems to replicate human-like skill acquisition capabilities.

old_text: Observation learning has close similarities to the imitation learning problem (also called as apprenticeship learning/ programming by demonstration) <cit.> <cit.> <cit.> which has been studied extensively using techniques like Inverse reinforcement learning <cit.> and Behavioral cloning <cit.>. It can be seen in literature that these two problems are not well defined from each other separately and the terms are even used interchangeably. But observation learning clearly differs from imitation learning in the aspect that in imitation learning, the learner (the robot) can observe the demonstrator in an ego centric (first person) view, whereas in observation learning the learner can only observe the demonstrator in allocentric (third person) view. Hence the problem of observation learning has to be treated separately from imitation learning and separate tools and techniques have to be developed for solving it efficiently. In the literature, observation learning is also referred to as third person imitation learning <cit.> and imitation from observation <cit.>. But in this article we coin this new term observation learning to differentiate it from imitation learning and indicate the unique nature of this problem. In the following sections we explain in detail the problem of observation learning, along with its mathematical formulation and literature survey.
new_text: Observation learning shares conceptual similarities with the problem of imitation learning, also known as apprenticeship learning or programming by demonstration (cite, cite, cite). Research in this area has extensively explored approaches such as inverse reinforcement learning (cite) and behavioral cloning (cite) to model and replicate observed behaviors. In academic literature, these two learning paradigms are often ambiguously defined, with the terms frequently used interchangeably. However, a critical distinction lies in the perspective from which the demonstrator is observed. In imitation learning, the learner—such as a robot—directly experiences the environment from the same viewpoint as the demonstrator (an egocentric or first-person perspective), enabling direct action replication. In contrast, observation learning involves the learner passively observing the demonstrator from an external, allocentric (third-person) viewpoint, akin to a human watching a video of another performing a task. This fundamental difference in observational perspective introduces unique challenges, such as disentangling the demonstrator’s actions from contextual environmental factors or compensating for limited sensory data. Consequently, observation learning requires distinct methodologies tailored to the constraints of third-person observation. While some studies refer to this problem as "third-person imitation learning" (cite) or "imitation from observation" (cite), this article adopts the term "observation learning" to emphasize its distinct nature and distinguish it from traditional imitation learning frameworks. Subsequent sections will formally define the problem, outline its mathematical formulation, and review relevant prior work.

old_text: We show that decomposition of a matrix as a product of sums can be useful in reducing the complexity of the model and can lead to faster implementations. The proposed approach allow for a flexible tradeoff between the number of trainable parameters and the accuracy of the network. On the other hand, the choice of such a decomposition is crucial and an efficient way to search for the best decomposition is important. The experiments also indicate that the number of trainable parameters (i.e. the degrees of freedom) is more than necessary, leading to overfitting and the need for drop out layers. In addition, product of sums of random matrices appear to be a promising architecture that is applicable to general problem domains. Future work include finding the best decomposition efficiently.
new_text:
Decomposing a matrix as a product of sums can effectively reduce computational complexity and enable faster implementations by breaking down operations into smaller, more manageable components. This approach introduces a key advantage: a flexible tradeoff between the number of trainable parameters in the model and its predictive accuracy. By adjusting the decomposition strategy, practitioners can prioritize efficiency when resources are limited or retain more parameters to enhance performance when needed. However, the choice of decomposition is critical, as suboptimal configurations can undermine these benefits. Therefore, developing an efficient search method for identifying the optimal decomposition is essential to leverage this tradeoff effectively.  

Experimental results further highlight challenges related to model capacity: when the number of trainable parameters exceeds the problem's requirements, the model tends to overfit the training data. This issue necessitates regularization techniques such as dropout layers to maintain generalization. Moreover, the architecture of product-of-sums decompositions demonstrates broader applicability, as it can be adapted to diverse problem domains without structural limitations. These findings underscore the importance of refining decomposition strategies to balance performance and efficiency. Moving forward, prioritizing research on computationally efficient methods for identifying optimal decompositions will be crucial for maximizing the utility of this approach.

During the last two decades, Time Series Classification (TSC) has been considered as one of the most challenging problems in data mining <cit.>.
With the increase of temporal data availability <cit.>, hundreds of TSC algorithms have been proposed since 2015 <cit.>.
Due to their natural temporal ordering, time series data are present in almost every task that requires some sort of human cognitive process <cit.>.
In fact, any classification problem, using data that is registered taking into account some notion of ordering, can be casted as a TSC problem <cit.>.
Time series are encountered in many real-world applications ranging from electronic health records <cit.> and human activity recognition <cit.> to acoustic scene classification <cit.> and steel quality prediction <cit.>.
In addition, the diversity of the UCR archive's datasets' <cit.> types (the largest repository of time series datasets) shows the different applications of the TSC problem.
new_text: Over the past two decades, Time Series Classification (TSC) has emerged as a central challenge in data mining, driven by the complexity of capturing temporal patterns and the variability inherent in sequential data <cit.>. This growth can be attributed to the surge in temporal data availability across domains, which has spurred the development of hundreds of specialized TSC algorithms since 2015 <cit.>. Time series data, characterized by their intrinsic temporal ordering, naturally align with tasks that involve processes requiring sequential reasoning or predictive modeling <cit.>. For instance, any classification problem involving data collected in a time-dependent or ordered manner—such as sensor logs, event sequences, or biological measurements—can be reframed as a TSC task <cit.>. The ubiquity of time series is evident in applications like electronic health records, where patient vitals evolve over time <cit.>; human activity recognition, which relies on sequential movement data <cit.>; acoustic scene classification, where sound patterns unfold dynamically <cit.>; and industrial forecasting, such as predicting steel quality through process variables <cit.>. These examples underscore the versatility of TSC in addressing real-world problems. Furthermore, the diversity of datasets in the UCR archive—the most extensive repository of time series data—mirrors the broad applicability of TSC, as it encompasses data from disciplines as varied as finance, healthcare, and engineering <cit.>.

Local pooling such as average or max pooling takes an input time series and reduces its length T by aggregating over a sliding window of the time series.
For example if the sliding window's length is equal to 3 the resulting pooled time series will have a length equal to T/3 - this is only true if the stride is equal to the sliding window's length.
With a global pooling operation, the time series will be aggregated over the whole time dimension resulting in a single real value.
In other words, this is similar to applying a local pooling with a sliding window's length equal to the length of the input time series.
Usually a global aggregation is adopted to reduce drastically the number of parameters in a model thus decreasing the risk of overfitting while enabling the use of CAM to explain the model's decision <cit.>.

Metrics of interest
The two metrics of interest in video analytics applications are inference accuracy and cost of processing. Inference accuracy is a function of the models used for the analytics, the labeled data used for training, and video characteristics such as frame resolution and frame rate <cit.>. All the above metrics also influence the cost of processing – larger models and higher quality videos result in higher accuracy, at the price of increased resource consumption or, equivalently, processing latency.
