Out of the 18 classifiers evaluated by <cit.>, we have chosen the four best performing algorithms: (1) Elastic Ensemble (EE) proposed by <cit.> is an ensemble of nearest neighbor classifiers with 11 different time series similarity measures; (2) Bag-of-SFA-Symbols (BOSS) published in <cit.> forms a discriminative bag of words by discretizing the time series using a Discrete Fourier Transform and then building a nearest neighbor classifier with a bespoke distance measure; (3) Shapelet Transform (ST) developed by <cit.> extracts discriminative subsequences (shapelets) and builds a new representation of the time series that is fed to an ensemble of 8 classifiers; (4) Collective of Transformation-based Ensembles (COTE) proposed by <cit.> is basically a weighted ensemble of 35 TSC algorithms including EE and ST.
In addition to these four state of the art classifiers, we included the classic NN-DTW (with a warping window set through cross-validation on the training set) since it is still one of the most popular methods for classifying time series data <cit.>.
Finally, we added a recent approach named Proximity Forest (PF) which is similar to Random Forest but replaces the attribute based splitting criteria by a random similarity measure chosen out of EE's elastic distances <cit.>.
new_text:
We selected four of the top-performing algorithms from the 18 classifiers evaluated in <cit.> to ensure robust comparison. First, the Elastic Ensemble (EE) <cit.>, an ensemble method combining multiple nearest neighbor classifiers, utilizes 11 distinct time series similarity measures to enhance prediction accuracy. Second, the Bag-of-SFA-Symbols (BOSS) <cit.> creates a discriminative "bag of words" representation by applying a Discrete Fourier Transform to discretize time series, followed by a custom distance-based nearest neighbor classification. Third, the Shapelet Transform (ST) <cit.> identifies informative subsequences (called shapelets), transforms the original time series into a shapelet-based representation, and inputs this into an ensemble of eight classifiers. Lastly, the Collective of Transformation-based Ensembles (COTE) <cit.> integrates a diverse set of 35 time series classification (TSC) algorithms—including EE and ST—into a weighted ensemble, leveraging their combined strengths.  

To contextualize these state-of-the-art methods, we included the classical Nearest Neighbor with Dynamic Time Warping (NN-DTW) <cit.>, where the warping window size was optimized through cross-validation on the training set. This algorithm remains widely used due to its interpretability and effectiveness in time series classification. For completeness, we also incorporated Proximity Forest (PF) <cit.>, a novel approach that adapts the Random Forest framework by substituting attribute-based splitting with similarity measures derived from EE’s elastic distance measures. This variation explores the potential of proximity-based decision trees in time series domains.

old_text: The problem of multi-fidelity modeling <cit.> arises in the broad range of applied disciplines, such as engineering design, medical diagnostics, and even product development, when an object of interest can be approximated with a cheaper, yet typically less reliable alternative. The main motivation behind multi-fidelity modeling is that low-fidelity data can bring additional benefits in terms of accuracy/cost trade-off, when it is used properly along with high-fidelity data <cit.>. For example, article <cit.> demonstrates that high-quality linguistic annotation results can be achieved with much lower expenses when non-expert annotators i.e. low-fidelity data are employed. The authors concluded that four non-experts per item were enough on average to achieve an expert-level annotation quality for their tasks, although this requirement can be relaxed further, by requiring multiple annotations only for a fraction of the dataset. Similarly in engineering design <cit.>, a high-fidelity source of data can be a physical experiment, whereas a low-fidelity can be a mathematical model or a computer simulation.
new_text: The problem of multi-fidelity modeling <cit.> arises across diverse applied disciplines—including engineering design, medical diagnostics, and product development—when a target system can be approximated using a lower-cost but less reliable method. This approach addresses scenarios where high-fidelity data, such as physical experiments or expert annotations, are expensive, time-consuming, or resource-intensive to obtain. By integrating low-fidelity data, which is often more abundant and cheaper to collect, multi-fidelity modeling aims to enhance the overall accuracy or efficiency of a solution while balancing the inherent trade-offs between cost and reliability. For instance, in linguistic annotation, studies <cit.> show that high-quality results traditionally requiring expert labor can be achieved at lower costs by leveraging inputs from non-expert annotators—representing low-fidelity data. In one example, researchers demonstrated that assigning four non-expert annotators to each item yielded results comparable to those of a single expert. Importantly, this approach can be further optimized: instead of requiring multiple annotations for the entire dataset, annotations can be prioritized for specific subsets, reducing costs without sacrificing accuracy. A similar logic applies to engineering design <cit.>, where high-fidelity data may involve expensive physical experiments, while low-fidelity alternatives include mathematical models or simulations. By strategically combining these data sources, engineers can iteratively refine designs at a fraction of the cost of relying solely on high-fidelity methods.

old_text: No sensing: Player j only observes r^j(t). This is the most difficult case, as there is no extra observation. Indeed, a low empirical performance of an arm can either be a consequence of a low mean μ_k or, alternatively, to a high frequency of collisions. Notice that, the better an arm, the more a player tends to play it. But if all players have the same behavior, then the better an arm is, the more collisions there will be. The collision factor could balance off the intrinsic performance of an arm. This is the main difficulty of multiplayer MAB, especially without sensing.
new_text: In the absence of sensing, each player j can only observe their own reward r^j(t), making this the most challenging setting due to the lack of additional observational data. A low observed performance for an arm may result either from a genuinely low mean reward μ_k or from frequent collisions with other players. Notably, better-performing arms are more likely to be selected by each player. However, if all players exhibit this behavior, the same arms that yield higher rewards also become hotspots for collisions, exacerbating their frequency. This creates a situation where the impact of collisions may effectively counteract an arm's inherent performance characteristics. This interplay between collisions and reward maximization constitutes a fundamental challenge in multi-player MAB settings, particularly when sensing mechanisms are absent.

Place recognition refers to the task of identifying a real world location from images of said place - essentially location classification. Ideally this process should be invariant to various image and world properties such as camera position, orientation, weather conditions, etc. Visual localization is the process of identifying the camera location (and sometimes orientation) either relative to a local or global map. One way of achieving this is via image-retrieval: finding the most similar image with a known pose to a unknown query. In such a case, invariance to camera orientation/position are not desired, as these are critical to calculating pose as accurately as possible.
new_text: Place recognition involves identifying a location from images—essentially location classification—and ideally remains invariant to factors such as camera position, orientation, and weather. Visual localization determines the camera’s location (and sometimes orientation) relative to a local or global map. One approach is image retrieval: finding the most similar image with a known pose to an unknown query. Here, invariance to camera orientation and position is undesirable, as these parameters are critical to accurately determining the pose.

For instance, the average voice pitch in the fundamental frequency sequence is highly speaker-dependent. old_text: When seeking an algorithm that satisfies all four desiderata D1–4, inevitably some tradeoff must be made. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) naturally satisfies D1–2, and this has buoyed recent advances in deep learning. Yet when it comes to large neural network models with hundreds of millions of parameters, distributed SGD can suffer large communication overheads. To make matters worse, any faulty SGD worker can corrupt the entire model at any time by sending an infinite gradient, meaning that SGD without modification is not robust.
new_text: Meeting all four desiderata (D1–D4) with a single algorithm inherently involves trade-offs. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) inherently satisfies D1–D2, contributing to its central role in recent deep learning advancements. However, for large neural networks with hundreds of millions of parameters, distributed SGD incurs significant communication costs. Compounding this issue, a single malfunctioning SGD worker can compromise the entire model by transmitting infinite gradients, highlighting the lack of robustness in unmodified SGD.

In <cit.>, the controller determines a dynamic reporting threshold that allows for reduced communication overheads. It is unclear how to utilize the method in the sliding window model. Yet, the optimization goal is very similar in essence to this work: maximize accuracy and minimize traffic overheads. Stroboscope <cit.> is another network-wide measurement system that also guarantees that the overheads adhere to a strict budget.
FlowRadar <cit.> avoids communication during the entire measurement period.
Instead, the state of each measurement point is shared at the end of the measurement. Thus, FlowRadar follows the Interval pattern, which we showed to be slow to detect new heavy hitters.
new_text: In <cit.>, a dynamic reporting threshold is implemented by a controller to minimize communication overheads by adjusting reporting criteria in real-time. However, applying this method within the sliding window model remains uncertain, as the model’s focus on time-bounded data processing may conflict with the dynamic threshold’s continuous adaptation. Despite this uncertainty, the core objective of this method—balancing high accuracy with low network traffic—parallels the optimization goals of this work. A different approach is taken by Stroboscope <cit.>, a network-wide system that enforces strict overhead limits by design, ensuring all measurement data stays within predefined resource constraints. FlowRadar <cit.>, on the other hand, operates without any communication during the active measurement phase, instead aggregating and sharing data only at the conclusion of each measurement interval. This strategy aligns with what we term the Interval pattern, a method prioritizing communication reduction at the cost of delayed responsiveness. Our analysis demonstrates that this delay hinders the system’s ability to quickly identify emerging heavy hitters, as updates occur only after fixed intervals rather than in response to real-time traffic patterns.

Given these theoretical advances in IL, it is natural to ask whether similar ideas can be extended to RL.
In this paper, we show that RL can also be formulated as a predictable online learning problem, and
 provide a first-order learning framework, PicCoLO (PredICtor-COrrector poLicy Optimization), for both RL and IL.
PicCoLO is a meta-algorithm: it takes a standard online learning algorithm designed for adversarial problems (like Adam <cit.>) as input and returns a new hybrid algorithm that can use model information to accelerate convergence. This new “PicCoLOed” algorithm optimizes the policy by recursively repeating two steps:
In the Prediction Step, the learner uses a predictive model to estimate the gradient of the next loss function and then applies it to update the policy; in the Correction Step, the learner runs the updated policy in the environment, receives the true gradient, and then corrects the policy using the gradient error.
We note that PicCoLO is an approach orthogonal to control variate methods; it can still improve learning even if the true gradient is noise-free (see Section <ref>).
new_text: With recent theoretical progress in imitation learning (IL), a logical question arises: can analogous concepts be applied to reinforcement learning (RL)? Here, we demonstrate that RL can be reformulated within a predictable online learning framework and introduce PicCoLO (PredICtor-COrrector poLicy Optimization), a first-order learning framework applicable to both RL and IL. PicCoLO operates as a meta-algorithm, accepting standard adversarial online learning algorithms (e.g., Adam <cit.>) as input and generating a hybrid algorithm that leverages model-based predictions to accelerate convergence. The resulting "PicCoLOed" algorithm iteratively executes two phases: (1) A Prediction Step, where a predictive model estimates the gradient of the subsequent loss function and applies it to update the policy; and (2) A Correction Step, where the updated policy is executed in the environment to obtain the true gradient, which is then used to correct the policy via gradient error. Notably, PicCoLO operates independently of control variate techniques and retains effectiveness even when true gradients are noise-free (Section <ref>).

The design of PicCoLO is made possible by a novel reduction that converts a given predictable online learning problem into a new adversarial problem, so that standard online learning algorithms can be applied optimally without referring to specialized algorithms.
Thus, we can treat PicCoLO as an automatic process for designing new algorithms that safely leverages imperfect predictive models (such as off-policy gradients or gradients simulated through dynamics models) to speed up learning. Particularly, MoBIL is its special case when the base algorithm is FTRL.
new_text: The design of PicCoLO is enabled through a novel reduction that transforms a given predictable online learning problem into an adversarial problem, enabling standard online learning algorithms to be applied optimally without requiring specialized algorithms. This approach allows us to view PicCoLO as an automated framework for algorithm design that safely incorporates imperfect predictive models—such as off-policy gradients, gradients simulated through dynamics models, or other imperfect predictive models—to accelerate learning. Notably, MoBIL emerges as a specific instance of PicCoLO when the base algorithm is FTRL.

old_text: Failures in scientific workflows increase the makes­pan and waste a lot of workforce and time. The different types of failures that can occur during an execution are task failures, VM failures and workflow-level failures. Fault tolerance for scientific workflows can be provided either at the task-level or workflow-level <cit.>. Task-level scheduling techniques involve retry, checkpointing and the use of alternate resources for the same task. On the other hand, workflow level scheduling involves the usage of alternate tasks, redundancy, user-defined exception handling and rescue workflows. In this paper, a new fault tolerant workflow scheduling approach called Checkpointing and Replication based on Clustering Heuristics (CRCH) is proposed. It uses replication, resubmission, checkpointing and provides fault-tolerance in an efficient manner.

In this paper, we presented an unsupervised learning framework for jointly predicting depth, optical flow and moving object segmentation masks. Specifically, we formulated the geometrical relationship between all these tasks, where every pixels is explained by either rigid motion, non-rigid/object motion or occluded/non-visible regions. We used a holistic motion parser (HMP) to parse pixels in an image to different regions, and design various losses to encourage the depth, camera motion and optical flow consistency. Finally, an iterative learning pipeline is presented to effectively train all the models.
We conducted comprehensive experiments to evaluate the performance of our system. On the KITTI dataset, our approach achieves SOTA performance on all the tasks of depth estimation, optical flow estimation and 2D moving object segmentation. Our framework can be extended to other motion video data sets containing deformable and articulated non-rigid objects such as MoSeg <cit.> etclet@token.., and multiple object segmentation <cit.>, yielding a more comprehensive understanding of the videos.
new_text: We propose an unsupervised learning framework for jointly predicting depth, optical flow, and moving object segmentation masks by modeling the geometric relationships among these tasks, categorizing each pixel as rigid motion, non-rigid/object motion, or occluded/non-visible. A holistic motion parser (HMP) partitions image pixels into distinct regions, while tailored losses enforce depth, camera motion, and optical flow consistency. The framework integrates an iterative learning pipeline to train all components effectively. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on KITTI for depth estimation, optical flow estimation, and 2D moving object segmentation. The framework is extendable to datasets containing deformable/articulated non-rigid objects, such as MoSeg <cit.> and multiple object segmentation <cit.>, enabling a more comprehensive video analysis.

If we build the tree incrementally in a left-to-right manner from the labels, if we find a negative n_i, we will need to attach the word w_i+1 (or a new subtree with that word as its leftmost leaf) to the (-n_i+2)th node in the path going from w_i to the root. Any smaller value would leave this node without enough children (which cannot be fixed later due to the left-to-right order in which we build the tree), and any larger value would create a node with too many children.
Thus, we can map negative values to a single label.
Figure <ref> shows an example for the case of binarized trees (k=2).
new_text: For trees where all branchings have exactly *k* children, a more efficient linearization is possible, as the fixed branching factor reduces the complexity of label encoding. This approach leverages the relative scale encoding method, adapting it to k-ary tree structures. Here, the tree is constructed incrementally in a left-to-right order based on the sequence of labels. When a negative value *n*<sub>*i*</sub> is encountered during this process, it indicates the position to which the next word *w*<sub>*i+1*</sub>—or a new subtree rooted at this word—should be attached. Specifically, *w*<sub>*i+1*</sub> is connected to the (*−n*<sub>*i*</sub> + 2)<sup>th</sup> node along the path from *w*<sub>*i*</sub> to the root. This logic hinges on the constraint that each node must have exactly *k* children. Under this constraint, only one negative *n*<sub>*i*</sub> value is valid: the one that points to the first node along the path that still lacks its *k*<sup>th</sup> child. Smaller values would leave this node with insufficient children, and since the tree is built left-to-right, no future insertion can resolve this underfill. Conversely, larger values would prematurely assign children to nodes already fully populated, violating the *k*-child limit. Because this single valid negative value uniquely identifies the insertion point, it can be encoded with a single label. This reduction in label diversity directly contributes to the improved efficiency. An example of this method is illustrated in Figure <ref> for binarized trees, where *k* = 2.

Sentence embeddings have become an essential part of today's natural language processing (NLP) systems, especially together advanced deep learning methods. Although pre-trained sentence encoders are available in the general domain, none exists for biomedical texts to date. In this work, we introduce BioSentVec: the first open set of sentence embeddings trained with over 30 million documents from both scholarly articles in PubMed and clinical notes in the MIMIC-III Clinical Database. We evaluate BioSentVec embeddings in two sentence pair similarity tasks in different text genres. Our benchmarking results demonstrate that the BioSentVec embeddings can better capture sentence semantics compared to the other competitive alternatives and achieve state-of-the-art performance in both tasks. We expect BioSentVec to facilitate the research and development in biomedical text mining and to complement the existing resources in biomedical word embeddings.

new_text: Data placement is regulated by various policies that determine memory allocation strategies. A prevalent setup for high-performance computing <cit.>, employed in our analysis, utilizes "quadrant mode." This mode partitions physical cores into four logical segments, each allocated two memory controllers. Each segment functions as an independent Non-Uniform Memory-Access (NUMA) node, enabling operating systems to optimize data locality. Table <ref> compares processors, emphasizing key distinctions, particularly in their Floating-Point Units (FPUs). The KNL chip features two 512-bit AVX vector units, delivering 32 double-precision and 64 single-precision operations per cycle across its 64 cores, yielding [2.6]Tflop/s for double-precision and [5.3]Tflop/s for single-precision performance. The KNM variant replaces one AVX unit with two Virtual Neural Network Instruction (VNNI) units, which support hybrid-precision FMA and single-precision operations but lack double-precision capabilities. This redesign reduces KNM’s capacity to [1.7]Tflop/s for double-precision and increases it to [13.8]Tflop/s for single-precision computations. Consequently, KNM achieves 2.59× higher single-precision throughput compared to KNL, while KNL maintains 1.54× greater double-precision capacity than KNM.

In this paper, we propose a dual-attention hierarchical recurrent neural network for dialogue act classification. Our model is partially inspired by the observation that conversational utterances are normally associated with both a dialogue act and a topic, where the former captures the social act and the latter describes the subject matter. However, such a dependency between dialogue acts and topics has not been utilised by most existing systems for DA classification.
With a novel dual task-specific attention mechanism, our model is able, for utterances, to capture information about both dialogue acts and topics, as well as information about the interactions between them. We evaluate the performance of our model on two publicly available datasets, i.e., Switchboard and DailyDialog. Experimental results show that by modelling topic as an auxiliary task, our model can significantly improve DA classification.

Reinforcement learning is the problem where an agent must interact with an unknown environment through trial-and-error in order to maximize its cumulative reward <cit.>. We first consider the standard setting where the environment can be formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the 4-tuple (𝒮, 𝒜, 𝒫, ℛ). At a given timestep t, the environment exists in state s_t ∈𝒮. The agent takes an action a_t ∈𝒜 according to policy π(a_t|s_t), causing the environment to transition to a new state s_t+1∼𝒫(s_t, a_t) and yield a reward r_t ∼ℛ(s_t, a_t, s_t+1). Hence, the agent's goal can be formalized as finding a policy that maximizes the expected discounted return 𝔼_π[ ∑_i=0^Hγ^i r_i ] up to some horizon H. The discount γ∈ [0, 1] affects the relative importance of future rewards and allows the sum to converge in the case where H →∞, γ≠ 1. An important property of the MDP is that every state s ∈𝒮 satisfies the Markov property; that is, the agent needs to consider only the current state s_t when selecting an action in order to perform optimally.

At any given timestep *t*, the environment resides in state *sₜ* ∈ 𝒮. The agent selects an action *aₜ* ∈ 𝒜 according to policy *π(aₜ | sₜ)*, transitioning the environment to a new state *sₜ₊₁* ∼ 𝒫(*sₜ*, *aₜ*) and generating a reward *rₜ* ∼ ℛ(*sₜ*, *aₜ*, *sₜ₊₁*). The agent’s objective is formalized as finding a policy that maximizes the expected discounted return 𝔼*ₚ*[∑_{i=0}^H γ^i r_i] over a finite horizon *H*. The discount factor γ ∈ [0, 1] determines the relative weight of future rewards and ensures convergence when *H* → ∞ and γ ≠ 1. A defining characteristic of the MDP is that all states *s* ∈ 𝒮 satisfy the Markov property: the agent requires only the current state *sₜ* to make optimal decisions at each step.

We now consider the problem of extending the packing bound over the whole
	graph (rather than just neighbourhoods of R and B). This bound is based
	on a similar approach taken in <cit.>. Intuitively, the flow
	bound might be small if there is a chokepoint between R and B. However,
	the actual optimal bipartitioning might be much larger if this
	chokepoint is biased towards one of R, B. We would like to correct for
	this by adding another bound which considers the
	sizes of the neighbourhoods of R and B rather than their

new_text: We now address the challenge of extending the packing bound from localized neighborhoods of sets R and B to the entire graph. This generalization relies on a method analogous to that used in <cit.>, where structural constraints are analyzed to derive bounds. A critical insight is that the flow bound—representing the maximum possible partitioning—can be artificially low when a "chokepoint" (a narrow bottleneck) exists between R and B. Such chokepoints restrict the flow by limiting the capacity of connections between the two sets. However, the actual optimal bipartitioning may be significantly larger if the chokepoint disproportionately favors one set (e.g., R being overrepresented), leading to a skewed estimation. To rectify this bias, we propose introducing an additional bound that evaluates the sizes of R’s and B’s neighborhoods instead of relying solely on their direct connectivity. This approach compensates for potential imbalances introduced by chokepoints, ensuring a more accurate assessment of the maximum partitioning capacity across the graph.

new_text: Recent improvements in computational capacity have been significantly driven by the development of accelerators or co-processors—such as general-purpose graphics processing units (GPGPUs) or the Intel Xeon Phi manycore processor—that enhance the computational capabilities of the CPU. These devices have evolved in power and complexity over the last two decades, leading to increased reliance on them to enable efficient floating-point computation on HPC systems <cit.>. As these systems grow in complexity, computational power, and physical size, latency and bandwidth costs limit the performance of applications requiring regular inter-node communication—such as CFD simulations. Bandwidth refers to the amount of data that can be transferred per unit time, while latency is the fixed cost of a communication event: the time required for the leading bit of a message to travel. Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) on HPC systems using explicit numerical methods requires domain decomposition (a strategy for dividing the computational domain across processors), which necessitates inter-node communication of small data packets for boundary information at every time step. The frequency of these communication events renders their fixed cost—latency—a significant barrier to the performance of these simulations.

new_text: In prior work, we explored strategies for optimizing the memory hierarchy on a single GPU within a swept time-space solver designed for stencil computations. This approach builds on foundational research by Alhubail et al., who introduced the swept rule for CPU-based systems in one and two dimensions. Separately, Wang demonstrated that complex numerical schemes could be decomposed into simpler “atomic” update formulas—sequences of operations requiring only a three-point stencil—which are well-suited for the swept rule. In this study, we apply this decomposition method, termed “lengthening,” in the implementation of the swept rule and directly compare its performance to an alternative approach we previously developed, called “flattening,” which was tailored for GPU-only execution. The latter technique, discussed in our earlier GPU-centric investigation, simplifies complex schemes through a different optimization strategy. Section [reference] provides a quantitative evaluation of how these two methods perform in practice. Additionally, Alhubail and Wang extended these ideas by using the swept rule to automatically generate C source code for solving partial differential equations such as the heat and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations on CPU-based systems. Collectively, these contributions form the theoretical and methodological foundation for the current work, which aims to expand and refine their approach.

new_text: We begin by comparing our proposed IncReg method with two alternative group regularization approaches—specifically, structured sparsity learning (SSL) <cit.> and automated filter pruning (AFP) <cit.>—using a convolutional neural network (ConvNet) <cit.> trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset <cit.>. In this evaluation, we investigate both row-wise and column-wise sparsity patterns to assess how different regularization strategies affect model performance. All experiments are implemented using the Caffe framework <cit.>, ensuring a consistent experimental setup. As summarized in Table <ref>, our results demonstrate that IncReg consistently achieves superior speedup ratios and classification accuracy compared to SSL and AFP under constant regularization constraints. While AFP matches IncReg’s performance at moderate speedups (approximately 4.5×), a significant divergence emerges at higher pruning levels (around 8×–10×). At these larger speedup ratios, IncReg outperforms AFP by a considerable margin. This performance gap likely stems from IncReg’s incremental regularization approach, which gradually introduces sparsity constraints during training. This gradual adaptation allows the network to retain critical features and maintain representational capacity, particularly when aggressive pruning is applied. In contrast, constant regularization methods like AFP impose fixed sparsity levels from the outset, which may hinder the network’s ability to compensate for removed parameters at high pruning ratios.

old_text: There are mainly two categories of structured pruning. One is importance-based methods, which prune weights in groups based on some established importance criteria <cit.>. The other is regularization-based methods, which add group regularization terms to learn structured sparsity <cit.>. Existing group regularization approaches mainly focus on the regularization form (e.g. Group LASSO <cit.>) to learn structured sparsity, while ignoring the influence of regularization factor. In particular, they tend to use a large and constant regularization factor for all weight groups in the network <cit.>, which has two problems. Firstly, this `one-size-fit-all' regularization scheme has a hidden assumption that all weights in different groups are equally important, which however does not hold true, since weights with larger magnitude tend to be more important than those with smaller magnitude. Secondly, few works have noticed that the expressiveness of CNNs is so fragile <cit.> during pruning that it cannot withstand a large penalty term from beginning, especially for large pruning ratios and compact networks (like ResNet <cit.>). AFP <cit.> was proposed to solve the first problem, while ignored the second one. In this paper, we propose a new regularization-based method named IncReg to incrementally learn structured sparsity.
new_text: Structured pruning is broadly categorized into two main types: importance-based approaches and regularization-based techniques. Importance-based methods involve removing weights in groups according to predefined criteria for significance <cit.>, whereas regularization-based methods introduce group-specific penalties to encourage structured sparsity <cit.>. Current group regularization strategies predominantly concentrate on the penalty structure—such as Group LASSO <cit.>—to achieve structured sparsity, often overlooking the impact of the regularization coefficient. Specifically, these methods frequently apply a uniform and high regularization coefficient across all weight groups within the network <cit.>, leading to two critical issues. First, the "one-size-fits-all" approach implicitly assumes that all weight groups have equal significance, which is not accurate, as weights with higher magnitudes generally contribute more to model performance. Second, limited research has recognized that CNNs are inherently fragile <cit.> during pruning, making them vulnerable to large penalty terms early in training, particularly when pruning ratios are high or when working with compact architectures like ResNet <cit.>. AFP <cit.> was developed to address the first issue but did not consider the second. To resolve these challenges, this study introduces IncReg, a novel regularization-based approach that incrementally learns structured sparsity.

old_text: We view molecular optimization as a graph-to-graph translation problem. The goal is to learn to map from one molecular graph to another with better properties based on an available corpus of paired molecules. Since molecules can be optimized in different ways, there are multiple viable translations for each input graph. A key challenge is therefore to model diverse translation outputs. Our primary contributions include a junction tree encoder-decoder for learning diverse graph translations along with a novel adversarial training method for aligning distributions of molecules. Diverse output distributions in our model are explicitly realized by low-dimensional latent vectors that modulate the translation process. We evaluate our model on multiple molecular optimization tasks and show that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin.
new_text: Molecular optimization is approached as a graph-to-graph translation task, where the objective is to learn mappings from one molecular graph to another with improved properties using a dataset of paired molecular examples. Given the multiple valid ways to optimize molecules, each input graph can generate several suitable translations, necessitating the ability to model diverse output distributions as a critical challenge. To address this, we introduce a junction tree encoder-decoder architecture for learning diverse graph translations and propose a novel adversarial training strategy to align molecular distribution patterns. Diverse translation outcomes are enabled by low-dimensional latent vectors that directly influence the translation process. Evaluation on various molecular optimization benchmarks demonstrates substantial performance gains over prior state-of-the-art methods.

Following their work, we interpret each molecule as having been built from subgraphs (clusters of atoms) chosen from a vocabulary of valid chemical substructures. The clusters form a junction tree representing the scaffold structure of molecules (Figure <ref>), which is an important factor in drug design.
Molecules are decoded hierarchically by first generating the junction trees and then combining the nodes of the tree into a molecule. This coarse-to-fine approach allows us to easily enforce the chemical validity of generated graphs, and provides an enriched representation that encodes molecules at different scales.
new_text: Building on prior research, we model molecular structures by decomposing each molecule into discrete subgraphs—collections of connected atoms—selected from a predefined set of chemically valid substructures. These subgraphs are organized into a junction tree, a hierarchical framework that captures the scaffold architecture of the molecule (Figure <ref>). The scaffold is a critical component in drug design, defining the molecule's core structural framework and its interactions with biological targets. The decoding process follows a two-step strategy: first, the model generates a valid junction tree representing the scaffold, then assembles individual atomic clusters by connecting the nodes of this tree into a complete molecular graph. This coarse-to-fine approach ensures chemical validity is enforced at the scaffold level prior to incorporating finer atomic details, allowing stepwise validation that prevents invalid configurations. The hierarchical representation further enables encoding molecular information at multiple abstraction levels—from high-level scaffold architecture to detailed atomic interactions—providing a more comprehensive characterization of molecular properties.

new_text: When working in high-dimensional latent spaces, the internal encoding of data in variational autoencoders unexpectedly becomes sparse. We highlight and investigate this phenomenon, which suggests that, at least for a given architecture, an intrinsic internal dimension of data may exist. This insight allows us to assess whether the network has sufficient internal capacity—either by augmenting it to achieve sparsity or conversely by reducing the network's dimensions through the removal of links to zeroed-out neurons. Sparsity also explains the reduced variability in random generative sampling from the latent space that is sometimes observed with variational autoencoders.

By Definition <ref>, θ' ∉ H(θ, F) if and only if there exists an allocation rule f ∈ F such that θ· f(θ') > θ· f(θ).
By the taxation principle, we can represent f by a list of allocations and the price for each allocation. Construct f' from f by eliminating all allocations except f(θ) and f(θ') from this list. Then f' is implementable-with-payments (those from the list), f'(θ) = f(θ), f'(θ') = f(θ'), and f' ∈F̅. Thus θ' ∉H(θ, F̅). By Corollary <ref>, θ' ∉H(θ, F̅^θ).

According to Definition <ref>, this occurs if and only if there exists an allocation rule f ∈ F such that θ · f(θ') > θ · f(θ). The taxation principle allows us to represent f as a list of allocations and their corresponding prices. Construct f' by removing all allocations from this list except those associated with f(θ) and f(θ'). The resulting mechanism f' is implementable with payments corresponding to the retained allocations, satisfies f'(θ) = f(θ) and f'(θ') = f(θ'), and belongs to F̅. Consequently, θ' is not in H(θ, F̅). In order to assess the effect of batch normalisation (BN) before and after the activation function, two FPD-M-net networks were trained: one with BN after ReLU activation (similar to M-net) and one with BN before ReLU activation. For convenience, the BN after and before ReLU activation network called as FPD-M-net-A and FPD-M-net-B, respectively. Both the networks were trained with the same settings as described in section <ref>. The quantitative results for validation and test set are presented in Table <ref>. Results indicate that the FPD-M-net-B is better in PSNR and MSE metric than FPD-M-net-A, whereas for SSIM the FPD-M-net-A has slightly better than FPD-M-net-B. Overall FPD-M-net-B has a fairly good results relative to FPD-M-net-A. Hence, BN before ReLU activation function is used in FPD-M-net.
new_text: To evaluate the impact of batch normalization (BN) placement relative to the ReLU activation function, two variants of the FPD-M-net architecture were trained. The first model applied BN after ReLU, aligning with the structure of the standard M-net, while the second incorporated BN before ReLU. For clarity, these configurations were labeled FPD-M-net-A (BN after ReLU) and FPD-M-net-B (BN before ReLU). Both networks were trained under identical conditions, following the methodology detailed in section <ref>, to ensure a direct comparison. Quantitative performance metrics for both validation and test sets are summarized in Table <ref>. The results revealed distinct advantages for each configuration: FPD-M-net-B achieved higher PSNR values and lower MSE, indicating better image reconstruction accuracy, whereas FPD-M-net-A showed a marginal improvement in SSIM, a perceptual quality metric. Despite the slight SSIM edge of FPD-M-net-A, the overall performance of FPD-M-net-B was stronger, particularly in metrics critical to the task. These findings justify the adoption of BN before ReLU in the final FPD-M-net architecture.

old_text: The reason for our belief that this is a core problem lies with the topology of data as the dimensionality grows. As the number of dimensions increases for a given set of data, many intuitive analytical techniques such as Euclidian norms and Gaussian kernels become inappropriate as the unit radius hypervolume goes toward zero and the probability that data points falling in sharp corners of a hypervolume goes toward one <cit.>. This implies that nearly all data points will be at or beyond the periphery, requiring extrapolation. Dealing with any kind of cost or value function to perform optimization will mean that nearly all points are Pareto optimal, meaning that it becomes increasingly more difficult to define “good” because nearly every point has some unique quality. In many cases, the larger number of dimensions can be helpful, but primarily when the structure is extracted and the dimensionality is reduced <cit.>. As nearly all new observations will be on the periphery, we believe extrapolation techniques, such as exputation, are likely to improve results while maintaining interpretability.
new_text: The fundamental challenge arises from the topological properties of data as dimensionality increases. When dimensions grow, intuitive methods like Euclidean norms and Gaussian kernels lose effectiveness because the unit-radius hypervolume diminishes toward zero while the likelihood of data points occupying the hypervolume's sharp corners approaches one <cit.>. Consequently, almost all data points reside at the periphery, necessitating extrapolation. In such scenarios, cost or value functions for optimization face difficulties in distinguishing "good" outcomes, as nearly every point becomes Pareto optimal, each possessing unique advantages. While higher-dimensional spaces can be beneficial, particularly when structural information is extracted and dimensionality is reduced <cit.>, the prevalence of peripheral observations suggests that extrapolation techniques, such as exputation, may enhance predictive accuracy without sacrificing interpretability.

In this section, we evaluate two strategies of choosing the reference image. One obvious strategy is to pair every two different images, but it will result in exponential increase of the training time and high information redundancy.
To make the training phase efficient, we generate only one reference image for each image. Specifically, reference images are selected in two ways: 1) select the next image in the same image sequence as the reference image; 2) randomly select a different image of the dataset that is not a reference image of any other images. It should be noted that the next image is visually similar to the current image. Randomly chosen reference image has no such property.
To evaluate the effectiveness of the two reference image selection strategies on the adaptive metric loss (MDLoss), we train the proposed network with the comprehensive loss function.
In addition, we use the result of the networks trained without MDLoss (G+R+C) as baseline to compare the results.
new_text: This section assesses two approaches for selecting reference images during training. A straightforward method involves pairing each image with all others, but this leads to exponential growth in training duration and excessive information redundancy. To enhance efficiency, we adopt a strategy generating a single reference image per input. The selection follows two methods: (1) choosing the subsequent image in the same sequence (visually similar to the current image) or (2) randomly sampling a non-reference image from the dataset. The random selection lacks inherent visual similarity to the current image. The performance of these strategies was evaluated using the adaptive metric loss (MDLoss) within the comprehensive loss function. Comparative analysis also included baseline networks trained without MDLoss (G+R+C).

One simple and obvious way to represent pose is to form a 7-dimensional vector, combining position and orientation together.
However, previous works demonstrate that the 7-dimensional vector representation does not achieve good performance due to the difference of scale between position and orientation. Therefore, two pose components are usually regressed separately. In this paper, instead of training two separate convolutional neural networks to estimate position and orientation, we train one model to predict the two components simultaneously. This is reasonable because both position and orientation come from the same image content.
new_text: A straightforward approach to encoding pose is to construct a 7-dimensional vector that integrates position and orientation into a single representation. Nevertheless, empirical evidence from prior studies reveals that this concatenated vector fails to yield optimal results, primarily due to the disparity in scale between positional and orientational components. As a consequence, these two elements are commonly modeled individually. In contrast, we propose a unified model that jointly predicts position and orientation within a single framework, rather than deploying two distinct convolutional neural networks for each task. This approach is justified by the fact that both position and orientation are derived from the same image data, allowing shared feature representations to effectively inform both predictions.

new_text: Monotonic programs, by definition, are inherently "safe" when dealing with incomplete information, allowing them to execute without requiring coordination. In contrast, non-monotonic programs must account for the possibility that the truth of a property might change as new information arrives. This characteristic means such programs cannot reliably proceed until all incoming information is confirmed to have arrived, thus necessitating coordination.

**Single-View Image Clustering.**
Image Clustering with deep neural networks (DNN) has received increasing interest in recent studies. Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC) <cit.> simultaneously learns cluster centroids and DNN paramaters by iterating between computing an auxiliary target distribution and minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence to it. <cit.> then proposed Improved Deep Embedded Clustering (IDEC), an enhanced version of DEC that preserves the local embedding structure by applying an under-complete autoencoder. DCN was presented by <cit.> where the model simultaneously learns to cluster and reduce dimensionality to facilitate K-means cluster analysis. **Single-View Image Clustering.**  
Image clustering using deep neural networks (DNNs) has garnered growing interest in recent studies. Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC) <cit.> simultaneously learns cluster centroids and DNN parameters by iterating between computing an auxiliary target distribution and minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence to it. <cit.> later proposed Improved Deep Embedded Clustering (IDEC), an enhanced version of DEC that preserves the local embedding structure using an under-complete autoencoder. DCN was presented by <cit.>, where the model concurrently learns to cluster and reduce dimensionality to facilitate K-means cluster analysis. Dizji et al. introduced DEPICT <cit.>, which integrates a multinomial logistic regression function on top of a multilayer convolutional autoencoder to minimize regularized KL divergence, mapping data into a discriminative embedding subspace while predicting cluster assignments. A new clustering framework, JULE, was proposed by <cit.>, combining recurrent updates to cluster results via agglomerative clustering with image representations from convolutional neural networks. However, JULE struggles with scalability due to the high computational cost of affinity calculation and the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning, which is impractical in real-world clustering settings. Unlike our model, these methods fail to incorporate semantic image components and are typically evaluated on toy datasets.

new_text: Contemporary database optimization frameworks typically consist of two distinct phases: a query-rewrite optimizer and a cost-based optimizer <cit.>. SQL's inherent design provides significant benefits for optimization, supported by the foundation of relational algebra, which enables reordering of operations due to the associative and commutative properties of many operations. Queries can be substantially transformed through semantic-preserving equivalences to their original formulation. The query-rewrite process applies established, rigorously validated transformations to incoming queries, aiming to simplify their structure such that the generated execution plan achieves greater efficiency. Despite this limitation, query rewriting remains a critical and indispensable element of the optimization pipeline.

Here, the initial condensation operates on a graph with no edges, resulting in V̂_0 being a trivial partition where each node consists of a single vertex. The Performance Threshold method uses τ as its threshold value. This value is representative of the performance level of the model the user wants to achieve. A larger value of τ would lead to a more conservative method. A smaller value of τ will cause the method to be more aggressive. By default, we set τ to 0.8, or 80% F-Measure. In many cases, a model that has a performance level of 80% F-Measure is considered reasonable. Setting τ is more difficult and dataset-dependent than setting ϵ because the level of performance that is acceptable depends heavily on the task and dataset whereas the level of ϵ that indicates a leveling off in performance is not so heavily dependent on the task and dataset.
new_text: The Performance Threshold method employs τ as the threshold value, which reflects the target performance level desired by the user. A larger τ results in a more conservative approach, whereas a smaller τ leads to a more aggressive approach. By default, τ is set to 0.8, corresponding to 80% F-Measure, a level often deemed acceptable in practice. Determining τ proves more challenging and dataset-dependent than setting ϵ, as acceptable performance thresholds vary significantly across tasks and datasets, while the ϵ value indicating a performance plateau exhibits less dependence on task or dataset specifics.

old_text: All the above methods are designed for horizontally partitioned data whose data providers record the same features for different entities. We consider a vertical data partition as shown in Figure <ref>, in which multiple parties record different features at different sites. For example, one party may record users' mobile phone data while another record users' online-shopping behavior and purchasing results. Different from the horizontal partitioning, which assumes that ensemble happens over data samples, the vertical partition builds a model over a common set of users. How to collaboratively build the model is an open question. Some previous works discuss privacy-preserving decision trees over vertically partitioned data <cit.>. However, their proposed methods have to reveal class distribution over the given attributes, which will cause potential security risk. In addition, they can only handle discrete data, which is less practical for real-life scenario. In contrast, our method guarantees more secure protection to the data and can easily apply to continuous data. In  <cit.>, Patrini et al. proposed a framework to jointly perform logistic regression over the encrypted vertically-partitioned data by approximating a non-linear logistic loss by a Taylor expansion. Clearly, in this approximation, the algorithm will inevitably cause a loss of accuracy. To the contrary, we propose a novel approach that is lossless in nature. In particular, our proposed SecureBoost framework is a federated learning system designed to avoid any loss of accuracy. We believe that the SecureBoost framework is the first attempt for privacy-preserving federated learning over vertically partitioned data which balance accuracy and security.
new_text: All the above methods are designed for horizontally partitioned data, where each data provider collects the same set of features for distinct entities. We consider a vertical data partition as shown in Figure <ref>, in which multiple parties record different features at different sites. For example, one party may record users' mobile phone data while another records users' online-shopping behavior and purchasing results. Unlike horizontal partitioning—where ensemble learning occurs across data samples—vertical partitioning constructs a model on a shared set of users. Collaboratively building such a model remains an open challenge. Some previous works discuss privacy-preserving decision trees over vertically partitioned data <cit.>, but their proposed methods require disclosure of attribute-based class distributions, which poses potential security risks, and are limited to discrete data, limiting their practicality in real-world scenarios. In contrast, our method ensures stronger data protection and natively supports continuous data. In  <cit.>, Patrini et al. proposed a framework to jointly perform logistic regression over encrypted vertically-partitioned data by approximating the non-linear logistic loss using a Taylor expansion. This approximation inevitably introduces accuracy loss. To the contrary, we propose a novel approach that is inherently lossless. Specifically, our proposed SecureBoost framework is a federated learning system designed to preserve full accuracy during collaborative training. We believe SecureBoost represents the first effort to achieve privacy-preserving federated learning over vertically partitioned data while maintaining both accuracy and security.

The task of leveling the hexapod's body is not only nonlinear, but also very highly dimensional, with multiple paths for achieving stability, greatly complicating the task for multiple agents to reach consensus and perform beneficial actions to stabilize the body.
Since a single agent has no control over the other portions of the robot, and cannot instruct other agents to do any specific action, the difficulties are amplified by the agents' need to collaborate without communication.

new_text: The task of stabilizing the hexapod's body presents a dual challenge: it is both nonlinear and highly dimensional, meaning that small adjustments can yield disproportionately large outcomes, and the system involves numerous variables and configurations. Complicating the matter further, multiple potential strategies exist to achieve stability, creating a complex landscape for coordination. As a result, multiple agents must navigate these uncertainties simultaneously, requiring consensus on which strategies to prioritize and how to allocate actions effectively. This complexity is magnified by the fact that no single agent controls other parts of the robot or can directly instruct peers, as they operate without communication channels. Agents must rely solely on independent observations and inferential reasoning to contribute meaningfully to the collective goal, which increases the risk of conflicting or redundant actions. Despite these constraints, the proposed framework demonstrates robust performance, achieving satisfactory stabilization after only a limited number of training episodes—equivalent to roughly one hour of real-world operation. This efficiency underscores its ability to adapt agent behavior quickly in a decentralized, communication-limited setting.

Many real-world applications give rise to large heterogeneous networks where nodes and edges can be of any arbitrary type (e.g., user, web page, location).
Special cases of such heterogeneous graphs include homogeneous graphs, bipartite, k-partite, signed, labeled graphs, among many others.
In this work, we generalize the notion of network motifs to heterogeneous networks.
In particular, small induced typed subgraphs called typed graphlets (heterogeneous network motifs) are introduced and shown to be the fundamental building blocks of complex heterogeneous networks.
Typed graphlets are a powerful generalization of the notion of graphlet (network motif) to heterogeneous networks as they capture both the induced subgraph of interest and the types associated with the nodes in the induced subgraph.
To address this problem, we propose a fast, parallel, and space-efficient framework for counting typed graphlets in large networks.
We discover the existence of non-trivial combinatorial relationships between lower-order (k-1)-node typed graphlets and leverage them for deriving many of the k-node typed graphlets in o(1) constant time.
Thus, we avoid explicit enumeration of those typed graphlets.
Notably, the time complexity matches the best untyped graphlet counting algorithm.
The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in terms of runtime, space-efficiency, parallel speedup, and scalability as it is able to handle large-scale networks.
new_text: Real-world applications generate large heterogeneous networks where nodes and edges are of arbitrary types (e.g., user, web page, location). Heterogeneous graphs encompass homogeneous, bipartite, k-partite, signed, and labeled graphs as special cases. We generalize network motifs to these networks by introducing typed graphlets—small induced typed subgraphs serving as fundamental building blocks of complex heterogeneous systems. Typed graphlets extend graphlets (network motifs) by capturing both the induced subgraph and associated node types. To compute these, we propose a fast, parallel, space-efficient framework leveraging non-trivial combinatorial relationships between lower-order (k−1)-node typed graphlets. This enables deriving many k-node typed graphlets in O(1) time while avoiding explicit enumeration, achieving time complexity matching the best untyped graphlet algorithms. Experiments validate the framework’s effectiveness in runtime, space efficiency, parallel speedup, and scalability for large-scale networks.

In this paper, we have proposed, for the first time, a multi-objective model for NMF that takes into account several data fitting terms. We then proposed to tackle this problem with a weighted-sum approach with carefully chosen weights, and designed MU to minimize the corresponding objective function. We used this model to design a DR-NMF algorithm that allows to obtain NMF solutions with low reconstruction errors with respect to several objective functions. We illustrated the effectiveness of this approach on synthetic, document and audio datasets.
For audio datasets, DR-NMF provided particularly stunning results, being able to obtain solutions with significantly lower IS and KL errors (simultaneously), while generating meaningful solutions under different noise models or statistics.
It is our hope that the algorithm for DR-NMF that we proposed in Algorithm <ref> resolves the long-standing debate <cit.> on whether to use IS- or KL-NMF for audio datasets. Using DR-NMF provides a safe alternative when one is uncertain of the noise statistics of audio datasets; the noise statistics is rarely, if at all, known in practice.
new_text: This paper introduces, for the first time, a multi-objective Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) model that incorporates multiple data-fitting terms to account for diverse reconstruction criteria. To address the inherent trade-offs between these competing objectives, we employed a weighted-sum approach, where the weights were strategically selected to balance the contributions of each term. This framework was implemented using multiplicative update (MU) rules tailored to minimize the composite objective function, enabling simultaneous optimization across multiple criteria. Building on this model, we developed a Dual-Regulated NMF (DR-NMF) algorithm designed to produce NMF solutions that achieve low reconstruction errors across several objective functions—such as Itakura-Saito (IS) and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergences—without requiring a priori specification of a single error metric. To validate the approach, we tested DR-NMF on synthetic data, text corpora, and audio signals. For audio datasets, DR-NMF demonstrated particularly effective performance, generating solutions with significantly reduced IS and KL errors concurrently, even under varying noise conditions. These results suggest that DR-NMF can produce meaningful decompositions across different statistical assumptions about the underlying data. Our algorithm offers a resolution to the ongoing debate <cit.> regarding the choice between IS-NMF and KL-NMF for audio applications. Since practical audio datasets often lack precise noise statistics—a critical assumption for traditional unimodal NMF methods—DR-NMF provides a robust alternative that mitigates the risks of suboptimal model selection when the true data-generating process is unknown.

In this paper, we present a novel perspective on how SFs relate to model-free and model-based RL.
First, we show that learning SFs is equivalent to learning value functions directly from trial-and-error interactions with the environment.
Hence, learning SFs is akin model-free RL.
Then, we show that if SFs are used to learn a state representation, then this state representation encodes a compression of the transition and reward function, also called a model reduction <cit.>.
Rather than just representing one control policy that can be improved, model reductions, and thus SFs, encode a representation of the control task itself, a key property of model-based RL algorithms.
This approach provides a novel perspective on model-based RL: Rather than finding approximations of the one-step transition and reward function, a state representation is learned that compresses the dynamics of a control task into a linear action model <cit.>.
Because the state space is compressed using a model reduction, the linear action model is guaranteed to produce the same reward sequences as the original control problem given any arbitrary action sequence.
If no approximation errors are present, the linear action model will simulate reward sequences in the same way as the original control problem.
If approximation errors are present, the learned linear action model resembles a “softened” model reduction and produces reward sequences that approximately resemble reward sequences produced by the original control problem.
For this case we present prediction errors bounds linear in the objective function used to train the model.

Then, we show that if SFs are used to learn a state representation, this representation encodes a compression of the transition and reward function, also called a model reduction <cit.>. Rather than just representing one control policy that can be improved, model reductions—and thus SFs—encode a representation of the control task itself, a key property of model-based RL algorithms. This approach provides a novel perspective on model-based RL: Rather than finding approximations of the one-step transition and reward function, a state representation is learned that compresses the dynamics of a control task into a linear action model <cit.>. Because the state space is compressed using a model reduction, the linear action model is guaranteed to produce the same reward sequences as the original control problem for any arbitrary action sequence. If no approximation errors are present, the linear action model will simulate reward sequences in the same way as the original control problem. If approximation errors are present, the learned linear action model resembles a "softened" model reduction and produces reward sequences that approximately resemble those produced by the original control problem. For this case, we present prediction error bounds linear in the objective function used to train the model.

This paper focuses on the task of manipulating tissue to place specified points on the tissue (tissue points) at desired positions in the image frame as described in Fig. <ref>. In operating rooms, tissue points can be selected as tissue features identifiable via recognition of common patterns on the tissue. However, in this paper, colored markers are used for robust tracking of the points with a vision algorithm. In the task, the tissue points are simultaneously indirectly manipulated by the robot arms grasping the tissue at manipulation points. This task is complicated by the complex dynamics between the motions of the robot arms and tissue points. This paper proposes a learning-based model predictive control framework to solve the dynamics and manipulate the soft tissue. Two learning approaches are compared. One is a reinforcement learning (RL) method where the robot learns the dynamics of the tissue after exploring by itself. The other is a learning from demonstration framework (LfD) that initializes the dynamics of the tissue by studying human expert demonstrations.
new_text: This paper focuses on the task of manipulating tissue to position specified points on the tissue (referred to as tissue points) at desired locations within the image frame, as illustrated in Fig. <ref>. In operating rooms, tissue points can be selected as identifiable features by recognizing common patterns on the tissue. However, in this work, colored markers are used to enable robust tracking of these points using a vision algorithm. During the task, tissue points are indirectly manipulated in parallel by robot arms that grasp the tissue at designated manipulation points. This task is complicated by the complex interplay between the motions of the robot arms and the tissue points. To address this, the paper proposes a learning-based model predictive control framework capable of managing the dynamics of the soft tissue. Two learning approaches are compared: one is a reinforcement learning (RL) method where the robot infers tissue dynamics through self-exploration, while the other is a learning from demonstration (LfD) framework that initializes the tissue dynamics by analyzing human expert demonstrations.

When and where should you spend the money?
The answer to this question is the key to budget allocation in marketing
and this topic has been studied for decades in traditional business.
The environment and decision-making process in online business are much more dynamic and complex
than traditional ones. And the marketing budget allocation is sophisticated and needs to be readjusted quite often,
e.g. weekly or even daily, much more often than a few times per year like traditional marketing does.
That brings great challenges, especially for companies
with large and diversified markets <cit.>.
Fortunately, in online business, commercial activities can be tracked and depicted
by the collected data from multiple sources.
By leveraging these data, data-driven methods can help us to overcome above challenges.
The intelligent techniques allow us to gain deeper insights into the market and make more informed decisions.
Moreover, when the market is monitored and analyzed automatically,
new patterns can be detected more quickly, and the budget allocation is thus readjusted timely <cit.>.
In this paper, we present a novel unified framework for marketing budget allocation,
which contains two sequential steps: learning market response models from historical data,
and optimizing budget allocation based on learned models.
The whole framework is illustrated in <ref>.
new_text: When and should you spend money? Determining where to allocate marketing budgets is the key to effective budget allocation, a topic extensively studied in traditional businesses. The environment and decision-making processes in online business are far more dynamic and complex than their traditional counterparts. Marketing budget allocation is complex and requires frequent readjustment, such as weekly or even daily, in contrast to traditional marketing, which is typically adjusted a few times a year. This presents significant challenges, especially for companies with large and diverse markets <cit>. Fortunately, in online business, commercial activities can be tracked and analyzed through data collected from multiple sources. Leveraging these data, data-driven methods can help overcome the aforementioned challenges. These techniques enable deeper market insights and more informed decisions. Moreover, automated market monitoring and analysis facilitate quicker pattern detection, allowing budgets to be readjusted in a timely manner <cit>. In this paper, we present a novel unified framework for marketing budget allocation comprising two sequential steps: learning market response models from historical data and optimizing budget allocation using the learned models. The framework is illustrated in <ref>.

old_text: In this study, we endeavoured to expand on the currently much unexplored domain of shoulder surfing. We were particularly interested in how susceptibility to these attacks could be measured objectively, and applied the developed metrics on a range of textual and graphical authentication methods. The main aim of the study was to provide a fair comparison of textual and graphical schemes from the perspective of shoulder surfing, while also considering the input method. For that reason, we chose the hybrid scheme association lists to observe the differences in susceptibility to observation attacks when the same passwords are entered using either a mouse(M), or a keyboard(K). In this regard, our work can be considered a continuation of the previous research efforts by <cit.>.
new_text: This study addresses the under-researched area of shoulder surfing, focusing on developing objective metrics to assess vulnerability to observational attacks. Previous work in this field has primarily emphasized theoretical frameworks rather than empirical measurement, leaving gaps in understanding how different authentication methods perform under real-world observational threats. To address this, we designed a set of quantifiable metrics and applied them across both textual and graphical authentication systems. The central goal was to evaluate and compare the resilience of these two types of authentication schemes to shoulder surfing, while also examining how input method influences risk. Toward this end, we selected hybrid association lists—a password scheme that combines elements of both text and graphics—as a test case to observe how the same password entry process is affected by the input device used. Specifically, participants entered their passwords using either a mouse (M) or a keyboard (K), allowing us to isolate and measure the differential impact of input modality on susceptibility to observation. This approach builds on earlier studies by <cit.>, extending their findings by incorporating measurable comparative analysis of authentication method and input modality in the context of observational security threats.

We validated this approach by training a predictive model on SCUT-FBP5500 <cit.> and testing it on 200 random CelebAHQ images <cit.>. Sixty VGG models were trained (one per human rater), using ImageNet-initialized weights. Reinforcement learning an area in machine learning research that is used by artificial agents or robots to learn optimal strategies by trial-and-error <cit.>. This work uses model based RL to automate tissue manipulation. Model based RL is an algorithm that learns the dynamics of a task by trial and error, and applies the learned dynamics to a controller to calculate control inputs. The reinforcement learning algorithm using model predictive control is shown in Fig. <ref> and summarized in Algorithm <ref>. After initialization of the neural network variables, a computer vision algorithm extracts the positions of the robot wrists and the tissue points from an image. Greedy action that chooses optimal action gradually more frequent over random action is used. For greedy behavior in RL, ϵ is decreased from 1 to 0.1 linearly as a function of the number of robot actions taken. If ϵ is greater than a random number generated between 0 and 1, a random action is taken. Otherwise, the optimal action based on the MPC is taken. This forces the robot to explore randomly at the beginning, but gradually optimize policy as dynamics are learned. Each action set, u ∈{[0,0], [1,0], [-1,0], [0,1], [0,-1]} is multiplied by a scale factor, step, in image space that determines the step size of the robots in pixels. The actions in u, in order, correspond to the robot stopping, moving left, moving right, moving upward, and moving downward in image space. We have found that step size of the robots' movement and control period should be properly selected to learn meaningful information. After the action is determined, desired robot positions are updated and visual servo is performed to control the robots. In the next frame, the algorithm again obtains positions, and calculates velocities of the robot wrists and tissue points by taking the difference between previous and current positions. An experience set that contains the previous positions and velocities is saved to the replay memory. Training of the dynamics model starts after collecting more than a predefined number of experience sets. Random but fixed size sets of experience sets are selected from the replay memory and used to train the network. This process is repeated until the number of total actions reaches a predefined exploration number. After this learning period, the robot always chooses the optimal action based on the learned dynamics.

In this paper we show how to preprocess S into a compressed representation that allows fast range minimum queries. This allows for sublinear size data structures with logarithmic query time.
The most natural approach is to use string compression and construct a data structure for answering range minimum queries directly on the compressed string. We investigate this approach using grammar compression. We then consider an alternative approach. Even if S is not compressible, its Cartesian tree necessarily is. Therefore, instead of compressing S using string compression, we compress the Cartesian tree of S using tree compression.
We show that this approach can be exponentially better than the former, is never worse by more than an O(σ) factor (i.e. for constant alphabets it is never asymptotically worse), and can in fact be worse by an Ω(σ) factor.

In such cases, τ is not sufficient to determine the ℓ_p,2-distance between the curves.

To evaluate the effect of motion, different rotational motion artifacts have been introduced into motion-free images with 16-shots and random trajectory. Motion-corrupted k-space data has been reconstructed using CG-SENSE (without motion correction) and then fed to the adversarial network, which is tasked to generate the motion-free images. Table <ref> summarizes the average results obtained for varying degrees of rotational motion (Δθ = {2, 5, 8, 10, 12, 14}) on test data. It can be noted from Table <ref> that the proposed framework shows excellent performance for small amount of motion by capturing the underlying statistical properties of MR images, and recover sharp and excellent images. However, with the increase in the amount of motion, a smooth decay in the performance of model is observed, as expected, because at higher degree (i.e., 14) MRI scans severely degraded and it becomes very difficult to recoverable the motion free image.
Moreover, the performance of our technique is better than the previous state-of-the-art iterative technique <cit.> for higher amounts of motion (i.e., Δθ = 14) (see Fig. <ref>). For a small amount of motion, the approach of Cordero et al. <cit.> performs slightly better in terms of AP, however, the long computational time restrains its efficiency.
new_text:
To evaluate the impact of motion, researchers first introduced varying levels of rotational motion artifacts into motion-free images acquired with 16-shot sequences and a random k-space trajectory. These motion-corrupted k-space data were then reconstructed using CG-SENSE, a technique that does not account for motion, and the resulting low-quality images were input into an adversarial network. The adversarial network was specifically trained to infer motion-free images by learning the intrinsic statistical patterns of MR data. As detailed in Table <ref>, the average performance of this framework was assessed across different rotational angles (Δθ = {2, 5, 8, 10, 12, 14}) on test data. For small motion increments (e.g., Δθ = 2°), the model achieved high accuracy, producing sharp images by effectively capturing the structural regularities of MR images. However, as the motion severity increased, the model’s performance declined progressively. At the highest motion level (Δθ = 14°), the original MRI scans became heavily distorted, limiting the feasibility of accurate motion-free reconstructions, which explains this performance drop. 

Comparing the proposed method to existing approaches, it outperforms the state-of-the-art iterative technique <cit.> under extreme motion conditions (Δθ = 14°), as illustrated in Fig. <ref>. In contrast, for minor motion scenarios (e.g., Δθ = 2°), the approach by Cordero et al. <cit.> marginally outperforms in average precision (AP) metrics. Nonetheless, its practical utility is constrained by significantly longer computational times, which reduces its efficiency in real-world applications.
