old_text: Coded caching was introduced as a technique of systematically exploiting locally available storage at the clients to increase the channel throughput via coded transmissions. Most known coded caching schemes in literature enable large gains in terms of the rate, however at the cost of subpacketization that is exponential in K^1/r (K being the number of clients, r some positive integer). Building upon recent prior work for coded caching design via line graphs and finite-field projective geometries, we present a new scheme in this work which achieves a subexponential (in K) subpacketization of q^O((log_qK)^2) and rate Θ(K/(log_qK)^2), for large K, and the cached fraction M/N being upper bounded by a constant 2/q^α-1 (for some prime power q and constant α>1) . Apart from this asymptotic improvement, we show that through some numerical comparisons that our present scheme has much lower subpacketization than previous comparable schemes, with some increase in the rate of the delivery scheme, for the same memory requirements. For instance, we obtain practically relevant subpacketization levels such as 10^2 - 10^7 for 10^2 - 10^4 number of clients. Leveraging prior results on adapting coded caching schemes for the error-free broadcast channel to device to device networks, we see that the scheme proposed functions as a low-subpacketization scheme for D2D networks also.

new_text: Theoretical studies have yielded several complexity results regarding register automata <cit.>. Specifically, issues like emptiness and equivalence have been shown to be NP-hard, with the computational difficulty varying based on the register automaton's specific type. These findings are not directly comparable to the complexity outcomes related to minimisation in our work. A distinguishing factor is our reliance on total order symmetry, under which local symmetries are inherently trivial (Lemma <ref>). Consequently, the computational burden associated with group handling is eliminated. Instead, the complexity shifts to the input for our algorithms, as automata defined under the equality symmetry necessitate a greater number of orbits when represented within the total order symmetry framework. Another key distinction lies in the handling of duplicate register values: register automata permit these duplicates, while nominal automata represent such states across distinct orbits. A compelling unresolved question is whether determining the equivalence of unique-valued register automata can be accomplished in polynomial time <cit.>.

The memory of Soar is divided into a long-term memory and a working memory, see Fig. <ref>.
The working memory consists of objects that represent states, whereas the long-term memory consists of a procedural memory, semantic memory and episodic memory.
To perform a task, there is an initial state, a destination state, a problem space and operators that can be applied to change the states.
Production rules from the procedural memory are used to suggest an operator with certain preferences that can be applied.
A distinct operator is applied to the state.
This sequence is repeated until the destination state has been reached.
If no distinct operator could be identified (called impasse), a subgoal is created, which is solved by trial and error.
Impasses are caused by a lack of knowledge.
If an impasse is solved once, chunking is used to preserve the knowledge by creating new production rules, to not run into the same impasse again.
new_text: The memory system of Soar is structured into two primary components: long-term memory and working memory, as illustrated in Fig. <ref>. Working memory stores dynamic representations of current states, serving as a temporary workspace for active processing, while long-term memory is subdivided into three distinct stores—procedural, semantic, and episodic—each serving different functions in knowledge retention. When executing a task, Soar begins with an initial state and aims to reach a goal state by navigating a defined problem space. This process involves applying operators, which are specific actions that transform one state into another. Production rules, housed in the procedural memory component of long-term memory, are activated to propose appropriate operators, often accompanied by preference conditions that guide the selection process. Once an operator is chosen, it is applied to the current state to generate a new state in the problem space. This cycle continues iteratively until the goal state is achieved. However, if no applicable operator can be identified—a situation termed an impasse—Soar generates a subgoal to address the gap in knowledge through exploratory trial and error. Impasses typically arise from insufficient knowledge to resolve a particular challenge. When an impasse is resolved successfully, the system employs a mechanism called chunking to encode the solution as a new production rule, thereby preventing recurrence of the same problem in future tasks.

Items within a particular hierarchy level may exhibit different characteristics than others. For example, the electronics category may be selling products at a lower margin than the jewelry category. Each hierarchy feature is categorical and represented by an integer. We denote the set of indices of hierarchical features as ℋ. A one-hot encoding of all the hierarchical features can result in a very large number of features; this can be challenging to incorporate in models. For some models, we choose to use a one hot encoding of only a single hierarchy feature, e.g., the department level. We describe this in more detail when we introduce models in Sections <ref> and <ref>.
new_text: We incorporate hierarchical features to capture the structured relationships between items. These features represent nested organizational levels, including sub-category, category, department, super-department, and division. Each higher-level hierarchy aggregates multiple lower-level groupings; for instance, a department may contain multiple categories, which in turn include several sub-categories. This hierarchical structure enables the modeling of relationships where higher levels represent broader groupings while preserving detailed information at lower levels. Importantly, items at the same hierarchical level can exhibit distinct characteristics depending on the category. For example, products in the electronics category often have different pricing and margin structures compared to those in the jewelry category. All hierarchical features are treated as categorical variables, encoded as integers for computational efficiency. We define the set of indices corresponding to these hierarchical features as ℋ. A direct one-hot encoding of all hierarchical levels would generate an excessively large feature space, which poses challenges for model training due to increased dimensionality and computational demands. To address this, we selectively use one-hot encoding for a single hierarchy level in certain models—such as the department level—to reduce complexity while retaining meaningful structure. This method is discussed further in the model-specific sections (Sections <ref> and <ref>).

Constructing this dataset involved training and evaluating a diverse collection of convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures on the CIFAR-10 dataset <cit.>, a process that required extensive computational resources, including TPU years of processing time. Architecture.
The architecture of the BiLSTM is shown in Fig. <ref>.
As seen in this figure, the LSTM is bidirectional, in order to extract and model the dependencies from both forward and backward directions.
First, the input 38-dimension feature vector is fed into 2 LSTM cells, corresponding to either forward or backward direction.
Each of LSTM cells is composed of 256 units at one time step (corresponding to one video frame).
Then, the outputs of the bi-directional LSTM cells are fused and sent to the fully connected layer with a sigmoid activation.
Consequently, the fully connected layer outputs p_n, as the probability of being the PQF frame.
Finally, the PQF label l_n can be yielded upon p_n.
new_text: The BiLSTM architecture is illustrated in Fig. <ref>. This design employs a bidirectional configuration to capture and model temporal dependencies from both forward and backward sequences. A 38-dimensional feature vector serves as input to two LSTM components, each responsible for processing temporal information in one direction (forward or backward). Each LSTM contains 256 units operating at each time step, corresponding to individual video frames. The outputs from the bidirectional LSTMs are combined and passed through a fully connected layer equipped with a sigmoid activation function, generating p_n, which represents the likelihood of a frame being a PQF. The PQF label l_n is ultimately determined based on this probability.

Constructing Hard Instances: There have been several researches on constructing hard instances of combinatorial problems.
Hard instance generation was first studied in relation to the phase transition phenomena <cit.>, which utilizes order parameters to generate hard instances.
The three coloring instance generation by Mizuno and Nishihara () and the graph isomorphism instance generation by Neuen et al. () generate hard instances with rule-based algorithms. However, these works depend on problem specific knowledge, whereas our method is independent of the problem.
Another approach is to generate instances by solving other related problems. For example, the Latin square problem is found useful for constructing a benchmark for the graph-coloring problem <cit.> and SAT  <cit.>. However, the conversion of the solution of the Latin square problem into those of other problems also requires problem-specific knowledge. When there is no knowledge about constructing a benchmark for a problem, random instances tend to be used as a benchmark.
new_text: Constructing Hard Instances: Research on generating challenging instances of combinatorial problems has a long history. Early efforts linked hard instance generation to phase transition phenomena <cit.>, where order parameters are employed to produce difficult cases. Rule-based algorithms, such as the three-coloring instance generator by Mizuno and Nishihara <ref> and the graph isomorphism generator by Neuen et al. <ref>, rely on problem-specific domain knowledge to construct hard instances, in contrast to our problem-agnostic approach. An alternative strategy involves leveraging solutions from related problems to derive benchmarks. For example, Latin square problems have been utilized to design benchmarks for graph-coloring <cit.> and SAT <cit.> instances. However, this transformation requires domain-specific insights to map solutions to target problems. In the absence of problem-specific construction knowledge, random instances are commonly adopted as benchmarks.

In this paper we introduce a new linear time correctness condition for MLL.
It is based on that of <cit.>.
Although de Naurois and Mogbil showed their correctness condition is NL-complete,

In order to establish the linear time complexity,

The rewriting system have only three rewrite rules, which is remarkably simple.
In the rewriting system, an active node flows in a DR-tree, reducing nodes by the rewriting rules.
In order to fix our rewriting strategy, we introduce the notion of local jumps in -links.
Thanks to the notion, any -link node does not become active twice.
So we can prove the linear time complexity easily.
Compared to <cit.> and <cit.>, our correctness condition is
surprisingly simple and intuitively appealing.
While the correctness condition in <cit.> has to use non-local jump rule called the new rule,
all three rewriting rules in our system are strictly local.
In addition, all correctness conditions in <cit.> are rather complex since
there must be several different passes in the algorithm or they must be combined in one pass.

new_text: In this paper, we introduce a new linear-time correctness condition for MLL, building on that in <cit.>. While de Naurois and Mogbil demonstrated their condition is NL-complete, linear-time complexity isn't directly derivable from their presentation in <cit.>. To establish this complexity, we define a rewriting system over DR-trees—special cases of DR-graphs—with three remarkably simple rewrite rules. An active node traverses the DR-tree, reducing nodes via these rules. To fix the strategy, we introduce local jumps in -links, ensuring -link nodes remain inactive after one traversal, which enables straightforward proof of linear time complexity. Compared to <cit.> and <cit.>, our condition is simpler and more intuitive. While <cit.> employs a non-local "new rule," all three of our rules are strictly local. Additionally, <cit.>’s correctness conditions require multiple algorithm passes or complex single-pass combinations, whereas our system requires only three rewrite rules.

Proof-of-Authority (PoA) was recently proposed as a Byzantine fault tolerant consensus mechanism that integrates with the Ethereum protocol <cit.>. It is available in the two major Ethereum implementations, called `geth` and `parity`, under the name of the Clique and Aura protocols, respectively. The concept is similar to traditional Byzantine fault tolerant consensus in that only n sealers are permissioned to create new blocks but requires authentication and strictly less than n/2 Byzantine participants. Although it does not necessarily improve the protocol performance for the sake of compatibility with the Ethereum participants using proof-of-work, its lack of double spending
raised interest from the industry <cit.>. Some recent study <cit.> of PoA revealed that unsynchronized clocks could affect Aura's consistency whereas Clique was only eventually consistent, however, to our knowledge no attacks have been proposed against Aura or Clique until now.
new_text: Proof-of-Authority (PoA), a Byzantine fault tolerant consensus mechanism integrated with the Ethereum protocol <cit.>, is implemented in the two major Ethereum clients—`geth` (Clique protocol) and `parity` (Aura protocol). Like traditional Byzantine fault tolerant systems, PoA restricts block creation to *n* permissioned sealers, requiring authentication and fewer than *n/2* Byzantine nodes. While it does not improve performance over proof-of-work for compatibility, its elimination of double spending has attracted industry interest <cit.>. Recent studies <cit.> highlight unsynchronized clocks affecting Aura’s consistency, with Clique offering only eventual consistency. Notably, no attacks against either Clique or Aura have been reported to date.

old_text: This paper presents a simple yet principled approach to boosting the robustness of the residual network (ResNet) that is motivated by the dynamical system perspective. Namely, a deep neural network can be interpreted using a partial differential equation, which naturally inspires us to characterize ResNet by an explicit Euler method. Our analytical studies reveal that the step factor h in the Euler method is able to control the robustness of ResNet in both its training and generalization. Specifically, we prove that a small step factor h can benefit the training robustness for back-propagation; from the view of forward-propagation, a small h can aid in the robustness of the model generalization. A comprehensive empirical evaluation on both vision and text AG-NEWS datasets confirms that a small h aids both the training and generalization robustness.[Preprint. Work in progress.]

old_text: Note that even if the attacker does not know the topology, there is a way to attack Clique. The attack is slightly different from the previous one as it relies on the possibility for the attacker to become the only sealer able to seal a block on both sides of the partition.
new_text: An attacker can compromise Clique without knowing the network’s topology. Unlike previous attacks that relied on topological information, this method depends on the attacker’s ability to become the sole sealer who can produce a valid block in both partitions of the network. This strategy exploits the consensus mechanism by allowing the attacker to control the sealing process on both sides of the split, thereby maintaining blockchain integrity manipulation without needing detailed network structure knowledge.

old_text: Neural machine translation systems have become state-of-the-art approaches for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) task. In this paper, we propose a copy-augmented architecture for the GEC task by copying the unchanged words from the source sentence to the target sentence. Since the GEC suffers from not having enough labeled training data to achieve high accuracy. We pre-train the copy-augmented architecture with a denoising auto-encoder using the unlabeled One Billion Benchmark and make comparisons between the fully pre-trained model and a partially pre-trained model. It is the first time copying words from the source context and fully pre-training a sequence to sequence model are experimented on the GEC task. Moreover, We add token-level and sentence-level multi-task learning for the GEC task. The evaluation results on the CoNLL-2014 test set show that our approach outperforms all recently published state-of-the-art results by a large margin.
new_text: Neural machine translation systems have become state-of-the-art approaches to the Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) task. In this paper, we propose a copy-augmented architecture for the GEC task by copying unchanged words from the source to the target sentence. Since the GEC task suffers from a lack of sufficient labeled training data to achieve high accuracy, we pre-train the copy-augmented architecture using a denoising autoencoder on the unlabeled One Billion Benchmark and compare the fully pre-trained model with a partially pre-trained model. This is the first study to experiment with copying words from the source context and fully pre-training a sequence-to-sequence model on the GEC task. Moreover, we incorporate token- and sentence-level multi-task learning for the GEC task. The evaluation results on the CoNLL-2014 test set show that our approach outperforms all recently published state-of-the-art results by a large margin.

new_text: In this section, we evaluate the impact of incorporating a copying mechanism into the Transformer architecture on the Grammar Error Correction (GEC) task. Our approach to estimate the room layout edges consists of two steps. In the
first step, we estimate the vanishing lines in a monocular image of the scene
using the approach of Hedau et al. <cit.>. Briefly, we detect
vanishing lines by extracting line segments and estimating three mutually
orthogonal vanishing points. Subsequently, we color the detected line segments
according to the vanishing point using a voting scheme. In the second step, we
overlay the estimated colorized vanishing lines on the monocular image which is
then input to our network for feature learning and prediction. Utilizing the
vanishing lines enables us to encode prior knowledge about the orientation of
the surfaces in the scene which accelerates the training of the network and
improves the performance in highly cluttered scenes.
new_text: Our method for estimating room layout edges involves two distinct steps. First, we determine vanishing lines in a monocular scene image using the approach of Hedau et al. <cit.>. Specifically, we extract line segments and compute three mutually orthogonal vanishing points. We then assign colors to the line segments based on each vanishing point using a voting scheme. In the second step, these colorized vanishing lines are overlaid onto the monocular image, which then serves as input to our network for feature learning and prediction. Incorporating these vanishing lines allows us to embed prior knowledge about the orientation of surfaces within the scene, thereby accelerating network training and enhancing performance in highly cluttered environments.

new_text: Let 𝒯 = (Q, Σ, δ) be a complete, inverse-deterministic S-automaton. old_text: We show that for any k ≥ 0, the class of B_k-CPG graphs is strictly contained in the class of B_k+1-CPG graphs even within the class of planar graphs, thus implying that there exists no k ≥ 0 such that every planar CPG graph is B_k-CPG. Additionally, we examine the computational complexity of several graph problems restricted to CPG graphs. In particular, we show that Independent Set and Clique Cover remain 𝖭𝖯-hard for B_0-CPG graphs. Finally, we consider the related classes B_k-EPG of edge-intersection graphs of paths with at most k bends on a grid. Although it is possible to optimally color a B_0-EPG graph in polynomial time, as this class coincides with that of interval graphs, we show that, in contrast, 3-Colorability is 𝖭𝖯-complete for B_1-EPG graphs.
new_text: Our results demonstrate that for each integer k ≥ 0, the class of B_k-CPG graphs is properly contained within the B_{k+1}-CPG class even when restricted to planar graphs. This hierarchy implies the nonexistence of a universal k ≥ 0 for which all planar CPG graphs are B_k-CPG. Our analysis of computational complexity reveals that Independent Set and Clique Cover remain NP-hard even on the restricted class of B_0-CPG graphs. We also investigate the B_k-EPG classes, which consist of edge-intersection graphs of paths having at most k bends on a grid. While optimal coloring of B_0-EPG graphs is polynomial-time solvable due to their equivalence to interval graphs, we demonstrate that 3-Colorability becomes NP-complete for B_1-EPG graphs.

old_text: Although deep learning models have brought tremendous advancements to the field of open-domain dialogue response generation, recent research results have revealed that the trained models have undesirable generation behaviors, such as malicious responses and generic (boring) responses. In this work, we propose a framework named “Negative Training" to minimize such behaviors. Given a trained model, the framework will first find generated samples that exhibit the undesirable behavior, and then use them to feed negative training signals for fine-tuning the model. Our experiments show that negative training can significantly reduce the hit rate of malicious responses (e.g. from 12.6% to 0%), or discourage frequent responses and improve response diversity (e.g. improve response entropy by over 63%).
new_text: Despite significant progress in open-domain dialogue response generation driven by deep learning models, recent studies have identified problematic behaviors in these systems, including the generation of harmful outputs or overly generic responses. To address this challenge, we introduce a method termed "Negative Training" designed to suppress such undesirable patterns. This approach operates by first identifying model-generated examples that exhibit the targeted problematic behaviors, followed by leveraging those samples to inject negative feedback during model refinement. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique effectively reduces malicious response rates (e.g., decreasing from 12.6% to 0%) while simultaneously mitigating repetitive responses and enhancing output diversity (e.g., boosting response entropy by more than 63%).

old_text: In summary, generation adversarial frameworks demonstrate the promising results, and especially visual feature generation outperforms image generation based on the same adversarial frameworks for ZSL. However, these frameworks rarely consider transfer information based on structure propagation for finding the more discriminative feature in ZSL. Therefore, for considering the transfer loss constrains,we expect to construct a novel generation adversarial frameworks to capture discriminative information for tackling ZSL or GZSL.
new_text: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have shown significant potential in zero-shot learning (ZSL), particularly excelling in visual feature generation compared to image generation under identical adversarial architectures for ZSL tasks. However, existing frameworks typically neglect leveraging transfer information through structural relationship propagation to identify more discriminative features in ZSL. To address this limitation, we propose designing a novel GAN framework that incorporates transfer loss constraints, aiming to enhance the capture of discriminative features for both ZSL and generalized ZSL (GZSL) scenarios.

Specifically, we evaluate the model using the School, Disjoint, Landmine, and Caltech-Birds datasets, which are partitioned into 50% training and 50% test sets through random sampling. For each task, we reconstruct the task representation using Ds_i, where i∈{1,…,t}, enabling iterative learning across a sequence of tasks. By analyzing the performance curves in Fig. <ref> and Fig. <ref>, it becomes evident that the FCL^3 model consistently outperforms both ELLA-Rand and ELLA-Info as new tasks are incrementally introduced into the lifelong learning system. This observed advantage arises from two key design choices in FCL^3. First, the inclusion of an additional model knowledge library S allows the system to progressively accumulate and retain a broader range of task-specific knowledge compared to ELLA-Rand, which lacks such a structured storage mechanism. This knowledge library integrates both a feature learning component {D, L} and the model knowledge S, enabling more effective reuse of learned patterns over time. Second, when encountering unfamiliar task environments, FCL^3 autonomously identifies these novel scenarios and systematically incorporates them into its knowledge library. This adaptive process allows the model to incrementally capture richer structural information from real-world data, a capability not explicitly supported in the competing methods. Together, these features enhance the model’s ability to generalize across diverse tasks, particularly as the learning process extends to an expanding task repertoire.

We present an ensemble deep neural network architecture, called SINet, which leverages both the SMILES and InChI molecular representations to learn to predict the HOMO values, and leverage transfer learning from large datasets to build more robust predictive models for relatively smaller dataset.
SINet is composed of two identical branch for both types of inputs; each branch is consists of 1-D CNN layers followed by LSTM layers.
The features learned by the two branch from the two input representations are combined together and fed into a fully connected network for making prediction for the regression output of HOMO value.
The deep neural network architecture of SINet enables us to perform transfer learning from a large dataset to relatively smaller dataset in similar domain. Transfer learning has already been used in the fields of computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning and many other application domains <cit.>.
new_text: We introduce SINet, an ensemble deep neural network architecture designed to predict HOMO values by integrating both SMILES and InChI molecular representations, with the goal of enhancing predictive robustness through transfer learning from extensive datasets to smaller, analogous datasets. The architecture comprises two identical branches for processing each input representation: each branch incorporates a sequence of 1-D CNN layers followed by LSTM layers. Features extracted by these branches are merged and processed through a fully connected network to generate the regression output corresponding to the predicted HOMO value. This design facilitates transfer learning, enabling knowledge transfer from large datasets to smaller ones within the same domain. Transfer learning methodologies have demonstrated effectiveness across diverse fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning <cit.>.

old_text: As a final note, while in the previous paragraphs we have discussed the difficulty of network data anonymization, there are specific types of social network data where anonymization is indeed possible. In ego-network data collection different actors are asked about their own social ties and perhaps those of their neighbors. Ego-networks are then analysed without reconstructing a common network for all of the participants. In this case, there is typically no need to know who the individuals are, which means that we can design a data collection that is already anonymised at the source. As a result, these data are outside the scope of the GDPR given the definition of anonymous data as "data rendered anonymous in such a way that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable"[Rec 26 GDPR].

old_text: The HTTP protocol following the architectural style defined by REST is being widely used as a communication protocol for web services and also for creating REST APIs for distributed system communication. The ease of use and compatibility with the already existing systems made its adoption as a communication protocol faster than with any other protocol, even with the known limitations this protocol has in some scenarios. One of these scenarios is when building RESTful applications with certain reliability requirements in dynamic environments where connectivity is intermittent and unreliable. A common developer practice for dealing with that kind of situations where timeout events occur is to resend request message following certain self made procedure, instead of any standard procedure. Due to the intrinsic nature of REST HTTP as a polling protocol, the so-called unsafe methods can modify resources in the server side even when the acknowledgments fail. This problem makes the client unaware of the modified resources and forces the client to resend repeated requests. In order to avoid duplicated modification of resources, some policies are usually applied on the server side to make the client aware whether the resources were already modified or not.
new_text: HTTP, which adheres to the REST architectural style, is widely used as a communication protocol for web services and for developing REST APIs in distributed system communication. Its ease of use and compatibility with existing systems have driven faster adoption compared to other protocols, despite known limitations in specific scenarios. One such limitation arises when building RESTful applications requiring reliability in dynamic environments with intermittent or unreliable connectivity. In these situations, developers often address timeout events by resending request messages using ad-hoc procedures rather than standardized approaches. Due to REST’s inherent reliance on HTTP’s polling mechanism, the so-called “unsafe” methods (e.g., POST, PUT, and DELETE) can inadvertently modify server-side resources even when acknowledgments fail. This issue leaves clients unaware of resource changes, prompting repeated request resubmissions. To mitigate potential duplicate modifications, server-side policies are commonly implemented to inform clients whether resources have already been altered, ensuring awareness of prior modifications.

old_text: The rising number of IoT devices is accelerating the research on new solutions that will be able to efficiently deal with unreliable connectivity in highly dynamic computing applications. To improve the overall performance in IoT applications, there are multiple communication solutions available, either proprietary or open source, all of which satisfy different communication requirements. Most commonly, for this kind of communication, developers choose REST HTTP protocol as a result of its ease of use and compatibility with the existing computing infrastructure. In applications where mobility and unreliable connectivity play a significant role, ensuring a reliable exchange of data with the stateless REST HTTP protocol completely depends on the developer itself. This often means resending multiple request messages when the connection fails, constantly trying to access the service until the connection reestablishes. In order to alleviate this problem, in this paper, we combine REST HTTP with random linear network coding (RLNC) to reduce the number of additional retransmissions. We show how using RLNC with REST HTTP requests can decrease the reconnection time by reducing the additional packet retransmissions in unreliable highly dynamic scenarios.
new_text: The increasing prevalence of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has intensified the demand for solutions capable of managing unreliable connectivity in highly dynamic computing environments, where network conditions and device availability fluctuate frequently. To enhance the performance of IoT systems, developers rely on a range of communication protocols—both proprietary and open source—each tailored to specific requirements such as latency, reliability, or resource constraints. Among these, the REST HTTP protocol remains a popular choice due to its simplicity, widespread adoption, and compatibility with existing web-based infrastructure. However, this preference introduces limitations in scenarios where network instability or device mobility are common. Since REST HTTP is inherently stateless—meaning each request operates independently without retaining prior interactions—ensuring reliable data exchange in such environments becomes a manual task for developers. When connections drop, developers must repeatedly resend HTTP requests until the service is reachable again, leading to redundant transmissions and prolonged latency. To address these challenges, this paper integrates REST HTTP with Random Linear Network Coding (RLNC), a technique that encodes data into redundantly encoded packets. This approach enables partial recovery of lost data without requiring full retransmission of messages. By applying RLNC to REST HTTP requests, we demonstrate that the number of redundant retransmissions is significantly reduced, thereby decreasing the time required to reestablish effective communication in unstable, fast-changing network conditions. This combination leverages the strengths of both technologies to optimize reliability and efficiency without altering the fundamental architecture of REST-based systems.

old_text: The text of the GDPR is complex and not specifically targeted to researchers but its content will impact research practices in significant ways that depend on the specific research field. On the one hand, universities and other research institutions are of course providing general information about the GDPR to their employees, and have a Data Protection Officer who can be contacted for specific matters. On the other hand, GDPR-compliant strategies need to be instantiated to the specific research problem, and many of these are difficult to interpret without domain-specific knowledge. Therefore, researchers should themselves be aware of the implications of the GDPR and have reflected about it. In fact, several papers have already been published to address this issue and to examine the impact of the GDPR on research in general <cit.> and on specific research fields <cit.>. However, none have addressed the implications of the GDPR for social network analysis, where data processing differs from other quantitative approaches. For example, as discussed by Borgatti and Molina <cit.>, respondent anonymity is not an option if we want to know who is talking about whom, which is necessary to define edges in the network. In addition, subjects providing information about their social relations may generate data about individuals not included in the study: a participant mentioning that she often performs some activity with someone may reveal a lot about this other person depending on the type of activity. Another issue is the fact that in social networks it is often possible to identify specific roles based on the network structure, with a limited number of individuals in each role, examples being high-degree and high-betweenness[Degree and betweenness are so-called centrality measures, that can be used to identify important actors in a network] nodes as well as other special network configurations. Once these few nodes have been identified, it becomes very simple to connect them to specific individuals using some basic knowledge of the studied organization. More in general, network data is often impossible to fully anonymize. In this article we will also identify specific issues related to data protection emerging when social network analysis is applied to less traditional contexts, such as the analysis of large-scale networks of social relations derived from social media data.

* Section <ref>: Theoretical vs Empirical. Our empirical results are surprising, in that, the pedagogic model is a state of the art cognitive science model that is fit to the human data and has relatively high predictive accuracy, yet the pedagogic robot does worse than the literal robot with humans who are trying to be pedagogic.
    We use our theory to derive a hypothesis for why this could be. The hypothesis is that in practice different humans vary in how literal or pedagogic they are, which our theory implies will degrade the performance of the pedagogic robot more than the literal robot. We find positive evidence for this hypothesis, indicating that robustness to a population of humans is an important consideration in choosing a pedagogic versus literal robot.
new_text: The findings from our empirical study reveal a counterintuitive outcome. The pedagogic model, which is a state-of-the-art cognitive science framework calibrated to human behavioral data and known for its strong predictive accuracy, performs worse than the literal robot in interactions with humans who explicitly aim to act pedagogically. This result is unexpected because the pedagogic model is theoretically designed to align with the cognitive strategies of humans who prioritize instruction. To explain this discrepancy, we applied our theoretical framework to generate a hypothesis. The hypothesis posits that in real-world scenarios, individuals vary in their tendency to act as literal communicators or intentional pedagogues. Such variability, as our theory suggests, places greater demands on the pedagogic robot—since it assumes a higher degree of pedagogical intent from its human collaborators—thereby reducing its performance relative to the literal robot, which operates under simpler assumptions. Empirical validation of this hypothesis supports the idea that the ability to function effectively across a diverse population of humans, with varying communication styles, is a critical factor in deciding whether to deploy a pedagogic or literal robot in practical settings.

Our proposed approach is composed of three stages. The first stage learns to generate skeleton points from the input image, for which we design a deep architecture whose decoder is based on a novel, parallel design of CurSkeNet and SurSkeNet, which are respectively responsible for the synthesis of curve- and surface-like skeleton points. To train CurSkeNet and SurSkeNet, we compute skeletal shape representations for instances of ShapeNet <cit.>. We will make our ShapeNet-Skeleton dataset publicly available. In the second stage, we produce a base mesh by firstly converting the obtained skeleton to its coarse volumetric representation, and then refining the coarse volume using a learned 3D CNN, where we adopt a strategy of independent sub-volume synthesis with regularization of global structure, in order to reduce the complexity of producing high-resolution volumes. In the last stage, we generate our final mesh result by extracting a base mesh from the obtained volume <cit.>, and deforming vertices of the based mesh using a learned Graph CNN (GCNN) <cit.>. Learning and inference in three stages of our approach are based on different shape representations, which take the respective advantages of point cloud, volume, and mesh. new_text: We propose a skeleton-bridged, stage-wise deep learning approach for generating mesh reconstructions of complex-topology objects (e.g., chairs and tables with elongated, thin structures) from single RGB images. Our method leverages the meso-skeleton—a skeletal structure combining curves and sheets from the 3D medial axis transform (MAT)—for its topology-preserving properties and reduced learning complexity compared to direct surface mesh learning. The approach consists of three stages: (1) skeleton point generation via a decoder combining parallel CurSkeNet and SurSkeNet modules, trained on ShapeNet skeletal representations [cit.]; (2) base mesh generation by converting the skeleton to a coarse volumetric representation, refined via 3D CNN with independent sub-volume synthesis and global regularization; and (3) final mesh deformation using a learned Graph CNN (GCNN) [cit.], applied to a base mesh extracted from the volume [cit.]. Each stage operates on distinct shape representations (point cloud, volume, mesh) and shares the input image to correct cumulative errors. We release the ShapeNet-Skeleton dataset. Extensive ablation studies validate the efficacy of the stage-wise design.

old_text: In the era of data deluge, where it is particularly difficult to store and process all data on a single device/node/processor, distributed schemes are becoming attractive for inference, learning, and optimization. Distributed optimization over multi-agent systems, thus, has been of significant interest in many areas including but not limited to machine learning <cit.>, big-data analytics <cit.>, and distributed control <cit.>. However, the underlying algorithms must be designed to address practical limitations and realistic scenarios. For instance, with the computation and data collection/storage being pushed to the edge devices, e.g., in Internet of Things (IoT), the data available for distributed optimization is often inexact. Moreover, the ad hoc nature of setups outside of data centers requires the algorithms to be amenable to communication protocols that are not necessarily bidirectional. The focus of this paper is to study and characterize distributed optimization schemes where the inter-agent communication is restricted to directed graphs and the information/data is inexact.
new_text: In the era of data deluge, where the volume of data often exceeds the storage and computational capacity of a single device, node, or processor, distributed approaches have emerged as a practical solution for tasks such as inference, learning, and optimization. By distributing computational workloads across multiple agents, these schemes enable scalability and efficiency in handling large datasets. Specifically, distributed optimization over multi-agent systems has garnered significant attention in fields ranging from machine learning <cit.> to big-data analytics <cit.> and distributed control <cit.>, as these areas often require collaborative decision-making across decentralized entities. However, the design of such algorithms must account for real-world constraints that deviate from idealized assumptions. For example, in modern applications like the Internet of Things (IoT), where computation and data storage are increasingly localized on edge devices, the data available for optimization is frequently incomplete, noisy, or subject to measurement errors—often referred to as "inexact." Additionally, unlike structured environments such as centralized data centers, real-world multi-agent systems often operate in ad hoc, dynamic networks where communication between agents is not guaranteed to be symmetric or bidirectional. This necessitates algorithms that can function effectively over directed graphs, where information flow follows asymmetric or partial connection patterns. Addressing these challenges, this paper focuses on characterizing distributed optimization frameworks that explicitly account for two critical factors: the asymmetry of inter-agent communication (restricted to directed graphs) and the inherent inexactness of the data being optimized.

We derive our decomposition using an axiomatic framework: we propose a set of four axioms any measure of copy information should observe, and then identify the unique measure that satisfies those axioms.
At the same time, we show that our measure is one of a family of functionals, each of which corresponds to a different way of quantifying error in transmission, and which have connections to the field of rate-distortion theory. We also demonstrate that our measures have several natural operational interpretations. These interpretations include the probability of correct copying and the thermodynamics of replication. The thermodynamic interpretation of our measures
suggests novel approaches for understanding the thermodynamic efficiency of biological replication processes,

new_text: We develop our decomposition through an axiomatic approach, defining four axioms that any valid copy information metric must satisfy and then proving that our proposed measure is the unique solution adhering to these principles. Simultaneously, we establish that this measure belongs to a broader class of functionals, each representing distinct methods for quantifying transmission error, with ties to rate-distortion theory. Operational interpretations of our measures include the likelihood of accurate copying and the thermodynamic principles governing replication. This thermodynamic perspective opens new avenues for analyzing the energy efficiency of biological replication mechanisms, particularly DNA and RNA synthesis. Applying our framework to empirical biological data, we analyze copy and transformation information through amino acid substitution rates, revealing notable differences in the information transmitted via copying versus transformation across amino acids.

new_text: Deciding whether a set is primitive is an NP-hard problem if it contains at least three matrices (with the complexity of two-matrix sets remaining unknown), as is computing its exponent. For sets of matrices with at least one positive entry in every row and column (referred to as NZ <cit.> or allowable matrices <cit.>), the primitivity problem becomes decidable in polynomial time <cit.>, although computing the exponent remains NP-hard <cit.>. Methods for approximating the exponent have been proposed <cit.>, as well as upper bounds that depend solely on the matrix size; in particular, if we denote by exp_NZ(n) the maximal exponent among all primitive sets of n×n NZ matrices, it is known that exp_NZ(n) ≤ (15617n³ + 7500n² + 56250n - 78125)/46875 <cit.>. Better upper bounds have been established for some classes of primitive sets <cit.>. The NZ condition is often satisfied in applications, particularly in their connection to synchronizing automata.

old_text: * We jointly learn grasping and throwing policies with a deep neural network that maps from visual observations (of objects in a bin) to control parameters: the likelihood of grasping success for a dense pixel-wise sampling of end effector orientations and locations <cit.>, and the throwing release velocities for each sampled grasp. Grasping is directly supervised by the accuracy of throws (grasp success = accurate throw), while throws are directly conditioned on specific grasps (via our dense predictions). As a result, our end-to-end policies learn to execute stable grasps that lead to predictable throws, as well as throwing velocities that can account for the variations in object-centric properties and dynamics that can be inferred from visual information.
new_text: We jointly learn grasping and throwing policies using a deep neural network that processes visual observations—such as objects within a bin—and outputs control parameters. Specifically, the network predicts two key outcomes: (1) the probability of successful grasping for a dense, pixel-level sampling of end effector positions and orientations, and (2) the optimal throwing release velocities corresponding to each sampled grasp. Grasping performance is directly supervised by the accuracy of the subsequent throws; a grasp is deemed successful only if it results in a throw that meets target criteria. Conversely, throwing actions are explicitly conditioned on the specific grasp used, as determined by the network’s dense spatial predictions. This creates a feedback loop where the system simultaneously optimizes for stable, reliable grasps and dynamically adjusted throwing velocities. By leveraging visual cues to infer object-specific properties—such as shape, mass distribution, or friction—the policies learn to compensate for variability in object dynamics, ensuring consistent throwing outcomes. As a result, the end-to-end framework enables coordinated, adaptive robotic manipulation without explicit prior knowledge of object physics.

In this paper, we show that distance-based classifiers for few-shot learning
suffer from high variance, which can be significantly reduced by using an
ensemble of classifiers. Unlike traditional ensembling paradigms where diversity
of predictions is encouraged by various randomization and data augmentation techniques,
we show that encouraging the networks to cooperate during training is also important.
new_text: In this paper, we demonstrate that distance-based classifiers for few-shot learning are prone to high variance in predictions, which can be substantially mitigated through ensemble methods. While traditional ensembling approaches rely on randomization and data augmentation to foster diversity among individual models, we show that inter-network cooperation during training is equally critical for achieving robust performance. Our findings highlight that both diversity generation and coordinated learning contribute significantly to reducing variance in few-shot classification tasks.

The dominant paradigm in few-shot learning builds upon meta-learning
<cit.>,
which is formulated
as a principle to learn how to adapt to new learning problems. These approaches
split a large annotated corpus into classification tasks, and the goal is to
transfer knowledge across tasks in order to improve generalization. While
the meta-learning principle seems appealing for few-shot learning, its empirical benefits
 have not been clearly established
yet. There is indeed strong
evidence <cit.> that
training CNNs from scratch using meta-learning performs substantially worse
than if CNN features are trained in a standard fashion—that is, by minimizing
a classical loss function relying on corpus annotations; on the other hand, learning only
the last layer with meta-learning has been found to produce better
results <cit.>. Then, it was recently shown
in <cit.> that simple distance-based classifiers could
achieve similar accuracy as meta-learning approaches.
new_text: Few-shot learning primarily relies on meta-learning as its foundational approach <cit.>, which is a method designed to enable adaptation to novel learning tasks. These methods partition extensive annotated datasets into distinct classification tasks, aiming to transfer knowledge across tasks to enhance generalization. Despite the theoretical appeal of meta-learning for few-shot learning, its practical advantages remain uncertain <cit.>. Indeed, evidence <cit.> suggests that training CNNs from scratch using meta-learning yields significantly lower performance compared to training CNN features through conventional methods—i.e., optimizing a standard loss function based on dataset annotations; conversely, studies show that applying meta-learning solely to the final layer results in improved outcomes <cit.>. Additionally, recent findings <cit.> reveal that straightforward distance-based classifiers can attain comparable accuracy to meta-learning approaches.

In this paper, we focus on a challenging but critical problem for mobile object detection, i.e., the incremental learning of new object classes. Each mobile user may have his/her personalized objects of interest not included in the deep learning model that is shipped with the mobile devices, and meanwhile new objects of interest may appear from time to time (e.g., the emergence of MP3 Walkman to replace the old tape Walkman). To incrementally add the new object classes into the model, a simple and straightforward way is to fine-tune the model with training data from both old classes and new classes. However, this naive method would not work in practice. First, due to privacy issues, the training data for old classes of the deployed model may not be available with a high possibility. Second, even the old data is available, training using a dataset containing all classes is time consuming as the training efficiency is highly correlated with the amount of training data required. For mobile object detection, learning to detect new objects incrementally in a timely and quality-conscious manner is crucial in many application scenarios. Users of mobile devices may encounter new objects of interest anywhere anytime and delayed learning on those objects would have a negative impact on the user experience. For mobile robots and drones performing military or disaster relief missions, this could play a decisive role on saving lives and properties.
new_text: This paper addresses the significant challenge of incrementally incorporating new object classes into mobile object detection systems. Mobile users often encounter objects of interest that are not included in the pre-deployed deep learning models on their devices. These objects may also evolve over time, such as the transition from tape Walkmans to MP3 Walkmans. A common approach is to fine-tune the model using training data from both existing and new classes. However, this method is impractical due to two primary issues. First, privacy constraints often render training data for existing classes inaccessible. Second, even if such data is available, retraining with an expanded dataset is computationally intensive, as training efficiency declines with increasing data volume. For mobile object detection, rapid and high-quality incremental learning is essential in various scenarios. Delays in detecting new objects can degrade user experience and are particularly critical in applications like disaster response or military operations, where timely detection can impact life-saving efforts.

old_text: The success of one-stage detector is attributed to four critical techniques recently invented by computer vision researchers: grid-based prediction <cit.>, anchor boxes <cit.>, feature pyramids <cit.> and focal loss <cit.>. First, the feature maps generated by convolutional neural networks preserve the spatial information of the input image and thus <cit.> divide the feature maps into grids, and each grid cell is used to directly predict objects (both classification and bounding box) falling into the area. In this manner, there's no need for a box proposal network. Second, regression learning of the four coordinates of a bounding box from random initialization makes the training extremely hard; to address this issue,  <cit.> instead predicts bounding box offsets to some pre-defined anchor boxes with varying aspect ratios, which embed some prior information about the shape of candidate objects. Third, to better locate objects of different scales and especially the small ones,  <cit.> proposed to predict objects with feature maps of different resolutions via a top-down pathway, i.e., the feature pyramids. Finally, the focal loss was proposed <cit.> to solve the class imbalance problem (e.g., there are too many boxes containing only the image background compared to the boxes actually containing an object). In particular, a scaling factor was added to the cross entropy loss such that the training focuses more on learning hard examples.
new_text: The success of one-stage detectors stems from four key techniques: grid-based prediction <cit.>, anchor boxes <cit.>, feature pyramids <cit.>, and focal loss <cit.>. First, grid-based prediction uses feature maps from convolutional neural networks—retaining spatial information—to divide the map into grids, with each cell directly predicting objects (classification and bounding boxes) in its area, eliminating the need for a box proposal network. Second, regression of bounding box coordinates from random initialization is challenging; <cit.> addressed this by predicting offsets to pre-defined anchor boxes with varying aspect ratios, embedding prior object shape information. Third, feature pyramids <cit.> improve detection of objects at different scales (especially small ones) via multi-resolution feature maps generated through a top-down pathway. Finally, focal loss <cit.> mitigates class imbalance (e.g., excessive background vs. object boxes) by introducing a scaling factor to cross-entropy loss, prioritizing hard examples during training.

Stable matching in a community consisting of N men and N women is a classical combinatorial problem that has been the subject of intense theoretical and empirical study since its introduction in 1962 in a seminal paper by Gale and Shapley <cit.>. In this paper, we study the number of stable pairs, that is, the man/woman pairs that appear in some stable matching. We prove that if the preference lists on one side are generated at random using the popularity model of Immorlica and Mahdian <cit.>, the expected number of stable edges is bounded by N + N ln N, matching the asymptotic bound for uniform preference lists. If in addition that popularity model is a geometric distribution, then the number of stable edges is 𝒪(N) and the incentive to manipulate is limited. If in addition the preference lists on the other side are uniform, then the number of stable edges is asymptotically N up to lower order terms: most participants have a unique stable partner, hence non-manipulability.
new_text: Stable matching in a community comprising N men and N women is a foundational combinatorial problem that has attracted extensive theoretical and empirical analysis since its introduction in 1962 by Gale and Shapley <cit.>. In this work, we examine the number of stable pairs—man/woman pairs that appear in at least one stable matching. We establish that when preference lists on one side are randomly generated using the popularity model of Immorlica and Mahdian <cit.>, the expected number of stable edges is bounded by N + N ln N, aligning with the asymptotic bound for uniform preference lists. When this popularity model is further assumed to follow a geometric distribution, the number of stable edges reduces to 𝒪(N), with limited incentives for manipulation. If, in addition, the preference lists on the other side are uniform, the number of stable edges becomes asymptotically N, with lower-order terms dominating deviations: most individuals have a unique stable partner, making non-manipulability more likely.

In this paper, we presented an ICP mapping approach in forests, and demonstrated that it produced maps that were accurate enough to perform tree diameter estimation, especially in mature, well-spaced forests where we reached an accuracy of 2.04.
We also identified key challenges to address in robot mapping in forests: dealing with rough tree bark, reduced visibility in dense forest and estimating platform motion during one scan.
We compared multiple diameter estimation methods, and concluded that fitting multiple cylinders using Hyper circle fitting combined with non-linear cylinder fitting, and taking the median of the diameters of those cylinders works best.
All of our methods were validated in the most extensive dataset of DBH measurement from mobile lidar in the literature.
new_text: This study proposed an ICP-based mapping technique for forested environments, achieving sufficient accuracy for estimating tree diameters, particularly in mature, sparsely populated forest areas where a precision of 2.04 was attained. Critical challenges in robotic forest mapping were highlighted, including the need to account for irregular tree bark surfaces, limited visibility in densely packed canopies, and precise estimation of platform movement during scanning. Comparative analysis of diameter estimation strategies revealed that combining hypercircle fitting with nonlinear cylinder fitting, followed by median selection of derived cylinder diameters, yielded the most reliable results. The proposed methods were validated using the most comprehensive existing dataset of diameter at breast height (DBH) measurements obtained via mobile LiDAR.

The challenges in obtaining reliable and timely access to state information have long been recognized in large-scale dynamic resource allocation problems. One prominent example is the celebrated “power-of-two-choices” (PoT) routing algorithm <cit.> for load-balancing. Designed to address the lack of full queue-length information in a system with a large number of parallel queues, the PoT algorithm routes an incoming job to the shorter one between two randomly sampled queues. The same design consideration underlies pull-based variants of PoT <cit.>, and the partially centralized scheduling policy by <cit.> that has access to complete queue-length information only a small fraction of the time. Beyond the realm of computer networks, information constraints are also prominent in systems with humans in the loop. For instance, communication failures and misunderstanding between physicians and nurses have been cited as a leading cause of adverse events in healthcare, and specialized messaging and decision protocols have been developed to minimize the impact of errors <cit.>; see <cit.> for other examples of information loss among healthcare providers. While information constraints play a central role in
the aforementioned models and applications, in contrast to our work, they often serve as an implicit motivation behind a chosen design, rather than an explicit constraint with respect to which an optimal policy is to be identified. As a result, there has been little understanding as to what policies are “optimal” for a given level of information availability, and what the fundamental impact information has on system performance.
new_text:
The difficulties in acquiring accurate and up-to-date information about system states are well-documented in problems involving large-scale dynamic resource allocation, particularly when decisions must be made rapidly. A classic case is the “power-of-two-choices” (PoT) routing algorithm <cit.>, a widely studied strategy for balancing workloads in distributed systems. This algorithm was developed to address scenarios where a system operator lacks complete knowledge of queue lengths—for example, in a setting with many parallel processing queues. Instead of relying on perfect information, PoT operates by randomly selecting two queues and assigning an incoming job to the one with the shorter backlog. This design acknowledges the practical reality that monitoring all system components continuously is infeasible due to time, cost, or communication limitations. The same logic extends to variations of PoT, such as pull-based implementations <cit.>, which rely on sampled information from a subset of queues, and hybrid policies like the partially centralized scheduling approach proposed in <cit.>, which combines occasional access to full queue-length data with periods of partial information.  

Beyond computational systems, these information constraints are equally significant in human-operated processes. In healthcare, for example, miscommunications or incomplete exchanges between physicians and nurses have been identified as a major contributor to medical errors <cit.>. To mitigate such risks, structured communication protocols (e.g., checklists, standardized handoff procedures) have been developed to reduce ambiguities and ensure critical information is shared systematically <cit.>; similar challenges also arise in other domains, as detailed in <cit.>. Despite these examples spanning both automated and human-centric systems, a recurring pattern emerges: while information limitations often motivate the design of specific policies, they are rarely formalized as explicit constraints in the optimization framework. Traditional models tend to focus on achieving performance gains *given* a fixed information structure, rather than investigating how different levels of information access fundamentally shape the trade-offs between system efficiency, robustness, and complexity. As a result, there remains limited theoretical understanding of what constitutes an optimal policy under specific information conditions or how information availability itself directly affects system performance—questions that our work explicitly addresses.

**Spiking Neural Network (SNN).**
Biological perception principles and computational primitives drive not only the design of event camera pixels but also some of the algorithms used to process the events.
Artificial neurons, such as Leaky-Integrate and Fire or Adaptive Exponential,
are computational primitives inspired in neurons found in the mammalian's visual cortex.
They are the basic building blocks of artificial SNNs.
A neuron receives input spikes (“events”) from a small region of the visual space (a receptive field),
which modify its internal state (membrane potential) and produce an output spike (action potential) when the state surpasses a threshold.
Neurons are connected in a hierarchical way, forming an SNN.
Spikes may be produced by pixels of the event camera or by neurons of the SNN.
Information travels along the hierarchy, from the event camera pixels to the first layers of the SNN and then through to higher (deeper) layers.
Most first layer receptive fields are based on Difference of Gaussians (selective to center-surround contrast), Gabor filters (selective to oriented edges), and their combinations. The receptive fields become increasingly more complex as information travels deeper into the network.
In artificial neural networks, the computation performed by inner layers is approximated as a convolution.
One common approach in artificial SNNs is to assume that a neuron will not generate any output spikes if it has not received any input spikes from the preceding SNN layer. This assumption allows computation to be skipped for such neurons.
The result of this visual processing is
almost simultaneous with the stimulus presentation <cit.>,
which is very different from traditional convolutional networks,
where convolution is computed simultaneously at all locations at fixed time intervals.
new_text: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are shaped by principles of biological perception and computational models akin to those in the mammalian visual system. Artificial neurons, such as Leaky-Integrate and Fire or Adaptive Exponential variants, mimic biological counterparts and serve as fundamental units in SNN architectures. These neurons receive spatio-temporal input spikes—events—from a localized visual region (a receptive field), which alters their internal membrane potential and triggers an output spike (action potential) upon exceeding a threshold. Neurons are organized hierarchically into SNNs, with spike generation initiated by event camera pixels or upstream neurons. Data propagates through the network, starting from event-driven inputs, through early layers, to deeper hierarchical levels. Early-layer receptive fields often employ Difference of Gaussians (sensitive to center-surround contrast), Gabor filters (responsive to edge orientation), or combinations thereof, while deeper layers develop increasingly complex receptive fields. In artificial SNNs, computations in inner layers are typically modeled as convolutions, with a common simplifying assumption that neurons receiving no input spikes from prior layers will remain silent, enabling computational efficiency by skipping redundant operations. The resulting processing achieves near-real-time responses relative to stimulus input <cit.>, contrasting sharply with traditional convolutional networks, which compute convolutions uniformly across all spatial locations at fixed temporal intervals.

Early works, such as <cit.>, estimated normal optical flow: the component of the normal flow perpendicular to the edge (i.e., parallel to the brightness gradient).
Normal flow is moderately straightforward to compute using the pixel map of last timestamps of the events, also called the surface of active events <cit.> (SAE).
More recent methods, such as <cit.>, estimate the full optical flow (i.e., both tangential and normal components).
Full optical flow is more informative than normal flow, but it is considerably harder to compute.
new_text:
**Normal vs. Full Flow.**  
Early works, such as <cit.>, estimated normal optical flow—the component perpendicular to edges (i.e., parallel to the brightness gradient). Normal flow is relatively straightforward to compute using pixel maps of event timestamps, also known as the surface of active events (SAE) <cit.>. Recent methods <cit.> estimate full optical flow (tangential and normal components). While full flow provides more information, it is significantly harder to compute.

new_text: We examine the key distinctions between Wikidata and static knowledge bases derived from Wikipedia, exploring how these differences affect the effectiveness and efficiency of entity linking systems. Wikidata’s dynamic, structured nature contrasts with static extractions, which often lack real-time updates and rich interlinking. To demonstrate the practical relevance of these distinctions, we construct a simple entity linker named OpenTapioca [Implementation and datasets are available at [URL]; a demo is accessible at [URL]]. This system relies exclusively on Wikidata data, which enables competitive performance relative to systems utilizing larger, more heterogeneous data sources in specific tasks. Importantly, OpenTapioca’s design allows for straightforward training using only a Wikidata dump, with the capability to remain current as Wikidata evolves in real time. To further support research in this area, we also introduce tools that facilitate the adaptation of existing entity linking datasets to align with Wikidata’s structure. Complementing this, we present a novel entity linking dataset composed of affiliation strings extracted from research articles, addressing a practical application where accurate entity resolution is critical. These contributions underscore the value of leveraging Wikidata’s unique attributes for advancing entity linking methodologies.

In this section, we train CRsAE to learn the filters that underlie two different datasets. The first is a dataset of simulated recordings of extracellular voltage from neurons with known ground-truth filters. We use this example to compare the ability of CRsAE to learn the ground-truth filters to the AE called learned convolutional sparse coding (LCSC) from <cit.>. The encoder of LCSC uses 3 ISTA iterations. Unlike in CRsAE, the decoder is unconstrained, i.e. it is not tied to the encoder. In LCSC, each filter is associated with its own regularization parameter. The overall objective of LCSC is to minimize the least-squares reconstruction loss from input to output. We also use the simulated example to compare the computational efficiency of CRsAE to the state-of-art optimization-based CDL algorithm from <cit.>, which is implemented in the Sporco library <cit.> (we refer to this method by Sporco). Sporco solves the CSC update through ADMM <cit.>, and solves the dictionary update by an accelerated proximal gradient method constraining unit norm on the filters. The second dataset consists of recordings of extracellular voltage from neurons in the rat Hippocampus <cit.>. We use this dataset to compare CRsAE to continuous basis pursuit (CBP) <cit.>, the state-of-the-art optimization-based algorithm for spike sorting, which is the process of identifying the location of action potentials (sparse codes) and their corresponding neurons in extracellular recordings.
new_text: In this section, we evaluate CRsAE's ability to learn filters from two distinct datasets. The first dataset consists of simulated extracellular voltage recordings from neurons with known ground-truth filters. This example enables a direct comparison between CRsAE and the AE-based method learned convolutional sparse coding (LCSC) from <cit.>. LCSC employs an encoder with three ISTA iterations and an unconstrained decoder (not tied to the encoder). Each filter in LCSC has an individual regularization parameter, and the overall objective minimizes least-squares reconstruction loss from input to output. We further assess computational efficiency by comparing CRsAE to the state-of-the-art optimization-based convolutional dictionary learning (CDL) algorithm from <cit.>, implemented in the Sporco library <cit.> (referred to as Sporco). Sporco solves the convolutional sparse coding (CSC) problem via ADMM <cit.> and uses an accelerated proximal gradient method with unit-norm constraints on filters for the dictionary update. The second dataset comprises extracellular voltage recordings from rat hippocampal neurons <cit.>, which we use to compare CRsAE with continuous basis pursuit (CBP) <cit.>, the leading optimization-based algorithm for spike sorting. Spike sorting identifies action potentials (sparse codes) and their corresponding neurons in extracellular recordings.

new_text: I. Stochastic Processing Network Scheduling. The core challenge in dynamic resource allocation involves scheduling within a discrete-time Stochastic Processing Network (SPN), also referred to as a switched network <cit.>, where a limited set of processing resources are utilized to manage incoming tasks of N distinct types. At each time slot t, tasks arrive in a stochastic fashion; unprocessed tasks of type i are held in a corresponding queue i, with queue lengths represented by the vector Q(t) = (Q_1(t), …, Q_N(t)). The number of type i tasks arriving at time t, denoted A_i(t), has an expected value [A_i(t)] = λ_i, and the vector λ = (λ_1, …, λ_N) is termed the arrival rate vector. The scheduler selects an allocation vector D(t) = (D_1(t), …, D_N(t)) ∈ Π from a finite set Π, where D_i(t) specifies the number of tasks in queue i that can be processed during the current time slot. The queue lengths evolve according to the relation Q(t + 1) = (Q(t) + A(t) − D(t))^+, where for a vector x = (x_1, …, x_N), the notation (x)^+ denotes the vector (max{x_1, 0}, …, max{x_N, 0}) <cit.>.

new_text: The sentences in the dataset were pre-classified using a sentence-level argument mining model based on <cit.>, with classifications made accessible through the ArgumenText Classify API (see [[URL]]. This API assigns three key outputs to each sentence: first, an argument confidence score (arg_score) ranging from 0.0 to 1.0, where values below 0.5 were excluded from further processing; second, a classification of the sentence's stance as either PRO or CON; and third, a confidence score for the stance classification (stance_score). These attributes, combined with a separate document-level confidence score (doc_score), informed the selection of sentences for subsequent crowd annotation. To generate a ranked list of sentences, the three scores (doc_score, arg_score, and stance_score) were first individually normalized across the range of available sentences. This normalization adjusted each score to reflect its relative position within the dataset. Second, the normalized ranks of the three scores were summed to produce a composite ranking for each sentence. This ranking methodology, formalized in Equation <ref>, incorporates the normalized ranks of document confidence (d_i), argument confidence (a_i), and stance confidence (s_i) as components of the overall sentence ranking.

sentences makes argument mining brittle – when the

makes mistakes. In addition, sentence identification is

new_text: A focus of our work is robustness. (i) The assumption that arguments correspond to complete sentences makes argument mining brittle—when the assumption is not true, sentence-level argument mining leads to errors. In addition, sentence identification is error-prone for noisy text (e.g., web-crawled text), leading to noisy, non-sentence-level units being equated with arguments. (ii) The properties of argument topics vary significantly across topics. An ARC method trained on one topic will not necessarily perform well on another. We structure ARC-8 to facilitate testing the robustness of argument mining by including a cross-domain split and show that cross-domain generalization is challenging for ARC-8.

Perhaps these results present an opportunity to learn from research in neuroscience: the human brain must be implementing principles that allow humans to generalize systematically, but which are lacking in current deep learning models.
One prominent idea from neuroscience research on language processing that may offer such a principle is that the brain contains partially separate systems for processing syntax and semantics.
The part of the prefrontal cortex responsible for language production, called Broca's area, is thought to be important for parsing syntactic information, and applying selective attention in order to help a separate comprehension system interpret semantics <cit.>.
Variants of this idea have been implemented in computational models of the prefrontal cortex <cit.>, but have not been taken up in deep learning research.
new_text: Perhaps these results highlight an opportunity to draw insights from neuroscience research, particularly regarding how the human brain achieves systematic generalization—a capability that remains elusive in modern deep learning systems. A key insight from neuroscience suggests that the brain may rely on functionally distinct systems to process different aspects of language, such as syntax and semantics. For instance, evidence indicates that Broca’s area, a region in the prefrontal cortex associated with language production, plays a critical role in parsing syntactic structures. This syntactic processing is thought to work in tandem with another system—such as the comprehension networks in the temporal lobes—to disentangle semantic meaning. Importantly, the brain appears to deploy selective attention mechanisms that focus cognitive resources on syntactic structure during tasks like sentence generation, while enabling separate systems to interpret meaning more broadly. Variants of this dual-system framework have been modeled computationally to simulate prefrontal cortex function, yet such approaches remain largely unexplored in the context of deep learning. Bridging this gap could reveal whether modular, attention-driven architectures inspired by neuroanatomy might improve generalization in artificial systems, compared to the holistic, monolithic processing of current neural networks.
