It has long been thought that humans possess specialized cognitive machinery for learning the syntactic or grammatical structure of language <cit.>. One of the most foundational findings in all of cognitive neuroscience was that lesions to a particular area of frontal cortex, called Broca's area, results in a profound deficit in the fluid production of sentences, while leaving comprehension relatively intact <cit.>. Broca's area was subsequently found to be important for parsing syntactically complex sentences, leading some to conclude that it is important for syntactic processing in general <cit.>. A more recent view adds nuance to this idea and situates the functioning of Broca's area within the context of prefrontal cortex in general, noting that it may simply be an area of prefrontal cortex specialized for language <cit.>. The prefrontal cortex is known to be important for cognitive control, or the active maintenance of top-down attentional signals that bias processing in other areas of the brain <cit.>. In this framework, Broca's area can be thought of as an area of prefrontal cortex specialized for language, and responsible for selectively attending to linguistic representations housed in other areas of the brain <cit.>. The prefrontal cortex has received much attention from computational neuroscientists <cit.>, and one model even showed a capacity for compositional generalization <cit.>. The current work was heavily inspired by these key principles from cognitive and computational neuroscience research on Broca's area and the prefrontal cortex.
new_text: For many years, researchers have posited that humans have a specialized cognitive system dedicated to learning the syntactic or grammatical structure of language <cit.>. A cornerstone discovery in cognitive neuroscience revealed that damage to a specific region of the frontal cortex, known as Broca’s area, leads to severe impairments in the fluent production of sentences, while comprehension remains largely unaffected <cit.>. This dissociation—where speech production is compromised yet understanding persists—suggests that distinct neural mechanisms underlie these processes. Further studies clarified that Broca’s area is particularly critical for processing syntactically complex sentences, prompting the conclusion that it plays a general role in syntactic computation <cit.>. However, more recent research has refined this perspective by situating Broca’s area within the broader framework of the prefrontal cortex <cit.>. The prefrontal cortex is broadly associated with cognitive control, a function that involves maintaining top-down attentional signals to guide and prioritize processing in other brain regions <cit.>. In this context, Broca’s area can be interpreted as a prefrontal region specialized for language, tasked with selectively attending to linguistic representations stored elsewhere in the brain <cit.>. This aligns with the well-established role of the prefrontal cortex in orchestrating goal-directed cognition and managing attentional resources. Computational neuroscience has further advanced this understanding by modeling prefrontal functions, with one model even demonstrating the capacity for compositional generalization, a hallmark of abstract syntactic reasoning <cit.>. By integrating these insights from both cognitive and computational neuroscience, the current work builds on the established principles of how Broca’s area and the prefrontal cortex support structured language processing.

In a noisy environment, a lossy speech signal can be automatically restored by a listener if he/she knows the language well. That is, with the built-in knowledge of a “language model”, a listener may effectively suppress noise interference and retrieve the target speech signals. Accordingly, we argue that familiarity with the underlying linguistic content of spoken utterances benefits speech enhancement (SE) in noisy environments. In this study, in addition to the conventional modeling for learning the acoustic noisy-clean speech mapping, an abstract symbolic sequential modeling is incorporated into the SE framework. This symbolic sequential modeling can be regarded as a “linguistic constraint” in learning the acoustic noisy-clean speech mapping function. In this study, the symbolic sequences for acoustic signals are obtained as discrete representations with a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder algorithm. The obtained symbols are able to capture high-level phoneme-like content from speech signals. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework can significantly improve the SE performance in terms of perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ) and short-time objective intelligibility (STOI) on the TIMIT dataset.
new_text: In noisy environments, a listener familiar with the language can restore lossy speech signals using a "language model" to suppress noise and retrieve targets. We propose incorporating symbolic sequential modeling as a "linguistic constraint" within speech enhancement (SE) frameworks alongside conventional acoustic noisy-clean speech mapping. Symbolic sequences are generated via Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) to discretize acoustic signals, capturing high-level phoneme-like content. Experiments on the TIMIT dataset demonstrate significant SE performance improvements, measured by perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ) and short-time objective intelligibility (STOI).

We have shown in previous sections that uncertainty in the observations can have a strong influence on the resulting set of principal components.
Therefore, to better understand this relationship, we investigate to what amount the dimensionality reduction depends on the shape of the probability distributions of the observations.
In Section <ref> we have shown that our method is a more general formulation of conventional PCA.
We achieved this by scaling the covariance matrices of each observation with a factor s that describes the importance of the uncertainty.
Now, we will leverage this model to show how the fitted projection varies for different scaling factors in the interval s ∈ (0, ∞).
This interval can be split up in two parts to investigate two different scenarios.
For 0 < s ≤ 1 we can interpolate between uncertainty-aware PCA and regular PCA.
Conversely, by choosing 1 < s < ∞ we can extrapolate what the projection would look like if the uncertainty was higher.
In the following, we propose a novel visualization technique that is tailored to analyze effects of different scaling factors s and hence influences of different levels of uncertainty.
new_text: Previous sections demonstrated that observation uncertainty strongly influences principal components. To understand this relationship, we analyze how dimensionality reduction depends on the shape of observation probability distributions. Section <ref> established our method as a general PCA formulation by scaling each observation’s covariance matrix with a factor *s* representing uncertainty importance. Leveraging this model, we examine how the fitted projection varies with scaling factors *s* ∈ (0, ∞). The interval divides into two regions: for 0 < *s* ≤ 1, the method interpolates between uncertainty-aware PCA and standard PCA; for 1 < *s* < ∞, it extrapolates projections under higher uncertainty assumptions. We propose a novel visualization technique to analyze effects of different *s* values and their associated uncertainty levels.

To find an approximate solution, the overall idea is to construct an LP whose objective function at its optimal solution provides an upper bound for ESP^⋆. The LP that takes advantage of a concise representation of the solution space, has a polynomial number of variables and constraints.
Then, we use a rounding technique to transform the optimal solution of the LP to
a vector of reserve prices. We show that if we consider the reserve prices
obtained from the rounding technique and the vector of all-zero reserve prices
and choose the one with the maximum revenue, we obtain the desired
approximation factor. In Theorem <ref>, we further show that our
analysis of our approximation factor is tight. That is, we provide an example
for which our algorithm obtains exactly fraction of the optimal value

Finally, in Theorem <ref>, we bound the integrality

new_text: The general approach involves constructing a linear program (LP) such that its objective function at optimality provides an upper bound for ESP^⋆. This LP is designed with a concise representation of the solution space, ensuring it has a polynomial number of variables and constraints. After solving the LP, a rounding technique is applied to convert the optimal solution into a vector of reserve prices. To achieve the desired approximation guarantee, we compare two options: the reserve prices derived from the rounding method and a baseline strategy using all-zero reserve prices. By selecting the option with higher revenue, we ensure the resulting solution achieves the required approximation factor. In Theorem <ref>, we demonstrate that this approximation analysis is tight. Specifically, we construct an example where the algorithm attains exactly the fraction of the LP's optimal value, matching the upper bound for ESP^⋆. Additionally, in Theorem <ref>, we characterize the integrality gap of the LP, showing that the gap limits the performance of any algorithm to no more than 0.828 fraction of the LP's value. This establishes that our algorithm’s approximation factor is nearly optimal, given the LP's theoretical constraints.

new_text: To address the limitations imposed by <cit.> and <cit.>, we introduce an algorithm termed "Profile-based LP-Rounding" (Pro-LPR), which leverages a compact representation of the solution space. This representation, referred to as "profile space," draws inspiration from revenue calculation methods in eager auctions. Utilizing the profile space allows us to consider all bids, rather than just the top two, when determining reserve prices. Additionally, this approach enables the optimal solution to be characterized via a polynomial-sized integer program. We then relax the integrality constraints of the integer program's variables to construct a linear program (LP) and round the LP's fractional solution to derive reserve prices. The algorithm's final reserve price is selected as the best among the zero reserves and those derived from the LP rounding. The most complex aspect of the analysis involves establishing a bound for the approximation ratio, achieved through rigorous probabilistic analysis of the rounding process, resulting in a non-linear mathematical program that bounds the ratio. Finally, we apply non-linear optimization techniques to constrain the solution of this mathematical program. We stress that our algorithm's analysis is tight; specifically, there exists an example where the algorithm's approximation factor cannot exceed that of .<cit.>.

old_text: **RAM Model.** In the RAM model (the leading model for applications where all data fit in the internal memory) the dynamic planar point location problem has been extensively studied <cit.>. It is a major and long-standing open problem in computational geometry to design a data structure that supports queries and updates in O(log N) time <cit.>, i.e., to achieve the same bounds as for the dynamic dictionary problem. In a recent breakthrough, Chan and Nekrich in FOCS'15 <cit.> presented a data structure supporting queries in O(log N (loglog N)^2) time and updates in O(log N (loglog N)) time. They also showed the tradeoff of supporting queries in O(log N) time and updates in O((log N)^1+ϵ) time or vice-versa for ϵ>0.
new_text: The RAM model, which is the leading model for applications where all data reside in internal memory, has seen extensive research on the dynamic planar point location problem <cit.>. A significant and enduring challenge in computational geometry is developing a data structure capable of performing queries and updates in O(log N) time <cit.>, equivalent to the performance of the dynamic dictionary problem. A notable breakthrough by Chan and Nekrich at FOCS'15 <cit.> introduced a data structure that allows queries in O(log N (loglog N)^2) time and updates in O(log N (loglog N)) time. They additionally demonstrated a trade-off, enabling queries in O(log N) time with updates in O((log N)^{1+ε}) time or the reverse, for any ε>0.

old_text: A key challenge is that we cannot know a priori how biased our training dataset is relative to an arbitrary set of traceroutes needing router-country predictions. Thus, instead of attempting to provide a “one-size-fits-all” classifier trained with some subset of training data, we chose to implement an ensemble of classifiers, each of which is trained using complementary approaches to sampling our dataset. In this model, each classifier in the ensemble predicts router countries independently and the ensemble returns a set that is the union of these countries. As we discuss in the following paragraphs, we use RTT latency with SoL constraints from traceroute data to eliminate infeasible countries from this set. If the set still contains more than one country, Passport can optionally return the set or report that it was unable to isolate a single country for the router. In our evaluation, we show that Passport returns exactly one country 88.1% of the time, and zero countries only 3.1% of the time.

To enable a direct comparison with the vector-based framework described in <cit.>, we conducted experiments using three widely used datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CelebA-32. These datasets were selected to evaluate performance across varying image characteristics and complexities. For the vector-based framework, we tested three distinct measurement rates to assess how performance scales with measurement density. Specifically, we used three total measurement counts: 256 × 3 = 768, 102 × 3 = 306, and 18 × 3 = 54. The multiplication by 3 here reflects the framework’s use of three independent sensing matrices, one for each color channel (red, green, blue), ensuring that color information is preserved during the measurement process.  

In our approach (MCL), we faced a limitation: the measurement tensor 𝒵 cannot always be resized to exactly match the total number of measurements used in the vector-based framework due to the multidimensional structure of MCL. Therefore, we sought configurations of 𝒵 that approximately matched the total measurement counts (768, 306, and 54) by adjusting its dimensions. For each target measurement count, multiple 𝒵 configurations can yield similar totals, enabling us to compare different spatial and channel arrangements under equivalent measurement budgets.  

For each of the three measurement values in the vector-based framework, we tested two configurations of 𝒵. Specifically, we used the following:  
- For the 768-target: 𝒵 sizes of 20 × 19 × 2 = 760 and 28 × 27 × 1 = 756.  
- For the 306-target: 𝒵 sizes of 14 × 11 × 2 = 308 and 18 × 17 × 1 = 306.  
- For the 54-target: 𝒵 sizes of 6 × 9 × 1 = 54 and 9 × 6 × 1 = 54.  

These choices ensure a systematic exploration of how MCL performs when constrained to similar total measurement volumes as the vector-based framework. A full overview of all selected 𝒵 configurations is provided in Table <ref>.

new_text: Adaptive DLS techniques dynamically adjust chunk calculations based on real-time performance metrics to mitigate load imbalance caused by systemic factors such as non-uniform memory access (NUMA) delays and execution perturbations. These methods include adaptive weighted factoring (AWF) <cit.> and its variants (AWF-B, AWF-C, AWF-D, AWF-E) <cit.>, as well as adaptive factoring (AF) <cit.>. AWF recalibrates processing element (PE) weights during execution to reflect their performance, eliminating the need to predefine these weights. It calculates weights using past batch performance, updating weights iteratively to align with the system’s current state. AWF-B, unlike AWF, updates PE weights after each chunk rather than batch execution. AWF-C similarly updates chunk-wise but incorporates scheduling overhead—the time to assign loop iterations—into weight calculations. AWF-D mirrors AWF-C in scheduling overhead inclusion. AF, derived from FAC, dynamically measures PE performance during execution to compute μ and σ for each PE.

Testing of reactive systems is an important and complex activity in the development process for systems of this nature.
The complexity of such systems and, consequently, the complexity of the testing task have required high costs and resources in the software development. Therefore automation of the testing activity has become essential in this process.

The inherent complexity of such systems, and by extension the associated testing efforts, necessitates significant costs and resources in software development. As a result, automation of testing has become essential within this process. Numerous studies have explored testing methodologies for reactive systems <cit.>, specifically conformance checking between implementation under test (IUT) instances and specifications grounded in suitable formalisms to ensure enhanced reliability.

old_text: Several recent works have shown how highly realistic human head images can be obtained by training convolutional neural networks to generate them. In order to create a personalized talking head model, these works require training on a large dataset of images of a single person. However, in many practical scenarios, such personalized talking head models need to be learned from a few image views of a person, potentially even a single image. Here, we present a system with such few-shot capability. It performs lengthy meta-learning on a large dataset of videos, and after that is able to frame few- and one-shot learning of neural talking head models of previously unseen people as adversarial training problems with high capacity generators and discriminators. Crucially, the system is able to initialize the parameters of both the generator and the discriminator in a person-specific way, so that training can be based on just a few images and done quickly, despite the need to tune tens of millions of parameters. We show that such an approach is able to learn highly realistic and personalized talking head models of new people and even portrait paintings.
new_text: Recent studies have demonstrated the ability of convolutional neural networks to generate highly realistic images of human heads. Typically, to create a personalized talking head model, these approaches rely on extensive training data from a single individual. However, in real-world applications, such models are often required to be generated from sparse data, such as a limited number of images or even a single photograph. This work introduces a system capable of few-shot learning for personalized talking head models. The system first undergoes extensive meta-learning on a large-scale video dataset, enabling it to formulate the few- and one-shot learning of novel talking heads as adversarial training tasks involving high-capacity generators and discriminators. A critical component is the system's ability to initialize both generator and discriminator parameters in a person-specific manner, allowing rapid training with minimal input data while optimizing tens of millions of parameters. Experimental results confirm that this method can effectively produce highly realistic, individualized talking head models for previously unseen subjects, including portrait paintings.

The goal is to solve the optimal value for all states s = (l,t,I), where l ∈ L, t ∈{0,1,2,·, 180}, and I ∈{0, 1}. There are in total 6,421 × 181 × 2 = 2,324,402 states, and half of them are decision-making states. We define one subproblem as solving the optimal value for one state and thus we have in total 2,324,402 subproblems. Noticing that at the final time step, i.e., t=T=180, the maximum expected reward that a driver can earn is obviously zero, we thus have V^*(s) = 0 for all states s where t = T. For any state s with t<T and a chosen action a, the calculation of the state-action value Q(s,a) depends on the value of some future states, i.e., s'_1, s'_2, and s'_3 in Equation (<ref>). In other words, the subproblem, i.e., solving the optimal value for state s, depends on some subproblems, i.e., solving the optimal value of some future states, e.g., s'_1, s'_2, and s'_3. For a future state s', there might be several states s from which the agent will reach the future state s', indicating the calculation of the optimal value of all these states s requires the calculation of the optimal value of the future state s', resulting in calculating the optimal value of the same state s' multiple times and thus wasting computation power. To avoid the repeated calculation of the optimal value for the same state, we adopt the dynamic programming algorithm. Since the optimal values for all states with t=T are known and the optimal value of a state s depends on the optimal value of some future states, we solve the optimal value of states backwards in time and simply store the solved optimal values in a hash table. Then for a state s and a chosen action a, we simply read the optimal values of future states s'_1, s'_2, and s'_3 from the hash table and use Equation (<ref>) to calculate the state-action value Q(s,a), based on which the optimal value of the state s can be derived from Equation (<ref>). new_text: Fig. <ref> illustrates a numerical example of the proposed m-M algorithm. Consider a 3×4 MIMO system with M = 2. Thus, we have 8 branches with a 3-node level length. First, the m-M algorithm initializes 𝐯 with all ones and calculates the first ED of each branch. The m-M algorithm identifies the minimum ED in 𝐝, which is 0.1 in our example. This ED corresponds to the 4th branch (j_min = 4); thus, the m-M algorithm expands this node after increasing the 4th element of 𝐯 by one (i.e., v_j_min = v_4 = 2 and d_2,4 = 0.4). In the second iteration, the m-M algorithm finds the new minimum ED in 𝐝 (i.e., 0.2), which is located in the first branch (j_min = 1). Then, the first element of 𝐯 is updated to 2 and the first element of 𝐝 is updated accordingly (i.e., v_1 = 2 and d_2,1 = 0.5). The algorithm shifts focus between branches according to the location of the minimum ED across all branches, as illustrated in iterations 3, 4, and 5. Note that the m-M algorithm detects that one element of 𝐯 has reached N_r (i.e., full expansion for that branch) in iteration 5, which corresponds to the 4th branch. According to (<ref>), the algorithm must check whether the new minimum ED occurs at a fully expanded branch before deciding to stop. In our example, the algorithm will not stop at iteration 5 because the minimum ED is at the first branch (i.e., 0.5). Therefore, the algorithm performs a single expansion to the first branch after updating the first element of 𝐯 (i.e., v_1 = 3 and d_3,1 = 0.55); then, it re-evaluates the location of the minimum ED. In this example, iteration 6 shows that the minimum ED (i.e., 0.55) occurs at the end of a fully expanded branch, corresponding to the first branch (i.e., ĵ_m-M = 1). Thus, the m-M algorithm stops and declares that the estimated transmitted combination is the first one (i.e., the first symbol was transmitted from the first antenna).

Theoretically, we analyzed the properties of CL and proofed that it is tighter upper bound of the 0-1 loss compared with conventional summation based surrogate losses. We extended our CL to a more general form (NPCL) to handle large rate of label corruption. Empirically, experimental results on benchmark datasets show the robustness of the proposed loss. new_text: In this study, we introduced a curriculum loss (CL) designed to enhance robust learning. Through theoretical examination, we demonstrated that CL offers a tighter upper bound for the 0-1 loss than traditional summation-based surrogate losses. To address higher rates of label corruption, we generalized CL into a more comprehensive form referred to as NPCL. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmark datasets validated the robustness of the proposed loss function. Additionally, as a byproduct of this work, we developed a novel soft multi-class hinge loss. Testing on the CIFAR100 dataset indicated that this soft hinge loss is more efficient to optimize compared to the standard hard hinge loss.

Moreover, the 0-1 loss is more robust to outliers compared with an unbounded (convex) loss (e.g. hinge loss) <cit.>. This is due to unbounded convex loss put much weight on the outliers (with large loss) when minimizing the loss <cit.>. If the unbounded (convex) loss is employed in deep network models, this becomes more prominent. The 0-1 loss treats each training sample equally. Thus, each sample does not have too much influence on the model. Therefore, the model is tolerant to a small number of outliers. Although the 0-1 loss has many robust properties, it is difficult to optimize. One possible way to alleviate this problem is to seek a tighter upper bound of the 0-1 loss that is still efficient to optimize.

new_text:
We evaluate models on test data using the 0-1 loss, which serves as an empirical approximation of the Bayes risk with respect to the test distribution. This loss measures the average number of misclassifications, aligning directly with the goal of minimizing the probability of error. Crucially, the 0-1 loss does not penalize errors beyond a fixed cost of 1, meaning that the influence of label errors is capped. This property ensures that, under no assumptions about the data or corruption process, minimizing the 0-1 loss provides the most robust objective against label noise. Any alternative loss function, even with minor modifications, could introduce dependencies on specific error patterns that may not generalize to corrupted labels.

Compared to unbounded convex losses—such as the hinge loss—the 0-1 loss is also more robust to outliers. Unbounded convex losses amplify the influence of outliers by assigning disproportionately large penalties to misclassified examples with extreme features or labels. This imbalance skews the model’s parameters during training, as optimization algorithms prioritize reducing the loss contributions from these outliers. The problem is exacerbated in deep networks, where training loss is often minimized to near-zero values. In such cases, the model becomes highly sensitive to individual data points, including outliers, because their large loss contributions dominate the total objective. In contrast, the 0-1 loss applies uniform weight to all samples, ensuring no single point, including outliers, unduly affects the model. By treating every sample equally, the 0-1 loss inherently limits the maximum impact of any one observation, making it more tolerant of small perturbations or a limited number of outliers in the training data.

Despite its robustness, the 0-1 loss is non-convex and non-differentiable, making it computationally intractable to optimize directly. A practical approach to this challenge is to replace the 0-1 loss with a tighter convex upper bound, such as a surrogate loss function that approximates its behavior while remaining amenable to optimization techniques. These surrogate losses retain the 0-1 loss’s robustness advantages by assigning lower penalties to outliers compared to unbounded convex alternatives, while their convex structure ensures efficient convergence. By minimizing such a surrogate, we indirectly approximate the minimization of the 0-1 loss, balancing tractability with robustness in the face of label corruption or distributional anomalies.

old_text: Dataset Summarization Techniques refer to approaches that extract suitable dataset information, known as meta-features, which can be used for different machine learning tasks. Meta-features can be represented as general dataset characteristics  <cit.> or even as measures extracted from models induced from training on the data  <cit.>. Meta-features can also be learned directly from the data. The neural statistician (NS)  <cit.> proposes an extension to the variational auto-encoder  <cit.> that models the latent distribution of the underlying generative process of each dataset, i.e. the item to be encoded is the dataset itself. The instances of the same dataset are conditioned on a shared latent variable, the context, which captures dataset-specific statistics. NS is improved upon by a hierarchical latent variable model  <cit.>, that uses subsampling to construct a lower bound on set instead of the complete data. Available techniques for meta-feature learning require vast amount of data and are bound by a fixed schema of the dataset, unlike our approach that can accommodate any schema.
new_text: Dataset Summarization Techniques refer to approaches that extract suitable dataset information, known as meta-features, which can be used for various machine learning tasks. Meta-features can also be learned directly from the data. The neural statistician (NS) <cit.> introduces an extension to the variational auto-encoder <cit.> that models the latent distribution of the underlying generative process of each dataset, where the encoded item is the dataset itself. Instances from the same dataset are conditioned on a shared latent variable—the context—which captures dataset-specific statistics. NS is further improved by a hierarchical latent variable model <cit.>, which uses subsampling to construct a lower bound on the full dataset instead of the entire data. Available techniques for meta-feature learning require vast amounts of data and are constrained by a fixed schema of the dataset, unlike our approach, which can accommodate any schema.

Textpresso <cit.> is a text-mining system that works as a search engine of individual sentences, acquired from the full text of scientific articles, and articles. new_text: While biomedical ontologies offer significant potential for relation extraction (RE), their application in this field remains relatively limited. For example, Textpresso <cit.> is a text-mining system that functions as a search engine indexing individual sentences extracted from the full text of scientific articles. It integrates biomedical ontological information—such as terms related to genes, phenotypes, and proteins—to enable more precise searches. This ontological integration allows users to query articles or specific sentences using terms that align with these domain-specific concepts, rather than relying solely on keyword matching. As a result, the system supports semantic queries, which enhance the ability to retrieve relevant information. Additionally, Textpresso contributes to database curation by automatically identifying and extracting key biomedical relationships from text. Another approach, the IICE <cit.> system, employs kernel-based support vector machines combined with an ensemble classifier to detect and categorize drug-drug interactions. It links chemical compounds to the ChEBI ontology, improving the accuracy of relationship identification. Similarly, Tripodi et al. <cit.> developed a system focused on uncovering drug-gene/protein interactions, utilizing ontologies like ChEBI (for chemical entities) and the Gene Ontology (GO) to structure and validate these interactions, thereby aiding database curation. Notably, BO-LSTM <cit.> represents a novel advancement, as it is the first model to integrate ancestry information from biomedical ontologies with deep learning architectures. This hybrid approach enables the extraction of relations such as drug-drug interactions and gene-phenotype associations by leveraging hierarchical relationships inherent in ontologies, enhancing the model's ability to capture contextual nuances in biomedical text.

For example, the training period is May 1 2011 to May 1, 2014 and the validation period is from June 1, 2014 to June 1, 2015.
We use the validation set to determine the hyperparameters and build the model, and then we use the trained model to forecast returns of equity in the same universe from July 1, 2015 to July 1, 2016. Then the model is retrained by using data in the second training period (May 1, 2012 to May 1, 2015). This workflow repeats. new_text: The model undergoes retraining at the start of each test year to ensure it adapts to the most recent data. To illustrate, the initial training period spans three years—from May 1, 2011, to May 1, 2014—after which the validation phase begins on June 1, 2014, and concludes on June 1, 2015. During this validation phase, hyperparameters are optimized, and the model is constructed. Once finalized, the model is applied to forecast equity returns within the same asset universe for the subsequent 12-month test period, from July 1, 2015, to July 1, 2016. Following this, the process is repeated: the training period advances by one year to May 1, 2012, to May 1, 2015, allowing the model to incorporate updated data. This iterative workflow ensures the model remains current with the evolving dataset. To prevent look-ahead bias—a situation where future data unintentionally influences earlier model decisions—we enforce a consistent one-month gap between the end of the training period and the start of validation, as well as between validation and testing. This temporal separation maintains methodological rigor by ensuring that no data from later timeframes is used in earlier stages of model development.

Recent work in deep reinforcement learning effectively tackles challenging problems including the board game Go <cit.>, Atari video games <cit.>, and simulated robotic continuous control <cit.>; however, these successful approaches often rely on frequent feedback indicating whether the learning agent is performing well, otherwise known as dense rewards.

new_text: Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have successfully addressed complex problems such as the board game Go <cit.>, Atari video games <cit.>, and simulated robotic continuous control <cit.>. However, these methods typically require frequent feedback—dense rewards—to assess an agent’s performance. Defining dense rewards often risks incentivizing locally optimal but globally suboptimal behavior, making sparse rewards—signals indicating task success or failure—preferable in many scenarios. Despite their advantages, sparse rewards present unique challenges.

old_text: In this work, we redefined the structural analysis problem using the graph model. We demonstrated our results on the problem of table parsing and we also argued how several other problems can also be defined using this model. Convolutional neural networks are the most suited at finding representative image features and graph networks are the most suited at fast message passing between vertices. We have shown how we can combine these two abilities using the gather operation. So far, we only used positional features for the vertices, but for a real-world dataset, natural language processing features like GloVe can also be used. There is a lot of room for contribution in improving the performance of graph neural networks, not just the accuracy but also the compute requirement. In conclusion, graph neural networks work well for structural analysis problems and we expect to see much more research on related problems.
new_text: This work introduces a novel approach to structural analysis by reformulating the problem within a graph-based framework. Specifically, we demonstrated the effectiveness of this methodology on the task of table parsing, where the structural relationships between elements are critical for accurate interpretation. Moreover, we discussed how this model is broadly applicable, as many structural analysis challenges—such as document layout understanding or molecular structure prediction—can similarly be represented and solved through graph-based modeling. The choice of techniques in our implementation leverages the complementary strengths of different neural architectures: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at extracting high-quality spatial features from images, while graph networks efficiently propagate information between connected nodes through message-passing mechanisms. By integrating these capabilities, we developed a hybrid architecture that employs a gather operation to combine local image features with global structural dependencies. Currently, our experiments have relied on positional features to represent node attributes, but the framework could naturally extend to incorporate natural language processing (NLP) embeddings like GloVe when applied to datasets involving textual content. Future research should focus on advancing graph neural networks (GNNs) not only to improve predictive accuracy but also to reduce computational demands, which remain a barrier for large-scale deployment. In summary, our findings underscore the potential of GNNs as a powerful tool for structural analysis tasks, and we anticipate growing interest in optimizing and applying these models to diverse domains.

new_text: Determining or verifying the number of columns—when no schema is provided and the column count is unknown a priori, it is possible to infer the input’s number of columns. Similarly, when rejecting records that deviate from the expected column count, the same method applies. In both scenarios, during deterministic finite automaton (DFA) simulation, threads must monitor three additional parameters alongside the relative or absolute column offsets passed to the next chunk. Specifically, each thread tracks: (1) the count of field delimiters encountered prior to the first record delimiter in its segment, termed the *relative min/max*; (2) the minimum and maximum column counts observed across all records after the chunk’s first record delimiter; and (3) an additional bit to indicate whether the min/max values were undefined (i.e., when no record delimiter exists in the chunk). After performing a prefix scan over the column offsets, the relative min/max is resolved into an absolute column offset, which is then integrated into the chunk’s overall min and max column counts. A reduction operation over the maximum column count enables inference of the total number of columns. Comparing the computed minimum and maximum column counts across chunks ensures consistency with the expected column count per record.

Finally, although much progress has been made in sentiment analysis by using deep learning techniques, substantial obstacles remain. Notably, a fundamental problem is how to build a robust network architecture to generalize the knowledge acquired during the training. The combination of a set of classifiers, a strategy known as ensemble, has been used to alleviate this problem.
As pointed by Dietterich <cit.>, some reasons for that are: (i) the lack of training data compared to the size of the problem space produces many optimizations with the same accuracy, and by using an ensemble we can average the votes of the classifiers, so as to reduce the risk of choosing the wrong one; (ii) the optimization may fail to converge to the correct minimum and an ensemble with distinct starting points may approximate the optimal minimum; and, (iii) the space being searched could not be approximated by any machine learning algorithm but an ensemble can expand this space.
new_text: Despite significant advancements in sentiment analysis through deep learning techniques, several challenges continue to persist. A critical issue involves developing an effective network architecture capable of generalizing learned knowledge during training. Ensemble methods, which involve combining multiple classifiers, have been employed to address this issue. As noted by Dietterich <cit.>, key reasons for this approach include: (i) limited training data relative to the problem space size can result in multiple equivalent optimizations, and averaging classifier outputs helps mitigate the risk of selecting an erroneous solution; (ii) optimization processes might fail to reach the correct minimum, and ensembles with diverse initialization points can better approximate optimal solutions; and (iii) certain search spaces may resist approximation by individual algorithms, yet ensembles can extend their representational capacity.

In recent years, inspired by the breakthroughs of convolutional neural networks (ConvNet) <cit.> in machine learning, many authors proposed novel architectures for sentiment analysis. Cai and Xia <cit.> proposed to combine two ConvNets, one fed with textual and other with visual features, to predict sentiments from tweets. Chen  <cit.> used transfer learning from ImageNet weights <cit.> in their ConvNet to deal with biased training data, which only contains images with strong sentiment polarity. You  <cit.> used a probabilistic ConvNet sampling to reduce the impact of noisy data by removing training instances with similar sentiment scores.
Recurrent Neural Network <cit.>, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) <cit.>, designed to recognize patterns in temporal sequences of data were also used for sentiment analysis <cit.>. Discriminative face features <cit.>, extracted from ConvNets architectures, were also used to estimate people happiness in the wild. While there are some initiatives showing the importance of outdoor images to the semantic classification of urban areas, such as the study of Santani  <cit.> that extracts labels for outdoor urban images, none of the previous studies focused on sentiment analysis of urban outdoor images.
new_text:
Recent advances in convolutional neural networks (ConvNets) within machine learning have inspired a surge of novel architectures for sentiment analysis. Many researchers have adapted these tools to handle multimodal data, where traditional methods struggle to integrate textual and visual cues effectively. For instance, Cai and Xia proposed a dual-ConvNet framework in which one network processes textual features from tweets, while the other analyzes visual elements, enabling a more comprehensive prediction of sentiment. Meanwhile, Chen introduced a technique that leverages transfer learning—using pre-trained ImageNet weights as a starting point—to address imbalanced training datasets. This approach is particularly relevant when datasets contain predominantly images with strong positive or negative sentiments, as it allows the model to generalize better despite limited exposure to neutral or ambiguous examples. Similarly, You explored a probabilistic sampling strategy in their ConvNet architecture, selectively discarding training instances with ambiguous or overlapping sentiment scores. This method reduces the risk of overfitting to noisy data, thereby improving model robustness.  

Beyond ConvNets, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architectures, have also been employed for sentiment analysis due to their ability to model temporal dependencies in sequential data. In parallel, researchers have adapted ConvNet-derived features to analyze facial expressions for estimating happiness in uncontrolled environments. While these approaches highlight the versatility of deep learning in sentiment-related tasks, they primarily focus on social media content or individual behavior. A different challenge emerges in the analysis of urban outdoor imagery, where prior studies—like Santani’s work on semantic labeling of cityscapes—have explored the role of outdoor images in categorizing urban environments. However, these efforts have not addressed the emotional or affective interpretation of such scenes, underscoring a gap in research that combines environmental vision with sentiment analysis.

The semi-dense target maps are created by merging the LiDAR scans from 11 consecutive frames into one, producing y in which roughly 30% of the pixels are non-zero. It contains 2126 unique frames, of which there are 10 different versions corresponding to various simulated weather and lighting conditions. We take sequence 0002 as our validation set, leaving a total of 18930 training examples. We create targets y for training by setting all pixels in x_dense corresponding to a depth > 80m to 0, and then also randomly sample 5% of the remaining non-zero pixels uniformly to create x_sparse. We use the DNN model presented by Ma et al. <cit.>. The inputs x_img, x_sparse are separately processed by initial convolutional layers, concatenated and fed to an encoder-decoder architecture based on ResNet34 <cit.>. We also employ the same basic training procedure as Ma et al. to train all our models, see Appendix <ref> for details. For the MC-dropout comparison, we take inspiration from <cit.> and place a dropout layer with p = 0.5 after the three last encoder blocks and the four first decoder blocks.

In this paper, we develop a principled method for selecting a subset
of training data points to speed up training of large machine learning
models. We call our method data Sketching for Iterative Gradient
descent (SIG).
Specifically, we show that the error of estimating the
expected risk with the selected subset is lower-bounded by a
submodular facility location function. As a result, by maximizing the
submodular lower-bound, we obtain a set that guarantees a fast
convergence rate to the optimum solution. Our SIG approach is based on
knowing the gradient of every training data point with respect to the
current model parameters, and these gradients are used to produce a
submodular function for which there are a variety of efficient greedy
procedures <cit.> available to
compute a subset approximately optimally. Based on these
subsets, we show improved convergence rates. Specifically,
we prove that for a μ-strongly convex risk function and a subset S that estimates the full gradient by an error of at most ϵ, IG with a diminishing stepsize of α_k=α/k^s for 0<s<1 and α>0, converges to a Rϵ/μ neighborhood of the optimum solution. Here, R=min{D, (rγ_maxC + ϵ)/μ} for a dataset of diameter D, and an upper bound C on the norm of the gradients. Moreover, we show that for a μ-strongly convex risk and smooth component functions, IG with the same diminishing stepsize rule on subset S converges to a ϵ/μ neighborhood of the optimum solution.
new_text: This paper introduces a principled method for accelerating the training of large machine learning models by selecting a subset of training data points. We term this approach Sketching for Iterative Gradient descent (SIG). Specifically, we demonstrate that the error in estimating the expected risk using the selected subset is lower-bounded by a submodular facility location function. By maximizing this submodular lower-bound, we derive a set that ensures rapid convergence to the optimal solution. The SIG method requires knowledge of the gradient of each training data point with respect to the current model parameters. These gradients are used to construct a submodular function, for which a variety of efficient greedy algorithms <cit.> can be employed to compute a subset that is approximately optimal. This subset selection leads to improved convergence rates. Specifically, for a μ-strongly convex risk function and a subset S that approximates the full gradient with error at most ϵ, iterative gradient (IG) with a diminishing stepsize α_k = α/k^s (where 0 < s < 1 and α > 0) converges to a Rϵ/μ neighborhood of the optimal solution. Here, R is defined as min{D, (rγ_maxC + ϵ)/μ}, with D representing the dataset diameter and C an upper bound on gradient norms. Furthermore, when the risk function is μ-strongly convex and the component functions are smooth, IG with the same diminishing stepsize applied to subset S converges to a ϵ/μ neighborhood of the optimum solution.

The second approach we present leverages the reliability of a given 𝐲, as detailed in Algorithm <ref>. This method is inspired by the uncertainty sampling query framework, which aims to prioritize instances where the model's confidence is low. To operationalize this, we empirically compute Γ_ρ,η_ABP,ℓ_MBCE(S,A_1,A_2) for multiple untrained BP decoders with varying iteration counts (L = {L₁, ..., Lᵣ}). By systematically analyzing these untrained models, we identify patterns in their decoding performance. For the query process, we set a prior on η_ABP,ℓ_MBCE to guide batch selection. Below, we detail the rationale behind this prior and the steps for batch construction.  

First, the prior is defined as a Normal distribution with mean μ and covariance matrix Σ over 𝐲, where these instances are decodable by augmenting the standard BP decoder with additional iterations. The choice of prior reflects the assumption that the selected 𝐲 lie near the decision boundary: these instances remain unresolved by BP until more iterations are introduced, suggesting they are challenging cases. The WBP is then trained to address this gap, effectively learning to decode these instances without requiring extra iterations during inference. The prior specification is formalized in Algorithm <ref>.  

For batch sampling, we proceed in three steps, outlined in Algorithm <ref> (lines <ref>-<ref>). The final step employs weighted random sampling, where each 𝐲 is assigned a probability proportional to its normalized weight. This ensures that instances with higher uncertainty or strategic value (as determined by the prior) are prioritized for inclusion in the batch. By sampling without replacement, we avoid redundant selections and promote diversity in the training data, which is critical for robust learning.

In a stream based approach batches are generated one by one. A selective sampling approach is one in which the data to be queried is selected based on some metric.
An underlying assumption in active learning stream-based selective sampling approach is that data is free to obtain. In our error-correcting codes domain data is unlimited when the channel model is known (as AWGN) or can be fairly easily collected when channel model is unknown, and we do not need to annotate it by hand. This is a huge advantage and a strong claim in favor of using this method in decoding.
Traditionally, this method is used on unlabeled stream or pool of data. In this case one would want to choose which samples are worth labeling and training. In our case all samples are labeled. Therefore, our goal is to perform the training procedure with the highest
κ for the received words.
new_text: In a stream-based approach, batches of data are generated sequentially, differing from methods that process large pre-collected datasets. This approach is particularly effective in active learning when combined with selective sampling techniques. Here, the algorithm uses a metric—such as uncertainty or informativeness—to select which data instances to query for labels. A key assumption in this method is that data is freely available. In our error-correcting codes domain, this holds true: when the channel model (e.g., AWGN) is known, data can be automatically generated in unlimited quantities. If the channel model is unknown, data collection remains straightforward without manual annotation, which is typically resource-intensive. This is a major advantage, strongly supporting the use of this method in decoding tasks. Traditionally, stream-based selective sampling is applied to unlabeled data, where the goal is to identify and label the most informative samples. However, since all our samples are already labeled, our focus shifts from selecting which data to label to optimizing training to achieve the highest possible κ (a performance metric) for received words. The automatic and accessible data allows efficient prioritization of training strategies that maximize this metric.

Omnidirectional Cameras:
360 degree vision, or at least panoramic vision, is necessary for higher levels of automation. This can be achieved through camera arrays, though precise extrinsic calibration between each camera is then necessary to make image stitching possible. Alternatively, omnidirectional cameras can be used, or a smaller array of cameras with very wide angle fisheye lenses. These are however difficult to intrinsically calibrate; the spherical images are highly distorted and the camera model used must account for mirror reflections or fisheye lens distortions, depending on the camera model producing the panoramic images<cit.>. The accuracy of the model and calibration dictates the quality of undistorted images produced, on which the aforementioned 2D vision algorithms are used. An example of fisheye lenses producing two spherical images then combined into one panoramic image is shown in <Ref>. Some distortions inevitably remain, but despite these challenges in calibration, omnidirectional cameras have been used for many applications such as SLAM<cit.> and 3D reconstruction <cit.>.
new_text: Achieving 360-degree or panoramic vision is critical for enabling higher levels of autonomous systems, as it provides comprehensive environmental awareness. This capability can be realized through traditional camera arrays, though such systems require precise extrinsic calibration—aligning each camera’s position and orientation relative to one another—to facilitate seamless image stitching. An alternative approach involves using omnidirectional cameras or a reduced number of cameras equipped with wide-angle fisheye lenses, which capture large fields of view in a single image. However, these cameras introduce significant calibration challenges due to their extreme distortion patterns. Specifically, intrinsic calibration—adjusting the internal parameters of the camera to correct distortions—must account for either mirror-based or fisheye lens-induced distortions, depending on the camera design. The fidelity of this calibration process directly impacts the quality of undistorted images, which are essential inputs for standard 2D vision algorithms. For example, systems using fisheye lenses often generate two spherical images, which are then merged into a unified panoramic view (see <Ref>); even after this combination, minor distortions may persist. Despite these technical hurdles, omnidirectional cameras remain valuable tools in applications such as SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping)<cit.> and 3D reconstruction<cit.>, where the benefits of full-coverage imaging outweigh the calibration complexity.

We proposed MOPED method for variational inference in Bayesian DNN which provides a way for choosing meaningful prior distributions and approximate posterior distributions over weights.
 We demonstrated with thorough empirical experiments that MOPED enables scalable variational inference for Bayesian DNNs while achieving faster training convergence and provide reliable uncertainty quantification, without compromising on the accuracy provided by the deterministic DNNs. We showed the uncertainty estimates obtained from the proposed method are reliable to identify out-of-distribution data.
We also showed hybrid Bayesian DNN architectures can provide reliable uncertainty estimates while striking a balance between complexity and benefits of Bayesian inference.
new_text: We proposed the MOPED method for variational inference in Bayesian DNNs, which provides a means of selecting meaningful prior distributions and approximate posterior distributions over weights. We demonstrated through comprehensive empirical experiments that MOPED enables scalable variational inference for Bayesian DNNs while achieving faster training convergence and providing reliable uncertainty quantification without compromising the accuracy of deterministic DNNs. We showed that the uncertainty estimates obtained from the proposed method are reliable for identifying out-of-distribution data. We also showed that hybrid Bayesian DNN architectures can provide reliable uncertainty estimates while balancing complexity with the benefits of Bayesian inference.

We therefore propose a new approach to predict the relative difficulty change of a gap g=(i, ℓ) when increasing the gap size by one letter Δ_inc(g) ≈ d(g') - d(g), g' = (i, ℓ + 1) and correspondingly when decreasing the gap size by one letter Δ_dec(g) ≈ d(g) - d(g'), g' = (i, ℓ - 1).

new_text: We propose a new method to estimate how the difficulty of a specific gap changes when its size is adjusted by one letter. Specifically, for a gap defined by positions *i* and length *ℓ*, denoted *g* = (*i*, *ℓ*), we approximate the difficulty increase as Δ<sub>inc</sub>(*g*) ≈ *d*(*g'*) − *d*(*g*) when expanding the gap to *g'* = (*i*, *ℓ* + 1). Similarly, the difficulty decrease Δ<sub>dec</sub>(*g*) ≈ *d*(*g*) − *d*(*g'*) is approximated when contracting the gap to *g'* = (*i*, *ℓ* − 1). This concept of relative difficulty change allows for efficient manipulation of gap sizes in real-time applications. Instead of recalculating the full difficulty prediction for every possible gap size combination, our method incrementally predicts the effect of modifying a single gap. By focusing on incremental adjustments, we avoid the computational overhead of a complete system recalculation, enabling dynamic gap size adjustments without significant delays.

A principled approach, Markov logic networks (MLNs) <cit.>, combine first-order logic with probabilistic graphical models. Despite their effectiveness in various tasks, MLNs face challenges in inference efficiency due to complex triplet connections, and their performance is limited in predicting missing knowledge graph (KG) triplets as many remain undiscoverable by rules. In contrast, pLogicNet employs knowledge graph embeddings for inference, leveraging learned entity and relation embeddings for greater effectiveness.

Instead, our approach consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art across diverse web content and various evaluation platforms.

Since the breakthrough results achieved with AlexNet for the 2012 ImageNet Challenge <cit.>, CNN's accuracy has been continually improved with architectures like VGG <cit.>, ResNet <cit.> and DenseNet <cit.>, at the expense of growing complexity (deeper and wider networks) that require more training samples and computational resources <cit.>. new_text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) extract distinguishing features from annotated training data, achieving record-breaking accuracy in visual recognition tasks such as image categorization, object localization, and medical diagnostic support. Following AlexNet’s groundbreaking performance at the 2012 ImageNet Challenge <cit.>, subsequent architectures like VGG <cit.>, ResNet <cit.>, and DenseNet <cit.> have iteratively improved performance metrics. However, these advancements come with escalating architectural complexity—deepening network depth and expanding width—which necessitate larger labeled datasets and substantially greater computational capacity <cit.>. Critically, the operational speed of CNNs often experiences a sharp decline as these architectural complexities grow.

old_text: Here, we show that the Ω_sparse attribution prior can build sparser models that perform significantly better in settings with limited training data. We use a publicly available healthcare mortality prediction dataset of 13,000 patients <cit.>, where each of the 36 features (119 after one-hot encoding) represent medical data such as a patient's age, vital signs, and laboratory measurements. The outcome is a binary label indicating survival after 10 years. Sparse models in this setting may reduce cost by accurately risk-stratifying patients using fewer lab tests, or may enable accurate models to be trained with very few labeled patient samples. We build 3-layer binary classifier neural networks regularized using L1, sparse group lasso (SGL) and sparse attribution prior penalties to predict patient survival. The regularization strength was determined by a broad sweep (from 10^-10 to 10^3 for all methods) followed by a fine sweep in the area of lowest loss (see Supplement for details).
new_text: We demonstrate that the Ω_sparse attribution prior can generate sparser models that achieve significantly better performance in low-data regimes. We apply this approach to a publicly available healthcare mortality prediction dataset comprising 13,000 patients <cit.>, where the 36 original features (119 post-one-hot encoding) represent clinical data including age, vital signs, and laboratory measurements. The binary outcome indicates patient survival after a 10-year period. In this context, sparse models could reduce healthcare costs by enabling accurate risk stratification with fewer lab tests or by allowing accurate training with limited labeled patient data. To evaluate this, we constructed 3-layer binary classifier neural networks employing L1, sparse group lasso (SGL), and sparse attribution prior regularization to predict patient survival. Regularization strength was selected via an initial broad sweep (ranging from 10^-10 to 10^3 for all methods) followed by a focused fine sweep in the lowest-loss region (see Supplement for details).

Training with expected gradients:
If we let the attribution function Φ in our attribution prior Ω(Φ(θ, X)) be expected gradients, this would appear computationally expensive. Computing a good approximation during training may require computing potentially hundreds of extra gradient calls every training step, as discussed in the previous paragraph. Ordinarily, this would make training with such attributions intractable. However, we observe that most deep learning models today are trained using some variant of batch gradient descent, in which the gradient of a loss function is approximated over many training steps using mini-batches of data. We can use a batch training procedure to approximate expected gradients over the training procedure as well. During training, we let k be the number of samples we draw to compute expected gradients for each mini-batch of data. Remarkably, we find that as small as k = 1 suffices to regularize the explanations, which corresponds to only one additional gradient call per training step. More details about how we train with respect to the attribution term can be found in the Supplement.
new_text: Training with expected gradients: When employing expected gradients as the attribution function Φ in our attribution prior Ω(Φ(θ, X)), the computational cost appears prohibitive. Approximating this effectively during training could necessitate hundreds of additional gradient evaluations per step, as outlined earlier. Typically, this level of computation would render such attribution-based training infeasible. However, modern deep learning models commonly rely on variants of batch gradient descent, where the gradient of a loss is estimated iteratively using mini-batches of data. We repurpose this framework to approximate expected gradients over the training process itself. For each mini-batch, we define k as the number of samples used to compute expected gradients. Notably, we observe that even k = 1—which entails just one additional gradient computation per training iteration—is sufficient to enforce regularization on the model’s explanations. Further methodological details regarding the training procedure for the attribution objective are detailed in the Supplement.

Two algorithms, RecurSIA and RRT, are presented, designed to increase the compression factor achieved using SIATEC-based point-set cover algorithms. RecurSIA recursively applies a TEC cover algorithm to the patterns in the TECs that it discovers. RRT attempts to remove translators from each TEC without reducing its covered set. When evaluated with COSIATEC, SIATECCompress and Forth's algorithm on the JKU Patterns Development Database, using RecurSIA with or without RRT increased compression factor and recall but reduced precision. Using RRT alone increased compression factor and reduced recall and precision, but had a smaller effect than RecurSIA.
new_text: Two algorithms, RecurSIA and RRT, are introduced to enhance the compression factor of SIATEC-based point-set cover algorithms. RecurSIA applies a TEC cover algorithm recursively to the patterns within the TECs it identifies, while RRT seeks to eliminate translators from individual TECs without compromising their covered sets. When evaluated against COSIATEC, SIATECCompress, and Forth’s algorithm on the JKU Patterns Development Database, RecurSIA—used with or without RRT—increased compression factors and recall but reduced precision. In contrast, RRT alone improved compression factors yet diminished both recall and precision, though with a less pronounced effect compared to RecurSIA.

A number of approaches to unsupervised representation learning from images based on self-supervision have proven very successful.
Self-supervision generally involves learning from tasks designed to resemble supervised learning in some way, but in which the “labels” can be created automatically from the data itself with no manual effort.
An early example is relative location prediction <cit.>, where a model is trained on input pairs of image patches and predicts their relative locations.
Contrastive predictive coding (CPC) <cit.> is a recent related approach where, given an image patch, a model predicts
which patches occur in other image locations.
Other approaches include colorization <cit.>,
motion segmentation <cit.>,
rotation prediction <cit.>,
and exemplar matching <cit.>.
Rigorous empirical comparisons of many of these approaches have also been conducted <cit.>.
A key advantage offered by BigBiGAN and other approaches based on generative models, relative to most self-supervised approaches,
is that their input may be the full-resolution image or other signal, with no cropping or modification of the data needed
(though such modifications may be beneficial as data augmentation).
This means the resulting representation can typically be applied directly to full data in the downstream task with no domain shift.
new_text: Unsupervised representation learning techniques for image data relying on self-supervision have demonstrated significant success. Self-supervised learning typically entails training models on tasks that mimic supervised objectives, with the distinction that annotations are generated algorithmically from the input data itself without human intervention. An early example involves training models to predict the relative spatial positions of image patches <cit.>. Contrastive predictive coding (CPC) <cit.>, a more recent method, requires models to forecast which patches co-occur in different regions of an image. Additional strategies include reconstructing colorized versions of grayscale images <cit.>, identifying motion patterns in video sequences <cit.>, predicting the degree of image rotation <cit.>, and distinguishing between similar object instances <cit.>. Comprehensive benchmarking studies comparing these methods have also been reported <cit.>. A notable benefit of approaches like BigBiGAN and other generative modeling frameworks, compared to most self-supervised techniques, is their ability to process full-resolution input signals without requiring cropping or data alterations (although such transformations may still prove advantageous for data augmentation). This enables representations to be directly applicable to complete data in downstream tasks without introducing domain discrepancies.

A number of relevant autoencoder and GAN variants have also been proposed.
Associative compression networks (ACNs) <cit.> learn to compress at the dataset level by conditioning data on other previously transmitted data which are similar in code space, resulting in models that can “daydream” semantically similar samples, similar to BigBiGAN reconstructions.
VQ-VAEs <cit.> pair a discrete (vector quantized) encoder with an autoregressive decoder to produce faithful reconstructions with a high compression factor and demonstrate representation learning results in reinforcement learning settings.
In the adversarial space, adversarial autoencoders <cit.> proposed an autoencoder-style encoder-decoder pair trained with pixel-level reconstruction cost, replacing the KL-divergence regularization of the prior used in VAEs <cit.> with a discriminator.
In another proposed VAE-GAN hybrid <cit.> the pixel-space reconstruction error used in most VAEs is replaced with feature space distance from an intermediate layer of a GAN discriminator.
Other hybrid approaches like AGE <cit.> and α-GAN <cit.> add an encoder to stabilize GAN training.
An interesting difference between many of these approaches and the BiGAN <cit.> framework is that BiGAN does not train the encoder or generator with an explicit reconstruction cost.
Though it can be shown that (Big)BiGAN implicitly minimizes a reconstruction cost,
qualitative reconstruction results (Section <ref>) suggest that this reconstruction cost is of a different flavor, emphasizing high-level semantics over pixel-level details.
new_text: Several autoencoder and GAN variants have been introduced to enhance data compression and generative capabilities. Associative compression networks (ACNs) <cit.> achieve dataset-level compression by conditionally encoding data based on similarities in latent code space, enabling the generation of semantically coherent reconstructions akin to BigBiGAN outputs. VQ-VAEs <cit.> combine a discrete vector-quantized encoder with an autoregressive decoder to achieve high compression ratios while producing accurate reconstructions and demonstrating effective representation learning in reinforcement learning tasks. In adversarial architectures, adversarial autoencoders <cit.> substitute the KL-divergence regularization of VAEs <cit.> with a discriminator, training an encoder-decoder pair via pixel-level reconstruction loss. Another VAE-GAN hybrid <cit.> replaces pixel-level reconstruction error with feature-matching loss derived from an intermediate layer of a GAN discriminator. Hybrid methods like AGE <cit.> and α-GAN <cit.> incorporate encoders to improve GAN training stability. A key distinction between these approaches and the BiGAN <cit.> framework lies in the absence of explicit reconstruction objectives for the encoder or generator in BiGAN. While theoretical analysis implies implicit reconstruction minimization in (Big)BiGAN, qualitative results (Section <ref>) indicate a focus on semantic coherence over precise pixel-level reconstruction.

We formulate segmentation in video as clustering in the space-time graph of pixels.
We introduce an efficient spectral algorithm, Spectral Filtering Segmentation (SFSeg), in which the standard power iteration for computing the principal eigenvector of the graph adjacency matrix is transformed into a set of 3D convolutions directly on 3D feature maps in the video volume. Our original theoretical contribution makes the initial intractable problem possible. In experiments, our algorithm consistently improves over top published Video Object Segmentation methods in both unsupervised and semi-supervised scenarios at a relatively minor additional computational cost. The consistent improvements in practice indicate that our spectral approach brings a new and complementary dimension to clustering in space and time, which is not fully addressed by current state of the art algorithms. In the immediate future we will explore ways to learn more powerful features end-to-end, within our spectral clustering formulation.

Our original theoretical contribution enables this previously intractable problem. In experiments, our algorithm outperforms top published Video Object Segmentation methods in both unsupervised and semi-supervised scenarios with minimal additional computational cost. These consistent improvements demonstrate that our spectral approach introduces a novel, complementary dimension to spatiotemporal clustering not addressed in existing state-of-the-art algorithms. We plan to explore learning end-to-end features that enhance our spectral clustering formulation in future work.

old_text: This paper presents a tractable and scalable spatiotemporal mathematical framework for massive uplink PMT IoT networks. Each device within the network accommodates a number of priority queues, generating packets, differentiated by their assigned priorities. Interactions between queues, in terms of the packet departure probabilities, occur due to aggregate network-wide mutual interference. Consequently, interdependency occurs between the microscopic (i.e., queues evolution) and macroscopic (aggregate network interference) scales. Tools from queueing theory are utilized to characterize the queues interaction within each device. Due to the adopted priority-aware transmission, service vacations occur within each device to lower priority packets to address higher priority packets. We propose a vacation-based queueing model that decomposes the different priority queues at each device to a single-queue system with server vacation. Employing such a vacation-based queueing model offers a tractable and scalable alternative to conventional state of the art, which are hindered by the curse of dimensionality problem. Furthermore, we utilize stochastic geometry to account for the network-wide aggregate interference. To this end, an iterative algorithm is proposed that aims at characterizing the steady state probabilities and the coverage probabilities for the different priority classes. In addition, we consider two channel access strategies; namely dedicated and shared. For the former strategy, an IoT device randomly and uniformly selects one of the channels dedicated for the addressed packet priority. On the other hand, an IoT device in the shared strategy randomly and uniformly selects one of the complete set of channels regardless of the packet priority. Based on the transmission success probability, average number of packets within a queue, average waiting time and service availability, shared access strategy shows better performance when employed in large scale grant-free uplink IoT networks. As a result, resource allocation on a traffic level for grant-free IoT systems provides lower performance compared to the shared access strategy. Finally, we show different insights on the scalability and overflow conditions of the network, which defines the network parameters at which the network can serve all packets generated by the IoT devices without dropping newly incoming packets.
new_text:
This paper introduces a spatiotemporal mathematical framework designed to manage the complexities of massive uplink PMT IoT networks. The framework is both tractable and scalable, enabling efficient analysis of systems with a large number of interconnected devices. To model the packet transmission process, each IoT device is equipped with multiple priority queues, where packets are generated based on their assigned priority levels. These queues interact through packet departure probabilities, influenced by the aggregate interference from all devices in the network. Such interactions create a two-way dependency: the microscopic behavior of individual queues (e.g., packet arrivals, processing rates) affects the macroscopic state of network interference, while the macroscopic interference in turn alters the microscopic queue dynamics.  

To address these interdependencies, tools from queueing theory are applied to model how different priority queues within each device interact. A key innovation is the use of a priority-aware transmission mechanism, which introduces service vacations—temporary pauses in processing lower-priority packets when higher-priority ones are pending. This approach is modeled through a vacation-based queueing system, where multiple priority queues are decomposed into a simplified single-queue structure with server vacations. This decomposition avoids the computational intractability of traditional models, which suffer from exponential complexity due to the "curse of dimensionality" when scaling to numerous devices and queues.  

The framework further integrates stochastic geometry to capture the spatial distribution and interference effects across the network. An iterative algorithm is developed to compute steady-state probabilities and coverage probabilities for each priority class, enabling precise performance evaluation. To test the framework, the study compares two channel access strategies: dedicated and shared. In the dedicated strategy, an IoT device randomly selects a channel reserved for the specific packet priority, whereas the shared strategy allows any channel to be chosen, regardless of priority. By analyzing metrics such as transmission success probability, average queue occupancy, waiting time, and service availability, the shared strategy is shown to outperform dedicated access in large-scale networks. This advantage highlights the trade-offs between prioritization and resource efficiency in grant-free uplink systems. The results also reveal critical thresholds for network scalability and overflow, identifying the conditions under which the network can reliably handle all incoming traffic without packet loss.
