old_text: Deep neural networks have become the state of the art for a lot of machine learning problems. However, these methods usually imply the need for a large amount of labeled data in order to avoid overfitting and be able to generalize. Furthermore, it is assumed that train and test data come from the same distribution and feature space. This becomes a huge problem in cases when labeling is costly and/or time-consuming. One way to address this challenge is to use a source domain which contains a vast amount of annotated data and reduce the domain shift between this domain and a different, but similar, target domain in which we have few or even no annotations.
new_text: Deep neural networks have emerged as the state-of-the-art approach for many machine learning tasks. However, their effectiveness often depends on large quantities of labeled training data to prevent overfitting—where models memorize training examples without learning generalizable patterns—and to enable performance on unseen data. Additionally, traditional approaches assume that training and testing datasets are drawn from the same statistical distribution and share the same feature space, ensuring consistent model behavior. This becomes a significant challenge in domains where data annotation requires substantial resources, expertise, or time, making it difficult to gather sufficient labeled examples. To overcome this limitation, researchers employ domain adaptation techniques that leverage a source domain with abundant annotations and aim to reduce the domain shift—the differences in data distribution—between the source and a related target domain with limited or no labeled data. This strategy allows models to transfer knowledge from well-annotated source data to target scenarios, improving performance despite limited local annotations.

The benefits of the IINC metric as compared with other metrics are shown in Fig. <ref>.
Note that the IOU and Cosine similarity metrics are not useful at all for the first3samples, where the scores are the same, but the maps have vastly different properties.
Similarly, the PBCA is not useful for the last3cases, because the ratio of mis-classification is not represented in the score.

new_text: The advantages of the IINC metric relative to alternative metrics are illustrated in Fig. <ref>. Notably, the IOU and Cosine similarity metrics fail entirely for the first 3 samples, where identical scores mask substantial differences in the properties of the maps. Similarly, the PBCA is ineffective for the final 3 cases, as its score does not account for the ratio of mis-classification. For example, the last case overestimates by a factor of 100%, the third-to-last case overestimates by 200%, and the second-to-last case both over- and underestimates by 150%. In contrast, the IINC achieves superior ordering by mirroring the IOU’s ranking when applicable (last 4 cases) and aligning with the PBCA when valid (first 3 cases). This demonstrates that the IINC is a more reliable and comprehensive metric for comparing attention maps than prior methods.

OODIDA (On-board/Off-board Distributed Data Analytics) is a platform for distributing and executing concurrent data analytics tasks. It targets fleets of reference vehicles in the automotive industry and has a particular focus on rapid prototyping. Its underlying message-passing infrastructure has been implemented in Erlang/OTP. External Python applications perform data analytics tasks. Most work is performed by clients (on-board). A central cloud server performs supplementary tasks (off-board). OODIDA can be automatically packaged and deployed, which necessitates restarting parts of the system, or all of it. This is potentially disruptive. To address this issue, we added the ability to execute user-defined Python modules on clients as well as the server. These modules can be replaced without restarting any part of the system and they can even be replaced between iterations of an ongoing assignment. This facilitates use cases such as iterative A/B testing of machine learning algorithms or modifying experimental algorithms on-the-fly.
new_text: OODIDA (On-board/Off-board Distributed Data Analytics) distributes and executes concurrent data analytics tasks for fleets of reference vehicles in the automotive industry, with a focus on rapid prototyping. Its message-passing infrastructure is implemented in Erlang/OTP, while Python applications handle data analytics. Clients (on-board) perform most tasks, and a central cloud server (off-board) executes supporting functions. Automatic packaging and deployment require system restarts, which can disrupt operations. To mitigate this, we introduced user-defined Python modules that execute on both clients and servers. These modules support hot-swapping—replacement without restarting any system components—and can be updated between iterations of ongoing assignments, enabling iterative A/B testing of machine learning algorithms or real-time experimental adjustments.

old_text: Inconsistent updates are a problem in practice, i.e. results sent from clients may have been produced with different custom code modules in the same iteration of an assignment. This happens if not all clients receive the updated custom code before the end of the current iteration. To solve this problem, each provided module with custom code is tagged with its md5 hash signature, which is reported together with the results from the clients. The cloud only uses the results tagged with the signature that achieves a majority. Consequently, results are never tainted by using different versions of custom code in the same iteration.
new_text: Inconsistent updates pose a problem: clients may submit results generated with different custom code modules during the same assignment iteration. This occurs when not all clients receive updated code before the iteration concludes. To resolve this, each custom code module is tagged with an MD5 hash, reported alongside client results. The cloud processes only results tagged with the hash achieving a majority. This ensures results remain untainted by mixed code versions in a single iteration.

Using TPRs to encode natural-language has several advantages.
First, natural-language TPRs can be interpreted by exploring the distribution of tokens grouped by the role and symbol vectors they are assigned by a trained model (as in <cit.>).
Second, TPRs avoid the Bag of Word (BoW) confusion <cit.>: the BoW encoding of Jay saw Kay is the same as the BoW encoding of Kay saw Jay.
However, in a TPR embedding using, say, grammatical roles, f_Jay⊗r_subject + f_saw⊗r_verb + f_Kay⊗r_object is different from f_Kay⊗r_subject + f_saw⊗r_verb + f_Jay⊗r_object, because the role filled by a symbol changes with its context.

old_text: With active-code replacement, the user can define a custom Python module for the cloud and for client devices. It is implemented as a special case of an assignment. The front-end f performs static and dynamic checks, attempting to verify correctness of syntax and data types. If these checks succeed, the provided code is turned into a JSON object and ingested by user node u for further processing. Within this JSON object, the user-defined code is stored as an encoded text string. It is forwarded to cloud node b, which spawns an assignment handler b' for this particular assignment. Custom code can be used on the cloud and/or clients. Assuming clients have been targeted with active-code replacement, node b' turns the assignment specification into tasks for all clients c specified in the assignment. Afterwards, task specifications are sent to the specified client devices. There, the client process spawns a task handler for the current task, which monitors task completion. The task handler sends the task specification in JSON to an external Python application, which turns the given code into a file, thus recreating the Python module the data analyst initially provided. The resulting files are tied to the ID of the user who provided it. After the task handler is done, it notifies the assignment handler b' and terminates. Similarly, once the assignment handler has received responses from all task handlers, it sends a status message to the cloud node and terminates. The cloud node sends a status message to inform the user that their custom code has been successfully deployed. Deploying custom code to the cloud is similar, the main difference being that b' communicates with the external Python application on the cloud.
new_text: Active-code replacement enables users to design a personalized Python module for deployment on both cloud infrastructure and client devices, functioning as a specialized assignment. The front-end system executes static and dynamic validation to ensure syntactic and data-type accuracy. Upon successful validation, the code is encapsulated into a JSON object and transmitted to the user node u for subsequent processing. This JSON structure contains the user-defined code as an encoded text string, which is then routed to the cloud node b. Node b initiates an assignment handler b' to manage this assignment. The custom code can be executed on the cloud, client devices, or both. When client devices are designated for active-code replacement, handler b' partitions the assignment into tasks for each targeted client c. These task specifications are relayed to the client devices, where a task handler is spawned to oversee task execution by passing the JSON task details to an external Python application. This application generates a file from the provided code, reconstructing the original user-submitted Python module and associating it with the user's unique identifier. Upon task completion, the task handler signals b' and terminates. Similarly, once b' receives all task responses, it communicates a status update to the cloud node, which in turn alerts the user of successful deployment. Cloud-specific deployment mirrors this process, differing only in that b' interacts directly with the cloud-hosted external Python application.

old_text: The main benefit of active-code replacement is that code for new computational methods can be deployed right away and executed almost instantly, without affecting other ongoing tasks. In contrast, a standard update of the cloud or client installation necessitates redeploying and restarting the respective components of the system. In an idealized test setup, where the various workstations that run the user, cloud and client components of OODIDA are connected via Ethernet, it takes a fraction of a second for a custom on-board or off-board method to be available for the user to call when deployed with active-code replacement, as shown in Table <ref>. On the other hand, automated redeployment of the cloud and client installation takes roughly 20 and 40 seconds, respectively. The runtime difference between a standard update and active-code replacement amounts to three orders of magnitude. Of course, real-world deployment via a wireless or 4G connection would be slower as well as error-prone. Yet, the idealized evaluation environment reveals the relative performance difference of both approaches, eliminating potentially unreliable data transmission as a source of error.
new_text: The main advantage of active-code replacement lies in its ability to deploy and execute new computational methods immediately, without disrupting other ongoing system operations. This contrasts sharply with traditional updates for cloud or client installations, which require full redeployment and subsequent restarts of system components—a process that inherently introduces delays. In an idealized test environment where all workstations (user, cloud, and client components of OODIDA) are connected via high-speed Ethernet, active-code replacement enables a custom method (either on-board or off-board) to become available for user execution in just a fraction of a second, as demonstrated in Table <ref>. This efficiency is measured against the time required for standard redeployment processes: cloud components typically take about 20 seconds to update, while client components require approximately 40 seconds. The runtime difference between these methods spans three orders of magnitude (a factor of 1,000), underscoring the efficiency of active-code replacement. While real-world deployments over wireless or 4G networks would face additional latency and higher error rates due to connection instability, this idealized setup isolates performance differences by eliminating transmission errors as a variable. By doing so, the comparison clearly highlights the relative scalability and responsiveness of active-code replacement over conventional update mechanisms.

In this model, a social network can be abstracted as a
	directed graph G=(V, E) with a node set V and a directed edge set E, |V|=n and |E|=m. Let N_in(v) and N_out(v) be the set of in-neighbors and out-neighbor of v, respectively. Each edge e=(u, v) ∈ E has a probability p(u, v) ∈ (0, 1) that represents the information transmission from u to v.
	The diffusion process from a seed set S to the rest of the network happens round by round as follows. At step 0, all nodes in S are activated while the rest of the nodes are inactive. At step t ≥ 1, an active node u in the previous step t-1 has a single chance to activate each currently inactive out neighbour node v with the successful probability p(u, v). Once a node becomes activated, it remains
	in that state in all subsequent steps. The influence propagation stops when no more node can be activated.

Optimization algorithms are typically controlled by metaparameters that determine their behavior (e.g. the learning rate). An optimization algorithm therefore represents a family of update rules until all metaparameters have been specified. Practitioners generally tune a subset of the metaparameters to maximize performance over a validation set, while often leaving some metaparameters at fixed default values. We define an optimizer to be an update rule together with a list of metaparameters to tune. In other words, someone using Adam and tuning ϵ is using a “different” optimizer than someone using Adam with the default ϵ. We focus on first-order optimizers within the following standard model of iterative methods for optimization <cit.>.
new_text: Optimization algorithms are governed by metaparameters, such as the learning rate, which dictate their behavior. An algorithm represents a family of update rules until all metaparameters are fixed. Practitioners typically tune a subset of metaparameters to optimize validation set performance, often retaining others at default values. We define an optimizer as an update rule and a set of metaparameters to tune. For example, tuning Adam's ϵ results in a different optimizer than using the default ϵ. We focus on first-order optimizers within the standard model of iterative optimization methods <cit>.

new_text: In the original implementation of Da et al. (da2015double), the authors noticed and addressed this problem by modifying the vertex area computation at the triple junction: the vertex area applied to all incident regions is set as the shared edge length at the triple junction multiplied by a global constant, which is defined as a fixed fraction of the mean edge length across the entire mesh (0.5 in the original implementation). This approach ensures that discrete mean curvatures computed at the triple junction capture relevant angles while remaining independent of the specific triangulation's areas.

old_text: Exploring adversarial attack vectors and studying their effects on machine learning algorithms has been of interest to researchers. Deep neural networks working with time series data have received lesser interest compared to their image counterparts in this context. In a recent finding, it has been revealed that current state-of-the-art deep learning time series classifiers are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. In this paper, we introduce two local gradient based and one spectral density based time series data augmentation techniques. We show that a model trained with data obtained using our techniques obtains state-of-the-art classification accuracy on various time series benchmarks. In addition, it improves the robustness of the model against some of the most common corruption techniques,such as Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Basic Iterative Method (BIM).
new_text: Adversarial attack vectors and their impacts on machine learning algorithms remain a key research area. Deep neural networks processing time series data have received less attention than their image-based counterparts in this field. Recent studies show current state-of-the-art deep learning time series classifiers are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper proposes two gradient-based and one spectral density-based time series data augmentation techniques. Models trained on data generated by these techniques achieve state-of-the-art classification accuracy across major time series benchmarks while enhancing robustness against common adversarial methods, including Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Basic Iterative Method (BIM).

Proposition <ref> means that once the pilot sequence is designed with the specific structure described in the proposition, then there exists a one-to-one mapping Φ(.) that can map the quantized measurement matrix 𝐘 to the channel 𝐡, i.e., it can use 𝐘 to predict 𝐡. Interestingly, as we will see in sec:Results, only a few pilot symbols (very small N) are needed in massive MIMO systems to make this mapping Φ(.) exist with high probability. This has the potential of significantly reducing the channel training overhead compared to classical 1-bit ADC channel estimation techniques. To be able to leverage this mapping function, however, we need to know it. Characterizing this mapping analytically is very non-trivial mainly because of the non-linear quantization. With this motivation, we propose to exploit the powerful learning capabilities of deep neural networks to learn this mapping and harvest the promising gains in reducing the channel training overhead. Before describing the adopted deep learning model in sec:DL_model, we first highlight in the next subsection an interesting gain of using the proposed deep learning based 1-bit ADC channel estimation approach in massive MIMO systems.
new_text: Proposition <ref> establishes that structuring the pilot sequence according to its specification enables a one-to-one mapping Φ(.) from the quantized measurement matrix 𝐘 to the channel 𝐡, allowing 𝐘 to predict 𝐡. As shown in Sec. Results, massive MIMO systems require only a small number of pilot symbols (very small N) for Φ(.) to exist with high probability, potentially reducing channel training overhead compared to classical 1-bit ADC techniques. However, leveraging Φ requires its characterization, which is non-trivial due to non-linear quantization. To address this, we propose using deep neural networks (DNNs) to learn Φ and exploit their learning capabilities for overhead reduction. We first highlight the benefits of this deep learning-based 1-bit ADC channel estimation approach in the next subsection before presenting the adopted DL model in Sec. DL_model.

old_text: The deep learning framework used to perform the task was adopted from our previous work <cit.>. Briefly, the main part of the system is a U-Net, originally introduced in <cit.>, for recovering missing parts of the time-frequency representations of speech segments. Similarly to the data preprocessing for training the speechVGG, here we divided all the available voice recordings into 1028 ms segments, extracted their STFT magnitudes, applied logarithm and normalized, as specified in <ref>, to obtain 128x128 matrices. Each training sample was furthermore degraded by applying a mask to it and replacing masked values with zeros. Such samples, along with their mask were processed through the network to recover original time-frequency representations of speech. Waveforms were obtained directly from the recovered STFT magnitudes by applying the local weighted sums algorithm <cit.>.
new_text: The deep learning framework adopted from our previous work <cit.> employs a U-Net <cit.> as its core component for reconstructing missing parts of speech segment time-frequency representations. Voice recordings were segmented into 1028 ms excerpts, processed via STFT magnitude extraction, logarithmic transformation, and normalization <ref>, yielding 128×128 matrices. Training samples were masked by setting selected values to zero; these masked samples, alongside their masks, were input to the network for reconstructing original time-frequency representations. Waveforms were reconstructed from the recovered STFT magnitudes using the local weighted sums algorithm <cit.>.

old_text: To train the network on the word classification task, we employed different sizes of training dictionaries (the numbers of unique words) extracted from subsets of voice recordings. In particular, for each considered dictionary size, corresponding to the number of classes in the classification task, we extracted all instances of words in the dictionary from the chosen subset of data. We obtained magnitude spectrograms for each segment by taking absolute values of a complex short-time Fourier transform (STFT, 256 samples window with 128 samples overlap, 128 frequency bins). Natural logarithm was then applied to the spectrogram, which was subsequently standardized. In the standardization process, the mean was subtracted from each frequency channel, then divided by the variance. Both the mean and variance were obtained from the training data.
new_text: To train the network on the word classification task, we used training dictionaries of varying sizes (where the size corresponds to the number of unique words) derived from subsets of voice recordings. Specifically, for each dictionary size (equivalent to the number of classification classes), we extracted all instances of the corresponding words from the selected data subset. For each audio segment, magnitude spectrograms were computed by taking the absolute values of a complex short-time Fourier transform (STFT; 256-sample window with 128-sample overlap, 128 frequency bins). These spectrograms were then transformed by applying a natural logarithm and subsequently standardized. Standardization involved subtracting the mean and dividing by the variance for each frequency channel, with both the mean and variance computed from the training data.

PoW is becoming a significant source of revenues for the entities participating to the consensus process. This phenomena will grow even more with the increasing number of users joining the digital currency markets. However,
while PoW computational requirements are fueling methodologies and techniques to achieve more and more computational power with less energy consumption, new malicious practices involves PoW-offloading to unaware users.
Indeed, a very recent cybersecurity attack involves the illicit use of resources from an unaware users to carry out PoW, i.e., cryptojacking <cit.>. This attack mainly consists on the unauthorized mining of cryptocurrencies allowing malicious parties to steal resources in terms of CPU, GPU, and memory from a target machine with the aim of effortlessly collecting crypto-wealth. This behaviour is gaining momentum for two main reasons: the ease of deployment of crypto-clients; and, the difficulty to detect those crypto-clients.
While being a general threat, cryptojacking is becoming particularly critical in Corporate ICT where the vast majority of laptops, desktops, and smartphones are distributed among the employees under a limited (if any) supervision. Indeed,
several unauthorized mining activities have already been discovered. Russian nuclear scientists have been arrested for “Bitcoin mining plot” <cit.>, the US government banned a Professor for secretly mining with National Science Foundation supercomputers <cit.>, a former Federal Reserve employee was sentenced to 12 months probation and a $5,000 fine after pleading guilty to installing unauthorized software that connected to an online Bitcoin network in order to earn units of the digital currency <cit.>, a Harvard student used 14,000-Core supercomputer to mine Dogecoin <cit.>, the factory lines of Hoya, the leading manufacturer of optical products in Japan, were shut down for three days as hackers tried to establish an unauthorized cryptocurrency mining <cit.>, just to cite a few.
new_text: Proof-of-Work (PoW) has emerged as a substantial revenue stream for entities engaged in blockchain consensus mechanisms. This trend is expected to intensify as the user base in digital currency markets expands. However, while advancements in PoW efficiency aim to maximize computational power with minimal energy use, new malicious tactics involve offloading PoW tasks onto unsuspecting users. Recent attacks involve the unauthorized exploitation of user resources for PoW—commonly termed "cryptojacking" <cit.>—where adversaries deploy covert mining operations to siphon CPU, GPU, and memory resources from compromised devices, enabling them to accumulate cryptocurrency without direct costs. The proliferation of this behavior stems from the simplicity of deploying mining clients and the inherent challenges in detecting such activities. Although a general threat, cryptojacking poses a critical risk in corporate information and communication technology (ICT) environments, where vast numbers of workstations and mobile devices remain under minimal oversight. Multiple instances highlight the severity: Russian nuclear scientists were arrested for orchestrating a Bitcoin mining operation <cit.>, a U.S. professor was prohibited from using National Science Foundation supercomputers for clandestine mining activities <cit.>, a former Federal Reserve employee received 12 months probation and a $5,000 fine for secretly connecting supercomputers to a Bitcoin network <cit.>, a Harvard student leveraged a 14,000-core supercomputer for Dogecoin mining <cit.>, and Japanese optical manufacturer Hoya temporarily suspended factory operations due to unauthorized mining attempts <cit.>, among other incidents.

old_text: Immediate access to vast quantities of information has resulted in online social media users feeling the effects of information overload <cit.>. Biological limits to cognition, in particular, memory and attention span, play an important role in information overload. Besides the recollection of ideas and experiences required to maintain conversation, memory is also required to maintain a store of the conversations and individuals to whom responses are due in the case of asynchronous communication. With the increasing dominance of the internet as a communication form, and, in particular, modern social media, asynchronous communication is quickly becoming the norm. Despite the typical preference of immediate response, studies have shown that most individuals are satisfied with responses that are delayed up to a day <cit.>. The downside of asynchronous communication is that it can quickly lead to a backlog of conversations lacking responses, which may exceed the individual's capacity to respond, overwhelming them, and potentially driving them into a state of information overload. Although memory capacity and the processes of information overload and the physiological stresses that result have been studied extensively in lab experiments <cit.>, the effects of information overload on online conversation dynamics and the potential stresses it places on collective social behavior remain largely unstudied.
new_text: The proliferation of online social media has led users to experience information overload due to overwhelming access to vast data <cit.>. Biological constraints on cognitive functions, particularly memory retention and attention, significantly contribute to this overload. Memory is essential not only for recalling content and interactions during conversations but also for tracking unresolved discussions and individuals expecting responses in asynchronous communication. As internet-based communication, especially through modern social platforms, becomes increasingly dominant, asynchronous exchanges now represent the standard mode of interaction. While instant responses are generally preferred, research indicates that users typically accept delays of up to one day for replies <cit.>. However, asynchronous communication risks accumulating unaddressed conversations, creating backlogs that surpass an individual’s capacity to respond, thereby inducing stress and contributing to information overload. Although memory limitations and associated psychological stressors have been extensively examined in laboratory settings <cit.>, the broader implications of information overload on digital dialogue dynamics and its societal-level effects remain underexplored.

old_text:
While memory capacity of an adult is considered to be fixed per individual, the effect of information overload on working memory results in a focus on the information deemed relevant to the task at hand and lack of comprehension of other information <cit.>. Therefore, when cognitive ability is lowered due to information overload, it is due to the excessive processing required to filter out irrelevant information to focus attention. Persistent information overload through multiple channels of online information providing notifications on a variety of activities of other users can often lead to the excessive processing, constant scattering of attention, and a feeling of perpetual loss of concentration <cit.>.
<cit.> discover that individuals with long hours of daily computer usage, especially with the use of smartphones, tend to have significantly lower ability for sustained attention. While interruptions, may improve performance at simple tasks, they lower performance on complex tasks <cit.>.
<cit.> demonstrate how constant social media notifications can disrupt focus and frustrate individuals, who prefer and benefit from notification systems that are able to deliver notifications at breakpoints when they are disengaged from any particular task.
<cit.> show that individuals who self-identify as highly multi-tasking are actually ineffective at filtering out irrelevant information from multiple channels and focusing attention to the task at hand in comparison to self-identified low multi-tasking individuals.
new_text: Although the memory capacity of adults is generally considered stable, information overload impairs working memory by compelling individuals to prioritize task-relevant information while neglecting other inputs <cit.>. This diminished cognitive capacity arises from the intense mental effort required to sift through irrelevant stimuli to maintain focus. Sustained exposure to information overload via digital platforms—such as notifications about others’ online activities—often results in chronic mental strain, fragmented attention, and an enduring sense of inattentiveness <cit.>. Research reveals that individuals with extensive daily screen time, particularly smartphone use, exhibit notably reduced capacity for maintaining focused attention. While brief interruptions may enhance performance on straightforward tasks, they impede efficiency in complex cognitive tasks <cit.>. Studies reveal that continuous social media alerts disrupt attention and induce frustration, with users favoring systems that deliver notifications during natural task disengagement points <cit.>. Findings also indicate that individuals who self-identify as heavy multitaskers are actually less effective at filtering extraneous information across multiple channels and maintaining task focus compared to those who report lower multitasking tendencies <cit.>.

new_text: Tab. <ref> presents the first-order (S_i) and total (S_Ti) Sobol sensitivity indices for M_max and α in relation to the means of three conversation dynamics characteristics: mean unique users in cascades, cascade volume, and virality. The results consistently demonstrate that all three characteristics are more influenced by variations in M_max than by α. This is evident in the first-order indices (S_i), where the mean unique users in cascades shows the strongest response to changes in both parameters. For instance, its S_i values for both M_max and α are significantly higher than those observed for the other two characteristics. However, the cumulative first-order effects (∑S_i) for cascade volume and virality are notably less than 1, suggesting these metrics remain highly uncertain even when accounting for variations in the model parameters. This implies that factors outside the influence of M_max and α may play a significant role in determining volume and virality outcomes. In contrast, the ∑S_i for mean unique users is much higher, indicating that this metric has minimal unexplained variability across the tested parameter ranges. Additionally, the total Sobol indices (∑S_Ti) exceed 1 for all three characteristics, highlighting that interactions between M_max and α contribute meaningfully to the observed sensitivity. These findings lead to the rejection of hypothesis 2, which likely posits no interaction effects, while supporting hypotheses 1 and 3, which emphasize the distinct impacts of M_max and the presence of nonlinear interactions, respectively (Sec. <ref>).

In addition to training single models for each of the WHAMR! core tasks, we evaluate combinations of models in which enhancement and separation systems are cascaded, with the output of one system being fed into the next.
The main motivation is that jointly separating and enhancing may be too difficult for a single network to learn, and modularization may allow the networks to focus on specific tasks. Two-stage approaches have previously been explored for denoising plus dereverberation <cit.>, separation plus dereverberation <cit.>, and denoising plus separation <cit.>.
new_text: We assessed both individual models for each WHAMR! core task and combined architectures where enhancement and separation modules are arranged sequentially, with the output of one stage serving as input to the next. This approach is motivated by the hypothesis that simultaneous separation and enhancement might overwhelm a single neural network, whereas modular systems enable each network to specialize in a distinct task. Prior work has demonstrated efficacy of two-stage methods in scenarios involving denoising followed by dereverberation <cit.>, separation combined with dereverberation <cit.>, and denoising paired with separation <cit.>.

The first dataset comprises 69 manually annotated Solidity smart contracts for evaluating tool precision, while the second includes 47,518 Ethereum Blockchain contracts with publicly available Solidity source code from Etherscan. In this paper, we introduce a new E2E-TTS toolkit named ESPnet-TTS, which is an extension of the open-source speech processing toolkit ESPnet <cit.>.
The toolkit is developed for the research purpose to make E2E-TTS systems more user-friendly and to accelerate research in this field.
The toolkit not only supports state-of-the-art E2E-TTS models such as Tacotron 2 <cit.>, Transformer TTS <cit.>, and FastSpeech <cit.> but also provides Kaldi automatic speech recognition (ASR) toolkit <cit.> style recipes.
The recipe is based on the design unified with the ASR recipe and includes all of the procedures required to reproduce the results.
The toolkit provides a number of recipes for more than ten languages, which include single-speaker TTS as well as multi-speaker one and speaker adaptation.
Pre-trained models and generated samples of all of the recipes are also provided so that users can easily use it as a baseline or perform TTS demonstrations.
Furthermore, thanks to the unified design among TTS and ASR, we can easily integrate ASR functions with TTS, for example,
ASR-based objecative evaluation by character error rate (CER), which is useful to automatically find alignment failures (e.g., repetitions and deletions) in E2E-TTS <cit.>.
This paper describes the basic design of the toolkit and comparative experimental evaluation with other TTS toolkits.
Subjective evaluation results verify that our best model outperforms other TTS toolkits, achieving a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.25 on the LJSpeech dataset.
new_text: This paper presents a novel end-to-end TTS (E2E-TTS) toolkit called ESPnet-TTS, extending the ESPnet open-source speech processing platform <cit.>. Designed to enhance the accessibility of E2E-TTS systems and expedite research advancements, the toolkit incorporates Kaldi-style automatic speech recognition (ASR) recipes aligned with the ASR framework <cit.>. It supports cutting-edge E2E-TTS models, including Tacotron 2 <cit.>, Transformer TTS <cit.>, and FastSpeech <cit.>, alongside Kaldi ASR <cit.>. The recipes follow a unified architecture with ASR workflows, covering all procedural steps to reproduce results. The toolkit provides extensive multi-language support across over ten languages, encompassing single-speaker and multi-speaker TTS systems, as well as speaker adaptation. Pre-trained models and synthetic audio samples are included for each recipe, enabling users to adopt them as baselines or demonstration tools. The integration of TTS and ASR modules via shared design principles allows functionalities such as ASR-based character error rate (CER) evaluation, which automates alignment failure detection in E2E-TTS systems <cit.>. The paper outlines the toolkit’s architecture, comparative experiments with existing toolkits, and subjective evaluations, where the best-performing model achieved a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.25 on the LJSpeech dataset, outperforming competing frameworks.

new_text: This paper presents a new end-to-end text-to-speech (E2E-TTS) toolkit named ESPnet-TTS, built upon the open-source speech processing framework ESPnet. The toolkit incorporates state-of-the-art E2E-TTS models, including Tacotron 2, Transformer TTS, and FastSpeech, and provides recipes modeled after the Kaldi automatic speech recognition (ASR) toolkit. These recipes utilize a unified design approach aligned with the ESPnet ASR framework, ensuring high reproducibility. The toolkit includes pre-trained models and sample implementations of all recipes, enabling users to treat them as benchmarks. Furthermore, the unified design facilitates integration of ASR functions with TTS, such as ASR-based objective evaluation and semi-supervised learning utilizing both ASR and TTS models. The paper outlines the toolkit’s design and presents experimental evaluations compared to other toolkits. Results demonstrate that our top-performing model achieves a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.25 on the LJSpeech dataset, outperforming existing alternatives. The toolkit is publicly available on GitHub[[URL]].

old_text: We propose two application-layer coding schemes for delay-constrained point-to-point packet communications over frequency bands with restrictions on the transmitter's maximum duty-cycle. The schemes operate over GF(2) and utilize intermittently available receiver feedback for erasure correction. Simulation results for independent Bernoulli erasure channels, Gilbert-Elliott channels, and Long Range (LoRa) communications demonstrate orders-of-magnitude reductions in the delivery failure rate as compared to feedback-assisted repetition redundancy and a blind coding scheme that does not utilize feedback.

The schemes operate over GF(2) and use intermittently available receiver feedback for erasure correction. Simulation results on independent Bernoulli erasure channels, Gilbert-Elliott channels, and Long Range (LoRa) communications demonstrate orders of magnitude reductions in the delivery failure rate compared to feedback-assisted repetition redundancy and a blind coding scheme that does not use feedback.

We compared state-of-the-art
multilingual representation learning models
and a monolingual model
that is transferred to new languages
at the lexical level.
We demonstrated that these models perform comparably
on standard zero-shot cross-lingual transfer benchmarks,
indicating that neither a shared vocabulary nor joint
pre-training are necessary in multilingual models.
We also showed that a monolingual
model trained on a particular language learns some
semantic abstractions that are generalizable to
other languages in a series of probing experiments.
Our results and analysis contradict previous theories and provide new insights
into the basis of the generalization abilities of multilingual models.
To provide a more comprehensive benchmark to evaluate cross-lingual models,
we also released the Cross-lingual Question Answering Dataset (XQuAD).
new_text: We evaluated leading multilingual representation learning models alongside a monolingual model adapted to new languages through lexical transfer. Our findings revealed comparable performance across standard zero-shot cross-lingual transfer benchmarks, suggesting that shared vocabularies and joint pre-training are not essential for multilingual models. Additionally, through probing experiments, we found that monolingual models trained on a specific language acquire semantic abstractions applicable to other languages. These results challenge existing theories and offer novel perspectives on the generalization mechanisms underlying multilingual models. To facilitate improved evaluation of cross-lingual models, we introduced the Cross-lingual Question Answering Dataset (XQuAD).

Conventionally, computer vision research has intensively explored color and human perception, but has paid surprisingly little attention to distance in perceptual color spaces.
Here, we mention some key points about color in computer vision history.
Early on, research focused on intensity-based descriptors, which then evolved to also capture color information.
Unsurprisingly, color boosted the performance of object and scene recognition <cit.> and semantic segmentation <cit.>.
Researchers extracted descriptors from opponent color spaces, most notably HSV and CIELAB, which separate luminance and chrominance.
Most recently, color is attracting more attention in the area of image synthesis.
Notable examples, such as style transfer <cit.> and cross-domain image generation <cit.>, find that color plays an important role in preserving the look of an image.
In general, we observe that until now the focus has been on the color space itself, and not on color distance, which we explore here.
new_text: Traditionally, computer vision research has extensively investigated color and human perception, yet has largely overlooked the concept of distance within perceptual color spaces. This section outlines pivotal developments in the role of color throughout the history of computer vision research. Initially, the field centered on intensity-based features, later advancing to incorporate color information for more comprehensive analysis. As expected, integrating color data enhanced the accuracy of object and scene recognition <cit.> as well as semantic segmentation tasks <cit.>. Researchers have traditionally derived features from opponent color spaces, particularly HSV and CIELAB, which decouple luminance from chromatic components. Recently, color has gained renewed interest in image synthesis applications. Techniques like style transfer <cit.> and cross-domain image generation <cit.> demonstrate that color is crucial for maintaining visual consistency. Overall, existing research has predominantly concentrated on the structure of color spaces rather than the metrics governing color distances, which this work addresses.

old_text: Audio source separation is usually achieved by estimating the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) magnitude of each source, and then applying a spectrogram inversion algorithm to retrieve time-domain signals. In particular, the multiple input spectrogram inversion (MISI) algorithm has been exploited successfully in several recent works. However, this algorithm suffers from two drawbacks, which we address in this paper. First, it has originally been introduced in a heuristic fashion: we propose here a rigorous optimization framework in which MISI is derived, thus proving the convergence of this algorithm. Besides, while MISI operates offline, we propose here an online version of MISI called oMISI, which is suitable for low-latency source separation, an important requirement for e.g., hearing aids applications. oMISI also allows one to use alternative phase initialization schemes exploiting the temporal structure of audio signals. Experiments conducted on a speech separation task show that oMISI performs as well as its offline counterpart, thus demonstrating its potential for real-time source separation.
new_text: Audio source separation typically estimates the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) magnitude of each source and applies a spectrogram inversion algorithm to recover time-domain signals. The multiple input spectrogram inversion (MISI) algorithm has been used effectively in recent works but has two limitations we address here. First, it was introduced heuristically; we derive it rigorously via an optimization framework, proving its convergence. Second, while MISI operates offline, we propose an online variant, oMISI, suitable for low-latency separation—a requirement for hearing aids. oMISI enables phase initialization schemes exploiting audio temporal structure. Experiments on a speech separation task show oMISI matches MISI’s performance, demonstrating its real-time separation potential.

**Sentence Processing.**
Given that our fact checker expects a single sentence as input, we segment the generated text into sentences.
We consider the first k=5 sentences.
We perform coreference resolution to replace pronouns with the corresponding referring entity in order to give the complete information to the fact checker.

new_text: To prepare the text for fact-checking, we first segment the generated text into individual sentences, as the fact-checking system processes one sentence at a time. We prioritize the first five sentences (k=5) to focus on the most prominent claims while maintaining a manageable workload. To enhance clarity for the fact checker, we perform coreference resolution using spaCy, replacing pronouns (e.g., "it," "he") with their corresponding entities. This step ensures that the fact checker receives full contextual information without needing to infer the antecedent of pronouns. Additionally, we apply a simple heuristic to address ambiguity at sentence beginnings: any determiner (e.g., "The") followed by a noun phrase is replaced with the original entity, typically the Wikipedia page title, to explicitly link to the referenced topic. For instance, "The car company was founded in 2003" becomes "Tesla was founded in 2003." All these preprocessing tasks are executed using spaCy [[URL]]. Finally, we filter out sentences exceeding 50 tokens, as longer sentences are deemed too complex or fragmented to assess reliably for factual accuracy.

new_text: Since 2013, numerous open-source AutoML libraries have emerged, including Auto-WEKA <cit.>, auto-sklearn <cit.>, TPOT <cit.>, and H2O AutoML <cit.>. These tools, alongside cloud-based AutoML services offered by major providers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, have expanded access to automated machine learning for data scientists. However, their integration into broader software systems remains limited. Most applications treat AutoML as an external process: data scientists generate models using these tools and then deploy the final models into production software. A key challenge lies in the computational demands of AutoML systems. While they often achieve strong results on small benchmark datasets, their performance on large-scale real-world data is hampered by lengthy training times and high resource consumption. This discrepancy highlights a critical gap: research often focuses on small, curated datasets, whereas industrial applications require models trained on massive, heterogeneous data within tight operational constraints. Empirical evidence from a recent large-scale AutoML benchmark <cit.> further underscores this issue: state-of-the-art AutoML systems failed to outperform a carefully optimized random forest baseline on 40-50% of tasks when limited to one CPU hour. Such time and resource inefficiencies restrict their adoption in latency-sensitive systems or environments where compute capacity is constrained—conditions that characterize most commercial applications handling large datasets.

old_text: In this paper, we propose a new wrapper approach for semi-supervised feature selection. A common strategy in semi-supervised learning is to augment the training set by pseudo-labeled unlabeled examples. However, the pseudo-labeling procedure is prone to error and has a high risk of disrupting the learning algorithm with additional noisy labeled training data. To overcome this, we propose to model explicitly the mislabeling error during the learning phase with the overall aim of selecting the most relevant feature characteristics. We derive a 𝒞-bound for Bayes classifiers trained over partially labeled training sets by taking into account the mislabeling errors. The risk bound is then considered as an objective function that is minimized over the space of possible feature subsets using a genetic algorithm. In order to produce both sparse and accurate solution, we propose a modification of a genetic algorithm with the crossover based on feature weights and recursive elimination of irrelevant features. Empirical results on different data sets show the effectiveness of our framework compared to several state-of-the-art semi-supervised feature selection approaches.
new_text: In this paper, we introduce a novel wrapper-based method for semi-supervised feature selection, addressing challenges inherent in leveraging unlabeled data within this learning paradigm. A widely adopted strategy in semi-supervised learning involves expanding the training dataset by assigning pseudo-labels to unlabeled instances, thereby artificially increasing the labeled data volume. However, this approach carries significant risks: pseudo-labels are inherently uncertain, and incorporating them into the training process can introduce noisy labels that degrade model performance. To mitigate this issue, our method explicitly incorporates the estimation of label error rates during model training, enabling a more robust learning process that accounts for the uncertainty of pseudo-labels. Specifically, we derive a 𝒞-bound for Bayes classifiers operating on partially labeled datasets, where the bound mathematically quantifies the impact of potential mislabeling errors. This theoretical risk bound then serves as an objective function for optimizing feature subset selection. By minimizing this bound over the space of possible feature combinations using a genetic algorithm (GA), our framework prioritizes feature subsets that balance discriminative power with label error resilience. To further enhance both sparsity and accuracy in feature selection, we modify the standard GA by integrating a feature-weighted crossover mechanism—favoring features with higher predictive relevance—and a recursive elimination process that systematically prunes irrelevant features. Experimental validation across multiple datasets demonstrates that our framework outperforms existing semi-supervised feature selection methods, highlighting the effectiveness of explicitly modeling label errors and the proposed GA enhancements.

To detect these intentions, we implement two distinct methods based on separate sensing modalities. The first approach employs forearm Electromyography (EMG), in which the patient’s attempted voluntary hand opening is detected through EMG signals processed by a pattern recognition algorithm <cit.> and used to activate extension assistance. The second intent inference method introduced here is specifically tailored for cases where EMG-based detection proves insufficiently reliable for sustained use. new_text:
**Recovery.**  
A decentralized storage system must ensure users can reliably retrieve files stored on the network. However, simply deploying primitives like proof of possession (PDP) and proof of retrievability (PoR) is insufficient to guarantee recovery. While PDP and PoR are designed to verify that cloud storage servers are storing data correctly, they fail to address scenarios where storage providers act maliciously or become unavailable <cit.>. Several existing systems <cit.> do not propose mechanisms to enable users to actually retrieve their files once stored. For instance, Permacoin <cit.> relies on a subset of altruistic peers to voluntarily return stored files. This approach is inherently fragile, as the pool of altruistic participants may diminish over time without financial incentives, ultimately leaving files unretrievable.  

In contrast, other proposals <cit.> suggest incentivizing storage nodes to return files by having clients pay for retrieval. However, these solutions lack a clear method to ensure fair exchange between payment and content delivery. Specifically, a storage node might accept payment and then vanish without returning the requested file, leaving the user without recourse.  

To address these challenges, KopperCoin <cit.> introduces a mechanism using a 2-out-of-2 multisignature scheme. Under this model, a user and a storage node collaboratively create a transaction that locks a payment for the node and requires both parties to provide collateral. When the user successfully receives the stored file, the multisignature transaction is activated, releasing the payment to the node while returning the collateral to each party. This ensures that only honest behavior—where the user retrieves the file and the node is compensated fairly—is rewarded.

old_text: In this paper, we propose an unsupervised graph neural network, HDGI, which learns node representations in heterogeneous graphs. HDGI combines several state-of-the-art techniques. It employs convolution-style GNNs along with a semantic-level attention mechanism to capture individual node local representations. Through maximizing the local-global mutual information by gradient descent over neural networks, HDGI learns high-level node representations containing graph-level structural information. It additionally exploits the structure of meta-path to analyze the connection semantics in heterogeneous graphs. Node attributes are fused into representations through the local-global mutual information maximization simultaneously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of learned representations across a variety of node classification and clustering tasks in three heterogeneous graphs. HDGI is particularly competitive in node classification tasks with state-of-art supervised methods, where they have the additional supervised label information. We are optimistic that mutual information maximization will be a promising future direction for unsupervised representation learning.
new_text: This paper introduces HDGI, an unsupervised graph neural network for heterogeneous graphs that learns node representations by combining convolution-style GNNs with a semantic-level attention mechanism. HDGI maximizes local-global mutual information via gradient descent, capturing graph-level structural information in high-level node representations. It leverages meta-path structures to model heterogeneous connection semantics and integrates node attributes through the same mutual information framework. Evaluations on three heterogeneous graphs demonstrate effectiveness across node classification and clustering tasks, with HDGI competitively matching state-of-the-art supervised methods that utilize labeled data. The results highlight mutual information maximization as a promising direction for unsupervised representation learning.

old_text: Several approaches have been proposed that learn how to solve routing problems, but even the most recent methods do not yet outperform state-of-the-art optimization techniques. This performance gap can be partially explained by the simple search strategies of machine learning based methods, e.g., sampling <cit.> or beam search (BS) <cit.>. To address this, we propose to integrate learned heuristics into a higher level metaheuristic. We develop a large neighborhood search (LNS) metaheuristic for the VRP that learns heuristics for repairing incomplete solutions and employs them to guide a search through the solution space. Note that the developed metaheuristic does not contain any components that have been specifically developed for a certain routing problem. As in previous approaches, our method learns the complex heuristics needed to solve a class of problem instances on its own.
new_text: Numerous methodologies have been introduced aiming to resolve routing challenges via learning-based techniques, yet contemporary approaches still lag behind established optimization algorithms in performance. This discrepancy is partly attributed to the relatively straightforward search methodologies adopted by machine learning systems, such as sampling <cit> or beam search (BS) <cit>. To overcome this limitation, we present a strategy that incorporates learned heuristics within a metaheuristic framework at a higher level. Our framework employs a large neighborhood search (LNS) metaheuristic for the vehicle routing problem (VRP), which autonomously learns heuristics to reconstruct partial solutions and facilitates exploration of the solution space through these learned strategies. Notably, the proposed metaheuristic lacks domain-specific components tailored to particular routing challenges. Instead, akin to prior techniques, the methodology independently acquires the sophisticated heuristics necessary to address a class of problem instances.

A class of methods implicitly consider the group-effect of input elements by exploiting hidden neurons, because these hidden neurons each correspond to a collection of input elements. These methods assign importance values to neurons in the last convolutional layers <cit.> or hidden biases in all layers <cit.>. new_text: Features in the input are typically composed of multiple elements, and the importance of the overall feature cannot be accurately inferred by evaluating the importance of individual elements. For instance, a classifier can still recognize a coffee cup in an image even if a single pixel is missing. One class of methods implicitly accounts for the group effect of input elements by leveraging hidden neurons, as each hidden neuron corresponds to a collection of input elements. These methods assign importance values to neurons in the last convolutional layers <cit.> or to hidden biases across all layers <cit.>. However, these methods generate attribution maps only for convolutional networks. Moreover, due to rescaling operations, the resulting maps lack fine-grained detail. Perturbation mask methods, on the other hand, identify either the minimal set of input elements whose preservation maintains the output or the maximal set of input elements whose removal does not alter the output. However, the solutions obtained through this optimization are susceptible to becoming adversarial in nature <cit.>.

Semantic structure extraction for documents has been explored in various works <cit.>. Document structure extraction has been performed for digitising documents to make them reflowable which is useful in web based services <cit.>. In this work, we look at a complex class of documents, i.e., Forms. Forms are documents that are used to capture data by various organisations in domains such as government services,finance, administration, and healthcare. Such industries which have been using paper forms or flat PDF forms would want to digitize them by converting them into an appropriate digitised version <cit.> (such as an HTML). Once these forms are made reflowable, they can be used on many devices with different form factors<cit.>. This availability across devices automatically increases the ease of doing business or provide services since people can interact with them easily. new_text: Semantic structure extraction for documents has been extensively studied in prior research <cit.>. Specifically, efforts in document structure extraction have focused on digitizing documents to enable reflowability, a critical feature for adapting content to diverse display environments such as web-based platforms <cit.>. Reflowability allows content to dynamically adjust its layout, ensuring readability across screens of varying sizes and resolutions. In this work, we address a particularly complex category of documents: forms. Forms are standardized documents designed to collect structured data from users within domains like government services, finance, administration, and healthcare. These sectors have traditionally relied on paper-based forms or static PDF formats, which limit accessibility and functionality. The proposed work aims to digitize such forms by converting them into interactive digital equivalents, such as HTML-based formats <cit.>. This transformation not only preserves the original structure and functionality of the form but also unlocks adaptability across devices with different screen sizes and input methods <cit.>. By enabling access on smartphones, tablets, and desktops, this approach enhances user convenience and broadens service accessibility, directly supporting operational efficiency in delivering services. Beyond accessibility, digital forms offer enhanced data management capabilities. For instance, digitized forms can enforce real-time validation rules to ensure data accuracy, maintain design consistency across instances, and automate repetitive tasks like auto-filling form sections based on user inputs or historical data. These improvements collectively reduce manual errors, streamline workflows, and lower operational costs in data-intensive industries.

old_text: Deep learning has shown impressive results in many perception tasks. Despite its performance, several works show deep learning algorithms susceptible to adversarial attacks. These attacks craft small perturbations to the inputs that push the network to produce incorrect outputs. There is significant progress made in 2D image adversarial attacks, where extensive work shows diverse ways to attack 2D based neural networks <cit.>. In contrast, there is little focus on their 3D counterparts <cit.>. 3D point clouds, obtained with sensors like LiDAR, are now widely used in deep networks for safety-critical applications like self-driving cars <cit.>. There has been significant progress in 2D image adversarial attacks, where extensive work has demonstrated diverse ways to attack 2D-based neural networks <cit.>. However, as we will see in this paper, 3D deep networks are vulnerable to perturbations in their input, increasing the risk of using these models. In this paper, we present a novel approach to attack deep learning algorithms applied to 3D point clouds and primarily focus on the transferability of attacks between networks.

When collisions arise, the affected transmitters retain the undelivered packets and reattempt transmission following their defined strategies until successful delivery is achieved or the packets are superseded by newer data.

To address the issues above, we design `FourierSAT` [The tool is available at [URL]], an incomplete SAT solver based on Fourier analysis of Boolean functions, a technique to represent Boolean functions by multilinear polynomials.
By such a reduction to continuous optimization, we propose an algebraic framework for solving systems consisting of different types of constraints.
The idea is to leverage gradient information to guide the search process in the direction of local improvements. Empirical results demonstrate that `FourierSAT` is more robust than other solvers on certain classes of benchmarks.
new_text: To address the issues outlined above, we introduce FourierSAT, an incomplete SAT solver that leverages Fourier analysis of Boolean functions. This mathematical technique allows any Boolean function to be represented as a multilinear polynomial, effectively transforming combinatorial logic into an algebraic form. By converting SAT problems into this continuous representation, we reduce solving to a continuous optimization task. This enables an algebraic framework for handling systems with diverse constraints, such as logical ANDs, ORs, and XORs, within a unified model. The solver's core mechanism utilizes gradient information to guide search direction toward local improvements. Specifically, gradients indicate variable adjustments most likely to enhance solution quality, enabling focused optimization. Empirical evaluations show FourierSAT's increased robustness compared to existing solvers on benchmarks with complex logical structures where gradient-based navigation is advantageous.

Limitations of previous constructions.  
The approach of Buchin et al. <cit.> (and similarly that of Bose et al. <cit.>) involves employing expanders to create a monotone spanner for points on a line, which is then extended to higher dimensions. section: Consensus in Collaborative Swarms with Blockchain
old_text: In a traditional blockchain architecture, a transaction is validated when the corresponding block where it has been included is mined. In our case, transactions in the proposed network architecture are data exchanges between one robot and a subset of its peers. The data itself is shared within the peer-to-peer network but outside of the blockchain. A certain sample is shared within the blockchain as part of the transaction body so that the whole network can run the data quality evaluation and ranking procedure. Robots do not wait for transactions to be validated within a block before sharing the data. Rather than coining new cryptocurrency though the consensus mechanism, we propose the utilization of of the periodic PoW mechanism to provide robots with a preconfigured and fixed amount of cryptocurrency. While in the case of the Ethereum blockchain the Ether can be utilized both to perform trade between peers, and to purchase the network's execution time, in this paper we only consider the latter scenario. Therefore, the only use of the cryptocurrency is to be able to perform data transactions and be sure that data will be forwarded through the peer-to-peer network.
new_text: In conventional blockchain systems, a transaction's validity is confirmed upon the mining of its containing block. In contrast, the proposed network architecture facilitates data exchanges between robots and a subset of peers. The data itself is disseminated through the peer-to-peer network but remains external to the blockchain. A representative data sample is embedded in the blockchain within the transaction body to enable network-wide data quality assessment and ranking. Robots do not delay data sharing pending transaction validation. Instead of generating new cryptocurrency through consensus, a periodic Proof-of-Work (PoW) mechanism distributes a predetermined, fixed cryptocurrency amount to robots. While Ethereum's Ether serves both peer trading and computational resource allocation, this study restricts cryptocurrency use to enabling data transactions, ensuring reliable data propagation through the peer-to-peer network.

old_text: Having a connected infrastructure that supports the blockchain is an interesting approach that has the potential to enable multiple applications in the era of 5G and beyond connectivity. With network slicing, softwarization and virtualization, and the ability to support a variety of different verticals, blockchains and other systems could be deployed within the base stations. In those cases, permissioned blockchains might be considered a more suitable solution, where the role of the infrastructure could be more related to validating and increasing the level of security. In any case, in this paper we also consider fully distributed and anonymous permissionless blockchains. A more in depth analysis on this topic is given within the discussion of the design principles.
new_text: Developing a connected infrastructure that integrates blockchain technology presents a promising approach for enabling diverse applications in the 5G and beyond connectivity era. Emerging technologies such as network slicing, softwarization, and virtualization allow the telecommunications infrastructure to become more flexible and programmable, enabling the deployment of blockchain systems directly within base stations. This integration could facilitate tailored support for multiple vertical industries—such as healthcare, smart cities, and industrial automation—by dynamically allocating resources to meet specific application requirements. In such contexts, permissioned blockchains may offer advantages, as they allow controlled access to network participants, aligning with the infrastructure's role in validating transactions and enhancing security through predefined trust mechanisms. However, this paper also explores the feasibility of fully distributed, anonymous permissionless blockchains, which prioritize decentralization and open participation, despite their potentially higher computational and network resource demands. The trade-offs between these approaches, including security, scalability, and governance, are elaborated further in the discussion of design principles, where their implications for future infrastructure architecture are critically evaluated.

old_text: We next study the effect of the level of redundancy on the completion time in System<ref>, for the optimal data distribution for a given batch size. The level of redundancy can vary from full diversity, by assigning the entire data set to every worker, to full parallelism, by dividing the data set evenly among workers. We call this range the diversity-parallelism spectrum and try to find the optimum operating point within this spectrum. To this end, we model the service time of each data sample τ with Exponential and Shifted-Exponential distributions. Further, to find the service time distribution of each batch, we use the size-dependent service time model proposed in <cit.>. In addition to the average, we also study the effect of the redundancy level on the variance of completion time. It is worth mentioning that the variance is considered to be even more important practical systems than the average job completion time, since it enables performance guarantees <cit.>.
new_text: We next analyze how redundancy levels affect the completion time in System<ref>, focusing on the optimal data distribution for a given batch size. Redundancy can be adjusted along a spectrum between two extremes: full diversity, where the complete dataset is replicated across all workers to maximize reliability, and full parallelism, where the dataset is partitioned equally among workers to minimize resource usage. We refer to this continuum as the diversity-parallelism spectrum and aim to identify the optimal operating point that balances these competing priorities. To model this trade-off, we characterize the service time for individual data samples (τ) using Exponential and Shifted-Exponential distributions, which capture scenarios with constant or time-varying processing rates. Building on this, we apply the size-dependent service time model from <cit.> to derive the batch-level service time distribution, acknowledging that larger batches inherently influence completion dynamics. Beyond evaluating the average completion time, we also examine how redundancy impacts its variance, as this metric is critical for practical systems. Variance directly affects the predictability and reliability of performance guarantees <cit.>, making it a more critical consideration than the mean in real-world applications where consistent behavior is paramount.

new_text: To ensure participants became comfortable with their assigned interface, we provided a training phase that included a practice page. On this page, participants could freely explore their assigned interface by drawing as many patterns as they desired without constraints. Additionally, we ensured that the system-assigned dot(s) for each participant remained static across all trials within the training phase. Specifically, once the system randomly allocated a dot (e.g., dot 4 in the 1-dot group), that assignment did not change even if the participant clicked the reset button to restart a pattern. This consistency was critical: without it, participants might repeatedly reset the interface until they received their preferred system-assigned dot(s), which would undermine the validity of the SysPal policies being tested. By fixing the assigned dot(s), we ensured all participants interacted with the same constraints during training. This approach also extended to the subsequent Pattern Creation stage, where the system-assigned dot(s) remained unchanged to maintain experimental control and prevent biased outcomes.

To address the above issues, we propose a novel generative adversarial network for text-guided image manipulation (ManiGAN), which can generate high-quality new attributes matching the given text, and at the same time effectively reconstruct text-irrelevant contents of the original image.
The key is a text-image affine combination module (ACM) where text and image features collaborate to select text-relevant regions that need to be modified, and then correlate those regions with corresponding semantic words for generating new visual attributes semantically aligned with the given text description. Meanwhile, it also encodes original image representations for reconstructing text-irrelevant contents.
new_text: To address these challenges, we propose a novel generative adversarial network framework for text-guided image manipulation, termed ManiGAN. This approach simultaneously achieves two critical objectives: generating high-quality visual attributes that align with a given textual description while preserving the text-irrelevant elements of the original image. Central to this framework is the text-image affine combination module (ACM), which serves as the core mechanism for coordinating interactions between textual and visual information. The ACM operates by first integrating textual and image features to identify regions of the image that correspond to text-relevant modifications. By mapping semantic words to specific visual regions, the module ensures that generated attributes are semantically consistent with the input description. Concurrently, the ACM retains detailed representations of the original image’s structure and non-modified components, enabling accurate reconstruction of areas unaffected by the textual instructions. This dual functionality—selective modification of targeted regions and faithful reconstruction of others—enables the model to maintain both semantic coherence and structural fidelity in the final output.

This section introduces a reliability-aware placement-based genetic algorithm that jointly optimizes node mapping and routing while considering SFC reliability requirements to achieve a desired level of reliability with minimal resource consumption. The proposed algorithm’s pseudo code is detailed in Algorithm <ref>. The algorithm iteratively generates solutions through initial population creation, fitness evaluation, selection, crossover, and mutation. First, a random population of *P* individuals is generated, and each individual’s fitness is evaluated. A set of parent individuals is then selected based on their fitness values (lines 1 through 5 of Algorithm <ref>). With specified probabilities, crossover is applied to parents to produce offspring, which are subsequently mutated. The feasibility of the new individuals is validated, and their ranks are updated (lines 6 through 21 of Algorithm <ref>). If the algorithm converges, the fittest individual is output and the process terminates; otherwise, the procedure iterates until convergence (lines 22 through 27 of Algorithm <ref>). Subsequent subsections elaborate on the encoding mechanism, constraint validation process, and fitness function design.

To evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning from pose estimation to action recognition, we conduct a controlled comparison between two feature extraction approaches. The first approach uses temporal convolution on pose features extracted by LCR-Net++ (represented by the blue curve, `Pose Feats'), while the second employs features from a Faster R-CNN model with a ResNet50 backbone trained for action classification (red curve, `Action Feats'). By using identical network architectures for both methods—differing only in the learned weights—we isolate the impact of domain-specific feature representation. This `Action Feats' baseline is intentionally not optimized for state-of-the-art action recognition performance, but its simplicity ensures a fair comparison focused on feature quality rather than architectural innovation. Notably, frame-level action detection approaches like this one were common in the spatio-temporal action detection literature prior to the widespread adoption of 3D CNNs <cit.>.  

Results in Figure <ref> reveal a significant decline in classification accuracy when substituting pose features with action features: a 20% drop on JHMDB-1 and PennAction datasets, and approximately 5% on NTU for sequence length T=32. These disparities persist even when temporal integration (T=32) is disabled, as evidenced by the T=1 results on HMDB-1 and PennAction. This observation suggests that `Pose Feats' inherently contain more discriminative information per frame than `Action Feats', as their advantage remains evident without relying on temporal smoothing. To explain this phenomenon, we analyze feature dynamics within action tubes (Figure <ref>). Action features extracted from frame-specific detectors exhibit strong correlations across consecutive frames in a given action sequence, limiting their capacity to encode temporal variation. In contrast, LCR-Net++ pose features evolve meaningfully over time in response to bodily motion, enabling temporal convolution to more effectively distill action-specific temporal patterns.  

The practical implications of this are visible in Figure <ref>'s confusion matrices on the PennAction dataset. When using `Action Feats', errors frequently occur between semantically similar actions—such as distinguishing between different tennis or baseball movements—due to feature homogeneity. These confusions are significantly reduced when using `Pose Feats', indicating that pose-based representations better capture the kinematic differences that distinguish similar actions. This aligns with the hypothesis that temporal integration benefits are maximized when the underlying features themselves evolve distinctly over time, a property more prevalent in pose data than in frame-wise action classifiers.
