Consider the classical method of exhaustion of approximating a circle with inscribed regular polygons. It follows that, in three dimensions, we can approximate a sphere in the same way. Thus, the choice of planar spherical approximation ought to be the convex Platonic solid with the most faces: the icosahedron. The icosahedron has been used by cartographers to represent Earth at least as early as Buckminster Fuller's Dymaxion map <cit.>, which projects the globe onto the icosahedral net. Recent work in computer vision <cit.> has demonstrated the shape's utility for resolving the distortion problem for CNNs on spherical images as well.
new_text: Building upon the classical method of exhaustion—where a circle is approximated by inscribed regular polygons—its three-dimensional counterpart involves approximating a sphere using similar polyhedral techniques. The optimal planar spherical approximation is logically the convex Platonic solid with the greatest number of faces: the icosahedron. Cartographers have utilized this geometry to model Earth since at least the development of Buckminster Fuller’s Dymaxion map <cit.>, which unfolds the globe onto an icosahedral net. More recently, advances in computer vision <cit.> have highlighted the icosahedron’s effectiveness in mitigating distortion issues in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) applied to spherical imagery.

Successful use of robot autonomy in these areas depends critically on the ability of robots to adapt safely to changing operational conditions. Existing systems, however, rely on brittle hand-designed dynamics models and safety rules that often fail to account for the complexity and uncertainty of real-world operation. Recent work <cit.> has demonstrated that learning-based system identification and control techniques may be successful at complex tasks and control objectives. new_text: Unmanned vehicles have the potential to revolutionize domains such as transportation, agriculture, mining, and construction by enabling autonomous operations. Achieving reliable autonomy in these applications hinges on a robot’s capacity to dynamically and safely respond to shifting environmental conditions. Current approaches often depend on rigid, manually crafted dynamic models and safety constraints, which struggle to address the unpredictability and intricacies of real-world scenarios. Recent advancements <cit.> highlight that learning-driven system identification and control strategies can effectively tackle complex tasks and control goals. Nevertheless, two pivotal challenges remain when deploying such methods on autonomous platforms: the need to perform real-time learning using continuous data streams and the imperative to ensure operational safety despite the inherent uncertainties of adaptive learning algorithms.

Remote inference leads to privacy concerns if the inference data samples are privacy-sensitive. In particular, the inference data samples may contain private information beyond the inference application.
Therefore, in this paper, we aim to protect the confidentiality of the raw form of each inference data sample. The data form confidentiality is an immediate and basic privacy requirement in many applications. In the experiments conducted in this paper (cf. Section <ref>), we use the human's ability to interpret the protected inference data samples as a measure of privacy preservation. The inference results generated by the backend may also contain information about the corresponding edge devices. However, in this paper, we do not consider the privacy contained in the inference results, since the edge devices should have no expectation of it if they are willing to join the remote inference system.
new_text: Privacy concerns arise in remote inference when inference data samples are privacy-sensitive. Specifically, these data samples may contain sensitive information unrelated to the inference application itself. To address this, we focus on protecting the confidentiality of the raw form of each inference data sample, a requirement that is immediate and fundamental in many applications. In our experiments (cf. Section <ref>), we assess privacy preservation by evaluating the ability of humans to interpret the protected inference data samples. While the backend-generated inference results may also reveal information about the associated edge devices, we do not consider the privacy implications of these results in this work. Edge devices participating in a remote inference system should not reasonably expect confidentiality in the output, given their voluntary participation in the system.

Meta-learning has demonstrated particular efficacy in few-shot learning, with notable approaches categorized into metric-based methods <cit.>, augmented memory systems <cit.>, and optimization-based strategies <cit.>. Motivated by the utility of Lyapunov functions for certifying stability properties, <cit.> proposed control barrier functions (CBFs) as a tool for characterizing long-term safety of dynamical systems. A CBF certifies whether a control policy achieves forward invariance of a safe set C by evaluating if the system trajectory remains away from the boundary of C. Most of the literature on CBFs considers systems with known dynamics, low relative degree, no disturbances, and time-triggered control, in which the control inputs are recalculated at a fixed and sufficiently small period.
This is limiting because, low control frequency in a time-triggered setting may lead to safety constraint violation in-between sampling times.
On the other hand, high control frequency leads to inefficient use of computational resources and actuators.
<cit.> extend the CBF framework to a self-triggered setup in which the longest time until a control input needs to be recomputed to guarantee safety is provided.
CBF techniques handle nonlinear control-affine systems but many existing results apply only to relative-degree-one systems, in which the first time derivative of the CBF depends on the control input. This requirement is violated by many underactuated robot systems and motivated extensions to relative-degree-two systems, such as bipedal and car-like robots. <cit.>. <cit.> generalized these ideas by designing an exponential control barrier function (ECBF) capable of handling control-affine systems with arbitrary relative degree.

Link Prediction
Link prediction (LP) is a problem of predicting whether two nodes are likely to have an edge in the graph <cit.>. LP has been used in many applications like friend and content recommendations <cit.> , shopping and movie recommendation <cit.> , knowledge graph completion <cit.> and even to identify criminals based on their activities <cit.>. Historically, link prediction has been mainly performed using topological features of the graph like common neighbors. This has yielded very strong baselines like Adamic/Adar measure <cit.>, Jaccard Index among others. Other approaches include Matrix Factorization <cit.> and more recently graph neural networks <cit.> have been also been explored for this application. However, all of the above mentioned approaches dealt with a single dense graph where you try to predict unknown/future links. Unlike these previous approaches, our approach considers link prediction tasks on multiple sparse graphs which are drawn from similar real world scenario.
new_text: Link prediction (LP) aims to predict the presence or absence of an edge between two nodes in a graph <cit.>. LP has been applied in various domains, including friend and content recommendations <cit.>, shopping and movie recommendation <cit.>, knowledge graph completion <cit.>, and criminal identification through activity analysis <cit.>. Historically, LP methods have primarily relied on topological features such as common neighbors, leading to robust baselines like the Adamic/Adar measure <cit.> and the Jaccard Index <cit.>. Other approaches, including matrix factorization <cit.> and graph neural networks <cit.>, have also been explored. However, the aforementioned approaches have focused on a single dense graph where one predicts unknown or future links. In contrast, our method addresses LP tasks across multiple sparse graphs derived from similar real-world scenarios.

Established techniques for simulation and prediction with Gaussian process (GP) dynamics implicitly
make use of an independence assumption on successive function evaluations of the dynamics model.
This can result in significant error and underestimation of the prediction uncertainty, potentially
leading to failures in safety-critical applications. This paper proposes methods that
explicitly take the correlation of successive function evaluations into account. We first describe
two sampling-based techniques; one approach provides samples of the true trajectory distribution,
suitable for `ground truth' simulations, while the other draws function samples from basis function
approximations of the GP. Second, we present a linearization-based technique that directly provides
approximations of the trajectory distribution, taking correlations explicitly into account. We
demonstrate the procedures in simple numerical examples, contrasting the results with established
methods.
new_text: Traditional methods for simulating and predicting Gaussian process (GP) dynamics rely on an independence assumption between consecutive function evaluations of the dynamic model. This assumption can lead to substantial errors and underestimated predictive uncertainty, posing risks in safety-critical systems. To address this, the paper introduces approaches that explicitly incorporate the correlation between successive evaluations. We first outline two sampling-based strategies: one generates samples from the true trajectory distribution, ideal for "ground truth" simulations, while the other samples functions from basis function approximations of the GP. Additionally, we propose a linearization-based approach that directly approximates the trajectory distribution by accounting for correlations. The effectiveness of these methods is validated through numerical experiments, comparing their performance against conventional techniques.

Early RL algorithms mostly belong to value-based method, which directly derive the optimal policy from a learned value function.
Policy iteration (PI) is considered the first value-based algorithm, in which policy evaluation (PEV) and policy improvement (PIM) keep alternating until action-value function converges to the optimal action-value function. In PEV step, action-value function is updated with fixed policy until it converges. And in PIM step, a better policy is obtained according to the updated action-value function<cit.>. Value iteration (VI) is a form of truncated
policy iteration algorithm, in which action-value function is updated only once in PEV step instead of updating until convergence <cit.>.However, PI and VI require complete knowledge of the environment in PEV step to calculate action-value estimation in a bootstapping way. Monte Carlo (MC) algorithm were proposed to approximate action-value function by averaging episodic returns, thus no model is needed <cit.>. But they suffer from large variance and cannot performing updating until the end of episode. SARSA and Q-learning are two famous temporal difference (TD) algorithms, and they are combination of PI and MC algorithms and are most widely used in RL <cit.>. They calculate action-value estimation of a state-action pair in PEV step by only bootstrapping to its next sampled state-action pair, instead of all of its adjacent state-action pairs or the whole episodic return from it, which greatly reduces estimation variance and speeds up learning process at the cost of adding bias. Main difference of SARSA and Q-learning lies in whose experiences they use to calculate action-value function estimation. For SARSA, it uses experiences conducted by target policy, i.e., the policy we aim to update, which requires target policy should always be stochastic due to exploration issues and thus limits optimality of the algorithm because optimal policy is usually deterministic <cit.>. Q-learning relieves this limitation by learning greedy policy while exploring by ϵ-greedy policy, which is one of the early breakthroughs in RL algorithm <cit.>.
new_text: Early RL algorithms mostly belong to value-based methods, which directly derive the optimal policy from a learned value function. Policy iteration (PI) is considered the first value-based algorithm, in which policy evaluation (PEV) and policy improvement (PIM) alternate until the action-value function converges to the optimal action-value function. In the PEV step, the action-value function is updated with a fixed policy until it converges. In the PIM step, a better policy is obtained according to the updated action-value function <cit.>. Value iteration (VI) is a form of truncated policy iteration algorithm, in which the action-value function is updated only once in the PEV step instead of being updated until convergence <cit.>. However, PI and VI require complete knowledge of the environment in the PEV step to calculate action-value estimates using a bootstrapping approach. The Monte Carlo (MC) algorithm was proposed to approximate the action-value function by averaging episodic returns, thus eliminating the need for an environment model <cit.>. But they suffer from high variance and cannot perform updates until the end of an episode. SARSA and Q-learning are two prominent temporal difference (TD) algorithms, which combine elements of PI and MC algorithms and are the most widely used in RL <cit.>. They estimate the action-value function of a state-action pair in the PEV step by bootstrapping from only its next sampled state-action pair, rather than all adjacent state-action pairs or the entire episodic return, which significantly reduces estimation variance and accelerates learning at the expense of introducing bias. The main difference between SARSA and Q-learning lies in the experiences used to calculate action-value function estimates. For SARSA, it uses experiences generated by the target policy—the policy we aim to update—which necessitates a stochastic target policy due to exploration requirements, thereby limiting the algorithm's optimality because the optimal policy is typically deterministic <cit.>. Q-learning alleviates this limitation by learning a greedy policy while using an ϵ-greedy policy for exploration, marking one of the early breakthroughs in RL algorithms <cit.>.

new_text: The study cited in <cit.> notes that images with smoother histogram distributions may have reduced readability. As detailed in <cit.>, while attackers cannot extract meaningful data from uniform histograms by analyzing pixels, they can recover significant statistical characteristics of the original image by shifting the histogram analysis from pixel-level counts to bit-level counts. Furthermore, an example presented in <cit.> demonstrates that two encrypted images may retain identical histograms even when using an encryption algorithm deemed secure for specific applications. Consequently, the pixel-based histograms illustrated in <cit.> are insufficient to conclusively demonstrate that the proposed encryption method offers enhanced security.

In this section, we focus on presenting one of such a designs called SharpEdge. SharpEdge is a design directly motivated by the equation 8. new_text: Designs that satisfy Equation <ref> (as defined in Theorem <ref>, and more broadly, in Theorem <ref>) ensure that the network enforces a bounded maximum delay on all traffic. This property is critical for real-time systems where predictable performance is essential. In this section, we present a specific implementation of such a design, termed *SharpEdge*, which directly addresses the requirements outlined in Equation 8. SharpEdge is explicitly motivated by the constraints and conditions described in Theorem 3: by structuring edge-node traffic management to align with these constraints, the network inherently guarantees bounded-delay behavior. Central to this approach is a novel traffic-shaping algorithm, the *Quantum shaper*, which introduces a method for regulating data flow that enables compliance with Theorem 3 while minimizing overhead. The following discussion will elaborate on the inner workings of the Quantum shaper algorithm, demonstrating how it achieves this balance.

new_text: In 2006, Raghavan <cit.> showed that twinless strongly connected components of a directed graph can be found in linear time. Building on this, Georgiadis <cit.> demonstrated in 2010 a linear-time algorithm to check whether a strongly connected graph is 2-vertex-connected, while Italiano et al. <cit.> provided linear-time algorithms for identifying all strong articulation points and strong bridges in directed graphs. By 2014, Jaberi <cit.> presented algorithms for computing 2-vertex-connected components in O(nm) time <cit.>, followed in 2015 by an experimental study <cit.> showing strong practical performance of their algorithm. Concurrently, Henzinger et al. <cit.> proposed algorithms for 2-vertex and 2-edge-connected components in O(n²) time. Jaberi <cit.> later introduced methods to compute 2-directed blocks, 2-strong blocks, and 2-edge blocks, along with approximation algorithms for optimization problems tied to these structures. Linear-time algorithms for 2-edge blocks were provided by Georgiadis et al. <cit.>, who also extended their work <cit.> to include 2-directed and 2-strong blocks. In 2019, Jaberi <cit.> advanced the field further by introducing a linear-time algorithm for computing 2-twinless-connected components.

In <cit.>, in addition to the description of the database, the authors have provided baseline results using three simple detection systems: i) a small CNN model composed of 6 convolution layers and 1 fully-connected layer to detect low-level image manipulations, ii) a XceptionNet model trained using only face images, and iii) a XceptionNet model trained using the full image. new_text: Facebook, in collaboration with other companies and academic institutions, launched the DeepFake Detection Challenge (<cit.>). The authors describe the database and present baseline results from three systems: i) a small CNN with 6 convolutional and 1 fully-connected layer for detecting low-level image manipulations, ii) a XceptionNet model trained on face images only, and iii) a XceptionNet model trained on full images. The XceptionNet model trained on face images achieved the best performance (93.0% precision, 8.4% recall).

In contrast, a non-work conserving network is a network which, in some cases, may leave the output links idle despite the presence of packets at the input.] queue management/scheduling algorithms akin to those used in commercial switches for serving incoming packets.

old_text: Some transport control protocol (TCP) designs target satisfying low/ultra-low latency packet transmissions in the network (e.g. <cit.>). In the big picture, the common property of all these TCP designs is that they attempt to reduce the delay of packets in the network. As mainly fully end-to-end approaches, most of TCP designs do not require any change in the network. However, TCP designs cannot provide any guarantee for the delay of packets. Due to TCP's acknowledgment based structure, TCP protocols are basically not work-conserving; however, when packets are sent to the network, they will be served in a work-conserving manner in the core network, because these TCPs do not require network device modifications and current general commercial network switches are work-conserving.
new_text: Some transport control protocol (TCP) designs aim to optimize low or ultra-low latency for packet transmission across networks (e.g., <cit.>). Fundamentally, these approaches share a common objective: to minimize packet delay by improving how quickly data moves through the network. Most TCP designs rely on end-to-end mechanisms, meaning their operation depends only on interactions between sender and receiver without requiring modifications to intermediate network devices such as routers or switches. This simplifies deployment and avoids the need for infrastructure changes, which is a significant practical advantage. However, even with these optimizations, TCP cannot guarantee strict latency bounds for packet delivery. This limitation arises from TCP’s acknowledgment-based structure, where a sender waits for feedback before transmitting new data. As a result, TCP protocols are not work-conserving—they do not utilize available network resources immediately when they become free. That said, once packets are injected into the network, they are processed in a work-conserving manner by the core infrastructure. This occurs because modern commercial network switches are inherently work-conserving, and TCP designs that avoid altering network devices rely on this existing behavior. Thus, while TCP itself introduces latency variability, the underlying network infrastructure ensures that packets are served efficiently once they reach the core network.

This study has several limitations.

because (i) we want to demonstrate the feasibility of VulDeeLocator and (ii) the

Second, VulDeeLocator requires to compile program source code into intermediate code, and cannot be used when a program source code cannot be compiled.
Third, the four kinds of vulnerability syntax characteristics used by VulDeeLocator can cover 98.3% of vulnerable programs collected from NVD
and SARD. This 98.3% coverage should be used with caution

new_text: This study has several limitations. First, VulDeeLocator is designed to detect vulnerabilities in C programs due to both the need to demonstrate feasibility and reliance on C-compatible tools; supporting other languages is promising future work. Second, the method requires compiling source code into intermediate code and is inapplicable when compilation is unfeasible. Third, the four vulnerability syntax patterns cover 98.3% of vulnerabilities in NVD/SARD datasets, but this figure should be interpreted cautiously: (i) NVD analysis only considers vulnerabilities located via deleted/moved code lines, excluding those identified via additions, and (ii) SARD data may lack representativeness for real-world software. Improving syntax pattern coverage remains an open problem. Fourth, our case study uses BRNN-vdl for feasibility demonstration; application-specific neural network designs are needed for vulnerability detection. Fifth, while we partially explain VulDeeLocator’s effectiveness, further research on model explainability is essential.

Prior work on bug detection.
Since vulnerabilities can be seen as a special kind of bugs <cit.>, we briefly review prior studies on bug detectors.
Similar to vulnerability detection, there are two detection methods: static vs. dynamic.
Static methods often use information retrieval techniques together with bug reports to detect bugs in source code (e.g., <cit.>).
Dynamic methods include:
spectrum-based methods <cit.>, which examine pass-and-fail execution traces to determine whether or not a line of source code has a bug;
mutation-based methods <cit.>, which consider whether or not the execution of a line of code affects the result of a test case.
However, bug detection methods cannot be used to detect vulnerabilities because (i) bugs are not necessarily vulnerabilities and (ii) bug detection methods often rely on bug reports or test cases.
new_text: Prior research in the field of bug detection has examined approaches relevant to identifying vulnerabilities, which can be viewed as a subset of software bugs <cit.>. Previous studies on bug detection primarily fall into two categories: static and dynamic analysis. Static analysis techniques typically integrate information retrieval strategies with bug reports to identify issues in source code <cit.>. In contrast, dynamic analysis encompasses methods such as spectrum-based analysis <cit.>, which evaluates pass-and-fail execution traces to assess whether a specific code line contains an error, and mutation-based analysis <cit.>, which determines whether executing a line of code alters the outcome of a test. Nonetheless, these bug detection frameworks are unsuitable for identifying vulnerabilities due to two factors: (i) not all bugs qualify as vulnerabilities, and (ii) these methods often depend on the availability of bug reports or test cases for operation.

In this paper, we introduce a modality independent of the scene, therefore robust to scene variation, based on spatial temporal graph representations that could be used either individually, in cascades or as a complementary modality for surgical activity recognition. To show the effectiveness of the modality we introduce, we propose to model and recognize surgical activities in surgical videos by first defining the graph representations of the surgical tools, and then learning hierarchical temporal relationships between these joints over time using Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCN) <cit.>. Figure <ref> shows an overview of spatial temporal graph representations of surgical tools.
new_text: This paper presents a novel modality designed to be independent of specific scene characteristics, making it inherently robust to variations in the operating environment. The proposed method relies on spatial-temporal graph representations, which capture dynamic relationships between surgical tools and their movements over time. These representations are flexible: they can be utilized in isolation, combined in cascading architectures, or integrated with other modalities to enhance surgical activity recognition. To demonstrate the modality’s effectiveness, we develop a framework for surgical activity modeling in video data. Specifically, we begin by constructing graph representations of surgical tools, encoding their spatial configurations and motion patterns as structured representations. These representations are then processed through Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCN), which learn hierarchical temporal dependencies between tool joints across timeframes. By explicitly modeling how surgical instruments interact and evolve over time, the method enables robust recognition of complex procedures. Figure <ref> illustrates the spatial-temporal graph representations used in this approach, providing a visual summary of how tool positions and dynamics are encoded.

old_text: Although frame based image cues provide us context such as the surgical setting, objects, anatomical structures operated on, they are quite prone to overfitting, therefore the generalizability across different tasks and different datasets remains a challenge. Mitchell <cit.> gives an example to communicate this problem by studying a deep neural network trained to classify images on whether they contain an animal or not. She figures out that in part, the network learned to classify images with blurry backgrounds as “contains an animal” as their dataset had a high number of wildlife photographs that focused on the animals subjects and blurred out the background. Although this network performed well, the representations learned were highly dependent on the background, and they were not representative of animal features to be generalized across other datasets. Similarly, in terms of surgical activities, placing a Tie Knot might occur during a task of “suturing on tissue” and also during the more specific and challenging task of “Urethrovesical Anastomosis (UVA)” <cit.> that involves stitching and reconnecting two anatomical structures together. If we heavily rely on image cues of the surgical scene, these surgical activities would have very different representations. In order to overcome the challenge of generalizability across different tasks and different datasets, we need to define more generic representations of surgical activities that are robust to scene variation.
new_text: Frame-based image cues offer valuable contextual information in surgical settings, such as the procedural environment, visible objects, and the anatomical structures being operated on. However, these cues often lead to models that are highly sensitive to the specific characteristics of the training data, making them prone to overfitting. As a result, generalizing these models across diverse surgical tasks or datasets remains a significant challenge. Mitchell <cit.> illustrates this issue through a study of a deep neural network trained to classify images based on whether they contained an animal. She found that the network partially relied on correlations between image characteristics—specifically, blurry backgrounds—rather than learning robust features of animals themselves. This occurred because the training data disproportionately included wildlife photographs where the animal was in focus and the background was blurred. While the model performed well on its specific training set, its learned representations were tightly coupled with dataset-specific cues, limiting their applicability to other, differently distributed datasets. Translating this insight to surgical activity recognition, the same problem arises when models rely heavily on visual scene context. For instance, the surgical activity of "placing a Tie Knot" may occur in both the broader "suturing on tissue" task and the more specialized "Urethrovesical Anastomosis (UVA)" procedure, which involves reconnecting two anatomical structures. These tasks differ in their surgical settings and visual context, leading models that depend on image-based cues to generate distinct and potentially incompatible representations for the same activity. To address these challenges and improve generalizability, it is essential to develop representations of surgical activities that abstract away from dataset-specific visual variations while retaining core task-agnostic features.

old_text: Ahmidi et al. <cit.> did a comparative benchmark study on the recognition of gestures on JIGSAWS dataset <cit.>. In this study, in order to classify surgical gestures, three main methods are chosen: Bag of Spatio-Temporal Features (BoF), Linear Dynamical System (LDS) <cit.> and a composite Gaussian Mixture Model- Hidden Markov Model: GMM-HMM <cit.>. For BoF, features of both spatially and temporally high texture variations are extracted with Space-Time Interest Points (STIP) <cit.>. This cuboid of features are then combined with additional features such as HOG: histogram of orientation gradients <cit.> and HOF: histogram of optical flow <cit.>. A codebook is created and dimensionality of these visual representations are reduced via clustering. An SVM classifier is trained on videoss histograms of the codebook words. Linear Dynamical System (LDS) on both the image intensities and kinematic data is proposed for the same problem. In this approach, the video frames are modeled as the output of a LDS, then the pairwise distances between the LDS models are measured. Finally, a classifier is trained to predict the class of the gesture frames. In the same work, a composite Gaussian Mixture Model- Hidden Markov Model: GMM-HMM models each gesture as an elementary HMM where each state corresponds to one Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on kinematic data <cit.>. Studies that use primarily kinematic data have also been suggested. Ahmidi et al. <cit.> proposed segmenting and recognizing surgical gestures using similarity metrics on the temporal model of surgical tool motion trajectories defined with descriptive curve coding, which transforms them into a coded string. In addition to the benchmark, more recent works have also proposed using both video and kinematic data <cit.>. Lea et al. <cit.> proposed to use both modalities to perform segmentation and recognition using object cues and higher-order temporal relationships between action transitions using a variation of Conditional Random Field.
new_text: Ahmidi et al. <cit.> conducted a comparative benchmark study on surgical gesture recognition using the JIGSAWS dataset <cit.>. Three methods were evaluated: Bag of Spatio-Temporal Features (BoF), Linear Dynamical System (LDS) <cit.>, and a composite Gaussian Mixture Model-Hidden Markov Model (GMM-HMM) <cit.>. For BoF, features capturing high texture variations in space and time were extracted via Space-Time Interest Points (STIP) <cit.>, combined with HOG (histogram of orientation gradients) <cit.> and HOF (histogram of optical flow) <cit.>. A codebook generated from clustered visual representations reduced dimensionality, and an SVM classifier was trained on codebook word histograms. The LDS approach modeled video frames as outputs of a LDS, with gesture classification based on pairwise distances between LDS models derived from image intensities and kinematic data. The GMM-HMM method represented each gesture as an HMM, where states corresponded to GMMs applied to kinematic data <cit.>. Other studies prioritizing kinematic data proposed segmenting and recognizing surgical gestures using similarity metrics on temporal motion trajectories encoded via descriptive curve coding <cit.>. Beyond the benchmark, recent work combined video and kinematic data <cit.>, such as Lea et al.’s <cit.> approach integrating object cues and higher-order temporal relationships between action transitions using a Conditional Random Field variant.

The radio access network (RAN) is regarded as one of the potential proposals for massive Internet of Things (mIoT), where the random access channel (RACH) procedure should be exploited for IoT devices to access to the RAN. However, modelling of the dynamic process of RACH of mIoT devices is challenging. To address this challenge, we first revisit the frame and minislot structure of the RAN. Then, we correlate the RACH request of an IoT device with its queue status and analyze the queue evolution process. Based on the analysis result, we derive the closed-form expression of the RA success probability of the device.
Besides, considering the agreement on converging different services onto a shared infrastructure, we further investigate the RAN slicing for mIoT and bursty ultra-reliable and low latency communications (URLLC) service multiplexing. Specifically, we formulate the RAN slicing problem as an optimization one aiming at optimally orchestrating RAN resources for mIoT slices and bursty URLLC slices to maximize the RA success probability and energy-efficiently satisfy bursty URLLC slices' quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. A slice resource optimization (SRO) algorithm exploiting relaxation and approximation with provable tightness and error bound is then proposed to mitigate the optimization problem.
new_text: The radio access network (RAN) is considered a promising solution for massive Internet of Things (mIoT), where the random access channel (RACH) procedure enables IoT devices to access the RAN. However, modeling the dynamic process of RACH for mIoT devices remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we first revisit the frame and minislot structure of the RAN. We then correlate each IoT device’s RACH request with its queue status and analyze the queue evolution process. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form expression for the device’s RACH success probability. Furthermore, acknowledging the trend toward converging services onto shared infrastructure, we investigate RAN slicing for mIoT and bursty ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC) service multiplexing. Specifically, we formulate the RAN slicing problem as an optimization task aiming to optimally orchestrate RAN resources for mIoT slices and bursty URLLC slices, maximizing RACH success probability while energy-efficiently meeting bursty URLLC slices’ quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. To solve this problem, we propose a slice resource optimization (SRO) algorithm based on relaxation and approximation techniques with provable tightness and error bounds.

old_text: We consider the classical sequential binary hypothesis testing problem in which there are two hypotheses governed respectively by distributions P_0 and P_1 and we would like to decide which hypothesis is true using a sequential test. It is known from the work of Wald and Wolfowitz that as the expectation of the length of the test grows, the optimal type-I and type-II error exponents approach the relative entropies D(P_1P_0) and D(P_0P_1). We refine this result by considering the optimal backoff from the corner point of the achievable exponent region (D(P_1P_0),D(P_0P_1)) under two different constraints on the length of the test (or the sample size). First, we consider a probabilistic constraint in which the probability that the length of test exceeds a prescribed integer n is less than a certain threshold 0<ε <1. Second, the expectation of the sample size is bounded by n. In both cases, and under mild conditions, the backoff, also coined second-order asymptotics, is characterized precisely. Examples are provided to illustrate our results.

Table <ref> shows their overall multi-label classification performance on BigEarthNet under different metrics. By analyzing the table, one can observe that the ResNet model provides the highest scores in most of the metrics. As an example, ResNet152 leads to an increase of about 2% in precision, the ResNet50 achieves a reduction of more than 5% in Hamming loss and ResNet152 provides a reduction of more than 4% in ranking loss compared to VGG19. VGG19 provides the highest score only under the one error with a reduction of less than 2% compared to ResNet50 and ResNet152. This shows that due to the residual connections of the ResNet model and their increased depth in terms of number of layers compared to the VGG model, they achieve better characterization of the semantic content of the BigEarthNet images. In detail, increasing the depth of the VGG model (VGG19) achieves better scores in only recall and one error, and thus provides considerably similar scores in other metrics compared to the shallower version (VGG16). Increasing the depth of the ResNet model from 50 to 101 has similar shortcomings as the VGG model. ResNet101 provides almost the same result with ResNet50 in only recall, whereas ResNet50 achieves a reduction of more than 4% in ranking loss. However, further increasing the depth of the ResNet model to 152 is capable of increasing the classification performance (while providing better scores under most of the metrics than ResNet50). This shows that only increasing the depth of a CNN model up to some extent is not sufficient to obtain better multi-label classification performance unless the amount of increase allows more accurate characterization of multiple classes present in the image. Moreover, ResNet152 provides better scores compared with the K-Branch CNN. However, the difference is smaller than 4% in recall, Jaccard index, label ranking average precision and F_1 score, whereas the K-Branch CNN model achieves more than 2% recall with significantly reduced number of layers (which is three order of magnitude). This shows that very shallow CNNs can achieve close classification performance to very deep CNNs if the spectral content of RS images is effectively characterized as in K-Branch CNN.
new_text: In the first experiment, we evaluate K-Branch CNN, VGG16/VGG19, and ResNet50/101/152 for BigEarthNet multi-label classification. Table <ref> reports their performance under standard metrics. ResNet models outperform others in most metrics: ResNet152 improves precision by ~2% over VGG19, while ResNet50 and ResNet152 reduce Hamming loss and ranking loss by >5% and >4%, respectively. VGG19 achieves the highest one error score (<2% improvement over ResNets). These results highlight that ResNet’s residual connections and greater depth enhance semantic image characterization. For VGG models, depth improvements (VGG19) only benefit recall and one error metrics, with minimal gains in other metrics compared to VGG16. Similarly, ResNet depth increases from 50 to 101 yield limited gains (e.g., ResNet50 reduces ranking loss by >4%, but ResNet101 matches ResNet50 in recall). Further increasing depth to 152 layers improves most metrics over ResNet50, demonstrating that deeper networks achieve better performance only when the depth enhances multi-class characterization. While ResNet152 outperforms K-Branch CNN by <4% in recall, Jaccard, and F1 scores, K-Branch CNN achieves >2% recall with ~1,000× fewer layers, demonstrating that shallow networks can match deep models if spectral content is effectively characterized.

Our contributions are as follows. (1) Propose new experimental protocol that uses a fixed amount of full supervision for hyperparameter search and carefully analyze six WSOL methods on three architectures and three datasets. (2) Propose new evaluation metrics as well as data, annotations, and benchmarks for the WSOL task which we will release upon acceptance. (3) Show that WSOL has not progressed significantly since CAM, when the calibration dependency and the different amounts of full supervision are factored out. Moreover, searching hyperparameters on a held-out set consisting of 5 to 10 full localization supervision per class often leads to significantly lower performance compared to the few-shot learning (FSL) baselines that use the full supervision directly for model training. Finally, we suggest a shift of focus in future WSOL research: consideration of learning paradigms utilizing both weak and full supervisions, and other options for resolving the ill-posedness of WSOL (e.gbackground-class images).
new_text: We introduce three contributions. First, a novel experimental protocol employing fixed full supervision for hyperparameter search, systematically evaluating six WSOL methods across three architectures and datasets. Second, new evaluation metrics, data, annotations, and benchmarks for WSOL, to be publicly released upon acceptance. Third, we demonstrate that WSOL has made limited progress beyond CAM when controlling for calibration and supervision variations. Notably, hyperparameter tuning using 5–10 full localization annotations per class in a held-out set consistently underperforms few-shot learning (FSL) baselines that leverage full supervision directly for training. Finally, we propose redirecting future WSOL research toward hybrid learning frameworks combining weak and full supervision, alongside alternative strategies for addressing WSOL’s inherent ill-posedness (e.g., background-class images).

The session ticket is then stored by the client and included in subsequent connections, allowing the server to retrieve the resumption secret. new_text: When using session tickets, the server encrypts the resumption secret with a long-term symmetric key called the session ticket encryption key (STEK), producing a session ticket. The client stores this ticket and reuses it in subsequent connections, enabling the server to recover the resumption secret. This method employs a single STEK for multiple sessions and clients, reducing server storage requirements but introducing vulnerabilities to replay attacks and lacking forward secrecy. To address these issues, we focus on the session cache mechanism described next.

new_text: When discrete changes occur in contact states—such as when parts of a contact surface transition between being in contact and not in contact—the finite element (FE) force vector **𝐟_c(𝐮)** becomes non-differentiable at these transition points (see <ref>). This lack of differentiability introduces challenges in standard numerical solution algorithms, which typically rely on smoothness to converge efficiently. If the applied load step is too large, or if multiple segments of the contact surface simultaneously switch states (e.g., from sticking to sliding), the solver may encounter a phenomenon known as cycling or zig-zagging (<cit.>). This occurs because the algorithm repeatedly alternates between two distinct contact states in successive iterations, failing to converge. To address such scenarios, numerical methods like semi-smooth Newton approaches are often employed, as they can handle the non-differentiable points inherent to these transitions. In this work, we adopt an alternative strategy that involves temporarily "freezing" the active sets—regions where contact is enforced—during early iterations (see <cit.>). Specifically, we maintain fixed active sets at the start of the solution process until the residual norm falls below a predefined tolerance threshold. This strategy assumes that any remaining state changes during this phase are sufficiently small to avoid triggering cyclic behavior. Furthermore, we enhance stability by adaptively adjusting the load step when the contacting body initiates or terminates full sliding motion, particularly when the direction of sliding reverses. Such adjustments ensure that abrupt changes in contact mechanics are accommodated without overwhelming the solver’s convergence criteria.

new_text: Accessing a Bloom Filter, such as those within the Delay Monitor, requires retrieving data from multiple indexes corresponding to hash function outputs. For example, in Fig. <ref>, the yellow SYN entry would require accessing three indexes associated with the yellow hash outputs. To address this, the two monitor tables are divided into smaller chunks, with each hash function restricted to index a single chunk as illustrated in Fig. <ref>. The conceptual point of this lemma is that the hardness of all-pairs constraint satisfaction is always concentrated on a relatively small number of demand pairs.
A few recent papers <cit.> have done technical work to design lower bounds with this property, but Lemma <ref> shows that this property can actually be obtained for free, in a black-box way.
However, we remark that some of these papers (including <cit.>) go a bit further to obtain hardness concentrated on demand pairs between a small number of terminal nodes, and we have been unable to prove an extension of Lemma <ref> that implies this stronger property in general.
Such an extension would be very interesting and would likely imply significant progress for spanners, even if it requires additional natural axioms about the MCSP complex in question.
new_text: The core insight of this lemma is that the computational difficulty in all-pairs constraint satisfaction problems is inherently localized to a limited set of demand pairs. While several recent works <cit.> have explicitly constructed lower bounds exhibiting this concentration, Lemma <ref> demonstrates that this property arises automatically through a general, black-box method. We note, however, that certain studies (including <cit.>) have further shown that the hardness can be restricted to demand pairs connected to only a few terminal nodes. We have not been able to extend Lemma <ref> to establish this more specific property universally. Achieving this extension would be highly impactful, potentially leading to substantial advancements in spanner constructions, even if it necessitates incorporating new standard assumptions regarding the MCSP complex.

Assistive-technologies have attracted the attention of several Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) researchers recently. People with limited physical abilities find it difficult to interact with traditional typing equipment, including keyboard, mouse, and joysticks as they require consistent physical interactions. For example, a person with a physical condition such as Quadriplegia (all four limbs are paralyzed) cannot use any of the off-the-shelf-devices for typing. Recent advancements in motion tracking, computer vision, and natural language processing have enabled researchers to develop techniques that assist people in typing. For example, touchless interaction such as lip reading <cit.>, speech recognition <cit.>, Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) <cit.>, eye tracking <cit.>, and head operated interfaces <cit.> have been utilized for assistive typing.
new_text: Assistive technologies have drawn attention from Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) researchers. People with limited physical abilities struggle with traditional typing equipment—keyboard, mouse, and joysticks—due to their reliance on continuous physical input. For instance, quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs) precludes the use of off-the-shelf devices for typing. Advances in motion tracking, computer vision, and natural language processing have enabled assistive typing techniques. Touchless interaction methods such as lip reading <cit.>, speech recognition <cit.>, Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) <cit.>, eye tracking <cit.>, and head-operated interfaces <cit.> have been developed.

The task of generating cluster sequences using head movement video can be seen as a sequence to sequence modeling task in which the input sequence is a sequence of RGB frames and output sequence is a sequence of clusters the user was looking at. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) such as LSTM <cit.>, GRU <cit.> are widely used for a sequence to sequence modeling tasks. However, it might be the case that the number of video frames is not equal to the number of clusters in the target sequence, and hence an input frame cannot be aligned to a corresponding cluster. For this, we use Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) Loss <cit.>, which solves the non-alignment problem of input and output. For forming the feature embedding, we use the output from the HopeNet model as described in the previous section.
Our model consists of a four-layered Bi-Directional GRU network. The embedding dimension is 198 (concatenation of 66 dimension softmax output for all three Euler angles) and the hidden dimension of the GRU cell used is 512.
new_text: The task of generating cluster sequences from head movement video data can be conceptualized as a sequence-to-sequence modeling problem, where the input consists of a temporally ordered sequence of RGB frames and the output corresponds to a sequence of visual clusters the user fixated on during the interaction. To model this temporal dependency, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) are natural candidates due to their capacity to process sequential data and retain temporal context. However, a key challenge arises when the temporal resolution of the input (i.e., the number of video frames) does not match the temporal structure of the target output (i.e., the number of discrete gaze clusters). In such cases, individual input frames cannot be directly aligned with specific output clusters, creating a mismatch in temporal granularity. To resolve this misalignment, we employ the Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss function, which enables end-to-end training by explicitly modeling the probabilistic alignment between input and output sequences, even when they differ in length. For feature representation, the model leverages precomputed visual embeddings from the HopeNet architecture described in the preceding section. Our implementation specifically utilizes a four-layer bidirectional GRU architecture. Each input frame is first embedded as a 198-dimensional vector, derived by concatenating the 66-dimensional softmax outputs for pitch, yaw, and roll Euler angles predicted by HopeNet. The GRU layers process these embeddings with a hidden state size of 512 units, allowing the model to dynamically encode and decode temporal patterns across the input sequence while respecting the inherent asynchrony between frames and cluster labels.

old_text: To address the first violation, we allow each packet one of the two operations, either to remove itself, if it is expected, or to insert the next expected one iteratively. To achieve this, we keep track of the number of packets seen by each flow. Particularly, when a packet arrives, it checks the number of non-zero-payload packets its flow has already sent. If this number is even, as for S:5500 and S:7500 in Fig. <ref>, then the packet will insert the next expected one in the CBF. If the number is odd, as for S:6500 in Fig. <ref>, the packet will try to find its footprint in the CBF and remove it. We use a counting bloom filter to efficiently keep track of the number of packets.
new_text: To address the first type of violation, the system provides each packet with two possible operations: either removing itself from the CBF if it is identified as expected, or iteratively inserting the next expected packet into the CBF. These decisions are based on tracking the number of packets processed for each flow. Specifically, when a packet arrives, it evaluates the number of non-zero-payload packets already associated with its corresponding flow. This count determines the packet's action: if the count is even (e.g., S:5500 and S:7500 in Fig. <ref>), the packet is directed to insert the next expected packet into the CBF. Conversely, if the count is odd (e.g., S:6500 in Fig. <ref>), the packet instead attempts to locate and remove its own footprint within the CBF. This parity-based logic ensures systematic alternating between insertion and removal operations, maintaining consistency in flow tracking. A counting bloom filter (CBF) is employed to efficiently manage this tracking, as it supports approximate counting of packets while minimizing memory overhead and computational complexity compared to alternative data structures.

old_text: To learn the functional model that is often nonlinear and complex, nonparametric kernel methods are widely appreciated thanks to the “kernel trick" that makes some well-behaved linear learning algorithms applicable in a high-dimensional implicit feature space, without explicit mapping from data to that feature space <cit.>. However, it is challenging to directly apply them to a decentralized multi-agent setting and solve under the consensus optimization framework using algorithms such as decentralized alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) <cit.> without any raw data sharing or aggregation. This is because decentralized learning relies on solving local optimization problems and then aggregating the updates on the local decision variables over the network through one-hop communications in an iterative manner <cit.>. Unfortunately, these decision variables of local objective functions resulted from the kernel trick are data-dependent and thus cannot be optimized in the absence of raw data exchange under the decentralized consensus framework.
new_text: Nonlinear and complex functional models can be effectively learned using nonparametric kernel methods, which leverage the “kernel trick” to enable linear algorithms to operate in high-dimensional feature spaces by implicitly mapping data without explicit computation of the feature space transformation <cit.>. However, deploying these methods in decentralized multi-agent settings under consensus optimization frameworks—such as decentralized alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)—<cit> poses significant challenges when raw data sharing or central aggregation is prohibited. This arises because decentralized learning relies on resolving local optimization tasks and iteratively combining their decision variable updates through one-hop communication across the network <cit.>. The issue stems from the fact that the local objective functions’ decision variables, generated via the kernel trick, depend on the data itself, making them incompatible with decentralized consensus optimization in data-sharing-free environments.

Why might we want to train our agents via self-play? Won't their language diverge from L^*? One way to intuitively understand why S2P is beneficial is to think in terms of constraints. In our set-up, there are two known constraints on the target language L^*: (1) it is consistent with the samples from the supervised dataset 𝒟, and (2) L^* can be used to obtain a high reward in the environment. In this setup, L^* must satisfy two constraints: (1) consistency with supervised samples in 𝒟, and (2) achievability of high environmental reward. Enforcing both constraints enhances performance.

Incorporating these factors could introduce new challenges for S2P learning frameworks, which remain outside the scope of this work. We aim not to identify optimal S2P methodologies across these scenarios but to encourage adoption of 'supervised self-play algorithms' as a framework for advancing sample-efficient human-in-the-loop language learning.

The obvious distinction between cognition and model levels is that feature embedding, rather than model updates, will be encrypted and applied to further ensemble in cognition-level federation. The embedding could be the last fully-connected layer in deep neural networks or the local cognition extracted on a party. The ensemble on the third party is a training process with an independent model based on local embeddings, and the training will interact with local models and iterate until convergence.
To be more specific, as shown in Figure <ref>, during federation, high-level features embedded in local data are first encrypted and sent to the third-party server. Local embedding can be viewed as coarse cognition (or meta knowledge) that is brought together to create fine cognition (or global knowledge). Pratical applications are often in need of this federation. In MPC, the knowledge is generated by performing homomorphic operations such as addition, multiplication, and maximum on the encrypted data, which requires that the encryption must be homomorphic. That is, the operation on the ciphertext can achieve exactly the same result as on the plaintext. Although the third party is probably untrustable, this computing procedure does not leak data privacy on the ciphertext space. If the third-party is virtual or omitted, the proposed framework is fully decentralized, which is quite useful especially in two-party collaboration.
According to the forementioned description, secure MPC is radically a special case of the information-level federation with regard to computation.
new_text: In MPC, the knowledge is generated by performing homomorphic operations such as addition, multiplication, and maximum on the encrypted data, which requires the encryption to be homomorphic. That is, the operation on the ciphertext produces the same result as when applied to the plaintext. Although the third party is likely untrustworthy, this computing procedure does not compromise data privacy in the ciphertext space. If the third party is hypothetical or omitted, the proposed framework becomes fully decentralized, which is particularly useful in two-party collaborations. Based on the foregoing description, secure MPC is essentially a special case of the information-level federation in terms of computation.

The RVE concept (see <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>) is commonly used in the aerospace/automotive industry to avoid using computationally expensive simulation platforms necessary to capture microstructural features. In essence, the features are captured in the RVE and averaged out over the RVE before any discretization technique is employed at the macroscale with the averaged properties as parameters. More often than not, a number of simulations are run with different microstructures and the statistical mean of the results from those simulations on the macroscale are used as guiding principles for the design of the aerospace/automotive part. The reason for running multiple simulations each with a different microstructure is that the microstructure is only known stochastically and not deterministically. With advances in the field of material science and increased emphasis on modeling of biological tissues and engineered structures like foams and textiles, the need is felt to extend the analyses for cases in which both solid and fluid phases exist in tandem in the microstructure.
The problem is complicated since the physics of solid dictates focus on solid displacements while the physics of fluid dictates focus on fluid velocities. The displacements and velocities are dimensionally incompatible since the velocity represents the rate of change of fluid displacement. In lieu of that, we employ the technique in which a displacement field is defined for the fluid phase also to go with the displacement field defined naturally for the solid phase (see <cit.>).
We combine that technique with the FE^2 homogenization framework (see <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>) in which each gauss point for the finite element calculations at the macroscale is associated with a RVE and the information exchange between the two scales occurs at each of those gauss points via the deformation gradient. A 2D depiction of the algorithmic framework is given in Figure <ref>. The reason for calling the framework “FE^2” is that both the macroscale and the RVE scale are solved using finite element method.
The accuracy of the RVE approximation depends on how well the assumed boundary conditions reflect each of the myriad boundary conditions to which the RVE is subjected in-situ. The imposed boundary conditions on the RVE should be such that the Hill-Mandel condition (see <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>) of energetic equivalence between the two scales is satisfied. Periodic boundary conditions satisfy the Hill-Mandel condition and are generally the optimal choice from the standpoint of macroscale accuracy (see <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>).

The Representative Volume Element (RVE) approach is widely adopted in aerospace and automotive sectors to circumvent the computational burden of detailed microstructural simulations. This method encapsulates microstructural details within an RVE, averaging these characteristics before applying macroscale discretization techniques with the averaged properties as input parameters. Typically, multiple simulations are conducted with varying microstructures, and the statistical average of macroscale outcomes guides part design. This strategy accounts for the inherently probabilistic nature of microstructural knowledge, where deterministic descriptions are unattainable. Recent advancements in material science—particularly in modeling biological tissues, foams, and textiles—have highlighted the need to analyze systems where both solid and fluid phases coexist within the microstructure. Such cases introduce complexity, as solid mechanics focuses on displacements while fluid mechanics prioritizes velocities, quantities that differ dimensionally. To resolve this, a displacement field is explicitly defined for the fluid phase alongside the native solid displacement field (<cit.>). 

This displacement-based fluid treatment is integrated within the FE² homogenization framework, where each macroscopic finite element calculation’s Gaussian point links to an RVE. Information exchange between scales occurs at these Gaussian points through the deformation gradient tensor. A schematic representation of this algorithm is provided in Figure <ref>. The framework is termed “FE²” because both macroscopic and RVE-scale analyses employ the finite element method. The fidelity of RVE predictions hinges on boundary conditions that mirror the in-situ constraints acting on the RVE. Crucially, these boundary conditions must satisfy the Hill-Mandel criterion (<cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>), ensuring energetic consistency between scales. Periodic boundary conditions are generally favored for this criterion and for maximizing macroscopic accuracy (<cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>, <cit.>).

ConvLab-2 provides user simulators for automatic evaluation and integrates Amazon Mechanical Turk for human evaluation, similar to ConvLab.
Moreover, it provides an analysis tool and an human-machine interactive tool for diagnosing a dialogue system.
Researchers can perform quantitative analysis using the analysis tool.
It presents useful statistics extracted from the conversations between the user simulator and the dialogue system. This information helps reveal the weakness of the system and signifies the direction for further improvement.
With the interactive tool, researchers can perform qualitative analysis by deploying their dialogue systems and conversing with the systems via the webpage.

A human-machine interactive tool enables qualitative analysis by allowing researchers to deploy dialogue systems and engage with them via a webpage. This interface displays intermediate outputs—such as user dialogue acts and belief states—facilitating manual correction of component errors and identifying performance bottlenecks. The tool also captures real-time human-machine dialogues and user feedback for iterative system refinement.

Classifying questions to predefined set of relations is one of the main approaches for this task <cit.>. Moreover, matching question content with relations has also been proposed and shown promising results <cit.>.
In this paper, the relation extraction is viewed from a new perspective such that relation extraction is done within a question-question matching model, instead of only matching questions and relations. Indeed, while many of the previous works use a matching between question mention and relations, we use an instance-based method for classifying relations.
The proposed model benefits from a text matching model, namely MatchPyramid <cit.>, and enhances it with a two-channel model for considering lexical match and semantic match between questions.
new_text: Classifying questions into a predefined set of relations is a widely adopted approach for this task <cit.>. Additionally, methods that directly match question content with specific relations have also been developed and demonstrated promising results <cit.>. In contrast to these approaches, this paper introduces a novel perspective by reframing relation extraction as a question-question matching problem. Instead of relying solely on the traditional method of aligning questions with predefined relations—common in earlier works <cit.>—the model focuses on comparing questions to identify relational patterns through instance-based classification. This shift allows the model to leverage contextual interactions between questions, potentially capturing more nuanced relational cues. The proposed method builds on the MatchPyramid model <cit.>, a text matching framework known for its effectiveness in natural language inference, and extends it with a two-channel architecture. This enhancement enables the model to simultaneously evaluate both lexical-level matches (e.g., word overlaps, syntax) and semantic-level matches (e.g., meaning alignment, contextual similarity) between paired questions, thereby improving the precision of relation classification.

**Qualitative study of non–augmented neural ODE variants.**
We qualitatively inspect the performance of different neural ODE variants: depth–invariant, depth–variant, Galërkin (GalNODE) and data–controlled. We utilize a nested 2–spheres problem in which all 2^13 data points are available during training. Models are then qualitatively evaluated based on the complexity of the learned flows and on how accurately they extrapolate to unseen points in the continuous space of the 2–spheres, i.e. the learned decision boundaries.
new_text: This study presents a qualitative analysis of various non-augmented neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) architectures, including depth-invariant, depth-variant, Galerkin (GalNODE), and data-controlled configurations. The evaluation is conducted using a nested 2-spheres dataset with 2^13 training samples accessible during the learning process. Model performance is assessed based on two criteria: the structural complexity of the learned dynamic trajectories and their ability to generalize to unobserved regions within the continuous 2-spheres domain, particularly in terms of the learned decision boundaries.

However, there are very few studies on BFT in decentralized learning systems. It is challenging to apply the above solutions to the decentralized scenario, due to two reasons. First, existing
defenses themselves have security and efficiency drawbacks for protecting centralized systems. It has been
shown that distance-based defenses are vulnerable to elaborately designed Byzantine attacks <cit.>. Performance-based defenses have large computation overhead
and scalability issue when conducting performance evaluation for each update. Besides, they require the parameter server to have an extra validation dataset, which is not realistic. These limitations still exist if the defenses were extended into decentralized systems. The second reason lies in the huge differences between centralized and decentralized learning systems. Existing defenses are mainly designed for one parameter server. However, each device in decentralized learning acts as not only a worker node, but also a “parameter server”. In addition, the number of neighbors connected to each device varies dramatically. So some assumptions made in the centralized defenses will not hold. To the best of our knowledge, currently there are only two research papers <cit.> attempting to achieve Byzantine-resilient decentralized learning by adopting the distance-based strategy, which is vulnerable to sophisticated Byzantine attacks, as demonstrated in the evaluation section of this paper.
new_text: Decentralized learning systems have seen limited research on Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT), primarily due to challenges in adapting existing solutions. First, defenses designed for centralized systems often exhibit shortcomings in both security and efficiency when applied to decentralized settings. For instance, distance-based methods are susceptible to advanced Byzantine attacks <cit.>, while performance-based approaches incur significant computational costs, scalability issues from evaluating every update, and reliance on an external validation dataset—practically infeasible. These drawbacks persist even if these methods are repurposed for decentralized architectures. The second challenge stems from structural differences between centralized and decentralized frameworks. Centralized defenses typically assume a single parameter server, whereas in decentralized learning, each device functions both as a worker node and a local parameter server, with highly variable neighbor counts. This undermines assumptions in centralized strategies. Currently, only two studies <cit.> explore Byzantine-resilient decentralized learning using distance-based methods, which remain vulnerable to sophisticated attacks, as shown in this paper's evaluation.

old_text: The growing area of text matching develops models to investigate the relationship and the degree of matching between sequences of words. This comparison mechanism is a substantial core for various tasks, including ad-hoc retrieval, paraphrase identification, question answering, and semantic web search <cit.>. In this regard, three main categories are considered in the context of deep matching models, namely representation-focused, interaction-focused, and hybrid <cit.>. In representation-focused models, an abstract contextual representation of texts are extracted through neural networks and then these representations are used to estimate the matching score between them. BiMPM <cit.> and ARC I <cit.> are examples of these models. On the other hand, interaction-focused models compute the similarity between two sequences of words in a procedure, such that different patterns and structures of interactions are learned with the help of neural networks based on local interactions of two sequences <cit.>. MatchPyramid <cit.> and aNMM <cit.> are examples of these models. Hybrid models aim to benefit from the advantages of both techniques. ARC II <cit.> is an example of this category.
new_text: The growing field of text matching focuses on developing models to analyze the relationship and degree of similarity between sequences of words. This foundational comparison mechanism underpins a wide range of natural language processing tasks, including ad-hoc retrieval, paraphrase identification, question answering, and semantic web search <cit.>. Within the realm of deep matching models, researchers typically categorize approaches into three primary types: representation-focused, interaction-focused, and hybrid <cit.>. Representation-focused models rely on neural networks to generate abstract, contextual representations of individual texts. These representations, which encode semantic and syntactic features, are then used to calculate a matching score between the texts. Models like BiMPM <cit.> and ARC I <cit.> exemplify this approach, prioritizing the quality of individual text encodings to infer similarity. Interaction-focused models, in contrast, emphasize direct interaction patterns between word sequences. Here, neural networks learn complex structures of local interactions—such as alignments or attention mechanisms—to compute similarity scores. This method captures nuanced relational details that may be lost in representation-only models; examples include MatchPyramid <cit.> and aNMM <cit.>. Finally, hybrid models integrate the strengths of both paradigms, combining robust contextual representations with detailed interaction patterns to enhance matching accuracy. ARC II <cit.> represents such a hybrid approach, demonstrating how merging representation and interaction layers can address the limitations of each individual strategy.

We define the condition number κ_Ł,F(S) for the system F and the loss function Ł on the set S,
    based on the smallest and largest eigenvalues of the tangent kernel, analogous to that for a linear system.
    Using the PL condition, we show that if a system F is well-conditioned on a ball of a certain radius, then a solution exists within the ball and, moreover, can be efficiently found by gradient descent or SGD. While the landscape of the loss function Ł can be complex, it is enough to control the condition number in a ball to ensure convergence to a global solution.

new_text: We introduce the condition number κ_Ł,F(S) for the system F and the loss Ł on the set S, derived from the minimum and maximum eigenvalues of the tangent kernel, mirroring the formulation for linear systems. Leveraging the PL condition, we demonstrate that if F is well-conditioned on a ball of a specified radius, a solution lies within that ball and can be efficiently identified using gradient descent or SGD. Despite the intricate nature of the loss landscape Ł, maintaining control over the condition number within this ball guarantees convergence to a global minimum. old_text: Few-shot learning (FSL) aims to learn novel visual categories from very few samples, which is a challenging problem in real-world applications. Many data generation methods have improved the performance of FSL models, but require lots of annotated images to train a specialized network (e.g., GAN) dedicated to hallucinate new samples. We argue that localization is a more efficient approach because it provides the most discriminative regions without using extra samples. In this paper, we propose a novel method to address the FSL task by achieving weakly-supervised object localization within performing few-shot classification. To this end, we design (i) a triplet-input module to obtain the initial object seeds and (ii) an Image-To-Class-Distance (ITCD) based localizer to activate the deep descriptors of the key objects, thus obtaining the more discriminative representations used to perform few-shot classification. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets under various settings. Besides, our method achieves superior performance over previous methods when training the model on miniImageNet and evaluating it on the different datasets (e.g., Stanford Dogs), demonstrating its superior generalization capacity. Extra visualization shows the proposed method can localize the key objects accurately.
new_text: Few-shot learning (FSL) aims to enable machines to recognize novel visual categories using only a small number of training examples, a task that poses significant challenges in practical settings where large annotated datasets are often unavailable. Traditional approaches to improve FSL performance rely on data generation techniques, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which synthesize additional samples to augment the limited training data. However, these methods require extensive labeled data to train the generator networks, creating a paradoxical dependency: solving an FSL problem necessitates first overcoming the scarcity of training examples. To address this, we propose a shift in focus from data generation to object localization. By identifying the most discriminative regions within images—such as key object parts—localization can enhance feature representations without the need for extra samples or complex generative models. Specifically, our approach integrates weakly-supervised object localization into the FSL framework, enabling the model to automatically emphasize critical visual cues during classification. The method consists of two key components: (i) a triplet-input module that extracts initial object regions by comparing support (example) and query (test) images, and (ii) an Image-To-Class-Distance (ITCD) based localizer that sharpens these regions by aligning deep feature maps with class prototypes. These components work synergistically to produce discriminative representations, which are then used for few-shot classification. Experimental results validate the efficacy of this approach, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks. Notably, our model demonstrates strong generalization by achieving competitive results when trained on one dataset (e.g., miniImageNet) and evaluated on unrelated domains (e.g., Stanford Dogs). Furthermore, qualitative analyses confirm that the proposed method reliably highlights relevant object regions, reinforcing its ability to extract meaningful features from minimal examples.
