Relaxed functional dependencies <cit.> relax the
traditional definition of FDs. Some replace data equality with data similarity,
some allow a certain (small) fraction of tuples in the dataset to violate the
learned FDs, and some allow both. Some variants of FDs consider noisy data, but
they require the allowable noise parameter to be explicitly specified by the
user. For example, approximate FDs <cit.>
allow violations by a certain fraction of tuples (specified as a system
parameter), but determining the right setting for this parameter is
non-trivial. Metric FDs <cit.> allow small variations in the
data (attribute values within a distance of a user-specified threshold are
considered identical), but the existing work focuses on verification of a given
metric FD, rather than the discovery of metric FDs. All of these approaches
treat violation as Boolean, and do not measure the degree of violation. In
contrast, we do not require any explicit noise parameter and provide a way to
quantify the degree of violation of data invariants.
new_text: Relaxed functional dependencies <cit.> modify traditional FDs by substituting data equality with similarity, permitting a fraction of tuple violations, or both. Variants addressing noisy data typically require explicit user-defined noise parameters. Approximate FDs <cit.> allow violations up to a user-defined fraction (a system parameter), yet optimal parameter selection remains challenging. Metric FDs <cit.> permit attribute variations within a user-defined threshold but focus on verification rather than discovery. These methods treat violations as Boolean, without quantifying violation degrees. Our approach eliminates the need for explicit noise parameters and quantifies violation degrees of data invariants.

old_text: Many works <cit.> have shown that utilizing localization can help to learn the more discriminative embedded feature for classification. In this context, <cit.> presented the Selective Convolutional Descriptor Aggregation method to achieve unsupervised localization in fine-grained datasets. For utilizing localization to address FSL, SalNet <cit.> employed a readily available saliency detector to obtain the foreground and background, thus fulfilling DA by combining them differently. The ablation study of SalNet demonstrated that performance improvements stem from the localization ability of the saliency detector. Similarly, <cit.> used the class attention map (CAM) generated by classification networks to locate the key region and fused with other different scale features for fine-grained few-shot classification. Different from applying readily available localization, <cit.> used the assistant bounding box annotations to achieve the localization within the few-shot classification, thus to address the FSL task over heavy-tailed datasets. These methods can improve few-shot classification performance by leveraging localization. However, in real-world applications, bounding box annotations and readily available localization (e.g., saliency map) may be hard to meet or impracticable. Therefore, we propose a novel method to achieve weakly-supervised object localization, thus addressing the FSL problem with realistic settings.
new_text: Many works <cit.> have shown that utilizing localization can help learn more discriminative embedded features for classification. In this context, <cit.> presented the Selective Convolutional Descriptor Aggregation method to achieve unsupervised localization in fine-grained datasets. To utilize localization for addressing FSL, SalNet <cit.> employed a readily available saliency detector to obtain the foreground and background, thus achieving DA by combining them differently. The ablation study of SalNet demonstrated that performance improvements stemmed from the localization ability of the saliency detector. Similarly, <cit.> used the class attention map (CAM) generated by classification networks to locate the key region and fused with other features of different scales for fine-grained few-shot classification. Different from applying readily available localization, <cit.> used assistant bounding box annotations to achieve localization in few-shot classification, thereby addressing the FSL task over heavy-tailed datasets. These methods can improve few-shot classification performance by leveraging localization. However, in real-world applications, bounding box annotations and readily available localization (e.g., saliency map) may be hard to obtain or impractical. Therefore, we propose a novel method to achieve weakly-supervised object localization, thus addressing the FSL problem with realistic settings.

new_text:
Adaptive inference cost  
The success of ensemble learning is driven by the reduction in variance achieved through averaging outputs from a set of distinct models. The expected variance reduction and accuracy improvement increase monotonically with the number of models in the ensemble. This property enables a straightforward adaptation of the trade-off between computational cost and predictive performance. Specifically, since each model in the ensemble can be evaluated sequentially, computational resources can be managed by selecting the number of models to evaluate when approximating the ensemble prediction of *ensemble_output*.

In general, there exists a rich literature in the machine learning community on
representation learning using generative models <cit.>,
black-box models such as auto-encoders <cit.>, Bayesian representation
learning <cit.>, and so on. These techniques are
sophisticated and require significant training effort including data cleaning,
encoding the entire data to numerical domain, hyper-parameter tuning, and so
on. In contrast, data invariants are more abstract, yet informative,
descriptions that can be constructed using efficient and highly-scalable
techniques. There is a clear gap between representation learning (that models
data likelihood) and the (constraint-oriented) data-profiling techniques. Our
aim is to bridge this gap by introducing data invariants—which can model
approximate arithmetic relationship over numerical attributes—as a new kind
of constraint to the existing data-profiling techniques.
new_text: A rich literature in machine learning addresses representation learning using generative models <cit.>, black-box models like autoencoders <cit.>, and Bayesian representation learning <cit.>. These methods require substantial training effort, including data cleaning, data encoding to numerical domains, and hyper-parameter tuning. In contrast, data invariants are abstract yet informative descriptive constructs constructable via efficient, scalable techniques. Representation learning, which models data likelihood, and constraint-oriented data-profiling techniques remain distinct. We aim to bridge this gap by introducing data invariants—approximating arithmetic relationships over numerical attributes—as new constraints to enhance data-profiling approaches.

Our approach includes three sequential modules: sketch segmentation, foreground generation, and background generation. These three modules are illustrated in Fig. <ref>.
Given a scene sketch, all object instances are first located and recognized by the sketch segmentation module, and after that image content is generated from each foreground object instance (i.e., instances belonging to the foreground categories) individually in a random order by the foreground generation module. new_text: Our method comprises three sequential components: sketch segmentation, foreground synthesis, and background synthesis, as depicted in Fig. <ref>. For a given scene sketch, the sketch segmentation module first identifies and classifies all object instances. The foreground generation module then creates visual content for each foreground object instance (those categorized as foreground elements) in a random sequence. Finally, the background generation module takes the remaining background sketch regions and the foreground outputs as inputs, generating the complete image through a single background rendering pass. The following sections elaborate on the implementation of each component.

To overcome the limitations caused by the constraint of specifying a normalized explicit density, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) <cit.> proposed to learn implicit density generative models within a minimax framework, where the generative model is a direct differentiable mapping from noise space to sample space. So far many variants of GANs have been proposed in order to minimize various discrepancy measures <cit.>. new_text: Flow-based models depend on invertible transformations with computable Jacobian determinants, whereas sum-product networks utilize hierarchical graph architectures featuring sum and product nodes to achieve tractable density estimation. To address challenges posed by the need to define a normalized explicit probability distribution, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) <cit.> introduced a framework for learning implicit generative models through a minimax game, in which the generator implements a differentiable mapping from latent noise space to the data sample domain. Numerous GAN variants have since emerged, aiming to reduce diverse statistical discrepancies between distributions <cit.>. Notably, f-GANs <cit.> optimize a variational approximation of f-divergence between the target and generated distributions, a flexible class of metrics for quantifying the difference between two probability measures.

old_text: There are occasional failures in feature detection, owing mainly to the symmetry of the tool parts, for example, the Roll_1, Pitch_1 and Yaw_2 features. As shown in Fig. <ref>, detecting those features are more challenging compared to other ones. The misdetections are, however, of low confidence. Hence they are handled by the probability weighting of the detected points in the observation model of the particle filter. In Fig. <ref>, for instance, one of the grippers of the tools is misdetected, but has substantially lower confidence; the correctly detected points have confidence scores higher than 70%. Similarly, in the second case, two features are detected on the wrong side of the shaft (they are symmetric and partially visible in this frame), but again with low confidence and hence does not throw off the pose estimation. Overall, the feature detection is robust and results in accurate perception.
new_text: The feature detection process occasionally encounters challenges, primarily due to the inherent symmetry of specific tool components, such as the Roll_1, Pitch_1, and Yaw_2 features. This symmetry, combined with partial visibility in certain frames, makes these features harder to distinguish from their counterparts compared to other less ambiguous features. For instance, as illustrated in Fig. <ref>, the symmetrical nature of the tool’s grippers creates ambiguity in detection; however, the system mitigates this by leveraging confidence scores assigned to detected points. When a misdetection occurs—such as when one gripper is incorrectly identified—it is typically accompanied by a low confidence score, distinguishing it from reliable detections. The particle filter’s observation model then applies probability weighting to these scores, downscaling the influence of low-confidence points. In Fig. <ref>, the misdetected gripper has a confidence score significantly below the threshold (e.g., less than 30%), while the correctly identified points consistently exceed 70% confidence. A similar mechanism resolves ambiguity in another case where two features are incorrectly localized on the wrong side of the shaft. Although the symmetry of the shaft’s design and limited visibility in that frame lead to erroneous detections, the associated low confidence scores ensure these errors do not distort the overall pose estimation. These examples underscore how the system’s reliance on probabilistic weighting maintains robustness, allowing accurate perception despite occasional feature detection challenges.

However, the state-of-the-art crowdsourcing methods place more emphasis on raw data sharing and aggregation from a bunch of collaborating users, and normally there is no model in mind; even if there is a model assumed, it remains simple and heuristic. Representative works are as follows. In geography, voluntary users collaboratively build a street map, fill in street information, etc. OpenStreetMap ([URL]) and Wikimapia (http:// [URL]) are two successful crowdsourcing projects among others. new_text: Crowdsourcing refers to a method of gathering services from an expansive, open, and dynamically changing group of internet users, where contributions collectively shape a system or dataset. While the concept aligns with the FedLoc framework, contemporary crowdsourcing techniques predominantly prioritize aggregating raw data from multiple users, often without a predefined model or relying on minimalistic, heuristic-driven models when applied. Key examples in geographic contexts include collaborative platforms where volunteers construct and update street maps—projects like OpenStreetMap ([URL]) and Wikimapia (http:// [URL]) exemplify this approach. Emerging trends extend crowdsourcing to virtual mapping, such as RSS-based or magnetic field maps, particularly for complex multi-storey structures <cit.>.

old_text: We propose the use of multivariate boosted trees (MBTs) to induce arbitrary regularization and consistency properties in the tree output. This can be done both via penalization of the multivariate output or requiring it to be a superposition of basis functions. Inducing regularization in multivariate output is not new, but while this is common for example in neural network architectures <cit.>, they are currently not exploited in tree-based algorithms. One exception is the possibility of LightGBM and XGBoost to express monotonicity conditions of the univariate prediction, with respect to a given input <cit.>. This is obtained by inhibiting the tree growth if the new leaf causes a non-monotonic relationship in the selected feature. However, this may produce unnecessarily shallow trees if not enough split candidates are tested, which could be the case if the tree is grown using histogram search, one of the most popular methods for finding candidate splits.
new_text: We propose using multivariate boosted trees (MBTs) to induce arbitrary regularization and consistency in tree outputs via either penalizing the multivariate output or enforcing it as a superposition of basis functions. While regularization of multivariate outputs is common in neural networks <cit.>, it remains underexplored in tree-based algorithms. An exception is LightGBM and XGBoost, which can enforce monotonicity constraints for univariate predictions relative to input features <cit.>, achieved by halting tree growth when a new leaf violates the monotonic relationship in the selected feature. This approach, however, risks producing overly shallow trees if insufficient split candidates are tested—particularly when using histogram-based search, a prevalent method for identifying candidate splits.

Power profiles of uncontrollable loads were generated with the LoadProfileGenerator <cit.>; power profiles of photovoltaic roof-mounted power plants were obtained through the PVlib python library <cit.>, while the electrical loads due to heat pumps was retrieved simulating domestic heating systems and buildings thermal dynamics, modelling them starting from building's metadata. new_text: To compare the method in <cit.> with the MBT approach, we simulated three months of operational data for a low-voltage grid in Switzerland. The grid’s configuration and the placement of QP (quadrature-phase) buses, visualized in Fig. <ref>, were obtained from the local Distribution System Operator (DSO), who also provided cable parameters essential for accurate modeling. For power profiles, three distinct sources were used: uncontrollable loads were generated using the LoadProfileGenerator <cit.>, a tool designed to synthesize realistic consumption patterns without predictive control; photovoltaic generation profiles were created via the PVlib Python library <cit.>, which models solar plant output based on irradiance and system properties; and electrical demand from heat pumps was simulated by modeling domestic heating systems and building thermal dynamics, derived from metadata such as insulation levels and occupancy patterns. These data were integrated into OpenDSS <cit.>, a widely used distribution grid simulation platform, to replicate the grid’s electrical behavior. The simulation captured voltage, power, and current values across all QP nodes at 1-minute intervals, enabling high-resolution analysis of grid performance under varying conditions.

old_text: Because the formulation of NAS is similar to reinfocement learning (RL), early NAS methods were firstly proposed based on it. However, such approaches are very computationally expensive. A variety of methods were thus proposed based on progressive learning or weight sharing to reduce computational cost. In the following, we only focus on related works on these two approaches.
new_text: The structural parallels between neural architecture search (NAS) and reinforcement learning (RL) led to the initial development of NAS methods grounded in RL frameworks. These early approaches, however, proved highly computationally intensive due to the repeated training of numerous candidate architectures. To address this limitation, subsequent research introduced alternative strategies such as progressive learning and weight sharing, which aim to mitigate these resource demands while maintaining performance. This paper specifically examines advancements and methodologies within these two computational efficiency-focused paradigms.

old_text: In this work, we propose Progressive One-shot Neural Architecture Search (PONAS) that combines the advantages of progressive NAS and the one-shot method. Progressive NASs like <cit.> and <cit.> construct convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by stacking some predefined numbers of cells. The best structure of the cell is searched by progressively expanding blocks (operations). The determined best cell then acts as a layer. The structure of each layer, therefore, keeps the same. In the proposed PONAS, instead of searching the best cell, we search the best block for each layer progressively. In this way, structures of different layers may be different, and richer expressivity may be obtained. To tackle the first problem mentioned above, we propose a two-stage training scheme that separates the searching process into the meta training stage and the fine-tuning stage to make the search process more efficient and stable.
new_text: In this study, we introduce Progressive One-shot Neural Architecture Search (PONAS), a framework that integrates the benefits of progressive NAS with the efficiency of one-shot methods. Traditional progressive NAS approaches, such as <cit.> and <cit.>, build convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by stacking a predefined number of cells. These methods identify the optimal cell structure through a stepwise expansion of blocks (operations), after which the selected cell serves as a recurring layer, maintaining a uniform structure across all layers. In contrast, PONAS searches for the best block for each layer individually in a progressive manner, enabling heterogeneous architectures where layer structures can vary, potentially enhancing model expressiveness. To address challenges in search stability and efficiency, we implement a two-stage training strategy that divides the process into a meta training phase and a subsequent fine-tuning phase.

In this paper, we proposed two modified neural network architectures based on SFANet and SegNet respectively for accurate and efficient crowd counting. Inspired by SFANet, the first model is attached with two novel multi-scale-aware modules called, ASSP and CAN. This model is called M-SFANet. The encoder of M-SFANet is enhanced with ASSP containing parallel atrous convolution with different sampling rates and hence able to extract multi-scale features of the target object and incorporate larger context. To further deal with scale variation throughout an input image, we leverage contextual module called CAN which adaptively encodes the scales of the contextual information. The combination yields an effective model for counting in both dense and sparse crowd scenes. Based on SFANet decoder structure, M-SFANet decoder has dual paths, for density map generation and attention map generation. The second model is called M-SegNet. For M-SegNet, we simply change bilinear upsampling used in SFANet to max unpooling originally from SegNet and propose the faster model while providing competitive counting performance. Designed for high-speed surveillance applications, M-SegNet has no additional multi-scale-aware module in order to not increase the complexity. Both models are encoder-decoder based architectures and end-to-end trainable. We also conduct extensive experiments on four crowd counting datasets and one vehicle counting dataset to show that these modifications yield algorithms that could outperform some of state-of-the-art crowd counting methods.
new_text: In this paper, we propose two modified neural network architectures based on SFANet and SegNet for accurate and efficient crowd counting. Inspired by SFANet, the first model incorporates two novel multi-scale-aware modules, ASSP and CAN. This model is called M-SFANet. The encoder of M-SFANet is enhanced with ASSP, which contains parallel atrous convolutions with different sampling rates, enabling the extraction of multi-scale features of the target object and the incorporation of a broader context. To address scale variation across an input image, we leverage a contextual module labeled as CAN, which adaptively encodes contextual information of different scales. The combination leads to an effective model for counting in both dense and sparse crowd scenes. Based on the SFANet decoder structure, the M-SFANet decoder has dual paths: one for density map generation and one for attention map generation. The second model is called M-SegNet. For M-SegNet, we simply replace the bilinear upsampling used in SFANet with max unpooling from SegNet, resulting in a faster model while maintaining competitive counting performance. Designed for high-speed surveillance applications, M-SegNet does not include any additional multi-scale-aware modules to avoid increasing complexity. Both models are encoder-decoder based, end-to-end trainable architectures. We conducted extensive experiments on four crowd counting datasets and one vehicle counting dataset to demonstrate that these modifications result in algorithms that outperform several state-of-the-art crowd counting methods.

Goal-Conditioned Imitation using Latent Goals:
Given the goals from the proposal network, the imitation policy should generate actions to reach that goal by conditioning on the goal.
Conditioning the low-level controller on high-dimensional image observations as goals is undesirable - the model could learn spurious associations for what is important in a goal image, and VAE image reconstructions are often low quality and noisy. Instead, we condition the low-level controller on a lower dimensional latent goal that encodes the most salient features of goal observations. In order to do this, we developed a goal relabeling scheme that leverages the latent space of the high-level cVAE to generate goals for the low-level controller.
new_text: The imitation policy generates actions to achieve goals from the proposal network by conditioning on them. However, conditioning the low-level controller on high-dimensional image observations is problematic: the model may learn spurious associations about important features, and VAE reconstructions are typically low quality and noisy. We instead use a lower-dimensional latent goal encoding the most salient features of goal observations. To achieve this, we propose a goal relabeling scheme leveraging the latent space of the high-level cVAE to generate goals for the low-level controller.

The role of prior knowledge and transition model:

To assess their impact, we fix LDA as the base model with batchsize=500, σ=1, K=100, and pre-trained word embeddings as prior. Figure <ref> compares TPS performance across three versions. old_text: We evaluate the success of our method, SGM, in a variety of navigation environments. First, we observe in Table <ref> that SGM has a significantly higher success rate than previous methods, on average increasing the success rate by 40% across the environments tested. As our ablation experiments demonstrate, SGM's success is due in large part to its sparse structure that enables efficient correction of distance metric errors. In addition, we see that the performance gains of SGM hold across a range of environment difficulties from a simple point maze to complex visual environments like ViZDoom and SafetyGym. new_text: To assess the effectiveness of our method, SGM, we conducted experiments across a diverse set of navigation environments. The results, summarized in Table <ref>, demonstrate that SGM consistently outperforms prior approaches in terms of success rate. Specifically, the method achieves an average 40% improvement in task completion across the tested scenarios, a statistically significant advantage that highlights its robustness. Crucially, ablation experiments reveal that this performance gain is largely attributable to SGM’s sparse architectural design. By focusing computational resources on correcting critical distance metric errors—common challenges in navigation—SGM reduces the accumulation of navigational inaccuracies, enabling more reliable path planning. Furthermore, the benefits of SGM are not limited to specific environment types. The method maintains consistent performance improvements across a wide spectrum of challenges, ranging from basic grid-based navigation in point mazes to complex, visually rich environments such as ViZDoom and SafetyGym. Finally, when comparing computational efficiency, SGM’s use of sparse memory for planning results in a nearly tenfold increase in processing speed relative to conventional methods, underscoring the scalability of the approach.

section: Dynamic Transformation of Prior knowledge into Bayesian models for data Streams (TPS)
old_text: Following <cit.> and <cit.>, we consider a general model B(β, z, x) with two kinds of variables: a global variable β of size K × V to model the latent structure that is shared among data points x_1:N, and probably a local variable z_i to model the latent structure that governs the ith data point x_i. Such a model is general and successfully applied in static conditions. However, there are several challenges in a streaming environment. A data stream is a sequence of minibatches D = {D^1, D^2, ..., D^t,...}, and each minibatch t consists of M observed data points: D^t = {x_1^t,x_2^t,...,x_M^t}.

First, since the predicted result in previous frames would be adopted in the future segmentation prediction, the online construction of our global-local tree would be time-consuming if no special design in training. We find that some parameter tuning would help us improve the efficiency. In training, we only take 4096 points for global-local tree construction in each frame and we find this configuration can take care both performance and efficiency. Secondly, our network need to take continuous frames as input since the frame-to-frame information is required during the training. If we update the network weights after each frame forwarding in a continuous sequence, the training performance would be pretty bad since gradient generated in the loss backward may be too small to be stable for weight update. new_text: Figure <ref> presents the detailed architecture of our network. Two key distinctions differentiate our approach from other semantic segmentation frameworks. First, as future segmentation predictions rely on results from previous frames, the online construction of our global-local tree becomes computationally intensive without optimized training strategies. Through parameter tuning, we find that restricting global-local tree construction to 4096 points per frame during training effectively balances performance and efficiency. Second, the network must process continuous frames to leverage frame-to-frame information during training. However, adjacent frames often exhibit minimal pixel-level changes, which can lead to unstable weight updates if gradients from individual frame losses are applied sequentially. To address this, we aggregate gradients across 8 consecutive frames before performing weight updates. This approach yields substantial performance gains compared to a naive sequential update strategy.

Variations of this approach include Search on the Replay Buffer <cit.>, which assumes access to uniform sampling of the environment for graph nodes; Semi-Parametric Topological Memory <cit.>, which assumes a demonstration to bootstrap the graph; and Mapping State Space Using Landmarks for Universal Goal Reaching <cit.>, which subsamples the policy’s past training observations to choose graph nodes. new_text: Recent work combines graph-based and parametric planning by using past observations for graph nodes and learned distance metrics for edges. Variants include Search on the Replay Buffer <cit.>, which relies on uniform environmental sampling for nodes; Semi-Parametric Topological Memory <cit.>, which bootstraps from demonstrations; and Mapping State Space Using Landmarks <cit.>, which subsamples policy training data for nodes. Hallucinative Topological Memory (HTM) <cit.> employs a contrastive energy model for edges, and <cit.> use dynamic programming with learned graphs. Our approach introduces a two-way consistency check to enforce sparsity, addressing prior limitations: existing methods either store full replay buffers in graphs—leading to quadratic scalability issues in node count—or subsample without graph structure considerations.

This could be attributed to noisy labels or uncertainties in expert annotations, which negatively impacted training in fully supervised settings but are effectively regularized using semi-supervised approaches.

old_text: Overall Pipeline. The goal of our proposed pipeline is to automatically reconstruct a watertight textured sinus surface from an unlabeled endoscopic video. The pipeline, shown in Fig. <ref>, has three main components: 1) SfM based on dense point correspondences produced by a learning-based descriptor; 2) depth estimation; and 3) volumetric depth fusion with surface extraction. SfM identifies corresponding points across the video sequence and uses these correspondences to calculate both, a sparse 3D reconstruction of these points and the camera trajectory generating the video. By replacing local with learning-based descriptors during the point correspondence stage of SfM, we are able to improve the density of sparse reconstruction and the completeness of the estimated camera trajectory. We refer to this process as Dense Descriptor Extraction. Reliable and complete reconstructions directly from SfM are important, because these results are subsequently used for two purposes: 1) they provide self-supervisory signals for fine-tuning two learning-based modules, i. e. Dense Descriptor Extraction and Depth Estimation; 2) they are used in the Depth Fusion & Surface Extraction module to guide the fusion procedure. Depth Estimation provides dense depth measurements for all pixels in every video frame that are then aggregated over the whole video sequence using Depth Fusion & Surface Extraction.
new_text: The overall pipeline aims to automatically reconstruct a watertight textured sinus surface from an unlabeled endoscopic video. The pipeline, shown in Fig. <ref>, comprises three key components: 1) Structure-from-Motion (SfM) based on dense point correspondences produced by a learning-based descriptor; 2) depth estimation; and 3) volumetric depth fusion with surface extraction. SfM identifies corresponding points across the video sequence and leverages these correspondences to compute both a sparse 3D reconstruction of the points and the camera trajectory used to capture the video. By substituting local (hand-crafted) descriptors with learning-based descriptors during the point correspondence stage of SfM, we enhance the density of the sparse reconstruction and the completeness of the estimated camera trajectory—a process we term Dense Descriptor Extraction. Reliable and complete SfM reconstructions are critical as they serve two key roles: first, they provide self-supervisory signals for fine-tuning the learning-based modules—Dense Descriptor Extraction and Depth Estimation—and second, they guide the fusion procedure within the Depth Fusion & Surface Extraction module. The Depth Estimation module generates dense depth measurements for every pixel in each video frame, which are subsequently aggregated across the entire sequence via Depth Fusion & Surface Extraction to produce the final reconstruction.

old_text: In this work, we proposed a learning-based surface reconstruction pipeline for endoscopy. Our method operates directly on raw endoscopic videos and produces watertight textured surface models that are in good agreement with anatomy extracted from CT. While this method so far has only been evaluated on videos of the nasal cavity, the proposed modules are generic, self-supervised and should thus be applicable to other anatomies. This approach directly processes raw endoscopic video sequences to generate watertight textured surface models that demonstrate strong anatomical accuracy relative to CT-derived references. Although the method has thus far been validated solely on datasets of the nasal cavity, the modular design, self-supervised nature, and generalizability of the individual components suggest applicability across diverse anatomical regions. Future directions involve developing uncertainty quantification for reconstructed surface models and the prospective acquisition of longitudinal endoscopic video data in clinical settings.

Unknown Detection. Following the protocol defined in <cit.>, we evaluate the model’s capacity to identify unknown samples across four standard image datasets: MNIST <cit.>, SVHN <cit.>, CIFAR-10 <cit.>, and Tiny-ImageNet <cit.>. For each of these datasets, we adopt a consistent strategy of partitioning classes into known and unknown categories to assess detection performance. Specifically, in the case of MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10, each dataset is randomly divided into 6 known classes (used for training) and 4 unknown classes (used for testing). For the CIFAR-10 dataset, the approach is slightly adapted: the model is trained on 4 known classes, while the test set is composed of 10 randomly selected unknown classes from the CIFAR-100 <cit.> dataset. This scenario is referred to as the *CIFAR+10* task. A more challenging variant, *CIFAR+50*, is also tested, where the test set is expanded to 50 unknown classes randomly sampled from CIFAR-100, maintaining the same 4-class training setup. 

Turning to the Tiny-ImageNet dataset, 20 classes are designated as known for training, with the remaining 180 classes treated as unknown during testing. This partitioning aligns with the general principle of isolating a subset of classes for model training while reserving distinct subsets to evaluate unknown detection. Performance is quantified using the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC), a metric that measures the model’s ability to distinguish between known and unknown samples. To ensure robustness, all results presented in Table <ref> are averaged across five independent random partitions of known and unknown classes. The reported values demonstrate that our method consistently achieves higher AUROC scores compared to prior approaches, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance in unknown sample detection.

In this evaluation, two metrics were used: average residual error between the registered surface reconstruction and the CT model, and average relative difference between the corresponding cross-sectional areas of the CT surface models and the surface reconstructions. The purpose of this evaluation is to determine whether our reconstruction can be used as a low-cost, radiation-free replacement for CT when calculating clinically relevant parameters. To find the corresponding cross-section of two models, the surface reconstruction was first registered to the CT model. The registered camera poses from SfM were then used as the origins and orientations of the cross-sectional planes. The relative differences of all cross-sectional areas along the registered camera trajectory were averaged to obtain the final statistics. As a comparison, when the sparse reconstructions from SfM are directly registered to CT models, the residual error was 0.53(±0.24) mm. The cross-sectional surface areas are estimated with an average relative error of 7(±2) %. This error mainly originates from regions that were not sufficiently visualized during scoping, such as the inferior, middle, and superior meatus. These regions are included in our analysis due to the automation of cross-sectional measurements. In practice, these regions are not commonly inspected as they are hidden beneath the turbinates; if a precise measurement of these areas is desired, small modifications to video capture would allow for improved visualization. new_text: To assess the agreement between their method and computed tomography (CT), the authors evaluated the accuracy of surface reconstructions by comparing them to corresponding CT-derived models. This comparison relied on two quantitative metrics: the average residual error between the registered surface reconstructions and the CT models, and the average relative difference between the cross-sectional areas of the CT models and the reconstructions. The overarching goal of this evaluation was to determine whether their proposed reconstruction technique could serve as a viable, cost-effective, and radiation-free alternative to CT when calculating clinical parameters such as airway geometry. To align the models for comparison, the surface reconstructions were first registered to the CT models. This registration step ensured spatial correspondence between the two datasets. Once registered, the camera poses derived from Structure from Motion (SfM) were used as reference points to define the orientation and position of cross-sectional planes. By aligning these planes with the registered reconstructions, the researchers could compute cross-sectional areas at corresponding anatomical locations. The relative differences between the CT-derived and reconstructed areas along the entire camera trajectory were then averaged to produce the final statistical results. This evaluation was performed on seven video sequences collected from four individuals. The residual error after registration was measured at 0.69(±0.14) mm, which reflects the spatial misalignment between the models. As a benchmark, when sparse SfM reconstructions were directly registered to CT models, the residual error was slightly lower at 0.53(±0.24) mm, suggesting that denser reconstructions may not always reduce error. For cross-sectional area estimation, the average relative error was 7(±2) %, indicating a moderate deviation in area measurements. Notably, this error primarily arose from anatomical regions that were inadequately visualized during endoscopic imaging, such as the inferior, middle, and superior meatus. These regions are typically obscured by anatomical structures like turbinates during clinical inspections but were included in the automated analysis due to the algorithmic nature of the cross-sectional measurement process. In practice, these hidden regions are not routinely inspected clinically, but if precise quantification is required, minor adjustments to the endoscopic imaging protocol—such as optimizing camera angles—could enhance their visibility. The authors also note that their surface reconstructions can guide such adjustments, as the occupancy information in the fusion volume explicitly identifies areas that remain unvisualized in the endoscopic footage. This capability aligns with prior work, which demonstrates that 3D reconstructions can inform targeted imaging strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy.

new_text: To apply our uniqueness measure to cases, we first summarize all event data associated with each case, consolidating this information under its corresponding case identifier. This approach simplifies the analysis of cases involving multiple events, as it allows us to treat all events belonging to the same case as a unified unit. Importantly, since case-level attributes such as Sex and Age remain constant over time, they can be applied uniformly to all events within a case without requiring repeated processing. In contrast, event-level attributes such as Activity, Timestamp, and Arrival Channel may vary with each occurrence, necessitating a temporal analysis to capture how these attributes evolve. <Ref> illustrates this distinction through an example. In the provided table, each row represents a single case, with case attributes like Sex and Age stored as static values in dedicated columns. Meanwhile, event attributes are presented as ordered lists, capturing the sequence of activities, timestamps, and arrival channels for each event within the case. For instance, case ID 11 contains two events: the first and second activities occur on March 04, 2019, with the second activity labeled "Antibiotics." Notably, this second event lacks an associated Arrival Channel, as indicated by the value "None" in the corresponding column. This structure highlights how multiple event details are aggregated per case while maintaining the temporal dynamics of event-specific attributes.

**Privacy in process mining.** Awareness of privacy issues in process mining has increased <cit.>, particularly since the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) was put into effect. Although the Process Mining Manifesto <cit.> demands to balance utility and privacy in process mining applications, the number of related contributions is still rather small.
To preserve privacy in event logs while still discovering the correct main process behavior has been addressed by Fahrenkrog-Petersen et al. <cit.>. Their algorithm guarantees k-anonymity and t-closeness while maximizing the utility of the sanitized event log. In general, k-anonymity aggregates the data in such a way that each individual cannot be distinguished based on its values from at least k-1 other individuals of the data set <cit.>. Yet, it has been shown in the past that neither k-anonymity, nor t-closeness are sufficient to provide strong privacy guarantees <cit.>.
new_text: **Privacy in process mining.** Awareness of privacy issues in process mining has increased since GDPR enforcement <cit.>, emphasizing the need to balance utility and privacy per the Process Mining Manifesto <cit.>, though contributions remain limited. In this work, we propose a novel tracking architecture which can utilize scene information for tracking. Our tracker represents such information as dense localized state vectors, which can encode, for example, if the local region is target, background, or distractor. These state vectors are propagated through the sequence and combined with the appearance model output to localize the target. Our network is trained to maximize tracking performance directly by exploiting scene context in video segments. The method achieves a new state-of-the-art on three benchmarks, with an AO score of 63.6% on GOT-10k.

new_text: Existing methods rely on an appearance model to track the target object, but this approach struggles in scenarios with distractor objects. Appearance-based tracking fails to accurately localize the target even when the model is continuously refined with data from previous frames, as distractors confound visual similarity. Other studies use models developed to predict protein-ligand binding affinities in order to tackle the drug repurposing problem. Ligands are small molecules which bind with a protein to trigger a signal, which can be activation or inhibition. <cit.>use a multi-task neural network for the general prediction of these affinities. The authors identify a list of SARS-CoV-2 related proteins (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, 3C-like protease, papain-like protease, helicase, spike glycoprotein, exonuclease, endoRNAse, 2'-O-ribose methyltransferase, and envelope protein), which they attempt to target using a database of 4,895 drugs.
They suggest 10 promising drugs, along with their target proteins and binding affinity scores (which indicate the likelihood that the drug will act as an inhibitor). In an attempt to increase model interpretability, they also estimate the precise regions of each target protein where binding is likely to occur.
In a similar vein, <cit.>use their own Molecule Transformer-Drug Target Interaction (MT-DTI) model <cit.> of binding affinities to identify US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved antivirals which may be effective in targeting six coronavirus-related proteins (3C-like protease, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, helicase, 3'-to-5' exonuclease, endoRNAse, and 2'-O-ribose methyltransferase).
The MT-DTI model ingests string data in the form of simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) data and amino acid sequences, and applies a text-modeling approach that leverages ideas from the BERT algorithm <cit.>. The model identifies drugs that are expected to be effective in targeting each protein studied.
Finally, <cit.>use a dense fully connected neural network, trained to predict binding affinities on the PDBBind database, in order to identify potential inhibitors of the 3C-like protease. They develop a homology (template) model of the target protein using its SARS variant, and explore databases of existing compounds (e.g. ChemDiv and TargetMol) as well as tripeptides to find treatments which may be effective at targeting this protein.

The study highlights 10 potential drug candidates, specifying their target proteins and binding affinity scores (which reflect inhibitory potential), while also mapping protein regions likely involved in binding to improve model interpretability. Similarly, <cit.> employ their Molecule Transformer-Drug Target Interaction (MT-DTI) model—<cit.> which processes molecular and protein sequences using a text-modeling framework inspired by the BERT algorithm <cit.>—to screen FDA-approved antivirals against six coronavirus-related proteins (3C-like protease, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, helicase, 3'-to-5' exonuclease, endoRNAse, and 2'-O-ribose methyltransferase). Lastly, <cit.> apply a dense fully connected neural network trained on the PDBBind database to identify 3C-like protease inhibitors. old_text: It is often the case that different games benefit from different algorithm parameters. In particular, the individual length has a high impact in the performance of the vanilla RHEA, as shown in <cit.>. This was mainly tied to the density of rewards in the various games in <cit.>: games with dense rewards generally benefit from shorter individuals which would allow for more generations and more statistics gathered to facilitate quick strategic reactions; as opposed to games with sparse or no rewards, where longer individuals are required in order to be able to find those rewards further ahead. This difference in reward density can also be observed at a more granular level, during the play-through of only one game: some areas of the game may contain more rewards, whereas others would require more exploration. Therefore, the dynamic depth modification presented in <cit.> is included in the system, which has the option to change the length of the individuals at every 5 game ticks: if the standard deviation of the fitness landscape observed previously falls below a threshold (0.04), decisions are considered to be uncertain without much variety in rewards observed and the individual length is increased by 2; if the opposite happens and the fitness landscape observed previously raises above a threshold (0.9), more generations are prioritised for more informed decision making in a highly varied environment and the individual length is decreased by 2 instead. All parameters for dynamic length adjustments were set based on <cit.> and could represent one point for further increasing the parameter search space in further studies.
new_text: Different games often require varying algorithm parameters for optimal performance. Specifically, the individual length significantly affects the performance of the vanilla RHEA, as demonstrated in <cit.>. This is primarily due to differing reward densities across games in <cit.>: games featuring dense rewards typically perform better with shorter individuals, enabling more generations and accumulated statistical insights to support rapid strategic decisions, while games with sparse or absent rewards necessitate longer individuals to effectively locate distant rewards. Such variations in reward density can also occur within a single game’s environment, as certain areas may contain higher concentrations of rewards compared to others requiring more exploration. To address this, the system incorporates the dynamic depth modification proposed in <cit.>, which adjusts individual length every 5 game ticks based on the observed fitness landscape. If the standard deviation of prior fitness values drops below 0.04, indicating low variability and uncertain decisions, individual length increases by 2; conversely, if the standard deviation exceeds 0.9, reflecting high environmental diversity, individual length decreases by 2 to prioritize data-driven decisions over extended generations. All dynamic length adjustment parameters are derived from <cit.>, highlighting a potential avenue for expanding parameter search spaces in future research.

old_text: In this paper we revisit the application of game-playing Evolutionary Algorithms with a deeper analysis of algorithm modifications and hybrids. We further argue that automatic exploration of algorithm variations is essential for optimisation problems with large search spaces, although still not exhaustive due to computation speed limitations. There have been several recent advances in game-playing Evolutionary Algorithms <cit.> and a multitude of modifications and hybrids proposed to improve performance across a large number of games. The result of this is that the possibility space for algorithm parameters has grown beyond manual optimisation efficiency. Although preforming grid-search is sometimes possible for finding good values for some parameters <cit.>, more recent works find the need to reduce more and more the number of parameter combinations chosen for analysis <cit.>. Therefore, the interesting insights into which variation of the algorithm is actually the best are limited to human exploration of very small sections of the entirety of the search space.
new_text: In this paper, we re-examine the use of game-playing Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs), focusing on a more detailed analysis of modifications and hybrid approaches. A central argument is that automating the exploration of algorithm variations becomes critical for optimization tasks involving large search spaces. However, computational constraints prevent such methods from being fully exhaustive, even when employing automation. Recent advancements in game-playing EAs have led to numerous proposed modifications and hybrids aimed at enhancing performance across diverse games. These developments have dramatically expanded the parameter space of potential algorithm configurations, surpassing the feasibility of manual optimization strategies. While grid-search methods can occasionally identify effective parameter settings for specific cases, computational limitations increasingly force researchers to narrow the range of parameter combinations they analyze. This trend toward reducing the scope of tested variations means that valuable insights into the most effective algorithm configurations remain confined to limited subsets of the overall search space. Consequently, the ability to comprehensively determine optimal algorithmic approaches is hindered by the trade-off between computational resources and the ambition to explore the full breadth of possibilities.

Byzantine broadcast protocols with optimal good-case latency under weaker models.
To make the synchronous model more practical, we consider two types of additional faults suggested in the literature so that the synchrony bound need not hold for all messages and parties at all times.
The first type of faults, named mobile link failures <cit.>, assume a certain fraction of send and receive links can be down at each replica.
The second type of faults, named mobile sluggish faults <cit.>, model the slow connection of some honest replicas whose message sending and receiving does not respect the assumed delay bound Δ.
We develop Byzantine broadcast protocols with optimal good-case latency that can tolerate the above faults respectively.
The optimal good-case latency remains Δ with mobile sluggish faults and becomes 2Δ under mobile link failures by a new lower bound we prove.
new_text: This paper presents Byzantine broadcast protocols achieving optimal good-case latency in weakened synchronization models. To enhance the practicality of the synchronous model, we incorporate two fault types from existing literature, allowing the synchrony assumptions to not universally apply to all messages and participants. The first fault type, termed mobile link failures <cit.>, refers to scenarios where a specific proportion of send and receive links may be unavailable at each replica. The second, called mobile sluggish faults <cit.>, describes situations where certain honest replicas experience slowed communication, violating the standard delay bound Δ for message transmission and reception. Our protocols achieve optimal good-case latency while tolerating these fault models. Notably, the optimal latency remains Δ when dealing with mobile sluggish faults, but increases to 2Δ under mobile link failures, a result supported by a novel lower bound established in this work.

Our main result is that a better way to use transformers for code prediction is to expose the syntactic structure of code to the network. The details of how to do this are interesting, as encoding the structure of a program's abstract syntax tree is not natural for sequence models. We show a range of design choices for communicating the AST structure to the Transformer. We find that the more faithfully we communicate the tree structure to the Transformer, the better the accuracy we obtain!
new_text: Building on this strong baseline, we investigate whether informing the Transformer about code's syntactic structure can further enhance prediction accuracy. Our key finding is that exposing the syntactic structure of code to the Transformer provides a more effective approach for code prediction than traditional methods. This approach presents unique challenges, as encoding the structure of an abstract syntax tree (AST)—a hierarchical representation of code—is fundamentally at odds with the sequential processing paradigm of Transformer models. To address this, we explore various design choices for communicating the AST structure to the Transformer, ranging from structural annotations in input sequences to tree-aware attention mechanisms. Empirically, we observe a direct correlation between the fidelity of tree structure representation and the model's prediction accuracy: more precise encoding of the AST results in higher predictive performance.

This component might also implement other complex reasoning functionality, e.g., to generate explanations or to compute a query relaxation (see later). Besides these central components, typical CRS architectures comprise modules for input and output processing. These can, for example, include speech-to-text conversion and speech generation. A central component is the Dialogue Management System (also called “state tracker” or similarly in some systems), responsible for processing user actions, updating the dialogue state and preference profile, and deciding and executing the next action. The Recommendation and Reasoning Engine retrieves recommendations based on the dialogue state and preference model, and may also support complex reasoning tasks, such as generating explanations or computing query relaxation (see later). Additional typical components in CRS architectures include input/output processing modules, such as speech-to-text and speech generation. On the input side, especially for natural language, these often include intent detection and named entity recognition.

**Knowledge Elements.**
Various types of knowledge are used in CRS. The Item Database is something that is present in almost all solutions, representing the set of recommendable items, sometimes including details about their attributes. In addition to that, different types of Domain and Background Knowledge are often leveraged by CRS. Many approaches, for example, explicitly encode dialogue knowledge in different ways, e.g., in the form of pre-defined dialogue states, supported user intents, and the possible transitions between the states. This knowledge can be general or specific to a particular domain. The knowledge can furthermore either be encoded by the system designers or automatically learned from other sources or previous interactions. A typical example for learning approaches are those that use machine learning to build statistical models from corpora of recorded dialogues.
Generally, domain and background knowledge can be used by all computational elements. Input processing may need information about entities to be recognized or knowledge about the pre-defined intents. The user modeling component may be built on estimated interest weights regarding certain item features, and the reasoning engine may use explicit inference knowledge to derive the set of suitable recommendations.
new_text: Conversational recommendation systems (CRS) rely on multiple forms of knowledge. The Item Database, a component found in nearly all CRS implementations, contains the collection of recommendable items, often accompanied by attribute details. Additionally, CRS frequently utilize Domain and Background Knowledge. For instance, several methods incorporate structured dialogue knowledge through pre-defined dialogue states, recognized user intents, and state transition possibilities. This knowledge may apply broadly or be tailored to specific domains and can be either hard-coded by developers or automatically extracted from external sources or interaction data. A common approach involves training statistical models using machine learning algorithms on recorded dialogue datasets. Domain and background knowledge are integral to all core computational elements. Input processing may require entity recognition or intent classification based on predefined intents. User modeling can employ estimated preference weights for specific item features, while the reasoning engine might utilize formal inference rules to generate recommendation candidates.

old_text: To solve the first main issue, Deep Graph Kernels (DGK) <cit.> leverages techniques from natural language processing to learn latent representations for substructures. Then the similarity matrix between substructures is computed and integrated into the computation of the graph kernel matrix. If the number of substructures is high, it will cost a lot of time and memory to compute the similarity matrix. In addition, DGK uses natural language processing models to learn latent representations for substructures without proving that the frequency of substructures extracted from graphs follows a power-law distribution, which is observed in natural language. For example, the Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree kernel (WL) <cit.> decomposes graphs into subtree patterns and then counts the number of common subtree patterns across graphs. If the subtree is of depth zero (i.e., only one root vertex), we can represent it using the vertex degree. However, the vertex degree distribution of a graph does not always follow a power-law distribution. Thus, the learnt representations for substructures are not accurate. To solve the second main issue, people develop graph neural networks (GNNs) <cit.> to extract the higher-order information from graphs.
new_text: To address the first issue, Deep Graph Kernels (DGK) <cit.> apply natural language processing (NLP) techniques to generate latent representations of substructures, which are then used to compute a similarity matrix integrated into the graph kernel. High substructure counts increase time and memory costs for this matrix computation. DGK employs NLP models to learn these representations without verifying that substructure frequencies follow a power-law distribution—a pattern observed in natural language but not guaranteed in graph data. For example, the Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree kernel (WL) <cit.> decomposes graphs into subtree patterns, with depth-zero subtrees (single-rooted) represented by vertex degrees. However, vertex degree distributions in graphs do not universally exhibit power-law behavior, potentially leading to inaccurate substructure representations. To address the second issue, researchers employ graph neural networks (GNNs) <cit.> to extract higher-order graph information.

The instability in GAN training has been a long-standing problem despite remarkable research efforts. We identify that instability issues stem from difficulties of performing feature matching with mini-batch statistics, due to a fragile balance between the fixed target distribution and the progressively generated distribution. In this work, we propose Feature Quantization (FQ) for the discriminator, to embed both true and fake data samples into a shared discrete space. The quantized values of FQ are constructed as an evolving dictionary, which is consistent with feature statistics of the recent distribution history. Hence, FQ implicitly enables robust feature matching in a compact space.
new_text: The persistent instability in GAN training remains a significant challenge despite extensive research. Our analysis reveals that this instability arises from the inherent difficulties in feature matching using mini-batch statistics, resulting from a delicate equilibrium between the fixed target distribution and the incrementally updated generated distribution. To address this, we propose Feature Quantization (FQ) for the discriminator, which enables the embedding of both authentic and synthetic data samples into a unified discrete space. The quantized representations of FQ are organized into an evolving dictionary that aligns with feature statistics derived from the recent distribution history. This approach inherently facilitates stable feature matching within a compact, structured space.

new_text: The key reason these defenses fail is their reliance on generative models to completely eliminate adversarial perturbations. This requires the generator to perfectly capture the underlying data manifold. However, due to the limited capacity of existing generative (or non-generative) models, they often fail to efficiently represent the full data manifold and tend to over- or underestimate different modes of the underlying distribution. Further, the classifier used to classify these projected images typically remains adversarially vulnerable, as in the original model. Consequently, these approaches are either ineffective or fail to scale to complex image domains. To address these limitations, we employ an RBF layer to model the density of smaller input image patches. Graph kernels can be based on walks <cit.>, paths <cit.>, graphlets <cit.>, and subtree patterns <cit.>, etc. RetGK <cit.> introduces a structural role descriptor for vertices, i.e., the return probabilities features (RPF) generated by random walks. The RPF is then embedded into the Hilbert space where the corresponding graph kernels are derived. The shortest-path graph kernel (SP) <cit.> counts the number of pairs of shortest paths that have the same source and sink labels and the same length in two graphs. The Tree++ <cit.> graph kernel is proposed for the problem of comparing graphs at multiple levels of granularities. It first uses a path-pattern graph kernel to build a truncated BFS tree rooted at each vertex and then uses paths from the root to every vertex in the truncated BFS tree as features to represent graphs. To capture graph similarity at multiple levels of granularities, Tree++ incorporates a new concept called super path into the path-pattern graph kernel. The super path contains truncated BFS trees rooted at the vertices in a path. The graphlet kernel (GK) <cit.> proposes to use the method of random sampling to extract graphlets from graphs. The idea of random sampling is motivated by the observation that the more sufficient number of random samples is drawn, the closer the empirical distribution to the actual distribution of graphlets in a graph. The Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree kernel (WL) <cit.> is based on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test of graph isomorphism <cit.> for graphs. In each iteration, the Weisfeiler-Lehman test of graph isomorphism augments vertex labels by concatenating their neighbors' labels and then compressing the augmented labels into new labels. The compressed labels correspond to the subtree patterns. WL counts common original and compressed labels in two graphs.
new_text: Graph kernels can be constructed using walks <cit.>, paths <cit.>, graphlets <cit.>, and subtree patterns <cit.>, among other techniques. RetGK <cit.> introduces a structural role descriptor for nodes, specifically the return probability features (RPF) generated via random walks. These RPFs are embedded into a Hilbert space to derive corresponding graph kernels. The shortest-path graph kernel (SP) <cit.> quantifies pairs of shortest paths that share identical source and target node labels and path lengths in two graphs. The Tree++ <cit.> graph kernel is designed to compare graphs across varying levels of granularity by initially applying a path-pattern kernel. It constructs a truncated BFS tree rooted at each node and employs paths from the root to all nodes in the tree as graph features. To enhance multi-granular comparison, Tree++ integrates a "super path" concept, which encompasses truncated BFS trees rooted along vertices in a path. The graphlet kernel (GK) <cit.> utilizes random sampling to identify graphlets within graphs, motivated by the principle that increased sampling yields a distribution closer to the true graphlet distribution. The Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree kernel (WL) <cit.> derives from the Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test <cit.>. In each iteration, the test enriches node labels by aggregating neighboring labels and condenses them into new labels, representing subtree patterns. The WL kernel tallies matching original and condensed labels across two graphs.

Handling the geometrical relationship between camera and ground is also an effective approach to tackle this problem. This geometrical constrain is broadly used in autonomous driving tasks, for ground is commonly seen in images captured by on-board cameras. The main task of these methods is to estimate a relative camera height using camera-ground geometrical constrains, and thus infer scale with absolute camera height prior. <cit.> extracted ground using trained classifier, but it doesn't possess an excellent generalization power. <cit.> extracted the ground points densely in region of interest similar to <cit.>, but it requires dense stereo to be added to the system, which can potentially raise cost and increase complexity. In <cit.>, the most similar work to this one, used surface normal to extract ground points and thus calculate camera height. However, due to the sparsity originated in its key-point-based strategy, data association through consecutive frames are needed, makes this method hardly integrated into monocular depth estimation tasks which use only single image as input. In additon, this method regards the ground as a whole, flat panel with single surface normal, which is a strong assumption for autonomous driving scenarios. In contrast, our method is free of data association, which means it can be integrated into both monocular depth estimation and visual SLAM tasks. Furthermore, our method achieve per-pixel surface normal calculation and ground segmentation, makes the algorithm robust to different road conditions for autonomous driving.
new_text: Handling the geometrical relationship between the camera and the ground offers a practical strategy for addressing the problem of scale estimation in autonomous driving. This approach leverages the frequent presence of ground surfaces in on-board camera images, enabling the use of geometric constraints to infer the camera’s height relative to the ground. By combining this relative height with an absolute camera height prior (such as known vehicle height), these methods can derive accurate depth scaling. However, existing implementations face significant limitations. For example, one approach trains a classifier to extract ground regions, but its performance varies across diverse environments due to poor generalization. Another method identifies ground points densely within a region of interest, akin to previous techniques, but relies on dense stereo input, increasing hardware costs and system complexity. A related study, conceptually closest to this work, employs surface normals to detect ground points and estimate camera height. This method, however, relies on a keypoint-based strategy that produces sparse data, necessitating data association across consecutive frames—making it incompatible with monocular depth estimation systems that process single images. Additionally, it assumes the ground is a flat, uniform plane with a single surface normal, an oversimplification in dynamic driving scenarios where road surfaces may be uneven or obstructed. In contrast, our method eliminates the need for data association, enabling seamless integration into monocular depth estimation and visual SLAM tasks. It further computes per-pixel surface normals and ground segmentation, enhancing robustness to diverse road conditions such as potholes, slopes, or debris without violating geometric assumptions.

We assume the existence of a reinforcement learning algorithm for learning the optimal mapping 𝒮→𝒜. We use Q-Learning <cit.> for ease of explanation in this section, but similar arguments can be developed for policy and actor-critic based algorithms. Typically, the reward structure is a natural consequence of the problem from which the MDP was derived. For example, in the popular environment Gridworld <cit.>, the task is to navigate through a 2-D grid towards a goal state. The most common reward structure in this problem is to provide a small negative step reward for every action that does not end in the goal state, and a large positive terminal reward for reaching the goal state. Often, existing SPN-based device fingerprinting methods are working on the correlation between the noise residuals extracted from the images. The intra-class correlations (the correlations between noise residuals of images from the same source device) can be greatly affected by images' ISO speeds and the alignment operation used in multi-frame computational photography algorithms. Thus, insightful investigations are required to understand the problems behind and develop effective forensic methods accordingly. Image device fingerprinting is an important topic in multimedia forensics. It allows forensic investigators to establish an image's history, identify the source device and authenticate the content. Sensor Pattern Noise (SPN) <cit.>, as its name suggests, is a noise intrinsically embedded in images, primarily due to Photo Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU). Such an intrinsic property makes SPN a popular candidate for device fingerprinting and many researches are done on SPN-based source camera identification<cit.>, tampering localization <cit.> and source camera clustering <cit.>. Public datasets like Dresden Image Dataset <cit.> and VISION Image Dataset <cit.>, which can be used as benchmarking platforms, are very important for the study of device fingerprint analysis and the development of relevant techniques.
new_text: Image device fingerprinting serves as a critical technique in multimedia forensics, enabling forensic analysts to trace an image’s origin, determine the device that captured it, and verify its authenticity. A key component in this process is Sensor Pattern Noise (SPN), a subtle form of noise that is inherently present in digital images. SPN arises primarily from Photo Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU), a phenomenon caused by small, device-specific variations in the manufacturing of image sensors. These variations create a unique "fingerprint" that persists in images even after compression or other post-processing, making SPN an invaluable tool for identifying the source camera. Because this noise is intrinsic to the hardware, researchers have widely adopted SPN-based methods for tasks such as source camera identification, detecting tampered regions in images, and grouping images captured by the same device. To support these efforts, public datasets like the Dresden Image Dataset and the VISION Image Dataset provide standardized benchmarks for evaluating and refining device fingerprinting techniques. These datasets are essential for advancing the field, offering researchers a consistent framework to develop, test, and compare new forensic methodologies.

old_text: The main goal of this paper is to address the problem of concurrently occurring feature and label noise in the image classification task which, to the best of our knowledge, has not been considered in the existing literature. To this end, we propose five novel ensemble selection algorithms among which four are inspired by the local optimization algorithm derived from the TSP and one employs a stochastic search. Three out of five methods outperform the strong baseline reference algorithm that applies a set of individually selected best models (top/̄n). We have also empirically proven that a margin gained by the committees over the best single model rises along with an increase of both types of noise as well as with raising dataset difficulty, thus making proposed ensembles specifically well-suited to noisy images with noisy labels.
new_text: This paper addresses concurrent feature and label noise in image classification, a problem we are aware has not been previously addressed in the literature. We propose five novel ensemble selection algorithms: four inspired by TSP-derived local optimization and one using stochastic search. Three methods surpass the strong baseline that selects top/n models individually. Our empirical results show that the performance margin between ensembles and the best single model increases with higher noise levels and dataset difficulty, making the proposed ensembles particularly suitable for noisy images with noisy labels.

As shown in Theorem <ref> and discussed in <cit.>, liveness of types does not imply liveness of processes due to divergent conditional behavior in types and processes. In Theorem <ref>, we identify three classes of Go programs where liveness coincides. new_text: Adversarial perturbations can be crafted through two primary strategies: white-box and black-box attacks. In the extensively studied white-box setting <cit.>, the attacker has complete knowledge of the CNN architecture, the gradients of the loss function with respect to the target class label(s) and input image(s), and the model parameters of the system being attacked. By contrast, the less investigated black-box setting <cit.> restricts the attacker to observations of the target classifier’s decisions alone. Because black-box approaches <cit.> rely on no internal model information, their resulting perturbations tend to exhibit greater transferability compared to white-box attacks. Furthermore, black-box attacks are more practical in real-world applications, where model-specific information is often inaccessible.

old_text: Humor Theory Incongruity theory has an essential guiding position in the field of computational humor <cit.>. It believes that the inconsistency between the reader's expectation and the ending of one story is the key to humor generation. On this basis, SSTH (Script-based Semantic Theory of Humor) theory is proposed <cit.>. SSTH defines the structure of a joke as set-up and punchline. The set-up provides humorous context information, including multiple possible explanations (scripts). The punchline, usually at the end of a joke, points to a surprising explanation that triggers the humorous effect. According to this theory, we explore how to generate a punchline given the set-up sentence.
new_text: Incongruity theory serves as a foundational framework in computational humor research <cit.>, emphasizing that humor arises when a narrative’s outcome contradicts the reader’s expectations. This principle forms the basis for Script-based Semantic Theory of Humor (SSTH) <cit.>, a model that operationalizes the joke-creation process by structuring it into two key components: a setup and a punchline. The setup introduces contextual information that implicitly suggests multiple plausible interpretations—what SSTH refers to as "scripts"—to orient the listener. The punchline then disrupts this expectation by delivering a surprising, yet logically coherent, resolution that aligns with only one of these scripts, thereby creating the humor. By formalizing this structure, SSTH bridges the gap between abstract theoretical concepts (such as expectation violation) and practical joke construction. Applying this framework, the study focuses on developing methods to algorithmically generate a punchline that not only resolves the setup’s context but also strategically exploits the incongruity between anticipated and delivered outcomes to maximize comedic effect.

old_text: Probabilistic embeddings for actor-critic RL (PEARL) is a meta-learning algorithm that enables sample efficient meta-learning by reusing past data with off-policy RL algorithms <cit.>. The key idea is to condition the policy on the past transitions of the current task, which is termed the context c^τ_1:n. The context is encoded into a latent variable Z, and we train the policy π_θ(a|s,z). During meta-training PEARL learns the policy parameters and the inference network q_ϕ(z|c) which is factorized as q_ϕ(z|c_1:N)= ∏_n=1^N Ψ(z|c_n) and Ψ are Gaussian factors, resulting in a Gaussian posterior. The parameters θ and ϕ are learned with an off-policy algorithm that additionally learns a critic. At meta-test time, z ∼ q(z|c) is sampled before every rollout, and the new data is used to update the posterior.
