Using learned positional embeddings at the embedding layer in the Input Module is critical, as substituting fixed positional embeddings results in a 10.1 BLEU score drop at the same layer. Consistent gains are observed in Table <ref> and Table <ref> when additional fixed sinusoidal positional embeddings are added to the input of each transformer layer in the Input Module, even with an unfrozen BART. This may be because the Input Module, augmented with extra fixed embeddings, can more effectively accommodate variations in input language word order. Notably, a key advantage over mBART is the smaller target vocabulary size (section <ref>). These results are compared to those of mBART and baseline models in the following section.

section: Point cloud downsampling: A matrix optimization perspective
old_text: Caption: The flowchart of MOPS-Net, a matrix optimization inspired deep learning method for task-oriented 3D point cloud downsampling. After mapping an input point cloud (represented by a set 𝒫 or a matrix 𝐏) into a high dimensional space via a hierarchical feature extraction module as well as additional MLPs (γ(·)), we regress a differentiable sampling matrix 𝐒∈ℝ^n× m (m<n) via an MLP ρ(·). Multiplying 𝐒 to the high-dimensional representations of the input data Φ(𝐏) produces downsampled high-dimensional features Φ(𝐐), which are then projected to 3D space via the coordinate regression module Θ(·), generating sampled point cloud (𝒬 or 𝐐). MOPS-Net is permutation-invariant, which can be end-to-end trained together with a fixed task network. A joint loss, which considers both the performance of a specific task and the geometry of the sampled points, is used. A optional post-matching operation can be applied to ensure the downsampled set is a subset of the input set 𝒬⊂𝒫.
new_text: MOPS-Net is a matrix-optimization-inspired deep learning framework for task-driven 3D point cloud downsampling, as illustrated in the flowchart. The method begins by transforming the input point cloud (denoted as 𝒫 or 𝐏) into a high-dimensional space through a hierarchical feature extraction module and auxiliary MLPs (γ(·)). A differentiable sampling matrix 𝐒∈ℝ^n×m (m<n) is then regressed using an MLP ρ(·). This matrix is applied to the high-dimensional representations Φ(𝐏) of the input data, generating downsampled features Φ(𝐐). These features are subsequently mapped back to 3D space via a coordinate regression module Θ(·), resulting in the sampled point cloud (𝒬 or 𝐐). The architecture is permutation-invariant, enabling end-to-end training alongside a fixed task-specific network. A composite loss function evaluates both task performance and geometric fidelity of the sampled points. Optionally, a post-matching step ensures 𝒬⊂𝒫 by confirming the downsampled set is a subset of the original.

The current go-to method for solving classification tasks in NLP is to leverage deep neural networks pre-trained in a self-supervised fashion on a large amount of text. The dominant architecture is a transformer <cit.>, which is typically trained with a language modelling objective <cit.>.
Transfer to a task of interest is achieved by finetuning all the weights of the pretrained model on that single task, often yielding state-of-the-art results <cit.> . However, finetuning all the weights in this way can lead to learning instabilities on smaller datasets.
Additionally, each task of interest requires all the parameters of the network to be fine-tuned,
which results in a specialized model for each task. Since these models are separate from each other, the only possible transfer of information is from the underlying pre-trained model to the single task of interest — and not among multiple tasks.
new_text: The current standard approach for tackling classification tasks in natural language processing (NLP) involves using deep neural networks that have been pre-trained in a self-supervised manner on vast text corpora. These models are typically built on transformer architectures, which are trained using objectives like language modeling, where the model learns to predict masked or next tokens in a sequence. Once pre-trained, these models are adapted to specific downstream tasks by fine-tuning all their internal weights—adjusting parameters to align with the target task's data and requirements—often achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, this full-weight fine-tuning can become problematic when applied to smaller datasets, where the limited examples may cause unstable learning dynamics or overfitting, as the model's extensive parameters are forced to generalize from sparse information. Furthermore, this approach necessitates retraining the entire model for each individual task, resulting in a unique, task-specific model each time. Because these models operate independently, they do not share information during training, and the only knowledge transfer occurs unidirectionally—from the pre-trained weights to the specific task—without enabling cross-task interactions or parameter sharing. This architectural constraint limits the model's ability to leverage insights across related tasks, reinforcing a one-task-per-model paradigm rather than a more collaborative, multi-task learning framework.

Having described the VSA procedure for both meshes and point sets in the previous chapter, we now turn to our contributions for this pipeline. First, we will establish by an example that convergence of neither the meshed nor the point set version is guaranteed. new_text: Having described the VSA procedure for both meshes and point sets in the previous chapter, we now present our contributions to this pipeline. First, we demonstrate through an example that convergence of neither the mesh-based nor the point set version is guaranteed. We then propose an alternative formulation of the VSA algorithm with guaranteed convergence. Furthermore, we address a different aspect of the VSA procedure: its high dependence on both the number of initial seeds and their placement at the beginning. To circumvent this dependency, we add two additional operations to the point set pipeline that have been previously applied manually <cit.> and automatically <cit.> in the context of meshes.

Generative Model Accuracy
In addition to heuristic-specific accuracy scores, Figure <ref> also shows the accuracy of the aggregate decision produced by the generative label model. Human respondents tend to agree with the generative model most when the dilemma is between pets and humans (“Species") and when the dilemma is between saving more lives and saving fewer lives (“Utilitarian"). Notably, the accuracy of the heuristic model is highest for those scenarios with the highest effect sizes, as measured in the Moral Machine experiment <cit.>. In other words, the heuristic model tends to agree with human respondents when moral preferences about the scenario in question are strong. One other important observation about the performance of the heuristic functions is that for scenarios where many heuristics abstained (“Age," “Fitness," “Gender," “Social Status"), the resulting heuristic label matched human responses less often. There are two likely explanations for this phenomenon: first, the fact that accuracy tends to decrease with label density in general; second, the fact that fewer moral factors were involved in these scenarios, putting the burden of decision-making on only a few heuristics. The heuristic generative model tends to match human respondents more when a diverse set of heuristics are applicable.
new_text:
Generative Model Accuracy  
In addition to heuristic-specific accuracy scores, Figure <ref> illustrates the accuracy of the aggregate decision generated by the generative label model. Human respondents show the highest agreement with the generative model when dilemmas involve pets versus humans („Species“) or saving more versus fewer lives („Utilitarian“). Notably, the heuristic model’s accuracy peaks for scenarios with the highest effect sizes, as reported in the Moral Machine experiment <cit.>. This suggests the heuristic model aligns more closely with human respondents when moral preferences are strongly defined. Another key finding is that scenarios where many heuristics abstained („Age,“ „Fitness,“ „Gender,“ „Social Status“) yielded lower agreement between heuristic labels and human responses. This discrepancy can be attributed to two factors: first, accuracy generally declines with lower label density; second, fewer moral factors were present in these scenarios, shifting the decision-making burden to a limited subset of heuristics. The generative model demonstrates stronger alignment with human respondents when a diverse set of heuristics are applicable.

Inter-class separation
Anchor-based object detectors are often easy to be confused by hard negatives which may share similar image appearance with foregrounds <cit.>. In order to overcome this, the correction network should be more focusing on learning to distinguish hard negatives. However, merely oversampling hard negatives during training is not sufficient, since the efficacy of oversampling is highly relying on the availability of redundant training samples thus not feasible in the low-data regime, and training with the standard soft-max cross-entropy loss cannot introduce any extra margin to separate each class <cit.>. To further enhance inter-class discrepancy, in our work, a margin-based ranking loss is used to incorporate with previously mentioned cosine similarity metric.
new_text: Anchor-based object detectors frequently encounter difficulties when distinguishing hard negatives that visually resemble foreground objects <cit.>. To address this issue, the correction network must prioritize learning the differentiation of hard negatives. However, simply oversampling hard negatives during training proves inadequate. This is because the effectiveness of oversampling depends heavily on the presence of redundant training examples, which are scarce in low-data scenarios. Additionally, training using the standard softmax cross-entropy loss does not introduce additional margins to separate classes <cit.>. To further increase inter-class separation, our approach integrates a margin-based ranking loss with the previously discussed cosine similarity metric.

new_text: **Scalability.** First, we observe a clear advantage for approaches employing exact belief updates and object-oriented factoring, such as MR-POUCT, compared to alternatives relying on particle-based representations without such structuring. In the simulated domain, particle depletion occurs rapidly, leading the particle-based methods to degenerate into near-random performance, as documented in prior work <cit.>. However, in settings with smaller search spaces or fewer target objects—such as the (4,4,4) and (32,2,16) configurations—simpler methods like flat POUCT and MA-POUCT remain competitive with MR-POUCT. This suggests that problem complexity is a key determinant of performance: as the challenge increases, MR-POUCT consistently outperforms these baselines by a significant margin. Specifically, in harder settings with m=16 or m=32, MR-POUCT achieves an average improvement of 25% to 35% in cumulative reward. Our analysis of agent behavior attributes this superiority to MR-POUCT’s ability to generate more efficient search policies. For example, experiments reveal that using action abstraction alone—without a resolution hierarchy—results in agents overly reliant on *MoveOp* actions while neglecting critical *Look* actions, which are essential for observing the environment. This imbalance leads to suboptimal exploration and reduced reward. In contrast, MR-POUCT’s combination of state and observation abstraction via octree belief structures avoids this pitfall. Additionally, MR-POUCT systematically identifies more target objects than baselines as the problem scales, demonstrating robustness under increasing difficulty. The (32,·,16) class of problems, in particular, proves challenging for all approaches due to its sparse observation geometry: each viewing frustum captures only 2% of the environment, severely limiting the efficiency of any search strategy.

Once we have a solution for the K-Backup-Placement problem, we turn to a more channeling task of allocating virtual memory for nodes in wireless networks. Here the goal is partitioning the node set into classes, and obtain a scheduling in which each class is active at a time and can make use of memories of other classes that are inactive in that time. The challenge here is coming up with the right trade-off between the number of classes (that needs to be small) and the size of the virtual memory (that becomes larger as the number of classes increase). To obtain the desired balance we compute a certain coloring in which all vertices of the same color class have considerable amount of virtual memory, while keeping the number of classes sufficiently small.
new_text: Following a solution to the K-Backup-Placement problem, we address the allocation of virtual memory for nodes in wireless networks, framed as a channeling task. The objective here involves partitioning the node set into classes and establishing a schedule where each class is active in turn, allowing it to leverage the virtual memory of inactive classes during its active period. The critical challenge lies in navigating the trade-off between minimizing the number of classes (to ensure efficiency) and the resulting increase in virtual memory size (which scales with the number of classes). To achieve an optimal balance, we employ a specific coloring strategy, ensuring that all vertices within the same color class possess substantial virtual memory while maintaining the number of classes within a manageable limit.

These are comprised of cylinders of varying size, filled with a large number of holes. The volumes were generated at a resolution of 1024^3 before trilinearly downsampling (to prevent aliasing artifacts). At a resolution of 512^3, a reconstruction using filtered backpropjection (FBP) of a strongly undersampled parallel-beam CT projection with Poisson noise was created. A diagonal axis of the volume served as the CT axis (perturbed by angular noise). We expect the varying size of the phantoms, the artifacts on the FBP reconstructions as well as the large-scale bubble structures to favor networks with a large, three-dimensional receptive field (i.e. many downsampling operations), which justifies the use of 3D iUNets and 3D U-Nets. The FBP reconstructions as well as the ground truth volumes were downsized to 256^3. Both 3D U-Nets as well as 3D iUNets were subsequently trained to retrieve the ground truth from the FBP reconstructions using the squared ℓ_2-loss. The peak signal-to-noise-ratios (PSNR) as well as the structural similarity indices (SSIM) of this experiment cohort are compiled in Table <ref>. Each line represents one classic 3D U-Net and one 3D iUNet of comparable size. While there is no way to construct perfectly comparable instances of both, the 3D U-Net uses 2 convolutional layers before downsampling (respectively after upsampling), whereas the 3D iUNet employs 4 additive coupling layers (each acting on half of the channels). In the case of the classic U-Net, 'channel blowup' indicates the number of channels before the first downsampling operation (identical to the number of output feature maps before reducing to one feature map again). In both architectures, layer normalisation was applied. The batch size was 1 in all cases, because for the larger models this was the maximum applicable batch size due to the large memory demand. Random flips and rotations were applied for data augmentation.As indicated the table, even the worst-performing iUNet performed considerably better than the best-performing classic U-Net, both in terms of PSNR but especially in terms of SSIM. While both model classes benefitted from an increased channel blowup, only the invertible U-Net benefits from raising the number of scales from 4 to 8 (at which point the receptive field spans the whole volume). The fact that the classic U-Net drops in performance despite a higher model capacity may indicate that the optimisation is more problematic in this case. The invertible U-Net shows one of its advantages in this application: By initializing the layer normalisation as the zero-mapping in each coupling block, the whole iUNet was initialised as the identity function. At initialisation, each convolutional layer's input is thus a part of the whole model input (up to an orthogonal transform). Since the optimal function for learned post-processing can be expected to be close to the identity function, we assume that this initialisation is well-suited for this task. We further used the memory-efficiency of the invertible U-Net to double the channel blowup compared to the largest classic U-Net that we were able to fit into memory. This brought further performance improvements, showing that a higher model capacity can aid in such tasks.In Figure <ref>, a test sample processed by the best-perfoming classic iUNet as well as classic U-Net are shown, along with the ground truth and the FBP reconstruction. Apart from the overall lower noise level, the iUNet is able to discern neighbouring holes from one another much better than the classic U-Net. Moreover, in this example a hole that is occluded by noise in the FBP reconstruction does not seem to be recognised as such by the classic U-Net, but is well-differentiated by the iUNet.
new_text: The experiment evaluated invertible U-Nets (iUNets) in a high-dimensional 3D CT post-processing task on 3D reconstructions with large-scale undersampling artifacts. Artificial 3D 'foam phantoms' (<cit.>) were generated: 180 training and 20 test volumes, each comprising cylinders with holes. Volumes were initially generated at 1024³ resolution, trilinearly downsampled to 512³ to prevent aliasing, then reconstructed using filtered backprojection (FBP) with undersampled parallel-beam CT projections and Poisson noise. The CT axis aligned with a diagonal (perturbed by angular noise). Large phantom variation, FBP artifacts, and 3D bubble structures favor models with extensive 3D receptive fields, justifying the use of 3D iUNets and U-Nets. FBP and ground truth volumes were further downsampled to 256³. Both 3D U-Nets and iUNets were trained to restore ground truth from FBP reconstructions using squared ℓ₂-loss, with PSNR and SSIM results reported in Table <ref>. Each row compares a U-Net and iUNet of similar size. The U-Net used 2 convolutional layers per downsampling/upscaling stage, while the iUNet employed 4 additive coupling layers (each operating on half-channels). 'Channel blowup' denotes initial channel count in the U-Net (matching feature map counts before final downscaling). Both models used layer normalization, trained with batch size 1 due to memory constraints. Data augmentation included random flips and rotations. As shown, the worst iUNet outperformed the best U-Net in PSNR and SSIM, particularly in SSIM. While both benefited from higher channel blowup, only the iUNet improved with 8 vs. 4 scales (full-volume receptive field). Classic U-Nets degraded with increased capacity, suggesting optimization challenges. The iUNet’s identity initialization via zero-mapping layer normalization ensured inputs aligned with model inputs (up to orthogonal transforms), advantageous for identity-near post-processing. Memory efficiency allowed doubling channel blowup compared to the largest U-Net, further enhancing performance. Figure <ref> compares best-performing iUNet and U-Net outputs: the iUNet resolved adjacent holes better and identified noise-occluded holes missed by the U-Net.

We believe, moreover, that it is an important advantage of our approach that it is inspectable to a much greater extent than many of its competitors. In particular, it is possible to inspect what words (fragments) correspond to what placeholders, and to change them to modify the behaviour of the system if this is desired; similarly, it is possible to scrutinise the set of schemas, and to modify one or more schemas in light of new evidence.
After training, what TRG model learns is the generation rules – the schemas and fragments, which could still be easily modified by human users. Through reading the schemas and fragments, human users can generally understand what sentences the rules result. If particular sentences should be generated or be avoid to generate, manually adding or removing the relative schemas and fragments is enough to do so.
A lack of inspectability is often cited as one of the main drawbacks of approaches based on Neural Networks <cit.>. After training, what the neural-network-based approaches learn is massive weights of matrices. Human users cannot trace what particular sentences can be generated according to the matrices. Consequently, to modify a trained approach is impossible.
new_text: We argue that a significant benefit of our approach lies in its high degree of inspectability, which surpasses that of many competing methods. This inspectability allows users to examine and adjust the system’s core components directly. Specifically, users can identify the mappings between word fragments (such as partial phrases or tokens) and their corresponding placeholders within the model, enabling targeted modifications to influence system behavior when necessary. Similarly, users can review the entire set of schemas—structured templates that define how sentences are generated—and alter them in response to new data or evolving requirements. For instance, if certain outputs should be avoided or encouraged, the relevant schemas and fragments can be manually adjusted or removed. This contrasts with neural network-based approaches, where inspectability is notably limited. After training, such models typically produce a complex web of matrix weights that encode patterns within the data, but these weights are not interpretable to humans in terms of linguistic rules or structures. As a result, users cannot determine which sentences the model might generate based on these weights, nor can they modify the system’s behavior without retraining the entire model—a process that is often impractical or impossible once deployment has occurred. The lack of transparency in neural network methods thus represents a critical limitation when compared to systems that offer human-readable, modifiable components like those in our approach.

old_text: We use a classic example to illustrate our framework: a perforated strip subjected to uniaxial extension <cit.>. Consider a plate of dimensions 200 mm×360 mm, with a circular hole of diameter 100 mm located in the center of the plate. The plate is subjected to extension displacements of δ=1 mm along the short edge, under plane-strain condition, and without body forces, f_i=0. The parameters are λ=19.44 GPa, μ=29.17 GPa and σ_Y=243.0 MPa. Due to symmetry, only a quarter of the domain needs to be considered in the simulation. The synthetic data is generated from a high-fidelity FEM simulation using COMSOL software <cit.> on a mesh of approximately 13,000 quartic triangular elements. old_text: In this work, we describe an Intent Mining framework that reduces the labeling effort significantly by using two sources of information - the metadata/ short description about conversations and the conversations themselves (Refer to Table 1 for a sample conversation in the helpdesk scenario). In cases where raw conversations are presented without any metadata, we have experimented with different approaches to extract suitable description for representing the summary/ short description of a conversation. We have discussed about feature engineering approaches, such as learning domain word embedding from the conversation data, converting textual description to feature vector using learned word embedding and also , extracting domain independent user's intent from conversations using a Dialog Act Classifier <cit.>. We have also experimented with pre-trained language model (Universal Sentence Encoder <cit.>) for sentence representation. We have used the textual descriptions to cluster conversations into unique groups, using a density-based clustering approach (discussed in section 3.2). Clusters are labeled to generate seed data for each intent. Features extracted from the labeled conversations along with intent labels are used to generate training data and train a statistical classifier. Unlabeled conversations are then labeled by the base classifier basis a cut-off confidence score of the model. The final training set can be used to train any supervised classification algorithm. We show that an intent model trained in this manner works with good efficacy and provides a good coverage of intents. We have also experimented and reported the accuracy of our algorithm on open source intent classification dataset and as well as on short text classification dataset.
new_text: In this work, we describe an Intent Mining framework that reduces the labeling effort substantially by using two sources of information: the metadata or short description about conversations and the conversations themselves (Refer to Table 1 for a sample conversation in the helpdesk scenario). In cases where raw conversations are presented without any metadata, we have experimented with approaches to generate descriptive summaries for representing a conversation's content. We have discussed feature engineering approaches, such as learning domain-specific word embeddings from the conversation data, converting textual descriptions into feature vectors using the learned embeddings, extracting domain-independent user intent from conversations via a Dialog Act Classifier <cit.>, and experimenting with pre-trained language models (e.g., Universal Sentence Encoder <cit.>) for sentence representation. We have used textual descriptions to cluster conversations into distinct groups using a density-based clustering approach (discussed in Section 3.2). Clusters are labeled to generate seed data for each intent. Features extracted from labeled conversations, combined with intent labels, are used to construct training data and train a statistical classifier. Unlabeled conversations are then labeled by the base classifier based on a cutoff confidence score of the model. The final training set can be used to train any supervised classification algorithm. We demonstrate that an intent model trained in this manner achieves effective performance and provides comprehensive coverage of intents. We have also experimented with and reported the accuracy of our algorithm on open-source intent classification datasets and short text classification datasets.

We have presented a dynamic adaptive cruise control system (D-ACC) that is designed to adjust the headway distance adaptively based on reinforcement learning in response to dynamically changing traffic conditions for highways with on-ramps. We demonstrated that D-ACC improves traffic flow significantly even with a small penetration rate compared with a state-of-the-art ACC system especially for highways with merging traffic. The broader impact of D-ACC is noteworthy due to its immediate applicability to real-world vehicles by a simple firmware update for existing ACC systems and availability of V2X based on a smartphone which can be connected to the vehicle's ACC system via the OBD port. Our future work is to implement the system for an actual vehicle platform and evaluate the performance in real-world traffic environments.
new_text: We present a dynamic adaptive cruise control system (D-ACC) that adjusts headway distance adaptively via reinforcement learning for highways with on-ramps and dynamically changing traffic. D-ACC significantly improves traffic flow even at low penetration rates compared to state-of-the-art ACC systems, particularly in merging traffic scenarios. Its broader impact is notable due to immediate real-world applicability through firmware updates for existing ACC systems and smartphone-based V2X connectivity via the OBD port. Future work involves implementing the system on a vehicle platform to evaluate real-world traffic performance.

old_text: Tracking an unknown target captured from medium- or high-aerial view is challenging, especially in scenarios of small objects, large viewpoint change, drastic camera motion, and high density. This paper introduces a context-aware IoU-guided tracker that exploits an offline reference proposal generation strategy and a multitask two-stream network. The proposed strategy introduces an efficient sampling strategy to generalize the network on the target and its parts without imposing extra computational complexity during online tracking. It considerably helps the proposed tracker, COMET, to handle occlusion and view-point change, where only some parts of the target are visible. Extensive experimental evaluations on broad range of small object benchmarks (UAVDT, VisDrone-2019, and Small-90) demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for small object tracking.
new_text: Tracking an unknown target captured from medium- or high-altitude aerial perspectives presents significant challenges, particularly when dealing with small objects, abrupt changes in viewing angles, rapid camera movements, and high target density. These factors collectively complicate accurate and consistent tracking, as the target’s appearance can vary drastically or become partially obscured. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel tracking framework, COMET, which integrates a context-aware intersection-over-union (IoU) guided approach with a two-stream multitask network. A key component of the method is an offline reference proposal generation strategy, which proactively samples candidate regions during preprocessing to capture the target and its contextual components. This strategy avoids the need for additional computations during online tracking, ensuring efficiency while enabling the model to generalize across varying target configurations. By leveraging these precomputed references, COMET becomes more robust to occlusion and viewpoint changes—scenarios where only parts of the target remain visible—since the network can rely on learned representations of both the target and its surrounding context. Experimental validation on diverse small-object tracking benchmarks (UAVDT, VisDrone-2019, and Small-90) confirms the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating superior performance in maintaining tracking accuracy under challenging real-world conditions.

The wireless repeater was invented by Guarini-Foresio in 1899 and advanced relaying technology, capable of improving the conditions of radio environments, has been included in cellular standards since 3G <cit.>.
The term cooperative communications is broadly used to refer to network architectures containing entities between the transmitter and receiver that enhance the physical channel, by exploiting diversity, beamforming, and/or multiplexing gains. These entities are co-optimized with the transmitter and receiver, thus satisfying the definition of controllable radio environments.
Two main categories are transparent relaying and regenerative relaying.
In the former category, each relay is an entity that receives a signal from the transmitter and processes it in analog (or digitally) before re-radiating it towards the receiver. Amplify-and-forward is a classic protocol for creating additional signal paths by re-radiating an amplified signal in a way that can be transparent to the receiver. No baseband processing is required, only amplification. In regenerative relaying, each relay is decoding the received signal and processes it in the digital baseband, before retransmitting it in an optimized manner towards the receiver. Decode-and-forward (DF) is a common example.
Classical relays operate in half-duplex mode, where reception and retransmission are separated in time, but full-duplex relays capable of receiving and transmitting simultaneously are emerging.

An RIS is a thin surface composed of N elements, each being a reconfigurable scatterer: a small antenna that receives and re-radiates without amplification, but with a configurable time-delay <cit.>.
For narrowband signals, this delay corresponds to a phase-shift.
Assuming the phase-shifts are properly adjusted, the N scattered waves will add constructively at the receiver. This principle resembles that of traditional beamforming: each element has a fixed radiation pattern but the collection of phase-shifts determines where constructive interference among the scattered waves occurs. The color pattern at the RIS in Fig. <ref> represents the phase-shifts necessary to steer a beam towards the receiver. Each element is substantially smaller than the wavelength (e.g., a fifth of the wavelength in each direction <cit.>) so it scatters signals almost uniformly, giving the surface the ability to form equally strong beams in any direction.

old_text: Biology and Medicine: Our method has the potential to directly impact research on biological sequence analysis by enabling the Transformer to be applied to much longer sequences without constraints on the structure of the attention matrix. The initial application that we consider is the prediction of interactions between proteins on the proteome scale. Recently published approaches require large evolutionary sequence alignments, a bottleneck for applications to mammalian genomes <cit.>. The potentially broad translational impact of applying these approaches to biological sequences was one of the main motivations of this work. We believe that modern bioinformatics can immensely benefit from new machine learning techniques with Transformers being among the most promising. Scaling up these methods to train faster more accurate language models opens the door to the ability to design sets of molecules with pre-specified interaction properties. These approaches could be used to augment existing physics-based design strategies that are of critical importance for example in the development of new nanoparticle vaccines <cit.>.
new_text: The method we present has significant implications for biological sequence analysis in the life sciences by addressing a key limitation of Transformer models: their inability to efficiently process long sequences due to structural constraints on the attention mechanism. Traditional Transformer architectures require pairwise comparisons between all tokens in a sequence, leading to computational challenges when scaling to large inputs. Our approach enables the application of Transformers to much longer biological sequences without compromising the integrity of attention computations, thereby broadening their utility in genomics and proteomics. As a proof of concept, we focus on predicting protein-protein interactions at the proteome scale, a critical problem in systems biology. Current methodologies for this task rely on large evolutionary sequence alignments to infer interaction patterns, a requirement that limits their applicability to mammalian genomes where such data is often sparse <cit.>. By overcoming this bottleneck, our framework supports the development of more scalable and accurate models for biological sequence analysis. The translational potential of this work is substantial, as integrating advanced machine learning techniques like Transformers into bioinformatics pipelines can accelerate the discovery of molecular interactions. In particular, improving the efficiency and accuracy of these models could enable the design of molecules with precisely defined interaction properties, complementing existing physics-based approaches. Such advancements are especially valuable in biomedical engineering applications, such as the design of nanoparticle vaccines, where hybrid strategies combining computational modeling and empirical design principles are essential <cit.>.

The CTM component of the BDM approximation is computed using Turing machines that run on a 2-dimensional tape and produce arrays rather than strings. The BDM approximation of the graph's Kolmogorov complexity BDM_(n,2)(𝐀) is computed over a partition of 𝐀 into block matrices small enough to have a CTM value (for a more explicit formulation please see Section <ref>). Using the adjacency matrix as the descriptor of a graph introduces a potential challenge as adjacency matrices corresponding to isomorphic graphs can have different Kolmogorov complexity. old_text: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) <cit.> shows competitive performance compared with best model-free reinforcement learning (MFRL) algorithms <cit.> with significantly fewer environment samples on challenging robotics locomotion benchmarks <cit.>. MFRL algorithms learns complex skills by maximizing a scalar reward designed by human engineering. However its promising performance requires large amounts of environment interactions, that may take a long time in real-world applications. In such a case, MBRL is appealing due to its superior sample efficiency that relies on the generalization of a learned predictive dynamics model. However, the quality of the policy trained on imagined trajectories is often worse asymptotically than the best MFRL counterparts due to the imperfect models.
new_text: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) <cit.> demonstrates performance comparable to state-of-the-art model-free reinforcement learning (MFRL) algorithms <cit.> while requiring far fewer interactions with the environment, particularly in complex robotics locomotion tasks <cit.>. MFRL methods achieve skill acquisition by optimizing a scalar reward signal designed through human engineering. The efficacy of these methods, however, depends heavily on extensive exploration of the environment, a process that can be prohibitively time-consuming in real-world deployment scenarios. This challenge highlights the advantages of MBRL, which leverages a learned predictive model of the environment to reduce sample complexity. By simulating interactions through the model, MBRL avoids exhaustive real-world trials, making it more practical for applications where data collection is costly or slow. Nevertheless, a key limitation of MBRL arises from the inherent inaccuracies of learned dynamics models. Policies trained using these imperfect models often fail to match the asymptotic performance of their MFRL counterparts, as errors in simulated trajectories compound over time and degrade learning outcomes. This trade-off between sample efficiency and final policy performance remains a central challenge in MBRL research.

Biases in VQA datasets
The success of these works is in part due to the creation of large annotated VQA corpus. The VQAv1 <cit.> dataset gathers more than 200k real-world images annotated with 760K questions in natural language. Moreover, each question is annotated with 10 ground truth answers in order to model the ambiguity and the disagreement between annotators. Nevertheless, as the data collection is fastidious and costly, VQAv1 suffers from numerous language biases as pointed out by many works such as <cit.>, and  <cit.>.
In order to downplay the influence of the language bias, <cit.> released an updated version of the same dataset (baptized VQAv2) by carefully balancing the answer distribution per question type.
<cit.> went one step further by designing a fully synthetic dataset called CLEVR in which automatically generated questions are asked on synthetically generated 3D images. This corpus is thought as a diagnostic dataset aimed at evaluating the visual reasoning capability of the models.
However, the limited environment of CLEVR <cit.> prevents from generalizing to complex realistic images such as in VQAv2 <cit.>.
Finally, <cit.> built the GQA dataset, a semi-synthetic dataset where automatically generated questions are asked on real images, which can be seen as an intermediate step between CLEVR and VQAv2.
new_text: The success of these works arises from the creation of a large annotated VQA corpus. VQAv1 <cit.> comprises 200k real-world images annotated with 760k natural language questions, each paired with 10 ground truth answers to model ambiguity and inter-annotator disagreement. However, due to labor-intensive and costly data collection, VQAv1 exhibits language biases identified by <cit.> and <cit.>. To reduce language bias, <cit.> introduced VQAv2, balancing answer distributions per question type. <cit.> developed the fully synthetic CLEVR dataset with auto-generated questions on 3D images, designed to evaluate visual reasoning capabilities. However, CLEVR’s limited environment <cit.> prevents generalization to complex real-world images like those in VQAv2. <cit.> created the GQA semi-synthetic dataset, using auto-generated questions on real images, positioned as an intermediate step between CLEVR and VQAv2.

Impact on VQAv2 dataset As discussed before, the VQAv2-CP dataset has been proposed by  <cit.> with the goal to evaluate the performance of VQA models in a condition where they cannot fully rely on question biases.
Indeed, as shown in <cit.>, the original VQAv2 <cit.> dataset contains numerous question biases (e.g. the question what color is the banana in the picture can be correctly answered as yellow without even analyzing the picture in VQAv2).
At the same time, it is very important to verify that our semantic loss, which is effective for training VQA models on the unbiased VQAv2-CP dataset, does not hinder the model's performances when the training is done on the biased VQAv2 dataset.
new_text: Building upon prior discussions, the VQAv2-CP dataset was introduced to assess VQA models under conditions where question biases cannot be exploited. As demonstrated in <cit.>, the original VQAv2 dataset <cit.> contains inherent question biases that allow models to bypass image analysis in some cases. For instance, a question like "What color is the banana in the picture?" can be answered correctly as "yellow" without referencing the image, solely based on common knowledge or language patterns. Such biases skew evaluations, as models can achieve high performance by relying on shortcuts rather than developing robust visual understanding. This highlights the need for datasets like VQAv2-CP, which remove such biases to enforce genuine multimodal reasoning. However, it is critical to evaluate whether techniques effective in these unbiased settings—such as the proposed semantic loss—might negatively affect model performance when applied to the biased VQAv2 dataset. After all, if a method improves accuracy in unbiased scenarios, it should not compromise performance in standard, bias-rich benchmarks. Verifying this compatibility ensures the semantic loss remains a broadly applicable tool, bridging both evaluation contexts without unintended trade-offs.

**Related work —.** A detailed description of the whole
trajectory taken by the (stochastic) gradient descent was so far
obtained only in several special cases. First such case are deep
linear networks where the dynamics of gradient descent has been
analyzed <cit.>. While this line of works have led to very
interesting insights about the dynamics, linear networks lack the
expressivity of the non-linear ones and the large time behavior of the
algorithm can be obtained with a simple spectral algorithm. Moreover,
the analysis of dynamics in deep linear networks was not extended to
the case of stochastic gradient descent. Second case where the
trajectory of the algorithm was understood in detail is the
one-pass (online) stochastic gradient descent for two-layer
neural networks with a small hidden layer in the teacher-student
setting <cit.>. However, the one-pass assumption done
in those analyses is far from what is done in practice and is unable
to access the subtle difference between the training and test error
that leads to many of the empirical mysteries observed in deep
learning. A third very interesting line of research that recently
provided insight about the behavior of stochastic gradient descent
concerns two layer networks with divergingly wide hidden layer. This
mean-field limit <cit.> maps
the dynamics into the space of functions where its description is
simpler and the dynamics can be written in terms of a closed set of
differential equations. It is not clear yet
whether this analysis can be extended in a sufficiently explicit way
to deeper or finite width neural networks.
new_text: Detailed analysis of the full trajectory of (stochastic) gradient descent has been achieved only in specific scenarios. First, deep linear networks have seen gradient descent dynamics analyzed <cit.>. However, linear networks lack the expressivity of nonlinear ones, and their long-term behavior is tractable via spectral methods. Additionally, these analyses haven’t extended to SGD. Second, one-pass online SGD for two-layer networks with small hidden layers in teacher-student settings <cit.> has been studied. However, this one-pass assumption deviates from practical settings and overlooks subtleties between training and test errors critical to deep learning phenomena. Third, recent work on two-layer networks with divergently wide hidden layers uses a mean-field limit <cit.>, reformulating dynamics in function space via closed differential equations. However, applicability to deeper or finite-width networks remains unclear.

old_text: Attention compute the dependency between representations, and it encourages the model to focus on the important selective features. Among the attention methods, the scaled dot-product attention is widely utilized in many models. This paper suggests a generalized structure of the scaled dot-product attention with similarity and magnitude terms. We derive that the scaled dot-product attention is a product of two parts: 1) the RBF kernel to measure the similarity of two instances and 2) the exponential L^2 norm to compute the importance of individual instances. From this decomposition, we improve the attention in two ways: implicit modeling on the kernel spectral density and generalized L^p norm, which results in a learnable and flexible attention structure. First, we estimate the spectral density of kernel with implicit probabilistic models to estimate the appropriate kernel for a given dataset without kernel selection manually. Second, we introduce a generalized L^p norm on the hidden feature space, where p is a hyper-parameter that affects the scale of individual importance and the sparsity of attention weights. Also, we show how to expand this implicit kernel modeling to multi-head attention in conjunction with a copula augmentation. Our generalized attention shows better performance on text classification, translation, regression, and node classification tasks.
new_text: Attention computes dependencies between representations, enabling models to focus on key features. Among these methods, scaled dot-product attention is widely used. This paper proposes a generalized structure of scaled dot-product attention by incorporating similarity and magnitude terms. Our analysis shows the scaled dot-product attention decomposes into two components: 1) an RBF kernel to measure instance similarity and 2) an exponential L² norm to assess individual instance importance. To improve attention, we introduce two modifications: implicit modeling of kernel spectral density via probabilistic models and a generalized L^p norm in the hidden feature space, where p is a hyper-parameter influencing weight sparsity and feature importance scaling. First, we estimate kernel spectral density implicitly, avoiding manual kernel selection. Second, the generalized L^p norm enables flexible feature weighting. We further extend this framework to multi-head attention with copula augmentation. The resulting generalized attention demonstrates improved performance in text classification, translation, regression, and node classification tasks.

old_text: **Toy Data.** In order to explore the biomolecular embedding properties of the GSAE framework, we first compare the model on a toy dataset. The toy dataset is generated by starting with a randomly generated Erdos-Renyi (ER) graph containing 10 nodes, with edge probability p=0.5. Then for 9999 steps, we randomly chose an edge to remove or add to the previous graph in sequence. This generates a sequence of 10000 graphs that should roughly form single trajectory based on graph edit distance. These toy graphs are visualized in Figure <ref>. We visualize these embeddings in two different ways, with PHATE <cit.> a non-linear visualization reduction method that keeps local and global structure, as well as PCA. We see that only the GSAE uncovers the linear trajectory of the graph indicating that simple embedding of edit distances, WL kernels and other graph autoencoders do not uncover the trajectory as well. Further, we quantify the structure in these embeddings in Table <ref> by computing the graph dirichlet energy of the signal formed by the sequence index, i.e., the signal f=[0, 1, …, 10000] with Laplacian matrix of each embedding f^T Lf. Lower values indicate more smoothness. We see in Table <ref> that aside from a direct embedding of the graph edit distance, GSAE has the best smoothness. However, note that in general graph edit distances are very expensive to compute and cannot be trained to predict meta-properties as we desire in biomolecules.

and reason about the behavior of the feed-back loop, i.e., the output of the OR

new_text: Intuitively, we analyze the impact of a pulse with duration Δ₀ initiated at time 0 at the input and examine the dynamics of the feedback loop, specifically the output from the OR gate. Three scenarios arise: when Δ₀ is small, the pulse is suppressed by the channel within the feedback loop. When Δ₀ exceeds a threshold, the pulse is retained by the storage loop, resulting in a stable output of 1. For intermediate Δ₀ values, the storage loop may enter a persistent oscillatory state. Despite these variations, an appropriately designed exponential channel can effectively map this complex behavior into a valid SPF output.

Flush+Reload <cit.> is a popular
type of cache attacks. When a victim process and a concurrent attacker
process load the same shared library or a file, a single set of physical
memory addresses containing the file's content is mapped into both
processes' virtual address space. In this situation, the attacker can (1)
cause the eviction of a specific memory address (“flush”), (2) wait,
and (3) reload this memory address. Short reload time reveals that the
victim has accessed this address after the eviction but before the load.
If memory addresses monitored by the attacker do not contain shared

new_text: Flush+Reload <cit.> is a common variant of cache side-channel attacks. When a victim process and a simultaneously running malicious process load the same shared library or file, a single set of physical memory addresses containing the file’s data is mapped into the virtual address spaces of both processes. Under such conditions, the attacker can execute three sequential actions: (1) evict a specific memory address (“flush”), (2) pause, and (3) attempt to reload that memory address. A brief reload latency signifies the victim accessed that address after the eviction but prior to the reload. In cases where the targeted memory addresses do not reside in shared memory, alternative cache attacks like Prime+Probe <cit.> are employed instead.

old_text: Existing non-adversarial DA methods attempt to quantify domain shifts by designing specific statistical distances between the two domains. Correlation alignment <cit.> utilizes the difference of the mean and the covariance between the two datasets as the domain divergence, and attempts to match them during the training. The methods based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) <cit.> such as <cit.> measure the variance between the latent feature distributions of the two domains. Some studies <cit.> also propose to learn the discriminative representations by pseudo-labels and aligning the output class distributions. However, they still consider classifier-induced discrepancies for the latent alignment, which cannot guarantee the safe transfer of the discriminative features across domains. Moreover, stepwise adaptive feature norm (SAFN) <cit.> identifies that domain shifts rely on the less-informative features with small norms for the target-specific task, and the knowledge across domains can be safely transferred by placing the target features far away from these small-norm regions.
new_text: Non-adversarial domain adaptation (DA) techniques quantify domain discrepancies by developing customized statistical measures to compare source and target domains. Correlation alignment <cit.> estimates domain divergence by computing differences in mean and covariance matrices between domains, aiming to harmonize these statistics during training. Methods leveraging maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) <cit.> such as <cit.> evaluate latent distribution disparities between domains by analyzing feature space variance. Alternative approaches <cit.> propose learning discriminative representations via pseudo-labeling and aligning output class distributions across domains. However, these strategies depend on classifier-generated discrepancies for latent space alignment, which does not ensure reliable cross-domain transfer of discriminative features. The stepwise adaptive feature norm (SAFN) <cit.> method identifies that domain discrepancies are attributed to less-informative features characterized by small magnitudes in target-specific tasks, and that safe knowledge transfer can be achieved by displacing target features away from these low-norm regions.

old_text: In this paper we propose to use cross-learner regularizers to prevent the collapse of the representation space in ensemble-based Q-learning methods. Intuitively, these representations capture an inductive bias towards more diverse representations. We have investigated five different regularizers. The mathematical formulation of four of the regularizers correspond to inequality measures borrowed from economics theory. While in economics, in general, high inequality is seen as a negative, in this case we use the metrics to encourage inequality between the representations. The fifth regularizer is inspired consensus optimization.
new_text: This paper proposes cross-learner regularizers to prevent representation space collapse in ensemble-based Q-learning. These regularizers induce diverse representations by encoding inductive biases toward variation. We investigate five regularizers, four of which are formulated as economic inequality metrics. Though high inequality is typically undesirable in economics, we employ these metrics to encourage representation diversity. The fifth regularizer derives from consensus optimization.

new_text: We evaluated the L² norm inequality between models to compare the baseline MaxminDQN and EnsembleDQN with their regularized counterparts. Specifically, we trained the baseline versions of both MaxminDQN and EnsembleDQN using two neural networks, while their regularized versions were trained with the same architectures but incorporated a Gini index regularization term weighted at 1e-8. All experiments were conducted in the PixelCopter environment under a fixed random seed to ensure consistent comparison conditions. In our results, <Ref> denotes the L² norm inequality values alongside the average returns observed during training. Interestingly, despite each neural network in the baseline methods being exposed to distinct training batches—potentially leading to divergent parameter updates—the L² norms of the baseline MaxminDQN and EnsembleDQN showed similar levels of inequality. In contrast, the regularized variants, which introduce additional constraints via the Gini index-based regularization, exhibited significantly higher L² norm inequality, suggesting that the regularization mechanism amplified differences in model behavior compared to their non-regularized counterparts.

old_text: Code-mixing is the phenomenon of using multiple languages in the same utterance of a text or speech. It is a frequently used pattern of communication on various platforms such as social media sites, online gaming, product reviews, etc. Sentiment analysis of the monolingual text is a well-studied task. Code-mixing adds to the challenge of analyzing the sentiment of the text due to the non-standard writing style. We present a candidate sentence generation and selection based approach on top of the Bi-LSTM based neural classifier to classify the Hinglish code-mixed text into one of the three sentiment classes positive, negative, or neutral. The proposed approach shows an improvement in the system performance as compared to the Bi-LSTM based neural classifier. The results present an opportunity to understand various other nuances of code-mixing in the textual data, such as humor-detection, intent classification, etc.
new_text: Code-mixing refers to the use of multiple languages within a single utterance in speech or text. This communication pattern is prevalent across diverse platforms including social media, online gaming, and product reviews. While sentiment analysis of monolingual text is a well-established task, code-mixing introduces additional challenges to sentiment classification due to the non-standard writing style. In this work, we propose a candidate sentence generation and selection approach built on top of a Bi-LSTM-based neural classifier to categorize Hinglish code-mixed text into three sentiment classes: positive, negative, or neutral. The proposed approach demonstrates improved system performance compared to the Bi-LSTM-based neural classifier. These results highlight opportunities to explore further nuances of code-mixing in textual data, such as humor detection, intent classification, and other downstream tasks.

old_text: In this regard, we answer two questions– (1) how to represent and obtain expectations of a human (that captures the notion of egregious vs. explicable misclassification) and (2) how to utilize such a representation to ensure that the trained classifier adheres to the human's expectation. To answer the first question, we posit that the notion of explicability can be represented as a semantic distance between the actual and the predicted label, i.e. misclassifications to classes semantically closer to the ground-truth are considered reasonable while misclassifications to classes further away (eg. classifying the image of a dog as an airplane) makes the end-user deem the classifier inexplicable. In particular, class-level semantic similarity can be leveraged to capture the human's expectation (M^h). To obtain M^h, we strongly advocate the use of a human labeling approach and in cases where the classification task is generic and labels are difficult to obtain, we suggest leveraging existing linguistic knowledge-bases. Finally, to incorporate this notion of explicability into classifiers, we employ the idea of weighted loss functions to train classifiers.
new_text: We address two key questions: (1) how to represent human expectations for misclassification explicability and (2) how to train classifiers to adhere to these expectations. To quantify explicability, we model it as semantic distance between predicted and ground-truth labels: misclassifications to semantically similar classes are deemed reasonable, while distant ones (e.g., classifying a dog as an airplane) are perceived as inexplicable. This class-level semantic similarity captures human expectations (M^h). We advocate human labeling to obtain M^h, with linguistic knowledge bases suggested for tasks where labels are scarce. To integrate explicability into training, we employ weighted loss functions.

In our setting, the agent learns from both the human feedback and the environment reward simultaneously. To learn from environment reward, we use an off-policy Reinforcement Learning algorithm, the Deep Q-Networks (DQN) <cit.>. To learn from human feedback, we first interpret binary feedback as the label on the optimality of the performed actions, which is similar to the interpretation used by <cit.>. The ideas manifest in the form of various loss terms to update the DQN network. Algorithm <ref> presents the train-interaction loop of EXPAND. Within an episode loop, the agent interacts with the environment and stores transition experiences. Every few episodes, it collects human feedback queried on a trajectory sampled from the most recent policy. new_text:
In our framework, the agent simultaneously incorporates learning signals from two sources: environment-based reinforcement learning (RL) and human-provided feedback. For the environment component, we employ an off-policy RL algorithm, specifically Deep Q-Networks (DQN) <cit.>, which enables the agent to learn an optimal policy by interacting with and receiving reward signals from the environment. When integrating human feedback, we treat binary (e.g., approval/disapproval) responses as indicators of whether an action was optimal in a given state. This interpretation aligns with prior approaches <cit.>, where human evaluations are mapped to action optimality. Because DQN inherently models action values through Q-learning, framing human feedback in terms of action optimality creates a direct alignment between human judgments and the Q-network’s representation of advantage values <cit.>. This connection allows us to translate human feedback into actionable signals for policy refinement, as we elaborate in Section <ref>.  

For explanation-augmented feedback, we incorporate saliency-based supervision by strategically perturbing state regions deemed irrelevant to the task. The intuition is that if a region is unimportant for decision-making, the Q-value estimator should remain stable when those regions are altered. To enforce this, we introduce additional loss terms that penalize the DQN for being sensitive to such perturbations, effectively training it to focus on task-relevant features. These loss components work in tandem with the standard DQN loss to jointly update the policy network. Algorithm <ref> outlines the training procedure for EXPAND. During an episode, the agent interacts with the environment, collecting transitions that are stored for offline learning. Periodically, after a fixed number of episodes, human feedback is solicited on trajectories generated by the current policy. In each training phase, the DQN is updated twice: first using the conventional RL loss, and subsequently with the feedback-specific loss. This two-step update ensures that the agent balances environment-driven and human-guided learning objectives. The following discussion details the structure of these loss terms and the method for generating perturbed states to support their computation.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: We elucidate the link between neural networks and chain graphs in Section <ref>, covering core concepts within a simple binary sequential layer setting. In Section <ref> we further discuss the chain graph interpretation in its generality, showing that it can cover an extensive range of existing designs. We then demonstrate by examples in Sections <ref> and <ref> how the proposed chain graph interpretation allows us to systematically design network structures and discover new learning approaches such as partially collapsed feed-forward. We then discuss related work in Section <ref> and draw conclusions in Section <ref>.
new_text: The paper is structured to progressively build upon the chain graph framework and its implications for neural network design. In the first section, we establish the foundational connection between neural networks and chain graphs, focusing on core principles through the lens of a simple binary sequential layer setup. This approach allows us to introduce key concepts in a manageable context before addressing more complex scenarios. Building on this foundation, the subsequent section expands the chain graph interpretation to a general case, demonstrating its versatility by showing how it encompasses a wide variety of existing network architectures. To illustrate the framework’s practical utility, the next two sections present concrete examples, highlighting how the chain graph interpretation enables systematic design of network structures and reveals novel learning methodologies, such as partially collapsed feed-forward approaches. In the following section, we contextualize our work by reviewing related research, emphasizing the novelty of our contributions. Finally, the concluding section summarizes our findings and discusses potential directions for future work.

Bidirectional layered models have long existed <cit.>,
but these models have not received the same intense scrutiny and development as feedforward models.
The goal of this paper is to revisit bidirectional layered models with the aim of raising them to state-of-the-art in performance and more specifically, out of distribution generalization.
Simply taking existing models and incorporating bidirectional connectivity introduces challenges <cit.>. Instead,
we explore the notion that bidirectional information flow must be coupled with additional mechanisms to
effectively select from potential top-down signals, modulate
bottom-up signals and prevent a cacophony of intermixed signals.
We propose two specific mechanisms from the deep learning toolkit to dynamically route information flow: modularity and attention.
With these two mechanisms, we outperform state-of-the-art feedforward models on challenging vision and language tasks.
new_text: Bidirectional layered models have been present <cit.> for some time, yet they have received less scrutiny and development compared to feedforward architectures. This paper aims to re-examine bidirectional layered models with the objective of elevating them to state-of-the-art performance levels, particularly in out-of-distribution generalization. Simply implementing bidirectional connectivity in existing models introduces significant challenges <cit.>. Instead, we investigate the hypothesis that bidirectional information flow requires supplementary mechanisms to effectively select top-down signals, modulate bottom-up signals, and avoid conflicting or redundant signal interactions. To achieve this, we propose leveraging two established deep learning tools for dynamic information routing: modularity and attention. By integrating these mechanisms, our models achieve superior performance compared to state-of-the-art feedforward architectures on complex vision and language tasks.

Our method consists of active speaker detection using audio-visual methods and speaker verification using self-enrolled speaker models. Second, we integrate our method into a semi-automatic dataset creation pipeline which significantly reduces the number of hours required to annotate videos with diarisation labels. Finally, we use this pipeline to create a large-scale diarisation dataset called `VoxConverse`, collected from `in the wild' videos, which we will release publicly to the research community. Our dataset consists of overlapping speech, a large and diverse speaker pool, and challenging background conditions.

Finally, we use this pipeline to create a large-scale diarisation dataset called "VoxConverse," collected from "in-the-wild" videos, which we will release publicly to the research community. Our dataset consists of overlapping speech, a large and diverse speaker pool, and challenging background conditions.

Specifically, Table <ref> shows that our Learned Comparison Histogram estimation method has the best log likelihood, when using PoseCNN features. new_text: For symmetric objects, Table <ref> demonstrates that learning a non-parametric histogram distribution is most effective at modeling the multi-modal uncertainty inherent in these objects. In particular, the Learned Comparison Histogram estimation method achieves the highest log likelihood when using PoseCNN features, as shown in Table <ref>. A close competitor is the Histogram Regression approach using PoseCNN features, which also ranks highly for this task but delivers notably inferior performance compared to our method. This performance gap arises because the multi-modal nature of symmetric objects inherently reduces log likelihood values compared to non-symmetric objects. When a distribution spreads probability mass evenly across all symmetric modes—such as distributing probability density equally among the eight symmetric orientations of the wood block (as illustrated in fig:block)—the likelihood at each individual mode necessarily decreases. This tradeoff reflects the need to account for all possible symmetric configurations, which lowers the maximum likelihood at any single mode. Despite this challenge, our method excels by flexibly adapting to both highly symmetric and asymmetric scenarios. For objects with symmetries, it accurately allocates probability across multiple modes, while for objects without such structure, it concentrates probability mass on a single mode. This adaptability makes our learned comparison-based approach the most robust for capturing uncertainty across a diverse set of objects.

Geometric deep learning on point clouds is a particularly popular research direction, as such architectures make minimal assumptions on input data. The primary limitation of these architectures is that they struggle to define point neighborhoods efficiently. The earlier instance of this type of networks is PointNet <cit.> and its successor PointNet++ <cit.>. PointNet++ relies on the spatial proximity of points at each layer of the network, composing a point cloud's local structures based on the Euclidean nearest neighbors approach. Some work has been done to improve neighborhood query, including non-spherical kNN search <cit.>.
new_text: Geometric deep learning on point clouds has emerged as a popular research direction due to the minimal assumptions these architectures impose on input data. A key limitation of such approaches lies in their inefficiency in defining point neighborhoods. Early examples of this class of architectures include PointNet <cit.> and its successor PointNet++ <cit.>. PointNet++ addresses this challenge by leveraging spatial proximity at each network layer, constructing the point cloud's local structures through Euclidean nearest neighbor analysis. Recent efforts to improve neighborhood queries have explored techniques such as non-spherical kNN search <cit.>.

old_text: We propose two novel methods for estimating orientation distributions. The first method learns a uni-modal, parametric distribution in the form of an isotropic Bingham, regressed from deep learned features. This model is ideal for objects that are known to be non-symmetric. The second learns to estimate a multi-modal non-parametric distribution, in the form of a histogram distribution, obtained using a learned comparison function over deep learned features. We find that this second method works well for objects with unknown symmetries, accurately modeling both symmetric and non-symmetric objects, without any requirement of symmetry annotation.
new_text: We propose two novel methods for estimating orientation distributions. The first method learns a uni-modal parametric distribution as an isotropic Bingham regression from deep learned features. This model is ideal for objects that are known to be non-symmetric. The second estimates a multi-modal non-parametric distribution as a histogram distribution using a learned comparison function over deep learned features. We find this method effectively models symmetric and non-symmetric objects with unknown symmetries without requiring symmetry annotations.

Simultaneous neural machine translation (briefly, NMT) has attracted much attention recently. In contrast to standard NMT, where the NMT system can utilize the full input sentence, simultaneous NMT is formulated as a prefix-to-prefix problem, where the system can only utilize the prefix of the input sentence and more uncertainty is introduced to decoding. Wait-k <cit.> is a simple yet effective strategy for simultaneous NMT, where the decoder generates the output sequence k words behind the input words. We observed that training simultaneous NMT systems with future information (i.e., trained with a larger k) generally outperforms the standard ones (i.e., trained with the given k). Based on this observation, we propose a framework that automatically learns how much future information to use in training for simultaneous NMT. We first build a series of tasks where each one is associated with a different k, and then learn a model on these tasks guided by a controller. The controller is jointly trained with the translation model through bi-level optimization. We conduct experiments on four datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
new_text: Simultaneous neural machine translation (abbreviated as NMT) has attracted significant attention in recent years. In contrast to standard NMT, where the system has access to the complete input sentence, simultaneous NMT is formulated as a prefix-to-prefix problem, in which the system can only use the input prefix and introduces greater uncertainty into the decoding process. Wait-k [cit.] is a simple yet effective strategy for simultaneous NMT, where the decoder generates the output sequence k words behind the input words. We observed that training simultaneous NMT systems using future information (i.e., with a larger k) typically outperforms training using the same k value. Based on this observation, we propose a framework that automatically learns how much of the future information to use in training for simultaneous NMT. We first construct a set of tasks, each associated with a different k, then train a model on these tasks directed by a controller. The controller is jointly trained with the translation model via bi-level optimization. We conduct experiments on four datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Here, the challenge is how much future information we should use. As shown in Figure <ref>, using more future information does not monotonically improve the translation accuracy of wait-k inference,
mainly because that more future information results in a larger gap between training and inference. In this work, we propose a framework that can automatically determine how much future information to use in training for simultaneous NMT. Given a pre-defined k for inference, we prepare K training tasks wait-k^' with different k^' values (i.e., 1,2,⋯,K). We introduce a controller such that given a training sample, the controller can dynamically select one of these tasks so as to maximize the validation performance on wait-k, i.e., the one we are interested in. The task selection is based on the data itself and the network status of the translation model. Transfer learning has emerged as a powerful methodology for adapting pre-trained deep neural networks to new domains. This process consists of taking a neural network pre-trained on a large feature-rich source dataset, freezing the early layers that encode essential generic image properties, and then fine-tuning the last few layers in order to capture specific information related to the target situation.
This approach is particularly useful when only limited or weakly labelled data are available for the new task. In this work, we demonstrate that adversarially-trained models transfer better across new domains than naturally-trained models, even though it's known that these models do not generalize as well as naturally-trained models on the source domain.
We show that this behavior results from a bias, introduced by the adversarial training, that pushes the learned inner layers to more natural image representations, which in turn enables better transfer.
new_text: Transfer learning has proven to be an effective strategy for adapting pre-trained deep neural networks to new domains. This involves leveraging a neural network initially trained on a large, feature-rich source dataset, keeping the initial layers fixed to preserve general image properties, while adjusting the final layers to capture task-specific characteristics. Such methods are especially beneficial when the target task involves sparse or weakly annotated data. Here, we demonstrate that models trained with adversarial techniques exhibit superior cross-domain transfer performance compared to those trained naturally, despite the known tendency of adversarially trained models to underperform on the source domain in terms of standard generalization. This advantage stems from the bias introduced during adversarial training, which encourages the internal layers to develop representations that are more aligned with natural image characteristics, thereby enhancing cross-domain adaptability.

They study the effect of depth within the network and optimization issues with regards to splitting networks between co-adapted neurons. <cit.> study the generalization of naturally and adversarially-trained models to additional data generated using a process similar to that of generating ImageNet. They conclude that models trained on ImageNet overfit the data. However, they study generalization of the model as-is without any fine-tuning applied to the last layers.
new_text: **ImageNet transfers.** We study transferring all but the last few layers of trained DNNs while fine-tuning the remaining layers. Applying this to ImageNet models <cit.>, <cit.> investigate the transfer of naturally-trained models to various datasets, forming a prequel to our work. <cit.> also examine transferring naturally-trained models but focus on individual neuron importance in transfer learning, examining the effect of depth and optimization challenges related to splitting co-adapted neurons. <cit.> investigate generalization of naturally and adversarially-trained models on generated data similar to ImageNet, concluding these models overfit. However, they analyze generalization without fine-tuning the final layers.
