new_text: For the IWSLT'14 English-to-German translation task, we adopt standard preprocessing steps. Following established practices, all words in the dataset are lowercased to ensure case consistency, followed by tokenization to segment text into subword units. To reduce the vocabulary size and improve model efficiency, we apply Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) with 10,000 merge operations. This BPE process is applied simultaneously to both source (English) and target (German) sequences, creating a shared subword vocabulary. The training data, initially comprising 167,000 sentences, is divided into a 160,000-sentence training set and a 7,000-sentence validation set to monitor model performance during training. The test set is constructed by concatenating five predefined splits—tst2010, tst2011, tst2012, dev2010, and dev2012—resulting in a total of 6,750 sentences for evaluation. For the IWSLT'15 English-to-Vietnamese task, we follow the same conventions by using tst2012 as the validation set and tst2013 as the test set. In the IWSLT'17 English-to-Chinese scenario, we tokenize the data and perform BPE independently on the source and target sequences with 10,000 merge operations each, allowing distinct subword representations. The validation set is formed by combining tst2013, tst2014, and tst2015, while tst2017 serves as the test set. For the WMT'15 English-German bilingual dataset, the preprocessing includes tokenization and joint BPE with 32,000 merge operations to align subword units across both languages, resulting in a training corpus of 4.5 million sentences. The validation set is designated as newstest2013, and the final evaluation is conducted on newstest2015. Further details about data splits and preprocessing are summarized in Appendix B.

new_text:
To assess the effectiveness of our learned representations in a semi-supervised setting, we adapt the fine-tuning protocol from IIC <cit.>. Our goal is to demonstrate how these representations perform when trained using a small portion of labeled data alongside a larger set of unlabeled examples. Specifically, we begin by pretraining the ResNet-34 encoder E(·) using all 105K unlabeled training samples from STL-10 (Sec. <ref>). Importantly, we also include the 5K labeled images from the same dataset in this phase but intentionally ignore their class labels. This step simulates a semi-supervised scenario where only unlabeled data is initially accessible, and a limited subset of labels becomes available later for refinement. 

In the subsequent supervised stage, following the protocol outlined in <cit.>, we build an MLP classifier on top of the pretrained E(·) while simultaneously fine-tuning the encoder itself. Here, we explicitly use the 5K labeled images and their ground-truth labels to optimize the model. To ensure robustness, we apply the data-augmentation procedure described in <cit.> during this phase. This two-stage approach combines pretraining on abundant unlabeled data with supervised refinement on a small labeled subset, leveraging both sources to maximize performance.

The results of this evaluation are summarized in Tab. <ref>. Our proposed method, CPW², achieves a new state-of-the-art result on this dataset under the semi-supervised paradigm. It significantly outperforms IIC <cit.>—a baseline using the same ResNet-34 encoder—and surpasses prior work as well. Notably, the InfoNCE method <cit.>, previously considered strong in self-supervised learning, achieves weaker performance in this context compared to the established baselines.

Referring to the special characteristics of variable-length paths in S, the modelling approach above has a number of limitations.
(i) Using a k-th order model, we can neither use the first k nodes in each path to fit the transition probabilities of the model, nor can we use the model to perform a next-element prediction for the first k nodes on a path.
(ii) The fact that the number of observations used to fit the transition probabilities of a k-th order model differs across different orders k complicates model selection, i.e., the selection of the optimal order k to model a data set.
(iii) The model neglects information on the start and end point of nodes, which hinders its application to an out-of-sample prediction of full paths, i.e. from start to end.
(iv) Finally, a model with a single order k is limited to capture sequential patterns of a single length k, which is why recent works argued for variable- and multi-order modelling techniques <cit.>.
new_text: The proposed modeling approach has several limitations when applied to variable-length paths in S, stemming from their inherent characteristics. First, in a k-th order model, the initial k nodes in each path cannot be used to estimate the model's transition probabilities, nor can they be used for next-element prediction during the first k steps of a path. Second, the varying number of observations available for fitting transition probabilities across different model orders (k) complicates the process of selecting an optimal k for a given dataset. Third, the model fails to account for the designated start and end points of nodes, limiting its applicability to predicting entire paths out-of-sample, that is, from beginning to end. Finally, as a model fixed to a single order k, it is constrained to capture sequential patterns of a uniform length k; thus, recent studies have advocated for variable- and multi-order modeling techniques <cit.>.

We first evaluate the performance of our method in a next-element prediction setting.
Given a prefix of k nodes (v_1, [.6em][c]..., v_k) previously traversed by a path, we want to predict which node v_k+1 in the network is visited next.
We evaluate our method in a cross-validation experiment for the six empirical data sets outlined above.
Leveraging the fact that our model captures terminal nodes on paths, we consider the special state † as a prediction of a path termination.
We include this in the evaluation, because the prediction of terminal nodes is crucial in data on variable-length path data, e.g., to predict where users exit a website, where passengers end their itinerary, or whether a purchase is made in an online shop.
We compare the performance of / to state-of-the-art sequence prediction algorithms that have addressed next-element prediction in categorical sequences.
Our choice of baseline methods is informed by the review of <cit.>, which compares the performance of state-of-the-art methods in several data sets.
The authors find that AKOM <cit.> outperforms other algorithms in three out of four tested data sets.
Conversely, <cit.> show that CPT+ outperforms AKOM in terms of the accuracy of the next element prediction.
We thus use both CPT+ and AKOM as baseline, utilising the implementations provided in <cit.>.
To enable a fair comparison for empty prefixes, we modified the implementation of AKOM to return a prediction based on the frequency of elements in the training data.
This is described in <cit.>, however the implementation in <cit.> returns an empty prediction instead.
CPT+ predicts the next element in a sequence based on an internal assignment of weights to candidate elements, i.e., the prediction is not based on probabilities.
We thus normalise the weights assigned by CPT+ to obtain a probabilistic prediction.
While this allows us to compare the performance of CPT+ with the other (probabilistic) methods, we highlight that the evaluation in <cit.> is based on prediction accuracy.
In addition to those sequence modelling techniques, we compare our method to a probabilistic prediction derived from (i) a random walk in a higher-order network with a single order k (NET), and (ii) the multi-order graphical model (MOG) introduced in <cit.>.
For k=1, NET is identical to a prediction generated by a random walk in the underlying network.
Note that, despite a similarity in name, the method proposed in the present work considerable differs from MOM.
First, MOM does not model the endpoint of paths, which limits its ability to predict variable-length paths.
Second, it uses a model fitting approach that estimates transition probabilities based on sub-path frequencies rather than the transition probabilities used in our approach.
Finally, it uses a model selection that builds on a nested model structure, which does not hold for our modelling framework.
In addition to those network-based models, we use a naive (parameter-free) random baseline (RND) that simply predicts the next node based on the relative frequency of nodes in the training set, i.e., a prediction that neither uses a Markov chain nor the network topology.
For AKOM, MOM, NET, and MOGen we report the results for the optimal (maximum) order parameter obtained via a grid search.
For CPT+, we use the default parameters chosen in <cit.>.

Despite the irregular nature based on input, there does exist some local structure normally.

new_text: Irregular kernel insight. Irregular kernels often retain local structure despite input variability, such as grouping rows or subblocks with many nonzero entries via ordering. The KASS system <cit.> considers adaptively chunking together in the static or initialization phase.
Chunks in the second (dynamic phase) are reduced fixedly based on information from past iteration runs but are not adapted within an iteration like iCh.
Chunks are stolen if a queue runs out of its own chunks.
A history-aware <cit.> studies chunk size from past iteration and the number of times the task will be ran using a much more complex “best-fit" approximation fit.
This proves benefits for loops that are repeated, but iCh does not consider this as i regular kernels may not repeat loops as in `spmv`.
Lastly, BinLPT <cit.> schedules irregular tasks from a loop using an estimate of the work in each loop and a maximal number of chunks provided by the user.
This method is one of the newest and provides good performance in publication.
In contrast, iCh wants to provide an easier method that does not require estimates of loop work and more user input.
new_text: In <cit.>, loops are scheduled via a distributed MPI approach, with chunk size determined by the ratio of cumulative completed tasks to processor speed. The KASS system <cit.> employs adaptive chunking during static/initialization phases, while dynamic-phase chunks are fixedly adjusted based on past iterations but remain unadapted within iterations (unlike iCh). Chunk stealing occurs when queues exhaust their own chunks. History-aware methods <cit.> employ a complex best-fit approximation using prior iteration data and task repetition counts, offering benefits for repeated loops—unlike iCh, which lacks this mechanism as regular kernels (e.g., `spmv`) may not repeat. BinLPT <cit.>, a newer approach, schedules irregular tasks by estimating loop work and user-defined chunk limits, achieving strong performance. In contrast, iCh simplifies scheduling by eliminating loop work estimates and user input requirements.

old_text: In this section, we analyse the CNLL of the ensembles of unregularized networks as a function of network size. Turning off regularization, i. e. weight decay and dropout, results in the clearly observed effect that for large values of n, CNLL_s of the ensemble of size n has optimum at some network size s. We firstly visualize this effect in figure <ref> showing the (n , s) plane of CNLL for the setting without regularization, for VGG and WideResNet on CIFAR-100. For higher n (e. g. n>5), the horizontal cuts are non-monotonic w. r. t. s. Secondly, we analyse the CNLL of the “infinite”-size ensemble, using power laws discovered in the paper. Figure <ref> visualizes the parameters of the power laws approximating CNLL_n for different values of s, for VGG and WideresNet on CIFAR-100. We can clearly observe that parameter b, that reflects the possible gain of ensembling the networks of size s, decreases as s increases, while the parameter c, that reflects the CNLL of the “infinite”-size ensemble, is non-monotonic, i. e. achieves optimum at some s in the middle of the considered range of s. The similar effect was observed in figure <ref> for the regularized setting, but in a less visible form. We notice that the decrease of parameter b in the setting without regularization is much larger, than in the standard setting with regularization, and the effect of non-monotonicity of c is also stronger.
new_text: In this section, we analyze the CNLL of ensembles of unregularized networks as a function of network size. Turning off regularization, i.e., weight decay and dropout, results in a clearly observed effect: for large values of n, the CNLL of the ensemble of size n reaches an optimum at some network size s. We first visualize this effect in Figure <ref>, showing the (n, s) plane of CNLL for the setting without regularization using VGG and WideResNet on CIFAR-100. For higher n (e.g., n > 5), the horizontal cuts are non-monotonic w.r.t. s. Second, we analyze the CNLL of the “infinite”-size ensemble using power laws discovered in the paper. Figure <ref> visualizes the parameters of the power laws approximating CNLL_n for different values of s, for VGG and WideResNet on CIFAR-100. We observe that parameter b, which reflects the possible gain of ensembling networks of size s, decreases as s increases, while parameter c, which reflects the CNLL of the “infinite”-size ensemble, exhibits non-monotonicity, achieving an optimum at some s in the middle of the considered range. A similar effect was observed in Figure <ref> for the regularized setting but in a less visible form. We notice that the decrease of parameter b in the setting without regularization is much larger than in the standard regularized setting, and the non-monotonicity of c is also more pronounced.

new_text: It is natural to ask whether regularity is also a sufficient condition for the existence of an α-relaxed perfect matching in the case of non-uniform hypergraphs (for some small α). The simple answer is that this is not the case. Figure <ref> (derived from a similar construction in <cit>) shows that there are regular hypergraphs that do not contain an α-relaxed perfect matching for α ≈ √n. However, a crucial aspect of the counter-example is that some hyperedges contain just one element of R. Those hyperedges cannot drop any elements in an α-relaxed matching. Our main result is that for α = O(log log n), a regular (non-uniform) hypergraph where all hyperedges contain at least α elements admits an α-relaxed perfect matching. We note that the setting with the assumption that hyperedges are large still contains the uniform case without the assumption (and therefore is much more general): This holds because the case where all hyperedges are smaller than α trivially admits an α-relaxed perfect matching by Hall's condition. In particular, our result directly implies a bound comparable to Bansal and Srivastava in the uniform case.

In this paper, we propose the first work on adversarial immunization on graphs.
Focusing on the graph structure, adversarial immunization aims to improve the certifiable robustness of graph against any admissible attack by vaccinating a fraction of node pairs, connected or unconnected.
To circumvent the computationally expensive combinatorial optimization, we further propose an efficient algorithm with meta-gradient in a discrete way to figure out suitable immune edges.
The effectiveness of our proposed method are evaluated on three well-known network datasets, including two citation networks and one social network.
Experimental results reveal that our immunization approach significantly improves the certifiable robustness of graphs under the evaluation metrics of both robust node ratio and worst-case margin.
In future work, we tend to explore the adversarial immunization focusing on both graph structures and node attributes.
new_text: In this paper, we introduce the first work on adversarial immunization for graphs. Adversarial immunization focuses on graph structures and aims to improve the certifiable robustness of graphs against any admissible attack by immunizing a fraction of node pairs, connected or unconnected. To overcome the computationally expensive combinatorial optimization, we further propose an efficient algorithm with meta-gradient using a discrete method to identify suitable immune edges. The effectiveness of our proposed method is evaluated on three well-known network datasets, including two citation networks and one social network. Experimental results reveal that our immunization approach significantly improves the certifiable robustness of graphs using the evaluation metrics of robust node ratio and worst-case margin. In future work, we plan to explore adversarial immunization that focuses on both graph structures and node attributes.

Several widely-used VQA databases have been proposed, including LIVE VQA <cit.>, LIVE Mobile <cit.>, CSIQ-VQA <cit.>, CDVL <cit.> etc. These generally begin with a set of less than 20 pristine video contents, on which various distortions are applied, primarily compression artifacts arising from past and present codecs, on both Standard Definition (SD) and High Definition (HD) resolutions. old_text: Currently available datasets addressing HFR content are very limited. One of the first HFR databases was proposed by Nasiri et al. <cit.>, containing SD and HD videos with frame rates no greater than 60 fps, and distorted by various compression levels. However, this database has not been made publicly available. Mackin et al. introduced the BVI-HFR <cit.> database, which contains videos of 4 different frame rates varying from 15 fps to 120 fps. The dataset includes 22 120 fps source sequences, where the lower fps videos were obtained by subsampling the source videos via frame averaging. Possible shortcomings of this database are that it only includes frame rate artifacts, it does not consider the effects of compression on frame rate, and it uses simple frame averaging to subsample in time. new_text: Currently available datasets for studying high frame rate (HFR) content remain extremely limited, hindering comprehensive analysis and development of related technologies. One of the earliest attempts to address this gap was introduced by Nasiri et al. <cit.>, who proposed a database containing standard definition (SD) and high definition (HD) videos with frame rates capped at 60 fps. These videos were intentionally degraded using varying levels of compression to simulate transmission artifacts, enabling evaluation of quality under different conditions. However, this dataset remains inaccessible to the public, severely limiting its utility for broader research. A more recent contribution, the BVI-HFR database by Mackin et al. <cit.>, expands the scope by including videos at four distinct frame rates (15, 30, 60, and 120 fps). This dataset is built from 22 original 120 fps source sequences, with lower frame rate versions generated by subsampling the original via frame averaging—a technique that merges multiple frames into a single frame to reduce temporal resolution. While this approach creates a controlled framework for studying frame rate perception, it introduces notable limitations. First, the dataset exclusively focuses on frame rate artifacts, omitting other critical factors like compression effects that co-occur in real-world scenarios. Second, the use of frame averaging imposes strong assumptions about temporal sampling, leading to motion blur artifacts that may not reflect practical systems, where decimation methods and hardware constraints vary widely. This discrepancy risks misalignment between experimental findings and real-world performance.

Defining a “perceptual” distance function between high-dimensional signals, images, has been a longstanding problem in computer vision and image processing. The majority of image translation work mentioned uses a per-pixel reconstruction metric, such as ℓ_1. Such metrics do not reflect human perceptual preferences and can lead to blurry results. Recently, the deep learning community has found that the VGG classification network <cit.> trained on ImageNet dataset <cit.> can be re-purposed as a “perceptual loss” <cit.>, which can be used in paired image translation tasks <cit.>, and was known to outperform traditional metrics such as SSIM <cit.> and FSIM <cit.> on human perceptual tests <cit.>. In particular, the Contextual Loss <cit.> boosts the perceptual quality of pretrained VGG features, validated by human perceptual judgments <cit.>.
In these cases, the frozen network weights cannot adapt to the data on hand. Furthermore, the frozen similarity function may not be appropriate when comparing data across two domains, depending on the pairing.
By posing our constraint via mutual information, our method makes use of negative samples from the data, allowing the cross-domain similarity function to adapt to the particular input and output domains, and bypass using a pre-defined similarity function.
new_text: Establishing a “perceptual” distance metric between high-dimensional signals, such as images, has posed an enduring challenge in computer vision and image processing. Most prior image translation methods rely on pixel-wise reconstruction criteria like ℓ_1, which fail to capture human perceptual preferences and often result in visually blurred outputs. Recent advances in deep learning demonstrate that the VGG classification network <cit.>, trained on the ImageNet dataset <cit.>, can be adapted to compute a “perceptual loss” <cit.> for paired image translation tasks <cit.>. This approach has consistently outperformed traditional measures such as SSIM <cit.> and FSIM <cit.> in human perceptual evaluations <cit.>. Specifically, the Contextual Loss <cit.> enhances the perceptual fidelity of pre-trained VGG features, as corroborated by human perceptual assessments <cit.>. However, these methods fix the network weights during inference, preventing the model from adapting to the specific characteristics of the target data or accounting for cross-domain discrepancies depending on the paired inputs. In contrast, our approach leverages mutual information to incorporate negative samples, enabling the cross-domain similarity function to dynamically adjust to the input and output domains without relying on a pre-defined similarity criterion.

For example, supervised classification methods such as random forest <cit.> and KNN<cit.> suffer from the curse of dimensionality. However, having large training data sets is not always possible in practice. As a result, designing a supervised classification algorithm that has good performance even when the training data set is extremely small is very important. new_text: The "curse of dimensionality" [describing non-intuitive behaviors when the length of data vectors (n) significantly exceeds the cardinality of the input space |𝒳|]<cit.> highlights that increasing the dimensionality of data vectors necessitates exponentially more training data to maintain the effectiveness of supervised classifiers<cit.>. Algorithms like random forest <cit.> and KNN<cit.> are particularly vulnerable to this phenomenon. However, acquiring extensive training datasets is often impractical in real-world applications. Consequently, developing supervised classification methods that perform well even with extremely limited training samples remains critical. Addressing this challenge, we present a classification algorithm tailored for data vectors exhibiting specific statistical properties. This method demonstrates competitive performance relative to existing approaches, even when provided with only a single training sample per class label.

Recent progress in training Deep Neural Networks (DNN) has proved very successful in establishing the state of the art results on several applications in the domain of computer vision <cit.>, natural language processing <cit.>, etc. The application and deployment of DNNs for public use in several security-critical scenarios has led researchers to explore their vulnerability against attackers. new_text: Recent advances in training deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in achieving state-of-the-art results across critical fields such as computer vision <cit.> and natural language processing <cit.>. As DNNs have been increasingly adopted in public-facing, security-sensitive applications, researchers have grown concerned about their susceptibility to adversarial threats. These attacks typically manifest in three primary ways: degrading model performance through adversarial inputs, poisoning training data, and manipulating predictions by introducing input triggers. Each method exploits vulnerabilities in the model's architecture or training process to compromise its reliability and integrity.

old_text: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a formal model for automated decision-making. RL is a growing field with several new techniques proposed to improve the applicability and generalization of RL towards real-world problems. Existing RL techniques, however, have been mostly applied and evaluated on games <cit.> and real-world use-cases of RL are hard to find. RL training, in general, is a cumbersome process: hyper-parameter tuning, improving sample efficiency as well as training stability <cit.> have become indispensable during the training process. Thereby, it has become necessary to have a solid background knowledge in RL and sufficient software development skills to develop and train RL agents. The above requirements restrict the RL audience to only a handful of researchers who are experts in RL. Though RL can solve decision-making problems in healthcare, transportation, networking, etc., people in these fields may find it cumbersome to train RL agents without sufficient expertise.

old_text: Our main goal is to build a RL framework that can be used by diverse audiences from different domains. To this end, we propose the EasyRL framework for both native as well as non-native RL users to easily develop, train, and evaluate RL agents. The existing RL frameworks Keras-RL, Tensorforce, Horizon, HuskaRL, SimpleRL, AI-ToolBox, and Coach provide a range of built-in deepRL (deep reinforcement learning) techniques and some of them, such as Coach, create visualization of the training process for debugging purposes <cit.>. However, they do not support a user-friendly Graphical User Interface (GUI). Even the popular OpenAI gym only supports a range of environments to evaluate RL agents. Further, all the existing frameworks require some amount of RL and programming knowledge.
new_text: Our primary objective is to develop a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that is accessible to a broad and varied user base across different domains. To address these challenges, we introduce EasyRL, a framework designed to simplify the development, training, and evaluation of RL agents for both experienced practitioners and newcomers. While existing RL frameworks—such as Keras-RL, Tensorforce, Horizon, HuskaRL, SimpleRL, AI-ToolBox, and Coach—offer a range of built-in deep reinforcement learning (deepRL) techniques, their functionality often remains limited in scope. For instance, tools like Coach provide visualization features to assist with debugging the training process, but even these advanced tools lack a user-friendly Graphical User Interface (GUI). Additionally, widely adopted platforms like OpenAI Gym primarily serve as repositories for evaluation environments, lacking the intuitive interfaces necessary for streamlined model development. Furthermore, these tools collectively demand a baseline understanding of both reinforcement learning algorithms and programming concepts, which can be a significant barrier for individuals new to the field. By addressing these limitations, EasyRL aims to lower the entry threshold for diverse users and expand the reach of RL-based solutions.

The simulation is conducted as follows. For each value of n (representing the length of the data vectors), one training data vector is generated for each label to form the training set. Next, 250 test data vectors are created for each label and classified using our proposed method, naive Bayes, and KNN. Error probabilities are computed for each classifier. The process is repeated for n ranging from 1 to 80, with 250 trials conducted at each vector length. The results are then aggregated, and the average error probability across all trials is plotted as a function of n to analyze performance trends.

Once again, our proposed classifier demonstrates a significant performance gap compared to the benchmark classifiers. The naive Bayes classifier consistently achieves an error probability close to 0.5 for all values of n. This occurs because the presence of unseen alphabets in the test data violates its assumption of feature independence and uniform distribution, leading to poor generalization. Similarly, the KNN classifier's error probability approaches 0.5 for n > 30, as higher-dimensional spaces cause distances between data points to become less meaningful, undermining its reliance on local neighbors. In contrast, our proposed classifier's error probability steadily decreases as n increases, indicating that it effectively mitigates these challenges and leverages longer vectors to improve accuracy.

old_text: **Limitations.** We conclude this section by mentioning a few limitations of the proposed approach and potential avenues to address them. First, `Greedy-TL` can be time consuming since it has to test all possible edges at each iteration (quadratic in the order of the tensor). However, this step is highly parallelizable and efficient task specific heuristics can be tailored to identify the best edge to increment. Second, the greedy algorithm is one of the simplest ways of tackling the combinatorial upper level discrete optimization problem, and is prone to identifying sub-optimal solutions. More advanced discrete optimization techniques can be used, which is a promising direction for building upon `Greedy-TL`; the A^* search algorithm would be a first alternative to investigate. Lastly, the tensor network structures learned by `Greedy-TL` do not contain hyper-edges and internal nodes, but the greedy algorithm can easily be adapted to address this limitation, which is left for future work.
new_text: The proposed method has several limitations worth noting, alongside potential strategies to mitigate them. First, the `Greedy-TL` algorithm entails significant computational overhead, as it requires evaluating all possible edges at each iterative step—a process with complexity quadratic in the tensor’s order. That said, this computation is highly parallelizable, and performance could be improved through tailored heuristics to prioritize the most promising edges. Second, the greedy heuristic is a basic strategy for addressing the combinatorial upper-level discrete optimization problem, which risks convergence to sub-optimal solutions. More sophisticated discrete optimization techniques could enhance the method, with the A^* search algorithm serving as a viable initial candidate for refinement. Finally, tensor networks produced by `Greedy-TL` lack hyper-edges and internal nodes, though this constraint could be overcome by modifying the greedy framework—a direction reserved for future investigation.

Recent advances in visual model interpretability have predominantly focused on gradient-based attention methods, which inherently depend on a classification module to generate explanations. However, such approaches are ill-suited for models that do not rely on classification-like loss functions, such as similarity models trained with metric learning objectives. In this work, we address this critical limitation by introducing the first gradient-based method for visualizing image similarity predictions. Our approach leverages solely the learned feature embedding, enabling compatibility with any CNN-based similarity architecture—a vital step toward achieving generic visual explainability. Beyond interpretability, we demonstrate how our visual explanations can be integrated into the model learning process itself by introducing novel trainable constraints derived from these explanations. We show that similarity models trained with these explanation-based constraints outperform baseline models without them while maintaining high-quality visual explanations. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments across three distinct tasks: generic image retrieval, person re-identification, and low-shot semantic segmentation.

With this module, the top-1 accuracy is further improved to 69.0%. By referring to each other, each stream is able to modify its own learning process.

new_text: In addition to summation fusion—a straightforward method for combining features—we incorporate a mutual promotion module to further optimize the framework's effectiveness. This module introduces a dynamic where the two processing streams (local and global) interact reciprocally during training. Specifically, by referencing each other’s intermediate representations, each stream can adaptively refine its learning process. For instance, the global stream leverages fine-grained cues extracted by the local stream, enabling it to capture more nuanced patterns in the data. Conversely, the local stream benefits from the global stream’s broader context, allowing it to produce higher-quality feature maps. These enhanced feature maps, in turn, provide more precise guidance for the sampling process, creating a positive feedback loop. This cyclical interaction ensures both streams reinforce each other’s strengths, leading to improved accuracy. As a result of this synergistic design, the model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 69.0%, demonstrating the effectiveness of mutual promotion in boosting overall performance.

new_text: All evaluations in this paper are conducted using standard precision and success metrics. The overlap success metric quantifies the percentage of frames for which the overlap score between estimated and ground-truth bounding boxes exceeds a predefined threshold. Conversely, the distance precision metric calculates the percentage of frames where the estimated location error relative to the ground-truth location is below a specific threshold. The default thresholds used in standard benchmarks—50% overlap and 20 pixels—are applied in the evaluations <cit.>. The success and precision results from comprehensive analyses of CNN models on the OTB-2013 dataset <cit.>—including model resolution, feature map counts, and evaluated layers—are summarized in Table <ref> and Table <ref>. These tables report results across over 29,000 frames for each evaluated CNN model configuration. Visual tracking datasets <cit.> commonly include challenging attributes such as illumination variation (IV), out-of-plane rotation (OPR), scale variation (SV), occlusion (OCC), deformation (DEF), motion blur (MB), fast motion (FM), in-plane rotation (IPR), out-of-view (OV), background clutter (BC), and low resolution (LR). Due to the extensive nature of the evaluations, this work highlights only the best and worst-performing CNN layers (see Appendix <ref> for full details). The tables provide a comprehensive framework for utilizing these CNN models and their features in visual tracking tasks. Additionally, the pros and cons of models, layers, and combinations for each attribute are explicitly detailed. These findings motivate future visual trackers to develop more sophisticated adaptive methods and selectively employ precise CNN layers to enhance performance under specific challenging conditions.

section: Why should the scaling affect homogeneous activations ?
old_text: In Section <ref>, we saw empirically that for a simple two-layer neural network with sin activations, we can induce a complete memorization scenario simply by increasing the scale of the initialization of the weights. For sin activations, this phenomenon may be explainable through the lens of random Fourier features and kernel machines, which suggests that large initialization leads to very poorly aligned examples. In this Section, we investigate what happens when we use more typical activations such as ReLU. We find that even for ReLU, increasing the scale of the initialization leads to a drop in generalization performance, and a similar downward movement in alignment as the initialization scale increases (see Figure <ref>). ReLU activation, due to its homogeneity property, should intuitively be robust to the scaling of initialization. However, this does not take into account the effect of the loss function ℓ, which is typically not homogeneous. We study 3 commonly used loss functions, namely softmax cross-entropy, multi-class hinge loss and squared loss, and show their effect on gradients when weights are close to their initialization. Defining an efficient training set is one of the most delicate phases for the success of HSI classification routines. Active learning is often designed to build effective sets of training by iteratively bettering the performance of the model through sampling. It has been extensively studied in HSI classification. In igeneral, active learning can be grouped into three main classes: committee learner-based approaches, margin sampling based approaches, class probability distribution based approaches <cit.>. Committee learner-based approaches selects the samples showing maximal disagreement between the different classification models in the committee <cit.>. SVMs rely on a sparse representation of the training data, margin sampling based approaches aim at finding the pixels more likely to become support vectors <cit.>. Class probability distribution based approaches use the estimation of posterior probabilities of class membership to rank the candidates <cit.>.
new_text: Defining an efficient training set is one of the most delicate phases for the success of HSI classification routines. Active learning is often designed to build effective training sets by iteratively improving the model’s performance through strategic sampling. This approach has been extensively studied in the context of HSI classification. Generally, active learning strategies can be grouped into three main categories: committee learner-based approaches, margin sampling-based approaches, and class probability distribution-based approaches <cit.>. Committee learner-based methods focus on identifying samples where the predictions of multiple models in a committee exhibit the greatest disagreement, as these cases are likely to provide the most valuable information for refining the model <cit.>. Another strategy, margin sampling-based approaches, leverages the principles of sparse representation used in support vector machines (SVMs), aiming to select pixels that are most likely to become support vectors due to their proximity to decision boundaries <cit.>. Finally, class probability distribution-based approaches rely on estimating the posterior probabilities of class membership for candidate samples, using these probabilities to prioritize pixels that exhibit high uncertainty in their predicted class labels, thus indicating potential high information gain <cit.>.

new_text: The NAS workflow typically relies on an objective function that incorporates accuracy loss alongside weighted energy and latency terms. Efficient evaluation of the inference accuracy, latency, and energy performance of candidate DNN architectures is essential for this process. Proxy models are commonly used to estimate latency and energy consumption for each candidate design, though they often lack precision across various devices <cit.>. In contrast, conducting real-device measurements for each candidate is effective but highly resource-intensive <cit.>. Recent approaches have instead integrated accuracy/latency/energy predictors into NAS and model compression frameworks <cit.>: these involve training machine learning models to forecast a candidate DNN’s performance in terms of accuracy, latency, and energy consumption on the target device. By leveraging search algorithms enhanced with pre-trained predictors for these metrics, an optimal DNN architecture can be identified from a large set of candidates for a target edge device without physically deploying or executing each model on the device <cit.>.

The authors of <cit.> argue that although multi-task learning generally benefits all tasks, certain tasks may compete for the model's capacity, as shared encodings might not provide equivalent information across tasks. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been increasingly deployed on and integrated
with edge devices, such as mobile phones, drones, robots and wearables.
To run DNN inference directly on edge devices (a.k.a. edge inference) with a satisfactory performance,
optimizing the DNN design (e.g., network architecture and quantization policy) is crucial. While
state-of-the-art DNN designs have leveraged performance predictors
to speed up the optimization process, they are device-specific (i.e., each predictor for only one
target device) and hence cannot
 scale well in the presence of extremely diverse edge devices.
Moreover, even with performance predictors, the optimizer (e.g., search-based
optimization) can still be time-consuming when optimizing DNNs for many
different devices.
 In this work, we propose a new DNN optimization framework which:
(1) leverages scalable performance predictors that can
estimate the resulting performance (e.g., inference accuracy/latency/energy)
given a DNN-device pair;
and (2) uses a neural network-based automated optimizer that takes the device features
and optimization parameters as input, and then directly outputs the optimal
DNN design without going through a lengthy search process for each individual
device.
new_text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are being increasingly deployed and integrated into edge devices—such as mobile phones, drones, robots, and wearables—to enable on-device processing. This deployment allows for direct execution of DNN inference, often termed "edge inference," without relying on cloud-based computation. However, achieving satisfactory performance for edge inference requires optimizing the DNN design, such as adjusting network architecture and quantization strategies, to meet device constraints. Many modern approaches use performance predictors—tools that estimate metrics like inference accuracy, latency, and energy consumption—to accelerate optimization. However, these predictors are typically device-specific, meaning a separate predictor is required for each unique edge device. This device-specific design becomes a limitation when dealing with the growing diversity of edge devices, as it hinders the scalability of optimization workflows. Furthermore, even when using these predictors, traditional optimizers such as search-based methods can remain computationally intensive. This is particularly challenging when optimizing DNNs across a large number of heterogeneous devices, as each optimization iteration may require extensive search processes tailored to specific hardware configurations. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel DNN optimization framework with two key components. First, we develop scalable performance predictors that can estimate key performance metrics (e.g., inference accuracy, latency, and energy consumption) for any DNN-device pair, eliminating the need for device-specific models. Second, we employ a neural network-based optimizer that accepts device features and optimization objectives as inputs and directly generates the optimal DNN design, bypassing the need for iterative search processes typically required for each device.

In the traditional minibatch SGD setting with batch size B, an upper limit on the write density per cell per sample is easily seen: 1/B. However, to store such a batch of updates without intermediate writes to NVM would require auxiliary memory proportional to B. Therefore, a trade-off becomes apparent. If B is reduced, LAM is satisfied at the cost of LWD. If B is raised, LWD is satisfied at the cost of LAM. Using low-rank training techniques, the auxiliary memory requirements are decoupled from the batch size, allowing us to increase B while satisfying both LWD and LAM[This can alternately be achieved by sub-sampling the training data by r/B where r is the OK rank. The purpose of using a low-rank estimate is that for the same memory cost, it is significantly more informational than the sub-sampled data, allowing for faster training convergence.]. Additionally, because the low-rank representation uses so little memory, a larger bitwidth can be used, potentially allowing for gradient accumulation in a way that is not possible with low bitwidth NVM weights. In the next section, we elaborate on the low-rank training method.
new_text: In traditional minibatch SGD with batch size B, the maximum write density per cell per sample is 1/B. Storing such updates without intermediate non-volatile memory (NVM) writes requires auxiliary memory proportional to B, creating a trade-off: reducing B satisfies low write density (LWD) but violates low auxiliary memory (LAM), while increasing B satisfies LAM but violates LWD. Low-rank training decouples memory requirements from batch size, enabling larger B that meet both LWD and LAM [Alternative methods include sub-sampling the training data at a rate of r/B, where r is the OK rank; low-rank estimates are significantly more informative than sub-sampled data at the same memory cost, accelerating training convergence]. Additionally, low-rank representations utilize less memory, enabling higher bitwidth and gradient accumulation, which is infeasible with low bitwidth NVM weights. The next section details the low-rank training approach.

old_text: The primary focus of this work is to encode cultural knowledge as an essential part of commonsense knowledge. To do this, we need to first find ways to collect cultural knowledge across a variety of cultural groups. However, this is not straightforward, since cultural knowledge can be fairly arbitrary and complex across groups. Prior literature from the study of cultural groups (see Section <ref>) seems to suggest that it is hard enough just to define culture given the array of complexities and nuance; however, it is even harder to identify the knowledge that comes along with it and to differentiate across cultural groups. Furthermore, as cultural norms and practices are so varied across various groups, it is hard to find knowledge structures that can be clearly compared across different groups. The first task, therefore, is to find topics that are relatively common across different groups; and that can be compared in a like-for-like fashion, thus demonstrating the relevance of culture-dependent representation of commonsense knowledge.
new_text: The primary focus of this work is encoding cultural knowledge as a core component of commonsense knowledge. This requires first identifying methods to collect cultural knowledge across diverse groups, a challenge due to its arbitrary and complex intergroup variability. Prior literature (see Section <ref>) notes that defining culture is inherently difficult given its nuanced complexities, while isolating associated knowledge and differentiating across groups proves even more challenging. Moreover, as cultural norms and practices vary widely, identifying comparable knowledge structures across groups remains elusive. The first task is therefore to identify topics common across groups that allow like-for-like comparisons, thereby demonstrating the relevance of culture-dependent commonsense knowledge representation.

They aim to achieve better computational efficiency compared to dense methods by only processing a subset of high-quality sensory information while providing a more dense and informative map compared to sparse methods. To execute SLAM efficiently on mobile robots and meet real-time and power constraint requirements, the efficient software/hardware architecture implementation in embedded systems, especially on FPGAs, has been explored in diverse ways in recent years, and some of them are summarized in Tab. <ref>.
new_text: To address the trade-off between computational intensity and mapping accuracy inherent in the extreme approaches of dense and sparse methods, a family of techniques termed *semi-dense SLAM* has emerged <cit.>. These methods aim to balance computational efficiency with the richness of the reconstructed environment by selectively processing only the most reliable sensory data—such as high-contrast regions or well-textured features—while still generating a denser, more informative representation than purely sparse approaches. By reducing the volume of data required for real-time processing, semi-dense SLAM systems are particularly well-suited for resource-constrained platforms, such as mobile robots, where power consumption and computational latency are critical limitations. To further enhance efficiency, researchers have increasingly focused on optimizing the implementation of these algorithms in embedded systems, especially leveraging hardware like FPGAs (Field-Programmable Gate Arrays), which enable parallelism and low-power execution. We figured out the reason to be a discontinuity in the domain of yaw. Yaw value jumps discontinuously from π to -π as can be seen in Figure <ref>. This discontinuity causes inferior performance since with ever so slight orientation change of face, the model is expected to change its prediction to π from -π or vice versa. Additionally, when θ_gt = π - ϵ gets predicted as -π, the loss becomes proportional to 2π instead of being proportional to ϵ thereby misguiding the learning. new_text: The model proposed by Kellnhofer et al. <cit.> directly predicted θ and ϕ. We observed that this approach resulted in significant losses when predicting backward gazes. The root cause was identified as a discontinuity in the yaw domain: the yaw value exhibits a discontinuous jump from π to -π (see Figure <ref>). This discontinuity leads to inferior performance because even a slight orientation change of the face requires the model to switch its prediction from π to -π or vice versa. Moreover, when θ_gt = π - ϵ is predicted as -π, the loss becomes proportional to 2π instead of ϵ, thereby misguiding the learning process. To address this issue, we employ a target space transformation, predicting sin(θ), cos(θ), and sin(ϕ) instead.

Traditionally, batch systems in most RJMS software support the execution of only rigid jobs, i.e., the number of processors allocated remain fixed during the entire job duration <cit.>. An example of this is SLURM <cit.> which is an open-source, scalable workload manager installed in six of the top ten supercomputers in the world. Therefore, to support expand/shrink operations and the management of different job types current batch systems need to be extended. In this paper, we extend the batch system in SLURM to support the combined scheduling of rigid MPI and malleable iMPI based applications. We present two novel job scheduling strategies to support performance-aware and power-aware dynamic reconfiguration decisions. The performance-aware strategy utilizes the heuristic criterion MPI to Compute Time (MTCT) ratio of running jobs for efficient expand/shrink decisions. The power-aware strategy supports dynamic power corridor management for HPC systems. If the power consumption of the system violates the limits of the power corridor, then appropriate node redistribution or scheduling decisions are taken to reinforce it.
We evaluate and compare the performance of our performance-aware strategy against other state-of-the-art strategies wrt system and user-centric metrics by utilizing a workload with varying number of rigid and malleable jobs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our power-aware scheduling strategy for maintaining the system level dynamic power corridor.
new_text: Conventional batch systems in most Resource Job Management Systems (RJMS) are designed to handle exclusively rigid jobs, where processor allocations remain static throughout the job’s execution <cit.>. SLURM <cit.>, an open-source and scalable workload manager deployed in six of the world’s top ten supercomputers, exemplifies such systems. To enable expand/shrink operations and accommodate diverse job types, existing batch systems require enhancements. This study proposes an extension to SLURM’s batch system to facilitate joint scheduling of rigid Message Passing Interface (MPI) and malleable Intel MPI (iMPI) applications. We introduce two novel scheduling approaches: a performance-aware strategy that leverages the heuristic metric of MPI to Compute Time (MTCT) ratio for optimal dynamic reconfiguration decisions, and a power-aware strategy that manages dynamic power corridors in high-performance computing (HPC) environments. When system power consumption exceeds corridor thresholds, the latter strategy triggers node redistribution or scheduling adjustments to realign with constraints. The efficacy of the performance-aware approach is evaluated against state-of-the-art methods using system- and user-centric metrics, tested across a workload with varying proportions of rigid and malleable jobs. Additionally, we demonstrate the power-aware strategy’s capability to maintain system-wide power corridor compliance under dynamic conditions.

old_text: Strategies for efficient resource management and job scheduling of malleable applications have been extensively studied in the literature. However, most of the papers utilize the equipartitioning strategy <cit.> and are evaluated using simulations <cit.>. In contrast to the above approaches, some prototypes which combine a dynamic resource manager along with an adaptive job scheduler have been developed. Utrera et al. <cit.> propose a FCFS-malleable job scheduling strategy based on the principal of virtual malleability (VM). In VM, the original number of processes are preserved, and the job is allowed to adapt to changes in the number of CPUs at runtime. old_text: In MIH <cit.>, the KNN search problem with Hamming distance is solved through solving the R-Near Neighbor (RNN) search problem with Hamming distance. The goal of the RNN search problem to find all data points lying at distance at most R from the query point. To solve the KNN search problem with Hamming distance, first, a hash table is populated with the binary codes in G. Then, starting from a Hamming radius equal to zero, R=0, the procedure increases R and then solves the RNN search problem by searching among the buckets at the Hamming distance R from the query. This procedure iterates until K binary codes are retrieved. In <cit.>, the author mentioned that the KNN problem with weighted Hamming distance can be solved by the same way. In other words, the procedure increases R and then searches among the buckets at the Hamming distance R from the query. The procedure iterates until (more than) K binary codes are retrieved and then culls them according to the weighted Hamming distance to find the query's K nearest neighbor in the weighted Hamming space. However, this method cannot return the exact K nearest neighbors in the weighted Hamming space. When increasing the search radius R progressively until K binary codes are found, it guarantees that the binary codes that are found yield smaller Hamming distance to the query than the ones that are not found. In contrast, it cannot guarantee that these binary codes have the smaller weighted Hamming distance with the query than the ones that are not found. The binary codes which have the larger Hamming distance with the query may have the smaller weighted Hamming distance.
new_text: In MIH <cit.>, the KNN search problem with Hamming distance is addressed by solving the R-Near Neighbor (RNN) search problem under the same metric. The RNN problem seeks all data points at Hamming distance ≤R from the query. To solve KNN, a hash table is first populated with binary codes in G. Starting at R=0, R increments iteratively; at each step, the RNN problem is solved by querying buckets at the current Hamming distance R. This continues until K codes are retrieved. In <cit.>, the same approach is extended to weighted Hamming distance. Here, R increments iteratively, buckets at distance R are queried, and once more than K codes are retrieved, they are culled based on weighted Hamming distance to identify the K nearest neighbors. However, this method cannot guarantee exact K nearest neighbors in the weighted Hamming space. While incremental R ensures retrieved codes have smaller Hamming distance than uncollected ones, this guarantee does not extend to weighted Hamming distance. Codes with larger Hamming distances may have smaller weighted Hamming distances, undermining exactness.

old_text: One of the first concerns that arise when using simulation as a proxy environment is realism and performance. On the one hand, we would like the simulator to behave as close as possible as the real world. For that, we need to include detailed 3D meshes that model the real life component. On the other hand, we want the simulator to be efficient enough so it can execute a large number of simulations, and detailed mesh models make collision detection more complex.
new_text: A primary challenge in employing simulation as an approximate environment involves balancing realism with computational performance. To accurately mirror real-world conditions, simulators must incorporate high-fidelity 3D mesh representations of physical components. However, this requirement conflicts with the need for efficient simulation execution, as complex geometric models increase computational demands—particularly in collision detection—limiting the number of feasible simulations (Smith et al., 2021).

For our version of MAB, each cache replacement algorithm is thought of as an “expert” that recommends which of the K items in the cache to evict on every miss. We assume that each algorithm is allowed a limited size “history” to keep track of recent evictions, and to help in its decision making.

The history also provides a natural aging mechanism for recent evictions. If the item is still in history, feedback on its eviction is considered valuable and is used; otherwise, it is assumed that a significant amount of time has passed, and the feedback is ignored.
For an eviction that occurred at time (or step or round) t', the delayed feedback offered at time t≥ t' is denoted by the indicator function, f_(t',t)∈{0,1}. If feedback arrives at time t, then f_(t',t) = 1, and is 0 otherwise.
The delay function is given by d(t)=t-t' ∈ [1,m], where m is the delay threshold (as well as the history size).
new_text: The history provides a natural aging mechanism for evictions. If an item remains in the history, its eviction feedback is considered valid and is used; otherwise, feedback is disregarded, as sufficient time has elapsed. For an eviction at time t', delayed feedback at time t ≥ t' is defined by the indicator function f_(t',t) ∈ {0,1}, where f_(t',t) = 1 if feedback arrives at t; otherwise, 0. The delay function is d(t) = t − t' ∈ [1,m], where m denotes the delay threshold (and history size).

new_text: Ensuring that each task effectively benefits from multi-task learning becomes increasingly challenging as the number of tasks grows. In `N-LTP`, we adopt a strategy inspired by BAM <cit.>, employing knowledge distillation to address this issue, as illustrated in Figure <ref>. This approach involves two key stages: first, we train individual models for each task to serve as "teacher" models. Then, during the learning phase, `N-LTP` integrates knowledge from both these teacher models and the original gold-standard labels. By doing so, the framework simultaneously leverages the specialized knowledge captured by each task's teacher model while remaining grounded in directly labeled data. A hyperparameter λ is introduced to balance the influence of the teacher models' guidance against the reliability of the gold-standard labels, allowing for flexible adaptation to the specific characteristics of the task set.

We consider the cache management problem, which is a classic resource allocation problem from storage systems.
The LeCaR algorithm is a recent cache replacement algorithm that uses online reinforcement learning to help decide which entry to evict when a new item is to be stored in the cache following a “cache miss” <cit.>.
LeCaR relies on only two very fundamental cache replacement policies, namely the Least Recently Used (LRU) policy and the Least Frequently Used (LFU) policy.
As a result, N=2 represents the number of experts in LeCaR.
LeCaR assumes that the best strategy at any given time is a probabilistic mix of the two policies and attempts to “learn” the optimal mix using a regret minimization strategy.
With a slight modification, the LeCaR <cit.> cache replacement algorithm is an instance of EXP-DFDC: the position of an item in history is a reflection of the delay in feedback for its eviction decision, and is bounded by the history size. The regret is greatest if an item is requested immediately after its eviction. Else, as time wears on, until a threshold is reached, the regret continues to decay. If it is not present in the history, then the feedback is ignored, thus making its regret equal to zero.
Cache management can be thought of as a special case of the MAB problem, and LeCaR can be considered as an application-specific version of EXP4-DFDC with two experts, delayed feedback and decaying losses, and has been shown to have vanishing regret over time. We note that LeCaR outperforms other state-of-the-art cache replacement algorithms for small cache sizes <cit.> with a fixed learning rate of 0.45. From our analysis, we demonstrate that it is possible to infer the learning rate in this class of algorithm without it being fixed a priori. Details of the mathematical proof of vanishing regret can be found in a forthcoming manuscript.
new_text: The cache management problem, a foundational resource allocation challenge in storage systems, involves determining which data entries to retain or remove when new items require storage after a cache miss. The LeCaR algorithm, a recent cache replacement approach, employs online reinforcement learning to select eviction strategies, integrating two elementary policies: the Least Recently Used (LRU) and Least Frequently Used (LFU) principles. Here, N=2 denotes the count of base policies, or "experts," considered. LeCaR posits that the optimal policy at any moment is a stochastic combination of these two strategies, optimized via regret minimization. With minor adjustments, LeCaR aligns with the EXP-DFDC framework, where an item’s historical position encodes the delay in feedback for its eviction decision, constrained by the history buffer size. Regret peaks when an item is requested immediately post-eviction but diminishes over time until a threshold, with zero regret if the item is absent from the history. Cache management is thus a specialized form of the multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem, and LeCaR serves as an application-specific EXP4-DFDC variant with two experts, delayed feedback, and decaying loss estimates, achieving proven vanishing regret. Experimental results confirm that LeCaR outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms for small cache sizes <cit.> using a fixed learning rate of 0.45. Our analysis further demonstrates that adaptive learning rate inference is feasible within this algorithm class, negating the need for a priori fixes. Detailed proofs for the vanishing regret property are outlined in an upcoming work.

Our meta-learning approach follows the paradigm in <cit.> by having two components: the base learner and a meta-learner. The aim of the base learner is to learn to perform a new task. It is, therefore, task-specific. The meta-learner, on the other hand, generalizes over a vast number of tasks. The main goal of the meta-learner is to learn a representation that is used by the task-specific base learner.
In a few-shot classification setting, a task T={S, Q} is characterized by a set of unlabeled query images Q = {x̃_j, ỹ_j}_j=1^Ñ which need to be classified, given only a few labeled image exemplars, called the support set S = {x_j, y_j}_j=1^N.
Here x_j and x̃_j are the j^th image samples in the support and query sets, respectively. The corresponding labels in the support and query sets are denoted by y_j and ỹ_j, respectively. The support set contains N=k× n image-label pairs, i.en examples for each of the k classes. Such a setting is called a k-way, n-shot classification problem. The query set Q contains Ñ image-label pairs with the images sampled from the same class set as the support samples. For a given task, the support and query labels share the same label space L={1,2,…, k}. The task support samples and the query samples for task T are sampled from a data split D of dataset 𝒟. Here, D∈{D_train, D_val, D_test} and, D_train, D_val and D_test are the train, validation and test splits of 𝒟. The dataset 𝒟 also defines the domain of the few-shot classification problem. The train, validation and test data splits are mutually disjoint and contain no common samples. Further, to measure the meta network's generalization to unseen categories, the class sets for the train, validation and test splits (C_train, C_val and C_test respectively) are chosen to be pairwise disjoint.

Another line of research partitions the parameter space into task-agnostic and task-specific parameters. The latter are learned explicitly for each task, while the former remain fixed.
Bertinetto et al <cit.> utilize a closed-form solution of the base learner, formulated as a ridge regression problem.
More recently, MetaOptNet <cit.> employs a Support Vector Machine (SVM) as the task-specific model. Gradients are back-propagated through the SVM learning during meta-training using implicit differentiation of the optimality conditions of the convex problem.
While achieving promising performance, both these works <cit.> are restricted to specific types of task-specific models.
In contrast, our approach allows for more general and flexible learning objectives. This enables us to, for instance, integrate entropy-based transductive learning during the meta-training stage. Moreover, in contrast to previous optimization-based few-shot classification methods, we propose to learn aspects of the task-specific learning formulation itself.
new_text: Recent work partitions the parameter space into task-agnostic (fixed) and task-specific (explicitly learned per task) parameters. Bertinetto et al. <cit.> employ a closed-form ridge regression solution for the base learner, while MetaOptNet <cit.> uses an SVM for the task-specific model, back-propagating gradients through meta-training via implicit differentiation of its convex optimality conditions. Both these approaches <cit.>, despite their success, are limited to specific task-specific models. Our approach enables general, flexible learning objectives, such as entropy-based transductive learning during meta-training, and unlike previous optimization-based methods, learns aspects of the task-specific formulation itself.

In this paper, we propose Pea-KD (Parameter-efficient and accurate Knowledge Distillation), a novel approach to KD. Pea-KD consists of two main parts: Shuffled Parameter Sharing (SPS) and Pretraining with Teacher's Predictions (PTP). Using this combination, we are capable of alleviating the KD's limitations. SPS is a new parameter sharing method that allows a greater model complexity for the student model. PTP is a KD-specialized initialization method, which can act as a good initial guide for the student.
	When combined, this method yields a significant increase in student model's performance.
	Experiments conducted on different datasets and tasks show that the proposed approach improves the student model's performance by 4.4% on average in four GLUE tasks, outperforming existing KD baselines by significant margins.
new_text: In this paper, we propose Pea-KD (Parameter-efficient and accurate Knowledge Distillation), a novel approach to knowledge distillation (KD) designed to address limitations in existing methods. Pea-KD integrates two complementary strategies: Shuffled Parameter Sharing (SPS) and Pretraining with Teacher’s Predictions (PTP). SPS is a parameter sharing mechanism that reorganizes weights between the teacher and student models to increase the student’s effective capacity without inflating its parameter count, enabling it to capture more complex patterns. PTP, conversely, pretrains the student model using the teacher’s predictions as soft labels, providing a task-specific initialization that aligns the student’s learning trajectory with the teacher’s strengths. By combining these components, Pea-KD simultaneously improves the student’s capacity to retain critical knowledge and ensures a more informed training process. This collaborative effect translates to measurable performance gains. Empirical evaluation across diverse datasets and tasks demonstrates the effectiveness of Pea-KD: on four GLUE benchmarks, the approach achieves an average performance improvement of 4.4%, significantly outperforming conventional KD methods. These results highlight how SPS and PTP synergistically overcome inefficiencies in knowledge transfer and model initialization.

As briefly covered in Section <ref>, KD transfers knowledge from a well-trained and large teacher model to a smaller student model. KD uses the teacher model’s predictions on top of the true labels to train the student model. It is proven through many experiments that the student model learns to imitate the soft distribution of the teacher model’s predictions, and ultimately performs better than learning solely from the original data.
There have already been many attempts to compress BERT using KD. Patient Knowledge Distillation (<cit.>) extracts knowledge not only from the final prediction of the teacher, but also from the intermediate layers. TinyBERT (<cit.>) uses a two-stage learning framework which applies knowledge distillation in both pretraining and task-specific finetuning. DistilBERT (<cit.>) uses half of the layers of BERT-base model and applies KD during pretraining and finetuning of BERT. <cit.> trains the student model with smaller vocabulary set and lower hidden state dimensions.
Unfortunately, these existing methods do not give sufficient accuracy due to the student model's insufficient complexity and absence of a clear guideline for initialization.
In this paper, we propose a new KD approach using parameter sharing and KD-specific initialization to alleviate the above issues. Our method improves the student model's performance significantly and shows the state-of-the-art performance among distillation methods on BERT.

Knowledge Distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from a well-trained, large teacher model to a smaller student model, as outlined in Section <ref>. It utilizes the teacher model’s predictions alongside true labels to train the student model. Numerous experiments have demonstrated that the student model learns to imitate the teacher model’s soft probability distribution, resulting in improved performance compared to learning from the original data alone.  
Many studies have attempted to compress BERT using KD. Patient Knowledge Distillation (<cit.>) leverages knowledge not only from the teacher’s final predictions but also from intermediate layers. TinyBERT (<cit.>) employs a two-stage learning framework that applies knowledge distillation during both pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning. DistilBERT (<cit.>) reduces the number of layers to half that of the BERT-base model and applies KD during pretraining and fine-tuning. <cit.> employs a smaller vocabulary and reduced hidden state dimensions to train the student model.  
However, these approaches often fall short in terms of accuracy due to the student model’s limited capacity and lack of clear initialization guidelines. In this paper, we propose a novel KD approach that incorporates parameter sharing and KD-specific initialization to address these limitations. Our method significantly enhances student model performance and achieves state-of-the-art results among BERT distillation methods.

Gupta et al. <cit.> utilize a probabilistic framework integrated with support vector machines (SVMs) to anticipate cascading failures, offering early warnings to enhance system resilience. Eskandarpour and Khodaei <cit.> present an ML-based predictive approach to assess power grid component outages triggered by approaching hurricanes, employing logistic regression to establish the classifier’s decision boundary for predicting both the count of failed components and their downtime. Glavic et al. <cit.> and Huang et al. <cit.> investigate reinforcement learning for power system emergency control, aiming to improve response strategies during crises. Additionally, regression and data mining techniques are applied by Guikema <cit.> to estimate post-hurricane pole replacement requirements.

D-EIGAN consists of two steps repeated in sequence until convergence. The first is local updating, in which each ℰ^(k) conducts a series of δ minibatch SGD iterations. For each minibatch, training proceeds as in the centralized case, with the encoder, allies, and adversaries parameters updated via SGD to minimize the log-losses ℒ_E^(k), ℒ_A_i^(k), and ℒ_V_j^(k) defined as in (<ref>) but in this case for each node. The second step is global aggregation, in which each ℰ^(k) uploads its locally-trained encoder to the parameter server to construct a global version, after every δ SGD iterations. We introduce a sparsification technique here in which each node selects a fraction ϕ of its parameters at random to upload for each aggregation. Letting 𝒬_k be the indices chosen by ℰ^(k), then the vector recovered at the server is θ̃_E^(k) where θ̃_E^(k)(q) = θ_E^(k)(q) if q ∈𝒬_k and 0 otherwise. With this, the global aggregation becomes a weighted average θ_E = ∑_k N_k/Nθ̃_E^(k). Then, the server also selects a fraction ϕ of indices at random to synchronize each node k with on the downlink. Letting 𝒬 be the indices selected, then each k sets θ_E^(k)(q) = θ_E(q) if q ∈𝒬, and makes no change to the qth parameter otherwise. The pseudo-code of our algorithm is given in Alg. <ref>.

The second step involves global aggregation, where each ℰ^(k) uploads its locally trained encoder to the parameter server to construct a global version after every δ SGD iterations. We introduce a sparsification technique here: each node randomly selects a fraction ϕ of its parameters to upload during aggregation. Let 𝒬_k denote the set of indices selected by ℰ^(k). The server then reconstructs a vector θ̃_E^(k), where θ̃_E^(k)(q) = θ_E^(k)(q) if q ∈𝒬_k and 0 otherwise. The global encoder parameters are computed as a weighted average θ_E = ∑_k N_k/Nθ̃_E^(k). On the downlink, the server independently selects a fraction ϕ of indices for synchronization. Let 𝒬 represent these selected indices. For each node k, θ_E^(k)(q) is updated to θ_E(q) if q ∈𝒬, with no changes to other parameters. The algorithm's pseudocode is provided in Alg. <ref>.

Our interpretation process begins with extracting collocations of the vehicle and the topic individually using a relatively large corpus. Specifically, we use DepCC,[[URL]] a dependency-parsed “web-scale corpus” based on CommonCrawl.[[URL]] There are 365 million documents in the corpus, comprising about 252B tokens. Among other preprocessing steps, every sentence was given with word dependencies discovered by MaltParser <cit.>. We only use a fraction of the corpus containing some 1.7B tokens.
Here, we considered a “collocation” to be words that are found to be dependent in either the topic or the vehicle, and assigned with a relevant part-of-speech tag: adjective or verb+ing. The main assumption is that many potential modifiers of a given noun will appear somewhere in the corpus as a dependent in the dependency graph.
new_text: Our interpretation process begins by extracting collocations associated with both the vehicle and the topic using a large, preprocessed corpus. To achieve this, we selected the DepCC corpus[[URL]], a dependency-parsed resource derived from CommonCrawl[[URL]], which contains 365 million documents and approximately 252 billion tokens. This corpus was preprocessed to annotate grammatical dependencies in every sentence using MaltParser <cit.>, enabling identification of syntactic relationships between words. For practical computational reasons, we focused on a 1.7B-token subset of the full corpus. Here, we define a "collocation" as a word that grammatically depends on either the topic or vehicle noun, as indicated by dependency parses. We further restricted these collocations to those assigned a relevant part-of-speech tag: either adjectives or verbs in the "-ing" form. This filtering reflects the observation that potential modifiers of a noun often co-occur as grammatical dependents in real-world text. The underlying assumption is that by analyzing these dependency patterns, we can systematically identify words likely to function as attributes or descriptors of the target nouns, providing a linguistically grounded foundation for our analysis.

new_text: Our three Open Science pillars establish the dissemination conditions for research outputs, with licenses serving as critical components. Software is considered free only when it is released in compliance with the four freedoms outlined in the Free Software Foundation (FSF) definition; this compliance must be explicitly stated in the license—a legal document included in the software’s distribution package alongside the source code, compiled code, documentation, and other associated files. Actions such as running, loading, reproducing, translating, or modifying a computer program require corresponding written authorization <cit.>. In the absence of a license, the default legal assumption is that "All rights are reserved," meaning that—legally speaking—only the authors and rights holders may execute the software. A license thus defines the conditions under which software can be shared and disseminated.
