Adversarial attacks on ML models in discrete input spaces have been found to cause models to misclassify input samples by manipulating tokens in sequence data <cit.>. Adversarial Reprogramming (AR) is a technique <cit.> that is able to repurpose a model (without significant changes to the architecture and parameters) by training an adversary to optimally transform input data such that we can choose the output of the model. This method has been proven to be successful in both, white-box and black-box settings <cit.>. The depth and the size of large general language models make them ideal candidates to be adversarially reprogrammed, as modifying the internal architecture or finetuning over 1 billion parameters is infeasible for a traditional transfer learning approach. The work in <cit.> assumes an exposed model, where they use the learned parameters of the pre-trained source model to generate context-based vocabulary map. However, the hypothesis of comparable vocabulary size does not hold when the source data are English vocabularies (on the order of ∼ 10 million) and the target data are amino acids (on the order of ∼ 20). To that end, we introduce dictionary learning to train our AP.
new_text: Adversarial attacks on machine learning (ML) models in discrete input spaces have been shown to cause models to misclassify input samples by manipulating tokens in sequence data <cit.>. Adversarial Reprogramming (AR) is a technique <cit.> that repurposes a model without significant changes to the architecture and parameters by training an adversary to transform input data in a way that allows us to control the model’s output. This method has been proven successful in both white-box and black-box settings <cit.>. The depth and scale of large general language models make them ideal candidates for adversarial reprogramming, as modifying the internal architecture or fine-tuning over 1 billion parameters is infeasible for a traditional transfer learning approach. The work in <cit.> assumes an exposed model, where the learned parameters of the pre-trained source model are used to generate a context-based vocabulary map. However, the hypothesis of comparable vocabulary sizes does not hold when source data include English vocabularies (approximately 10 million tokens) and target data include amino acids (approximately 20 tokens). To address this, we introduce dictionary learning to train our AP.

old_text: Deep learning has proven to be an extremely successful tool for various applications for the natural sciences. While works like MoleculeNet have made significant progress in publishing benchmarks on various molecular learning tasks, curating substantial, well-structured and labeled molecule datasets remains a critical constraint in training high performing models from scratch to establish baselines for a multitude of tasks <cit.>. A lack of substantive training datsets motivates transfer learning to be a natural approach to solve problems in the molecule data domain, as it has proven to be a successful technique to solve new tasks using learned representations from source model domains <cit.>. In this paper, we consider an empirically successful transfer learning method, adversarial reprogramming, where a learned function adversarially perturbs input samples to the model such that the model can perform a task chosen by the adversary <cit.>. The motivations of the transfer learning approach lie in the recent successes of powerful general language models <cit.>, and being able to leverage these learned representations when applied to molecule data that can be treated as sequence data. However, the adversarial reprogramming method is well suited to models operating within a continuous input space (such as images), but discrete input spaces require that we learn a mapping between source-model space and target-model space. Reprogramming of text classifiers and language models has been explored <cit.>, as well as knowledge injection for general language models <cit.>, but such approaches do not investigate mappings between domains that require a very high representational capacity (from language data to molecule data). This shift in domain poses a significant challenge through the reduction of dimensionality of the input space. We end up with an overdetermined system, as we have more observations in the source-model input space than in the target-model input space. To address this, we use a dictionary learning approach to encode a sparse representation of the embeddings of the input data to the pre-trained language model (text classifier). Training the adversarial program (AP) via dictionary learning enables us to approximate a linear transformation (mapping) between the input spaces of the source and target models, it learns the optimal coefficients of the atoms in our molecule data to represent the dictionary. When compared to the baselines of training AMP models from scratch, repurposing a sentiment classifier via R2DL outperforms the baseline for AMP/non-AMP (90.01 % vs 88.0 %) and achieves approximately the same progress on toxicity prediction (89.34 % vs 93.7 %).

In this work, we explore how layer-wise local updates <cit.> can help overcome these challenges and scale more efficiently with compute than backpropagation.
With local updates, each layer is updated before even completing a full forward pass through the network.
This remedies the forward and backward locking problems which harm memory efficiency and update latency in standard backprop.
Layer-wise local updates
are not proportional to gradients of the original loss, and are not even guaranteed to descend a loss function.
Nevertheless, in practice they are effective at training neural networks.
We refer to this approach of parallelizing compute, which is alternative and complementary to data and model parallelism, as local parallelism.
new_text: This study investigates the potential of layer-wise local updates <cit.> to address these issues and achieve more efficient scaling with computational resources compared to traditional backpropagation. Local updates allow for the adjustment of each layer prior to completing a full forward pass across the entire network. This approach mitigates the forward and backward locking problems that negatively impact memory efficiency and the latency of updates in conventional backpropagation methods. However, these layer-wise local updates are not aligned with the gradients of the original loss function and do not ensure a descent in the loss. Despite this theoretical limitation, empirical results demonstrate their effectiveness in training neural networks. We term this method of computational parallelization—distinct from yet complementary to data and model parallelism—local parallelism.

Our contributions i) We are the first to study evasion attacks to LDA models. The study has significant practical impact as it provides early warning on the security vulnerability of LDA models to users and service providers. The derivation of the attack strategies provides insights into designing defense strategies against such attacks. ii) We formulate the evasion attack to LDA models as a combinatorial optimization problem and prove its NP-hardness. iii) We propose EvaLDA, a novel evasion attack algorithm to LDA models with key technical novelties in handling the various new challenges in the new problem. iv) We conduct extensive empirical evaluations that prove the effectiveness of EvaLDA on two distinct datasets (i.e., NIPS and AP[Links to the datasets are in the experiment section.]) and a large variety of problem settings. For instance, results on the NIPS dataset show that, by replacing only 1% of the words to similar words in a victim document, EvaLDA can averagely promote the rank of a target topic from 10 to around 7.

**Computation.**
Training a model like GPT-2 is a computationally expensive task that requires access to expensive hardware for long training times.
All models discussed in this paper are trained with eight parallel NVIDIA V100 32GB GPUs on
the Peregrine high performance computing cluster at the University of Groningen.
For efficient implementation of the models, we use PyTorch (1.6.0; ), PyTorch Lightning (0.9.0; ) and Transformers (3.0.2; ).
We implement four strategies to decrease general training time.
Firstly, the models are trained with 16-bit automatic mixed-precision training. This decreases training time with a factor of two to three times.
Secondly, we split each document in windows of 128 tokens instead of 1024 tokens when we only train the lexical embeddings.
Thirdly, we use bucketed random sampling. Items in minibatches are sampled from buckets of sequences of similar length, which decreases the amount of padding within minibatches.
Finally, we use maximum batch sizes that fit into GPU memory and use gradient accumulation in order to do backpropagation only for every 2000 sequences.
The models are trained with the Adam optimiser <cit.> and initial learning rates are chosen based on the steepest loss slope with gradually increasing learning rates <cit.>.

To the best of our knowledge, our paper is the first that specifically addresses outcome prediction in multifocal cancer with medical imaging and machine learning. We propose an end-to-end autoencoder-based multiple instance neural network (AMINN) that predicts multifocal CRLM patient outcome based on radiomic features extracted from contrast-enhanced 3D MRIs. This model is jointly trained to reconstruct input radiomic features with an autoencoder branch and to make prediction with a multiple instance branch, which allows for learning prognosis-relevant representations of tumors. The multiple instance neural network then aggregates the representations of all tumors of a patient for survival prediction. new_text: We hypothesize that leveraging features from all lesions in multifocal cancer improves outcome prediction. To our knowledge, this is the first work addressing outcome prediction in multifocal cancer via medical imaging and machine learning. We propose an end-to-end autoencoder-based multiple instance neural network (AMINN) to predict multifocal CRLM patient outcomes from contrast-enhanced 3D MRI radiomic features. This model jointly trains an autoencoder branch to reconstruct input features and a multiple instance branch to predict survival, enabling learning of prognosis-relevant tumor representations. The multiple instance branch then aggregates patient-level tumor representations for survival prediction. A radiomic feature transformation technique tailored for deep learning is also proposed. Ablation experiments validate each framework component’s contribution.

To overcome these issues, we propose a novel SBR approach upon hypergraph to model the high-order relations among items within sessions. Conceptually, a hypergraph <cit.> is composed of a vertex set and a hyperedge set, where a hyperedge can connect any numbers of vertices, which can be used to encode high-order data correlations. We also assume that items in a session are temporally correlated but not strictly sequentially dependent. The characteristics of hyperedge perfectly fit our assumption as hyperedge is set-like, which emphasizes coherence of the involved elements rather than relative orders. Therefore, it provides us with a flexibility and capability to capture complex interactions in sessions. Technically, we first model each session as a hyperedge in which all the items are connected with each other, and different hyperedges, which are connected via shared items, constitute the hypergraph that contains the item-level high-order correlations. Then a line graph is built based on the hypergraph by modeling each hyperedge as a node and focuses on the connectivity of hyperedges, which depicts the session-level relations. To overcome these issues, we propose a novel session-based recommendation (SBR) approach based on a hypergraph to model higher-order relations among items within sessions. Conceptually, a hypergraph <cit.> is composed of a vertex set and a hyperedge set, where a hyperedge can connect any number of vertices, which can be used to encode higher-order data correlations. We also assume that items in a session are temporally correlated but not strictly sequentially dependent. The characteristics of a hyperedge perfectly align with our assumption, as a hyperedge is set-like, emphasizing the coherence of the involved elements rather than their relative orders. Therefore, it provides us with the flexibility and capability to capture complex interactions in sessions. Technically, we first model each session as a hyperedge in which all the items are connected to each other, and different hyperedges, connected via shared items, constitute the hypergraph capturing item-level higher-order correlations. A line graph is then constructed from the hypergraph by modeling each hyperedge as a node and focusing on the connectivity of hyperedges, which captures session-level relations. Subsequently, a Dual-channel Hypergraph Convolutional Network (DHCN) is proposed to capture the complex item correlations and cross-session information through its two channels, corresponding to the two graphs, respectively. Figure <ref> illustrates the hypergraph construction and the pipeline of the proposed method. By stacking multiple layers in the two channels, we can leverage the strengths of hypergraph convolution to generate high-quality recommendation results. However, since each hyperedge only contains a limited number of items, the inherent data sparsity issue might limit the benefits brought by hypergraph modeling. To address this problem, we innovatively integrate self-supervised learning <cit.> into our model to enhance hypergraph modeling. Intuitively, the two channels in our network can be seen as two distinct views that describe intra- and inter-session information, respectively, with each channel lacking knowledge of the other. By maximizing the mutual information between the session representations learned via the two channels through self-supervised learning, the two channels can gain new information from each other to improve their performance in item/session feature extraction. We further unify the recommendation task and the self-supervised task under a primary-and-auxiliary learning framework. By jointly optimizing the two tasks, the performance of the recommendation task achieves significant improvements.

Containerisation ensures compatibility of applications and their environment by encapsulating applications with their libraries and configuration files <cit.>, thus enables users to move and deploy programs easily among clusters. Containerisation is a virtualisation technology <cit.>. Rather than starting a holistically simulated OS on top of the host kernel as in a Virtual Machine (VM), a container only shares the host kernel. This feature makes containers more lightweight than VM. Containers are dedicated to run micro-services and one container mostly hosts one application. Nevertheless, containerised applications can become complex, e.g. thousands of separate containers may be required in production. Recently, fairness has started to become an important topic in ML, because as ML models are deployed in various applications (e.g., banking or law enforcement), the decisions made on their outputs may severely impact some minorities due to the presence of bias in data.
Different ML tasks have been considered, e.g., classification <cit.>, ranking <cit.>, sequential-decision making <cit.> or clustering <cit.>.
Most of such work focuses on the impartiality aspect of fairness, expressed at the individual or group level, which leads to a constrained-based or penalty-based formulation.
However, some recent work
<cit.> advocates the approach based on fair social welfare function that we also adopt in this work.
new_text: Fairness has emerged as a critical consideration in machine learning, as models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as banking or law enforcement, where biased data can disproportionately affect marginalized groups through algorithmic decisions. A range of machine learning tasks has been studied in this context, including classification <cit.>, ranking <cit.>, sequential-decision making <cit.>, and clustering <cit.>. Much of this body of work centers on the concept of impartiality, defined at either the individual or group level, which has led to the development of constrained-based or penalty-based optimization strategies. However, a distinct line of recent research <cit.> advocates for an approach grounded in fair social welfare functions—this perspective, which we also adopt in this work, prioritizes equitable outcomes through a societal utility lens.

Exploiting the third dimension.  
The analysis above shows that the temporal dimension contributes to an increase in runtime and therefore impedes performance (given an optimal 2D mapping). Adding a third spatial dimension can alleviate this bottleneck. In the context of WS and IS dataflow, this translates to mapping the M and N dimensions into the new spatial dimension. For example, if we have a 3D stacked architecture comprising two planar arrays, in WS dataflow, half the rows of matrix A would be mapped to the top-tier array, while the other half would be mapped to the bottom-tier array. For IS dataflow, the mapping is similar, but the roles of matrices A and B are reversed. Please note that no communication is required between arrays across different tiers. This is equivalent to a distributed array, and such acceleration lends itself to the well-studied model parallelism approach <cit.>.

One of the main challenges of forgetting in deep networks is how to estimate the effects of a given training sample on the parameters of the model, which has lead the research to focus on simpler convex learning problem such as linear or logistic regression, for which a theoretical analysis is feasible.
To address this problem, Mixed-Linear Forgetting uses a first-order Taylor-series inspired decomposition of the network to learn two sets of weights: a core set _c which is trained only with the core data _c using a standard (non-convex) algorithm, and a set of linear of user weights, which is trained to minimize a quadratic loss function on the changeable user data .
The core weights are learned through standard training (since forgetting is not required on core data), while the user weights are obtained as the solution to a strongly convex quadratic optimization problem.
This allows us to remove influence of a subset of the data with strong guarantees. Moreover, by construction, simply setting to zero the user weights removes influence of all changeable data with the lowest possible drop in performance, thus easily allowing the user to remove all of their data at the same time.
new_text: A significant hurdle in forgetting mechanisms for deep learning models is quantifying the impact of individual training samples on model parameters. To facilitate theoretical analysis, much work has shifted focus to simplified convex problems like linear or logistic regression. Mixed-Linear Forgetting tackles this issue via a decomposition method inspired by a first-order Taylor series expansion, learning two distinct weight components: (1) a core set of weights trained using standard non-convex optimization on fixed core data _c, and (2) a set of linear user weights trained to minimize quadratic loss over mutable user data. The core weights are updated conventionally (as forgetting is unnecessary for core data), whereas the user weights are derived from a strongly convex quadratic optimization problem. This framework ensures rigorous guarantees for data removal; critically, zeroing user weights entirely eliminates influence of all changeable data while incurring minimal performance loss, enabling instant removal of a user’s entire dataset with a single operation.

new_text: Study of λ. In SAHR, there is a hyper-parameter λ, i.e., the weight for regularizer loss. A larger λ implies that the model must incur a higher penalty to adjust the standard deviations. This suggests that we are more confident in the manually constructed ground-truth heatmaps. A smaller λ indicates that we allow the model to adjust the standard deviations independently for each keypoint. We compare the performance of HrHRNet-W32 + SAHR with different λ values on the COCO val2017 dataset. As shown in Table <ref>, when λ = +∞, meaning the model is not allowed to adjust standard deviations, it degrades to the original baseline model. Overall, the improvements from SA are not too sensitive to λ, as the results remain consistent when λ = 1 and λ = 0.5. However, when λ becomes too small, i.e., λ = 0.1, the model can significantly adjust the standard deviations, but may not be reliable enough. In such cases, the improvements could be compromised.

old_text: In this paper, we present a systematic robustness evaluation of language understanding in task-oriented dialog systems from three aspects: language variety, speech characteristics, and noise perturbation. And accordingly, we develop four data augmentation methods to approximate these language phenomena. new_text: This study conducts a systematic assessment of robustness in language understanding (LU) for task-oriented dialog systems across three dimensions: linguistic diversity, speech-related features, and noise-induced variations. Correspondingly, four data augmentation techniques were designed to mimic these linguistic and acoustic phenomena. Extensive experiments and detailed analysis were performed on the MultiWOZ 2.3 dataset, evaluating both classification-based and generation-based LU models. Significant performance degradation observed in all models when tested on augmented data suggests that addressing these robustness challenges remains a crucial and non-trivial task.

Humans perceive the world through many modalities, such as sound, vision and language.
Even though any individual modality might be incomplete or noisy, important information are still perceivable since they tend to be shared or enhance each other.
With this motivation, we propose a unified-modal pre-training method UNIMO to learn representations that capture modality-invariant information at the semantic level.
Different from previous methods, UNIMO can learn from different modalities of data, including images, texts and image-text pairs, thus achieving more robust and generalizable representations for both textual and visual input.
new_text: Humans perceive the world through multiple modalities, such as sound, vision, and language. While individual modalities may be incomplete or noisy, critical information remains perceivable due to shared or complementary cues across modalities. Motivated by this observation, we propose a unified-modal pre-training method, UNIMO, to learn representations that capture modality-invariant information at the semantic level. Unlike previous approaches, UNIMO leverages multiple data modalities—images, texts, and image-text pairs—thereby enabling more robust and generalizable representations for both textual and visual inputs.

old_text: Many Question-Answering (QA) datasets contain unanswerable questions, but their treatment in QA systems remains primitive. Our analysis of the Natural Questions <cit.> dataset reveals that a substantial portion of unanswerable questions (∼21%) can be explained based on the presence of unverifiable presuppositions. We discuss the shortcomings of current models in handling such questions, and describe how an improved system could handle them. Through a user preference study, we demonstrate that the oracle behavior of our proposed system that provides responses based on presupposition failure is preferred over the oracle behavior of existing QA systems. Then we discuss how our proposed system could be implemented, presenting a novel framework that breaks down the problem into three steps: presupposition generation, presupposition verification and explanation generation. We report our progress in tackling each subproblem, and present a preliminary approach to integrating these steps into an existing QA system. We find that adding presuppositions and their verifiability to an existing model yields modest gains in downstream performance and unanswerability detection. The biggest bottleneck is the verification component, which needs to be substantially improved for the integrated system to approach ideal behavior—even transfer from the best entailment models currently falls short.
new_text: Many Question-Answering (QA) datasets include unanswerable questions, yet QA systems often lack effective strategies to address them. Current approaches typically treat these questions in rudimentary ways, such as simply classifying them as unanswerable without deeper analysis. To investigate this issue, we conducted a detailed analysis of the Natural Questions dataset <cit.> and discovered that approximately 21% of unanswerable questions stem from the presence of unverifiable presuppositions—assumptions embedded in the question that cannot be confirmed using available evidence. This finding highlights a critical gap: existing models struggle to detect or reason about such presuppositions, which limits their ability to provide meaningful responses. To address this, we propose a system designed to explicitly handle presupposition-related unanswerability. Through a user preference study, we compared an oracle version of our system—where responses are generated based on identifying presupposition failure—to oracle versions of existing QA systems. The results showed a clear preference for our approach, indicating that users value explanations tied to unverifiable assumptions. To realize this system, we introduce a novel framework that decomposes the problem into three sequential steps: first, identifying potential presuppositions within a question; second, verifying whether these presuppositions can be supported by the given context; and third, generating an explanation for the unanswerability when verification fails. We outline progress on each subtask and describe preliminary methods for integrating these components into existing QA pipelines. While augmenting a baseline model with presupposition and verifiability information leads to modest improvements in unanswerability detection and downstream task performance, our experiments reveal a key limitation: the verification component remains underdeveloped. Even state-of-the-art entailment models, when repurposed for verification, fall short of achieving ideal performance, underscoring the urgent need for more robust methods in this stage.

old_text: Finally, recent works in the community, e.g. <cit.>, have explored the susceptibility of the conventional one-hot encoding of the otuput to adversarial attacks. By borrowing arguments from coding theory, the authors examine the effect of encoding the output using error-correcting output codes in the adversarial scenario. The experimental results suggest that such an encoding technique greatly enhances the robustness of a considered architecture while retaining high classification accuracy in the benign context; in addition, it does not require to craft a method explicitly designed to address adversarial attacks with deeply analyzed and taken care of characteristics.
new_text: Finally, recent studies in the field, such as <cit.>, have investigated how the traditional one-hot encoding of model outputs may be particularly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. These works leverage principles from coding theory to analyze the potential benefits of replacing the standard encoding with error-correcting output codes (ECOCs). By encoding class labels using codes designed to correct errors—a technique commonly used in communication systems to combat noise—the authors assess whether such an approach can mitigate adversarial influences in machine learning models. Experimental results indicate that ECOCs significantly improve the robustness of the evaluated architectures under adversarial attacks, without compromising their performance on standard, non-adversarial data. Importantly, this approach achieves these improvements without necessitating the development of attack-specific defenses or detailed prior knowledge of an attacker's strategies, offering a general-purpose solution rooted in established theoretical frameworks.

new_text: In our analysis, as shown in Figure <ref>, we observed a consistent trend in both the base and large model configurations: the performance of the Joint Top-k method improves when the number of selected top-k documents is increased. This improvement suggests that the Joint Top-k approach can better integrate information from multiple context documents compared to the Individual Top-k method, which treats each document in isolation. The ability to synthesize cross-document insights likely enhances the system’s capacity to construct accurate answers. Conversely, we also observed that as the top-k count rises, the marginal benefit of updating the query encoder during training diminishes. This phenomenon aligns with the relatively modest gains in retrieval performance seen during joint training, indicating that the encoder’s contribution to optimization becomes less critical when a larger number of documents are already being leveraged. These findings highlight trade-offs between model complexity and the value of additional context in retrieval-augmented systems.

old_text: (1) We design a novel edge-preserving cost volume upsampling module based on the learned bilateral grid. It can efficiently obtain high resolution cost volume for disparity estimation from a low resolution cost volume via slicing operation. With this module, the cost volume aggregations (e.g. 3D convolutions) can be performed at low resolution. The proposed cost volume upsampling module can be seamlessly embedded into many existing networks such as GCNet, PSMNet and GANet. The resulting networks can be accelerated 4∼29 times while maintaining comparable accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first time that the differential bilateral grid operation is applied in deep stereo matching network.
new_text: We propose a novel module for upsampling cost volumes that preserves edge details, leveraging the concept of the learned bilateral grid. This module is designed to efficiently generate high-resolution cost volumes required for accurate disparity estimation, starting from a low-resolution input, through a slicing operation that maintains critical structural details. By performing this upscaling step, the computationally intensive aggregation processes—such as 3D convolutions—can be executed at the lower resolution, thereby reducing the overall computational load. This approach enables the module to integrate seamlessly into existing stereo matching architectures like GCNet, PSMNet, and GANet, as these frameworks can be modified to perform key operations at the reduced resolution before final upscaling. Networks incorporating the proposed module achieve a significant speed improvement—4 to 29 times faster—while retaining performance levels comparable to their original high-resolution counterparts. Notably, this is the first instance of applying a differential bilateral grid operation within a deep stereo matching network, marking a departure from conventional upsampling strategies.

Spatial domain-based methods operate on pixels or regions directly and use linear or nonlinear methods to fuse the multi-focus images. Spatial domain-based methods can be roughly divided into three categories <cit.>, which often include pixel-based <cit.>, block-based <cit.> and region-based <cit.> algorithms. The block-based algorithms decompose the input images into blocks with equal size according to block-based strategy. Then the decomposed blocks are fused by the designed activity level measurement. However, the selected block-size has great impact on the quality of fused image, the unsuitable size of block restricts the performance of these block-based algorithms. The region-based algorithms firstly use image segmentation to split up the input images into regions. Then, the clarities of corresponding regions are measured and image fusion is performed by integrating the sharply focused regions. Clearly, the accuracy of image segmentation greatly affects the efficiency of the region-based algorithms. Different from the fusion algorithms mentioned above, pixel-based algorithms directly use activity level measurement strategy to generate the decision map for fusion. Some novel pixel-based spatial domain methods have been proposed, such as multi-scale weighted gradient (MWGF) <cit.>, guided filtering (GFF) <cit.> and dense SIFT <cit.>.
new_text: Unlike transform domain approaches, spatial domain techniques operate directly on pixel or region data without requiring conversion to a different feature space. These methods typically employ linear or nonlinear operations to combine multi-focus images and are broadly classified into three types <cit.>: pixel-based <cit.>, block-based <cit.>, and region-based <cit.> strategies. Block-based approaches partition input images into equally sized blocks using a predefined strategy, followed by fusion guided by activity level metrics. The effectiveness of these methods is heavily influenced by block size, as improper sizing can degrade fusion quality. Region-based techniques first segment images into regions, then assess regional clarity to integrate sharply focused areas, with segmentation precision directly determining algorithmic performance. Pixel-based methods differ by generating decision maps through activity level analysis, enabling direct fusion without segmentation or blocking. Recent advancements in this category include techniques like multi-scale weighted gradient (MWGF) <cit.>, guided filtering (GFF) <cit.>, and dense SIFT <cit.>.

old_text: What’s more, there are also some deep learning-based networks applied to image fusion tasks. Ram et al. <cit.> proposed a deep learning-based fusion network, DeepFuse, for fusing the exposure images. In DeepFuse, two pre-fusion convolutional layers which shared the same weights were used to extract low-level image features, then the features are fused in a single merge layer by an elementwise-add fusion strategy. Finally, the fused image was reconstructed by three convolutional layers. Inspired by DeepFuse, Li et al. <cit.> proposed an unsupervised encoder-decoder network, DenseFuse, for the infrared and visible fusion problem. DenseFuse consists of three parts: firstly, the encoder network was used to extract the image features, and fused them in a fusion layer by an L1-norm fusion strategy or elementwise-add fusion strategy, then reconstructed by the decoder network. These two fusion models do not require the post-processing procedures to optimize the intermediate decision map. Consequently, these two fusion models can also fuse other types of images such as multi-focus images and medical images. Similar to DeepFuse and DenseFuse, Zhang et al. <cit.> proposed the IFCNN which is a general fusion network based on CNN without any post-processing procedures. In IFCNN, the pretrained convolutional layer of ResNet101 was firstly used to extract the image features, then the image features were fused by different fusion rules according to the type of input image. The fusion rules include elementwise-maximum, elementwise-sum, and elementwise-mean. Finally, the fusion image was reconstructed by two convolutional layers. All these three fusion models do not require the post-processing procedures to produce fusion images and their models can be fully optimized for image fusion. However, there is a problem in these methods, namely, these methods adopted the fusion strategy based on simple mathematical operations, which ignored the deep image details in the process of feature fusion.
new_text: In addition to traditional approaches, several deep learning-based networks have been developed for image fusion tasks. Ram et al. <cit.> introduced DeepFuse, a deep learning-based fusion network designed to combine exposure images. In DeepFuse, two pre-fusion convolutional layers with shared weights are employed to extract low-level image features, which are subsequently fused in a single merge layer using an elementwise-add strategy. A fused image is then reconstructed through three convolutional layers. Inspired by DeepFuse, Li et al. <cit.> developed DenseFuse, an unsupervised encoder-decoder architecture tailored for infrared and visible image fusion. DenseFuse comprises three stages: first, an encoder extracts features; second, these features are fused in a fusion layer via either an L1-norm or elementwise-add strategy; finally, a decoder reconstructs the fused image. Notably, both DeepFuse and DenseFuse eliminate post-processing steps typically used to refine intermediate decision maps, enabling their application to diverse image types, such as multi-focus and medical images. A similar approach is adopted by Zhang et al. <cit.>, who proposed IFCNN, a general-purpose convolutional neural network (CNN) fusion framework that also omits post-processing. In IFCNN, a pretrained ResNet101 convolutional layer extracts image features, which are then fused using one of three rules—elementwise-maximum, elementwise-sum, or elementwise-mean—depending on the input image type. The final fusion image is reconstructed using two convolutional layers. These three models share the advantage of end-to-end optimization for image fusion without requiring additional post-processing. However, a critical limitation emerges in all these methods: the reliance on simple mathematical operations for feature fusion overlooks deeper image details, potentially compromising the quality of the final output.

In this paper, we propose a novel and effective image fusion model which can be trained in an end-to-end manner with supervised learning strategy. It avoids generating the intermediate decision map and utilizing post-process procedures to refine decision map for image fusion. Besides, to ﬁnely train the proposed fusion model, we have generated a large-scale multi-focus image dataset with ground-truth fusion image, and designed a novel fusion strategy based on the unity fusion attention, which can preserve more image information in the process of feature fusion. Specifically, the salient image features are firstly extracted from multiple input images. Then the proposed unity fusion attention is utilized to fuse these extracted convolutional features. Finally, the fused image features are fed into the cascaded convolutional blocks to reconstruct the fusion image. Extensive experiments are conducted to compare with other state-of-art fusion algorithms, which demonstrates that our proposed fusion approach can generate the high quality of fusion image. In addition, the qualitative evaluation and quantitative evaluation performed on expanded experiments also indicated that our proposed fusion framework is effective in other image fusion tasks.
new_text: In this paper, we propose a novel and effective image fusion model that can be trained in an end-to-end manner using a supervised learning strategy. It avoids the need to generate intermediate decision maps or employ post-processing procedures to refine them for image fusion. Furthermore, to finely train the proposed fusion model, we have generated a large-scale multi-focus image dataset with ground-truth fusion images and designed a novel fusion strategy based on unity fusion attention, which can preserve more image information during feature fusion. Specifically, salient image features are first extracted from multiple input images. Then, the proposed unity fusion attention mechanism is applied to fuse these extracted convolutional features. Finally, the fused image features are passed through cascaded convolutional blocks to reconstruct the fusion image. Extensive experiments comparing our method with state-of-the-art fusion algorithms demonstrate that our proposed approach can generate high-quality fusion images. Additionally, qualitative and quantitative evaluations on expanded experiments indicate that our fusion framework is effective in other image fusion tasks.

In fact, CBAM is suitable for application in single-image processing task and can improve the network’s feature representation capability. As we all know, multi-focus image fusion aims to integrate as many clear image features as possible from source images. Based on this, this fusion strategy can preserve more image details compared to other simple fusion strategy based elementwise operations.
new_text: Attention mechanisms have been widely applied in computer vision tasks since Hu et al. proposed SENet <cit.> in 2017. It has been proven that attention mechanisms are effective components for deep learning. SENet introduced channel-wise attention for the first time, calculating correlations between different channels via global average pooling and fully connected layers. Since it is a simple and "plug-and-play" component, it has gradually been adopted in image fusion tasks. In SESF-Fuse, the SE module was inserted into the encoder network to enhance the network's feature extraction capabilities. Furthermore, building on SENet, Sanghyun Woo et al. proposed the convolutional block attention module (CBAM) <cit.>. This module calculates attention maps separately along channel and spatial dimensions. Although CBAM is an effective and lightweight module, it is rarely applied in image fusion tasks. Indeed, CBAM is suitable for single-image processing tasks and enhances the network's feature representation capability. Multi-focus image fusion aims to integrate as many clear image features as possible from source images. Inspired by CBAM, we propose a fusion strategy that focuses on image features in both channel and spatial dimensions. This strategy preserves more image details compared to simple fusion approaches based on element-wise operations.

The purpose of this paper is to derive discrete orthogonal matrices directly by solving systems of linear equations,
rather than to discretize existing continuous orthogonal polynomials.
Our method has several advantages.
It has virtually no precondition to use.
Orthogonal matrices of arbitrary sizes can be generated to the need of an application.
It directly follows the definition of discrete orthogonality,
eliminating the need to discuss the orthogonal property over a continuous domain,
such as the interval [-1, +1] of the Chebyshev Polynomials <cit.>.

that must be discretely orthogonal to each other over a set of given sample values,

x_k = cosπ(2k+1)/2n,

new_text: This paper presents a method to derive discrete orthogonal matrices by directly solving systems of linear equations, bypassing the discretization of continuous orthogonal polynomials. The approach requires minimal preconditions, enabling the generation of orthogonal matrices of arbitrary sizes tailored to application requirements. By adhering directly to the definition of discrete orthogonality, it eliminates the need to analyze orthogonality over continuous domains like the interval [-1, +1] of Chebyshev Polynomials <cit.>. The method determines polynomial coefficients that enforce discrete orthogonality over specified sample values—e.g., x_k = cos(π(2k+1)/2n) for k = 0,…,n−1, as used in the n × n Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) matrix <cit.>—avoiding errors inherent to continuous function discretization.

Simply put, by installing large reflecting surfaces – with adjustable phase shifts on incident waves – in the wave propagation environment, one can shape the channel's behaviour. new_text: A key technology currently being investigated for 6G is the use of Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS), which can enhance the performance of communication schemes <cit.>. In essence, by deploying large reflecting surfaces equipped with adjustable phase shifts for incident waves within the propagation environment, the behavior of the wireless channel can be actively shaped. Given that the performance of many communication schemes—particularly those involving multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems—strongly depends on wireless channel characteristics, the design flexibility offered by these surfaces implies significant potential for performance improvements <cit.>.

old_text: Our main contributions consist of proposing a novel infection spread model with random connection graph, proposing a two-step sampled group testing algorithm which is based on novel ℱ-separable zero-error non-adaptive test matrices, characterizing the optimal design of two-step sampled group testing algorithms, and presenting explicit results on analytically tractable exponentially split cluster formation trees. For the considered two-step sampled group testing algorithms, we identify the optimal sampling function selection, calculate the required number of tests and the expected number of false classifications in terms of the system parameters, and identify the trade-off between them. Our ℱ-separable zero-error non-adaptive test matrix construction is based on taking advantage of the known probability distribution of cluster formations. In order to present an analytically tractable case study for our proposed two-step sampled group testing algorithm, we consider exponentially split cluster formation trees as a special case, in which we explicitly calculate the required number of tests and the expected number of false classifications. For zero-error construction, we prove that the required number of tests is less than 4(log_2n+1)/3 and is of O(log_2n), when there are nδ individuals. We show that, even when we ignore the gain by cluster size δ, our non-adaptive algorithm, in the zero-error setting, outperforms any zero-error non-adaptive group test and Hwang's generalized binary splitting algorithm <cit.>, which is known to be the optimal zero-error adaptive group test <cit.>. Since the number of infections scale as n/log_2nδ in exponentially split cluster formation trees with nδ individuals, our results show that, we can use group testing to reduce the required number of tests significantly in our system model even when the infection rate is high by using our two-step sampled group testing algorithm.
new_text: Our main contributions consist of proposing a novel infection spread model with a random connection graph, proposing a two-step sampled group testing algorithm that utilizes novel ℱ-separable zero-error non-adaptive test matrices, characterizing the optimal design of two-step sampled group testing algorithms, and presenting explicit results on analytically tractable exponentially split cluster formation trees. For the considered two-step sampled group testing algorithms, we identify the optimal sampling function selection, calculate the required number of tests and the expected number of false classifications in terms of the system parameters, and identify the trade-off between them. Our ℱ-separable zero-error non-adaptive test matrix construction is based on leveraging the known probability distribution of cluster formations. To present an analytically tractable case study for our proposed two-step sampled group testing algorithm, we consider exponentially split cluster formation trees as a special case, in which we explicitly calculate the required number of tests and the expected number of false classifications. For zero-error construction, we prove that the required number of tests is less than 4(log₂n + 1)/3 and is O(log₂n), when there are nδ individuals. We show that, even when we ignore the gain by cluster size δ, our non-adaptive algorithm, in the zero-error setting, outperforms any zero-error non-adaptive group test and Hwang’s generalized binary splitting algorithm <cit.>, which is known to be the optimal zero-error adaptive group test <cit.>. Since the number of infections scales as n/(log₂nδ) in exponentially split cluster formation trees with nδ individuals, our results show that we can use group testing to reduce the required number of tests significantly in our system model even when the infection rate is high by employing our two-step sampled group testing algorithm.

old_text: * We propose Locality-Constrained Cross Attention to address the issue of semantic noise aroused by the direct fusion of two sources of features. With the constructed geometric alignment graphs, LCCA can not only enables the interaction between features of different sources accurately, but also reinforce each kind of feature via cross-attention fusions.
new_text: To mitigate the semantic noise generated by directly combining features from two distinct sources, we introduce Locality-Constrained Cross Attention (LCCA). Leveraging geometric alignment graphs, LCCA facilitates precise feature interactions across different modalities while simultaneously enhancing individual feature representations through cross-attention mechanisms.

old_text: * MHCN shows great performance in both the general and cold-start recommendation tasks. Even without self-supervised learning, it beats all the baselines by a fair margin. Meanwhile, 	self-supervised learning has great ability to further improve MHCN. Compared with the vanilla version, the self-supervised version shows decent improvements in all the cases. Particularly, in the cold-start recommendation task, self-supervised learning brings significant gains. On average, S^2-MHCN achieves about 5.389% improvement in the general recommendation task and 9.442% improvement in the cold-start recommendation task compared with MHCN. Besides, it seems that, the sparser the dataset, the more improvements self-supervised learning brings.
new_text: MHCN demonstrates strong effectiveness in both general and cold-start recommendation scenarios. Notably, even without incorporating self-supervised learning techniques, it consistently outperforms all baseline models by a significant margin. This foundational performance highlights its inherent robustness. However, when self-supervised learning is integrated, the model’s capabilities are further enhanced. Specifically, the self-supervised version of MHCN (S²-MHCN) achieves measurable improvements across all evaluation metrics compared to its non-self-supervised counterpart. These gains are particularly pronounced in cold-start settings, where the scarcity of user-item interaction data makes learning more challenging. For instance, S²-MHCN reports an average 5.389% improvement in general recommendation performance and a more substantial 9.442% improvement in cold-start tasks. The disparity between these results underscores self-supervised learning’s capacity to address data sparsity by leveraging auxiliary tasks to extract meaningful representations. Furthermore, empirical observations indicate that the effectiveness of self-supervised learning correlates with dataset sparsity: the fewer interactions available, the greater the marginal benefit of self-supervised methods. This suggests that such techniques are especially valuable for overcoming data limitations in recommendation systems.

Later on, the same problem has been introduced under different names in a number of other applications: it has been called LIFO-search <cit.> in the area of graph pursuit-evasion games; it is a problem of searching in tree-like partial orders, which naturally generalizes the classical binary search problem on sorted arrays; it has been also named as ordered coloring and more recently as tree-depth <cit.>.
Through the connection to searching partial orders, it is worth pointing out that computing tree-depth (or equivalently, a search strategy for the corresponding partial order) can be used to finding, in an automated way, software bugs <cit.>.
In this application, again, the line graphs of trees and their tree-depth are of interest.
To intuitively see the link between tree-depth and parallel processing, we may see the graph-theoretic problem from two perspectives.
One perspective that is the driving approach e.g. in parallel matrix factorization or in software testing, looks at the tree-depth in a `top-down' fashion: find a good separator in the graph, process the workload that corresponds to the separator and then recurse (in parallel) on the connected components.
What is powerful regarding the tree-depth problem is that it balances the ratio between the sizes of such separators and the recursion depth, providing the minimum overall computation time.
It is worth noting that neither focusing on small separators (and hence pay with larger recursion depth) nor finding the computation scheme with the minimum recursion depth (but perhaps using some larger separators) is an efficient approach for such applications.
The other perspective is to see the tree-depth of a line graph of a tree in a `bottom-up' fashion: find a matching in a tree, contract its edges in parallel, and repeat this step until you reach a state where there is a single vertex left.
This interpretation lies behind the above-mentioned applications in databases, parallel assemblies, and information retrieval (see Figure <ref> for an illustration of this scheme).
new_text:
The same problem has been independently introduced in various fields under different names. In the context of graph pursuit-evasion games, it is known as LIFO-search <cit.>. In computational mathematics, it is framed as a problem of searching within tree-like partial orders, a concept that generalizes the classical binary search on sorted arrays. More recently, it has also been termed "ordered coloring" and "tree-depth" <cit.>. These diverse names reflect the problem’s adaptability to different domains but underscore its core mathematical essence.  

Through its link to partial orders, tree-depth (or equivalently, an optimal search strategy for the associated structure) has proven valuable in automated software testing. Specifically, computing tree-depth can help identify software bugs <cit.>. In this application, the focus lies on the line graphs of trees and their tree-depth, as these structures encapsulate key dependencies within the system. To understand how tree-depth connects to parallel processing, we can examine the problem from two complementary perspectives.  

The first, a top-down approach, is commonly used in applications like parallel matrix factorization and software testing. Here, the process begins by identifying a "separator" in the graph—a subset of nodes that, when removed, divides the graph into smaller connected components. The computational workload corresponding to the separator is processed first, after which the components are handled recursively in parallel. The efficiency of this strategy hinges on the trade-off between separator size and recursion depth. Tree-depth excels in this balance by minimizing total computation time, as it avoids extremes: overly small separators force excessive recursion, while excessively large separators may dominate the workload. Neither of these extremes is optimal for parallel applications.  

In contrast, a bottom-up perspective reveals another facet of tree-depth, particularly relevant to applications in databases, parallel assemblies, and information retrieval. Here, the process involves iteratively identifying a matching (a set of non-overlapping edges) in a tree, contracting those edges in parallel, and repeating this until a single node remains. This method reflects how tree-depth can be interpreted as a measure of structural decomposition. The relevance of this perspective is illustrated in <ref>, where the stepwise contraction of edges is demonstrated. Both perspectives—top-down partitioning and bottom-up decomposition—highlight how tree-depth provides a unifying framework for analyzing and optimizing hierarchical or graph-based processes.

The use of satellites to provide ubiquitous coverage and connectivity for the densely deployed IoT networks are expected to be a reality in the emerging 6G networks. Yet, the low battery capacity is of IoT nodes constitute a problem for the direct connectivity to satellites that are located up to 2000 km altitude. As an architectural novelty, in this paper we propose the use of RIS units to help with the path loss associated with high transmission distances. The use of RIS units through broadcasting and beamforming approaches are shown to provide a significant gain in terms of their signal transmission. These units can be placed on the reflectarrays that are already available on the satellites. It is shown that RIS-assisted satellites can provide up to 10^5 times higher downlink and uplink achievable rates for IoT networks.
new_text: The use of satellites to provide ubiquitous connectivity for dense IoT networks in emerging 6G systems is expected to be a reality. However, the low battery capacity of IoT nodes poses a challenge for direct connectivity to satellites located up to 2000 km altitude. This paper proposes using RIS units to mitigate path loss from high transmission distances. RIS units demonstrate significant signal transmission gains via broadcasting and beamforming approaches, leveraging existing satellite reflectarrays. Results show that RIS-assisted satellites achieve up to 10^5 times higher downlink and uplink rates for IoT networks.

In this paper we introduce NIMIWAE, one of the first methods to handle up to MNAR patterns of missingness in the VAE/IWAE class of methods, to address complex patterns of missingess observed in the Physionet EHR data. Using statistical simulations, we show that NIMIWAE performs well in imputing missing features under MNAR, and has reasonable performance under the MCAR or MAR settings. Performance in imputing MCAR and MAR missingness can be further improved in NIMIWAE by using the ignorable version of this model (IMIWAE), where we omit the mask decoder network. We also found that the results of the analysis on the Physionet data are highly dependent on the choice of missingness model, which specifies the assumption of the missingness mechanism. However, NIMIWAE is able to impute missing values well in simulations regardless of the underlying missingness mechanism, flexibly modelling the mechanism using a deeply-learned neural network. We have also shown that this performance can be further improved if a priori knowledge is used to narrow down the missingness model covariates, while the neural network structure allows this model to capture complex, nonlinear dependencies between missingness across features. The NIMIWAE-imputed dataset resulted in more realistic imputed values with respect to what we may expect in the Physionet Challenge patients, since NIMIWAE takes into account possible non-ignorable missingness in the data. Additionally, the IWAE architecture learns a lower-dimensional representation of the data, which can be used for further tasks, such as patient subgroup identification or visualization of data.

Patients whose ICU stays were less than 48 hours long were excluded from the dataset. For each patient, 36 features were measured, with one potential measurement hourly for 48 hours. new_text: The Physionet 2012 Challenge dataset <cit.> is a publicly available electronic health record (EHR) dataset. It contains de-identified information on 12,000 adult Intensive Care Unit (ICU) patients admitted to Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center between 2001 and 2008. Patients whose ICU stays were less than 48 hours long were excluded from the dataset; this exclusion criterion was implemented to ensure that each patient had a minimum observation window of 48 hours for consistent data collection. For each patient, 36 distinct clinical features were recorded. These features were measured up to once per hour for 48 hours, resulting in a maximum of 48 observations per feature. These features encompass a range of laboratory measurements and clinical indicators, such as albumin levels (in g/dL) and serum sodium levels (in mEq/L), which reflect metabolic status, and white blood cell counts (in cells/nL), which indicate immune response. Additionally, the dataset includes recorded clinical outcomes for each patient, such as the SAPS-I score <cit.> (a tool for estimating the severity of illness) and the SOFA score <cit.> (an assessment of organ dysfunction), along with the length of ICU stay, survival status, and whether the patient experienced in-hospital death. The challenge aimed to develop machine learning algorithms capable of accurately predicting specific clinical outcomes—such as in-hospital mortality—by analyzing these time-series data. Such predictive models could help clinicians identify patients at high risk of adverse outcomes, thereby facilitating early intervention and improving decision-making in ICU settings <cit.>.

old_text: In <cit.>, GRIMM is proposed as a gateway based regional mobility management architecture for satellite network based on locator/identifier split. GRIMM divides the coverage of the satellite system into regions based on the terrestrial gateways distribution. Each gateway is equipped with a tgms and is responsible for the localized location management of the MN within its region. The global location management is realized through the synchronization among all gateways. When a foreign TGMS receives global updates, it generates the mapping entry between MN's ID and its corresponding TGMS. To avoid the non-optimal routing, GRIMM's location resolution is conducted before forwarding data packets. In GRIMM, a MN accesses a satellite with a fixed id and the local TGMS records the MN's ID and its corresponding accessed satellite. When the MN ID is registered locally for the first time, the TGMS will trigger a global update among all TGMSes. To start a session between a MN and a CN, the accessed satellite will first send a request of location resolution to the local TGMS upon receiving the first data packet. If the local TGMS does not have the specific locator of the enquired CN's ID, the request will be redirected to the corresponding TGMS. After receiving the requested CN location, the source satellite begins to encapsulate the data packet with location information and then forwards it through inter-satellite links to that area. The destined satellite can decapsulate the packet and then sends it to the CN. When a MN moves from one satellite area to another, subsequent messages will notify the accessed satellite of CN to update MN's location in the cached mapping entry. This is to update the routing path between satellites. Although the regional location management greatly reduces the management cost and facilitates the scalability of the network, global updates may create high signaling overhead among the gateways. In addition, keeping records of every MN's ID and its corresponding TGMS in all foreign TGMS requires massive storage resources.
new_text: In <cit.>, GRIMM is proposed as a gateway-based regional mobility management architecture for satellite networks, leveraging a locator/identifier split. GRIMM partitions the satellite system's coverage into regions, aligning with the geographic distribution of terrestrial gateways. Each gateway is equipped with a tgms, which manages the localized location tracking of mobile nodes (MNs) within its assigned region. Global location management is achieved via synchronized communication among all gateways. Upon receiving global updates, a foreign TGMS generates a mapping entry linking the MN's ID to its corresponding TGMS. To prevent non-optimal routing, GRIMM resolves the MN's location prior to forwarding data packets. Within GRIMM, an MN accesses a satellite using a fixed ID, with the local TGMS recording the MN's ID and the associated satellite. A first-time local registration of an MN ID triggers a global update across all TGMSes. When a session between an MN and a correspondent node (CN) initiates, the accessed satellite requests location resolution from the local TGMS upon receiving the first data packet. If the local TGMS lacks the CN's locator, the request is forwarded to the corresponding TGMS. After acquiring the CN's location, the source satellite encapsulates the packet with location metadata and transmits it via inter-satellite links to the target area. The destination satellite decapsulates the packet and delivers it to the CN. As an MN migrates between satellite coverage areas, subsequent messages notify the accessed satellite to update the cached mapping entry for the MN's new location, thereby adjusting the inter-satellite routing path. While regional location management significantly reduces management overhead and enhances network scalability, global updates can introduce substantial signaling overhead among gateways. Furthermore, maintaining a distributed record of every MN's ID and its corresponding TGMS across all foreign TGMSes requires considerable storage resources.

new_text: Interest in the compound figure separation (CFS) problem gained momentum only after its introduction as a biomedical domain challenge at ImageCLEF 2013 <cit.>. Early approaches relied heavily on handcrafted features and rule-based strategies. Researchers utilized empty spaces between subfigures as a critical cue for decomposition <cit.>, and <cit.> et al. integrated an SVM-based classifier to merge fragmented components. Taschwer et al. <cit.> advanced this by incorporating both spatial gaps and edge information for segmentation. Later, learning-based techniques, particularly deep neural networks, emerged to address CFS. Tsutsui et al. <cit.> applied a conventional object detection framework, while Shi et al. <cit.> introduced joint prediction of layout structures and bounding boxes. However, <cit.> limited their approach to a finite set of predefined layouts, constraining its adaptability to diverse compound figures. Critically, none of these methods considered subfigure labels, neglecting the semantic links between subfigures and their caption-based descriptions.

Table <ref> shows the BIC for the DCHSBM using each of these affinity functions.
    Importantly, no single affinity function is preferred across all of the study data sets, suggesting the presence of different kinds of polyadic structure.
    AON, GN, and P all prefer edges with homogeneous cluster labels, whereas RP prefers edges in which the two most common labels are roughly balanced in representation.
    In the two congressional committee data sets, RP achieves the optimal BIC, while in each of the other data sets, one of the three affinities that promotes edge homogeneity is instead preferred.

new_text: Table <ref> shows the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) values for the Dendritic Hierarchical Stochastic Block Model (DCHSBM) when using each of the four affinity functions described in the analysis. These results highlight a key finding: no single affinity function consistently outperforms the others across all study datasets, indicating that the datasets exhibit diverse polyadic structural patterns. Specifically, the AON, GN, and P affinities are statistically consistent with the hypothesis that edges are more likely to form between nodes assigned to the same cluster (homogeneous label distributions). In contrast, the RP affinity is associated with edges in which the two most prevalent cluster labels in the network are approximately equally represented—a pattern distinct from strict homophily. This divergence in structural assumptions becomes particularly relevant when evaluating the BIC results across different datasets. For example, in the two congressional committee datasets, RP yields the lowest BIC, implying that the data’s structure aligns more closely with RP’s assumptions about label balance. However, in every other dataset analyzed, one of the three homophily-promoting affinities (AON, GN, or P) is favored instead. Further, the three homophily-based affinities themselves show nuanced performance differences. In the `house-bills` dataset, the Pairwise affinity achieves the lowest BIC among all four functions, whereas in `walmart-purchases`, Pairwise outperforms all affinities except Group Number. These patterns suggest that models based on pairwise comparisons of node labels can provide strong generative explanations for the observed structures in these datasets. This observation has broader implications: dyadic algorithms, which primarily model pairwise interactions, may perform comparably to or even exceed polyadic methods in these cases. Supporting this claim, we observe in both `house-bills` and `walmart-purchases` that dyadic clustering algorithms produce results more strongly correlated with ground truth labels than the AON HMLL method, a polyadic approach.

We consider that a smart home platform may be exploited by attackers for accessing user private data and inferring user privacy-sensitive behaviors. For example, an attacker may find a way to gain access to the data; also the platform administrators may be curious to mine user privacy.
We do not assume that the platform is attacker-controlled, but aim to handle the concern that the rich data

The platform is assumed to be honest, i.e., it faithfully operates all services and does not perform active attacks on users.

new_text: We consider that a smart home platform could be compromised by malicious actors seeking to access private user data and infer sensitive behavioral patterns, such as daily routines, personal preferences, or location history. For instance, attackers might exploit security flaws to gain unauthorized access to collected data, while platform administrators—despite adhering to operational protocols—could potentially misuse their access to monitor users out of curiosity or for other improper purposes. Importantly, our analysis does not assume the platform itself is under adversarial control; rather, we address concerns that the inherently rich and detailed data generated by smart home systems could inadvertently be exposed to attackers through misconfigurations, insider threats, or other data leaks. To clarify, the platform is modeled as "honest" in this context, meaning it correctly implements its intended functions without intentionally subverting user privacy or launching active attacks. However, this assumption does not eliminate the risk of malicious exploitation if sensitive data becomes accessible to unauthorized parties. We prove the equivalence between NSS and SPIR in the following two senses. 1) Given any SPIR protocol, we can construct an NSS protocol. 2) Given any linear NSS protocol, we can construct a SPIR protocol. new_text: This paper investigates the equivalence between non-perfect secret sharing (NSS) and symmetric private information retrieval (SPIR) in scenarios involving colluding and unresponsive servers. Leveraging this relationship, we demonstrate that the capacity of a *z*-server SPIR system with *r* responsive servers and *r* colluding servers is given by the formula (*r* − *t*)/*n*.

At present, however, several issues need to be solved to make deep learning methods more trustworthy, predictable, safe, and secure against adversarial attacks. Although several methods have been proposed to improve the trustworthiness of deep neural networks, most of them are tailored for specific classes of adversarial examples, hence failing to detect other corner cases or unsafe inputs that heavily deviate from the training samples.

This survey aims to study and systematically classify personality-aware recommendation systems. To the best of our knowledge, this survey is the first that focuses on personality-aware recommendation systems. We explore the different design choices of personality-aware recommendation systems, by comparing their personality modeling methods, as well as their recommendation techniques. Furthermore, we present the commonly used datasets and point out some of the challenges of personality-aware recommendation systems.

When to batch invocations.
As pipeline dataflow progresses, there can be moments when an operation may have fewer invocations available than the most efficient configuration's batch size.
For example, if a pipeline contains a slower face detection operation followed by a faster blurring operation, the blur operation's invocations will likely drain the speculative queue faster than it can build up.
In such cases, executing upstream operations first yields a larger batch size, amortizing RPC and I/O overheads.
However, waiting for upstream operation invocations to complete their execution may result in a slack violation.
new_text: Determining when to batch invocations is critical to pipeline efficiency. During pipeline dataflow execution, operations can encounter instances where the number of available invocations falls below the optimal batch size dictated by their configuration. For example, in a pipeline including a slower face detection operation followed by a faster blurring operation, the blur operation’s invocations will likely deplete the speculative queue before it can be replenished. In such cases, executing upstream operations first results in larger batch sizes, which amortize RPC and I/O overheads. However, waiting for upstream operations to finish executing may result in a slack violation.

It was shown in <cit.> that such a distributed approach outperforms centralized beam selection, where a NN at the BS infers the best beams for all the vehicles in its coverage area either by combining LIDAR data from all the vehicles or using a single LIDAR sensor mounted at the BS. However, compiling such a dataset in practice is challenging, as it requires transmitting large volumes of LIDAR point cloud data over the uplink channel. Additionally, a separate NN must be trained for each BS’s coverage area, since site-specific NNs degrade in performance when the scattering environment changes significantly, even for the same site. Consequently, continuous collection of updated LIDAR data and iterative retraining or fine-tuning of the NN weights are necessary during system operation. This inherent need for ongoing data transmission imposes persistent overhead on the system in a centralized approach.

In this section, we discuss the design choices of the mask head in CondInst.
To our surprise, the performance is insensitive to the architectures of the mask head. Our baseline is the mask head of three1 ×1convolutions with8channels ( i.e., width= 8). The theory implies the superiority of our methods to previous non-local and local methods in terms of communication complexity and even total execution time. new_text: This paper proposes and analyzes BVR-L-SGD for nonconvex federated learning, which utilizes a bias-variance reduced gradient estimator to leverage heterogeneity in local objectives. The theoretical analysis demonstrates superior performance over prior non-local and local methods in communication complexity and total execution time. Numerical experiments align with theoretical results and validate the empirical advantages of the proposed method. A key future direction is analyzing our methods for convex objectives, as numerical results reveal no clear trend between local update counts and minibatch sizes, and SVRG-like and SARAH-like approaches exhibit nearly identical performance—phenomena that may require a tighter convex theory for BVR-L-SGD. Extending the algorithms and theory to enforce second-order optimality (local minima) is also promising, since current methods ensure only first-order stationarity.

new_text: As shown in Fig. <ref>, the TSCN framework comprises two primary components: CME-Net and CSR-Net. old_text: In the conventional FSCSS modulation, each chirp is associated with a message symbol. Specifically, let b_0,b_1,⋯,b_Λ-1 be a group of Λ information bits associated with a message symbol, and m be the corresponding decimal number, i.e., m = ∑_i=0^Λ-1 b_i 2^i. The transmitted signal corresponding to message m, denoted by s_m[n], is simply given by s_m[n] = x_m[n]. Note that Λ = log_2 M, or M=2^Λ. This means that in a conventional FSCSS modulation, such as in LoRa modulation, the number of chirps is selected to be a power of 2.
new_text: In conventional FSCSS modulation, each chirp corresponds to a message symbol. To represent a message symbol, let b₀, b₁, ⋯, b_{Λ−1} denote a group of Λ information bits, and let m be the corresponding decimal number, i.e., m = ∑_{i=0}^{Λ−1} b_i 2^i. The transmitted signal corresponding to message m, denoted by s_m[n], is defined as s_m[n] = x_m[n]. It follows that Λ = log₂ M, or equivalently M = 2^Λ. This means that in conventional FSCSS modulation, such as in LoRa, the number of chirps must be a power of two.

In each heatmap, the element on the i-th row and the j-th column denotes w_ij, the pairwise weight for computing the contribution of the reward upon transition to the j-th state to the return at the i-th state in the episode. The weights in the remaining part of the top rows are zero because those rewards do not depend on the the actions in the key phase. For the same reason, the weights in the middle-right area are zero as well. The weights in the rest of the area resemble the exponentially discounted weights with a discount factor of 0.92. This steep discounting helps fast learning of collecting apples. The weights learned by metagradients (right) largely resemble the handcrafted weights, which indicate that the metagradient procedure was able to simultaneously learn (1) the important rewards for the key phase are in the door phase, and (2) a quick-discounting set of weights within the apple phase that allows faster learning of collecting apples.
new_text: Figure <ref> presents a visualization of the handcrafted weights for H-PWR (left) and the weights learned by Meta-PWR (right). In these heatmaps, the element located in the i-th row and j-th column corresponds to w_ij, representing the pairwise weight used to calculate how the reward earned upon transitioning to the j-th state contributes to the return estimated at the i-th state during an episode. For the handcrafted weights (left), the non-zero values in the top-right region reflect a key dependency: the rewards obtained in the door phase rely on actions taken in the key phase earlier in the task. Specifically, successful progression through the key phase is a prerequisite for entering the door phase, making the later rewards contingent on prior decisions. The remaining elements in the top rows of the heatmap are zero because these rewards—those not associated with the door phase—do not depend on actions from the key phase. Similarly, the middle-right region of the heatmap is also zero, following the same logic: rewards in this area are unrelated to the key-phase actions. Outside of these specific dependencies, the weights align closely with the pattern of exponentially discounted returns, using a discount factor of 0.92. This sharp discounting prioritizes recent rewards, accelerating the agent’s ability to learn optimal strategies for collecting apples efficiently. In contrast, the weights learned via metagradients (right) mirror the structure of the handcrafted weights. This similarity demonstrates that the metagradient optimization process successfully identified two critical features: (1) the importance of linking door-phase rewards to key-phase actions, and (2) the necessity of applying a rapid-discounting scheme within the apple phase to streamline learning. The ability to recover both task-specific dependencies and reward-prioritization strategies without explicit guidance underscores the effectiveness of the metagradient approach.
