An illustration of this investigation is presented in Figure <ref>, where we display the top predictive features for in-hospital mortality and physiological decompensation. This confirms our previous findings from automated metrics that phenotypic features are particularly effective for predicting in-hospital mortality, as 14 of the 20 most important features are phenotypes. This aligns with our expectations and is explained by the absence of a fixed future time point for prediction in this task. Specifically, since the prediction must encompass the entire hospital stay rather than predicting within a specific timeframe such as 12 hours, forecasts require data that is both highly informative and capable of accurately reflecting long-term outcomes. Unlike bedside measurements, which can lose temporal correlation due to their dynamic nature, phenotypes effectively satisfy these criteria by capturing comorbidities—key factors in mortality prediction<cit.>—and serving as the sole input for clinically validated mortality models<cit.>. Additionally, a study involving 230,000 ICU patients demonstrated that combining comorbidities with acute physiological measurements yielded superior results, outperforming established mortality scores (APACHE II, SAPS II)<cit.>.

new_text: This section presents experiments conducted with the Kirin robot to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed ACQL algorithm in handling unknown payloads. As illustrated in Fig. <ref>, the robot begins in a stationary position on a flat surface, carrying unspecified sandbag payloads. A predefined set of control torques is applied to actuate the robot’s legs, enabling it to lift its body to a target height while maintaining stability with all four legs grounded. However, due to the unknown mass and distribution of the payloads, the robot’s torso experiences notable deviations in both positional accuracy and orientation—specifically, shifts in vertical alignment and rotational misalignment (e.g., pitch, roll, or yaw). To address these disturbances, the robot initiates a continuous process of identifying the payload’s mass and inertial properties (moment of inertia) while simultaneously adjusting its posture using the adaptive control framework described earlier. This dual process persists until the angular errors in the robot’s orientation—measured in three rotational axes—drop below a predefined threshold. In the experiments, this threshold is set conservatively at 0.01 radians for each rotational direction, ensuring precise alignment. The ACQL algorithm’s parameters—c, λ, and M—are configured to 0.7I, 0.7I, and 1.3I, respectively. These values regulate the rate at which the algorithm iteratively updates its estimates of the payload’s inertial characteristics, balancing responsiveness with stability during the adjustment phase.

old_text: Classical kernels (RBF and Laplace) as well as FC kernels are cheap to compute in the sense that they are dot product kernels: a kernel matrix element k(x,x') between two inputs only depends on x · x, x · x', and x' · x'. Kernels formed out of convolutional and pooling layers introduce computational complexity by having to keep track of pixel-pixel correlations. Indeed, the addition of a convolutional layer introduces an O(d) complexity while a (global) pooling layer introduces O(d^2) complexity, where d is the spatial dimension of the image.
new_text: Classical kernels (RBF and Laplace) as well as FC kernels are computationally efficient due to their structure as dot product kernels: the kernel matrix element k(x, x′) between two inputs depends solely on x · x, x · x′, and x′ · x′. In contrast, kernels constructed from convolutional and pooling layers introduce computational complexity by necessitating tracking of pixel-pixel correlations. Specifically, the addition of a convolutional layer introduces a complexity of O(d), while a (global) pooling layer introduces a complexity of O(d²), where d represents the spatial dimension of the image.

old_text: Maximizing the legged robot's maneuverability is one of the most attractive research topics in the locomotion community. The well-known MIT Cheetah robot incorporates virtual leg compliance into its controller and realizes 2D running on the treadmill up to 6 m/s with trot gait in the Sagittal plane <cit.>. StarlETH is another representative quadruped robot developed by ETH Zurich, on which the hierarchical Operational Space Control <cit.> is adopted to separate dynamical constraints from trajectory tracking tasks. This enables StarlETH to trot over rough terrains with loose and slippery obstacles<cit.>. Along this line of research, a Whole-Body-Control method is integrated in the locomotion controller on ETH ANYmal, which significantly improves the robot's agility <cit.>. MIT mini Cheetah, a lightweight version of the MIT Cheetah series, is capable of highly dynamic gaits including 3D trotting and galloping up to 2.5 m/s through convex model predictive control <cit.>. Unitree A1 is another lightweight quadruped robot that has performed dynamic locomotion over rough terrains <cit.>. Besides agile quadruped locomotion, equipping the robot with a payload-carrying ability is also a critical research topic. Bigdog, the first field legged robot that leaves the lab, is hydraulically actuated with impressive robustness to the external disturbances. This robot weighs about 109 kg and can carry a payload weighing more than 150 kg <cit.>. HyQ is another hydraulic robot developed by IIT <cit.>. It weights about 80 kg and the peak torque of its hydraulic joint is around 180 Nm which provides the robot extremely large payload-carrying ability <cit.>. Different from traditional rotation joint, baby elephant developed by Shanghai Jiaotong University has a parallel-leg. This electric-hydraulic driven robot weights 130 kg and can carry payload up to 100 kg <cit.>. Due to the technology limitations, including the electric motor constraints, it is yet extensively explored in the area of the payload-carrying on the electrically-actuated quadruped robots.
new_text:
Maximizing the legged robot's maneuverability remains a central focus within the locomotion research community, as it directly impacts the robot's ability to navigate complex environments efficiently. A key example is the MIT Cheetah robot, which incorporates virtual leg compliance into its controller to simulate the adaptability of biological limbs. This innovation allows the robot to achieve 2D running at speeds up to 6 m/s on a treadmill using the trot gait within the sagittal plane, demonstrating how advanced control strategies can enhance speed and stability. Another representative system, StarlETH developed by ETH Zurich, employs hierarchical Operational Space Control to decouple the challenges of managing dynamic constraints from trajectory tracking tasks. This separation enables the robot to maintain control precision while trotting across rough terrains with loose or slippery obstacles, highlighting the importance of modular control frameworks in adapting to unpredictable surfaces. Building on these advancements, the ETH ANYmal platform integrates a Whole-Body-Control method into its locomotion controller, which coordinates leg movements and torso stability simultaneously, thereby significantly improving agility and responsiveness during dynamic tasks.  

To further illustrate progress in legged robotics, the MIT mini Cheetah—a lightweight variant of the original MIT Cheetah—utilizes convex model predictive control to execute complex 3D gaits such as trotting and galloping at speeds up to 2.5 m/s, showcasing how compact systems can still achieve high dynamic performance. Similarly, the Unitree A1, another lightweight quadruped robot, demonstrates robust dynamic locomotion capabilities over rough terrain, emphasizing the role of actuator efficiency and control algorithms in enabling adaptability. While agility in locomotion is critical, researchers also prioritize equipping robots with payload-carrying abilities for real-world applications. For instance, the Bigdog robot, developed as a hydraulically actuated field robot, represents an early breakthrough in robustness, capable of carrying payloads exceeding 150 kg despite its own weight of 109 kg. This capacity arises from hydraulic systems’ high torque output, as seen in the HyQ robot developed by IIT, which weighs approximately 80 kg and generates peak joint torques of 180 Nm, enabling significant load-bearing capabilities. Notably, the Baby Elephant robot from Shanghai Jiaotong University diverges from traditional rotational joints by employing a parallel-leg design driven by electric-hydraulic actuators, allowing it to carry payloads up to 100 kg.  

However, payload-carrying research remains less mature in electrically-actuated quadruped robots due to inherent limitations in electric motor performance, such as lower torque density and slower response times compared to hydraulic systems. This technological bottleneck highlights the ongoing challenges in balancing speed, agility, and payload capacity in electrically driven platforms. Thus, while substantial progress has been made in enhancing locomotion and load-bearing capabilities through diverse actuation and control strategies, the field continues to seek solutions that unify these attributes for practical deployment in real-world scenarios.

Cumulative cultural evolution describes the gradual improvement of knowledge and technology across generations of individual learners <cit.>.
The archaeological record reveals that the technological toolkit of the modern human began growing at an accelerated pace around 300,000 years ago <cit.>.
This acceleration is thought to be spurred by the development (or, perhaps, co-evolution) of cognitive capacities that support the use of rich social information <cit.>, including language <cit.>, and in turn increase the fidelity of knowledge transmission.
In support of this hypothesis, Morgan2015 found that when contemporary humans learned from others how to engineer sharp stone flakes, they produced higher quality flakes, more efficiently and more sustainably across generations when their learning was supplemented with verbal teaching (vs. gestural teaching or imitation learning).
new_text: Cumulative cultural evolution refers to the gradual enhancement of knowledge and technology over time through the learning and transmission of innovations across generations <cit.>. Archaeological evidence suggests that the pace of technological advancement among modern humans began to accelerate significantly approximately 300,000 years ago <cit.>. This shift is hypothesized to stem from the development—or simultaneous co-evolution—of cognitive abilities that facilitate the effective use of social information <cit.>. Key among these abilities are likely capacities such as language <cit.>, which would have improved the accuracy and efficiency of passing knowledge between individuals. Enhanced cognitive tools would, in turn, have strengthened the *fidelity* of knowledge transmission, ensuring that innovations were preserved, refined, and built upon across generations rather than being lost or simplified. A study by Morgan2015 supports this hypothesis, demonstrating that when participants learned to craft sharp stone flakes, verbal instruction alongside observation yielded higher quality results compared to reliance on gestural cues or imitation alone. Furthermore, this method enabled more consistent and sustainable improvements in flake production across multiple generations of learners, underscoring how symbolic communication may have amplified the power of cumulative cultural evolution.

This mode of transmission is one of the richest forms of linguistic transmission, as the mechanism itself provides a kind of cultural ratchet.
We cannot guarantee that other forms of linguistic transmission (e.g., single, unseeded messages) would or would not result in similar knowledge accumulation we observed <cit.>cf.,>beppu2009iterated.
It is also possible that language is not necessary for cumulative cultural learning in our setting, as suggested by results in other tasks <cit.>e.g.,>caldwell2008studying; however, task difficulty may be an important third variable when evaluating the necessity of language for cultural learning <cit.>.

new_text: In our experiment, we utilized a "living document" framework in which each generation’s message was initialized with the editable text from the preceding generation. This approach enabled participants to modify and build upon prior contributions, creating a dynamic chain of iterated learning. The design resembles a cultural ratchet mechanism, where each iteration retains and potentially enhances accumulated knowledge, making it one of the most linguistically rich forms of transmission. While we observed significant knowledge accumulation under this model, we caution that similar outcomes may or may not emerge from alternative transmission methods, such as non-iterated or unseeded message passing, as explored in related studies (cf. beppu2009iterated). Furthermore, our findings do not confirm that language is strictly necessary for cumulative cultural learning in this context. For instance, prior work on non-linguistic tasks has demonstrated knowledge accumulation without verbal communication (e.g., caldwell2008studying). However, task complexity may serve as a critical moderating factor; simpler tasks might support cumulative learning without language, while more complex ones could necessitate it. Importantly, the video game paradigm we employed is not limited to linguistic modes of transmission. It naturally extends to other pedagogical strategies, such as nonlinguistic demonstrations (e.g., guided actions within the game) or observational learning (e.g., watching recorded game replays), offering a flexible framework to investigate how transmission modality influences cultural evolution.

Picture a situated interactive agent such as a social robot conversing with a group of people. How can agents act in such a setting?
We sustain conversations spatially and temporally through explicit behavioral cues—examples include locations of partners, their orientation, gestures, gaze, and floor control actions <cit.>. Evidence suggests that we employ an anticipation of these and other cues to navigate daily social interactions <cit.>.
Consequently, the ability to forecast the future constitutes a natural objective towards the realization of
machines with social skills.
As such, interactive agents typically contend with uncertainties in inferences surrounding cues <cit.>. So beyond making real-time inferences, such systems may achieve more fluid interactions by leveraging the ability to forecast future states of the conversation <cit.>.
new_text: Consider a social robot, a type of situated interactive agent, engaging with multiple individuals. What strategies enable effective interaction in such a setting? Human conversations are maintained through spatial and temporal coordination of explicit behavioral signals, including the positioning and orientation of participants, their gestures, eye gaze patterns, and turn-taking dynamics <cit.>. Studies demonstrate that anticipation of these and related cues plays a critical role in managing real-world social exchanges <cit.>. Thus, predictive capability—forecasting future states—emerges as a core requirement for machines aiming to achieve human-like social competence. Interactive agents must navigate inherent uncertainties in interpreting behavioral cues <cit.>, and research highlights that incorporating predictive models of conversational dynamics can significantly enhance the fluidity and coherence of agent-mediated interactions <cit.>.

The "Explore/Exploit" game tasks players with collecting all blocks of any color. This is the easiest game in the set, as there are no permanent consequences for failure—no way to die—and players can choose from multiple winning strategies. A time incentive adds urgency to collect efficiently. The game introduces a precondition: players must first collect a gem surrounded by poison. Progress here requires acquiring an antidote to safely navigate the poisoned area. This structure emphasizes sub-goals, where completing preparatory steps unlocks new pathways in the environment.  

"Zelda" shares similar mechanics. Players must collect a key and reach a door, but their path is blocked by monsters that actively pursue and kill the character. Defeating these threats requires using the spacebar, a mechanic repeated across several games to denote active combat or environmental interaction. "Plaqueattack" similarly relies on the spacebar, but in this "Space Invaders"-style game, players shoot "toothpaste" to clear harmful "food" objects, prioritizing speed over complex strategy.  

"Sokoban" shifts the focus to intricate puzzle-solving: players must push boxes into designated holes. Success demands careful planning to avoid dead-ends that trap the character or the boxes, compounded by the time pressure to finish efficiently. "Avoid George" introduces a defensive challenge: George converts green blocks into purple over time, but players can reverse these changes using the spacebar. The objective is to preserve at least one green block when the timer ends, requiring a balance between defense and resource management.  

"Push Boulders" combines strategic planning with physics-based problem-solving. Players must maneuver boulders to remove hazards and reach the exit, requiring knowledge of how objects interact with the environment. The "Relational" game escalates complexity: players must eliminate blue gems by pushing them into fire, but the environment dynamically changes as blocks transform into new types, including fire itself. Mastery here demands a large knowledge set about object interactions, while time constraints heighten tension.  

Finally, the "Watergame" challenges players to navigate environments where deadly water blocks often surround the exit. Clearing this water with dirt requires complex planning, as missteps create dead-ends. "Lemmings" introduces cooperative elements: players must guide a group to an exit by using the spacebar to dig tunnels. Each action, however, reduces the player’s score, creating a tension between necessary interventions and optimal performance. Across these games, the spacebar frequently serves as a critical control for overcoming obstacles, highlighting its recurring role in enabling player agency.

One issue with the architecture is that a large number of features can lead to a combinatorial explosion as the number of functions learned in the second phase of training grows with the square of the number of features. In particular, one-hot encoded variables which encode categorical variables with a large number of potential values can cause the number of functions in the model to explode very quickly; this problem compounds when multiple such variables exist in the dataset. There are several potential solutions to this particular problem. In our work, we simply disabled one-hot encoding for the two affected datasets: Adult and Diabetes. new_text: A key limitation of the architecture arises when handling a large number of features, as the combinatorial complexity increases exponentially with the square of the feature count during the second phase of training. This is particularly problematic for one-hot encoded categorical variables with high cardinality, which rapidly escalate the number of functions in the model; the effect intensifies when multiple such variables are present in the data. Addressing this issue involves multiple potential strategies, but in our implementation, we opted to exclude one-hot encoding for the two datasets exhibiting this challenge: Adult and Diabetes. While this decision weakened the regression models’ performance, we considered the trade-off reasonable, as our primary objective was to evaluate the comparative efficacy of Regression Networks versus DNNs.

The local self attention module is designed to specialize every feature point. As common transformers <cit.>, our local self attention operations on queries(Q), keys(K) and values(V) with an input feature map X∈ℝ^C × H × W, and output a transformed version X with the same shape as X. For every location in X, we select its r × r neighborhood to conduct the self-attention. Feature vectors of the neighborhood locations in X are collected, and then we get a neighborhood feature tensor X^'∈ℝ^C × H × W × r × r. We send the input feature map X into the query transformation function ℱ_q, and send the neighborhood feature tensor X^' into the key and value transformation functions ℱ_k/ℱ_v respectively. The query/key/value transformation functions are implemented with 1 × 1 convolutions followed by ReLU activations respectively.
new_text: The local self-attention module is designed to specialize each feature point. Analogous to standard transformer architectures <cit.>, the local self-attention mechanism processes queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V) using an input feature map X∈ℝ^C × H × W, producing a transformed output X with the same spatial dimensions as the input. For each position in X, a localized r × r neighborhood is selected for self-attention computation. Feature vectors from these neighboring regions are aggregated, resulting in a neighborhood feature tensor X′∈ℝ^C × H × W × r × r. The input feature map X is passed through the query transformation function ℱ_q, while the neighborhood tensor X′ is processed by key (ℱ_k) and value (ℱ_v) transformation functions. All three transformation functions are implemented as 1 × 1 convolutions followed by ReLU activation layers.

Figure <ref> shows a comparison of the proposed MMNet with state-of-the-art methods under varying α values. The parameter α determines the threshold for acceptable displacement in keypoint matching. When α is set to a low value (e.g., α = 0.02), only matches where the predicted keypoint is very close to the ground truth are considered correct. This strict criterion often results in failed matches for keypoint pairs that require larger displacements. As α increases, the allowed matching displacement widens, providing greater flexibility in identifying correct correspondences. 

The performance of MMNet is evaluated across different α ranges. When α is increased from 0.02 to 0.1, all methods exhibit rapid improvements in PCK (Percentage of Correct Keypoints), indicating that the performance of keypoint matching algorithms is highly sensitive to the allowable displacement range. This suggests that moderate α values (0.02–0.1) are critical for distinguishing between methods, as smaller α values impose overly restrictive conditions, while larger α values begin to balance performance. 

However, when α exceeds 0.15 and approaches 0.3, all methods achieve similarly high matching accuracy, demonstrating that excessively large α values eliminate meaningful differences between algorithms. In this regime, even suboptimal methods can achieve high PCK scores due to the lenient matching criteria. Notably, MMNet demonstrates superior performance when α is in the range of 0.01 to 0.05, consistently outperforming other state-of-the-art methods. This highlights MMNet’s ability to accurately identify relevant neighborhood pixels even under stringent matching constraints, suggesting its robustness in modeling local spatial relationships.

Recently, some of the EV charging energy management challenges for the non-CAV system has been studied that focuses on game-theoretical approaches in <cit.>. In <cit.>, the authors proposed a two-stage non-cooperative game among EV aggregators while these aggregators decide EV charging energy profiling. In particular, the objective of this game model is to minimize EV charging energy cost for the EVs. Thus, the authors have considered ideal, or non-ideal, decisions for the aggregators to analyze the impact of EV charging decision. In <cit.>, the authors proposed an incentive-based EV charging scheduling mechanism by considering uncertain energy load of each charging station (CS) and EV charging time constraint. In particular, the authors have designed a distributed online EV charging scheduling algorithm by combining ϵ-Nash equilibrium and Lyapunov optimization to maximize the payoff of each CS. Furthermore, a game-based decentralized EV charging schedule was proposed in <cit.>. Particularly, the authors in <cit.> developed a Nash Folk regret-based strategy mechanism while minimizing the EV user payment and maximizing the power grid efficiency. The work in <cit.> developed a competitive pricing mechanism for electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs) by considering both large-sized EVCSs (L-EVCSs) and small-sized EVCS (S-EVCSs) with heterogeneous capacities and charging operation behavior of CSs. A Stackelberg game-based solution approach was proposed to analyze the price competition among the CSs in the form of a multiplicatively-weighted Voronoi diagram. However, the works in <cit.> do not investigate the problem of long time charging, minimization of idle charging time for CS (i.e., EVSE) nor they account for the irrational energy demand and charging time among the EVs (i.e., CVs and AVs). Dealing with irrational energy demand and charging time among EVs as well as EVSEs is challenging due to the intrinsic behaviors of each EV and EVSE evolve the risk of uncertainty. In order to overcome this unique EV charging scheduling challenge, we propose to develop a risk adversarial multi-agent learning framework that can adapt new uncertain risk towards a rational decision support system for the connected and autonomous vehicle charging.
new_text: Recent studies on EV charging energy management in non-CAV systems have focused on game-theoretical approaches <cit.>. In <cit.>, a two-stage non-cooperative game among EV aggregators was proposed to determine charging profiles, with the objective of minimizing EV charging costs. Ideal and non-ideal aggregator decisions were analyzed to assess their impact on charging strategies. A distributed online EV charging algorithm was developed in <cit.>, combining ϵ-Nash equilibrium and Lyapunov optimization to maximize CS payoffs under uncertain loads and time constraints. A decentralized EV charging schedule based on Nash Folk regret minimization was proposed in <cit.>, aiming to reduce user payments while enhancing power grid efficiency. In <cit.>, a competitive pricing mechanism was developed for EVCSs, considering heterogeneous L-EVCS and S-EVCS with varying capacities and operational behaviors. This was analyzed using a Stackelberg game model based on multiplicatively-weighted Voronoi diagrams. However, these works do not address long charging durations, idle EVSE time minimization, or irrational energy/demand behavior in EVs (CVs and AVs). Such challenges arise from uncertain EV and EVSE behaviors, introducing risk. To address these challenges, we propose a risk-adversarial multi-agent learning framework to adaptively support rational charging decisions for connected and autonomous vehicles.

section: The Fable: Bob and Alice Go to a Bar
old_text:
Many different settings can be considered based on this story.
Bob and Alice may know each other's preferences with respect to
the bars and to the meeting with the other person, be uncertain
about the preferences, or hold wrong beliefs about the
preferences. Their preferences may be collaborative (both want to
meet) or competitive (Bob wants to meet Alice, but Alice avoids
Bob). Bob may consider Alice's deliberation about Bob's
behavior, and vice versa, recursively. It turns out that all
these scenarios can be represented by a single model of
interacting agents. However, doing this properly, from the
viewpoint of both specification and inference, requires certain
care.
new_text: The richness of this scenario depends on specific factors influencing Bob and Alice’s interactions. For instance, their mutual understanding of each other’s preferences—whether aligned with bar choices or meeting goals—can vary significantly. They might possess perfect knowledge, partial uncertainty, or even hold incorrect assumptions about one another’s priorities. Moreover, the nature of their interaction itself introduces complexity: in some cases, both might aim to meet (collaborative preferences), while in others, only one party seeks the encounter while the other actively avoids it (competitive preferences). A further layer of intricacy arises when each agent recursively considers the other’s deliberation process—Bob might anticipate how Alice interprets his behavior, while Alice, in turn, might question Bob’s assumptions about her motivations. Crucially, all these dynamics—spanning knowledge states, preference alignment, and recursive reasoning—can be captured within a single framework for modeling interacting agents. However, constructing such a model rigorously requires careful attention to both how scenarios are formally defined (specification) and how inferences about agent behavior are derived (inference), as oversights in either domain risk distorting the model’s validity.

Given three disjoint agent-sets A, B and C, each of size n,

new_text: Ng and Hirschberg <cit.> studied a 3D generalization of the Stable Marriage problem, termed 3D Stable Family (3-GSM): Given three disjoint sets A, B, C of size n, where each agent in a set X ∈ {A, B, C} ranks pairs from the other two sets, the 3-GSM problem asks whether a 3D stable matching exists. A matching is a collection of n disjoint triples {a_i, b_i, c_i}, a_i ∈ A, b_i ∈ B, c_i ∈ C. It is stable if no triple {a, b, c} exists where each member prefers the other two agents to their respective partners in the matching.

new_text: Advancements in 3D simulation technology have led to the creation of diverse 3D datasets, including SUNCG <cit.>, Matterport <cit.>, and Gibson <cit.>, which serve as foundational resources for constructing embodied environments. Leveraging these datasets, researchers utilize different simulators to render the 3D assets into simulated embodied environments. An agent that engages with the environment through a physical body is referred to as an "embodied agent" <cit.>. These simulated environments provide RGB data (with many also providing depth) to enable the agent to perceive and interpret its surroundings. Certain simulators, such as MINOS <cit.>, further incorporate contact force sensors and localization sensors. By operating within these virtual spaces, navigation agents can generate extensive trajectory data samples for training. This approach significantly reduces the cost and logistical challenges of real-world data collection.

Recently, more researchers have focused on long-term navigation. Motivated by this, Wani <cit.> proposed MultiON, a benchmark for multi-object navigation. In MultiON, an agent must navigate to multiple target objects sequentially, making the navigation trajectory significantly longer. The agent performs a FOUND action to declare that it has reached the instructed target. Perception and effective planning under partial observation are critical for solving this task. There are two simulators that support multi-agent navigation: Habitat and iGibson.

new_text:
**Robust detection.**  
Like robust representations, detection methods maintain the original aggregation function of GCNs but focus instead on identifying the appropriate nodes for aggregation. Existing approaches include Jaccard detection <cit.>, which removes edges connecting nodes whose feature-based Jaccard similarity falls below a predefined threshold, and singular value decomposition <cit.>, which applies low-rank approximation to preprocess the graph structure.

**From GCNs to aggregation function.**
Recall that a core operation of GCNs is to recursively update each node's embedding by aggregating the ones of their neighbors. Since structural adversarial attacks directly change the input of aggregation function, the robustness of the aggregation function is closely related to the robustness of GCNs. Specifically, injecting/deleting an edge of a node will add/remove an embedding from the input set (i.e., the set of embeddings needed to be aggregated). If a GCN is built on a non-robust aggregation function, the whole model tends to be non-robust as well. Figure <ref> is a simple example of mean aggregation. As can be seen from Figure <ref>, although most input nodes are blue class and there is only one single perturbation, the output is classified to the red class. Thus it is crucial to identify whether the existing aggregation function of GCNs is robust and whether employing a more robust aggregation can improve the robustness against structural attacks.
new_text: A core operation in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) involves iteratively refining each node’s embedding representation by aggregating information from its neighboring nodes. This process relies on an aggregation function to combine the features of a node and its immediate neighbors, forming the basis for updating the node’s state. The structural integrity of a GCN is thus closely tied to how this aggregation function handles perturbations in the input graph structure. Specifically, adversarial attacks that manipulate the graph’s structure—such as adding or removing edges—directly alter the set of embeddings that the aggregation function processes. For instance, inserting a deceptive edge introduces an unexpected embedding into the aggregation input, while deleting an edge removes a legitimate neighbor’s embedding. These modifications can distort the aggregated output, particularly if the chosen aggregation function is inherently sensitive to such perturbations. To illustrate, consider a GCN using mean aggregation (as shown in Figure <ref>). Here, a single adversarial edge connecting a node to an outlying red-class node causes the aggregated result to deviate from the majority of blue-class neighbors, resulting in misclassification. This highlights a critical vulnerability: when the aggregation function lacks robustness to structural changes, the entire GCN’s predictions become susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Therefore, evaluating the robustness of existing aggregation functions and exploring alternatives that can withstand such perturbations are essential steps in strengthening GCNs against structural adversarial attacks.

Food inspections remain an essential food safety practice to prevent food-borne illnesses.
However, the variation in practices and guidelines across jurisdictions has led to mixed results.
One of the first studies done in Seattle-King County found that restaurants with lower food inspection scores were likely to have more outbreaks than restaurants with a better score <cit.>.
Another study done in Miami–Dade County found no correlation between restaurant inspection scores and the outbreak of food-borne illnesses <cit.>. used a large-scale dataset to conduct a study across the U.S. and called for a deeper examination into the restaurant inspection system <cit.>.
Beyond working with food inspection datasets alone, recent work proposed an ML-based approach to find restaurants that could be a cause of food-borne illnesses using Google search activity <cit.> and argued that the use of Yelp data does not improve the prediction of inspection scores <cit.>.
This paper builds upon the objective of the City of Chicago <cit.> to find restaurants that would result in a critical violation and explores the fairness of the resulting schedule. We discuss the city's work, and another prior reanalysis of it <cit.>, in <ref>.
new_text: Food inspections remain a cornerstone of food safety practices to mitigate food-borne illness risks. However, inconsistent implementation of inspection protocols and divergent regulatory frameworks across jurisdictions have resulted in inconclusive outcomes. One of the earliest investigations in Seattle-King County revealed that restaurants with subpar inspection scores were more likely to be associated with outbreaks compared to those with higher scores <cit.>. Conversely, a concurrent study in Miami-Dade County found no statistically significant correlation between inspection scores and food-borne illness outbreaks <cit.>. A subsequent, nationwide analysis employing extensive U.S. datasets highlighted the need for a comprehensive reevaluation of current inspection methodologies <cit.>. Beyond traditional inspection data, recent research has introduced machine learning (ML) approaches to identify potential outbreak sources through Google search activity <cit.>, while also demonstrating that Yelp data does not significantly enhance the accuracy of inspection score predictions <cit.>. Building upon the City of Chicago's initiative <cit.> to identify establishments at risk of critical violations, this paper examines the equity implications of inspection scheduling strategies. We provide a detailed review of the city's original methodology and a subsequent critique of its implementation in <ref>.

**Robustness measure.**
To address the above problems, the major challenge is how to quantitatively measure the robustness of aggregation functions. Previous work <cit.> has shown that the perturbed edges tend to connect nodes with low feature similarity. In other words, the adversarially injected node can be viewed as an outlier compared to other true neighbors. Now the key problem is that outliers are hard to define. Following the existing work <cit.>, the robustness of a function can be estimated under the extreme case. That is, whether adding multiple infinities values to the input data will cause the output to infinity. Formally, we employ the breakdown point to quantitatively measure the robustness of a given aggregation function, which refers to the maximum fraction of perturbations that an aggregation scheme can tolerate before incurring arbitrarily high error. Let 𝒩_v denote the set of input nodes. Fortunately, since the aggregation functions considered in this work are element-wise (e.g., the aggregation function of GCNs is element-wise weighted mean), we can reduce our analysis from high-dimension to 1-dimension. Therefore, we assume the output of f is a scalar corresponding to a certain dimension.

Consistent answers to a query from a possibly inconsistent database are answers
that are simultaneously retrieved from every possible repair of the database. Repairs
are consistent instances that minimally differ from the original inconsistent instance. It has been shown before
that database repairs can be specified as the stable models of a disjunctive logic program. In this
paper we show how to use the repair programs to transform the problem of consistent query answering
into a problem of reasoning w.r.t. a theory written in second-order predicate logic. It also investigated how a first-order
theory can be obtained instead by applying second-order quantifier elimination techniques.
new_text: Consistent query answers from an inconsistent database correspond to results extracted across all potential repairs of that database. Repairs represent consistent data instances that deviate minimally from the original inconsistent state. Previous research has demonstrated that database repairs can be modeled as stable models of a disjunctive logic program. This work demonstrates how to leverage these repair-based programs to reframe the challenge of consistent query answering as a reasoning problem within a second-order predicate logic framework. Additionally, it examines the derivation of a first-order theory through the application of second-order quantifier elimination methodologies.

old_text: Point completion refers to completing the missing geometries of an object from incomplete observations. Main-stream methods predict the missing shapes by decoding a global feature learned from the input point cloud, which often leads to deficient results in preserving topology consistency and surface details. In this work, we present ME-PCN, a point completion network that leverages emptiness in 3D shape space. Given a single depth scan, previous methods often encode the occupied partial shapes while ignoring the empty regions (e.g. holes) in depth maps. In contrast, we argue that these `emptiness' clues indicate shape boundaries that can be used to improve topology representation and detail granularity on surfaces. Specifically, our ME-PCN encodes both the occupied point cloud and the neighboring `empty points'. It estimates coarse-grained but complete and reasonable surface points in the first stage, followed by a refinement stage to produce fine-grained surface details. Comprehensive experiments verify that our ME-PCN presents better qualitative and quantitative performance against the state-of-the-art. Besides, we further prove that our `emptiness' design is lightweight and easy to embed in existing methods, which shows consistent effectiveness in improving the CD and EMD scores.
new_text: Point cloud completion involves reconstructing missing geometric structures from incomplete data observations. Existing approaches typically predict missing shapes by decoding global features extracted from input point clouds, yet these methods frequently struggle to preserve topological integrity and capture fine surface details. To address these limitations, we introduce ME-PCN, a point completion framework that exploits the concept of emptiness within 3D shape spaces. Conventional methods typically encode occupied partial geometries while disregarding unoccupied regions such as voids in depth maps. We posit that these "emptiness" cues correspond to shape boundaries, offering critical information for enhancing topological representation and surface detail resolution. Specifically, our ME-PCN simultaneously encodes occupied point clouds and adjacent "empty" points, enabling the generation of coarse yet structurally sound surface points in an initial phase, followed by a refinement stage to restore high-resolution surface characteristics. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that ME-PCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Furthermore, we show that this emptiness-based design is computationally efficient and easily integrable into existing frameworks, consistently enhancing both Chamfer Distance (CD) and Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) scores.

new_text: In our experiments, we utilize eight distinct datasets to represent both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) data sources. All images are standardized to a uniform resolution of 224 × 224 pixels and subjected to basic data augmentation techniques, including horizontal flipping and contrast adjustments, to increase dataset variability while preserving computational efficiency. For model training, we employ pre-trained EfficientNet architectures <cit.>, which were initially trained on the ImageNet benchmark dataset. These models are adapted to the target datasets through transfer learning, enabling the reuse of learned features from the source task. To regularize the training process and mitigate overfitting, we set the label smoothing parameter <cit.> to 0.2. The training strategy is structured in two stages: first, we fix the front layers and train them for three epochs with an initial learning rate of 0.01. Subsequently, we proceed to fine-tune the model starting from the second block, reducing the learning rate to 0.001 to allow for more precise adaptation of deeper features. The Adam optimizer <cit.> is used throughout the process due to its adaptive learning rate capabilities. To prevent overfitting and ensure robust convergence, we implement early stopping by monitoring validation loss. Specifically, if the validation loss does not improve for three consecutive epochs, we reduce the learning rate by a factor of 0.6 and continue training. The final classification accuracy achieved by the models across all datasets is summarized in Table <ref>. The critical technique for few-shot semantic segmentation is the way to propagate the local and global information between the query and support images.
Previous methods simply average the support feature to a global vector, serving as a general clue to guide every position of the query image. However, the global vector does not contain the information of spatial structures and only captures the most dominant information of the support features, which results in the limited parts of the support images being used to match the query images.
The unconstrained many-to-many matching methods aim to address the problem with a weighted connection between each query and support features. However, due to the dominant feature problem, most of the feature points from the support image will match the most discriminative parts in the query image, which causes the remaining query features to be unmatched.
new_text: The key technique in few-shot semantic segmentation is how to propagate local and global information between query and support images. Previous methods simply average support features into a global vector to serve as a general descriptor for guiding all positions of the query image. However, the global vector does not capture spatial structural information and only retains dominant information from the support features, resulting in only limited parts of the support images being used to match the query images. Unconstrained many-to-many matching methods aim to address this problem by establishing weighted connections between each query and support feature. However, due to the dominant feature issue, most feature points from the support image will align with the most discriminative regions in the query image, leaving the remaining query features unmatched.

new_text: For training, the DeepMoon model utilizes a dataset created by combining two manually annotated crater datasets: the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Wide Angle Camera Global Lunar Digital Elevation Model (LRO WAC Global Lunar DEM) and the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter DEM (LRO LOLA DEM). These datasets were partitioned into three equal subsets—training, validation, and testing—each containing 30,000 DEM images. The model optimizes using a pixel-wise binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss function to minimize prediction errors. Once trained, DeepMoon generates a crater rim prediction mask, which serves as input for subsequent post-processing steps. These steps include a low-level image processing stage and a template-matching procedure to refine and identify the final crater locations. The model achieves median fractional errors of 11% or less for longitude, latitude, and radius measurements, indicating strong alignment with the original human-annotated data. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to transfer knowledge from lunar terrain to Mercury’s surface, as evidenced by qualitative success when tested on extraterrestrial maps, highlighting its adaptability across planetary datasets.

old_text: The main idea behind SplitNN is to split and allot a DNN among multiple parties. Figure <ref> displays potential setups of the SplitNN protocol. In its simplest setting (Figure <ref>), SplitNN involves a single data holder (client) and a server. The client computes the first few layers of the DNN, and forwards the output, along with the target label, to the server. The server then resumes the computation with the remaining layers. This concludes a forward pass through the network, and then the server initiates the corresponding backward pass by computing the loss value. The server completes a backward pass through its part of the network, and sends the gradient values of its first layer back to the client. Finally, the client completes the backward pass, concluding a complete forward-backward pass through the network.
new_text: SplitNN is designed to partition and distribute a deep neural network (DNN) across multiple parties, enabling collaborative model training while maintaining data privacy. As illustrated in Figure <ref>, the protocol can be configured in various ways depending on the number of participants. The simplest implementation (Figure <ref>) involves two parties: a client, who holds sensitive data, and a server, which processes non-sensitive computations. In this setup, the client is responsible for executing the initial layers of the DNN—typically those that process raw input data—before transmitting the intermediate outputs and the corresponding target labels to the server. This partial computation ensures the data holder retains control over unprocessed information. The server then continues the forward pass by processing the remaining layers of the network, culminating in the final prediction. To enable model training, the server calculates the loss, which quantifies the discrepancy between the model’s prediction and the true label, marking the start of the backward pass. The server completes gradient computation for its assigned layers, then sends the gradients of its first layer to the client. The client uses these gradients to propagate error signals backward through its own layers, finalizing the backward pass. This two-step process—combining the client’s and server’s contributions—ensures a full forward and backward pass, enabling end-to-end training while limiting exposure of sensitive data to the client alone.

old_text: According to Shannon and Weaver’s information theory <cit.>, communication can be divided into three levels: i) transmission level, ii) semantic level, and iii) effective level. The first level is the technical issue, mainly to solve the problem of how to accurately transmit communication symbols. The second level is the semantic issue, which mainly solves the problem of how to accurately transmit the meaning of transmission symbols. The third level is the effective issue, which mainly solves the problem of how to effectively use the received meaning according to the expected way.

Within more than 70 years since Shannon established information theory, scholars’ study mainly focused on the first level of how to accurately and effectively transmit symbols from the transmitter to the receiver. However, in recent years, with the astonishing development of artificial intelligence, natural language processing (NLP) and other supporting technologies, the intelligent level of communication system and its cognitive ability to the outside world are constantly enhanced, which provides the promising possibility to carry out the second level of semantic communication. Accordingly, semantic communication has been attracting ever-growing interests as a potential trend in the field of next-generation mobile communications.
new_text: Since Shannon's foundational work in information theory over 70 years ago, research has predominantly concentrated on the first level of communication: ensuring accurate and efficient transmission of symbols from sender to receiver. This foundational focus emphasized the reliability of signal transmission and the minimization of errors during data transfer. However, recent years have seen remarkable advances in artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and related technologies. These developments have significantly enhanced the intelligence of communication systems and their ability to perceive and interpret the external environment. This progress creates a feasible pathway for achieving the second level of communication—semantic communication—which involves conveying not just symbols but the underlying meaning. As a result, semantic communication has become a topic of increasing interest, with growing recognition as a potential direction for next-generation mobile communication systems.

Synthetic segmentation is a unique cross-domain knowledge transferring framework for medical images to utilize knowledge across modalities <cit.>. The inspiration for synthetic segmentation is the content consistency among corresponding medical modalities, e.g, the head or abdominal CT have the similar organs and tissues with corresponding MRI. Therefore, synthetic segmentation usually utilizes image translation to get synthetic target modality images from source labeled images, then, the synthetic images will be accompanied with original real labels to train a segmentation network can be directly applied to target modality images. It is widely investigated in cross-modality such as CT-MR <cit.>, CBCT-MR <cit.>. new_text: Synthetic segmentation is a unique cross-domain knowledge transfer framework for medical images to utilize knowledge across modalities <cit.>. The inspiration for synthetic segmentation is the content consistency among corresponding medical modalities, e.g., head or abdominal CT scans have similar organs and tissues as corresponding MRI. Therefore, synthetic segmentation usually utilizes image translation to generate synthetic target modality images from source-labeled images. Then, the synthetic images are accompanied by original real labels to train a segmentation network that can be directly applied to target modality images. It is widely investigated in cross-modality settings such as CT-MR <cit.>, CBCT-MR <cit.>. Among them, CycleGAN-based synthetic segmentation, which is an unsupervised framework and requires only unpaired images, has received more attention than supervised approaches based on paired images <cit.>. In addition to some papers directly using CycleGAN as a component of their framework <cit.>, there are also methods that enhance CycleGAN with various constraints to achieve better synthetic segmentation <cit.>.

M is encoded into symbols X via the channel encoder to compensate for noise introduced by the physical channel. After transmission through the physical channel, the receiver obtains the distorted symbols Y, which are subsequently decoded by the channel decoder. The semantic decoder layer then reconstructs the transmitted sentences. Finally, the difference between the original sentence S and the reconstructed sentence Ŝ is calculated to evaluate transmission accuracy. The system is optimized using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in accordance with the loss function L_CE.

old_text: Machine learning approaches have recently been leveraged as a substitute or an aid for physical/mathematical modeling approaches to dynamical systems. To develop an efficient machine learning method dedicated to modeling and prediction of multiscale dynamics, we propose a reservoir computing model with diverse timescales by using a recurrent network of heterogeneous leaky integrator neurons. In prediction tasks with fast-slow chaotic dynamical systems including a large gap in timescales of their subsystems dynamics, we demonstrate that the proposed model has a higher potential than the existing standard model and yields a performance comparable to the best one of the standard model even without an optimization of the leak rate parameter. Our analysis reveals that the timescales required for producing each component of target dynamics are appropriately and flexibly selected from the reservoir dynamics by model training.
new_text: Machine learning approaches have been used as substitutes or supplements for physical/mathematical models in dynamical systems. To develop an efficient method for modeling and predicting multiscale dynamics, we propose a reservoir computing model using a recurrent network of heterogeneous leaky integrator neurons. In prediction tasks involving fast-slow chaotic systems with large timescale disparities between subsystems, the proposed model exhibits greater potential than existing models and achieves performance comparable to the best existing model without parameter tuning. Our analysis shows that training adaptively selects appropriate timescales from the reservoir dynamics for each target component.

Motivation. Due to the unbalanced distribution between boundary pixels and background pixels, only using boundary pixels for glass detection will lead to larger prediction errors of pixels close to the boundary than those far away from the glass. Therefore, the glass boundary should diffuse itself into the glass's interior to amplify its influence. Conversely, the glass's interior should diffuse itself from center to boundary to loosen its influence. Based on this observation, we propose to decouple the glass label into the interior-diffusion part and the boundary-diffusion part, both of which are auxiliary supervisions to enhance the overall glass detection quality and boundary clearness. To make full use of the decoupled supervisions, we further present a three-stream network, which consists of the proposed multi-scale interactive dilation modules to effectively integrate large-field contextual features for detecting glass of different sizes. Also, our proposed network learns to fuse multi-modal information to further enhance the performance.
new_text: The imbalance between boundary and background pixels in glass detection results in higher prediction errors near the boundary when relying solely on boundary pixels. To address this, we propose two diffusion strategies: the boundary should spread into the glass interior to amplify its impact, while the interior diffuses outward toward the boundary to attenuate its influence. Based on this principle, we decompose the glass label into an interior-diffusion component and a boundary-diffusion component, which serve as complementary supervisory signals to improve detection accuracy and boundary precision. To leverage these dual supervisions effectively, we design a three-stream neural network architecture incorporating multi-scale interactive dilation modules. This design enables the aggregation of long-range contextual features across diverse spatial scales, facilitating the detection of glasses with varying sizes. Furthermore, the network is trained to integrate multi-modal data, enhancing robustness and performance in complex scenarios.

Building machine learning models for natural language
understanding (NLU) tasks relies heavily on labeled data. Weak
supervision has been shown to provide valuable supervision when large
amount of labeled data is unavailable or expensive to obtain. Existing
works studying weak supervision for NLU either mostly focus on a
specific task or simulate weak supervision signals from ground-truth
labels. To date a benchmark for NLU with real world weak supervision
signals for a collection of NLU tasks is still not available. In this
paper, we propose such a benchmark,
named [:WeAkly
supervised Learning for Natural
language Understanding Testbed], to advocate and
facilitate research on weak supervision for NLU. consists of NLU
tasks with different types, including both document-level prediction
tasks and token-level prediction tasks and for each task contains weak
labels generated by multiple real-world weak sources. We conduct
baseline evaluations on the benchmark to systematically test the value
of weak supervision for NLU tasks, with various weak supervision
methods and model architectures. We demonstrate the benefits of weak
supervision for low-resource NLU tasks and expect to stimulate
further research on methodologies to best leverage weak supervision.
The benchmark and code for baselines will be publicly available at <aka.ms/walnut_benchmark>.
new_text: Building machine learning models for natural language understanding (NLU) tasks relies heavily on labeled data. Weak supervision has been shown to provide valuable supervision when large amounts of labeled data are unavailable or expensive to obtain. Existing works on weak supervision for NLU either focus narrowly on specific tasks or simulate weak signals from ground-truth labels. No benchmark for NLU with real-world weak supervision signals across multiple tasks currently exists. In this paper, we propose such a benchmark, WALNUT (Weakly Supervised Learning for Natural Language Understanding Testbed), to advance research on weak supervision for NLU. It includes diverse NLU tasks, spanning document- and token-level prediction, with weak labels generated by multiple real-world sources for each task. We evaluate baseline models on the benchmark to assess the efficacy of weak supervision using varied methods and architectures, demonstrating its benefits for low-resource NLU tasks and aiming to stimulate further research on leveraging weak supervision effectively. The benchmark and baseline code will be publicly available at <aka.ms/walnut_benchmark>.

The goal is to output a heatmap that represents the position of an agent at a given time in the future. The trajectory is then regressed conditioned to the final end point.
To achieve this, our GOHOME system focuses on lane-level operations as illustrated in Fig. <ref>.
The local HD-Map is provided as a graph of L lanelets. A lanelet represents a macro section of the road (10 to 20 meters on average), as our goal is to encode connectivity at a macro level (lane segments), and not micro level (every meter). Each lanelet is defined as a sequence of centerline points, and is connected to its predecessor, successor, left and right neighbors if they exist.
We encode each lanelet into a road graph, where geometric and connectivity information are represented. Our model yields a score for each of these lanelets, that is used to identify most probables lanes. A partial heatmap is then generated for the top ranking lanelets, and projected onto a global heatmap. Afterwards, we sample a set of endpoints from the heatmap and recreate a trajectory for each.
new_text: The GOHOME system aims to predict and visualize an agent's future position at a specific time by generating a heatmap that reflects probable movement. To achieve this, the system models the agent’s trajectory in reverse, starting from a predefined endpoint and regressing the path backward through the road network. This approach relies on lane-level operations, as illustrated in Fig. <ref>, which focus on high-level road connectivity rather than granular spatial details. The local high-definition map (HD-Map) is structured as a graph composed of *L* lanelets. Each lanelet represents a segment of a road averaging 10–20 meters in length, designed to capture macro-level connectivity (e.g., transitions between lanes) rather than micro-level geometry (e.g., every meter of road). Each lanelet is defined by a sequence of centerline points and maintains connections to its predecessor, successor, and adjacent left/right lanes, if applicable. These connections are critical for modeling navigable pathways. The system encodes each lanelet into a road graph, embedding both its geometric properties (e.g., shape, orientation) and topological relationships (e.g., connectivity to neighboring lanes). A scoring mechanism then evaluates the likelihood of each lanelet being part of the agent’s path, identifying the most probable candidates. For the top-ranked lanelets, partial heatmaps are generated to highlight regions of high probability, which are subsequently aggregated into a global heatmap. Finally, a set of potential endpoints is sampled from this heatmap, and for each endpoint, a corresponding trajectory is reconstructed to align with the predicted future position.

**Lane ranking.**
The lanelet classification is obtained with a linear layer on the graph encoding, followed by a sigmoid activation. The ground-truth is defined by a 1 for all lanelets where the future car position is inside the lanelet polygon and 0 otherwise. new_text:
**Lane ranking.**  
A linear layer applied to the graph encoding generates the lanelet classification, followed by a sigmoid function to produce probabilities. The ground-truth labels assign a value of 1 to lanelets containing the predicted future position of the vehicle and 0 otherwise. The loss function combines binary cross-entropy with the pixel-wise loss defined in Eq. <ref>, weighted by a coefficient of 10^{-2}. To reduce computational load, lane-level raster predictions are computed only for a subset of lanelets, selected based on the model's predicted classification scores (c_lane). The top k ranked lanelets are chosen, and their rasters are projected, as predictions for excluded lanelets are near-zero with negligible impact on performance, as validated in Sec. <ref>.

On the other hand, probability heatmap are a great way of representing information coming from different sources or models in a common system of reference and can be averaged together without any assumption nor risk of mode collapsing. These heatmaps can be averaged without assumptions or risk of mode collapsing, enabling straightforward application of endpoint sampling to extract the desired number of trajectories. The ensembling process is detailed in Fig. 3 of Appendix C.

new_text: In text summarization, a document, its gold summary, and model-generated summaries can be viewed as distinct perspectives on a shared meaning representation. We propose SeqCo, a sequence-level contrastive learning model for text summarization, which aims to minimize the distances between a document, its gold summary, and generated summaries during training. Experiments on three summarization datasets (CNNDM, NYT, and XSum) show that SeqCo consistently improves a strong Seq2Seq text generation model and achieves state-of-the-art results on CNNDM and NYT. Future work includes extending SeqCo to multilingual or cross-lingual text generation tasks. Our experiments show that using multiple contrastive objectives did not improve results, prompting further investigation into methods for regularizing diverse contrastive objectives.

In light of these structural differences, we aim to generate highly transferable adversarial examples using white-box ViTs as proxy models to attack different black-box ViTs, normally trained CNNs, and robustly trained CNNs. In particular, we introduce a dual attack method tailored for the architecture of ViTs—attacking the attention mechanism and patches simultaneously, both of which are the core components of popular transformer architectures. In particular, we use a Pay No Attention (PNA) attack and a PatchOut attack to manipulate the attention mechanism and image features in parallel.
The PNA attack improves adversarial transferability by treating the attention weights computed on the forward pass as constants. In other words, it does not propagate through the branch of the computation graph that produces the attention weights, as illustrated in Figure <ref>. This prevents patches from strongly interacting, as measured by the Shapley interaction index <cit.>, which is known to help boost adversarial transferability <cit.>.
In addition, the PatchOut attack randomly samples a subset of patches to receive updates on each iteration of the attack crafting process. This is akin to using dropout <cit.> on perturbation patches, and helps to combat over-fitting. It also shares similarities with random feature selection in Random Forests <cit.>, Dropout and Diversity Input (DI) <cit.>.
new_text: In light of these structural differences, our goal is to generate highly transferable adversarial examples using white-box vision transformers (ViTs) as proxy models to attack diverse black-box ViTs, conventionally trained CNNs, and robustly trained CNNs. To achieve this, we introduce a dual attack strategy specifically designed for ViT architectures, simultaneously targeting the attention mechanism and patch representations—two fundamental components of transformer-based models. This approach combines a Pay No Attention (PNA) attack with a PatchOut attack to manipulate attention dynamics and image features in parallel. The PNA attack enhances adversarial transferability by fixing the attention weights computed during the forward pass as constants, effectively preventing gradients from propagating through the computational branch that generates these weights, as illustrated in Figure <ref>. This technique suppresses patch interactions measured by the Shapley interaction index <cit.>, a metric demonstrated to improve transferability <cit.>. The PatchOut attack, meanwhile, randomly selects a subset of patches to update during each attack iteration—a process analogous to applying dropout <cit.> to perturbation patches, mitigating overfitting. This method shares conceptual similarities with random feature selection in Random Forests <cit.> as well as dropout and Diversity Input (DI) strategies <cit.>.

Performance on CNNs.
We further evaluate the performance of transferring the adversarial examples generated on white-box ViTs to attack black-box CNNs. The results are summarized in Table <ref>. We have the following observations. First, the attack success rates of all methods decrease significantly, which indicates that adversarial samples generated on ViTs are less transferable on CNNs than ViTs, presumably due to structural differences between ViTs and CNNs. Second, MI improves the transferability of the generated adversarial examples by utilizing the momentum term to stabilize update directions.
Third, compared to other baseline methods, our proposed dual attack significantly improves MASR despite the different structures between ViTs and CNNs. The dual attack has a 42.61% average MASR on normally trained CNNs and a 22.38% average MASR on robustly trained CNNs. These results indicate the feasibility of using ViTs to attack robustly trained CNNs.
new_text: We assess the effectiveness of transferring adversarial examples generated against white-box vision transformers (ViTs) to black-box convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Results in Table <ref> reveal three key insights. First, attack success rates across all methods experience a notable decline compared to attacks within ViTs, suggesting adversarial examples produced on ViTs exhibit reduced transferability to CNNs—likely attributed to inherent architectural differences between ViTs and CNNs. Second, momentum iteration (MI) enhances transferability by leveraging the momentum term to stabilize gradient update directions. Third, our proposed dual attack achieves a substantial increase in mean attack success rate (MASR) relative to baseline methods, even when attacking CNNs with distinct structures. Specifically, the dual attack attains 42.61% average MASR on standard CNNs and 22.38% average MASR on robustly trained CNNs, demonstrating the viability of exploiting ViTs to compromise both standard and adversarially trained CNNs.

Combining with Existing Methods.
The proposed dual attack tailored for ViTs can be easily combined with existing methods to further improve performance. We demonstrate this by combining our method with MI and SGM. The reason we choose MI and SGM is that these two methods perform much better than other baseline methods.
Using these combined methods, we conduct experiments with ViT-B/16 as the white-box model. Specifically, SGM + Ours uses fewer gradients than MultiLayer Perceptron (MLP) modules according to a decay factor that is set as 0.5.
Table <ref> shows the results of the integrated methods.
We observe that the proposed dual attack significantly improves the transferability of MI and SGM across ViTs, normally trained CNNs, and robustly trained CNNs. In particular, the dual attack increases the average MASR of MI and SGM by 28.54 % and 102.49 %, respectively, when attacking robustly trained CNNs.
The results demonstrate that the dual attack can easily be combined with existing methods to further boost performance.

Combining with Existing Methods.  
The proposed dual attack for ViTs can be combined with existing methods to enhance performance. We demonstrate this by integrating our method with MI and SGM, which outperform other baselines. **Implementation.**
We implement the LangID model as a 2-layer Transformer encoder with input from the multilingual decoder states to classify the target language.
We add to the decoder states a sinusoidal positional embedding for position information.
We implement two common approaches to do classification: CLS_Token and Meanpooling.

**Implementation.**  
We develop the LangID model as a 2-layer Transformer encoder that leverages multilingual decoder states as input to predict target languages. The CLS_Token method introduces a BERT-style [CLS] token, utilizing its topmost layer’s hidden representations for downstream classification (<cit.>). For Meanpooling, we compute the average of all decoder output states before passing them to the classifier. A detailed performance comparison between these approaches is provided in Section <ref>.

Here we address these issues by introducing a non-English GPT-3 with various parameter sizes and intensively investigating their capabilities on diverse real-world classification and generation tasks under in-context few-shot learning and prompt-based optimization. We introduce a Korean in-context large-scale LM with 82B parameters, i.e., HyperCLOVA. This is the first discovery on near 100B-scale non-English LM.
We present the corpus composition of Korean datasets used for HyperCLOVA,
and describe how we crawl and refine such data to collect 561B tokens of Korean corpus (<ref>).
We also design a new Korean tokenization method based on the agglutinative property for HyperCLOVA. We use byte-level BPE <cit.> with a morpheme analyzer (<ref>). Our results show that such tokenization strategy is important for the performance of downstream tasks in large-scale in-context learning (<ref>).
new_text: To address these challenges, we introduce a non-English variant of GPT-3, featuring models with diverse parameter sizes, and conduct an in-depth evaluation of their capabilities across a range of real-world classification and text generation tasks. These assessments are performed under two key learning paradigms: in-context few-shot learning, where models learn from limited examples provided in the input, and prompt-based optimization, which leverages structured prompts to enhance task performance. As a central contribution, we present HyperCLOVA, a large-scale Korean language model with 82 billion parameters. This model represents the first study of a non-English language model approaching the 100 billion parameter scale. To train HyperCLOVA, we first outline the composition of the Korean datasets used, detailing the process of crawling and refining raw data to construct a comprehensive training corpus of 561 billion Korean tokens (<ref>). Furthermore, we introduce a novel tokenization strategy tailored to Korean’s agglutinative structure, a linguistic feature where morphemes are concatenated to form words. This approach combines byte-level Byte Pair Encoding (<cit.>) with a morpheme analyzer (<ref>), enabling more effective subword segmentation. Our findings demonstrate that this tokenization method plays a critical role in improving the model’s performance on downstream tasks within the context of large-scale in-context learning (<ref>).

Designing of Three Players. In particular, the first network is the client model trained with labeled data in each client, which has good classification ability. In a deep neural network, such ability is usually determined by the last few layers.
The second one is the global model aggregated by all the client models, which usually has a strong ability to extract features using the first few layers.
The third model combines the client model and the global model, which tries to unify both models' advantages by borrowing the first few layers from the global model and the last few layers from the client model. Then, the combined model conducts finetuning with the labeled client data.
new_text: Design of Three Players. The first model is a client model trained on each client’s labeled data, providing strong classification performance, which in deep neural networks is primarily achieved through the final layers. The second model is the global model, aggregated from all clients, excelling in feature extraction via its initial layers. The third model combines the client and global models by integrating the global model’s initial layers with the client model’s final layers, then fine-tunes on labeled client data.

With the global metamorphosis of the beauty industry and the rising demand for beauty products worldwide, the need for an efficacious makeup recommendation system has never been more. Despite the significant advancements made towards personalised makeup recommendation, the current research still falls short of incorporating the context of occasion in makeup recommendation and integrating feedback for users. In this work, we propose BeautifAI, a novel makeup recommendation system, delivering personalised occasion-oriented makeup recommendations to users while providing real-time previews and continuous feedback. The proposed work's novel contributions, including the incorporation of occasion context, region-wise makeup recommendation, real-time makeup previews and continuous makeup feedback, set our system apart from the current work in makeup recommendation. We also demonstrate our proposed system's efficacy in providing personalised makeup recommendation by conducting a user study.
new_text: The evolving global beauty industry and increasing worldwide demand for cosmetics highlight the urgent need for effective personalized makeup recommendation systems. While progress has been made in tailored recommendations, existing approaches largely overlook integrating contextual factors such as occasions and mechanisms for iterative user feedback. This study introduces BeautifAI, an innovative makeup recommendation framework that addresses these gaps by offering occasion-specific recommendations, interactive real-time visualizations, and ongoing user input integration. Key innovations include contextual adaptation to specific occasions, localized region-based makeup suggestions, dynamic preview capabilities, and feedback-driven refinement, distinguishing the system from prior work. The practical effectiveness of BeautifAI is validated through a controlled user study, demonstrating its capacity to deliver context-aware, personalized recommendations.

Let G=(X, Y, E) be a bipartite graph. An edge e=xy is said to be a bisimplicial edge if G[N[{x,y}]] is a complete bipartite subgraph of G. Let ℳ=(x_1y_1,x_2y_2,…,x_ky_k) be an ordering of pairwise nonadjacent edges of G. Let A_j={x_1,x_2,…,x_j}∪{y_1,y_2,…,y_j} and let A_0=∅. The ordering ℳ is called a perfect edge elimination ordering of G if x_j+1y_j+1 is a bisimplicial edge in G[(X∪ Y)\ A_j] for j=0,1,…,k-1 and G[(X∪ Y)\ A_k] has no edge. A bipartite graph for which there exists a perfect edge elimination ordering is called a perfect elimination bipartite graph. Panda and Pradhan <cit.> showed that the Acyclic Matching problem is NP-hard for perfect elimination bipartite graphs. In this section, we strengthen their result and prove that the problem remains NP-hard for planar perfect elimination bipartite graphs with maximum degree three and girth at least l for any arbitrary positive integer l.
