The proposed system requires users to provide two inputs - a picture of their face and the occasion for which they require makeup recommendations. The system then recommends users a combination of makeup options for the skin, eyes and lips most suited to their face and the occasion. The previews of these recommendations are then displayed on the picture of the users' face, allowing them to visualise how the makeup would look on their faces. While the users apply this recommended makeup, the system continuously provides them feedback on how accurately they have applied the recommended makeup combination.
To integrate all these functionalities into the system, we design four modules, three of which are novel contributions of this work (Module 2,3,4). Firstly, we propose a facial feature extraction module (Module 1) by fine-tuning different state of the art algorithms for facial feature extraction. We extract these facial features to ensure that we recommend users makeup styles tailored to their face's unique features. This is a significant aspect of personalisation. Secondly, we contribute a novel occasion-oriented region-wise makeup recommendation module (Module 2) that recommends users a large number of makeup styles for different regions of the face (skin, eyes, lips) by comparing neural embeddings, based on the user's choice of occasion. This region-wise recommendation module provides greater customizability, better engagement and greater diversity in recommendations than the holistic recommendation as proposed by current work. Thirdly, we propose a style-transfer module (Module 3) to provide users with previews of how the recommended makeup styles would look on their face. Fourthly, we design an innovative continuous feedback module (Module 4) using colour correlogram features that assists users while applying makeup by dispensing detailed real-time feedback on how to achieve their desired look.

During the past decade, there have been great advances in the fields of computer vision and image processing for detection and extraction of facial features for a variety of applications namely surveillance, human-computer interaction, etc. We extract facial features to provide high quality makeup recommendations that are personalised for every user. Each makeup recommendation is unique to each user as it is suited to their peculiar facial structure and features. We propose a system where for a given image of the user as input, this module identifies three regions of interest i.e. the skin, the eyes and the lips. We find that various algorithms work with different efficiency on extracting facial features.
For identifying the facial/skin region - the entire face except the eyes and lips (depicted by region of interest A in Figure 3), we utilise the ensemble method proposed in DeepFace <cit.>, a deep neural network with remarkably high performance for identifying and segmenting entire faces as bounding boxes. This model is state of the art for facial detection and verification. The algorithm employs explicit 3D face modeling in order to apply a piecewise affine transformation, and derive a face representation from a nine-layer deep neural network. This method provides an accuracy of 97.35%. After extracting the skin region, we extract the eyes and lips region of interest. For identifying the skin and lips region of the face (regions of interest B and C in Figure 3), we use a Faster RCNN model (with a ResNet-50 backbone) <cit.>, which is a state of the art convolutional neural network for object detection, pre-trained on the MS Coco Dataset <cit.>. We then fine-tune this model by freezing the first 50% layers and performing transfer learning on the MUCT Face Database <cit.>. We fine-tune this model on the MUCT dataset as it contains facial images with 76 landmarks for 3755 images that allows for greater precision in identifying the relevant regions of interest. For training, we generated the bounding boxes for each of the eyes and the lips region on the MUCT Database on the basis of 76 facial landmarks and resize the images to 128x128, allowing the model to detect the regions of interest in real time.
new_text: Advances in computer vision and image processing over the past decade have enabled significant progress in facial feature detection and extraction for applications such as surveillance and human-computer interaction. We propose a system that extracts facial features to provide personalized makeup recommendations tailored to a user's facial structure. Given a user image, the system identifies three regions of interest (ROI): skin (excluding eyes and lips, ROI A, Figure 3), eyes (ROI B), and lips (ROI C). For facial skin region segmentation, we employ the DeepFace ensemble method <cit.>, a state-of-the-art deep neural network achieving 97.35% accuracy. This model uses explicit 3D face modeling to apply piecewise affine transformations and derive representations from a nine-layer network. For eyes and lips segmentation, we utilize a Faster R-CNN with a ResNet-50 backbone <cit.>, pre-trained on MS Coco <cit.> and fine-tuned on the MUCT Face Database <cit.>. The MUCT dataset (3755 images with 76 landmarks) was selected for precise ROI identification. During fine-tuning, the first 50% of layers were frozen, and bounding boxes for eyes and lips were generated using 76 facial landmarks. Images were resized to 128×128 to enable real-time ROI detection.

In this dataset, each patient record contains medical data at five different time cycles (i.e., 0-2, 2-4, 4-6, 6-12 and 12+ hours since hospital admission); as the patient can be admitted to the ICU at any time, only medical data prior to ICU admission was used to predict ICU admission and included in the training and testing sets. Patients who were admitted to the ICU at any time cycle were given a positive label, and patients with no record of ICU admission were given a negative label.
new_text: COVID-Net Clinical ICU uses a clinical dataset from Hospital <cit.> containing 1,925 records from 385 patients, with demographic information (age, gender), comorbidities (e.g., hypertension, immunocompromised), blood metrics (e.g., platelet, neutrophil counts), and vital signs (e.g., temperature, pulse rate), totaling 228 features. Each record includes data across five time cycles (0–2, 2–4, 4–6, 6–12, and 12+ hours post-admission). Only data collected before ICU admission were used to predict ICU admission in training and testing, as patients could enter the ICU at any time cycle. Patients admitted to the ICU at any time cycle received a positive label; those without ICU admission received a negative label.

For instance, a 1D convolution layer consists of a weight W ∈ℝ^C_in× C_out× S, where C_in and C_out denote the number of input channel and output channel, and S denotes the size of the convolution kernel. new_text: As the three solvers mentioned above cannot handle tensors, Greenformer transforms weight tensors into matrices to enable decomposition of convolutional layers. For instance, a 1D convolutional layer has a weight tensor W ∈ ℝ^{C_in × C_out × S}, where C_in and C_out denote the number of input channels and output channels, respectively, and S denotes the size of the convolution kernel. Greenformer reshapes the weight into a 2-dimensional matrix W' ∈ ℝ^{C_in S × C_out}. The matrix is then decomposed and converted back into the original tensor dimensions, resulting in tensors A ∈ ℝ^{C_in × r × S} and B ∈ ℝ^{r × C_out × 1}.

old_text: Despite the fact that many works have been published on low-rank matrix factorization, all the solutions are model-dependent, making applicability to different model architecture difficult and cumbersome. To improve the generalization and applicability of the low-rank matrix factorization method, we introduce Greenformer, an eloquent low-rank matrix factorization toolkit that supports multiple use cases of matrix factorization and is currently implemented for the PyTorch framework <cit.>. As shown in Figure  <ref>, with Greenformer, we can easily factorize any deep neural networks to perform both factorization-by-design and post-training factorization. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of our Greenformer toolkit for three different use cases: 1) factorization-by-design, 2) post-training factorization, and 3) few-shot via in-context learning factorization.
new_text: Despite the numerous publications on low-rank matrix factorization, existing solutions remain model-specific, hindering generalizability across diverse model architectures. To enhance the generalization and applicability of low-rank matrix factorization techniques, we present Greenformer—a versatile low-rank matrix factorization toolkit supporting multiple use cases and currently implemented for the PyTorch framework <cit.>. As illustrated in Figure <ref>, Greenformer enables seamless factorization of any deep neural network to achieve both factorization-by-design and post-training factorization. We further validate the effectiveness of Greenformer across three distinct use cases: (1) factorization-by-design, (2) post-training factorization, and (3) few-shot in-context learning factorization.

new_text: Several recent works have proposed conducting data-driven reachability analysis <cit.> to address limitations imposed by prior model knowledge. Furthermore, <cit.> introduces formal guarantees for over-approximating a system’s reachability despite the presence of noisy data. However, ensuring such guarantees for data-driven reachable sets often results in prohibitively conservative over-approximations when the noise level is high. In this work, we aim to mitigate this conservatism by leveraging reliable auxiliary information when available.

old_text: Probabilistic temporal logic extends temporal logic (Sec. <ref>) to a probabilistic setting. In 2016, Sadigh and Kapoor proposed this language, expressed specifications in this language using chance constraints, and demonstrated their applicability to safe vehicle control <cit.>. In earlier work by some of the same authors, the concept of probabilistic temporal logic was applied to finite-state MDPs with unknown transition probabilities, and a temporal difference learning algorithm was proposed <cit.>. A method that uses second-order cone programming has been devised to verify the satisfaction of probabilistic temporal logic specifications with applications to autonomous driving <cit.>, and similar ideas have been investigated by <cit.>.
new_text: Building upon traditional temporal logic (Sec. <ref>), probabilistic temporal logic (PTL) adapts logical reasoning to environments where outcomes are uncertain. In 2016, Sadigh and Kapoor formalized this framework, introducing a method to express system requirements through *chance constraints*—a probabilistic guarantee that specific conditions hold within a predefined confidence level. Their work demonstrated the practical value of PTL in ensuring safety-critical constraints for autonomous vehicle control <cit.>. Prior to this, some of the same researchers had explored PTL’s application to finite-state Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transition dynamics, addressing the challenge of learning optimal policies under partial observability. In that earlier work, a temporal difference learning algorithm was proposed to estimate and refine probabilistic system behavior <cit.>. Further advancements have since emerged, including a verification method leveraging second-order cone programming (SOCP) to assess whether PTL specifications are satisfied in autonomous driving scenarios <cit.>. Parallel developments have similarly applied probabilistic temporal reasoning to related domains, exploring analogous approaches for constraint satisfaction <cit.>.

old_text: **Relevance to Artificial Intelligence.** The broad problem of how to analyze and optimize the behavior of autonomous systems has significant relevance to the field of Artificial Intelligence. For example, designing algorithms to ensure that robots can safely and efficiently traverse uneven terrain is an instance of this problem. Moreover, optimizing treatment protocols for a particular cancer patient using data from their previous treatment cycle, expert knowledge from an oncologist, and machine learning techniques is another instance of this problem. Our survey offers a historical and modern overview of research at the intersection of risk analysis and autonomous systems. Naturally, this intersection is quite interdisciplinary and connects ideas from many domains, including reinforcement learning, decision theory, operations research, and stochastic control. We are hopeful that our survey about risk-averse autonomous systems will inspire future theoretical and applied research that enhances the operation of systems in practice and therefore the quality of life.
new_text: **Relevance to Artificial Intelligence.** The challenge of analyzing and optimizing the behavior of autonomous systems is deeply relevant to Artificial Intelligence (AI), as it underpins the design of systems that make decisions in complex, uncertain environments. For instance, developing algorithms that allow robots to navigate uneven terrain—while avoiding obstacles and adapting to changing conditions—directly reflects this challenge. Similarly, personalizing cancer treatment protocols by combining patient-specific data, oncological expertise, and machine learning models to maximize efficacy and minimize harm represents another application of this same problem. These examples highlight how AI seeks to balance performance, safety, and adaptability in real-world scenarios. Our survey provides a comprehensive overview of research addressing the intersection of risk analysis and autonomous systems, tracing both historical foundations and contemporary advancements. This area is inherently interdisciplinary, drawing on concepts from reinforcement learning (for sequential decision-making), decision theory (for modeling preferences under uncertainty), operations research (for optimization), and stochastic control (for dynamic system management). By integrating these domains, the field aims to create robust frameworks for systems that operate reliably in high-stakes settings. We hope this survey will catalyze further theoretical and applied research, ultimately improving the practical deployment of autonomous systems and enhancing their positive impact on societal well-being.

old_text: One of the first studies was conducted by Howard and Matheson in 1972 in the setting of finite-state MDPs <cit.>. The authors were inspired by decision theory <cit.> to encode the subjective preferences of a risk-averse or risk-seeking decision-maker using the Exponential-Utility functional. Independently, Jacobson and colleagues studied an Exponential-Utility performance criterion in the setting of linear systems subject to Gaussian noise with quadratic costs (LEQG) in 1973 <cit.> and 1974 <cit.>. The initial investigation was motivated by the intuition that the linear-quadratic-Gaussian controller, which is equivalent to the linear-quadratic-regulator controller without noise, may neglect key characteristics of disturbance distributions <cit.>. In 1981, the optimization of an Exponential-Utility criterion for a continuous-time stochastic system was studied by Kumar and van Schuppen <cit.>. Also, in 1981, Whittle published a seminal paper showing parallels between LEQG theory and linear-quadratic-regulator theory, in particular for partially observable systems <cit.>. In subsequent years, Whittle considered a Hamiltonian formulation <cit.> and developed a Pontryagin maximum principle for an Exponential-Utility criterion in a partially observable setting <cit.>. Researchers have drawn connections between LEQG theory and a) ℋ_∞ control <cit.>, b) minimax linear-quadratic-Gaussian model predictive control <cit.>, and c) soft-constrained linear-quadratic games <cit.>; please see our prior work <cit.> for an extended discussion about these connections. In 1999, Coraluppi and Marcus studied relations between the problems of optimizing Exponential-Utility and worst-case performance objectives for MDPs with finitely many states <cit.>. In the same year, di Masi and Stettner examined the problem of optimizing an infinite-time Exponential-Utility criterion for an MDP whose state space need not have finite cardinality <cit.>.

Whittle later formulated a Hamiltonian-based Pontryagin maximum principle for Exponential-Utility criteria in partially observable settings <cit.>. **Lightweight Network Topology Design.**
In recent years, a series of efficient convolutional architectures have been proposed for lightweight network topologies. Aside from the convolution components already introduced (e.g., DWSConv, group convolution and channel shuffle <cit.>), GhostNet <cit.> aims to reduce input redundancy by using fewer convolutional filters to process input features, which is beneficial to reduce the FLOPs, parameters and memory movements in networks. Fewer memory movements can reduce inference latency in a network. Therefore, drawing on the concept of GhostNet, our fundamental idea in this paper is to identify cheap combinations of operations and efficient convolutional components architectures to build our new CNN network.
new_text: Recent advancements have led to the development of several efficient convolutional neural network architectures for lightweight models. In addition to established techniques like depthwise separable convolution, group convolution, and channel shuffling <cit.>, GhostNet <cit.> reduces computational overhead by applying fewer convolutional filters to input features, effectively lowering FLOPs, model parameters, and memory movement within the network. Minimizing memory movement directly contributes to decreased inference latency. Inspired by GhostNet’s approach, this work proposes identifying computationally inexpensive operation combinations and optimizing convolutional component arrangements to construct an efficient CNN architecture.

old_text: This work presents a fast successive-cancellation list flip (Fast-SCLF) decoding algorithm for polar codes that addresses the high latency issue associated with the successive-cancellation list flip (SCLF) decoding algorithm. We first propose a bit-flipping strategy tailored to the state-of-the-art fast successive-cancellation list (FSCL) decoding that avoids tree-traversal in the binary tree representation of SCLF, thus reducing the latency of the decoding process. We then derive a parameterized path-selection error model to accurately estimate the bit index at which the correct decoding path is eliminated from the initial FSCL decoding. The trainable parameter is optimized online based on an efficient supervised learning framework. Simulation results show that for a polar code of length 512 with 256 information bits, with similar error-correction performance and memory consumption, the proposed Fast-SCLF decoder reduces up to 73.4% of the average decoding latency of the SCLF decoder with the same list size at the frame error rate of 10^-4, while incurring a maximum computational overhead of 36.2%. For the same polar code of length 512 with 256 information bits and at practical signal-to-noise ratios, the proposed decoder with list size 4 reduces 89.1% and 43.7% of the average complexity and decoding latency of the FSCL decoder with list size 32 (FSCL-32), respectively, while also reducing 83.3% of the memory consumption of FSCL-32. The significant improvements of the proposed decoder come at the cost of only 0.07 dB error-correction performance degradation compared with FSCL-32.

We then derive a parameterized path-selection error model to estimate when the correct decoding path is eliminated from the initial FSCL process. The trainable parameter is optimized using an efficient supervised learning framework. Simulation results show that for a polar code of length 512 with 256 information bits, the proposed Fast-SCLF decoder achieves a reduction of up to 73.4% in average decoding latency compared to the SCLF decoder with the same list size at a frame error rate of 10^-4, while incurring a maximum computational overhead of 36.2%. For the same polar code of length 512 with 256 information bits and at practical signal-to-noise ratios, the proposed decoder with a list size of 4 reduces the average complexity of the FSCL-32 decoder by 89.1% and its decoding latency by 43.7%, while also reducing memory consumption by 83.3%. The significant improvements of the proposed decoder come at the cost of only 0.07 dB degradation in error-correction performance compared to FSCL-32.

The MILP can be solved with measurable optimality as it produces the gap between the objective's relaxed and feasible solutions[Relaxed solutions are obtained by partially dropping the integer constraints of the original problem.
As a result, in case of a minimization (maximization) the relaxed solution is an estimate guaranteed to be smaller (larger) than the optimal feasible solution.

new_text: The Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem can be solved with measurable optimality by evaluating the difference, or "gap," between the objective function's relaxed and feasible solutions. This gap is determined by comparing the relaxed solution—computed by partially removing the integer constraints of the original problem—to the best feasible solution found under the full set of constraints. Specifically, in minimization problems, the relaxed solution serves as a lower bound, guaranteed to be no higher than the optimal feasible solution, whereas in maximization problems, the relaxed solution provides an upper bound, assured to be no lower than the optimal feasible solution. The MILP solver operates in parallel by actively seeking improved feasible solutions while simultaneously refining the relaxed solution through a process of progressively reducing the number of ignored integer constraints. By tightening the relaxed problem's formulation (i.e., reintroducing more constraints), the solver narrows the gap between the bounds. When the solver finally incorporates all constraints into the relaxed solution, the two bounds converge (Gap = 0), confirming that the optimal solution has been achieved.

old_text: This paper draws upon three themes in the bipedal control literature to achieve highly agile, terrain-aware locomotion. By terrain aware, we mean the robot can use information on terrain slope and friction cone as supplied by state-of-the-art mapping and trajectory planning algorithms. The process starts with abstracting from the full dynamics of a Cassie 3D bipedal robot, an exact low-dimensional representation of its centroidal dynamics, parameterized by angular momentum. Under a piecewise planar terrain assumption, and the elimination of terms for the angular momentum about the robot's center of mass, the centroidal dynamics become linear and has dimension four. Four-step-horizon model predictive control (MPC) of the centroidal dynamics provides step-to-step foot placement commands. Importantly, we also include the intra-step dynamics at 10 ms intervals so that realistic terrain-aware constraints on robot's evolution can be imposed in the MPC formulation. The output of the MPC is directly implemented on Cassie through the method of virtual constraints. In experiments, we validate the performance of our control strategy for the robot on inclined and stationary terrain, both indoors on a treadmill and outdoors on a hill.
new_text: This paper synthesizes three key themes from the bipedal control literature to enable highly agile, terrain-aware locomotion. By terrain-aware control, we mean the robot can utilize terrain slope and friction cone information provided by state-of-the-art mapping and trajectory planning algorithms. The approach begins by abstracting the full dynamics of the Cassie 3D bipedal robot into an exact low-dimensional representation of its centroidal dynamics, parameterized by angular momentum. Under a piecewise planar terrain assumption and after eliminating terms related to angular momentum about the robot’s center of mass, the centroidal dynamics become linear and reduce to four dimensions. A four-step-horizon model predictive control (MPC) strategy for these centroidal dynamics generates step-to-step foot placement commands. Crucially, the intra-step dynamics are incorporated at 10 ms intervals to enforce realistic terrain-aware constraints on the robot’s evolution within the MPC formulation. The resulting control signals are directly implemented on Cassie using virtual constraints. Experimental validation demonstrates the effectiveness of this control strategy on both inclined and stationary terrain, conducted indoors on a treadmill and outdoors on a natural slope.

In many real-world terrain monitoring scenarios, the distribution of information in the environment is not uniform, i.e. some areas are considered more informative for mapping than others. Therefore, maintaining a map with constant resolution over the whole terrain is inefficient. A common method to generate more compact map representations is using tree structures. A well-known algorithm in this category is OctoMap, which is based on the octree structure <cit.>. Each node in the octree represents the space contained in a voxel. This voxel is then recursively divided into eight sub-volumes until the maximal resolution is reached. If all child nodes have the same state, e.g. occupied, the nodes are pruned, resulting in both memory-savings and the preservation of highly precise maps. <cit.> use the octree structure in an online mapping system that adjusts the map resolution based on occupancy state.
Similarly, <cit.> apply quadtree to build multi-resolution 2D maps. Nd-tree generalizes these approaches by subdividing any d-dimensional volume recursively with N^d children <cit.>. Rather than compressing the maps only after they have already been built, as in the case of OctoMap, we change the map resolution online based on incoming measurements in a similar way to <cit.>. This enables us to tailor the map structure to conserve memory and computation time in applications requiring online mapping, such as adaptive path planning <cit.>.

old_text: In the paper, we propose and analyze divergence policy iteration in general cooperative MARL settings and a special case combined with value decomposition. Based on divergence policy iteration, we derive the off-policy update rule for the critic, policy, and target policy and propose divergence-regularized multi-agent actor-critic (DMAC), a novel off-policy cooperative MARL framework. We theoretically show that DMAC guarantees a monotonic policy improvement and is not biased by the regularization. Besides, DMAC is benefited for exploration and stable policy improvement by applying our update rule of target policy. Moreover, DMAC is a flexible framework and can be combined with many existing cooperative MARL algorithms to substantially improve their performance.
new_text: We propose and analyze divergence policy iteration in general cooperative MARL settings and its combination with value decomposition. From this, we derive the off-policy update rules for the critic, policy, and target policy, introducing divergence-regularized multi-agent actor-critic (DMAC), a novel off-policy cooperative MARL framework. We prove that DMAC ensures monotonic policy improvement without regularization bias. Additionally, DMAC enhances exploration and stable policy improvement through its target policy update rule. DMAC is a flexible framework that can integrate with existing cooperative MARL algorithms to significantly enhance their performance.

old_text: Discrete, uneven terrains present an additional challenge of controlling the robot in different orientations. Popular model-based quadrupedal control techniques like <cit.> assume linearized models of the robot about zero roll, pitch, yaw of the torso. Such models are not suitable for uneven terrains which can result in the robot pitching, or experiencing high angular velocities. We present a coordinate-free linear dynamics model that uses rotation matrices, instead of Euler orientations, building on recent works on variational-based linerization. Next, we formulate a Quadratic Program (QP) that uses this dynamics model and outputs torques that can achieve desired footstep and center of mass (CoM) velocity targets output by the motion library. This CoM model adds stability and robustness to our controller, and enables our robot to navigate long, challenging terrains reliably. In comparison, a controller using a linearized CoM dynamics model suffers and experiences frequent falls on the robot.
new_text: Discrete, uneven terrains pose a particular challenge for controlling robots in varying orientations. Popular model-based quadrupedal control techniques like <cit.> rely on linearized models of the robot around nominal zero roll, pitch, and yaw torso orientations. However, such models are unsuitable for uneven terrains, as they can subject the robot to pitch deviations and high angular velocities. We present a coordinate-free linear dynamics model that uses rotation matrices rather than Euler angles, leveraging recent advances in variational-based linearization. We then formulate a Quadratic Program (QP) that leverages this dynamics model to generate torques achieving desired footstep and center of mass (CoM) velocity targets specified by the motion library. This CoM model enhances the stability and robustness of our controller, enabling reliable navigation of long, challenging terrains. In contrast, a controller using a linearized CoM dynamics model struggles to maintain stability and results in frequent falls.

As a result, images are prone to have degraded features and contrast, which harm the low-level perceptual quality and deteriorate high-level computer vision tasks relying on accurate semantic information. Therefore, it is necessary to improve the visual quality and enhance the generalizability of the advanced vision algorithms.

This has led to research in geometric variational-based optimal control approaches <cit.> that linearize the quadruped dynamics using rotation matrices instead of Euler angles. The resulting linearization is coordinate free, holds in all orientations (not just close to 0 roll, pitch), and does not suffer from singularities. However, <cit.> do not consider discrete time dynamics of the linearized system required for MPC, and <cit.> use forward Euler to discretize the orientation dynamics. Euler discretization for orientations that lie on SO(3) does not preserve energy, and the predicted future angular velocities do not lie in the tangent space of SO(3).

**Runtime complexity.**
It is clear that the priority retrieval runs in Θ(1) and priority update runs in Θ(log_K N). For prefix sum index computation, the loops runs H=log_K N + 1 times. The memory access inside loop has K/C cache misses and K·(1-1/C) cache hit, where C is the number of nodes in one cacheline. Thus, the time complexity of prefix sum index computation is Θ((log_K N+1)(T_miss·K/C+T_hit· K·(1-1/C))), where T_miss is the execution time of one cache miss and T_hit is the execution time of one cache hit. Note that this function has a local minimum in terms of K. In practice, we profile the performance of various K values based on the size of the cacheline and choose the one that yields the best performance.

section: Challenges in Using AI to Empower Local Communities
old_text: Furthermore, researchers need to evaluate the social impact of AI systems to understand if the community co-design approach is practical. However, it is hard to determine if the intervention of AI systems actually influences the local people and leads to social changes by statistically analyzing community data. One difficulty is that local communities may have the implicit cognitive bias to overestimate and overstate the effect of the intervention since they are deeply involved in the co-creation of the AI system <cit.>. Moreover, it can be infeasible to conduct randomized experiments to prove the effectiveness of the intervention of AI on local communities <cit.>. Controlling volunteer demographics and participation levels can be unethical when analyzing impact among different groups of people. Community Citizen Science treats local people as collaborators rather than participants. Researchers in CCS take the supporting role to assist communities using technology, instead of supervising and overseeing the entire project <cit.>. Therefore, citizens join the CCS project at will and are not recruited like typical research studies. AI systems, in this case, are deployed in the wild with real consequences rather than a controlled test-bed environment that is designed for hypothesis testing. It remains an open research question as to how to integrate social science when studying the impact of AI systems <cit.>.
new_text: Researchers must assess the social impact of AI systems to evaluate the practicality of community co-design approaches. However, statistically analyzing community data to determine whether AI interventions influence local populations and drive social change is challenging. One barrier is the potential for implicit cognitive bias in local communities, which may overestimate intervention effects due to their active involvement in co-creation <cit.>. Additionally, conducting randomized experiments to validate AI’s effectiveness on communities is often infeasible <cit.>, as controlling demographics or participation levels could be unethical. Community Citizen Science (CCS) addresses these challenges by treating local people as collaborators rather than passive participants; researchers adopt a supportive role in facilitating community-driven technology use rather than overseeing projects <cit.>. This approach allows citizens to self-select into CCS initiatives rather than being recruited for studies, enabling AI systems to operate in real-world contexts with tangible consequences rather than controlled environments. Integrating social science methodologies into AI impact assessments remains an open research question <cit.>.

old_text: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown advantages in various graph-based applications. Most existing GNNs assume strong homophily of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been successfully applied to representation learning on graphs, as well as multiple real-world applications from web-scale recommendation <cit.> to molecular chemistry inference <cit.>. Most existing approaches are based on a framework of message-passing neural networks (MPNNs), including ChebyNet <cit.>, GCN <cit.>, GAT <cit.> and GIN <cit.>. They learn each node’s representation by aggregating feature information from its neighbors. The aggregation often needs to be permutation-invariant (e.g., Mean, Max or Sum) as there is no ordering information of the neighboring nodes. These methods are effective with an assumption of strong homophily for graphs (such as citation networks <cit.>), where neighboring nodes always possess similar features and belong to the same class. However, this inductive bias is not suitable for graphs with heterophily. In heterophilic graphs, most connected nodes are dissimilar and may belong to different classes, while the semantically relevant nodes are often multi-hops away. As Figure <ref> (a) shows, normal local aggregation in GNNs might introduce noises for node representation in heterophilic graphs. In such scenarios, even models that ignore the graph structure altogether (e.g., MLPs) can outperform state-of-the-art GNNs <cit.>.
new_text: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated effectiveness in various graph-based applications, including representation learning on graphs and real-world tasks such as web-scale recommendation <cit.> and molecular chemistry inference <cit.>. Most existing GNNs are based on a message-passing neural network (MPNN) framework, which includes ChebyNet <cit.>, GCN <cit.>, GAT <cit.>, and GIN <cit.>. These models learn node representations by aggregating information from neighboring nodes, typically using permutation-invariant operations such as Mean, Max, or Sum due to the absence of inherent node ordering. They perform well under the assumption of strong homophily, where neighboring nodes typically share similar features and class labels, a characteristic particularly evident in graphs like citation networks <cit.>. However, this inductive bias fails in heterophilic graphs, where connected nodes are often dissimilar and belong to different classes. In such cases, semantically relevant nodes may be multiple hops apart. As illustrated in Figure <ref> (a), standard local aggregation in GNNs can introduce noise into node representations when applied to heterophilic graphs. In these scenarios, even models that disregard graph structure entirely (e.g., MLPs) have been shown to outperform state-of-the-art GNNs <cit.>.

old_text: Many powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques have been engineered with the goals of high performance and accuracy. Recently, AI algorithms have been integrated into diverse and real-world applications. It has become an important topic to explore the impact of AI on society from a people-centered perspective <cit.>. Previous works in citizen science have identified methods of using AI to engage the public in research, such as sustaining participation, verifying data quality, classifying and labeling objects, predicting user interests, and explaining data patterns <cit.>. These works investigated the challenges regarding how scientists design AI systems for citizens to participate in research projects at a large geographic scale in a generalizable way, such as building applications for citizens globally to participate in completing tasks. In contrast, we are interested in another area that receives significantly less attention: how scientists co-design AI systems “with” local communities to influence a particular geographical region, such as community-based participatory projects <cit.>. Specifically, this article discusses the challenges of applying AI in Community Citizen Science <cit.>, a framework to create social impact through community empowerment at an intensely place-based local scale. We provide insights in this under-explored area of focus to connect scientific research closely to social issues and citizen needs.
new_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been advanced through techniques prioritizing performance and precision. The integration of AI algorithms into various real-world applications underscores their transformative potential. Assessing AI’s societal implications through a people-centered lens has gained critical attention <cit.>. Prior research in citizen science has explored AI’s role in public engagement, including strategies for maintaining participation, ensuring data accuracy, object classification, predicting user preferences, and interpreting data trends <cit.>. These studies have focused on challenges related to designing scalable, globally accessible AI systems for citizen involvement in research across extensive geographic regions. Conversely, our focus lies in a less-explored area: co-creating AI systems with local communities to address specific geographic contexts, such as place-based participatory projects <cit.>. This article examines challenges in applying AI to Community Citizen Science <cit.>, a framework aimed at fostering social impact through localized community empowerment. By emphasizing this under-investigated domain, we bridge scientific inquiry with societal challenges and civic needs.

section: Proposals to Bridge AI Research and Citizen Needs
old_text: Lessons learned from previously deployed AI systems in other contexts cannot be simply applied in the current one, as local communities have various cultures, behaviors, beliefs, values, and characteristics <cit.>. Hence, it is essential to understand and document how scientists can co-design AI systems with local communities and co-create long-term social impact in diverse contexts. It is also important to study the effectiveness and impact of various AI interventions with different design criteria in sustaining participation, affecting community attitude, and empowering people. The Community Citizen Science framework provides a promising path toward these goals. Implications of collaborating with local people in co-designing AI interventions, creating long-term impacts, and tackling the conflicts of interest among stakeholders can be strong empirical contributions to the academic community <cit.>. The data-driven evidence and the interventions that are produced by AI systems can impact the local region in various ways, including increasing residents' confidence in addressing concerns, providing convincing evidence, or rebalancing power relationships among stakeholders.
new_text: Lessons from AI systems implemented in different contexts cannot be directly applied here, as local communities vary in culture, behavior, belief, value, and characteristics <cit>. Thus, understanding and documenting how scientists can co-design AI systems with local communities to co-create sustained social impact across diverse settings is essential. Studying the effectiveness and impact of AI interventions with varying design criteria—such as sustaining participation, shaping community attitudes, and empowering individuals—is equally crucial. The Community Citizen Science framework offers a promising approach to achieving these objectives. Collaborating with local communities to co-design AI interventions, foster long-term impacts, and address stakeholder conflicts presents opportunities for significant empirical contributions to the academic community <cit>. Data-driven evidence and AI-generated interventions can influence local regions in multiple ways: enhancing residents' confidence in addressing issues, providing compelling evidence, or rebalancing stakeholder power dynamics.

The kernel size of the first 2 layers of the Encoder was 3x3, while for the last two layers two 5x5 kernels were used. 2x2 padding along with 1x1 stride and 2x2 max-pooling were used in all layers. old_text: Multimodal Language Analysis is a demanding area of research, since it is associated with two requirements: combining different modalities and capturing temporal information. During the last years, several works have been proposed in the area, mostly centered around supervised learning in downstream tasks. In this paper we propose extracting unsupervised Multimodal Language representations that are universal and can be applied to different tasks. Towards this end, we map the word-level aligned multimodal sequences to 2-D matrices and then use Convolutional Autoencoders to learn embeddings by combining multiple datasets. Extensive experimentation on Sentiment Analysis (MOSEI) and Emotion Recognition (IEMOCAP) indicate that the learned representations can achieve near-state-of-the-art performance with just the use of a Logistic Regression algorithm for downstream classification. It is also shown that our method is extremely lightweight and can be easily generalized to other tasks and unseen data with small performance drop and almost the same number of parameters. The proposed multimodal representation models are open-sourced and will help grow the applicability of Multimodal Language.

In this paper, we propose to extract unsupervised multimodal language representations that are universal and applicable to various tasks. To achieve this, we map word-level aligned multimodal sequences to 2D matrices and then use convolutional autoencoders to learn embeddings by combining multiple datasets. Extensive experimentation on Sentiment Analysis (MOSEI) and Emotion Recognition (IEMOCAP) indicates that the learned representations can achieve near-state-of-the-art performance using only a logistic regression algorithm for downstream classification. Our method is also shown to be lightweight and capable of being generalized to other tasks and unseen data with minimal performance loss and approximately the same number of parameters. The proposed multimodal representation models are open-sourced and will expand the applicability of multimodal language.

This study adopts two algorithms that represent two distinct approaches to bridging the domain gap: unsupervised domain adaptation <cit.>, which utilizes unlabeled images from the target domain to close the feature-level discrepancies, and domain randomization <cit.>, which instead randomizes various aspects of the input images such that the target image would be considered as another randomized version of the source image. Although we demonstrated excellent performance gains, compared to polar code and TurboAE, as well as state-of-the-art classical codes, via training ProductAEs of dimensions 100 and 196, the architecture and training procedure are general and can be applied to train larger ProductAEs. As the first work on training product codes and a pioneering approach for large channel codes, we demonstrate significant performance gains using ProductAEs of dimensions 100 and 196 compared to polar codes, TurboAEs, and classical state-of-the-art codes. The architecture and training procedure are generalizable to larger ProductAEs. The ProductAE's low encoding/decoding complexity, flexible code rate and length, and parallel implementation capabilities make its performance gains noteworthy and warrant further research. This work paves the way for larger neural codes surpassing state-of-the-art performance with applications in next-generation wireless networks.

The Task Adaptive PreTraining (TAPT) method, in which an NLM pretrains on the training set of an NLU task, leads to impressive gains <cit.>.
	Notably, TAPT is most effective after the regular pretraining stage on a general corpus.
	This implies that during TAPT, the model generates improved representations by integrating the task related text with the knowledge stored in its weights from the preceding general pretraining phase.

new_text: The Task Adaptive PreTraining (TAPT) approach, where a neural language model (NLM) is pretrained on the training data of a natural language understanding (NLU) task, achieves notable improvements <cit.>. Critically, TAPT demonstrates the strongest effectiveness when applied subsequent to standard pretraining on a broad corpus. This suggests the model enhances its contextual representations by combining task-specific text with knowledge retained in its parameters from the prior general pretraining stage. Building on this insight, we hypothesized that performance could be further boosted by increasing the model's access to relevant sentences from the general corpus during the TAPT phase. Based on this reasoning, we propose a straightforward yet effective strategy to encourage the model to capture desired relationships between sentences: concatenating relevant general corpus sentences into the context during TAPT.

Specifically, since ℳ is compact, for every pair (p,q) ∈ℳ ×ℳ there exists a C^1-regular minimizing geodesic γ connecting p to q. An interior geodesic is defined as a geodesic γ: I →ℳ whose image is entirely contained within the interior intℳ, or equivalently, does not intersect the boundary ∂ℳ. In contrast, when ∂ℳ ≠ ∅, geodesics may fail to be C^∞-regular and might not be uniquely determined by initial position and velocity due to potential bifurcations at ∂ℳ (see Figure <ref>). To avoid these challenges, our analysis exclusively considers interior geodesics. Adopting the convention that d(x,∂ℳ) = ∞ when ∂ℳ = ∅, we ensure that for x ∈ intℳ and 0 < r < d_ℳ(x,∂ℳ), the open ball B_r ⊂ T_xℳ centered at the origin yields, for each v ∈ B_r, a unique interior geodesic γ_ v : [0,1] → intℳ satisfying γ_ v’(0) = v. We show that multilingual embedding spaces are highly anisotropic, which limits their semantic expressiveness. Our findings reveal the other limitation of multilingual embeddings: they have a biased structure towards word frequency, and this distribution is similar across different languages. By applying a local method to increasing the isotropy, we significantly improve the multilingual CWRs performance and address their frequency bias.

new_text: Most existing deep learning approaches for person re-identification (Re-ID) rely on supervised learning, where models are trained using labeled datasets. However, as person Re-ID datasets continue to expand in size, the cost and effort required for manual annotation become prohibitively high, limiting the scalability of supervised methods. In contrast, semi-supervised and unsupervised learning strategies are more adaptable to real-world applications, where labeled data may be scarce or expensive to obtain <cit.>. While the performance of Re-ID models in weakly supervised settings—such as those with limited labels or no labels at all—remains lower than that of fully supervised methods, this approach holds substantial research value. Specifically, it encourages models to generalize more effectively across diverse datasets and scenarios, which is critical for deployment in uncontrolled environments <cit.>. To bridge the performance gap, future research could focus on refining clustering algorithms and classification frameworks tailored to weakly supervised learning. By improving how models organize unlabeled data and learn discriminative features, such strategies may enhance the accuracy and robustness of person Re-ID systems under realistic constraints.

Motivated by the lack of large-scale datasets with realistic 3D objects from a diverse set of categories and corresponding real-world multi-view images, we introduce Amazon-Berkeley Objects (ABO). This dataset is derived from Amazon.com product listings, and as a result, contains imagery and 3D models that correspond to modern, real-world, household items.
Overall, ABO contains 147,702 product listings associated with 398,212 unique images, and up to 18 unique attributes (category, color, material, weight, dimensions, etc.) per product. ABO also includes “360º View” turntable-style images for 8,222 products and 7,953 products with corresponding artist-designed 3D meshes. Because the 3D models are designed by artists, they are equipped with high-resolution, physically-based materials that allow for photorealistic rendering. Examples of the kinds of data in ABO can be found in Figure <ref>.
new_text: The absence of large-scale datasets featuring realistic 3D objects across diverse categories, paired with corresponding real-world multi-view imagery, creates significant challenges for tasks like object recognition, synthesis, and simulation. To address this limitation, we introduce the Amazon-Berkeley Objects (ABO) dataset, which leverages Amazon.com product listings to provide high-quality, real-world household objects in both image and 3D model formats. By sourcing from Amazon, ABO captures modern, commonly used items that reflect actual consumer products rather than stylized or generic examples. The dataset includes 147,702 product listings, each accompanied by an average of 2.7 images per product, culminating in 398,212 total images. These listings are annotated with up to 18 product attributes (e.g., category, color, material, weight, and dimensions), enabling rich semantic and physical analysis. A subset of 8,222 products includes 360º turntable-style image sequences, while 7,953 products feature artist-crafted 3D meshes. These meshes are particularly valuable: their high-resolution, physically based materials enable realistic rendering and simulation. Notably, the use of professionally designed models ensures topological accuracy and detailed surface properties, distinguishing ABO from datasets relying on automatic model generation. Examples of the dataset’s structure and content are illustrated in Figure <ref>.

The problem of finding a winning permutation π∈𝒫 is a variant of the Travelling Salesman Problem where neurons are mapped to cities visited by a salesman. The problem belongs to the class of NP-hard optimization problems and simulated annealing (SA) is often used to find a solution for such a combinatorial search problem. SA's performance however highly depends on the parameter choices, including the minimum and maximum temperatures, the cooling schedule and the number of optimization steps. The pseudocode of SA is shown in Algorithm <ref>. SA takes a set of solutions {θ_i}, i=1..n, n≥2 as input (we use n=5) and searches for a set of permutations {π_i} that reduce the barriers between all permuted n2 solution pairs. To find the best {π_i}, in each step of SA the current candidate permutations {π̂_i}, i=1..n are evaluated to minimize the objective function Ψ. We use two versions of simulated annealing that vary in their definition of Ψto evaluate the conjecture.
Simulated Annealing 1 (SA_1) In the first version SA_1, Ψ is defined as the average pairwise barrier between candidate permutations B(P(θ_i,π_i),P(θ_j,π_j)), i≠ j.
Simulated Annealing 2 (SA_2) In the second version SA_2, we average the weights of permuted models P(θ_i,π_i) first and defined Ψ as the train error of the resulting average model. The simplest form of SA_2 happens if n=2 and is discussed in spacereduction.

The task of determining a winning permutation π∈𝒫 corresponds to a variant of the Travelling Salesman Problem, where neurons are analogous to cities in the salesman's route. This problem falls within the category of NP-hard optimization challenges, with simulated annealing (SA) commonly employed to address such combinatorial search scenarios. The effectiveness of SA is strongly influenced by parameter configurations, including minimum and maximum temperatures, the cooling schedule, and the number of optimization iterations. The algorithmic framework for SA is presented in Algorithm <ref>. SA begins with a set of solutions {θ_i}, i=1..n, n≥2 (here, n=5) and seeks permutations {π_i} that minimize the barriers between all pairs of permuted solutions. At each step, current candidate permutations {π̂_i}, i=1..n are assessed to reduce the objective function Ψ. Two distinct SA implementations, differing in their formulation of Ψ, are utilized to evaluate the hypothesis.  
**SA_1** In the first variant, SA_1, the objective function Ψ is defined as the average pairwise barrier between candidate permutations B(P(θ_i,π_i),P(θ_j,π_j)) for i≠j.  
**SA_2** The second variant, SA_2, first computes the average weights of the permuted models P(θ_i,π_i) and sets Ψ as the train error of this averaged model. The simplest instance of SA_2 occurs when n=2, as detailed in sparereduction.

Therefore, we test the combination of SASA with either PASCAL or UDISCAL, retaining the hyperparameters used for the separate models. We find that combining with UDISCAL outperforms the former, and so we continue with it. Interestingly, En-De and En-Ru hardly benefit from the combination compared just to the SASA model. We hypothesize that this might be due to the fact that the syntax of each language pair is already quite similar, and therefore the model mainly relies on it to separate the sentence that UCCA gives it as well. On the other hand, En-Fi and En-Tr do benefit from the combination, both on average and in most of the test sets. Evaluating the performance using the chrF metric (see <ref>) yields a similar behavior, which further confirms its validity. It leads us to hypothesize that language pairs that are more typologically distant from one another can benefit more from both semantics and syntax; we defer a more complete discussion of this point to future work. In order to confirm that the combined version persistently outperforms each of the separate versions for typologically distant languages, we compare each of the pairs using the sign-test (only on the test sets of En-Fi and En-Tr). We get a p-value of 0.02 for the comparison with SASA and 0.0008 for the comparison with UDISCAL. This suggests that for these language pairs, there is indeed a significant benefit, albeit small, from the infusion of both semantics and syntax.
new_text: We next investigate whether combining semantic and syntactic heads improves model performance by testing SASA in combination with either PASCAL or UDISCAL, using the same hyperparameters as in the individual models. Combining with UDISCAL yields superior performance over the PASCAL combination, prompting further exploration of this configuration. However, language pairs such as En-De and En-Ru derive minimal additional benefit compared to the standalone SASA model. This suggests that their syntactic similarity may enable the model to effectively rely on existing structures for sentence disambiguation via UCCA annotations. In contrast, En-Fi and En-Tr demonstrate consistent improvements both in average performance and across most test sets. Evaluating with the chrF metric (<ref>) produces analogous results, reinforcing the robustness of these findings. These patterns lead us to propose that typologically distant language pairs benefit more significantly from integrating both semantic and syntactic information—a hypothesis we defer to future work for comprehensive analysis. To confirm the consistent advantage of the combined model for distant languages, we apply the sign-test to the test sets of En-Fi and En-Tr. Comparisons against SASA and UDISCAL yield p-values of 0.02 and 0.0008, respectively, indicating a statistically significant, albeit modest, performance gain from the integrated use of semantic and syntactic features in these cases.

Given the researcher community graph 𝒢 = {(a_i, r, a_j)}⊆ A ×ℛ× A, first we aim to extract community information of researchers from this graph. Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance on handling graph data. Typically, GNNs output node representations via a message-passing mechanism, i.e., they stack K layers to encode node features into low-dimensional representations by aggregating K-hop local neighbors' information of nodes. However, most GNN based models take the whole graph as the input, which can hardly be applied on large-scale graph data due to memory limitation. Also, the inter-connected graph structure prevents parallel computing on complete graph topology, making the GNNs propagation on large graph data extremely time-consuming<cit.>.
One prominent direction for improving the scalability of GNNs use sub-graph sampling strategies, For example, SEAL<cit.> extracts k-hop enclosing subgraphs to perform link prediction. GraphSAINT<cit.> propose random walk samplers to construct mini-batches during training.
Thus, we propose to sample a sub-graph of 𝒢 to represent the local community graph of researcher a_i, denoted by 𝒢_i, which can preserve the interactions and relations of a_i with other researchers.
An intuitive way to sample 𝒢_i is to directly sample a_i's h-hops neighborhoods, e.g., to sample all a_i's neighbors within h-hops as well as corresponding relations to compose 𝒢_i.
However, the community graph of researchers usually is denser than other kinds of graphs, each researcher may have dozens of neighbors.
In this sampling way, the size of 𝒢_i might grow geometrically and it would become expensive to process it in training when h increases.
new_text: To analyze the researcher community graph 𝒢 = {(a_i, r, a_j)}⊆ A ×ℛ× A, we first focus on extracting community-specific information for individual researchers. Recent advances in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated superior performance in processing graph data by generating low-dimensional node representations through a K-layer message-passing mechanism that aggregates K-hop neighbor information. However, conventional GNN models operate on the full graph, which is infeasible for large-scale data due to memory constraints. Additionally, the inherently connected nature of complete graphs hinders parallel processing, leading to prohibitively slow training on large graphs<cit.>. A common solution to enhance scalability involves subgraph sampling techniques: for instance, SEAL<cit.> constructs k-hop enclosing subgraphs for link prediction, while GraphSAINT<cit.> employs random walk samplers to create training mini-batches. We propose sampling a localized subgraph 𝒢_i to capture the community interactions of researcher a_i. A straightforward approach is to extract a_i’s h-hop neighborhood, including all connected researchers and their relations. Yet, due to the high density of researcher networks—where each individual often has over 10 connections—the size of 𝒢_i can expand exponentially with increasing h, resulting in significant computational costs during training.

To better understand the dataset's origin and composition, we examine key dataset distributions in Table <ref>. At the top of Table <ref>, we list the top five domains contributing webpages to the dataset. The stackexchange domain dominates, representing approximately 8% of all data points. This is followed by significant contributions from hotels, viamichelin, commentcamarche, and vrbo, though these account for smaller proportions of the total. Understanding these domain distributions helps contextualize the dataset's sources and potential biases.  

Furthermore, we analyze the topical distribution using the DMOZ/Curlie taxonomy—a well-known directory that categorizes web content hierarchically. By automatically extracting this taxonomy, we infer the thematic focus of the dataset. To validate this, we randomly sampled 1,000 question webpages and identify the top five topics in the second row of Table <ref>. The results reveal that most questions fall under regional topics, followed by society and business themes. Sports and recreational topics round out the top five. This high-level overview is supplemented in Table <ref> (Appendix <ref>), where a more nuanced breakdown is presented, including second-level topic categories that provide additional granularity.  

Regarding question-word distribution in the CCQA dataset, we observe that the most frequent query type is the "what" question, which appears in 36% of cases. These are followed, in decreasing order, by "how," "when," "which," and "where" questions. A complete listing of all eight question words and their relative frequencies can be found in Table <ref> (Appendix <ref>).  

Finally, we analyze the frequency of HTML markup tags in the dataset, extending the analysis presented in Table <ref>. The last row of Table <ref> highlights the most commonly used tags: the paragraph (p) tag dominates, accounting for 28.5% of all instances. The anchor (a) tag follows with 14.9%, reflecting the prevalence of hyperlinks in the data. Structural elements like breaks (br), list items (li), and span tags also appear frequently. These findings align with expectations for question-and-answer pages, which often emphasize readable text and navigational links. A full ranking of the top 25 HTML tags is provided in Table <ref> (Appendix <ref>).

new_text: The `LSPE` method enhances the performance of various existing graph neural network (GNN) architectures by enabling more effective learning of structural and positional representations. This improvement is particularly pronounced when `LSPE` is implemented with random walk positional embeddings (RWPE) as initial positional encodings. Both sparse GNNs, such as PNA, and Transformer-based GNNs, like GatedGCN, demonstrate significant gains when augmented with `LSPE`, as detailed in Table <ref>. For example, on the ZINC dataset, PNA—which is the best-performing GNN without positional encodings (PE)—achieves a relative improvement of 28.37% (mean absolute error of 0.101 compared to 0.141 without `LSPE`) when structural and positional information is decoupled through `LSPE`. This performance boost is even more substantial for other architectures: GatedGCN augmented with `LSPE` (GatedGCN`-LSPE`) improves by 64.14% (0.090 vs. 0.251), highlighting the method’s versatility across GNN types. On the MOLTOX21 dataset, PNA`-LSPE` achieves a more modest but still notable improvement of 3.44% (0.781 vs. 0.755), while other models either show minimal gains or maintain their performance levels when not using PE. Similarly, on MOLPCBA, PNA`-LSPE` achieves a 2.87% improvement, aligning with the consistent trend observed across datasets. These results collectively demonstrate that `LSPE` effectively augments the representation learning capabilities of diverse GNNs, particularly when structural and positional features are learned in a decoupled framework.

new_text: In this paper, we systematically analyze the extent to which neural networks not explicitly trained to be modular still exhibit modularity. First, this requires a method to decompose a network's computational graph into candidate modular partitions. For this purpose, we employ spectral clustering on a graph representation of the network, building on an extension of the methods described in <cit.>. Second, we need a scalable method to estimate the extent of modularity in a given partition. To achieve this, we apply interpretability tools to clusters of neurons, thereby quantifying proxy metrics for modularity.

There exists a body of research for developing more modular networks which either have distinct architectural building blocks <cit.> or are trained in a way that promotes modularity via regularization or parameter isolation <cit.>.
Yet in machine learning, it is more common to encounter networks whose architecture and training are not guided by considerations of modularity.
For example, in computer vision, networks are generally trained end-to-end with all of the filters in one layer connected to all filters in the next.

Pre-trained contextual representations have led to dramatic performance improvements on a range of downstream tasks.
This has motivated researchers to quantify and understand the linguistic information encoded in them.
In general, this is done by probing, which consists of training a supervised model to predict a linguistic property from said representations. Unfortunately, this definition of probing has been subject to extensive criticism, and can lead to paradoxical or counter-intuitive results.
In this work, we present a novel framework for probing where the goal is to evaluate the inductive bias of representations for a particular task, and provide a practical avenue to do this using Bayesian inference.
We apply our framework to a series of token-, arc-, and sentence-level tasks. Our results suggest that our framework solves problems of previous approaches and that fastText can offer a better inductive bias than BERT in certain situations.
new_text: Pre-trained contextual representations have led to dramatic performance improvements on a range of downstream tasks. This has motivated researchers to quantify and understand the linguistic information encoded in them. A common approach involves probing, where a supervised model is trained to predict a linguistic property from these representations. However, this definition of probing has faced significant criticism and can risk producing paradoxical or counterintuitive outcomes. In this work, we propose a novel probing framework aimed at assessing the inductive bias of representations for specific tasks, offering a practical method to achieve this using Bayesian inference. We apply our framework to token-, arc-, and sentence-level tasks. Our findings indicate that this approach addresses limitations in prior methods and demonstrate that fastText may provide a more favorable inductive bias than BERT in specific scenarios.

The graph shows that insufficient regularization leads to poor generalization using BERT, apparent from the gap between training and test loss that grows larger for too weak regularization.

new_text: The analysis involves linear probes applied to two tasks, examining how weight decay impacts model performance by tracking changes in evidence and cross-entropy loss. As demonstrated by the graph, when regularization is insufficient, BERT exhibits diminished generalization capability, as indicated by the increasing divergence between training and test loss curves. This phenomenon occurs because weaker regularization allows the linear probes to utilize their full parameter capacity, which, rather than improving performance, leads to overfitting. Specifically, the reduced evidence suggests that overly flexible probes prioritize fitting idiosyncratic patterns in the training data rather than capturing generalizable features. Consequently, the results imply that the most effective probes might not be purely linear, as even a linear architecture could introduce excess capacity that hinders learning. This highlights a trade-off between model flexibility and the ability to generalize effectively.

**Problem III.**
The formal goals of probing and its relation to regular NLP tasks are unclear.
This manifests in several ways.
Firstly, while some argue that probing should focus on “simple” tasks <cit.>, others argue that probing should focus on complex tasks to be informative <cit.>.
However, this leaves it unclear where the boundary between probing and regular NLP tasks lies and if there even should be a distinction.
Secondly, it is unclear what experimental probing results tell us.
Knowing that BERT excels at text generation, is it really surprising that we can predict the tense of a word from its representations?
Indeed, the NLP community is still in search of how probing can be of service to them.
new_text: **Problem III.** The formal goals of probing and its relationship to standard NLP tasks remain unclear. This ambiguity manifests in several ways. First, as a matter of definition, while some advocate that probing should focus on “simple” tasks <cit.>, others contend that probing should emphasize complex tasks to provide meaningful insights <cit.>. This discrepancy leaves the boundary between probing and standard NLP tasks ambiguous, raising questions about whether such a distinction should exist. Second, the interpretability of experimental probing results remains uncertain. For instance, given that BERT excels at text generation, does it truly surprise us that we can predict a word’s tense from its representations? Consequently, the NLP community continues to seek a clear understanding of how probing can be practically applied.

**Strategy Comparison: Principle V.S. Entity Pyramid.**
To verify the effectiveness of our pre-training strategy, i.e. Entity Pyramid, we do an additional ablation study with the base model on the Multi-News dataset. We prepare the pre-training data by following two different strategies, i.e. the Entity Pyramid strategy proposed in this paper, and the Principle strategy used in Pegasus <cit.>. Then, we train the models on the two pre-training data with all the other settings remaining the same (e.g. length limit of input and output, pre-training dataset, input structure, as well as the document separators). Finally, we run the same experiments under zero- and few-shot scenario on the Multi-News dataset as in Sec.<ref>, and the results are shown in
Figure <ref> (b).
The model pre-trained with our novel Entity Pyramid strategy shows a clearly improved performance on the Multi-News dataset under few-shot scenarios.
new_text: To further validate the effectiveness of our proposed Entity Pyramid strategy, we conducted an ablation study using the base model on the Multi-News dataset. Specifically, we generated two distinct pre-training datasets following two contrasting approaches: first, the Entity Pyramid strategy described in this paper, which organizes data through a multi-layered entity-based hierarchy, and second, the Principle strategy employed by Pegasus, which relies on a single abstraction level for training. Both models were then trained under identical conditions, ensuring consistent hyperparameters such as input/output length limits, pre-training dataset composition, document structure, and use of document separators. This controlled setup isolates the impact of the pre-training strategy itself. After training, we evaluated both models using the same experimental protocols for zero- and few-shot learning on the Multi-News dataset as described in Sec. <ref>. The results, summarized in Figure <ref> (b), demonstrate that the Entity Pyramid pre-training consistently outperforms the Principle-based approach in few-shot scenarios, highlighting its advantage in adapting to limited data conditions. This improved performance suggests that the hierarchical entity structure in Entity Pyramid enhances model generalization when training examples are scarce.

The ultimate goal of our empirical evaluation is to assess the effectiveness of the proposed augmentation techniques (Section <ref>) and underlying theoretical principles (Section <ref>) in a controlled setting with a significant mismatch between training and test conditions. To this end, we perform a series of experiments on aurora4 <cit.>, which is a well known benchmark dataset for assessing robustness of acoustic models. The dataset has been assembled for the purpose of evaluating the effectiveness of acoustic models in out-of-distribution generalization. In particular, the benchmark includes a setting known as clean condition training with a set of clean speech training utterances recorded using a high-quality close-talking Sennheiser microphone and a number of test utterances recorded using one of 18 different microphones. While some of the test utterances are recorded in clean conditions, the majority of them are noisy and cover various different noise conditions such as street traffic, train station, car, babble, restaurant, and airport. The signal-to-noise ratio (snr) in these test recordings ranges from 5 to 15 dB. Hence, the selected benchmark dataset allows for assessing two modes of out-of-distribution generalization: i) robustness to different types and levels of noise unseen during training, and ii) robustness relative to bias introduced by microphones and recording devices. In addition to this, the benchmark also includes a setting known as multi-condition training that has been designed such that the conditions (i.e., noise types and microphones) present in training match those for the test utterances. More specifically, the training sample in this setting includes recordings from Sennheiser and other microphones, and it covers various different noise types <cit.>. An important difference between acoustic conditions present in the two samples for this setting is in the range of signal-to-noise ratios (10-20 dB in training vs 5-15 dB in test utterances). Here, it is important to note that throughout our empirical evaluation we maintain the mismatch in the signal-to-noise ratios between training data (detailed below) and the test conditions of aurora4.
new_text: Our empirical evaluation aims to assess the effectiveness of the proposed augmentation techniques (Section <ref>) and their underlying theoretical principles (Section <ref>) in a controlled setting where significant mismatches exist between training and test conditions. To achieve this, we conduct experiments on the Aurora4 dataset <cit.>, a widely recognized benchmark for evaluating the robustness of acoustic models. This dataset was specifically assembled to assess how well acoustic models generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. The benchmark includes a "clean condition training" setting, where training utterances are recorded with a high-quality close-talking Sennheiser microphone, and test utterances are captured using one of 18 distinct microphones. While some test utterances are recorded in clean environments, the majority contain noise from sources such as street traffic, train stations, vehicles, babble, restaurants, and airports, with signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) ranging from 5 to 15 dB. This setup enables evaluation of robustness across two modes of out-of-distribution generalization: (i) adaptation to unseen noise types and SNR levels during training, and (ii) adaptation to microphone-specific biases introduced by different recording devices. Additionally, the benchmark features a "multi-condition training" setting in which training and test utterances share the same noise types and microphone configurations. Specifically, the training data in this setting includes recordings from both the Sennheiser and other microphones, covering a variety of noise conditions <cit.>. A key difference between the acoustic conditions in this setting is the SNR range—10–20 dB during training versus 5–15 dB in the test data. Importantly, throughout our evaluation, we maintain the SNR mismatch between our training data (detailed below) and the Aurora4 test conditions.
