new_text: We demonstrate that omitting machine translation (MT) during inference causes substantial accuracy losses for state-of-the-art IR frameworks in cross-lingual IR. To address this, we propose novel algorithms to distill knowledge from a monolingual IR teacher model (operating on MT output) into a cross-lingual student model requiring no MT. We apply knowledge distillation (KD) for both IR and text representation, introducing a cross-lingual alignment algorithm for the latter that leverages the masked language model's multilingual representations. Empirical evaluations show our student model recovers most performance lost in single-pass cross-lingual operation. Future work includes zero-shot application to new datasets and adapting the approach for end-to-end QA.

new_text: Conventional fake video detection methods output a possibility value or a suspected mask of tampered images. However, such unexplainable results lack explanatory power and cannot be used as convincing evidence. Therefore, tracing the sources of fake videos is a more effective approach. Traditional hashing methods retrieve semantically similar images but cannot discern subtle differences. Specifically, source tracing differs from traditional video retrieval in that it seeks the authentic source video among visually similar candidates. This presents a challenge when distinguishing between videos featuring the same person in similar scenes or identical scenes from different angles. To address this, we designed a novel loss—Hash Triplet Loss—to improve discrimination of such visually similar videos. We propose Vision Transformer-based models termed Video Tracing and Tampering Localization (VTL). In the first stage, we train hash centers using ViTHash (VTL-T). A fake video is input into ViTHash, which generates a hash code used to retrieve the source video from hash centers. In the second stage, the source video and fake video are input into a generator (VTL-L), which masks suspect regions to provide auxiliary information. Additionally, we constructed two datasets: DFTL and DAVIS2016-TL. Experiments on DFTL demonstrate the superiority of our framework in source tracing for similar videos. In particular, VTL achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on DAVIS2016-TL. Our source code and datasets are available on GitHub: [URL].

old_text: Injecting meta information or linguistic markers in NMT is a well studied topic <cit.>. A straightforward approach is to insert these markers in the text being generated. To project pause markers from source to target language, we simply add a [pause] token to delineate pauses in the source and target sentences. And then, let the NMT model learn the phrase boundaries implicitly by learning the [pause] token positions along with target token sequence. This way we incorporates pauses directly into the vocabulary of the model and allows it to learn semantics of the marker itself, at the same time model also implicitly learns to control the length of the phrase by demarcating the phrase boundaries.
new_text: The integration of metadata or linguistic markers into Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems is a well-established area of research (cite). A direct method involves embedding these markers into the source or target text to guide the model’s behavior. For instance, to preserve rhythmic or structural cues like pauses during translation, a specialized [pause] token is inserted at equivalent positions in both the source and target sentences. This enables the NMT model to treat pauses as explicit units during training. As the model processes the input and generates the target sequence, it simultaneously learns the placement of [pause] tokens relative to other tokens. This dual learning objective allows the model to internalize both the semantic role of pauses (e.g., signaling breaths or natural speech segmentation) and their functional impact on structuring output text. Over time, the model develops an implicit understanding of phrase length regulation by associating pause tokens with boundaries between segments, thereby aligning linguistic pauses with the natural cadence of the target language.

Sparse coding with an l_1 penalty and a learned linear dictionary requires regularization of the dictionary to prevent a collapse in the l_1 norms of the codes. Typically, this regularization entails bounding the Euclidean norms of the dictionary's elements.
In this work, we propose a novel sparse coding protocol which prevents a collapse in the codes without the need to regularize the decoder. Our method regularizes the codes directly so that each latent code component has variance greater than a fixed threshold over a set of sparse representations for a given set of inputs. Furthermore, we explore ways to effectively train sparse coding systems with multi-layer decoders since they can model more complex relationships than linear dictionaries.
new_text: When employing sparse coding with an l_1 penalty and a learned linear dictionary, regularization of the dictionary is essential to avoid a collapse in the l_1 norms of the codes. Conventional approaches achieve this by imposing constraints on the Euclidean norms of the dictionary elements. In contrast, our proposed sparse coding framework circumvents the need for decoder regularization by directly enforcing a constraint on the codes: we ensure that each latent code component maintains a variance exceeding a predefined threshold across sparse representations of a given input set. Additionally, we examine training methodologies for sparse coding architectures incorporating multi-layer decoders, which offer enhanced capacity to capture complex relationships compared to linear dictionaries.

The inter/intra-subject variability of electroencephalography (EEG) makes the practical use of the brain-computer interface (BCI) difficult.
In general, the BCI system requires a calibration procedure to tune the model every time the system is used.
This problem is recognized as a major obstacle to BCI, and to overcome it, approaches based on transfer learning (TL) have recently emerged.
However, many BCI paradigms are limited in that they consist of a structure that shows labels first and then measures “imagery", the negative effects of source subjects containing data that do not contain control signals have been ignored in many cases of the subject-to-subject TL process.
The main purpose of this paper is to propose a method of excluding subjects that are expected to have a negative impact on subject-to-subject TL training, which generally uses data from as many subjects as possible.
In this paper, we proposed a BCI framework using only high-confidence subjects for TL training.
In our framework, a deep neural network selects useful subjects for the TL process and excludes noisy subjects, using a co-teaching algorithm based on the small-loss trick.
We experimented with leave-one-subject-out validation on two public datasets (2020 international BCI competition track 4 and OpenBMI dataset).
Our experimental results showed that confidence-aware TL, which selects subjects with small loss instances, improves the generalization performance of BCI.
new_text: The inter/intra-subject variability of electroencephalography (EEG) hinders practical brain-computer interface (BCI) use, requiring recalibration for every session. While transfer learning (TL) has emerged to address this, many BCI paradigms face limitations due to labeled “imagery” tasks and the exclusion of source subjects with non-control signals, which often negatively impact subject-to-subject TL. This paper proposes a framework to exclude low-confidence subjects during TL training, deviating from conventional approaches that rely on all available subjects. A deep neural network with a co-teaching algorithm employing the small-loss trick identifies useful subjects for TL, filtering out noisy ones. Leave-one-subject-out validation on the 2020 international BCI competition track 4 and OpenBMI datasets demonstrated that confidence-aware TL, which prioritizes small-loss instances, enhances BCI generalization performance.

Striking a balance between well performing object trackers and run-time speeds that fall in the real-time envelope is a challenging problem when deploying on computationally limited devices.
In this section, we introduce the Exemplar Transformer, an efficient transformer architecture for visual object tracking, capable of operating at real-time on standard CPUs.
While lightweight, our Exemplar Transformer significantly closes the performance gap with the prohibitively expensive transformer-based trackers <cit.>.
Sec. <ref> first presents the original Transformer of Vaswani et al. <cit.>, and then introduces the efficient Exemplar Transformer.
Sec. <ref> introduces our tracker, E.T.Track.
Specifically, it first outlines the overall architecture, and presents how Exemplar Transformers are utilized within the tracker.
new_text: Achieving a balance between high-performance object tracking and real-time execution is a critical challenge when deploying tracking systems on devices with limited computational resources. This section introduces the Exemplar Transformer, an efficient Transformer architecture for visual object tracking capable of real-time operation on standard CPUs. Despite its lightweight design, the Exemplar Transformer significantly reduces the performance gap compared to costly Transformer-based trackers <cit.>. Sec. <ref> begins by presenting the original Transformer of Vaswani et al. <cit.> and then describes the Exemplar Transformer’s efficient design. Sec. <ref> introduces our tracker, E.T.Track, first describing the overall architecture and then detailing how Exemplar Transformers are integrated into the tracking pipeline.

The brain-computer interface (BCI) is a technology that analyzes human brain signals to comprehend the user's intention and makes it possible for the user to communicate with external devices or systems via these signals <cit.>.
For BCIs, a variety of brain imaging modalities are available <cit.>,
with electroencephalography (EEG) being a well-known and commonly utilized brain signal<cit.>. Three types of paradigms are commonly utilized in EEG-based BCI: event-related potential (ERP) <cit.> and steady-state visual potential (SSVEP) <cit.> based on stimulus presentation, and motor imagery (MI) <cit.> based on intuitive imagination. Recent studies have been proposed on paradigms like speech and visual imagery that emphasize increased intuitiveness<cit.>.

In this work, we only considered reading requests from user in the framework of the Linear Tape Scheduling Problem. However, the raw logs contains much more information
that one could expect to use. Knowledge about time processing of reading operations and positioning operations performed by the multiple device heads could be leveraged to better
model seeking speed and reading speed. With a fast parsing of the logs, the positioning time seems to impact the performance much more than the reading time. Hence, modeling
the seeking speed of the device seems to be important in order to provide realistic cost models of the process.
Temporal aspects of the raw dataset could also be exploited for a usage in online problems, for instance.
new_text: In this work, we focused exclusively on reading requests within the Linear Tape Scheduling Problem, specifically addressing how these requests are handled in the context of tape storage systems. However, the raw operational logs contain a wealth of additional data that could be utilized for more sophisticated modeling. For example, detailed information about the time required for individual read operations and the positioning of multiple device heads is embedded in the logs. These data points could be analyzed to refine estimates of device characteristics such as seeking speed (the time needed to move the tape head to a specific location) and actual reading speed (the time spent transferring data once the head is in place). Upon parsing the logs, it becomes evident that variations in positioning time—rather than the duration of the read itself—have a greater influence on overall performance. This suggests that accurate modeling of seeking speed is critical for developing cost-effective scheduling algorithms that reflect real-world behavior. Furthermore, the temporal dynamics captured in the dataset, such as the frequency and timing of requests, open possibilities for adapting these methods to online scheduling scenarios, where decisions must be made in real time based on incoming data streams.

The standard Query function f_Q projects every spatial location of the feature map independently to a query space.
Unlike machine translation where every feature represents a specific word or token, adjacent spatial representation in vision tasks often resemble identical objects.
We, therefore, hypothesize that a more coarse representation is sufficiently descriptive while significantly decreasing the computational complexity.
Consequently, we aggregate the information of the feature map X ∈ℝ^H × W × C, where H × W represents the spatial dimensions.
Specifically, we use a 2D adaptive average pooling layer followed by a flattening operation Ψ_S(X), with a kernel of size S, decreasing the output spatial dimension to S^2.
The compressed representation of X is then project to a query space as in the standard self-attention formulation.

Psychometric testing Psychometric testing <cit.> aims to study the perceptual processes under measurable psychical stimuli such as tones with different intensity or lights with various brightness.
In general, two types of psychometric experiments could be carried. First, the absolute threshold based method tries to detect the point of stimulus intensity that a participant could notice. For example, how many hairs are touched to the back of hand before a participant could notice. Secondly, the discriminative based experiments (also known as the just-noticeable difference (JND)) try to find the slightest difference that a participant could perceive between two stimuli. Participants might be asked to describe the difference in directions or magnitude between these two stimuli or tested by two-alternative-force choice (2AFC)  <cit.> that forces them to make a choice between the stimuli concerning a specific` parameter of interest. The 2AFC method has also been adopted to elicit the subjects' perception of more complex multimedia, such as videos or images  <cit.>. Some scholars extend the 2AFC to M-AFC methods  <cit.> by comparing M stimuli in one test. In our work, we take advantage of the 3-AFC method, where threes samples are presented in one test to elicit the annotator's perception regarding the conception similarity.
new_text: Psychometric testing <cit.> focuses on the study of perceptual processes in response to measurable physical stimuli. These stimuli can range from varying sound intensities, like different tones, to changes in light brightness. Two primary categories of psychometric experiments are commonly employed. The first approach, known as the absolute threshold method, seeks to identify the minimal stimulus intensity that a participant can detect. For instance, this might involve determining the number of hair strands that need to be lightly touched on a person’s back before they become aware of the sensation. The second category, discriminative-based experiments—often referred to as just-noticeable difference (JND) testing—aims to quantify the smallest perceptible difference between two stimuli. In these experiments, participants may be required to articulate the direction or magnitude of differences between stimuli or may be subjected to a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) <cit.> paradigm. In the 2AFC method, participants are compelled to choose between two stimuli based on a predefined parameter of interest. This approach has been adapted for evaluating perception in more complex media, such as videos or images <cit.>. Researchers have further generalized the method into M-alternative forced-choice (M-AFC) models <cit.>, where participants compare up to M distinct stimuli in a single trial. In this study, we implement a 3-AFC methodology, in which three samples are simultaneously presented to annotators to assess their perception of conceptual similarity among the stimuli.

Network models are powerful and flexible tools for representing complex interactions between individual elements in many different fields <cit.>.
For instance, in social support networks, each individual is a person or the representative of a household, and each link, tie or arc represents the presence or intensity of a relationship between two individuals. Understanding what core patterns drive the observed set of interactions is of high relevance for scientists and practitioners willing to fully exploit the increased availability of networked datasets.
A popular approach to modeling networks is that of generative models, in particular latent variable models <cit.>. They are probabilistic models that introduce latent variables to incorporate domain knowledge and capture complex interactions. Of particular interest, is the possibility of recovering clusters of individuals that behave similarly, a problem named community detection <cit.>. In this framework, the latent variables represent the nodes' community memberships and the structure of interactions between communities, and the aim is to infer those quantities from the data <cit.>.
new_text: Network models are versatile tools for representing complex interactions among individual elements across diverse disciplines <cit.>. For example, in social support networks, each individual is either a person or a household representative, with each link (or tie/arc) denoting the presence or intensity of a relationship between two individuals. Understanding the core patterns underlying observed interactions is crucial for scientists and practitioners seeking to leverage the growing availability of networked datasets. A popular approach to modeling networks is generative modeling, particularly through latent variable models <cit.>. These probabilistic models integrate domain-specific knowledge and capture intricate interactions by introducing latent variables. The ability to identify clusters of individuals with similar behaviors—known as community detection—is of particular interest <cit.>. In this framework, latent variables represent both nodes' community memberships and the interaction structure between communities, with the goal being to infer these quantities from the data <cit.>.

In the manuscript, we use networks generated with the benchmark proposed above where we fix N = 1000 nodes, K = 2 overlapping communities, ⟨ k ⟩ = 20 average degree, and different values of the pair-interaction parameter η such that we obtain networks with reciprocity values 𝗋 in the interval [0, 0.8]. In detail, we use η∈{0.1, 10, 20, 40, 80, 140, 280, 500, 1500} to get 𝗋 ∈{0, 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.8}. To generate the membership matrices u and v we first assign an equal-size unmixed group membership and then we apply the overlapping to 20% of the nodes by drawing those entries from a Dirichlet distribution with parameter α=0.1. The affinity matrix w is generated using an assortative block structure with main probabilities p_1 = ⟨ k ⟩ K / N and secondary probabilities p_2 = 0.1 p_1. Thus the latent variables Θ = (u, v, w, η) are fixed. Then, edges are drawn according to the generative model described above. We generate 10 different samples for each value of η.
new_text: The manuscript employs networks generated using the benchmark framework described, with fixed parameters: N = 1000 nodes, K = 2 overlapping communities, an average degree ⟨k⟩ = 20, and varying values of the pair-interaction parameter η to control reciprocity (r). Specifically, η is set to values in the set {0.1, 10, 20, 40, 80, 140, 280, 500, 1500}, which systematically produce reciprocity levels spanning the range 𝗋 ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.2, ..., 0.8}. To construct the membership matrices u and v, an initial step assigns an equal-sized unmixed group membership to all nodes (i.e., no overlap). Subsequently, 20% of the nodes are designated as overlapping, where their membership entries are sampled from a Dirichlet distribution with concentration parameter α = 0.1. This approach introduces variability in the degree of overlap, with α = 0.1 favoring distributions where nodes belong predominantly to one group but retain a small, non-zero presence in the other. The affinity matrix w is generated using an assortative block model, where within-community connection probabilities (p₁) are calculated as ⟨k⟩K/N to ensure the desired average degree, while between-community connections (p₂) are set to 0.1p₁ to maintain lower cross-community connectivity. Collectively, the latent variables Θ = (u, v, w, η) define the generative process, which is then used to simulate edge formation according to the model. For robustness, 10 independent network samples are generated for each η value, enabling statistical analysis across the reciprocity spectrum.

new_text: Ensemble-based methods share similarities with bagging techniques in machine learning. In <cit.>, the authors propose a method where neural networks are initialized with randomly assigned parameters, and bagging sampling is employed to generate training data subsets. This approach leverages the well-known benefits of bagging, such as reducing variance in model predictions and improving generalization. Similarly, in <cit.>, the focus shifts to utilizing features extracted from multiple layers of a neural network to identify out-of-distribution (OOD) samples. By constructing higher-order Gram Matrices from these features, the method captures intricate interactions between data representations, which empirically demonstrates improved OOD detection performance. More recently, <cit.> introduces an innovative approach by transforming training labels into different word embeddings (e.g., GloVe or FastText) to introduce diversity and redundancy during supervision. This strategy embeds semantic relationships into the training process, enabling the model to learn more robust representations. The incorporation of semantic structure not only enhances model diversity but also strengthens the neural network’s resilience to distributional shifts, aligning with the broader goals of ensemble methods.

Compared to convolutional layers, fully-connected (FC) layers are better at modeling the long-range dependencies but worse at capturing the local patterns, hence usually less favored for image recognition. In this paper, we propose a methodology, Locality Injection, to incorporate local priors into an FC layer via merging the trained parameters of a parallel conv kernel into the FC kernel. Locality Injection can be viewed as a novel Structural Re-parameterization method since it equivalently converts the structures via transforming the parameters. Based on that, we propose a multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) block named RepMLP Block, which uses three FC layers to extract features, and a novel architecture named RepMLPNet. The hierarchical design distinguishes RepMLPNet from the other concurrently proposed vision MLPs. As it produces feature maps of different levels, it qualifies as a backbone model for downstream tasks like semantic segmentation. Our results reveal that 1) Locality Injection is a general methodology for MLP models; 2) RepMLPNet has favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared to the other MLPs; 3) RepMLPNet is the first MLP that seamlessly transfer to Cityscapes semantic segmentation. The code and models are available at [URL].
new_text: Compared to convolutional layers, fully-connected (FC) layers excel at modeling long-range dependencies but fall short in capturing local patterns, making them less preferred for image recognition tasks. In this paper, we introduce Locality Injection, a methodology that integrates local priors into an FC layer by merging the trained parameters of a parallel convolutional kernel into the FC kernel. Locality Injection can be considered a novel structural re-parameterization method, as it transforms the network structure by reconfiguring the parameters. Building upon this approach, we propose an MLP block, termed RepMLP Block, comprising three FC layers for feature extraction, and a novel architecture, RepMLPNet. The hierarchical design of RepMLPNet differentiates it from other concurrently proposed vision MLPs. By generating feature maps at multiple levels, RepMLPNet serves as a suitable backbone model for downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation. Our experimental results demonstrate that: (1) Locality Injection is a general method applicable to MLP models; (2) RepMLPNet achieves a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency compared to existing MLPs; and (3) RepMLPNet is the first MLP to seamlessly transfer to Cityscapes semantic segmentation. The code and models are available at [URL].

new_text: We focus exclusively on the first misreport case outlined in Section <ref> due to its greater practical relevance compared to the second case. Specifically, in the second misreport scenario, a malicious node exaggerates its dataset size beyond typical client levels, creating a detectable discrepancy for the central server. This abnormality triggers protocol-based interventions—such as requiring the node to re-upload its local model update or provide verifiable evidence that the update aligns with the claimed dataset size. These safeguards render the second case less critical for robustness analysis, as the system already has clear mechanisms to flag and address such inconsistencies. In contrast, the first misreport case arises when all nodes report similar dataset sizes, making it impossible for the central server to statistically distinguish malicious nodes based on this metric alone. This distinction is crucial for evaluating the system’s resilience, as it necessitates advanced detection strategies beyond simple dataset size verification.

Here we advance on existing digital trace methods using a two-wave study in which we captured not only the URLs participants clicked on while browsing the web (engagement), but also the URLs they saw while using Google Search (exposure). Using surveys paired with engagement and exposure data collected around the 2018 and 2020 US elections, we found that strong Republicans engaged with more partisan and unreliable news than strong Democrats did, despite the two groups being exposed to similar amounts of partisan and unreliable news in their Google search results. Our results suggest the search engine is not pushing strong partisans into “filter bubbles,” but strong Republicans are asymmetrically selecting into “echo chambers.” These findings hold across both study waves, align with work on social media and web browsing, and provide a rare look at the relationship between exposure and engagement. Our research highlights the importance of users' choices, and our approach moves the field closer to the independent, longitudinal, and cross-platform studies it needs to evaluate the impact of online search and social media platforms.
new_text: Popular online platforms like Google Search have the potential to expose billions of users to partisan and unreliable news. However, studying the content shown to real users is difficult due to technical challenges in obtaining this data and the absence of data-sharing agreements that include it. Here, we build upon existing digital trace methods using a two-wave study in which we captured participants’ web browsing engagement (clicks on URLs) and Google Search exposure (visible URLs). Using surveys combined with engagement and exposure data collected around the 2018 and 2020 US elections, we found that strong Republicans engaged with more partisan and unreliable news than strong Democrats, despite both groups encountering similar levels of such content in their search results. Our results indicate that the search engine does not reinforce “filter bubbles” for strong partisans but rather highlights how strong Republicans disproportionately self-select into “echo chambers.” These patterns persist across both study waves, align with existing work on social media and web browsing, and offer a rare empirical view of how exposure and engagement interact. Our findings emphasize the role of user agency and demonstrate an approach that advances the field toward the independent, longitudinal, and cross-platform analyses necessary to assess the influence of online search and social media platforms.

In one approach, researchers evaluated these relationships by comparing the returns of asset i with the forward-shifted returns of asset j, identifying whether changes in one asset’s performance predict changes in another after a delay. A subsequent study built on this method by substituting the correlation coefficient with mutual information, a statistical measure capable of capturing both linear and non-linear dependencies. Together, this approach combined network visualization with rigorous statistical validation to characterize temporal dependencies in financial markets.

Unlike CNNs, the ViT <cit.> is typically more cumbersome and computationally extensive.
Therefore, recently, lots of studies try to make ViT lightweight and efficient.
These works usually revise the architecture of ViT <cit.> and introduce the image-specific inductive bias of CNNs back into ViT <cit.> to reduce the number of parameters and complexity.
In detail, the DeiT <cit.> introduces the distillation token and applies knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from pre-trained networks to lightweight ViTs.
The T2T <cit.> proposes progressive tokenization to model the local structure information.
The Cross-ViT <cit.> uses a dual-branch transformer to combine image patches of different sizes to produce stronger image features, and propose a cross attention module to reduce computation.
The MobileViT <cit.> combines the strengths of CNNs and ViTs by replacing local processing in convolutions with global processing using transformers.
All of these methods heavily modify the architecture of the standard ViT, while our quantized ViT still maintains the origin network architectures.
new_text:
Vision Transformers (ViTs) differ from CNNs in that they often demand significantly greater computational resources and model complexity. Specifically, the inherent design of ViTs—characterized by large parameter counts and intensive computation—makes them less practical for deployment on devices with limited hardware capabilities. To address this challenge, recent research has focused on optimizing ViT models to improve efficiency without sacrificing performance. A common strategy among these approaches involves adapting the architectural framework of ViTs by integrating image-specific inductive biases derived from CNNs. This hybridization aims to reduce both the number of parameters and the computational load while preserving the strengths of Vision Transformers in capturing global dependencies.  

For instance, DeiT introduces a distillation token and employs knowledge distillation, a technique where a smaller "student" model learns from a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model, thereby enhancing efficiency. Meanwhile, T2T addresses local feature extraction by implementing progressive tokenization, which incrementally builds hierarchical representations to model spatial structures. Cross-ViT adopts a dual-branch design, processing patches of varying scales and incorporating a cross-attention module to reduce redundant computations. MobileViT further bridges the gap between CNNs and ViTs by substituting convolution-based local processing with transformer operations, leveraging CNN-like inductive biases for spatial awareness.  

These advancements, while diverse in methodology, share a common trait: they fundamentally restructure the standard ViT architecture. In contrast, our approach—quantized ViT—retains the original architectural design while introducing efficiency improvements through quantization techniques. This distinction allows us to maintain compatibility with existing ViT frameworks while achieving computational savings.

new_text: This article presents several analytical implications. First, it proposes an LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) model trained exclusively on data from Maharashtra, a state with favorable dynamics, and uses this model to predict trends in other Indian provinces. This approach highlights the potential for leveraging region-specific data to infer broader patterns. Furthermore, the study evaluates the performance of this LSTM model by comparing it against alternative architectures—SimpleRNN, GRU, Stacked RNN, Stacked LSTM, and Stacked GRU—while systematically varying input window sizes and the number of hidden units. These comparisons aim to identify which configurations yield the most accurate predictions. In alignment with the growing emphasis on Explainable AI, the authors visualize the maximum and minimum output values of the LSTM layer and juxtapose these with the actual data trends, offering insights into the model’s decision-making process. Additionally, the research demonstrates the robustness of the proposed model and confirms that the authors’ approach (referred to as Approach 1) achieves superior predictive performance. Finally, the pretrained LSTM model is used to forecast active cases in India over a 100-day horizon, extending its applicability to real-world public health planning.

new_text: This study employs a proposed pretrained LSTM model to predict active cases across Indian provinces. Various deep learning architectures—including SimpleRNN, LSTM, GRU, Stacked RNN, Stacked LSTM, and Stacked GRU—were trained and tested on data from Maharashtra. A detailed comparative analysis was conducted based on input window size and the number of hidden units. The LSTM model outperformed other architectures on Maharashtra’s dataset. The pretrained LSTM model trained on Maharashtra data successfully captured transmission dynamics in other Indian provinces. Within the framework of Explainable AI (XAI), this approach evaluates a model’s robustness in capturing dynamic patterns. Proposed approach-1 yielded better results than proposed approach-2. For instance, the first case in Lakshadweep was reported on 18th January 2021, and it was noted that approach-2 required increased training days due to minimal data dynamics—a limitation mitigated by approach-1. The study also visualized maximum and minimum outputs from the LSTM layer for selected states (Kerala, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu). These visualizations demonstrated that approach-1 generalized effectively to capture diverse transmission dynamics. The pretrained LSTM model forecasted active cases in India from 16th December 2021 to 5th March 2022, indicating a third wave would emerge by January 2022. These forecasts enabled the Indian government to implement targeted restrictions and enhance COVID-19 testing at airports, bus, and railway stations.

old_text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been widely utilized in many computer vision tasks. However, CNNs have a fixed reception field and lack the ability of long-range perception, which is crucial to human pose estimation. Due to its capability to capture long-range dependencies between pixels, transformer architecture has been adopted to computer vision applications recently and is proven to be a highly effective architecture. We are interested in exploring its capability in human pose estimation, and thus propose a novel model based on transformer architecture, enhanced with a feature pyramid fusion structure. More specifically, we use pre-trained Swin Transformer as our backbone and extract features from input images, we leverage a feature pyramid structure to extract feature maps from different stages. By fusing the features together, our model predicts the keypoint heatmap. The experiment results of our study have demonstrated that the proposed transformer-based model can achieve better performance compared to the state-of-the-art CNN-based models.
new_text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used in computer vision but suffer from fixed receptive fields and limited long-range perception, crucial for human pose estimation. The transformer architecture, which effectively captures long-range dependencies, has emerged in computer vision. We propose a novel transformer-based model with a feature pyramid fusion structure for human pose estimation. Our model uses a pre-trained Swin Transformer backbone to extract input image features and employs a feature pyramid to obtain multi-stage feature maps. These fused features are used to predict keypoint heatmaps. Experimental results show the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art CNN-based approaches.

new_text: In our initial experiments, we employed image classification models based on ResNet architectures <cit.>. Training these models without data augmentation results in severe overfitting. We evaluated optimizer performance on ResNets (18, 50, and 101) using the publicly available CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 <cit.>, TinyImageNet <cit.>, and ImageNet <cit.> datasets. Recently, there has been a surge in research in multimodal machine translation (MMT), where additional modalities such as images are used to improve translation quality of textual systems.
A particular use for such multimodal systems is the task of simultaneous machine translation, where visual context has been shown to complement the partial information provided by the source sentence, especially in the early phases of translation caglayan2020simultaneous,imankulova-etal-2020-towards. In this paper, we propose the first Transformer-based simultaneous MMT architecture, which has not been previously explored in the field. Additionally, we extend this model with an auxiliary supervision signal that guides its visual attention mechanism using labelled phrase-region alignments. We perform comprehensive experiments on three language directions and conduct thorough quantitative and qualitative analyses using both automatic metrics and manual inspection. Our results show that (i) supervised visual attention consistently improves the translation quality of the MMT models, and (ii) fine-tuning the MMT with supervision loss enabled leads to better performance than training the MMT from scratch. Compared to the state-of-the-art,
our proposed model achieves improvements of up to 2.3 BLEU and 3.5 METEOR points.
new_text: Interest in multimodal machine translation (MMT) has grown significantly, with researchers incorporating additional modalities like images to enhance the performance of text-based translation systems. One critical application of these multimodal approaches is in simultaneous machine translation, where visual context aids in compensating for incomplete source sentence information, particularly during initial translation stages caglayan2020simultaneous,imankulova-etal-2020-towards. This work introduces the first Transformer-based architecture for simultaneous MMT, a configuration previously unexplored in the domain. We further augment this model by integrating an auxiliary supervision signal that refines its visual attention through labelled phrase-region alignment annotations. Extensive experiments across three language pairs include rigorous quantitative evaluation via automatic metrics and qualitative analysis through manual review. Results demonstrate that (i) supervised visual attention consistently boosts MMT performance, and (ii) fine-tuning the MMT system using supervision loss yields superior outcomes compared to training from scratch. The proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems by up to 2.3 BLEU and 3.5 METEOR points.

This hints at the fact that the improvements can be more pronounced if the models are (pre-)trained on larger linguistic resources, an exploration that we leave to future work.

Simultaneous machine translation (MT) aims at providing a computational framework that
reproduces how human interpreters perform simultaneous interpretation. In this task, the duty of the interpreter is to translate speech in near real-time, by constantly maintaining a balance between the time needed to accumulate sufficient context and the translation latency the listeners experience in return.
This streaming property is what differentiates simultaneous MT from the conventional MT approaches, which process complete source sentences. Traditional work in simultaneous translation have dealt with this streaming property by relying on syntactic or heuristic constraints bub1997verbmobil,ryu-etal-2006-simultaneous,bangalore-etal-2012-real to determine the amount of waiting prior to committing a partial translation. Similar approaches have also been explored using state-of-the-art neural MT (NMT) architectures sutskever2014sequence,Bahdanau2015NeuralMT,vaswani2017attention, such as rule-based deterministic policies implemented at (greedy) decoding time cho2016can or the wait-k policy which sequentially switches between reading a new word and committing a translation ma2019stacl. Adaptive policies, which attempt to learn when to read or commit
depending on the context, have also been explored mostly through reinforcement learning-based techniques gu2016learning,alinejad2018prediction,ive-etal-2021-exploiting.
new_text: Simultaneous machine translation (MT) aims to develop a computational framework that mirrors the real-time translation strategies used by human interpreters. In this context, the interpreter’s role involves translating spoken language with minimal delay, requiring a continuous balancing act between accumulating sufficient contextual information and minimizing the latency experienced by listeners. This dynamic, termed the "streaming property," distinguishes simultaneous MT from traditional MT methods, which typically operate on fully formed source sentences. Conventional approaches to simultaneous translation have historically addressed this challenge by employing syntactic or heuristic rules—such as verb-final constraints in Germanic languages—to determine how long to wait before committing to a partial translation. Early systems relied on these structural cues to manage the tension between translation accuracy and speed. With the advent of neural machine translation (NMT), researchers have extended these principles to end-to-end models, exploring strategies like rule-based deterministic policies implemented during greedy decoding (e.g., the wait-k policy) or incremental commitment thresholds. For instance, the wait-k method sequentially alternates between reading new input tokens and committing to translations, using a fixed waiting period before issuing output. More recently, efforts have shifted toward adaptive policies that dynamically adjust reading and translation decisions based on contextual factors. These data-driven approaches, primarily developed using reinforcement learning techniques, aim to optimize translation quality and fluency by learning optimal trade-offs between waiting for additional context and minimizing listener delay. Such methods differ from rigid rule-based systems by incorporating environmental feedback, allowing models to adapt more flexibly to varying linguistic structures and speaker rhythms.

old_text: Accurate and fine-grained information about the extent of damage to buildings is essential for humanitarian relief and disaster response. However, as the most commonly used architecture in remote sensing interpretation tasks, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have limited ability to model the non-local relationship between pixels. Recently, Transformer architecture first proposed for modeling long-range dependency in natural language processing has shown promising results in computer vision tasks. Considering the frontier advances of Transformer architecture in the computer vision field, in this paper, we present the first attempt at designing a Transformer-based damage assessment architecture (DamFormer). In DamFormer, a siamese Transformer encoder is first constructed to extract non-local and representative deep features from input multitemporal image-pairs. Then, a multitemporal fusion module is designed to fuse information for downstream tasks. Finally, a lightweight dual-tasks decoder aggregates multi-level features for final prediction. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first time that such a deep Transformer-based network is proposed for multitemporal remote sensing interpretation tasks. The experimental results on the large-scale damage assessment dataset xBD demonstrate the potential of the Transformer-based architecture.
new_text: Accurate, fine-grained building damage assessments are critical for humanitarian relief and disaster response. Despite their widespread use in remote sensing, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) struggle to model non-local pixel relationships. Transformer architectures, originally designed for long-range dependencies in natural language processing, have recently shown promise in vision tasks. We present DamFormer, the first Transformer-based approach for multitemporal damage assessment. The model employs a siamese Transformer encoder to extract non-local features from multitemporal image pairs, followed by a multitemporal fusion module and a lightweight dual-task decoder for feature aggregation and prediction. This work introduces the first deep Transformer-based network for multitemporal remote sensing interpretation; experiments on the xBD dataset validate its efficacy.

The proposed approach is also compatible with different routing algorithms, as we will demonstrate in the experimental section. Similar to Momentum ResNets, we use a momentum term that enables us to convert any existing residual capsule block into its reversible counterpart. Our architecture, called MoCapsNet, drastically reduces the memory consumption of deep capsule networks, such that we can train capsule networks at almost any arbitrarily deep configuration. We further show that MoCapsNet beat the performance of baseline capsule networks on MNIST, SVHN and CIFAR-10.

The proposed approach is compatible with various routing algorithms, as demonstrated in the experimental section. Similar to Momentum ResNets, our approach employs a momentum term that allows us to convert any existing residual capsule block into its reversible counterpart. Our architecture, MoCapsNet, significantly reduces the memory consumption of deep capsule networks, enabling us to train capsule networks at nearly arbitrary depths. To address this, modules like dilated convolution and self-attention mechanisms have been introduced to capture long-range dependencies and improve performance <cit.>. Despite this, these modules often incur substantial computational costs and are typically placed at the end of CNN-backbones, neglecting low-level feature relationships.

* Dynamic Task:
  Random task generation and arrival exist for a mobile device since independent tasks are possibly sensed, collected, and generated by multiple types of applications stochastically.
  They queue in the task buffer if they cannot be processed immediately due to the limited mobile device computation and communication capabilities.
  For delay-sensitive applications, the task buffer queuing state should be characterized in each mobile device to reduce the queuing delay and avoid buffer overflow.
  However, the time-varying task arrival model poses a challenge to the queuing model and further to the computational offloading and resource allocation optimization in MEC.
new_text: In mobile edge computing (MEC) systems, tasks are generated dynamically for mobile devices due to the stochastic nature of modern applications, which independently sense, collect, and produce tasks at unpredictable intervals. These tasks often arrive faster than a mobile device can process them, as computational and communication resources are inherently constrained. When immediate processing is infeasible, tasks accumulate in a task buffer, waiting to be executed. For delay-sensitive applications—such as real-time video streaming or autonomous control—monitoring the buffer’s queuing state in each device is essential to minimize delays and prevent overflow, which could lead to task loss or performance degradation. However, the unpredictable and time-varying arrival patterns of these tasks complicate accurate queuing model characterization. This uncertainty directly challenges optimization strategies for computational offloading and resource allocation in MEC, as these rely on predictable task behavior to balance workloads efficiently.

Although energy consumption can be enhanced through larger-capacity batteries or frequent recharging, the former increases device size, weight, and cost, while the latter is often impractical or impossible for devices such as mobile phones and hard-to-reach wireless sensors <cit.>. Tying the control scheme too closely to a physical setup would exaggerate the discrepancies between physical world and our numerical model. Moreover, the learned control strategies would be valid only for a particular hardware implementation and would not transfer across manufacturers of similar deposition systems. To address these issues we propose to learn high-level control strategies. More specifically, our policy tunes the velocity of the printing head and an offset from baseline printing path (see inset). new_text: Defining an appropriate action space is crucial for translating learned strategies into physical hardware implementations. Overly binding control schemes to specific physical configurations amplifies discrepancies between simulated models and real-world environments. Additionally, such rigid approaches restrict the applicability of learned control strategies to a single hardware setup, preventing generalization across different manufacturers of similar deposition systems. To address these limitations, we propose the use of high-level control strategies. Specifically, our policy modulates the printing head’s velocity and introduces a deviation from the baseline printing path (as illustrated in the inset). This approach decouples abstract control objectives from low-level actuation details, enabling the transfer of strategies across hardware with analogous capabilities. In both simulation and physical experiments, we evaluate velocity ranges of [0.2, 2] mm/s and path deviations of ±0.315 mm.

This paper has presented a comprehensive survey of the RL-enabled MEC system in terms of network uncertainty.
First, we have presented a brief overview of MEC-empowered networks and specified the optimization difficulties based on the analysis of the network uncertainties.
Then, we have summarized the RL-based MEC framework, which provides two solutions for network optimization.
The first solution is direct RL, based on MDP models for optimization problems.
The second solution is indirect RL, where based on the decomposition of the original optimization problem into many subproblems, parts of the subproblems are optimized by RL algorithms and others are optimized by conventional optimization algorithms or machine learning algorithms.
Afterward, according to free mobility, time-varying channels, and distributed edge services in heterogeneous MEC-empowered networks, a detailed survey of MEC has been presented using mobility-, spectrum-, computation-, and caching-aware RL.
Finally, potential challenges have been given as future research directions.
new_text: This paper presents a comprehensive survey of reinforcement learning (RL)-enabled mobile edge computing (MEC) systems, focusing on network uncertainty. First, we present a brief overview of MEC-empowered networks and highlight the optimization challenges identified through analysis of network uncertainties. Next, we summarize the RL-based MEC framework, which proposes two approaches for network optimization. The first approach is direct RL, which employs Markov Decision Process (MDP) models to address optimization problems. The second approach is indirect RL, wherein the original optimization problem is decomposed into subproblems, with some solved using RL algorithms and others optimized via conventional optimization or machine learning methods. Finally, considering the characteristics of heterogeneous MEC-empowered networks—including free mobility, time-varying channels, and distributed edge services—we present a detailed survey of MEC utilizing mobility-, spectrum-, computation-, and caching-aware RL. Potential challenges are highlighted as future research directions.

Having established that the relatedness between a country and a product is better assessed by means of machine learning, a natural question arises, namely whether the country data provides an optimal assessment, given the fact that companies, and not countries, are actually
	producing the exported products. Moreover, often recommendations are given to the private sector, so one could expect that algorithms should be trained on companies, and not countries. In this paper, we provide a systematic and quantitative comparison of machine learning and network-based approaches to forecasting new products both at country and firm-level. In particular, we will leverage a database of more than 70000 Italian firms and compare it with country-level data, providing a cross-database analysis for both training and testing. Our results provide quantitative evidence about which algorithm and which database should be used to optimally assess relatedness; moreover, we are able to economically motivate these results by investigating the different structure of the two databases and how the algorithms extract the relevant information.
new_text: Having established that machine learning methods offer a more accurate way to measure the relatedness between countries and products, a critical question emerges: does using country-level data provide the most reliable insights when, in reality, the production of exported goods is carried out by individual companies rather than entire countries? This discrepancy is particularly relevant given that policy recommendations and economic strategies are often targeted at the corporate level, raising the expectation that predictive models should ideally be trained on firm-level data instead of aggregated national statistics. To address this, this paper presents a systematic and quantitative evaluation of machine learning and network-based forecasting approaches at both the country and firm levels. Leveraging a comprehensive database of over 70,000 Italian firms, we conduct a comparative analysis against traditional country-level datasets, performing cross-database experiments for model training and testing. By doing so, we not only identify which algorithms and data granularities yield optimal predictions of relatedness but also provide an economic interpretation of these findings, examining how structural differences between firm- and country-level data influence algorithmic performance and the extraction of meaningful patterns.

A straight-forward idea is to simply save all intermediate instances, i. e., the footprint of the EA so to say. This approach is not target-oriented however since instances with large performance gaps are desirable; see diversity requirement (D1). We now present an idea that borrows ideas from quality diversity (QD). QD is a recently emerged branch of evolutionary computation. In the so-called Map-elites approach the target space is partitioned into boxes where each box stores the best solution found for all target space realizations closest to its box-center. This approach is highly successful, e. g., in evolving different robot behavior <cit.> where the target space corresponds to the behavioral space of the robots.
In our setting the target space corresponds to the feature space ℱ⊆ℝ^p we aim to cover. Each box of our QD-algorithm corresponds to one possible feature combination. The algorithm is designed for discrete features where, given a fixed instance size n, the number of possible realizations of each feature is countable and bounded. This is indeed the case for many TSP-features of interest, e. g., k-NNG based features or depth-based MST features <cit.> which are frequently among the top discriminating features in AS-models <cit.>.[E. g., given n cities, the number of weak connected components in the k-NNG can take values in {1, 2, …, n-k} only <cit.>.] We refer the interested reader to recent work by Heins et al. <cit.> who derived theoretical lower and upper bounds for a large collection of such features for feature normalization.
new_text: A straightforward approach to EA archiving is to store all intermediate instances, i.e., the algorithm’s footprint. However, this method is not target-oriented, as (D1) requires preserving instances with large performance gaps. We instead propose an idea inspired by quality diversity (QD), a branch of evolutionary computation. In the Map-Elites algorithm, the target space is partitioned into boxes storing the best solutions corresponding to each box’s center in the target space. This approach has successfully evolved diverse robot behaviors <cit.>. In our setting, the target space aligns with the feature space ℱ⊆ℝ^p we aim to cover, where each box represents a feature combination. The algorithm operates on discrete features with countable, bounded realizations under a fixed instance size n—common for TSP features like k-NNG and depth-based MST features <cit.> frequently distinguishing AS models <cit.>. For example, the number of weakly connected components in a k-NNG with n cities is constrained to {1, 2, …, n−k} <cit.>. Theoretical bounds for normalizing such features are derived by Heins et al. <cit.>.

We begin by evolving small instances with n=100 nodes using two insertion heuristics: Farthest-Insertion (FI) and Nearest-Insertion (NI) <cit.>. FI starts with a partial tour containing one randomly selected node. In (n−1) iterations, the remaining nodes are incrementally added until a TSP tour is complete. During the selection phase, FI identifies the node farthest from the current sub-route and inserts it into the partial route in the position that creates the minimal possible extension. In contrast, NI follows a similar procedure but differs in the selection phase by choosing the nearest node instead. The objective is to evolve instances that span a two-dimensional feature space effectively while minimizing the tour length ratio FI(I)/NI(I) or NI(I)/FI(I), respectively. Ratios below 1 indicate a performance advantage for the algorithm in the numerator.

Following the principle of OOD evaluation, the corruptions should not be used as augmentations during training, and therefore we choose mixing and deformation augmentations.
As shown in <ref>,
mixing and deformation augmentations can bring significant improvements to model robustness.
PointMixUp <cit.> and RSMix <cit.> are two mix strategies.
Similar to MixUp <cit.> in 2D augmentation, PointMixup mixes two point clouds using shortest-path interpolation.
Similar to CutMix <cit.> in 2D augmentation, RSMix mixes two point clouds using rigid transformation.
Both mix strategies substantially reduce CE on corruptions including “Add-G”, “Add-L”, “Rotate” and “Jitter”.
However, an unexpected side effect of the mix strategies is that classifiers become more vulnerable to scaling effects.
By non-rigidly deforming local parts of an object,
PointWOLF <cit.> enrich the data variation, which constantly improves classifier robustness on all evaluated corruptions.
new_text: Guided by the OOD evaluation framework, we avoid using corruptions as training augmentations, instead opting for mixing and deformation techniques. As demonstrated in <ref>, these augmentations notably enhance model robustness. Two mixing approaches—PointMixUp <cit.> and RSMix <cit.>—are inspired by 2D counterparts: PointMixUp employs shortest-path interpolation to blend point clouds akin to MixUp <cit.>, while RSMix applies rigid transformations to interleave data similarly to CutMix <cit.>. Both methods achieve significant reductions in cross-entropy (CE) for corruptions such as “Add-G”, “Add-L”, “Rotate”, and “Jitter”. However, a counterintuitive consequence arises: these strategies heighten classifier vulnerability to scaling effects. PointWOLF <cit.>, which applies non-rigid deformations to localized object regions, mitigates this by expanding data diversity, consistently strengthening robustness across all tested corruptions.

Under all three experimental settings, the true average treatment effects (ATEs) of interest for the 2-wave time-varying model λ_{a_1,a_2}—corresponding to binary treatments {A_1 := a_1, A_2 := a_2}—are derived from Eqs. (<ref>)-(<ref>) as λ_{1,0} = 0.2 - 0 = 0.2, λ_{0,1} = 0.2 - 0 = 0.2, and λ_{1,1} = 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3, as denoted by green horizontal dotted lines in Fig. <ref>. The red horizontal dotted line in Fig. <ref> represents zero-ATE, serving as a critical reference point since it signifies that the compared treatments yield equivalent causal outcomes. In certain applications, the accuracy of the ATE sign is more critical than its magnitude, as the sign determines treatment effectiveness. For instance, λ_{1,0} > 0 (as in Eq. (<ref>)) indicates that treatment {A_1 := 1, A_2 := 0} is more effective than {A_1 := 0, A_2 := 0} in expectation, and the reverse is true if λ_{1,0} < 0. Identifying the direction of the ATE thus takes precedence over quantifying its exact magnitude.  

In Fig. <ref>, boxplots illustrate μ, μ ± σ, and μ ± 3σ values for all λ_{a_1,a_2} to characterize the variability of the estimates. Notably, across all plots, c-GNF excludes the zero-ATE value within the one-standard-deviation interval (μ ± σ), demonstrating no ambiguity in identifying the optimal treatment in expectation. By contrast, IPW, RWR, and GCOM exhibit such ambiguity, as they include zero-ATE within this interval. This property of eliminating decision-making uncertainty is a desirable quality for causal effect estimation methods deployed in practical settings.

new_text: For our experiments and benchmarking, we simulate a virtual social system using the 2-wave model depicted in Fig. <ref>. Specifically, we generate three types of variables: continuous covariates (C₁, C₂), which represent neighborhood-level characteristics such as the median parental income in a given area; binary treatment variables (A₁, A₂), which indicate individual-level exposures such as whether a person resides in a high- or low-income neighborhood; and a continuous outcome variable Y, representing the total score achieved in a high-school graduation examination. The outcome Y is designed to measure the aggregated academic performance of individuals in relation to their neighborhood conditions. This approach enables us to systematically study neighborhood effects on high-school graduation. For example, we draw C₁ from a standard normal distribution (C₁ ∼ 𝒩(μ = 0, σ² = 1)) to simulate variability in neighborhood contexts.

old_text: Structural Equation/Causal Models (SEMs/SCMs) are widely used in epidemiology and social sciences to identify and analyze the average treatment effect (ATE) and conditional ATE (CATE). Traditional causal effect estimation methods such as Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) and more recently Regression-With-Residuals (RWR) are widely used - as they avoid the challenging task of identifying the SCM parameters - to estimate ATE and CATE. However, much work remains before traditional estimation methods can be used for counterfactual inference, and for the benefit of Personalized Public Policy Analysis (P^3A) in the social sciences. While doctors rely on personalized medicine to tailor treatments to patients in laboratory settings (relatively closed systems), P^3A draws inspiration from such tailoring but adapts it for open social systems. In this article, we develop a method for counterfactual inference that we name causal-Graphical Normalizing Flow (c-GNF), facilitating P^3A. A major advantage of c-GNF is that it suits the open system in which P^3A is conducted. First, we show how c-GNF captures the underlying SCM without making any assumption about functional forms. This capturing capability is enabled by the deep neural networks that model the underlying SCM via observational data likelihood maximization using gradient descent. Second, we propose a novel dequantization trick to deal with discrete variables, which is a limitation of normalizing flows in general. Third, we demonstrate in experiments that c-GNF performs on-par with IPW and RWR in terms of bias and variance for estimating the ATE, when the true functional forms are known, and better when they are unknown. Fourth and most importantly, we conduct counterfactual inference with c-GNFs, demonstrating promising empirical performance. Because IPW and RWR, like other traditional methods, lack the capability of counterfactual inference, c-GNFs will likely play a major role in tailoring personalized treatment, facilitating P^3A, optimizing social interventions - in contrast to the current `one-size-fits-all' approach of existing methods.

However, substantial work remains before traditional estimation methods can be used for counterfactual inference or to advance personalized public policy analysis (P^3A) in the social sciences. Second, we propose a novel dequantization technique to address discrete variables, a limitation of normalizing flows in general. Third, we demonstrate in experiments that c-GNF performs comparably to IPW and RWR in terms of bias and variance for estimating the ATE when true functional forms are known, and performs better when they are unknown. 3D perception, especially point cloud classification, has achieved substantial progress.
However, in real-world deployment, point cloud corruptions are inevitable due to the scene complexity, sensor inaccuracy, and processing imprecision. In this work, we aim to rigorously benchmark and analyze point cloud classification under corruptions. To conduct a systematic investigation, we first provide a taxonomy of common 3D corruptions and identify the atomic corruptions. Then, we perform a comprehensive evaluation on a wide range of representative point cloud models to understand their robustness and generalizability.
Our benchmark results show that although point cloud classification performance improves over time, the state-of-the-art methods are on the verge of being less robust.
Based on the obtained observations, we propose several effective techniques to enhance point cloud classifier robustness. We hope our comprehensive benchmark, in-depth analysis, and proposed techniques could spark future research in robust 3D perception. Code is available at [URL].
new_text: 3D perception, particularly point cloud classification, has achieved significant advances. However, in real-world deployments, point cloud corruptions are unavoidable due to scene complexity, sensor inaccuracy, and processing imprecision. In this work, we propose to rigorously benchmark and analyze point cloud classification under corruptions. To conduct a systematic evaluation, we first present a taxonomy of common 3D corruptions and identify atomic corruptions. Then, we perform a comprehensive evaluation on a diverse set of representative point cloud models to assess their robustness and generalizability. Our benchmark results show that although point cloud classification performance improves over time, state-of-the-art methods are approaching the threshold of being less robust. Based on the observed findings, we propose several effective techniques to enhance point cloud classifier robustness. We hope our comprehensive benchmark, in-depth analysis, and proposed techniques could spark future research in robust 3D perception. The code is available at [URL].

Clearly, by improving the efficiency of the internal MAPF solver (e.g., PBS) we can improve the efficiency of RHCR overall, as it solves multiple W-MAPF queries. However, speeding up MAPF solvers without leveraging additional structure within the RHCR approach can be difficult. Next, we observe that there is an underlying structure emerging from the fact that the W-MAPF queries are consecutive, i.e., a solution plan to one query q_i defines the next query q_i +1. In particular, considering that a short replan rate h is typically used by RHCR, consecutive W-MAPF queries can be quite similar to one another in terms of initial and goal agent locations. This, in turn, can lead to similar queries, in terms of the conflicts that need to be avoided and the agents between which they arise. Despite this, current RHCR implementations solve every subsequent W-MAPF query from scratch.
new_text: Improving the efficiency of internal MAPF solvers (e.g., PBS) directly enhances RHCR, as it handles multiple W-MAPF queries. However, accelerating these solvers without exploiting RHCR-specific structure remains challenging. Notably, consecutive W-MAPF queries share an underlying structure: the solution to query q_i defines the subsequent query q_{i+1}. Since RHCR employs a short replan rate h, consecutive queries exhibit similar initial and goal agent positions, leading to overlapping conflict patterns among agents. Despite this similarity, current RHCR implementations solve each subsequent W-MAPF query independently, discarding prior solutions.

old_text: In recent years, ultrasonic (US) sensing technologies emerged as a promising alternative to EMG. Huang et al. showed that US has the potential to achieve better results compared to EMG <cit.>. McIntosh et al. proposed to extract the optical flow of an ultrasound stream as a feature prior to the classification phase <cit.>. Others used ML algorithms demonstrating the feasibility of gesture classification from downsampled US images of the same area <cit.>. Gesture recognition was achieved with wearable single-transducer sensors <cit.>. Importantly, these devices differ from medical transducers in that they contain significantly fewer elements and provide coarser views for the lower arm. In addition, researchers demonstrated that similar techniques allow decoupling of different degrees of freedom and emphasize their dominance in an US image <cit.>. Unsupervised techniques were also studied, showing discrimination of unlabeled gestures <cit.>, which might imply the possibility to understand muscle behavior of arm amputees without labeling them explicitly. Despite this progress, the feasibility of instructing a robotic hand to deliver fine finger motions is still an open question.

new_text: These approaches leverage the observation that samples near the decision boundary are linked to uncertain predictions. For such samples, the model's logit values tend to converge toward uniformity, approximating 1/K as the samples approach the boundary, resulting in elevated ℒ^adv values. In contrast, for samples distant from the decision boundary, the model exhibits high confidence, with one logit value approaching 1 and the remaining logits approaching 0, thereby producing low ℒ^adv values. Consequently, minimizing ℒ^adv encourages models to maximize the separation between input samples and the decision boundary.

This section discusses some important observations pertaining the proposed method and network pruning.
First, training from scratch. Training a compact network (from random initialization) using Deadwooding instead of pruning a pre-trained (PT) complex model may result in low era and eba models. The analysis is further discussed in Appendix F and in line with the SoA <cit.>. It highlights that training a smaller model from scratch performs worse than retraining a pruned model.
Second, multi-step or iterative pruning. This paper’s presented evaluations are for single-shot pruning. However, we also evaluated our approach for multi-step pruning (detail in Appendix G), also known as Iterative Pruning <cit.>, with 20% parameter pruning at each step. The pruned models achieved through single-shot and iterative perform similarly in terms of eba and era.

First, training from scratch: training a compact network from random initialization using Deadwooding, rather than retraining a pruned pre-trained (PT) complex model, may result in lower era and eba values. This observation aligns with the state-of-the-art (SoA) literature and is further analyzed in Appendix F <cit.>. Second, multi-step or iterative pruning: while this paper’s evaluations focus on single-shot pruning, we also tested iterative pruning (details in Appendix G), where 20% of parameters are pruned in each step. The models obtained through single-shot and iterative pruning demonstrate comparable eba and era performance.

PBS
maintains priorities between agents which are used to resolve conflicts.
On the high-level search PBS explores a priority tree (PT), where a given node N of PT encodes a (partial) priority set ≺_N={a_h ≺ a_i, a_j ≺ a_l, …}. A priority a_i≺ a_j means that agent a_i has precedence over agent a_j whenever a low-level search is invoked (see below). In addition to the ordering, each PT node maintains single-agent plans that represent the current MAPF solution (possibly containing conflicts).
PBS starts the high-level search with the tree root whose priority set is empty, and assigns to each agent its shortest path. Whenever PBS expands a node N, it invokes a low-level search to compute a new set of plans which abide to the priority set ≺_N. If a collision between agents, e.g., a_i and a_j, is encountered in the new plans, PBS generates two child PT nodes N_1, N_2 with the updated priority sets ≺_N_1=≺_N∪{a_i≺ a_j}, ≺_N_2=≺_N∪{a_j≺ a_i}, respectively. The high-level search chooses to expand at each step a PT node in a depth-first search manner.
The high-level search terminates when a valid solution is a found at some node N, or when no more nodes for expansion remain, in which case, PBS declares failure.
new_text: PBS maintains agent priorities for conflict resolution by exploring a priority tree (PT), where each node N encodes a partial priority set ≺_N={a_h ≺ a_i, a_j ≺ a_l, ...}. A_i≺ a_j indicates a_i's precedence over a_j during low-level searches. Each PT node stores single-agent plans for the current (possibly conflicting) MAPF solution. PBS initiates the high-level search at the root with an empty priority set and shortest paths for each agent. Expanding a node N triggers a low-level search to compute plans conforming to ≺_N. Collisions between agents (e.g., a_i and a_j) generate two child nodes N₁, N₂ with updated priority sets ≺_N₁=≺_N∪{a_i≺ a_j}, ≺_N₂=≺_N∪{a_j≺ a_i}. The high-level search expands nodes in depth-first order. It terminates when a valid solution is found at a node or all expansion nodes are exhausted, returning failure in the latter case.

new_text: Zero-finding remains complex even in unverified settings, so Dandelion employs an external oracle to generate initial approximations of zeros. These approximations are structured as confidence intervals [a,b], where the derivative h'(x) is known to have a zero between a and b. Additionally, the algorithm that computes these confidence intervals does not need to be verified, since Dandelion can independently validate the results. To validate a list of guesses Z, Dandelion leverages a result from real-number analysis established by Harrison: A function f has a zero at a point x if its first derivative f' changes sign at this point.

old_text: While there is evidence on the benefits of dialogic reading for children across a broad age range, much of the research attention has been focused on younger children aged three to eight who are at the stage of “learning to read” and do not have fluent decoding skills  <cit.>. Dialogic reading is particularly suitable for this age group as this reading activity is typically carried out orally, thus allowing young children to fully allocate their cognitive resources on making sense of the text they hear  <cit.>. Thereby, dialogic reading promotes the kind of oral language skills, including vocabulary and narrative comprehension <cit.>, that are strongly linked to children's later reading skills and academic success as they move to the “reading to learn” stage after the age of eight <cit.>. Nevertheless, children aged three to eight span two different stages of the reading development  <cit.>: a pre-reading stage when children gain mastery over the sound structure of spoken language, make inferences of stories from pictures, and develop listening comprehension skills; and an early-reading stage when children learn to decode print text and begin to read fluently and strategically. Due to pre-reading children's limited decoding skills, they primarily rely on stories being read to them, while children in the early-reading stage start to read stories more independently. Our system provides audio narration to support pre-reading children, but also allows early-reading children to read without audio narration. We will discuss the different usage patterns between these two stages in the findings of our user study (Section <ref>) and how future versions of StoryBuddy can better accommodate the specific needs of children in these age groups (Section <ref>).
new_text: While evidence supports dialogic reading’s benefits across ages, research primarily focuses on three- to eight-year-olds in the “learning to read” phase who lack fluent decoding skills <cit.>. This age group benefits because dialogic reading’s oral format allows children to allocate cognitive resources to text comprehension <cit.>. It enhances oral language skills—vocabulary and narrative comprehension <cit.>—critical for later reading and academic success as children transition to “reading to learn” after age eight <cit.>. These children span two reading stages: pre-reading (developing phonological awareness, inference from pictures, and listening comprehension) and early-reading (learning decoding, fluency, and strategic reading). Pre-reading children rely on audio narration due to limited decoding; early-reading children progress to independent reading. Our system supports audio narration for pre-reading children while enabling independent reading for early-readers. We analyze usage patterns in these groups in our study (Section <ref>) and propose adaptations for future StoryBuddy versions (Section <ref>).
