In addition to enhancing engagement, some participants also valued the effect of joint reading on providing emotional support to their kids: “in addition to engagement, I think, (kids will get) the emotional support, while you're reading with your child, and the interaction with the child, especially before (going to) bed, ... your child will feel very loved and warm” (PA2).
new_text: When exploring practical strategies that parents used to foster children’s engagement in storytelling—excluding the use of intelligent agents—joint reading emerged as a frequently reported approach. This technique, described as alternating between parent and child during reading sessions, was highlighted as a method to sustain attention and encourage active participation. For instance, one parent explained, “Usually, we'll take turns since she doesn't like to read all the pages by herself. So I want to motivate her. And usually, I'll read one sentence and she will read the next sentence, and we will take turns to read the whole book” (PA2). Another parent described a similar approach: “So we do what's called joint reading. So I'll read, and then I'll have him read. And then I'll read and we go back and forth” (PA3). These accounts illustrate a shared practice designed to balance the cognitive and emotional demands of reading, allowing children to engage without feeling overwhelmed. Beyond fostering engagement, some parents emphasized joint reading’s role in providing emotional support. As one parent noted, the interactive nature of the activity—particularly during evening routines—strengthened familial bonds: “In addition to engagement, I think [kids will get] the emotional support while you're reading with your child, and the interaction with the child, especially before [going to] bed, ... your child will feel very loved and warm” (PA2). This dual benefit—cognitive participation and emotional connection—suggests that joint reading serves both educational and relational purposes in family contexts.

new_text: In <cit.>, the authors introduced the Algebra of Interactions over a set of ports P (AI(P) for short) for modeling component interactions. The syntax of the algebra was built over the set of ports P, one symbol representing empty interaction, another symbol denoting the set of empty interactions, a union operator, and a synchronization operator. For their second algebra, the Algebra of Connectors (AC(P) for short), each port was associated with a synchronization type: 'trigger' for initiating interactions and 'synchron' for synchronizing with other ports to interact. The authors also considered two subalgebras, where all connectors shared the same type (synchron or trigger), and discussed the relationships among the presented algebras. Furthermore, they introduced and studied a congruence relation for connectors, defined as the largest equivalence relation that allowed interchangeable use of equivalent connectors. Finally, the authors demonstrated applications of their algebras to enhance the language and execution engine of the BIP framework. We also refer the reader to <cit.> and <cit.> for related methodologies on connector characterization.

old_text: -1 Limitations. We experimented with real recordings in order to identify the limitations of the current model. We found that the model struggles in generalizing to recording environment conditions that significantly deviate from the ones encountered during training. The model fails to produce intelligible speech for highly reverberant, noisy samples, or when the recording microphone introduces noticeable distortions. Similarly, the model fails to generalize to unseen accents and speech tempos. There is also a degradation in speaker identity preservation for longer gap sizes, as well as a tendency towards producing a monotone prosody. new_text: Our experiments with real-world audio recordings revealed several limitations of the current model, particularly in scenarios where input conditions diverge significantly from those encountered during training. The model demonstrates reduced performance when faced with environmental factors such as excessive reverberation, background noise, or microphone-induced distortions—common challenges in real-world settings—which often result in unintelligible or degraded output speech. Additionally, it struggles to generalize across variations in speaker characteristics, including unfamiliar accents or atypical speech tempos, indicating a reliance on patterns present in the training data rather than robust adaptability. Performance degradation is further observed in tasks requiring long-term coherence: as silence or missing segments (gaps) increase in duration, the model’s ability to maintain consistent speaker identity weakens, and its output speech often adopts a monotonous prosody, lacking natural intonation and rhythm. These failure modes are documented in our supplementary materials, offering concrete examples of how the model’s behavior diverges from ideal performance under challenging, real-world conditions.

old_text: In this work, we consider how to conduct few-shot evaluations in light of the analysis with respect to the pretraining data. Prior work has attempted to control for overlap between training or pretraining data and the test instances, but as we have seen, those methods are insufficient. For example, <cit.> measure the impact of removing instances from evaluation datasets that share 13-gram overlap with their pretraining data on GPT-3's accuracy, and also argue that the low occurrence of exact phrases such as “NUM1 + NUM2 =” and “NUM1 plus NUM2” in the pretraining data indicate that the model's strong performance on arithmetic tasks is likely due to factors other than memorization. However, we have seen that model performance is impacted by much simpler statistical patterns, as small as unigram overlaps with the pretraining data.
new_text: In this work, we address the challenge of designing few-shot evaluations in the context of pretraining data analysis. While prior research has sought to mitigate overlap between pretraining data and test instances by controlling for shared content, our analysis demonstrates that these approaches remain inadequate. For instance, <cit.> evaluate the impact of removing evaluation dataset instances that exhibit 13-gram overlap with GPT-3’s pretraining data on the model's accuracy, and further posit that the infrequent appearance of exact phrases such as “NUM1 + NUM2 =” and “NUM1 plus NUM2” in the pretraining data suggests that the model's strong performance on arithmetic tasks likely stems from mechanisms other than memorization. In contrast, our findings demonstrate that even more rudimentary statistical patterns—such as unigram-level overlaps with pretraining data—significantly impact model performance.

We compute occurrences and co-occurrences (if they are within a window of 5 words) of the terms in the corpus, i.e. the time units and numbers.
We then generate instances for each of our reasoning datasets using the most frequent terms (in the top 200) as operands with less than 3 digits.

new_text: The pipeline for creating natural language instances in these datasets is illustrated in Figure <ref>. We compute occurrences and co-occurrences (specifically within a 5-word window) of the terms in the corpus—the time units and numbers. We then generate instances for each reasoning dataset using the most frequent terms (top 200) as operands with fewer than three digits. We focus on the top terms because we expect the models to have reliable and robust representations for these words. Each reasoning instance is generated as a natural language query using the prompt templates from Table <ref> and input into the language model to produce an answer. For example, to create a multiplication instance with arguments (x_1=23, x_2=18), we use the instance template to generate a natural language input for the model, such as “Q: What is 23 times 18? A: [3mm]”, aiming to produce “414” (y=23×18=414). old_text: In this work, we develop an algorithm that overcomes these limitations by augmenting a standard reinforcement learning agent with a retrieval process (parameterized via a neural network). The purpose of the retrieval process is to help the agent achieve its objective by providing relevant contextual information. To this end, the retrieval process uses a learned attention mechanism to dynamically access a large pool of past trajectories stored in a dataset (e.g., a replay buffer), with the aim of integrating information across these. The proposed algorithm (R2A), shown in Figure <ref>, enables an agent to retrieve information from a dataset of trajectories. The high-level idea is to have two different processes. First, the retrieval process, makes a “query” to search for relevant contextual information in the dataset. Second, the agent process performs inference and learning based on the information provided by the retrieval process. These two processes have different internal states but interact to shape the representations and predictions of each other: the agent process provides the relevant context, and the retrieval process uses the context and its own internal state to generate a query and retrieve relevant information, which is in turn used by the agent process to shape the representation of its policy and value function (see Fig. <ref>A). Our proposed retrieval-augmented RL paradigm could take several forms. Here, we focus on a particular instantiation to assay and validate our hypothesis that learning a retrieval process can help an RL agent achieve its objectives.
new_text: In this work, we develop an algorithm that overcomes these limitations by augmenting a standard reinforcement learning agent with a retrieval process (parameterized via a neural network). The retrieval process aims to assist the agent in achieving its objective by providing relevant contextual information. To this end, the process uses a learned attention mechanism to dynamically retrieve a large pool of past trajectories stored in a dataset (e.g., a replay buffer), with the aim of integrating information from these. The proposed algorithm (R2A), illustrated in Figure <ref>, enables an agent to retrieve information from a dataset of trajectories. The high-level idea involves two distinct processes: the retrieval process generates a query to search for relevant contextual information in the dataset, and the agent process performs inference and learning based on the retrieved information. These two processes maintain separate internal states but interact to mutually shape their representations and predictions: the agent process provides the relevant context, and the retrieval process combines this context with its own internal state to generate a query and retrieve information, which in turn shapes the agent process’s policy and value function representations (see Fig. <ref>A). Our proposed retrieval-augmented RL paradigm encompasses several possible forms; here, we focus on a specific instantiation to test and validate our hypothesis that learning a retrieval process can assist an RL agent in achieving its objectives.

**Resignation.**
A widespread assumption among service providers is that individuals will be able to process complex legal jargon and take an informed decision. Shifting the burden of obtaining informed consent to citizens is at odds with adequately empowering them to take control <cit.>. Instead, this has led to a regime of misinformed and often coercive consent <cit.>. Evidence of this is the proliferation of purposely misleading consent controls or dark patterns <cit.>. Such asymmetrical relations engender different adverse behaviours and feelings of resignation among users. Research shows that there are disconnects between the stated privacy policies and the controls that are used to implement them <cit.>. This means even if a trained individual is able to navigate through complex policies, there might not be adequate controls to enable the functioning of a private life. Service providers rather take advantage of people's need to access online services despite their inability to process the complexities. Contrary to the view of the privacy paradox, users have little choice than to accept obscure terms and conditions in exchange for online services if the risks are not well understood and they are overburdened with information <cit.>.
new_text: Many service providers operate under the belief that individuals can effectively navigate complex legal language and make informed decisions. However, transferring the responsibility of obtaining informed consent to users conflicts with enabling meaningful autonomy <cit.>. This approach has instead fostered a system characterized by misinformed and often coercive consent practices <cit.>. A key example is the use of intentionally deceptive interface designs, or "dark patterns," which manipulate user choices <cit.>. These imbalanced power dynamics contribute to negative outcomes, including user resignation. Studies highlight inconsistencies between organizational privacy policies and the actual controls provided to implement them <cit.>. Consequently, even individuals with the expertise to interpret detailed policies may find insufficient mechanisms to exercise privacy in practice. Service providers exploit users' reliance on online services, despite their cognitive limitations in processing intricate terms. Contrary to the notion of the privacy paradox, users often lack viable alternatives but to accept opaque agreements when risks are poorly comprehended and information overload is prevalent <cit.>.

Acquisiti reviews the growing recognition of both behavioral and utilitarian aspects in privacy choices, noting how framing individuals as rational yet self-interested utility maximizers gave rise to the "privacy paradox" <cit.>. User-specific nudges based on preferences further reflect paternalistic tendencies in intervention design <cit.>.

new_text: The interdisciplinary field of surveillance studies has long examined how commercial and political interests drive surveillance practices that generate ethical conflicts and distribute benefits and harms unevenly <cit.>. While sharing specific data in straightforward scenarios—such as verifying student discounts—raises minimal concerns, more sensitive disclosures, such as criminal records, can disproportionately affect equitable opportunities for ethnic minorities <cit.>. Similar complexities arise in medical research: a lack of transparent and verifiable data protection systems risks undermining [id=AD]legitimate and beneficial data uses <cit.>. Simultaneously, the web’s persistence ensures that personal missteps are archived indefinitely, enabling discrimination based on historical actions <cit.>. Yet, granting individuals the ability to erase damaging past information encounters significant barriers stemming from economic and political power imbalances. Individuals often lack the tools or authority to remove unwanted personal data from public spaces <cit.>. As collective entities, individuals remain politically vulnerable in sustaining the advocacy required for robust regulatory frameworks <cit.>. Political dynamics remain central to understanding how effectively privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) can be implemented as public goods, particularly in determining who gains from weakened or failed regulatory systems.

A Realistic Testbed for FL. Prior works on federated training of HAR models (e.g.,  <cit.>) have assumed that each FL client owns a large amount of labeled data, in the order of 3000-5000 seconds. Instead, we setup a realistic FL testbed with a large number of clients, each holding a small amount of labeled data. This is achieved through a novel class-based partitioning scheme that divides existing HAR datasets over a large number of users, and makes them suitable for realistic federated evaluations. In addition, our testbed includes latency and energy consumption profiles for nine embedded-scale hardware, which allows for obtaining a realistic estimate of the resource consumption of federated HAR algorithms.
We plan to open-source the source code of our partitioning algorithm as well as the federated HAR datasets for reproducibility.

new_text: Deep feature extraction leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and correlation techniques is a core component of advanced object recognition algorithms <cit.>. A critical approach to addressing object scale variations is the feature pyramid strategy, which was initially developed in the Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) <cit.>. This method extracts hierarchical features from discretized image pyramids, significantly enhancing object recognition performance. Following this foundational work, subsequent architectures introduced similar pyramid frameworks incorporating multi-scale lightweight feature maps and refined skip connection structures. The effective feature pyramid design in FCOS <cit.> is now widely adopted. For our DangerDet framework, we implement a comparable pyramid architecture to improve both efficiency and accuracy in detecting diverse dangerous behaviors (see Fig. <ref>).

old_text: Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) are one of the most popular SLAM sensors due to their competitive price and the associated acceptable performance. new_text: Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) are among the most commonly used SLAM sensors due to their competitive pricing and satisfactory performance. By analyzing IMU data, the framework enables systematic characterization of motion profiles, leveraging the inherent capabilities of these sensors for structured motion analysis.

old_text: Reliability of SLAM systems is considered one of the critical requirements in many modern autonomous systems. This directed the efforts to developing many state-of-the-art systems, creating challenging datasets, and introducing rigorous metrics to measure SLAM system performance. However, the link between datasets and performance in the robustness/resilience context has rarely been explored. In order to fill this void, characterization the operating conditions of SLAM systems is essential in order to provide an environment for quantitative measurement of robustness and resilience. In this paper, we argue that for proper evaluation of SLAM performance, the characterization of SLAM datasets serves as a critical first step. The study starts by reviewing previous efforts for quantitative characterization of SLAM datasets. Then, the problem of perturbations characterization is discussed and the linkage to SLAM robustness/resilience is established. After that, we propose a novel, generic and extendable framework for quantitative analysis and comparison of SLAM datasets. Additionally, a description of different characterization parameters is provided. Finally, we demonstrate the application of our framework by presenting the characterization results of three SLAM datasets: KITTI, EuroC-MAV, and TUM-VI highlighting the level of insights achieved by the proposed framework.
new_text: Reliability of SLAM systems plays a critical role in many modern autonomous systems, prompting efforts to develop state-of-the-art technologies, create challenging datasets, and introduce rigorous metrics to assess performance. However, the connection between these datasets and performance under robustness/resilience conditions has been scarcely investigated. To address this gap, characterizing the operating conditions of SLAM systems is essential to establish a framework for quantitatively measuring robustness and resilience. In this paper, we argue that proper evaluation of SLAM performance necessitates characterizing datasets as a foundational step. The study begins with a review of prior work on quantitative characterization of SLAM datasets. It then discusses the problem of characterizing perturbations and establishes their relationship to SLAM robustness/resilience. Next, we propose a novel, generic, and extensible framework for analyzing and comparing SLAM datasets quantitatively. Additionally, various characterization parameters are described. Finally, the framework’s application is demonstrated through the characterization of three datasets—KITTI, EuroC-MAV, and TUM-VI—highlighting the insights gained via our approach.

Incremental methods for CT modification have been explored in some previous works <cit.>.
In Draper1995, incremental addition of links is performed by first forming a cluster graph using a set of rules and then converting the cluster graph into a junction tree.
Although several heuristic-based graph transformations are suggested, a difficulty is to choose a set of heuristics, so that clique size constraints are met. Also, there is no specific algorithm to construct the CT.
A preferable method would be to make additions to an existing CT. Dynamic reconfiguration of CTs is explored <cit.>, but it is specific to evidence and query based simplification.
A more general method has been proposed in Flores2002.
Here, the minimal section of the clique tree that needs modification is identified using the Maximal Prime Subgraph Decomposition (MPSD) <cit.> of the BN.
Based on the moralized graph, the junction tree is converted into another graphical representation called the MPD join tree. We have a more detailed comparison with the partitioning and incremental compilation methods in section 7.
new_text: Prior studies have investigated incremental methods for CT modification <cit.>. In Draper1995, incremental link addition involves forming a cluster graph via rules and converting it into a junction tree. Selecting heuristics to satisfy clique size constraints remains challenging, and no specific CT construction algorithm is provided. Dynamic reconfiguration methods <cit.> are limited to evidence- and query-based simplification. A broader approach is proposed in Flores2002, which identifies the minimal clique tree section for modification using the BN’s Maximal Prime Subgraph Decomposition (MPSD) <cit.>. The junction tree is then converted into an MPD join tree based on the moralized graph. A detailed comparison with partitioning and incremental compilation methods is provided in Section 7.

Graphon Approximation: One possible approach to consider non-uniform agent interaction is the notion of Graphon mean-field, which is recently gaining popularity in the non-cooperative MARL setup <cit.>. The main idea is to approximate the finite indices of the agents as a continuum of real numbers and the discrete interaction graph between agents as a continuous, symmetric, measurable function, called graphon, in the asymptotic limit of infinite population. The unfortunate consequence of this approximation is that one is left to deal with an infinite dimensional mean-field distribution. In order to obtain practical solution from graphon-approximation, one must therefore discretise the continuum of agent indices <cit.>, which limits the use of this approximation. Our paper establishes that for affine reward functions, we do not need to go to the complexity of Graphon approximation.
new_text: Graphon Approximation: To model non-uniform agent interactions, the concept of Graphon mean-field has emerged as a promising approach in non-cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) <cit.>. This method approximates the finite set of agent indices as a continuum of real numbers and represents the discrete interaction graph between agents as a continuous, symmetric, measurable function—known as a graphon—in the asymptotic limit of infinite population. This approximation, however, leads to an infinite-dimensional mean-field distribution, which poses significant challenges for tractable analysis. To derive practical solutions, the continuum of agent indices must be discretized <cit.>, a step that inherently restricts the utility of the graphon-based framework. Our work demonstrates that for systems with affine reward functions, the complexities of Graphon approximation are unnecessary, enabling simpler and more scalable solutions.

**Reconstructing Clothed Humans from RGB-D Data.**
One straightforward approach to acquiring a 3D human model from RGB-D data is via per-frame reconstruction <cit.>. To achieve this, IF-Net <cit.> learns a prior to reconstruct an implicit function of a human and IP-Net <cit.> extends this idea to fit SMPL to this implicit surface for articulation. However, since input depth observations are partial and noisy, artifacts appear in unseen regions. Real-time performance capture methods incrementally fuse observations into a volumetric SDF grid. DynamicFusion <cit.> extends earlier approaches for static scene reconstruction <cit.> to non-rigid objects. BodyFusion <cit.> and DoubleFusion <cit.> build upon this concept by incorporating an articulated motion prior and a parametric body shape prior. Follow-up work <cit.> leverages a neural network to model the deformation or to refine the shape reconstruction. However, it is important to note that such methods only reconstruct the surface, and sometimes the pose, for tracking purposes but typically do not allow for the acquisition of skinning information which is crucial for animation.
In contrast, our focus differs in that we aim to acquire a detailed avatar including its surface and skinning field for reposing and animation.
new_text: Reconstructing clothed humans from RGB-D data often involves per-frame techniques that generate 3D models directly from individual depth and color frames <cit.>. For example, IF-Net <cit.> employs an implicit function prior to reconstruct human shapes, while IP-Net <cit.> adapts this approach by aligning SMPL parametric models to the implicit surface for articulation tracking. However, the inherent incompleteness and noise in depth data often result in visual artifacts in unobserved regions. Real-time capture systems instead integrate observations into a volumetric signed distance function (SDF) grid. DynamicFusion <cit.>, originally designed for rigid scenes <cit.>, was adapted for non-rigid human bodies, with BodyFusion <cit.> and DoubleFusion <cit.> enhancing this framework by integrating articulated motion priors and parametric shape models. Subsequent advancements <cit.> introduced neural networks to model deformations or refine geometry. Notably, these methods primarily recover surface geometry and/or pose information for tracking, but they lack the ability to capture skinning weights essential for animation. In contrast, our work targets a more comprehensive avatar representation, explicitly reconstructing both detailed surface geometry and the skinning field required for reposing and animation tasks.

This paper presented a learning-based approach to follow reference paths that can be changed during motion execution.
Trajectories are generated by a neural network trained to maximize the traversing speed while minimizing the deviation from the reference path.
Additional task-specific objectives can be considered by including sensory feedback into the state.
The mapping of network actions to joint accelerations ensures that no kinematic joint limits are violated.
We evaluated our method with and without additional objectives on robotic systems with up to 30 degrees of freedom
showing that well-performing trajectories can be learned for reference paths with different path characteristics.
We also demonstrated successful transfer for a ball-on-plate task performed by an industrial robot.
new_text: This study proposes a learning-based method for dynamically adjusting to reference paths during motion execution. A neural network generates trajectories by optimizing for maximal traversal speed while minimizing deviations from the desired path. Task-specific goals can be integrated by incorporating sensory feedback into the system's state representation. The network’s outputs are mapped to joint accelerations, ensuring compliance with kinematic constraints and preventing joint limit violations. Experimental validation on robotic platforms with up to 30 degrees of freedom demonstrated the ability to learn effective trajectories across diverse reference path characteristics, both with and without additional objectives. Successful adaptation was also shown for a ball-on-plate control task using an industrial robotic manipulator.

In this paper, we presented PINA to learn personalized implicit avatars for reconstruction and animation from noisy and partial depth maps. The key idea is to represent the implicit shape and the pose-dependent deformations in canonical space which allows for fusion over all frames of the input sequence. We propose a global optimization that enables joint learning of the skinning field and surface normals in canonical representation.
Our method learns to recover surface details and is able to animate the human avatar in novel unseen poses. We compared the method to explicit and neural implicit state-of-the-art baselines and show that we outperform all baselines in all metrics. Currently, our method does not model the appearance of the avatar. This is an exciting direction for future work. We discuss potential negative societal impact and limitations in the Supp. Mat.
new_text: This paper introduces PINA, a framework for learning personalized implicit avatars capable of reconstruction and animation from noisy, incomplete depth map sequences. The core concept involves encoding the implicit shape and pose-dependent deformations in a canonical space, enabling cross-frame data fusion. A global optimization strategy is proposed to simultaneously learn the skinning field and surface normals within this canonical representation, allowing for the recovery of detailed surfaces and animation in novel poses. Evaluation against explicit and neural implicit state-of-the-art baselines demonstrates superior performance across all metrics. Notably, the current implementation does not account for the avatar’s appearance, which remains an unexplored avenue for future research. Limitations and potential societal impacts are detailed in the Supp. Mat.

Usually, the vocabulary is generated from a union of HRL and LRL data. This often results in under-allocation of vocabulary bandwidth to LRLs, as LRL data is significantly smaller in size compared to HRL. This under-allocation of model capacity results in lower LRL performance <cit.>, as mentioned previously. In response, prior research has explored development of region-specific models <cit.>, generating vocabulary specific to language clusters <cit.>, and exploring relatedness among languages to build better LMs for LRLs <cit.>. However, none of these methods have utilized relatedness among languages for better vocabulary generation during multilingual pre-training.
new_text: The creation of a vocabulary is a crucial component of multilingual language model training, as the size of the vocabulary directly influences the model's capacity. Typically, the vocabulary is derived from a combination of high-resource language (HRL) and low-resource language (LRL) datasets. However, due to the disproportionately smaller size of LRL data compared to HRL data, this process frequently leads to insufficient allocation of vocabulary resources to LRLs, which in turn causes diminished LRL performance <cit.>, as previously noted. To address this, earlier studies have proposed approaches such as developing region-specific models <cit.>, generating vocabulary tailored to language clusters <cit.>, and investigating linguistic relatedness to enhance LRL language models (LMs) <cit.>. None of these approaches have leveraged language relatedness to optimize vocabulary creation during multilingual pre-training.

old_text: Our method is different in nature from existing single and two-stage detectors. The closest single-stage detector is anchor-free, center and scale prediction <cit.>. However, we only use the head from CSP <cit.> with different loss settings as the CSP head <cit.> is stronger and efficient compared to region proposal networks, also we use fast suppression head to further refine detections. Compared to two-stage detectors, we replace the region proposal network with a stronger detection network, we do not call it another region proposal network because focal detection network produces strong detection candidates compared to proposals that need further bounding box refinement and classification. new_text: Our method is fundamentally distinct from existing single- and two-stage detectors. The most similar single-stage approach employs anchor-free center and scale prediction <cit.>. However, we adopt the head from CSP <cit.> while modifying the loss settings to enhance performance, as the CSP head <cit.> is both stronger and more computationally efficient than traditional region proposal networks. Furthermore, we incorporate a fast suppression head to further refine detections. Compared to two-stage detectors, we substitute the region proposal network with a more robust detection architecture; we retain the term "region proposal network" to emphasize its role despite its improved performance, as the focal detection network generates high-quality candidates that require no further bounding box refinement or classification. Additionally, we replace the traditional second stage—which is computationally expensive and jointly predicts bounding boxes and classifies them—with a lightweight suppression head that selectively suppresses false positives while preserving bounding box locations.

To our knowledge, body part detection is an unprecedented task in traditional object detection tasks.
Different from general object detection, body part detection needs to overcome the ambiguity of body parts and model the prior of human body structure.
For example, normally people only have one left foot and one right foot, but the local features of the left one and the right one are often very similar.
Fortunately, this structural prior is very common in human pose estimation and has been widely explored.
To maximize the usage of this structural prior, we propose a pose-guided part detection method, which is shown in the top half of Figure <ref>.
new_text: Body part detection differs from general object detection by requiring resolution of body part ambiguity while modeling human structural priors. Humans possess symmetrically limited limbs (e.g., one left and one right foot) yet exhibit similar local features between mirrored parts. This structural prior, foundational in human pose estimation and extensively studied, is leveraged in our proposed pose-guided part detection method (Figure <ref>, top half).

Our method contains two modules, the path planner and the path scorer. The path planner is a fully CPU intensive module that in parallel
extracts candidate paths and context compasses (room and object). The results are batched and sent to a 12-head 6-layer transformer model for scoring. Path features are extracted by additional projection layers and PointNet as aforementioned. These feature extractors and transformer are combined and jointly optimized by the AdamW <cit.> optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-4. The model is trained on a single NVIDIA-P100 GPU for 10 hours.
new_text: Our method is structured into two primary components: the path planner and the path scorer. The path planner is designed as a fully CPU-intensive module that operates in parallel to extract candidate paths and associated spatial context information, which includes room layouts and object positions (referred to as "context compasses"). Once these candidate paths and contextual features are generated, they are organized into batches and transmitted to the second component, a 12-head, 6-layer transformer model, for evaluation. The transformer scoring module relies on features derived from additional projection layers and the PointNet architecture, which were detailed earlier. These feature extraction components, alongside the transformer model, are trained in unison, with their parameters jointly optimized using the AdamW optimizer at a learning rate of 1e-4. The entire system is trained end-to-end on a single NVIDIA P100 GPU, with the training process spanning a total of 10 hours to ensure convergence.

This paper presents a pose-guided coarse-to-fine framework for the part-level action parsing task.
In our PCF framework, the pose-guided part detector is one of the first attempts toward body part detection and brings considerable improvement in the AP@50 (+26.60%). Meanwhile, we convert the frame-level part state parsing problem into segment-level action recognition based on the persistence of human actions, which greatly improves the computational efficiency with less precision reduction.
At last, our method achieves SoTA results at the Kinetics-TPS dataset, which shows the effectiveness of our PCF framework. With these three contributions, we provide one of the first attempts for the part-level action parsing task.
new_text: This paper introduces PCF, a pose-guided coarse-to-fine framework for part-level action parsing. The pose-guided part detector, one of the first attempts at body part detection, achieves a significant AP@50 improvement of +26.60%. By transforming frame-level part state parsing into segment-level action recognition based on human action persistence, computational efficiency is enhanced with minimal precision loss. Achieving state-of-the-art results on Kinetics-TPS, the PCF framework demonstrates effective part-level action parsing through three novel contributions.

old_text: Accuracy. We show the performance of different classifiers under our DISCO and report their fake news detection accuracy in Table <ref>. For each row in Table <ref>, we report the performance under different training-testing splits, and each split is executed 10 times randomly to obtain the average and standard deviation. From Table <ref>, we can observe that (1) even the sample classifier can achieve very competitive performance under the DISCO modeling, for MLP (hidden dim = 32, # layers = 2) achieving the most accurate and stable predictions; (2) in many cases, too few or too many training samples could not contribute the most to the classifier under our DISCO modeling, for MLP (hidden dim = 64, # layers = 1) and MLP (hidden dim = 64, # layers = 2) reaching the peak when 20% of the whole data set are extracted as testing samples.
new_text: We evaluated the accuracy of multiple classifiers trained using our DISCO framework and present their fake news detection performance in Table <ref>. Each row in the table reflects results from distinct training-testing data splits, with each split independently repeated 10 times to compute mean accuracy and standard deviation, ensuring robustness against randomness in data partitioning. Analyzing the results reveals two key patterns. First, even a relatively simple classifier—a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with a hidden dimension of 32 and two layers—demonstrated both the highest average accuracy and the lowest variability across trials, suggesting that DISCO’s design enables stable, reliable predictions with minimal model complexity. Second, for more complex MLP variants—specifically those with a hidden dimension of 64—the optimal performance did not occur at the extremes of data sampling (e.g., using minimal or maximal training samples). Instead, peak accuracy emerged when 20% of the dataset was allocated to testing, indicating that overly constrained or saturated training regimes reduced generalization effectiveness under the DISCO framework. These findings highlight the importance of both model architecture and data proportioning when leveraging DISCO for fake news detection.

old_text: Despite plenty of efforts focusing on improving the domain adaptation ability (DA) under unsupervised or few-shot semi-supervised settings, recently the solution of active learning started to attract more attention due to its suitability in transferring model in a more practical way with limited annotation resource on target data. Nevertheless, most active learning methods are not inherently designed to handle domain gap between data distribution, on the other hand, some active domain adaptation methods (ADA) usually requires complicated query functions, which is vulnerable to overfitting. In this work, we propose a concise but effective ADA method called Select-by-Distinctive-Margin (SDM), which consists of a maximum margin loss and a margin sampling algorithm for data selection. We provide theoretical analysis to show that SDM works like a Support Vector Machine, storing hard examples around decision boundaries and exploiting them to find informative and transferable data. In addition, we propose two variants of our method, one is designed to adaptively adjust the gradient from margin loss, the other boosts the selectivity of margin sampling by taking the gradient direction into account. We benchmark SDM with standard active learning setting, demonstrating our algorithm achieves competitive results with good data scalability. Code is available at [URL]
new_text: Despite extensive research aimed at enhancing domain adaptation (DA) under unsupervised or low-annotation semi-supervised settings, recent interest has increasingly shifted toward active learning approaches. This shift is motivated by active learning’s practical advantages: it enables models to transfer knowledge effectively when annotation budgets for target domains are constrained. Unlike traditional DA strategies that require substantial labeled data in the target domain, active learning prioritizes selecting the most informative unlabeled samples for annotation, thereby optimizing resource allocation. However, many existing active learning frameworks lack explicit mechanisms to address domain shifts—systematic differences in data distributions between source and target domains—limiting their efficacy in realistic cross-domain scenarios. Simultaneously, some active domain adaptation (ADA) methods, which aim to bridge domain gaps through active querying, often rely on complex query functions that can suffer from overfitting, especially when training data is scarce. In response, we propose a streamlined yet effective ADA framework called Select-by-Distinctive-Margin (SDM). SDM integrates a maximum margin loss to encourage decision boundaries that distinguish domain-invariant features and a margin-based sampling strategy to prioritize uncertain yet informative data points. Theoretical analysis reveals that SDM operates similarly to a Support Vector Machine (SVM), identifying and retaining hard examples near decision boundaries, which are critical for learning robust domain-bridging representations. To further enhance flexibility, we introduce two variants of SDM: the first dynamically adjusts the gradient influence of the margin loss, enabling more stable training, while the second refines the sampling process by incorporating gradient direction to better capture informative features. Empirical evaluations across standard active learning benchmarks demonstrate that SDM achieves competitive performance with strong scalability in data selection, making it a practical solution for real-world domain adaptation challenges. Code for implementing the proposed methods is available at [URL].

In this paper, we incorporate CGF with mutation testing to address the aforementioned challenges.
Mutation testing is a fault-based testing technique which realises the idea of using mutants (buggy versions mutated from the PUT) to support testing activities <cit.>.
We exploit mutation testing to identify bug-revealing inputs generated by fuzzers, and use mutation scores as feedback to guide fuzzing towards detecting bugs.
Our approach comprises two stages: (1) in initialization stage, we create mutants and make preparations for fuzzing, and (2) in fuzzing stage, we generate inputs and execute them against PUT and mutants.
We compute mutation scores for every generated test inputs, and preserve bug-revealing inputs according to the computed mutation scores.
new_text: We integrate CGF with mutation testing to address these challenges. Mutation testing is a fault-based testing technique that employs mutants—buggy versions of the PUT—<cit.>. By using mutation testing, we identify bug-revealing inputs generated by fuzzers and use mutation scores as feedback to guide fuzzing toward bug detection. The approach has two stages: (1) during initialization, we create mutants and prepare for fuzzing, and (2) during fuzzing, we generate and execute inputs on the PUT and mutants. Mutation scores are computed for each test input, and bug-revealing inputs are retained based on these scores.

old_text: The online social platforms, like Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn and WeChat, have grown really fast in last decade and have been one of the most effective platforms for people to communicate and share information with each other. Due to the “word of mouth” effects, information usually can spread rapidly on these social media platforms. Therefore, it is important to study the mechanisms driving the information diffusion and quantify the consequence of information spread. A lot of efforts have been focused on this problem to help us better understand and achieve higher performance in viral marketing and advertising. On the other hand, the development of neural networks has blossomed in the last few years, leading to a large number of graph representation learning (GRL) models. Compared with traditional models, GRL methods are often shown to be more effective. In this paper, we present a comprehensive review for recent works leveraging GRL methods for popularity prediction problem, and categorize related literatures into two big classes, according to their mainly used model and techniques: embedding-based methods and deep learning methods. Deep learning method is further classifed into six small classes: convolutional neural networks, graph convolutional networks, graph attention networks, graph neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and reinforcement learning. We compare the performance of these different models and discuss their strengths and limitations. Finally, we outline the challenges and future chances for popularity prediction problem.
new_text: Online social platforms, such as Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, and WeChat, have grown rapidly in the last decade and have become one of the most effective platforms for people to communicate and share information with one another. Due to word-of-mouth effects, information tends to spread rapidly on these social media platforms. Therefore, it is important to study the mechanisms driving information diffusion and quantify the impact of information spread. Substantial efforts have focused on this problem to help us better understand and achieve higher performance in viral marketing and advertising. On the other hand, the development of neural networks has advanced significantly in the last few years, resulting in a large number of graph representation learning (GRL) models. Compared with traditional models, GRL methods have been shown to be more effective. In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of recent works leveraging GRL methods for the popularity prediction problem, and categorize related literature into two major classes based on the primary models and techniques they employ: embedding-based methods and deep learning methods. Deep learning methods are further classified into six categories: convolutional neural networks, graph convolutional networks, graph attention networks, graph neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and reinforcement learning. We compare the performance of these different models and discuss their strengths and limitations. Finally, we outline the challenges and future opportunities for the popularity prediction problem.

new_text: To create a structured representation of disease-disease associations, we constructed a knowledge graph by integrating data from the Diseases and MedScape repositories. These repositories consolidate evidence from diverse sources, including automated text mining of biomedical literature, manually curated resources, cancer mutation databases, and genome-wide association studies (GWAS). This integration allows the knowledge graph to capture a comprehensive range of clinically relevant disease relationships. The graph comprises 9,182 disease concepts, each uniquely identified using concept unique identifiers (CUIs) from the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS), a standardized framework for medical terminology. These concepts are connected through three distinct relationship types: “may cause” (MC), “may be caused by” (MBC), and “differential diagnosis” (DDx). The “may cause” relationship indicates a directional link where one disease potentially leads to another, while the “may be caused by” relationship is its inverse, reflecting a reverse causal possibility. In contrast, the “differential diagnosis” relationship is symmetric, meaning if disease A is associated with disease B, the reverse association is also valid. Relationships that do not fit these categories are labeled as “not available” (NA). For further details on dataset statistics, see <cit.> and Table <ref>.

old_text: The simplest backbone model applicable to weighted networks is the global threshold. The global threshold model preserves all edges whose weight exceeds a specified threshold. It can be classified as a `global' model because it applies the same criteria to all edges in the network, and can be classified as a `structural' model because it uses only structural information (here, the edges' weights). While it can be appealing for its simplicity, the global threshold model can be problematic when applied to networks in which the edge weights follow a long-tailed distribution (e.g., mostly weak edges, a few strong edges) and networks in which different parts of the network have different characteristic edge weights (e.g., multi-scale networks).
new_text: The most straightforward backbone approach for weighted networks is the global threshold method. This method retains every edge with a weight above a defined threshold. It is considered a `global' model since it applies uniform criteria across all edges in the network, and a `structural' model as it relies solely on structural data (here, the edges' weights). Although its simplicity is advantageous, the global threshold method may lead to challenges when used in networks with long-tailed edge weight distributions (e.g., predominantly weak edges with a few strong ones) or in networks where different regions have varying edge weight characteristics (e.g., multi-scale networks).

Bias in Vision-Language. Several approaches make initial steps towards measuring bias in vision-language representations. The authors of the original CLIP paper investigated manifestations of bias within their own model <cit.> by assessing the misclassification of faces by age or race with non-human and criminal categories. Given the lack of robustness in measures such as WEAT, other metrics such as ranking metrics for search and recommendation tasks <cit.> may be better suited. These works can be applied to vision-language by measuring the attribute distribution of returned images for a given text prompt.
The sparse literature on debiasing vision-language models falls into two categories: (1) dataset-level debiasing <cit.> and (2) model-level debiasing <cit.>. On the dataset side, imbalanced training data has been proposed as a point of blame <cit.> but balancing the data is not a panacea, with <cit.> finding exaggerated gender stereotypes in tasks unrelated to gender recognition, even after balancing the number of labels by gender. In large-scale, multi-modal datasets, like those used to train vision-language models, the disproportionate representation of certain genders and ethnicities in various roles can lead to misclassifications, such as overly strong associations of black people playing basketball <cit.> or certain genders and ethnicities with explicit content <cit.>. However, correcting bias at the dataset-level requires access to the original training data and retraining the model on alternative data. Even if an end-user had these resources, it may still be infeasible to capture all proxies for demographic bias <cit.>, so it is possible that the data necessary to combat bias has not been curated yet <cit.>. On model-level adjustments, <cit.> train an image captioning model to confidently predict gender when there is gender evidence, and be cautious in its absence. Specifically, they improve the captioning model by attending to the right visual evidence, such as the person in the image as opposed to the background. However, retraining the model with costly masked supervision is beyond the scope of this work.

Bias in Vision-Language. Several approaches have made initial strides in measuring bias in vision-language representations. The authors of the original CLIP paper investigated manifestations of bias within their model <cit.> by analyzing how age and race-based misclassifications linked faces to non-human or criminal categories. Given WEAT’s lack of robustness, ranking metrics used in search and recommendation tasks <cit.> may offer a more suitable alternative. These methods can assess bias in vision-language systems by evaluating the distribution of returned images for a given text prompt.  

The limited literature on debiasing vision-language models divides into two categories: (1) dataset-level debiasing <cit.> and (2) model-level debiasing <cit.>. Dataset-level approaches often attribute bias to imbalanced training data <cit.>, though balancing data is not a guaranteed solution. Studies <cit.> reveal that exaggerated gender stereotypes can persist in unrelated tasks even after balancing labels by gender. In large-scale, multimodal datasets used for vision-language models, disproportionate representation of certain genders and ethnicities in specific roles—such as strong associations between Black individuals and basketball <cit.> or specific genders/ethnicities and explicit content <cit.>—can lead to biased classifications. Correcting these biases at the dataset level requires access to original training data and retraining on revised datasets. Even with these resources, capturing all proxies for demographic bias remains challenging <cit.>, as critical data to address biases may not yet have been curated <cit.>.  

Model-level adjustments focus on refining internal representations to reduce bias. For example, one approach <cit.> trains an image captioning model to confidently predict gender when visual evidence (e.g., a person in an image) supports it, while exercising caution in its absence. This method improves performance by directing attention to salient visual elements, such as the subject rather than background. However, the approach requires retraining using costly masked supervision, which is beyond the scope of this work.

new_text: Notation. We adopt the notation from the MPT paper as follows: a probability space is denoted by (Ω, Σ, P), where Ω is the sample space, Σ is the σ-algebra, and P is the probability measure. A parametric model parameterized by θ in an arbitrary space is denoted by M_θ ∈ Σ, which is an element of the σ-algebra Σ. Random variables are represented using uppercase letters (e.g., X, Y), and the range of a random variable is denoted by R(·). We define S(P) as shorthand for the support of the probability measure P, where x ∈ S(P) indicates outcomes of X with nonzero probability. For a mapping f whose domain and range are vector spaces, the y-th entry of the output vector is denoted as f(x)[y].

new_text: Our study examined the impact of varying student model word error rate (WER) performance on the ultimate results. Table <ref> presents a comparison of neural self-training (NST) initialized with three distinct student models. `B1` served as a weaker baseline due to training solely on out-of-domain `YT` data. In contrast, `B0` was trained on in-domain `MD` data with human annotations, while `E1` leveraged JUST hydra for training. Across all experiments, NST was executed using 100% pseudo-labeled data. As detailed in Table <ref>, all models achieved identical final performance metrics of 4.1% and 2.1%, regardless of their initial student model configuration. This suggests that, when paired with a robust teacher model, NST exhibits minimal sensitivity to the quality of the starting student. Instead, the critical factor lies in employing advanced techniques such as self-supervised learning to develop a high-performance teacher model. Once a reliable teacher is established, NST with pseudo labels alone is sufficient to attain optimal results.

old_text: Humans excel at using language to convey information efficiently in context. A speaker does not have to communicate every detail. Rather, a listener can infer the intended meaning of an utterance by assuming that it contains only relevant information. This idea was first explicitly formulated by grice as the Maxim of Relation: “I expect a partner’s contribution to be appropriate to immediate needs at each stage of the transaction”. An illustration of this mechanism can be given in the form of a simple referential context. In a scene with a red circle and a green triangle, “circle” is enough information to identify the referent, whereas more complex scenes may require the speaker to name both object attributes—shape and color—to allow for an unambiguous interpretation. The Maxim of Relation requires a hierarchical reference system, that allows the selection of the most appropriate level of specificity for a given context.
new_text: Human communication relies on efficient information transmission through contextual inference, enabling speakers to omit superfluous details. Listeners typically assume that utterances contain only pertinent information, allowing them to deduce intended meanings. Grice introduced this principle as the Maxim of Relation, which posits that “I expect a partner’s contribution to be appropriate to immediate needs at each stage of the transaction” (Grice). For example, in a referential context featuring a red circle and a green triangle, the term “circle” alone suffices to identify the intended object. However, more intricate scenarios may necessitate specifying both attributes (e.g., shape and color) to ensure clarity. This principle underscores the need for a hierarchical reference system that dynamically selects the most suitable level of specificity based on contextual demands.

**Symbol redundancy.**
We develop this metric to approximate whether agents repeat information about attribute values in their messages. It assumes that each attribute value, a_v (e.g a=color, a_v=red), is encoded by a specific symbol and counts how often that symbol is repeated given that a_v is being encoded. The preferred symbol for each attribute value is defined s^a_v _s ℐ(a_v, s), where we code for each message whether s occurs at least once (the position of s is irrelevant). Symbol redundancy is defined as the average number of occurrences of s^a_v per message given that a_v is part of the target concept.

In natural language, referencing objects at different levels of specificity is a fundamental pragmatic mechanism for efficient communication in context.
We develop a novel communication game, the hierarchical reference game, to study the emergence of such reference systems in artificial agents. We consider a simplified world, in which concepts are abstractions over a set of primitive attributes (e.g., color, style, shape).
Depending on how many attributes are combined, concepts are more general (“circle”) or more specific (“red dotted circle”). Based on the context, the agents have to communicate at different levels of this hierarchy. Our results show, that the agents learn to play the game successfully
and can even generalize to novel concepts. To achieve abstraction, they use implicit (omitting irrelevant information) and explicit (indicating that attributes are irrelevant) strategies.
In addition, the compositional structure underlying the concept hierarchy is reflected in the emergent protocols, indicating that the need to develop hierarchical reference systems supports the emergence of compositionality.
new_text: In natural language, referencing objects at varying levels of specificity is a fundamental pragmatic mechanism for efficient contextual communication. We develop a novel communication game, the hierarchical reference game, to study the emergence of such reference systems in artificial agents. Concepts in our simplified world are abstractions over primitive attributes (e.g., color, style, shape), varying in generality (“circle”) or specificity (“red dotted circle”) based on combined attributes. Agents must communicate at different hierarchy levels depending on context. Our results show that the agents successfully learn to play the game and generalize to novel concepts, using implicit strategies (omitting irrelevant information) and explicit strategies (indicating irrelevant attributes) for abstraction. Additionally, the compositional structure of the concept hierarchy is reflected in emergent protocols, suggesting that hierarchical reference systems drive compositional emergence.

`BBT` (season 1, episodes 1 to 6) and `Buffy` (season 5, episodes 1 to 6) are challenging video face identification/clustering datasets. They are generated based on the videos of the sitcoms
The Big Bang Theory and
Buffy the Vampire Slayer on small cast lists, for BBT: 5 main casts, and for Buffy: 6 main casts. The data comprises of detected faces in video frames represented by a trained (on the VGG-Face dataset) ResNet-50 model. BBT has a total of 199346 frames and Buffy has 206254 frames. The extracted ResNet-50 feature vectors are 2048 dimensional. The data for BBT and Buffy are provided by <cit.>. Since the feature vectors are obtained from a trained CNN model on face dataset, one should expect to see 5 main clusters (for BBT) and 6 clusters (for Buffy) in the embedding space.
new_text: The BBT (The Big Bang Theory, season 1, episodes 1–6) and Buffy (Buffy the Vampire Slayer, season 5, episodes 1–6) datasets are widely recognized as benchmarks for evaluating video face identification and clustering algorithms. These datasets are specifically designed to challenge systems by leveraging the visual and contextual complexity of television sitcoms, where lighting, camera angles, and occlusions can complicate face detection. The creation of these datasets begins with the full-length videos of the respective shows, from which faces are automatically detected and represented as high-dimensional feature vectors. A pre-trained ResNet-50 model, originally trained on the VGG-Face dataset, is used to encode facial features into 2048-dimensional embeddings. This choice of model ensures that the feature representations are robust to variations in facial expressions and partial occlusions, as the VGG-Face dataset itself includes diverse facial images. The BBT dataset includes 199,346 video frames, while Buffy contains 206,254 frames, with each frame potentially containing faces of the main casts—5 for BBT and 6 for Buffy. Since the datasets restrict attention to small, well-defined cast lists, they provide a controlled yet realistic scenario for testing clustering algorithms: ideal performance would group face embeddings into 5 or 6 distinct clusters, corresponding to each main character. The data, provided by [cit.], is valuable for assessing how effectively algorithms can map visual data into semantically meaningful clusters when the number of expected groupings is known a priori.

old_text: In this paper, the use of personas comes full circle. Hand-designed utility functions steer artificial agents to behave in a specific way. These agents are then used to classify human playtraces with a ground truth label using Action Agreement Ratios (AAR) <cit.>. Though accurate, AAR calculations can be expensive for long playtraces. Often times in industry, game studios have hundreds to thousands of trace telemetry datapoints streaming in by the hour. For large companies this can be even greater. For example, King, the developer of Candy Crush Saga[[URL]], reports a daily average of 13 million active players[[URL]]. For large or streaming datasets, calculating AAR can be an incredibly expensive computational challenge, even with parallelization. Therefore, we propose that a mechanic frequency vector can be used in lieu of AAR to rapidly classify unseen playtraces with an acceptable level of accuracy. To prove this, we train classifiers on human playtrace data using AAR labels, and infer on a testing set of more human playtraces using AAR labels. For comparison, we also train a classifier on the actual playtrace (sequence of game states) and compare its results to the ones trained on the mechanic frequency vector.
new_text: In this paper, we revisit the concept of personas through a computational lens, demonstrating how AI-driven methods can bridge design and data analysis. Specifically, we develop artificial agents guided by hand-designed utility functions—mathematical rules that dictate behavior priorities—to simulate player decision-making in specific ways. These agents serve a critical analytical role: by generating synthetic playtraces (sequences of in-game actions) with defined behavioral "ground truth," they enable the calculation of Action Agreement Ratios (AAR), a metric that quantifies how closely real human playtraces align with specific agent behaviors <cit.>. While AAR provides precise classification of player behavior, its computational cost grows significantly with playtrace length, creating scalability issues. This limitation becomes especially acute in modern game development, where major studios process massive volumes of real-time telemetry data. For instance, game companies like King (developer of *Candy Crush Saga*) receive 13 million active play sessions daily, each generating continuous streams of gameplay data. At this scale, even parallelized AAR calculations become impractical. To address this challenge, we propose a computationally efficient alternative: using mechanic frequency vectors—numerical representations of how often core gameplay mechanics occur in a trace—to classify player behavior. Our evaluation compares three approaches: (1) classifiers trained on AAR-labeled data, (2) classifiers trained directly on raw playtrace sequences, and (3) classifiers trained on mechanic frequency vectors. By testing all methods on human-labeled playtraces, we assess how well these alternatives maintain accuracy while reducing computational demands.

Although self-attention <cit.> is a basic yet powerful component in the Transformer architecture, it is inefficient to some extent. As each input element has to attend to all n elements, the overall complexity scales as 𝒪(n^2). In a document, however, a semantic region relies more heavily on its surrounding context, which is already a robust inductive bias. However, previous works <cit.> apply the Transformer to learn this bias from scratch during the pre-training phase, which increases the learning cost. Therefore, how to leverage this prior knowledge to "lighten up" the pre-training model will be meaningful. In our work, we inject the graph structure in a document into the attention mechanism to form the graph attention layer instead of the original Transformer architecture to mitigate this problem.

Considering that the AVA-ActiveSpeaker dataset <cit.> does not include identity meta-data, we approximate the sampling of different identities by selecting visual data from concurrent tracklets[Since tracklets include a single face and were manually curated, it is guaranteed that two tracklets that overlap in time belong to different identities. new_text: **Visual contrastive loss.** We complement L_s with a contrastive loss (L_c) on video data. As shown in Figure <ref>, this loss enforces feature similarity for video nodes of the same person and encourages feature dissimilarity between non-matching identities. Since the AVA-ActiveSpeaker dataset <cit.> lacks identity metadata, we approximate identity sampling using concurrent tracklets: manually curated tracklets with single faces ensure that temporally overlapping tracklets belong to different identities. We tackle both challenges based on fusing 3D and 2D weak semantic information using our dual semantic fields.
We demonstrate that noisy 2D semantic predictions can be leveraged to improve the underlying geometry when applied to a fixed semantic field determined by the 3D bounding primitives. A comparison between predictions and simulation outcomes reveals a general agreement, but with a systematic difference in steep downhill sections. This is most notably seen for terrain 11, with regions of low locomotion for the model but not for the simulations.
This can be due to the model overestimating locomotion in steep downhill terrain.

new_text: A comparison of predicted and simulated locomotion reveals broad consistency overall, though notable discrepancies emerge in steep downhill sections. Specifically, the model consistently overestimates locomotion performance in such terrains, a pattern most clearly observed in terrain 11, where the model predicts low locomotion capability while simulations show normal or higher performance. This suggests the model may not fully account for real-world dynamics in these conditions. One contributing factor is the vehicle’s 1-second time window for accelerating before being reset (respawned), which limits its ability to build sustained momentum. Additionally, this short observation period prevents the vehicle from experiencing a potential drop in locomotion that could occur if allowed to continue operating beyond the 1-second window—such as when overspeeding leads to instability. These time constraints, though critical for simulation design, likely reduce the model’s accuracy by omitting longer-term effects of momentum and velocity regulation in steep downhill scenarios.

It first assigns each object to all pyramid levels P_3, P_4, P_5 and calculates loss_l for each level P_l. l=3,4,5. Then, the level that produces the minimal loss is converted to a one-hot vector, i.e., (1,0,0) if the minimal loss is from P_3; and (0,1,0) if it is from P_4, and so on. The vector is used as the ground-truth to train an auxiliary network that simultaneously predicts a vector (F_3, F_4, F_5). Each element F_l is a down-weighting factor for loss_l. In our context, precision reflects the ability of the classifier to correctly predict a given intent out of the predictions made, which, in turn translates to the ability of the dialog system to respond with the correct answer.
A high recall reflects the ability of the intent classifier to ideally predict (realistically, as many as possible) the correct intent for all the test examples associated with that intent.
The quality of the classification hence depends on that of the paraphrasing component, whether it be NMT- or LM-based.
new_text: To evaluate dialog system performance, we measure intent classification effectiveness using macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score. Micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score are reported (which are equivalent since each sample is assigned to a single class). Precision measures the classifier’s accuracy in predicting a given intent, directly impacting the dialog system’s ability to provide correct responses. High recall indicates the classifier’s effectiveness in identifying as many test examples of a given intent as possible. Classification quality depends on the paraphrasing component’s effectiveness, whether NMT- or LM-based.

Datasets aspects. The difficulty and complexity of molecular datasets can largely be divided into four aspects: chemical diversity, system size, dataset size, and domain shift. Chemical diversity (number of atom types or interacting pairs) and system size (number of independent atoms) determine the data's complexity and thus the expressive power a model needs to fit this data. The dataset size determines the amount of data from which the model can learn. Note that a large dataset might still need a very sample-efficient model if the underlying data is very complex and diverse. Finally, we look at the test set's domain shift to determine its difficulty. The learning task might be significantly easier than expected if the test set is very similar to the training set.
Note that many dataset aspects are not covered by these four properties, such as the method used for calculating the molecular data or the types of systems. OC20 has multiple details that fall into this category: It consists of periodic systems of a bulk material with an adsorbate on its surface, and has a canonical z-axis and orientation. These details also affect the importance of modeling choices, such as rotation invariance <cit.>. We chose to focus on the above four properties since they are easy to quantify, apply to every dataset, and have a large effect by themselves.
new_text: Dataset aspects. The difficulty and complexity of molecular datasets can largely be categorized into four aspects: chemical diversity, system size, dataset size, and domain shift. Chemical diversity (e.g., number of atom types or interacting pairs) and system size (e.g., number of independent atoms) determine the data's complexity and thus the expressive power required by a model to fit this data. Dataset size refers to the volume of data available for the model to learn from. Note that a large dataset may still require a highly sample-efficient model if the underlying data is highly complex and diverse. Finally, the test set's domain shift determines its difficulty. The learning task may prove significantly easier than expected if the test set closely resembles the training set. Note that many dataset aspects are not captured by these four properties, such as the methodology used for calculating molecular data or the system types. The OC20 dataset includes several such details: it comprises periodic systems of a bulk material with an adsorbate on its surface and features a canonical z-axis and orientation. These details influence the importance of modeling decisions, such as rotation invariance <cit>. We chose to focus on the above four properties since they are easily quantifiable, apply universally to all datasets, and exert a significant influence independently.

Tracking continues, and reinforces power of gatekeepers and opacity of mobile data ecosystem.
Our findings suggest that tracking companies, especially larger ones with access to large troves of first party, still track users behind the scenes.
They can do this through a range of methods, including using IP addresses to link installation-specific IDs across apps and through the sign-in functionality provided by individual apps (e.g. Google or Facebook sign-in, or email address).
Especially in combination with further user and device characteristics, which our data confirmed are still widely collected by tracking companies, it would be possible to analyse user behaviour across apps and websites (i.e. fingerprinting and cohort tracking).

new_text: Tracking perpetuates power imbalances among gatekeepers and the opacity of mobile data ecosystems. Larger tracking companies with first-party data troves continue covert tracking via methods such as IP address linkage of installation-specific IDs across apps or sign-in functions (e.g., Google/Facebook/email). When combined with user/device characteristics—still widely collected—they enable cross-app/website behavioral analysis (e.g., fingerprinting, cohort tracking). The App Tracking Transparency (ATT) framework may thus entrench existing power imbalances in digital tracking.

On the other hand, the depth maps in CO3D are estimates from COLMAP's multi-view stereo (MVS) algorithm, and are incomplete. Our method requires accurate depth to project the discovered semantic correspondences into 3D space, enabling a solution for the rigid body transform between object instances (<ref>).
One approach would be to disregard those correspondences that land on an area with unknown depth. However, as the correspondences are found at the ViT patch level (8 × 8 pixels, see <ref>), we found a small number of missing areas in the per-pixel depth maps led to throwing away a disproportionate amount of correspondences.
Instead, we use a fast in-painting method based on the Navier-Stokes equations <cit.>, implemented in OpenCV, to fill missing values.
new_text: In contrast to idealized depth data, the depth maps used in CO3D are computed as probabilistic estimates via COLMAP's multi-view stereo (MVS) pipeline, which inherently results in incomplete coverage of the scene. Since our approach relies on precise depth information to project identified semantic correspondences into a 3D coordinate system—this is critical for accurately estimating the rigid body transformation between object instances (see <ref>—this incompleteness poses a significant challenge. A straightforward solution would involve discarding correspondences that intersect regions where depth estimates are missing. However, this approach proves problematic: because semantic correspondences are detected at the scale of Vision Transformer (ViT) patches (8 × 8 pixels, as detailed in <ref>), even minor gaps in per-pixel depth data can result in discarding a large proportion of useful correspondences. To address this, we implement a computationally efficient in-painting strategy that leverages the Navier-Stokes equations (<cit.>). This method, available in OpenCV, effectively interpolates missing depth values by propagating known depth information across the surface, preserving geometric consistency while recovering sufficient data to maintain the integrity of our correspondence-based 3D reconstruction.
