Video Panoptic Segmentation. Video Panoptic Segmentation (VPS) <cit.> requires generating the instance tracking IDs along with panoptic segmentation results across video clips. Kim et al <cit.> use Cityscapes video sequences for 6 frames out of each short 30 frame clip and mainly focus on short-term tracks. They proposed Video Panoptic Quality (VPQ) for evaluation. Several works <cit.> are proposed to solve this task respectively. VIP-Deeplab <cit.> extends the Panoptic-Deeplab <cit.> with next frame center map prediction for DVPS task <cit.>. Then they use such predicted maps for offline tracking. Since Cityscapes VPS only contains short term clips, to allow long term VPS, STEP dataset <cit.> is proposed. They propose a new metric named Segmentation and Tracking Quality (STQ) that decouples the segmentation and tracking error. They also provide several baselines for reference. Our Video K-Net is verified to work well on both short- and long-term videos.
new_text: Video Panoptic Segmentation (VPS) <cit.> involves assigning instance-level tracking identifiers alongside panoptic segmentation outputs across sequential video frames. Kim et al. <cit.> leverage 6-frame samples from each 30-frame Cityscapes clip, prioritizing short-term tracking, and introduce the Video Panoptic Quality (VPQ) metric for evaluation. Multiple approaches <cit.> have since been developed to address this task. VIP-Deeplab <cit.> expands upon Panoptic-Deeplab <cit.> by integrating next-frame center map prediction for Dynamic VPS (DVPS) <cit.>, enabling offline tracking via these predictions. Given that Cityscapes VPS is limited to short clips, the STEP dataset <cit.> was introduced to support long-term VPS analysis. This dataset defines the Segmentation and Tracking Quality (STQ) metric, which separates segmentation and tracking error assessments, and includes baseline models for comparison. Our Video K-Net architecture achieves robust performance on both short- and long-term video sequences.

Panoptic Segmentation.
The goal of this task is to unify the semantic segmentation and instance segmentation into one framework with a single metric named Panoptic Quality (PQ) <cit.>. Since then, lots of works <cit.> have been proposed to solve this task with various approaches. However, most methods separate thing and stuff segmentation as individual tasks. Recently, starting from DETR <cit.>, query based approaches <cit.> unify both things and stuff segmentation as a set prediction problem. In particular, K-Net <cit.> unify segmentation tasks in the view of dot product between kernel and feature maps.
new_text: Panoptic segmentation unifies semantic and instance segmentation within a single framework measured by Panoptic Quality (PQ) <cit.>. Numerous approaches <cit.> have since been proposed, but most treat thing and stuff segmentation as separate tasks. Recently, DETR-based <cit.> query-based approaches <cit.> have unified both segmentation aspects as a set prediction problem. K-Net <cit.> unifies segmentation tasks by framing them through the dot product between kernel and feature maps.

Algorithm <ref> gives a general view of cascade propagation models: set A consists of all the activated nodes, and is initially equal to the seed set S. At each time step, recently activated source nodes try to activate their neighbours independently. If an activation fails, it is never retried (a destination node is assumed to have made its decision). At each time step, recently activated source nodes independently attempt to activate their neighbors. If an activation fails, it is not retried (the destination node is assumed to have made its decision). Successful activations allow propagation to continue, which terminates when no new nodes are activated in a time step.

old_text: Companies use ERP(Enterprise Resource Planning) system to integrate and manage their main business processes. The system receives several essential information from different parts of business such as inventory information. To update inventory information, workers depend on receiving and forwarding based management and manual inventory counting. In other words, workers record the information – such as type of stock, quantity, and date – whenever the stock comes in or out of the warehouse. In order to ensure accurate inventory, also, workers have to manually count the number of inventories regularly. For small warehouses where only a few types of inventories are treated, handwork can be effective. For usual cases, however, managing inventories by hand is very tedious and inefficient work. Especially for small pieces, such as bolts and nuts, it is nearly impossible to count accurately. Also, Workers get easily tired, so human errors can occur frequently. That makes information in the ERP system and real inventory count different.
new_text: Companies use ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) systems to integrate and manage core business processes, including inventory data. Inventory updates rely on receiving-forwarding based management and manual counting, where workers record stock type, quantity, and date during warehouse transactions. Manual inventory counting is also required regularly to ensure accuracy. Handwork remains effective only in small warehouses with limited inventory types; for larger operations, manual management becomes tedious and inefficient, particularly for small items like bolts and nuts, where accurate counting is nearly impossible. Worker fatigue further increases human error rates, creating persistent discrepancies between ERP system data and actual inventory counts.

To compute the latent network structure, Trust2Vec generates random walks by navigating the network
through random steps. The logic behind this approach is that the more we repeat these random walks
from the same starting device with a fixed length, the more likely the walks will include nodes that
are similar in terms of network proximity, either first-order proximity or second-order proximity
nodes. Let W_d_i(l) denotes the random walk starting from device d_i with a walk length l. A
random walk W_d_i(l) is a stochastic process composed of a chain of random variables
W_d_i(l)={w^1_d_i,w^2_d_i,… ,w^l_d_i}, where w^n_d_i is
the neighbor device that is randomly chosen among w^n-1_d_i neighbors. Relying on random
walks to compute the latent network structure is desirable for two reasons. Firstly, the
computations of the random walks can be distributed among edge devices, hence the process is
distributed and can be performed offline without relying on any remote cloud or server. Secondly, as
the random walks are limited with walk length l, the newly added trust relationships among devices
can be easily accommodated by regenerating random walks only for the updated trust relationships,
without the need to recompute the random walks for the whole graph. To navigate the trust
relationships among devices, Trust2Vec estimates the likelihood of observing a series of short
random walks by adapting the same approach in natural language modeling, where the goal is to
estimate the likelihood of a sentence being present in a corpus. The analogy here is to calculate the trust walk TW that starts from source device d_o, and estimate the probability of arriving at destination device d_d given the previously navigated devices through a random walk of length l:
new_text: Trust2Vec computes the latent network structure by employing random walks to traverse the network via randomized steps. The underlying principle is that repeated execution of these walks from a given device d_i with a fixed length l increases the probability of sampling nodes with high network proximity, encompassing both first-order and second-order relationships. Formally, let W_d_i(l) denote a random walk initiating at device d_i with length l; this is defined as a stochastic process W_d_i(l) = {w^1_d_i, w^2_d_i, ..., w^l_d_i}, where each term w^n_d_i represents a randomly selected neighbor from w^n-1_d_i’s adjacent nodes. Leveraging random walks for latent structure inference offers two key advantages: first, the computation can be distributed across edge devices, enabling offline execution without reliance on cloud infrastructure; second, constraints on walk length l allow for efficient updates—new trust relationships necessitate only recomputation of walks involving those specific interactions rather than global recomputation. To model trust dynamics, Trust2Vec adapts methodologies from natural language modeling to estimate the probability of generating a trust walk TW starting at source device d_o and terminating at destination device d_d. This involves calculating the likelihood of observing a sequence of devices along a random walk of length l, mirroring the task of predicting sentence probability in a text corpus.

It follows the dual-stream architecture, that is, one visual stream and one textual stream.
The visual stream takes a cropped vehicle image, a context image and a foreground motion map as input, and then extracts their features by three individual image encoders.

The textual stream encodes a global text, three local texts, and a prompt separately using five tied text encoders. We sample edges which requires us to extend and strengthen the concept of cut sparsifiers introduced in the seminal work of <cit.> and <cit.> to the motif setting. The task of adapting the importance sampling framework common to efficient graph sparsification algorithms to the motif setting turns out to be nontrivial due to the fact that cut sizes in a random subgraph of G depend non-linearly on the sampled edges. To overcome this, we adopt the viewpoint of hypergraph sparsification to define edge sampling probabilities which are derived from the strong connectivity values of a hypergraph whose hyperedges represent motif instances. new_text: We combine graph and hypergraph sparsification techniques by sampling edges and extending cut sparsifiers from <cit.> and <cit.> to the motif setting. Adapting importance sampling to this context is nontrivial because cut sizes in random subgraphs depend nonlinearly on sampled edges. To address this, we define edge sampling probabilities using hypergraph sparsification principles, where hyperedges represent motif instances and sampling weights derive from the hypergraph’s strong connectivity values. An iterative sparsification primitive, synthesizing both frameworks, reduces G’s edge count to nearly linear.

old_text: The subgraph (g) and (f) in Figure <ref> are the waveform and spectrogram after the masking music and the adversarial samples are synthesized. From the waveform diagram, the synthesized sample is obviously different from the confrontation sample of unmasked music. But the effect from the spectrogram is similar to drawing a few horizontal lines on the picture. From the experience of confrontation attacks in the field of image recognition, although such a line may cause model misjudgment, it does not introduce other phoneme characteristics, and the introduced disturbance is not a gradient information-based confrontation disturbance generated by the algorithm. , Therefore, it is not easy to cause the effect of the adversarial attack and affect the migration of the adversarial sample itself. As for the ASR system that converts time-domain signals into frequency-domain signals for feature extraction, the audio recognition problem has been transformed into an image recognition problem. Therefore, although masking music is more noticeable in human auditory perception, it only occupies a small part of the characteristics in the frequency domain signal. This is also the reason why our masking music can improve the masking effect while having less impact on migration attacks.
new_text: The subgraphs (g) and (f) in Figure <ref> depict the waveform and spectrogram of the synthesized audio after applying masking music and generating adversarial samples. In the waveform visualization, the synthesized sample exhibits clear deviations from the unmasked confrontation sample, suggesting structural differences introduced by the masking process. However, the spectrogram reveals a different dynamic: the adversarial perturbations manifest as faint horizontal lines across the frequency-time representation. These patterns resemble the adversarial noise patterns observed in image recognition tasks, where small, localized modifications can deceive models. Yet, in this audio context, such horizontal lines do not introduce phoneme-like acoustic features or leverage gradient-based optimization (as seen in traditional adversarial attacks). Instead, they represent non-gradient disturbances that lack the structural specificity required to trigger effective model misclassification. This distinction is critical: for adversarial attacks to propagate or migrate to other models, they typically rely on gradient-guided perturbations that align with the model’s decision boundaries. Since masking music introduces disturbances unrelated to these boundaries, it limits the adversarial samples’ ability to generalize or transfer. Furthermore, automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems typically convert time-domain audio signals into frequency-domain representations (spectrograms) for feature extraction, effectively transforming the recognition task into a form of image analysis. In this framework, masking music—while perceptible to humans in the time domain—occupies a minimal portion of the frequency-domain features critical for model decision-making. This dual property—strong masking in the time domain and weak disruption in the frequency domain—explains why the proposed masking music enhances auditory concealment while reducing the risk of enabling adversarial attack propagation.

A major challenge in future object prediction is that the motion of dynamic objects is highly correlated with the ego-motion of the camera. Provident detection of other road users at night has the potential
for increasing road safety. For this purpose, humans intuitively use
visual cues, such as light cones and light reflections emitted by
other road users to be able to react to oncoming traffic at an early
stage. This behavior can be imitated by computer vision methods by
predicting the appearance of vehicles based on emitted light reflections
caused by the vehicle's headlights. Since current object detection
algorithms are mainly based on detecting directly visible objects
annotated via bounding boxes, the detection and annotation of light
reflections without sharp boundaries is challenging. For this reason,
the extensive open-source dataset PVDN (Provident Vehicle Detection
at Night) was published, which includes traffic scenarios at night
with light reflections annotated via keypoints. In this paper, we
explore the potential of saliency-based approaches to create different
object representations based on the visual saliency and sparse keypoint
annotations of the PVDN dataset. For that, we extend the general idea
of Boolean map saliency towards a context-aware approach by taking
into consideration sparse keypoint annotations by humans. We show
that this approach allows for an automated derivation of different
object representations, such as binary maps or bounding boxes so that
detection models can be trained on different annotation variants and
the problem of providently detecting vehicles at night can be tackled
from different perspectives. With that, we provide further powerful
tools and methods to study the problem of detecting vehicles at night
before they are actually visible.
new_text: Provident detection of other road users at night enhances road safety by enabling early reaction to oncoming traffic. Humans intuitively detect oncoming traffic using visual cues like light cones and reflections from vehicle headlights. Similarly, computer vision methods can predict vehicle presence via emitted light reflections. However, current object detection algorithms primarily rely on bounding boxes for directly visible objects, making annotation of undefined light reflections challenging. To address this, the open-source PVDN (Provident Vehicle Detection at Night) dataset was released, containing nighttime traffic scenarios with light reflections annotated via keypoints. This study investigates saliency-based approaches to generate object representations from PVDN’s sparse keypoint annotations and visual saliency. We extend Boolean map saliency to a context-aware method by integrating human-sourced keypoint annotations. This approach automates generation of object representations, including binary maps and bounding boxes, enabling detection models to train on diverse annotation variants. It provides tools to tackle nighttime vehicle detection from multiple perspectives, improving pre-visibility detection capabilities.

Our first decision criterion is the F-score since we want to capture
as many keypoints as possible. Here, the recall can be used equivalently,
as precision is always 1.0. This is caused by the fact that bounding
boxes generated with our saliency method cannot be false positive
since bounding boxes are only created if there is a keypoint annotated.
The second decision criterion then is the bounding-box metric, since

In our evaluation, we consider all possible combinations of bounding boxes derived from each keypoint annotation. For each combination, we calculate both the F-score—a measure combining precision and recall—and the bounding-box metric introduced by Saralajew et al. <cit.>. Our primary decision criterion is the F-score because our goal is to maximize the detection of keypoint-related information. Specifically, since our saliency method generates bounding boxes *only* in locations where a keypoint is explicitly annotated, there are no false positives in the bounding-box detection. This means precision is inherently 1.0, making the F-score effectively equivalent to recall. Thus, optimizing the F-score in this context directly aligns with maximizing the number of correctly identified keypoint regions. 

The second criterion we apply is the bounding-box metric. After identifying combinations with the highest F-scores, we further select the combination with the highest metric value to ensure quality. The metric is designed to penalize overlapping bounding boxes that contain the same set of keypoints. By prioritizing combinations with higher metric scores, we favor non-overlapping bounding boxes, which is critical for avoiding redundant or conflicting annotations in the final output. This dual-criteria approach ensures both comprehensive keypoint coverage and spatially distinct bounding-box assignments.

It follows the basic structure of DETR3D, consisting of three components: (i) an image encoder, (ii) a transformer-style decoder, and (iii) object prediction heads. Given with a set of images 𝐈 = {I_1, I_2, ..., I_K}∈^H× W × 3 (captured by N surrounding cameras), Graph-DETR3D aims to predict the localization and categories of the interested bounding boxes. These images are first processed with an image encoder, including a ResNet <cit.> and a FPN <cit.>, into a set of features F with respect to L feature map levels. Then, we construct a dynamic 3D graph to extensively aggregate 2D information through our proposed dynamic graph feature aggregation module to refine the representation of object queries. Finally, the enhanced object queries are utilized to output the final prediction.

It follows the basic structure of DETR3D, consisting of three components: (i) an image encoder, (ii) a transformer-style decoder, and (iii) object prediction heads. Given a set of images 𝐈 = {I_1, I_2, ..., I_K}∈^H× W × 3 (captured by N surrounding cameras), Graph-DETR3D aims to predict the localization and categories of objects of interest. These images are first processed using an image encoder, including a ResNet <cit.> and a FPN <cit.>, into a set of features F with respect to L feature map levels. Then, we construct a dynamic 3D graph to comprehensively aggregate 2D information via our proposed dynamic graph feature aggregation module to refine the representations of object queries. Finally, the enhanced object queries are used to generate the final prediction.

new_text: In a proof of concept, we demonstrated that our saliency method generates binary masks for direct and indirect light instances, enabling semantic segmentation networks to solve provident nighttime vehicle detection as a semantic segmentation task. Current metrics like mIoU fail to address the fuzzy nature of light reflections, prompting our proposal of a metric tailored to detecting oncoming vehicles at night before direct sight. However, we acknowledge the need for further investigation into metrics that accommodate objects with undefined spatial positions and tasks permitting prediction variability. For instance, in provident vehicle detection, exact light reflection localization is unnecessary, as the goal is predicting the vehicle’s position rather than the light’s location, necessitating metrics that tolerate spatial volatility. Future work should focus on refining such metrics and developing algorithms to efficiently leverage the limited indirect light instances in the PVDN dataset for provident vehicle detection.

Why simulation?
To test our method, we need to evaluate both recommenders which interact with users (rendering static datasets of user interaction unsuitable), as well as test our evaluation metrics themselves – which are defined based on internal preferences (for which we never get ground truth in real interactions). We thus create a testing environment in which we can emulate user behavior and have access to their ground truth preferences.
Like previous work <cit.>, we simulate both a recommendation environment and human behavior. However, unlike such approaches, we use simulated human behavior for evaluation purposes only: our human model is learned exclusively from data that would be observed in a real-world RS (slates and choices), i.e. data of users (in our case the simulated users) interacting with previous RS policies – meaning our approach could be applied to real user data of this form. A fundamental advantage of testing our method in a simulated environment is that we can actually evaluate how well our model is able to recover the preferences of our “ground truth” users, giving us insights about how our methods could perform with real users.
new_text: To evaluate our method, we require interactive recommenders (static user interaction datasets are unsuitable) and must test metrics defined by internal preferences (which lack ground truth in real interactions). We therefore simulate a recommendation environment with emulated user behavior and ground truth preferences. As in prior work <cit.>, we simulate both the recommendation environment and human behavior, but use simulated behavior solely for evaluation: our human model is trained exclusively on data observable in real-world recommendation systems (slates and choices)—specifically, interactions of simulated users with prior RS policies—ensuring our approach could be applied to real user data of this form. A key advantage of simulation is the ability to evaluate how accurately our model recovers users’ ground truth preferences, providing insights into real-world performance.

Most modern recommender systems predict users' preferences with two components: user and item embedding learning, followed by the user-item interaction modeling. By utilizing the auxiliary review information accompanied with user ratings, many of the existing review-based recommendation models enriched user/item embedding learning ability with historical reviews or better modeled user-item interactions with the help of available user-item target reviews. Though significant progress has been made, we argue that current solutions for review-based recommendation suffer from two drawbacks.
First, as review-based recommendation can be naturally formed as a user-item bipartite graph with edge features from corresponding user-item reviews, how to better exploit this unique graph structure for recommendation? Second, while most current models suffer from limited user behaviors, can we exploit the unique self-supervised signals in the review-aware graph to guide two recommendation components better?
To this end, in this paper, we propose a novel Review-aware Graph Contrastive Learning  (RGCL) framework for review-based recommendation.
Specifically, we first construct a review-aware user-item graph with feature-enhanced edges from reviews, where each edge feature is composed of both the user-item rating and the corresponding review semantics.
This graph with feature-enhanced edges can help attentively learn each neighbor node weight for user and item representation learning.
After that, we design two additional contrastive learning tasks (i.e., Node Discrimination and Edge Discrimination) to provide self-supervised signals for the two components in recommendation process. Finally, extensive experiments over five benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed RGCL  compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.
new_text: Modern recommender systems typically rely on two core components: learning representations for users and items through embeddings, and modeling the interactions between them. Review-based recommendation models enhance these components by incorporating auxiliary review information alongside user ratings. Some approaches improve the ability to learn user and item embeddings by incorporating historical reviews, while others refine the modeling of user-item interactions using target reviews associated with specific interactions. Despite these advancements, we identify two critical limitations in current methods. First, reviews naturally form a user-item bipartite graph where edges contain semantic features derived from user-item interactions. However, there remains an open question of how to more effectively leverage this graph structure for recommendation. Second, many models are constrained by limited user behavior data; here, we ask whether unique self-supervised signals embedded in the review-aware graph can be utilized to better train both the embedding learning and interaction modeling components of recommendation systems. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework called Review-aware Graph Contrastive Learning (RGCL). Specifically, we construct a user-item graph where edges are augmented with review semantics—each edge includes both rating data and review text features. This enriched graph enables more precise attention-based learning of neighbor node weights during the embedding process for users and items. To further strengthen training, we design two contrastive learning tasks: Node Discrimination, which enhances representation learning for individual users and items, and Edge Discrimination, which focuses on refining the modeling of interactions. By integrating these self-supervised signals, our framework better aligns the two core recommendation components. Extensive experiments across five benchmark datasets demonstrate that RGCL outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of our approach.

Through comprehensive bilingual and multilingual experiments among 8 languages (English, Tagalog, Icelandic, Danish, Indonesian, Tamil, Greek, and Chinese), we make the following five main observations: (1) NMT performance is more robust to language imbalance than we usually expected: especially when languages share scripts, performance drops only happen when the data ratio of two languages is as disparate as 1:10^5. (2) Better performance is often achieved when languages are more balanced: we observe moderate Pearson correlations between translation performance and the degree of language balance. (3) English can “never” be starved because English tokens often appear in the “monolingual” data of other languages.
(4) In most cases, the two features (UNK rate and closeness to the character level) can hint at poor translation performances before performing the task.
(5) NMT is more sensitive to language imbalance in model training than in tokenizer training. See more observations and discussions in Section <ref>,  <ref>.
new_text: This study presents five key findings from an extensive series of bilingual and multilingual experiments spanning eight languages (English, Tagalog, Icelandic, Danish, Indonesian, Tamil, Greek, and Chinese): (1) Neural Machine Translation (NMT) demonstrates greater resilience to language imbalance than anticipated, particularly between languages sharing writing systems, with performance degradation occurring only when the data distribution ratio between two languages reaches extremes of 1:10^5. (2) Translation quality tends to improve as language balance increases, evidenced by moderate positive Pearson correlations between performance metrics and the degree of data parity. (3) English data remains highly prevalent in monolingual corpora of non-English languages, making English token starvation improbable in multilingual training scenarios. (4) Two pre-task indicators—vocabulary UNK rate and lexical similarity to character-level models—consistently predict suboptimal translation outcomes across most language pairs. (5) Language imbalance exerts a stronger negative impact during model training phases compared to tokenizer training. Further details and analysis are provided in Sections <ref>,  <ref>.

new_text: With the advancement of stereo matching algorithms and 3D sensors, the significance of point cloud data has grown substantially. Point cloud data captures three-dimensional coordinates, color, echo intensity, and other scene characteristics, naturally representing the environments we encounter daily. Compared to two-dimensional images, while point clouds lack the ability to describe surface textures, 3D point clouds directly provide target distance information, aligning more closely with our intuitive understanding of spatial relationships. Additionally, point clouds retain structural information of objects across multiple viewing angles, enabling more accurate target representation. High-quality point cloud data serves as the critical bridge between the virtual and real worlds; by processing this data, environmental perception is enhanced, and semantic interpretations enrich the information conveyed. This capability holds profound importance for fields such as computer vision, intelligent driving, remote sensing mapping, and smart cities.

**Personalized Body Models.**
Learning personalized body models given only videos of a single actor is particularly
challenging.
Most existing approaches start from estimating a parametric surface model such
as SMPL and extend it to learn specifics.
For instance, one can anchor neural features spatially by
associating each SMPL vertex with a learnable latent feature, and then either diffuse vertex features to the 3D space <cit.> or project the 3D query point to the SMPL surface for feature retrieval.
Incorrect shape estimates and missing details can then be corrected by a
subsequent neural rendering step.
As texturing improves classical approaches, neural texture mapping provides additional rendering
quality <cit.>.
Another line of work makes use of SMPL blend skinning weights as initialization for learning deformation fields <cit.>. The deformation field maps 3D points from 3D world space to canonical space, which enables learning a canonical neural body field that predicts the radiance and density for rendering as for the classical NeRF on static scenes. While the skinning weights in SMPL provide an initialization, <cit.> showed that fine-tuning the deformation fields via self-supervision helps rendering unseen poses.
However, relying on body models imposes the previously discussed limitations.
new_text:
Learning personalized body models from monocular videos of a single actor presents unique challenges due to the limited input data and the complexity of capturing human body shape and motion accurately. Most existing methods begin by estimating a parametric surface model like SMPL, which provides a coarse skeletal and mesh-based representation of the body. These models are then extended to encode subject-specific details through machine learning. For instance, one common approach involves spatially anchoring neural features by associating each vertex in the SMPL mesh with a learnable latent feature. These features can then be utilized in two complementary ways: by diffusing the vertex-based features into the surrounding 3D space <cit.>, or by projecting arbitrary 3D query points onto the SMPL surface to retrieve relevant features for processing. Errors in initial shape estimation or surface detail, such as missing textures or misaligned geometry, are typically addressed in a subsequent neural rendering stage. This step refines the model similarly to how texturing enhances classical 3D graphics, with neural texture mapping further improving rendering quality by integrating learned surface properties <cit.>.  

An alternative approach leverages SMPL’s blend skinning weights as an initialization for learning deformation fields <cit.>. These fields map 3D points from the dynamic world coordinate system to a canonical space where the body is in a standardized pose. This canonicalization allows the training of a neural radiance field (NeBF) that predicts both surface radiance and density for rendering, analogous to the NeRF framework for static scenes. While the SMPL skinning weights provide a useful prior for deformation modeling, recent work demonstrates that fine-tuning these fields using self-supervised learning improves generalization, particularly for novel poses where the body deforms beyond the initial assumptions of the parametric model <cit.>. Nevertheless, reliance on SMPL and similar parametric models inherits their limitations—such as anatomical inaccuracies or rigidity in representing non-standard body types—highlighting the need for methods that move beyond explicit mesh-based representations.

The homogeneous population structure of MFEA and GMFEA introduces randomness in crossover events across tasks, where genetic contributions from unrelated tasks may disrupt task-specific optimization due to distinct objective landscapes in point cloud registration. In MTPCR-NKS, independent populations per task ensure search progress toward minimized function values, albeit with the risk of premature convergence to local optima. This strategy still facilitates potential discovery of global optima, affirming the efficacy of task-specific populations. While MTPCR-Inter outperforms MTPCR-NKS, its improvements are limited by the absence of intra-task knowledge sharing, hindering full exploitation of inter-task synergies. Table <ref> further illustrates that MTPCR-Intra achieves high-quality solutions on most tasks, underscoring the value of auxiliary tasks as knowledge sources. new_text: We first developed and externally validated non-exercise VO_2max estimation models as a regression task using features commonly measured by wearable devices (anthropometry, resting heart rate [RHR], physical activity [PA]; see Table <ref>). Our objective was to investigate how traditional non-exercise VO_2max estimation methods could be improved through the integration of free-living physical activity data. Participant data were partitioned into independent training and test sets. The training set (n=8384, participants with baseline data only) was used for model development, while the test set (n=2675, participants with baseline and follow-up data) provided external validation. Models relying solely on anthropometry or RHR exhibited poor external validity, though performance improved when these features were combined. The highest predictive accuracy (R^2 of 0.67) was achieved by a deep neural network model integrating wearable sensor data, RHR, and anthropometric features (Figure <ref>). To contextualize these findings, we compared our results to conventional non-model-based equations that use Body Mass, RHR, and Age. A widely used equation (<cit.>) demonstrated markedly lower validity (R^2 of -3.2 and correlation of 0.389), underperforming even our anthropometry-only model (see Methods for details). These results highlight the advantages of machine learning in capturing complex covariate interactions.

old_text: The healthcare sector especially profits from privacy-preserving machine learning due to the natural sensitivity of the underlying patient data <cit.>. A wide range of applications demonstrate that federated learning is a potential fit for leveraging diverse types of medical data, including electronic health records <cit.>, genomic data <cit.>, and time-series data from wearables <cit.>. Examples related to medical image classification include brain tumor segmentation <cit.>, classification and survival prediction on whole slide images in pathology <cit.>, classification of functional magnetic resonance images (fMRI) <cit.>, and breast density classification from mammographic images <cit.>. The feasibility of federated learning on chest X-rays has previously been benchmarked for both CheXpert and Mendeley datasets. <cit.> enhance a ResNet18 architecture with a graph neural network for federated learning on CheXpert data with site-specific data distributions. <cit.> deploy a DenseNet121 model for a real-world, physically distributed implementation of federated learning on CheXpert. <cit.> determine the ResNet18 architecture as superior for federated learning on Mendeley data in comparison with ResNet50, DenseNet121, and MobileNet.
new_text: The healthcare sector particularly benefits from privacy-preserving machine learning approaches, as patient data inherently involves highly sensitive information, including medical histories, genetic profiles, and real-time health monitoring. Federated learning emerges as a suitable strategy to address these privacy challenges while enabling collaborative model training across institutions. This framework allows diverse medical datasets—such as electronic health records, genomic information, and continuous data from wearable devices—to be utilized without requiring direct data sharing, thereby mitigating risks of data breaches. In the domain of medical imaging, federated learning has shown promise in addressing tasks where data silos are common. For instance, researchers have applied it to brain tumor segmentation, pathology image analysis for cancer classification and survival prediction, functional MRI interpretation, and mammographic breast density assessment. These applications highlight federated learning’s ability to harmonize heterogeneous data sources while preserving data confidentiality. Specifically, feasibility studies on chest X-rays have benchmarked approaches using the CheXpert and Mendeley datasets. One study enhanced a ResNet18 architecture by incorporating a graph neural network to adapt to site-specific data distributions within CheXpert. Another implemented a DenseNet121 model in a real-world, physically distributed setting for CheXpert data. Meanwhile, a third study found ResNet18 outperformed alternatives like ResNet50, DenseNet121, and MobileNet in federated learning scenarios on the Mendeley dataset. These findings illustrate the adaptability of federated learning to different data characteristics and architectures in healthcare.

Learning rates differ by component: pre-trained BERT models and the tree-decoder are initially trained at 1e⁻⁵ and 1e⁻⁴, respectively, with both schedules halving every 25 epochs to gradually reduce learning magnitude as training progresses. Regularization strategies include a dropout rate of 0.5 to randomly zero out activations during training, preventing overfitting by enforcing robust feature representations, and a weight decay of 1e⁻⁵ to penalize large parameter magnitudes. Training durations vary by module, with the retriever trained for 20 epochs (a shorter span due to its simpler retrieval task) and the encoder-decoder and logic generator each trained for 100 epochs. During inference for solution expression generation, beam search is employed to explore the most promising expression trees and predict logic formulas by maintaining a fixed-width search space, ensuring efficient exploration of high-probability outputs.

Unlike CNNs or MONet, they readily incorporate depth information, enabling effective robotic manipulation. The method is extendible to challenges like multi-object tasks, occlusions, and varying object scales through intuitive training. The remaining elements of proxy discrimination are each about whether one of the aforementioned relationships induces another one of them, which I view as a second-order relationship.
They cannot be decomposed into a mere conjunction of the underlying first-order relationships since they capture something about the interaction of the two relationships not present in either alone.
For example, it is possible to have proxy use and a bottom line impact that do not have anything to do with one another since the impact could come from some other aspect of the model.
Only when the proxy use induces a bottom line impact is the proxy consequential.
new_text: The remaining elements of proxy discrimination involve assessing whether one of the prior relationships causes another. I categorize this as a second-order relationship because it depends on how relationships interact, not just their independent existence. These second-order relationships cannot simply be broken into the combination of their individual, first-order components because they capture the interaction between two relationships—a dynamic that neither relationship demonstrates on its own. For example, proxy use can exist alongside a bottom line impact without a causal connection; the impact may originate from other aspects of the model, such as unrelated parameters or design choices. Consequently, the mere presence of both proxy use and an impact is insufficient to label the proxy as consequential. Causality must be established: only when the proxy use directly generates the observed bottom line impact does the proxy hold relevance in discrimination analysis. This distinction is critical because it emphasizes that correlation or temporal overlap does not equate to significance.

Then we can apply CLCNet in a simple cascade structure system, in which we stack two (or several) classification models as shown in Fig.<ref>. The model with fewer computations is called shallow model, and the model with more computations is called deep model. When inferring a sample through this system, it will first use the shallow model to classify and return its classification result to CLCNet to predict whether it is classified correctly. If CLCNet outputs a high confidence score, we will accept the classification result directly and won’t perform subsequent steps. On the other hand, when CLCNet has insufficient confidence to the classification result of the shallow model, the input sample will proceed to be classified by the deep model,and the classification result of deep model will also be evaluated by CLCNet and output a confidence score. Finally, we compare the confidence scores predicted by CLCNet on classification results of both deep model and shallow model, and return the classification result with the higher confidence as output.
new_text: After establishing the basic framework, CLCNet can be integrated into a hierarchical cascade system. This configuration involves arranging two or more classification models in a sequential arrangement (as illustrated in Fig.<ref>). The first model in the sequence, termed the "shallow model," is designed for computational efficiency, prioritizing speed over model depth. Conversely, the subsequent "deep model" incorporates a more complex architecture, trading computational efficiency for potentially higher accuracy. During inference, a sample is first processed by the shallow model, which generates an initial classification output. This result is then evaluated by CLCNet, which computes a confidence score reflecting the predicted reliability of the shallow model's decision. If CLCNet determines that the confidence score exceeds a predetermined threshold, the system adopts the shallow model's output as the final prediction, bypassing further processing steps to conserve resources. However, when CLCNet identifies insufficient confidence in the shallow model's result—indicating potential uncertainty or complexity in the input—the sample is forwarded to the deep model for re-evaluation. The deep model produces an alternative classification, which CLCNet again assesses for confidence. At this stage, the system compares the confidence scores assigned to both the shallow and deep model outputs, selecting the prediction associated with the higher score as the final decision. This cascading approach optimizes computational efficiency by selectively engaging the more resource-intensive deep model only when necessary, while CLCNet serves as a gatekeeper to ensure decision quality.

Because the classification model and the subsequent fully connected layer are trained at the same time, when doing gradient descent, the previous classification model must consider not only to get correct classification, but also when the cross-entropy loss is low, its classification output needs to "look like" to be a correct classification for the subsequent fully connected layer to recognize. new_text: This end-to-end model presents a significant limitation. During training, the classification model and the subsequent fully connected layer are optimized simultaneously. As a result, during gradient descent, the classification model must not only achieve accurate classification but also ensure that its outputs align with patterns expected by the downstream fully connected layer. Specifically, when cross-entropy loss is low, the model’s output must appear correct to the fully connected layer to enable effective processing. Our lightweight counting head, f(g_s(x)), directly regresses a single, scalar count
for the input image, x, from the latent features of g_s(x) without the need for point-level annotations, which are difficult and expensive to gather.
Although it may seem that a location-based loss should aid in training, we found that point-level annotations were unnecessary and often detrimental in a class-agnostic setting.
Since point-level annotations are often arbitrarily placed and contain no information about the size and shape of an object, identifying a different part of all the correct objects would be punished by a point-level loss function. This arbitrary punishment hinders the network's understanding of the counting task.
While previous class-agnostic works aim to localise instances explicitly by using pixel-wise density estimation and location-based loss functions, we instead regress an estimate for the count directly, allowing the network to develop its own conceptual representation of the task. To this end, we use the simplest possible loss function, the absolute error, defined as: ℒ = Absolute Error= | c - ĉ|, where c is the ground truth count and ĉ = f(g_s(x)) is the predicted count.
We found that the network, without enforcing any location-based loss, still learnt to localise instances of the counted class in a meaningful way, as discussed in Section <ref> and seen in Figure <ref>.

In this paper, we investigate a practical problem setting of FL, personalized federated learning with server data. We adapt the meta-learning process to create `FedSIM` where meta-gradients are calculated using the server to improve model performance and reduce client computational overhead. We show that `FedSIM` solves the proposed FL problem by first performing local optimization using a custom loss function with a regularization term, and then using server data with these locally optimized models to calculate the required gradients. We also provide a variety of numerical experiments and ablations to illustrate the performances of our method compared with existing methods in personalized FL. Finally, we present empirical analyses on the distribution of server data and its impact on performance.
new_text: This study addresses a practical federated learning (FL) scenario involving personalized learning and server data. To enhance model performance while minimizing client-side computational load, we integrate a meta-learning approach to develop **FedSIM**, where the server computes meta-gradients. The method tackles the FL challenge through a two-step process: initially, local optimization is conducted using a customized loss function that includes a regularization term, followed by gradient computation using the server's data combined with these optimized local models. Comprehensive numerical experiments and ablation studies are presented to evaluate the proposed method's effectiveness against existing personalized FL techniques. Additionally, empirical analyses are conducted to examine how the distribution of server data influences overall performance.

In articulatory phonetics, the place of articulation refers to the point of contact between an active articulator (typically a portion of the tongue) and a passive location (such as the roof of the mouth) in the vocal tract, with common classifications including bilabial and velar consonants. The manner of articulation describes how articulators (e.g., tongue, lips, palate) interact during speech production, with frequent categories such as stopping and affrication. This study employs these four categories, as they are most prevalent and account for the majority of observed errors in early speech development.

new_text: Assembling parts into an object is a combinatorial problem that arises in various real-world contexts and has numerous applications in science and engineering. Previous related work has focused on limited cases involving identical unit parts or jigsaw-style parts with textured shapes, which greatly mitigate the problem's combinatorial challenges. In this work, we address the more challenging problem of shape assembly, involving textureless fragments of arbitrary shapes with indistinct junctions, and propose a learning-based approach to solving it. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on shape assembly tasks across diverse scenarios, including those with abnormal fragments (e.g., missing or distorted), varying numbers of fragments, and different rotation discretizations. (Supplementary material and implementations are available at (URL).)

Training models on data with representational issues can lead them to treat particular demographic groups unfairly and/or poorly <cit.>, a problem that is particularly egregious for historically marginalized groups, including people of color <cit.>, and women <cit.>. For example, models learned the stereotype that “women like shopping” when they were trained on data where most or all of shoppers are women, and they learned that “men don't like shopping” when they were trained on data where few or no shoppers are men <cit.>. First, the authors prove that the Cartesian mapping is already NP-hard for a
two-dimensional Cartesian grid and a one-dimensional stencil.
Then three fast construction algorithms which exploit the regularity of the problem are proposed.
Their algorithm with best overall results is the stencil strips algorithm, which partitions the grid into strips of lengths close to the scaled length of an optimal bounding rectangle of the coordinates of the target stencil.
In their experimental evaluation using the MPI_Neighbor_alltoall routine of MPI,
their algorithms are up to two orders of magnitude faster than general purpose graph mapping tools such as VieM <cit.> while resulting in a similar communication performance.
Moreover, their algorithms are up to three times faster than other Cartesian grid mapping algorithms while resulting in a much better communication performance.
new_text: Kirchbach et al. <cit.> investigate the process mapping problem under the assumption that parallel processing elements (PEs) communicate using a sparse stencil pattern, with PEs arranged in Cartesian grids. They begin by addressing the computational complexity of the problem: they demonstrate that even for a simplified two-dimensional Cartesian grid with a one-dimensional stencil, finding an optimal Cartesian mapping is NP-hard. This result highlights the inherent difficulty of solving the problem exactly, motivating the need for efficient approximation algorithms. To tackle this challenge, the authors propose three fast algorithms that leverage the regularity of both the grid structure and the stencil pattern. The most effective of these is the *stencil strips* algorithm, which partitions the computational grid into one-dimensional strips. These strips are designed to align with the optimal bounding rectangle of the stencil's target coordinates, with their lengths adjusted to match a scaled version of this rectangle, balancing load distribution and communication efficiency. In their evaluation, using the MPI_Neighbor_alltoall routine to benchmark communication performance, the proposed algorithms outperform general-purpose graph mapping tools like VieM <cit.> by up to two orders of magnitude in execution time while achieving comparable communication efficiency. Additionally, their Cartesian grid-specific methods outperform alternative Cartesian mapping algorithms, reducing runtime by up to three times while significantly improving communication performance. This combination of speed and efficiency positions their approach as a practical solution for large-scale stencil-based parallel applications.

old_text: To infer which sentences were especially lengthy, we need to know what the distribution of sentence lengths is for any given set of legally relevant factors. There are typically few sentences that share precisely the same set of legally relevant factors, so simply using the empirical distribution of sentence lengths for each set of cases sharing the same legally relevant factors is not possible. Thus, we require good model-based estimates of the conditional distribution of Y (the sentence length, in months) given X (the legally relevant factors). Traditional regression approaches assume that the distribution of the errors is constant and independent of X. In our case, we expect that the variance of the errors is non-constant and likely varies with X. For example, we expect that sentence lengths for cases where the Guidelines indicate a minimal sentence are less variable in terms of the absolute number of months than sentences for those cases where the Guidelines indicate a long sentence. We also expect that legally relevant factors influence judicial decision-making in complicated ways that are not well approximated by a simple linear function.
new_text: To identify sentences that are unusually long, it is essential to understand the distribution of sentence durations in relation to specific sets of legally relevant factors. Since there are often insufficient cases with identical combinations of these factors, relying on empirical frequency distributions for each unique factor set is impractical. Therefore, we must instead depend on robust statistical models that estimate the conditional probability distribution of Y (sentence length in months) based on X (the legally relevant variables). Conventional regression methods typically assume homoscedasticity, where error variance remains constant regardless of X values. However, our analysis suggests that error variance is heteroscedastic, changing in relation to X. For instance, cases with Guideline-recommended minimal sentences likely exhibit narrower variability in sentencing duration compared to cases where longer Guideline sentences are advised. Furthermore, these factors are expected to influence judicial decisions through complex, non-linear mechanisms that cannot be adequately captured by linear models.

new_text: The inspiration for the ideas explored here draws from Sellars’ work, as previously noted. Extending beyond the cited sources, the significance of giving and asking for reasons has been emphasized by <cit.> and further developed by <cit.>. Specifically, this involves a shift in perspective: when we describe an event or state as an instance of "knowing," we are not merely providing an empirical account of its features. Rather, as <cit.> observes, we are situating it within what Sellars termed the "logical space of reasons"—a framework where knowledge is defined by its intelligibility through justification and the capacity to articulate why one asserts a claim. This conceptual approach connects directly to longstanding philosophical discussions about rule following. The concept of rule following, a significant theme in the work of <cit.> (see <cit.>), underscores how actions gain normative force not through solitary intent but through their alignment with publicly recognizable standards. This ties to the idea that judgments about the applicability of norms must necessarily be public in character, as participants in social practices must mutually recognize and respond to shared expectations (see also <cit.>). In this context, the notion of "orienting towards" becomes central, particularly in Conversation Analysis (CA). CA’s foundational insight is that social interactions exhibit a structured order that is not externally imposed but emerges from participants’ active engagement with implicit rules or expectations. As <cit.> explains, this "order at all points" is normative in the sense that individuals produce and sustain it through their practical orientations to social conventions—a dynamic that mirrors the interplay of justification and shared understanding discussed earlier.

Much literature combined MAML<cit.> with transformer<cit.> models to enhance the fast adaptation ability of chatbot. <cit.> proposed a method that extended MAML to personalized dialogue learning; the chatbot could learn to quickly adapt to new personas by leveraging only a few dialogues.
<cit.> first proposed propose a novel multi-task learning framework for Dialogue State Tracking (DST) to steer mode's output in various dialogue acts.
<cit.> applied the multi-task learning algorithm to DST and the obtained meta-learning model is used for new domain adaptation.
<cit.> combined structure learning into chatbot to enhance the effectiveness of meta-learning by promoting knowledge customization among different sentence functions.

new_text: A significant body of research has integrated Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) with transformer architectures to improve chatbots' capacity for rapid adaptation to new tasks. For instance, one study extended MAML to the domain of personalized dialogue learning, enabling chatbots to swiftly adjust to new user personas by utilizing only a small number of example dialogues, thereby reducing the need for extensive labeled data. Another approach introduced a novel multi-task learning framework for Dialogue State Tracking (DST), where the model's outputs were guided to handle diverse dialogue functions, such as request, confirmation, or information provision. Building on this, researchers applied multi-task learning algorithms to DST, demonstrating that the resulting meta-learning models could be effectively adapted to new domains, enhancing generalization across unseen scenarios. Additionally, another work incorporated structural learning mechanisms into chatbots, which improved meta-learning's effectiveness by encouraging the customization of knowledge representations for different sentence-level functions, such as intent recognition or entity extraction. Collectively, these studies highlight the synergy between MAML and multi-task learning in enabling chatbot models to remain robust and adaptable even when confronted with unfamiliar tasks or domains, as the underlying frameworks facilitate knowledge transfer and efficient parameter updates during deployment.

RDF Mapping Language - RML:
The RDF Mapping Language (RML) <cit.> extends the W3C-standard mapping language R2RML to manage heterogeneous data sources represented in various formats, e.g., CSV, XML, JSON, and relational tables.
These rules, named as RML triples maps, define the instances of RDF classes and their properties in terms of a logical source. Attributes from the logical data source of a triples map describe the resources of the corresponding class.
RML is an RDF triple-oriented mapping language, where a triples map comprises mapping assertions <cit.> that define the instances of a class (a.k.a. subjectMap), and the property and object (a.k.a. predicateObjectMap) of the RDF triples where these instances participate as a subject. RML triples maps are expressed in RDF. This allows the exploration and tracing of the definition of the process of KG creation.
new_text: The RDF Mapping Language (RML) <cit.> builds upon the W3C-standard R2RML framework to handle diverse data sources across formats such as CSV, XML, JSON, and relational databases. RML triples maps serve as rule sets that define RDF class instances and their properties by referencing a logical data source. The attributes within this logical source map to resources corresponding to the class in question. As an RDF triple-centric language, RML organizes mapping rules into triples maps, which consist of assertions specifying class instances via subjectMaps and their associated predicate-object pairs through predicateObjectMaps <cit.>. These triples maps are themselves encoded in RDF, enabling transparent tracking and analysis of the knowledge graph (KG) generation process.

Deep neural networks usually perform poorly when the training dataset suffers from extreme class imbalance.
Recent studies found that directly training with out-of-distribution data (i.e., open-set samples) in a semi-supervised manner would harm the generalization performance.
In this work, we theoretically show that out-of-distribution data can still be leveraged to augment the minority classes from a Bayesian perspective. Based on this motivation, we propose a novel method called Open-sampling, which utilizes open-set noisy labels to re-balance the class priors of the training dataset. For each open-set instance, the label is sampled from our pre-defined distribution that is complementary to the distribution of original class priors.
We empirically show that Open-sampling not only re-balances the class priors but also encourages the neural network to learn separable representations.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing data re-balancing methods and can boost the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods.
new_text: Deep neural networks often exhibit poor performance when training data contains extreme class imbalance. Incorporating out-of-distribution data (open-set samples) during semi-supervised training negatively impacts generalization, as evidenced by recent studies. Here, we present a theoretical analysis demonstrating that out-of-distribution data can effectively augment minority classes under a Bayesian framework. Motivated by this insight, we introduce a novel approach named Open-sampling, which utilizes open-set noisy labels to recalibrate the class priors of the training dataset. For each open-set instance, labels are sampled from a predefined distribution designed to counterbalance the original class priors. Empirical results confirm that Open-sampling not only adjusts class prior distributions but also promotes the learning of discriminative feature representations. Comprehensive experiments indicate that our method significantly surpasses existing data rebalancing strategies and enhances the performance of current state-of-the-art techniques.

In the American legal system, civil lawsuits (“cases”) involve a set of actions among two or more parties and the judge(s) <cit.>. Most steps in the case are taken by way of formal document filings.
The first step typically occurs when the “plaintiffs”—people, groups of people, or entities—file a “complaint” against one or more “defendants” in a state or federal trial court. The case then proceeds as the parties file additional documents.
It is through these documents that the parties lay out the case background, explain their arguments, rebut opposing parties' arguments, and ask for specific actions from the judge(s) (see Table <ref> for a breakdown of document types).
The judge(s) also file documents which set schedules, ask questions, and memorialize rulings—intermediate orders that frame the conflict or instruct parties to take various steps or "final" orders that at least temporarily resolve the case <cit.>.
All a result, a case's documents can extend to hundreds, even thousands, of pages of text.
Collectively, these documents paint a full picture of the case, but they can be extremely time-consuming to read and digest in order to understand the gist.
new_text: In the American legal system, civil lawsuits—commonly referred to as “cases”—involve interactions among at least two parties (typically plaintiffs and defendants) and a judge, with most procedural actions formalized through written documents submitted to the court. The process generally begins when one or more plaintiffs—individuals, organizations, or legal entities—initiate a lawsuit by filing a “complaint” in a state or federal trial court. This complaint names the defendant(s) and outlines the legal basis for the claim. Following this initial filing, the case progresses as both sides exchange additional documents to build their legal arguments. These filings serve multiple purposes: they contextualize the dispute, articulate each party’s position, challenge the opposing side’s claims, and formally request specific judicial actions (such as rulings or remedies). Throughout this process, judges also issue documents that shape the case. These include scheduling orders, interrogations, and rulings—some of which outline procedural steps or clarify legal standards, while others may resolve parts of the case temporarily. Because civil litigation involves repeated rounds of document submissions and judicial interventions, the total volume of records can grow substantially, often resulting in hundreds or even thousands of pages. While these documents collectively capture the full scope of the legal dispute, their sheer volume and procedural focus can make it difficult for readers to quickly grasp the central issues and outcomes without careful review.

new_text: We experiment with summarization models that represent the current state of the art in abstractive text generation. Two prominent models—BART (<cit.>) and PEGASUS (<cit.>)—are based on the Transformer architecture (<cit.>) and have demonstrated leading performance on widely used summarization datasets. These models employ sequence-to-sequence frameworks to generate summaries by learning both to reconstruct and rephrase input text through pre-training objectives like denoising. However, the Multi-LexSum task presents unique challenges due to its requirement to process multi-document inputs with extensive source content. To address this, we also evaluate models specifically designed for long-document summarization. The Longformer Encoder and Decoder (LED) (<cit.>) and PRIMERA (<cit.>) are two such models capable of handling extended input lengths (16,384 tokens for LED and 4,096 tokens for PRIMERA). Both achieve this by modifying standard attention mechanisms with sparsity strategies, which reduce computational complexity while preserving semantic coherence across lengthy texts. PRIMERA further incorporates an MDS-specific pre-training objective that explicitly optimizes for multi-document summarization, enhancing its effectiveness in tasks like Multi-LexSum that demand cross-document synthesis.

We conduct extensive ablation studies on the CIFAR-100 dataset, with 50% labels, to study the contribution of different components of OpenLDN. The results are presented in Tab. <ref>. In this table, the first row demonstrates that without entropy regularization OpenLDN is unable to detect novel classes. We contribute this to overpowering of a single class (sec. <ref>). Next, we evaluate the impact of our pairwise similarity loss with bi-level optimization rule. We observe that without pairwise similarity loss the performance of OpenLDN degrades by 13.7% on novel classes which makes it the most critical component of our proposed solution. We also observe that our pairwise similarity loss does not sacrifice known class performance to improve the performance on novel classes. This outcome is expected since one of the objectives of our bi-level optimization rule is to retain performance on known classes (sec. <ref>). The fourth row demonstrates the effectiveness of transforming the open-world SSL problem into a closed-world one. Here, we observe that with this component we obtain a significant improvement in known class performance. In addition, we also notice a significant improvement in novel class performance. Interestingly, on this dataset, OpenLDN outperforms ORCA <cit.> (on joint classification task) even without the subsequent closed-world SSL training. Finally, Tab. <ref> shows that including iterative pseudo-labeling proves to be effective, where we observe ∼2% performance boost on novel classes. In conclusion, this extensive ablation study empirically validates the effectiveness of
different components of our solution.
new_text: We perform thorough ablation studies on the CIFAR-100 dataset using 50% labeled data to evaluate the contributions of individual components in OpenLDN. The findings are summarized in Tab. <ref>. The first row of the table indicates that excluding entropy regularization causes OpenLDN to fail in identifying novel classes, a limitation attributed to class dominance (sec. <ref>). Subsequently, we assess the role of our pairwise similarity loss paired with the bi-level optimization rule. Removing this loss leads to a 13.7% drop in novel class accuracy, highlighting its pivotal role in the framework. Notably, this loss does not compromise known class performance, aligning with the bi-level optimization’s goal of preserving closed-world performance (sec. <ref>). The fourth row emphasizes the benefits of reformulating the open-world SSL task as a closed-world problem, which significantly boosts accuracy for both known and novel classes. Remarkably, OpenLDN surpasses ORCA <cit.> (in joint classification) on this dataset without requiring additional closed-world SSL training. Lastly, Tab. <ref> confirms the value of iterative pseudo-labeling, which elevates novel class accuracy by ∼2%. These results collectively demonstrate that each component of OpenLDN contributes meaningfully to its overall efficacy.

In another set of experiments, to analyze the effectiveness of our pairwise similarity estimation with bi-level optimization rule we conduct experiments with alternate pairwise similarity estimation methods on CIFAR-100 dataset. The results are reported in Tab. <ref>. In this table, to provide a baseline to compare other pairwise similarity estimation techniques, we include the performance of OpenLDN without any pairwise similarity loss in the first row. The next row in the table demonstrates the performance of OpenLDN when the pairwise similarity is directly estimated from the cosine similarity of features. Surprisingly this method of estimating pairwise similarity performs worse than our baseline without any pairwise similarity loss (first row). We hypothesize this phenomenon to instability of cosine similarity of features without any feature pretraining. In the next set of experiments (third and fourth rows), we utilize a hard version of this pairwise similarity estimation method, where we threshold the pairwise feature similarities using two different thresholds (0.50 and 0.95). After that, we minimize a binary cross-entropy loss as the pairwise similarity loss. The results of these two experiments are reported in third and fourth row, where a further drop in performance is observed. One possible explanation is that without any feature pretraining this kind of pairwise similarity estimation leads to a lot of false positives (from novel classes) which in turn reduces the score of known classes. Finally, in the next row of the table, we use a nearest neighbor based pairwise similarity estimation technique similar to ORCA <cit.>. As indicated in the table, this nearest neighbor based similarity estimation improves over the baseline without any pairwise similarity loss. However, our pairwise similarity estimation based on the bi-level optimization rule outperforms this nearest neighbor based estimation technique by a significant margin; we obtain ∼9% absolute improvement on novel classes. These set of experiments further validate our claim that common pairwise similarity estimation techniques are not potent without feature pretraining, whereas, the proposed pairwise similarity estimation in OpenLDN is able to learn these pairwise similarities effectively.

Caption: OpenLDN Overview - Learning to Discover Novel classes: A set of labeled and unlabeled images are provided to the feature extractor, f_Θ, to obtain feature embeddings. The embeddings are passed to the classifier, f_Φ, to obtain output probabilities. We compute pairwise cosine similarity scores from the output probabilities for every possible pair in a batch. In parallel, the pairwise similarity prediction network, f_Ω, also outputs these scores based on pairs of feature embeddings. Afterwards, we calculate pairwise similarity loss (Eq. <ref>) to promote the discovery of novel classes. We also compute cross-entropy (CE) loss (Eq. <ref>) and entropy regularization loss (Eq. <ref>) to complement the pairwise similarity loss by learning from labeled and pseudo-labeled samples and avoiding trivial solutions, respectively. Next, we update the parameters of f_Θ and f_Φ to minimize the overall loss. Then we compute CE loss using only the labeled samples with updated f_Θ and f_Φ. Finally, we utilize a bi-level optimization rule to update f_Ω based on this CE loss (Eq. <ref>). The bi-level optimization rule helps to optimize f_Ω by transferring feature similarities from known to unknown classes.
new_text: In OpenLDN, labeled and unlabeled images are fed into a feature extractor, f_Θ, to generate feature embeddings. These features are then processed by the classifier, f_Φ, to produce output probabilities. Pairwise cosine similarity scores are computed between all possible pairs in a batch using the output probabilities, while the similarity prediction network, f_Ω, simultaneously generates these scores from pairs of feature embeddings. The pairwise similarity loss (Eq. <ref>) is applied to encourage detection of novel classes. Additionally, cross-entropy (CE) loss (Eq. <ref>) and entropy regularization loss (Eq. <ref>) are implemented to leverage information from labeled/pseudo-labeled data and prevent degenerate solutions. The parameters of f_Θ and f_Φ are optimized to minimize the combined loss. Subsequently, CE loss is calculated using only the labeled samples with the updated parameters. A bi-level optimization framework updates f_Ω based on this CE loss (Eq. <ref>), enabling the transfer of feature similarities from known to unknown classes.

Inspired by the observation that the co-occurrent texts incorporate incomplete fine-grained image information (e.g., tags, phrases, etc.), we exploit such information to enrich supevisory signals with textual information for improving visual representation learning.
Concretely, we design a novel and effective VLP framework named IDEA, which stands for increasing text diversity via online multi-label recognition for vision-language pre-training.
IDEA applies Image-Text Contrastive learning (ITC) with the global features obtained by image and text encoder to align the visual-linguistic features.
Meanwhile, IDEA utilizes the visual spatial feature to accomplish Multi-label Recognition (MLR), which requires identifying multiple tags contained in an image.

Qualitative Results. We report qualitative results in Figure <ref>. It shows that IDEA can additionally recognize image tags which do not exist in the original co-occurrent texts. These tags are entirely learned from the texts and recognized online, including objects (e.g., "boat"), scenes (e.g., "snow"), attributes (e.g., "stained"), actions (e.g., "swimming"), etc. More example visualization results are provided in Appendix <ref>.

These tags—comprising object categories (e.g., "boat"), scene types (e.g., "snow"), attribute labels (e.g., "stained"), action descriptors (e.g., "swimming"), among others—are learned solely from textual data and recognized online. old_text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are typically used in image recognition. The convolution layers iterate a specified kernel over an RGB image (Red, green, blue), and from the resulting matrix, an input can be generated usually by summation for an activation function. These convolution layers are customarily followed by a pooling layer which reduces the size of the outputted image; a necessary adaptation that in turn depletes the number of parameters needed in the model. Convolutional layers tend to record the exact location of a feature, and this can reduce the generality of a model if the feature map is sensitive to the location of a pattern in the image. The resulting architecture tends to be a combination of these layers which specify input shape and kernel sizes. Models are commonly finished with fully connected dense layers, which output an m-dimensional matrix.
new_text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely employed in image recognition tasks due to their ability to efficiently extract spatial features from visual data. During the convolution process, a predefined kernel (a small matrix of weights) is systematically applied to an input RGB image (representing red, green, and blue channels). This operation generates a feature map—a matrix where each value corresponds to the sum of element-wise multiplications between the kernel and the overlapping image region, followed by application of a nonlinear activation function. Following this, a pooling layer is typically introduced to downsample the feature map, reducing its spatial dimensions while retaining critical information. This downsampling is crucial for decreasing computational complexity and the number of parameters in the model, making training more efficient. However, convolutional layers inherently emphasize the precise spatial location of features, which can limit a model’s generalization if the detected patterns are overly sensitive to positional variations in the image. To mitigate this, multiple convolutional and pooling layers are stacked in sequence, each tailored by specifying input dimensions and kernel sizes to progressively refine feature extraction. Finally, most CNN architectures transition to fully connected dense layers, where the spatial information is flattened into an m-dimensional output vector that can be used for tasks such as classification.
