In this section, we provide experimental results to demonstrate that the proposed quantization framework is applicable to other quantization functions.
In the main text, each quantization function candidate is implemented with PAMS, a linear quantization function with a learnable scale parameter 31.
To demonstrate the generalizability of CADyQ with different quantization functions in this section, we employ another linear quantization function <cit.>, which we refer to as LinQ.
The major difference between PAMS and LinQ is that PAMS uses a learnable scale parameter to clip the outliers, whereas LinQ does not clip the outliers and thus takes the whole feature range as the quantization range.
Table <ref> shows the quantization results of CADyQ with LinQ (referred to as LinQ-CADyQ).
Our framework successfully achieves the reduction in average precision while simultaneously achieving the performance similar to or better than baselines or its 8-bit counterpart quantized with LinQ.
The results show that the proposed quantization framework is flexible in terms of quantization functions.
Note that CADyQ achieves a larger average precision reduction with PAMS than with LinQ.
The results corroborate the previous findings that learnable scale parameters are effective for SR networks, which can have variant outliers in feature distributions 31.
new_text: In this section, we present experimental results to illustrate the applicability of the proposed quantization framework to various quantization functions. In the main text, each quantization function candidate is implemented using PAMS, a linear quantization function incorporating a learnable scale parameter (31). To showcase the generalizability of CADyQ with different quantization functions in this section, we utilize a different linear quantization function <cit.>, termed LinQ. The key distinction between PAMS and LinQ lies in their handling of outliers: PAMS incorporates a learnable scale parameter to clip outliers, whereas LinQ retains the entire feature range for quantization by not implementing outlier clipping. Table <ref> presents the quantization outcomes of CADyQ combined with LinQ (LinQ-CADyQ). The framework successfully reduces average precision while maintaining performance comparable to or exceeding baselines and its 8-bit counterpart using LinQ. These results highlight the framework's adaptability to different quantization functions. It is noteworthy that CADyQ achieves a more substantial average precision reduction when using PAMS compared to LinQ. This underscores prior findings that learnable scale parameters enhance performance for SR networks dealing with varying feature distributions (31).

For better photography, most recent commercial cameras including smartphones have either adopted large-aperture lens to collect more light or used a burst mode to take multiple images within short times. These interesting features lead us to examine depth from focus/defocus.
   In this work, we present a convolutional neural network-based depth estimation from single focal stacks. Our method differs from relevant state-of-the-art works with three unique features. First, our method allows depth maps to be inferred in an end-to-end manner even with image alignment. Second, we propose a sharp region detection module to reduce blur ambiguities in subtle focus changes and weakly texture-less regions. Third, we design an effective downsampling module to ease flows of focal information in feature extractions. In addition, for the generalization of the proposed network, we develop a simulator to realistically reproduce the features of commercial cameras, such as changes in field of view, focal length and principal points.
  By effectively incorporating these three unique features, our network achieves the top rank in the DDFF 12-Scene benchmark on most metrics. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on various quantitative evaluations and real-world images taken from various off-the-shelf cameras compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our source code is publicly available at [URL].
new_text: Recent commercial cameras and smartphones enhance photography by employing large-aperture lenses to capture more light or using burst modes to capture multiple images in quick succession. These features prompt an investigation into depth estimation based on focus/defocus cues. This study introduces a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based approach for depth estimation using single focal stack inputs. The method distinguishes itself from state-of-the-art techniques through three innovations: first, enabling end-to-end depth map inference while incorporating image alignment; second, introducing a sharp region detection module to address ambiguities caused by subtle focus transitions and low-texture areas; third, designing an efficient downsampling module to facilitate focal information flow during feature extraction. To enhance generalization, a simulation tool is developed to replicate commercial camera characteristics—including adjustments to field of view, focal length, and principal points. By integrating these components, the network attains top performance on the DDFF 12-Scene benchmark across most evaluation metrics. Quantitative assessments and real-world experiments using images from consumer-grade cameras further validate the method’s superiority over existing techniques. The implementation is publicly accessible at [URL].

new_text: The hierarchical control framework we adopt consists of a higher-level RL policy that generates joint position predictions at a 40Hz update rate, and a lower-level PD controller operating at 1000Hz that converts desired joint positions into joint torques. Can reported vulnerabilities really affect our example application in production?
Vulnerable dependencies are problematic and may affect the security of our project in multiple ways.
However, the risk of vulnerable dependencies reaches its peak when the dependency is needed for the software to run in a production environment.
To find which dependencies are part of our production software, i.e., production dependencies, we use a module bundler.
A module bundler is a tool that assists the building process of a software by resolving the software dependencies and pruning the dependencies that are not needed in the production software. The process of pruning dependencies is referred to as tree shaking.
We use webpack <cit.>, a popular JavaScript module bundler, to build our production software and export a list of production dependencies.
new_text: Reported vulnerabilities can compromise our example application's security in production if they exist in dependencies critical to runtime. This paper concerns pseudo labelling in segmentation. Our contribution is fourfold. Firstly, we present a new formulation of pseudo-labelling as an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for clear statistical interpretation. Secondly, we propose a semi-supervised medical image segmentation method purely based on the original pseudo labelling, namely SegPL. We demonstrate SegPL is a competitive approach against state-of-the-art consistency regularisation based methods on semi-supervised segmentation on a 2D multi-class MRI brain tumour segmentation task and a 3D binary CT lung vessel segmentation task. The simplicity of SegPL allows less computational cost comparing to prior methods. Thirdly, we demonstrate that the effectiveness of SegPL may originate from its robustness against out-of-distribution noises and adversarial attacks. Lastly, under the EM framework, we introduce a probabilistic generalisation of SegPL via variational inference, which learns a dynamic threshold for pseudo labelling during the training. We show that SegPL with variational inference can perform uncertainty estimation on par with the gold-standard method Deep Ensemble.
new_text: This paper focuses on pseudo-labelling in segmentation. We make four contributions. First, we propose a novel formulation of pseudo-labelling as an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to enable a clear statistical interpretation. Second, we introduce a semi-supervised medical image segmentation method built purely on original pseudo-labelling, termed SegPL. We demonstrate that SegPL is a competitive approach against state-of-the-art consistency regularisation-based methods in semi-supervised segmentation, evaluated on a 2D multi-class MRI brain tumour segmentation task and a 3D binary CT lung vessel segmentation task. The simplicity of SegPL enables lower computational cost compared to prior methods. Third, we demonstrate that the effectiveness of SegPL can be attributed to its robustness against out-of-distribution noise and adversarial attacks. Lastly, within the EM framework, we present a probabilistic generalisation of SegPL via variational inference, which learns a dynamic threshold for pseudo-labelling during training. We show that SegPL with variational inference performs uncertainty estimation on par with the gold-standard method Deep Ensemble.

old_text: In this line of research, a grid generation method in <cit.> named the deformation method was built based on <cit.>. It had been furtherer developed, in <cit.>, to generate Higher Order Element grids. The deformation method constructs T with prescribed JD that is defined by a scalar-valued function 0<f_o∈ C^1. The essential step in the deformation method is that to solve a divergence-curl system (similar to the constraint equations (<ref>)). In that system, the divergence is approximated by f_o-1 and curl is assigned to 0 because realizing curl beforehand is another challenging task, where the curl models the local cell-rotation. Consequently, the grids generated by the deformation method are not unique when curl information is lacking, in <cit.>. To overcome this problem, the original VP was proposed in <cit.> and studied further in <cit.>. Its mathematical mechanism is designed to control both JD and curl, where the prescribed curl is defined by a sufficiently smooth vector-valued function g_o. The original VP works well and accurately in 2D, but in 3D cases, it produces stagnated approximations around the true solution. The limitation leave the original VP acceptable for some engineering tasks, but once it comes to the areas that require high accuracy such as medical image processing, undesired results are accumulated. Later, in <cit.>, the VP is fundamentally revised in its theory and developed with more effective algorithms. Surprisingly, the revised VP not only resolves the inaccuracy in 3D scenario, but also regularizes the solution pool of VP, {T}, is a Lie group inside H^2_0(Ω). More and more numerical tests are done by the revised VP with nearly ideal results as they are expected. It has become to a prioritized curiosity for us to find out whether a diffeomorphism can be uniquely determined with its JD and curl. That forms the uniqueness conjecture which this paper focuses. Fortunately, so far, the uniqueness issue does not undermine VP to produce well approximated grids and in turn allows mismatched pairs of prescribed JD and curl with discrepancies under certain range. Nonetheless, to the least, we would like to understand better about how well of an approximation can be made even if the conjecture is false.

Experimental Settings and Evaluation Metrics.
 For evaluations of `LTE4G`, we perform node classification under various manual imbalance settings, and a natural setting. Regarding the data splits, we follow the protocol of GraphSMOTE <cit.> and GraphENS <cit.> for the manual imbalance settings, and 1:1:8 (train/valid/test) splits for the natural setting. As for the evaluation metrics, besides conventional accuracy (Acc), we use several metrics widely used for imbalanced classification problems (i.e., balanced accuracy (bAcc), Macro-F1 and Geometric Means (G-Means) <cit.>) and report them along with standard deviations for 3 repetitions with different random seeds.
new_text: To assess the effectiveness of `LTE4G`, we conduct node classification experiments under both artificial and natural class imbalance scenarios. Artificial imbalances are generated using manual settings, following established protocols from GraphSMOTE <cit.> and GraphENS <cit.>, which define specific training data splits with controlled class ratios while retaining the same validation and test partitions. In contrast, the natural setting preserves the original class distribution of the dataset and employs a standard 1:1:8 train/valid/test split. For evaluation, we report conventional accuracy (Acc) alongside metrics tailored for imbalanced classification: balanced accuracy (bAcc), Macro-F1, and Geometric Mean (G-Means) <cit.>. These metrics account for class distribution disparities, providing a more nuanced assessment than accuracy alone. All results are averaged over three independent runs with distinct random seeds, with standard deviations included to reflect variability in performance. This approach ensures robust evaluation across diverse imbalance conditions and validates the method’s generalizability.

old_text: In sum the key-points are: (a) We propose an uncertainty-aware pseudo-label-based semi-supervised learning framework, that utilizes Beam-Search inference for pseudo-label assignment, and a character and sequence aware uncertainty estimate for sample selection. (b) We utilize teacher-forcing <cit.>, primarily employed to train sequence-models, in the pseudo-labeling phase to enforce prediction consistency across all the sampled models in the ensemble, to estimate the predictive distribution.(c) Finally, the methods are evaluated on several challenging handwriting and scene-text datasets in the SSL setting.
new_text: This study introduces three main contributions: (a) a semi-supervised learning approach that incorporates pseudo-labels with uncertainty awareness, employing Beam-Search inference for pseudo-label generation and a combined character- and sequence-level uncertainty metric for selecting training samples. (b) The method integrates teacher-forcing <cit.>, a technique traditionally applied in sequence-model training, during the pseudo-labeling phase to ensure prediction consistency among all models in the ensemble, thereby enabling accurate estimation of the predictive distribution. (c) Experimental validation is conducted on multiple challenging handwriting and scene-text datasets within a semi-supervised learning (SSL) framework to assess method performance.

old_text: **Visual Concepts Augmentation (VCA):.** Here we propose a simple yet effective VCs augmentation technique. Having a set of concepts extracted for each image, instead of considering all the concepts at once, we sample randomly a fraction of these concepts (i.e., p_vc%) at each iteration step. The benefit of VCA is three-fold; (1) it may prevent the model from overfitting on specific concepts and potentially disregard the image or other concepts during training, (2) the model sees different combinations of concepts, which helps to have more diversity. (3) the model is exposed to more information during finetuning or test, as it will see all the concepts at once.
new_text: **Visual Concepts Augmentation (VCA):** Here we propose a simple yet effective VC augmentation technique. Given a set of concepts extracted for each image, instead of considering all the concepts at once, we randomly sample a fraction of these concepts (i.e., p_vc%) at each iteration. The benefit of VCA is threefold: (1) it may prevent the model from overfitting to specific concepts and which could cause the model to disregard the image or other concepts during training, (2) the model sees different combinations of concepts, which enhances diversity, and (3) the model is exposed to more information during fine-tuning or testing, as it encounters all concepts simultaneously during inference.

Using VCs provides significant improvements over the baseline (+9.6% RSUM and +0.5% Acc. VQA). We next introduce our H-ITC loss, which contributes additional gains (+2.2% RSUM and +0.2% Acc. VQA), demonstrating the value of a stronger pre-alignment loss. We favor the MAE-based, unimodal MIM loss, which improves results further by 2.4% RSUM. We have presented the problem of unjustified assumptions in decorated objects, a reformulation of a similar problem for subclasses. We have suggested an approach for detecting such problems in EO code, based on inlining and property inference. We have shown that our approach to detection is sound — a successful detection means that the problem is present in the original code, assuming an interpretation of methods in EO programs as virtual methods, and no unknown primitives are used. In addition to that, if EO program is a result of a faithful translation from another object-oriented programming language, the detection remains sound for the program in the original language.
new_text: We introduce the problem of unjustified assumptions in decorated objects, a reformulation of the problem originally defined for subclasses. We propose an approach for detecting such issues in EO code, grounded in inlining and property inference. We demonstrate that our detection method is sound: successful detection confirms the presence of the problem in the original code under the assumptions that (1) methods in EO programs are interpreted as virtual methods and (2) no unknown primitives are used. Furthermore, if an EO program is the result of a faithful translation from another object-oriented language, the soundness of detection extends to the original language as well.

This is in contrast to int8 inference with networks trained in 32- or 16-bit floating point, which require post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration and sometimes quantization-aware training (QAT) in order to maintain model accuracy. old_text: FP8 is a natural progression from 16-bit floating point types, reducing the compute requirements of neural network training. Furthermore, due to its non-linear sampling of the real numbers, FP8 can also have advantages for inference when compared to int8. Wang et al. <cit.> proposed using 5-bit exponent format for training neural networks, confirming their methodology on the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image classification on CIFAR-10 and ILSVRC12 datasets. Mellempudi et al. <cit.> study the 5-bit exponent format for training on the larger CNNs as well as language translation networks based on recurrent and transformer blocks. Both papers investigate 16-bit weight updates as well as stochastic rounding. Use of two FP8 formats, 4- and 5-bit exponent fields, for training is introduced in <cit.>, studying a wider range of CNNs as well as speech and language translation models. <cit.> also investigates FP8 inference of networks trained in higher precision and introduces returning of batch normalization statistics to improve result accuracy. Noune et al <cit.> propose a modified FP8 representation that dedicates a single encoding to special values in order to increase the represented dynamic range and present an extensive study of exponent bias effect on result quality. 8-bit inference with various formats, including FP8, with networks trained in higher precision is the focus of <cit.>.
new_text: FP8 represents a natural evolution from 16-bit floating-point formats by further reducing the computational demands of neural network training. Its non-linear distribution of representable values can also provide inference advantages over int8, particularly in scenarios where dynamic ranges of input data vary significantly. Early work by Wang et al. <cit.> explored the use of a 5-bit exponent format for training, validating their approach on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) applied to image classification tasks using the CIFAR-10 and ILSVRC12 datasets. Building on this, Mellempudi et al. <cit.> extended the 5-bit exponent framework to larger CNN architectures and language translation models based on recurrent and transformer-based architectures, emphasizing broader applicability beyond computer vision. These studies also incorporated 16-bit weight updates and stochastic rounding techniques to manage numerical precision during training. A follow-up study <cit.> introduced two FP8 formats, differing in their 4- or 5-bit exponent fields, and evaluated their performance across a wider array of CNNs, as well as speech and language translation models. This same work <cit.> also pioneered FP8 inference strategies for networks trained at higher precision, proposing the retention of batch normalization statistics during inference as a method to mitigate accuracy loss. In parallel, Noune et al. <cit.> proposed a modified FP8 format that reserved a dedicated encoding for special values (e.g., infinities or NaNs), thereby increasing the representable dynamic range and systematically analyzing how exponent bias affects overall result quality. More recent research <cit.> has focused on optimizing 8-bit inference—specifically FP8—when networks are trained in higher precision, aiming to balance computational efficiency with minimal accuracy degradation through refined implementation techniques.

old_text: We extend the narrow dynamic range of the E4M3 format by representing fewer special values, adopting their bit patterns for normal values. Infinities are not represented (see Section <ref> for overflow handling details) and we retain only one mantissa bit-pattern for NaNs. This modification extents the dynamic range by one extra power of 2, from 17 to 18 binades. We gain the representation of seven more magnitudes (256, 288, 320, 352, 384, 416, 448), corresponding to the biased exponent value 1111_2. The maximum representable magnitude without this modification would be 240. For consistency with IEEE 754 conventions we retain positive and negative representations for zero and NaN. While we could gain one additional representable magnitude, 480, by having just one encoding for zero and one for NaN, this would require breaking the symmetry of positive and negative representations inherent in the IEEE 754 formats, complicating or invalidating algorithm implementations that rely on this property. For example, IEEE floating point formats allow comparison and sorting of floating point values using integer operations. The benefit of increasing the maximum value from 448 to 480 for DL is not significant to warrant deviating from IEEE convention and losing software implementations that rely on it.
new_text: We extend the narrow dynamic range of the E4M3 format by reducing the number of special values represented and reassigning their bit patterns to normal values. Infinities are omitted (see Section <ref> for overflow handling details), and we retain only a single mantissa bit-pattern for NaNs. This modification extends the dynamic range by an additional power of 2, increasing the number of binades from 17 to 18. As a result, seven new magnitudes (256, 288, 320, 352, 384, 416, and 448) become representable, corresponding to the biased exponent value 1111_2. Without this modification, the maximum representable magnitude would be limited to 240. To maintain consistency with IEEE 754 conventions, we preserve both positive and negative representations for zero and NaN. While using a single encoding for zero and a single encoding for NaN could enable an additional representable magnitude (480), this would disrupt the symmetry between positive and negative representations inherent in IEEE 754 formats. Such a change could complicate or invalidate algorithm implementations that depend on this symmetry, such as those leveraging integer operations for comparison and sorting of floating-point values. The benefit of increasing the maximum representable value from 448 to 480 in deep learning applications is not substantial enough to justify deviating from IEEE conventions or risking incompatibility with software relying on them.
